XVI.‘ After its crushing defeat in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections at the hands of the BJP, the
Trinamool Congress (TMC)’s influence appears to be on the decline. This was also reflected by the
results in the Falta seat after a recent repolling, where the Mamata Banerjee-led party finished
fourth behind the winner BJP and the runner-up CPI(M) with the Congress getting third position.
The Falta outcome has raised a crucial question: Will the TMC be able to regain ground in Bengal’s
political landscape, or whether that vacuum be filled up by the Left and Congress? It remains to be
seen, however, if the CPI(M) and the Congress could again forge an alliance in a bid to fill the
vacuum in state politics left by the TMC. www.lawpreptutorial.com
In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, the Left-Congress alliance managed to lead in just 12 of the
state’s 294 Assembly segments. While the Congress led in 11 segments, including the Baharampur
segment under the Baharampur Lok Sabha seat and the Suti segment under the Jangipur
parliamentary constituency, the CPI(M) led in just one segment — Raninagar under the
Murshidabad Lok Sabha seat. The Congress had also led in the Farakka and Samserganj segments
of Murshidabad district, besides the Mothabari, Sujapur, Ratua, Malatipur, Harishchandrapur and
Chanchal segments in Malda district, and the Chakulia segment in North Dinajpur district.
Source: https://indianexpress.com/article/political-pulse/tmc-decline-bengal-congress-left-
opposition-vacuum-10715163/
passages.LEG-P0002:
IX. In January 2026, protests were reported in several Iranian cities where groups of
demonstrators voiced support for restoring the Pahlavi dynasty, which ruled Iran before
the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Protesters cited dissatisfaction with economic conditions,
governance, and civil freedoms, while authorities maintained that the Islamic Republic
remained constitutionally intact. Images circulating on social media showed monarchist
symbols and portraits of the late Shah, alongside calls for a referendum on Iran’s political
future. Analysts noted that such demonstrations reflect the persistence of competing
political identities within Iranian society, even decades after the monarchy’s overthrow.
The government responded with security deployments and messaging that foreign actors
were amplifying unrest. International observers followed developments closely, mindful
of Iran’s strategic position in West Asia, its energy resources, and its complex relations
with regional and global powers.

Source: Al-Jazeera
passages.LEG-P0003:
X. Bangladesh is observing a period of national mourning following the death of Khaleda Zia,
the country’s first female prime minister and long-time political leader. Zia’s death at the age
of 80, after a prolonged illness, was confirmed by her political party. Tributes poured in from
leaders and citizens alike, highlighting her role in Bangladesh’s political history, including her
leadership of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and multiple terms as prime minister.
Her decades-long rivalry with another key political figure shaped much of the nation’s
governance dynamics over the past generation. Officials announced state mourning measures
while calling for peace and unity during the period of loss. Analysts suggest that her passing
could influence political alignments as the country prepares for upcoming elections, with
debates on democratic participation, party leadership, and the future direction of national
policies now gaining prominence.


Source: Al-Jazeera
passages.LEG-P0004:
PASSAGE 9

COP-30 is scheduled to be hosted in Belém, a city located at the gateway of the Amazon region in
Brazil. The choice of venue has drawn global attention to the role of tropical forests in climate regulation
and biodiversity conservation. Brazilian authorities have highlighted infrastructure upgrades and
sustainability planning as part of the preparations. Climate negotiators view COP-30 as a crucial
milestone for reviewing progress on global climate commitments made under previous conferences.
Discussions are expected to focus on climate finance, adaptation strategies for vulnerable countries, and
pathways for reducing emissions while supporting development goals. Observers note that holding the
summit in the Amazon region symbolically reinforces the urgency of protecting natural carbon sinks
and addressing deforestation as part of the global climate agenda.

Source: The Tribune
passages.LEG-P0005:
IX. India’s preparations for hosting the BRICS Summit in 2026 have drawn attention to the
evolving character of the grouping. Over time, BRICS has expanded beyond its original
economic coordination mandate to address development finance, geopolitical coordination,
and Global South representation. India’s presidency is expected to emphasise institutional
consolidation, inclusivity, and coordination among newly inducted members. Analysts note
that symbolism—through branding, themes, and diplomatic messaging—often reflects broader
strategic priorities of the host country. At the same time, substantive outcomes depend on
consensus-building among diverse political systems and economic models. As global economic
fragmentation deepens, BRICS forums have become important platforms for articulating
alternative development narratives and cooperation mechanisms, particularly for emerging and
developing economies navigating a multipolar world order.
Source: Indian Express
passages.LEG-P0006:
XV. My. Vikas Rastogi, an owner of ‘Bikaner Namkeen Bhandar’, has 8 gas stoves for making Kachoris
and Samosas or both. He has 24 man-hours to complete the job and Rs. 2750 as working capital for
one single day. To produce 1 round of eatables (Either 100 kachoris or 100 samosas) in one stove he
needs 2 man-hours and 4 man-hours respectively. While amount required for producing one round
is Rs. 360 and Rs. 200 respectively. The ratio of the price at which Mr Rastogi sells a Kachori to

passages.LEG-P0007:
XV. Between 1946 and 1949, the Constituent Assembly of India functioned as a forum entrusted with the
task of framing a constitutional framework for a newly independent nation. The Assembly was
composed of representatives drawn from diverse regions, communities, and ideological backgrounds,
many of whom had actively participated in the freedom struggle or in provincial governance under
colonial rule. Its meetings were marked by extensive deliberations, disagreements, and revisions,
reflecting the competing visions of governance, liberty, and social justice that existed at the time.
Several sub-committees were constituted to examine specific issues such as fundamental rights,
minority protections, the structure of the judiciary, and the distribution of powers between the Union
and the provinces. Draft proposals were circulated, debated clause by clause, and frequently
reconsidered in light of objections raised by members. The Assembly’s proceedings often reflected
concerns about maintaining national unity while simultaneously addressing historical inequalities and
safeguarding individual freedoms. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Debates within the Assembly also revealed differing attitudes toward judicial power, legislative
supremacy, and the extent to which constitutional provisions should limit future governments. Some
members expressed apprehension about granting excessive discretion to the judiciary, while others
emphasised the need for enforceable guarantees to prevent the abuse of state power. Comparative
constitutional models from other jurisdictions were occasionally referred to, though the members
repeatedly stressed the importance of adapting such ideas to Indian conditions.
The Assembly ultimately adopted the Constitution after multiple readings and revisions, leaving the
task of interpretation and implementation to future institutions within the constitutional framework.
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Oxford Constitutional Law, "The Indian Founding: a
comparative perspective," Oxford Constitutions (OUP, 2028), available
at: https: //oxcon.ouplaw.com/display/10.1093/law /9780198704898.001.0001/law-9780198704898-
chapter-4
passages.LEG-P0008:
Passage (Q.68-Q.72): The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines a partnership as a relationship between two or
        more individuals who comply with share the profits of a business run by them all or by one or more individuals
        acting for all. Individuals who have entered into a partnership with each other are called “partners” and collectively
        a “company,” and also the name under which their business is carried on is termed as the “company name.”
        The relation of partnership arises from contract and not from status; and, in particular, the members of a Hindu
        undivided family carrying on a family business as such, or a Burmese Buddhist husband and wife carrying on
        business as such are not partners in such business.
        If there is no clause to establish a partnership at the expiry of a partnership, it is referred to as a partnership at will.
        Under Section 7 of The Indian Partnership Act, 1932, two conditions have to be met for a partnership to be a
        partnership at will and they are:
        •    There is no agreement on a fixed period for the existence of a partnership.
        •    No provision is made for establishing a partnership.
        If a partnership has been established and continues to operate beyond the fixed period, the partnership will become
        a partnership at will after the end of that term.
        A partnership may be formed for ongoing business or a specific purpose. If the partnership is merely formed to hold
        out one company or complete one undertaking, it’s referred to as a specific partnership. The partnership is going to
        be dissolved after the completion of the said venture or activity. The partners may, however, conform to continue
        the said partnership. But within the absence of this, when the task is complete, the partnership ends.
passages.LEG-P0009:
X.	Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the 18th edition of the Pravasi Bharatiya Diwas on (1) in
Bhubaneswar, with his speech focusing on the theme of ‘Diaspora’s Contribution to a Viksit Bharat’. He
also noted the date’s significance, saying, “It was on this day in 1915 when Mahatma Gandhi came back
to India after a long time abroad.” www.lawpreptutorial.com
The event is held once every two years to “honour the contributions of the Indian diaspora to their
homeland”. According to the Ministry of External Affairs, more than 3.5 crore Overseas Indians (that
is, Non-Resident Indians or NRIs and Persons of Indian Origin or PIOs) are based abroad. Overseas
Indians are classified into three categories: Non-Resident Indians, Overseas Citizens of India and
Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs). NRIs are Indians who are residents of foreign countries.
A person of Indian origin who is a foreign national and gets registered as an Overseas Citizen of India
cardholder under Section 7A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 is an OCI. The person must be eligible to be a
citizen of India on January 26, 1950, or was a citizen of India on or at any time after January 26, 1950,
or belonged to a territory that became part of India after August 15, 1947. Minor children of such
individuals, except those who were citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh, were also eligible for OCI cards.
The PIO category was abolished in 2015 and merged with the OCI category.
Source: https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/pravasi-bharatiya-diwas-diaspora-award-
9768938/

uninterrupted energy supply, even as the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial global oil transit route,

"The leaders agreed to promote new initiatives for a comprehensive energy partnership. In this

passages.LEG-P0011:
XV. Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution
occupies a central position in democratic life. In a recent observation, the Supreme Court
reminded both citizens and governments that the value of free speech lies not merely in its
availability but in society’s willingness to tolerate dissent, disagreement, and even discomfort.
The Court emphasised that constitutional freedoms are not meant only for agreeable or popular
opinions; they protect unpopular, critical, and minority viewpoints as well. Suppressing speech
merely because it causes offence or embarrassment to those in power risks hollowing out the


democratic promise of the Constitution. At the same time, the Court clarified that freedom of
speech is not absolute. Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of
sovereignty, public order, decency, morality, and other specified grounds. However, the Court
warned that these restrictions cannot become routine tools of convenience. Governments must
demonstrate a clear nexus between the speech sought to be restricted and the harm
apprehended. Vague allegations, speculative threats, or broad claims of disturbance cannot
justify curtailment. The responsibility to respect free speech, the Court noted, rests as much on
the State as on citizens, who must learn to engage with opposing views without immediately
demanding censorship. The judgment also underlined an institutional concern: frequent resort
to criminal law against speech risks creating a chilling effect, where individuals self-censor out
of fear rather than legal prohibition. Such an environment undermines constitutional culture.
Ultimately, the Court’s intervention frames free speech as a shared constitutional commitment.
While the State may regulate expression in exceptional circumstances, the default
constitutional posture must remain one of restraint, tolerance, and faith in democratic dialogue
rather than suppression.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/citizens-
must-know-value-of-freedom-of-speech-sc-tells-centre-states/article69810508.ece, 14-07-
2025
passages.LEG-P0012:
XI. Equality is a foundational value of constitutional democracies, yet its meaning is often
misunderstood. Two dominant conceptions of equality in legal theory are formal equality
and substantive equality. Formal equality is grounded in the idea that “likes should be
treated alike.” Under this approach, the law must apply uniformly to all persons, without
distinction. If a rule is neutral on its face and applies equally to everyone, formal equality
considers it fair, even if its effects are unequal. This conception prioritises sameness and
non-discrimination in form. Substantive equality, by contrast, focuses on outcomes rather
than appearances. It recognises that individuals and groups do not start from the same
social, economic, or historical position. Treating unequal persons identically may
perpetuate, rather than reduce, disadvantage. Substantive equality, therefore, permits, and
sometimes requires, differential treatment to achieve genuine equality. Measures such as
reservations, affirmative action, or targeted welfare schemes are justified under this
approach because they seek to correct structural barriers faced by disadvantaged groups.
Constitutional courts have increasingly moved beyond a purely formal understanding of
equality. In India, Article 14 has been interpreted not merely as a guarantee against
arbitrary classification, but as a tool to achieve real equality. This shift explains why laws
that treat people differently are not automatically unconstitutional; the key question is
whether the differentiation is aimed at reducing disadvantage or reinforcing it. A law that
appears neutral may still violate equality if it disproportionately harms a vulnerable group,
while a law that explicitly distinguishes between groups may be upheld if it promotes
fairness in substance. However, substantive equality is not limitless. Differential treatment
must have a rational connection to the goal of equality and must not create new forms of
exclusion or stigma. The challenge for courts lies in balancing uniformity with
responsiveness, ensuring that equality is not reduced to mechanical sameness, nor distorted
into unchecked preference. Ultimately, equality in law is not merely about equal rules, but
about equal concern and respect.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://lawbhoomi.com/formal-and-substantive-
equality/, 31-03-2025
passages.LEG-P0013:
XIV. The Constitution of India did not emerge overnight; it was the outcome of a long constitutional
struggle that began under colonial rule and culminated in a representative Constituent Assembly.
The demand for such an Assembly, made by leaders like M.N. Roy and the Indian National
Congress, was finally accepted by the British through the [Q1] of 1946, which laid down the
framework for electing a body to draft a free India’s Constitution.
Under this plan, the Constituent Assembly of India was created in 1946 with an original strength
of 389 members, drawn from British Indian provinces and princely states through indirect
elections and nominations rather than universal adult franchise. The Assembly held its first
meeting on [Q2], with [Q2] as the temporary chairman, and later elected Dr. Rajendra Prasad as
its permanent president to steer the constitution-making process.
In its early sittings, the Assembly debated the basic philosophy of the future Constitution and, on
[Q3], Jawaharlal Nehru moved the historic [Q3], which was later adopted and became the basis of
the [Q3]. After Partition in 1947, the membership of the Assembly was reduced from 389 to [Q4],
and over nearly three years, in eleven sessions, these members deliberated on fundamental rights,
federalism, and the structure of government. The Constitution was finally adopted on [Q5] and
came into force on [Q5], transforming the Constituent Assembly into the Parliament of
independent India.
passages.LEG-P0014:
XIII. In criminal law, liability is traditionally founded on the coexistence of two core
elements: actus reus and mens rea. Actus reus refers to the external conduct of the accused,
the physical act or omission that the law prohibits. Mens rea represents the mental element
accompanying the act, such as intention, knowledge, recklessness, or negligence. The
classical principle governing criminal responsibility is captured in the maxim actus non
facit reum nisi mens sit rea, meaning that the act alone does not make a person guilty unless
the mind is also blameworthy. Ordinarily, both elements must be present at the same time.
A guilty intention formed after the completion of an act does not create criminal liability,
just as a mere intention without any corresponding conduct does not attract punishment.
This requirement reflects the law’s concern with moral culpability rather than mere harmful
outcomes. However, this principle admits important exceptions. Certain offences, known
as strict liability offences, do not require proof of mens rea. In such cases, the commission
of the prohibited act itself is sufficient for liability. These offences are commonly found in
regulatory statutes dealing with public health, safety, and welfare, where proving intention
would be impractical and enforcement would suffer. Here, the law prioritises prevention
over blame. Criminal liability may also arise from omissions, but only where there exists
a legal duty to act. Failure to perform a moral duty alone does not amount to an offence;
the duty must be imposed by law. For example, a guardian may be criminally liable for


failing to protect a child if such omission leads to harm. Thus, criminal law carefully
balances the requirement of a guilty mind with practical considerations of social protection,
ensuring that liability is imposed only when justified by law.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.lawctopus.com/clatalogue/clat-
ug/mens-rea-and-actus-reus/,
passages.LEG-P0015:
IX. Sporting events involving India and Pakistan have often unfolded against a complex
diplomatic backdrop, where cricket functions as both a competitive spectacle and a symbolic
arena of engagement. The lead-up to the T20 World Cup 2026 has again drawn attention to
how sporting calendars intersect with diplomatic signals, visa regimes, security assessments,
and public sentiment. While cricketing encounters are governed by international sporting
bodies, their political resonance frequently exceeds the boundary lines. Analysts observe that
sporting participation neither substitutes formal diplomacy nor remains entirely detached from
it. Instead, such events coexist with broader bilateral dynamics shaped by security concerns,
regional stability, and international mediation norms. The episode underscores how popular
sport can amplify diplomatic narratives, influence public discourse, and occasionally serve as
a low-stakes channel of communication amid otherwise strained relations.

Source: Indian Express
passages.LEG-P0016:
PASAGE 14
 India’s digital ecosystem is dominated by a few large platforms, especially in messaging and
social media. A key problem is platform lock-in: when users are unable to switch services or
communicate across apps because one platform holds most of the network. For instance,
when WhatsApp became massively used, competing apps like Hike Messenger and Arattai
found it almost impossible to gain traction. Platform interoperability, where different apps can
communicate seamlessly, offers a solution. Interoperability means that a user on one
messenger can send messages to a user on another, even if they are on different apps. Legal
analysts argue that India is now at a crossroads: traditionally, competition law focused on data
protection, privacy and dominance; but in the platform era there is also a need for
interoperability regulation. Proponents point to fintech and telecom examples: the Unified
Payments Interface (UPI) created interoperable payments across different apps and broke the
wallet-lock-in. Similarly, mobile number portability allowed telecom users to switch providers
easily. These experiences suggest that messaging and social-media interoperability are
feasible. Critics caution that forcing interoperability might dilute privacy or security standards
or impose heavy burdens on smaller apps. In India, the regulation of social media and
messaging apps is still evolving. Industry observers stress that regulating interoperability
requires protecting encryption, ensuring fair competition, safeguarding user choice, and
preventing winner-take-all dominance. If large platforms are required to allow interoperability,
new entrants may compete on features, quality, service not users locked into a network. The
discussion is thus not only technical, but fundamentally about user freedom, competition, and
regulation in the digital age.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.livelaw.in/articles/zoho-arattai-platform-
interoperability-and-social-media-regulation-311643, 29-11-2025
passages.LEG-P0017:
IX. In 2026, the Government of India announced an expanded Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
Vaccination Scheme aimed at reducing cervical and other HPV-related cancers nationwide. The
programme prioritises adolescents and young adults, integrating preventive health into existing school
and primary healthcare frameworks. Officials highlighted that HPV is a leading cause of cervical
cancer, which remains a significant public health burden, especially among women in rural and
underserved areas. The new scheme involves coordinated outreach, subsidised vaccines, and
community awareness campaigns to improve uptake. Health experts noted that such initiatives require
sustained investment, training of healthcare workers, and monitoring for cold-chain integrity.
International partners such as the World Health Organization and Gavi have commended India’s
strategic emphasis on preventive oncology. The development reflects a broader shift toward preventive
care and universal immunisation coverage in national health policy discussions.

Source: Indian Express
passages.LEG-P0018:
IX. The SHANTI Act, 2026, introduced by the Union Government, aims to strengthen institutional
mechanisms for maintaining social harmony and preventing coordinated violence in sensitive districts.
The legislation proposes enhanced monitoring frameworks, inter-agency coordination protocols, and
targeted preventive measures in areas classified as high-risk for communal or organized unrest. While
the government argues that the law provides clarity in emergency response and intelligence-sharing,
critics have raised concerns regarding safeguards against misuse and the protection of civil liberties.
The Act reportedly includes provisions relating to digital surveillance coordination, district-level peace
committees, and structured reporting requirements to Parliament. Legal experts suggest that the law’s
constitutional sustainability will likely be tested on grounds of proportionality and federal balance. The
SHANTI Act reflects the broader tension between national security frameworks and fundamental rights
protections in contemporary India.

Source: Hindustan Times
passages.LEG-P0019:
XIII. Intergenerational equity is a foundational principle in environmental law that emphasizes the
duty of the current generation to preserve the environment for future generations. It is based
on the idea that those who have received the environment in pristine form are under an
obligation to maintain it in that state for generations to come. This principle has three main
components: conservation of options, which means preserving biodiversity and genetic
resources; conservation of quality, which involves sustaining environmental quality; and
conservation of access, which ensures equitable access to resources for all generations. The
principle aims to balance environmental protection with development activities between
present and future generations. In international law, it finds support in the 1972 Stockholm
Declaration and the 1992 Rio Declaration, which state that the right to development must be
fulfilled equitably for present as well as future generations. In India, the Supreme Court has
recognised intergenerational equity as part of sustainable development, holding that the
present generation owes a duty to future generations to keep the environment clean. The
principle requires replacing short-term decisions with long-term responsibility, supported by
public participation, legal frameworks, and planning. It serves as a mechanism to prevent
excessive exploitation of natural resources and maintain ecological balance.
Source: "Intergenerational Equity in Environmental Law," The Academic Journal (2026).
passages.LEG-P0020:
XIII. In contract law, the distinction between void and voidable contracts is fundamental to
understanding when legal obligations arise and when they can be avoided. A void contract is
one that is invalid from its very inception. It creates no legal rights or obligations because it
lacks one or more essential elements of a valid contract, such as a lawful object, lawful
consideration, or capacity of the parties. Agreements that are illegal, opposed to public policy,
or impossible to perform are classic examples. Since a void contract is a legal nullity, it cannot
be enforced by either party, and ratification is not possible. A voidable contract, on the other
hand, is a valid and enforceable contract unless and until it is avoided by the party entitled to
do so. Such contracts usually suffer from defects in free consent. When consent is caused by
coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake as to fact, the law allows the
aggrieved party to either affirm the contract or rescind it. Until this choice is exercised, the
contract remains legally binding. The distinction has important practical consequences. In void
agreements, restitution is generally unavailable because the law does not recognise the
transaction. In contrast, when a voidable contract is rescinded, the parties may be required to
restore benefits received. Another key difference lies in enforceability by third parties: rights
cannot flow from a void agreement, whereas third-party rights may arise under a voidable
contract before it is rescinded. Thus, while void contracts reflect situations where the law
refuses recognition altogether, voidable contracts represent situations where the law protects
consent but leaves the final choice to the injured party. Understanding this difference ensures
clarity in determining remedies, enforceability, and the stability of contractual relationships.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://cleartax.in/s/difference-between-void-and-
voidable-contract, 21-04-2025
passages.LEG-P0021:
X. In contract law, the formation of a valid agreement depends fundamentally on the
presence of an offer and its acceptance. An offer is a clear expression of willingness by one
party, the offeror, to enter into a legally binding relationship on definite terms, with the
intention that it shall become binding as soon as it is accepted by the other party. An offer


must be distinguished from a mere invitation to offer. Advertisements, price lists, and
display of goods generally indicate an intention to invite offers, not to make binding
promises, unless the language shows a clear commitment. Acceptance is the unqualified
and absolute assent to the terms of the offer. For acceptance to be valid, it must correspond
exactly with the offer and must be communicated to the offeror, unless the offeror has
waived the requirement of communication. Silence, as a general rule, does not amount to
acceptance. Acceptance may be expressed in words or implied through conduct, such as
performing the conditions of the offer. The timing of acceptance is also significant. An
offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance is complete against the offeror. Once
acceptance is validly communicated, a binding contract comes into existence, and neither
party can unilaterally withdraw. In cases of communication by post, acceptance is complete
against the offeror when it is properly posted, even if it is delayed or lost, reflecting the
“postal rule.” However, acceptance must be given while the offer is still in force. An offer
may lapse after a reasonable time, on rejection, on the death of the offeror, or if a condition
attached to the offer is not fulfilled. The law of offer and acceptance thus ensures certainty
by clearly identifying when negotiations end and contractual obligations begin.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://blog.ipleaders.in/offer-acceptance/, 18-01-
2025
passages.LEG-P0022:
XII. Medical negligence law in India has undergone significant development as courts
increasingly recognise the right to health and medical treatment as an integral component
of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. Traditionally, claims of medical
negligence were assessed through the lens of tort law, requiring the patient to establish
duty of care, breach, and resultant harm. However, recent judicial trends have expanded
the scope of state and institutional responsibility, especially in cases involving denial of
treatment or emergency care. Courts have repeatedly held that government hospitals and
public health authorities cannot refuse treatment on the grounds of administrative
constraints, lack of infrastructure, or non-availability of beds when a patient’s life is at
stake. The obligation to provide timely medical assistance arises not merely from
contractual relationships but from constitutional duty. Even private hospitals, once they
undertake treatment, are expected to adhere to reasonable standards of care and cannot
arbitrarily withdraw services in emergency situations. Importantly, courts distinguish
between medical negligence and medical error. An error of judgment does not
automatically amount to negligence unless it falls below the standard of care expected
from a reasonably competent medical professional. At the same time, systemic failures,
such as the absence of oxygen supply, delay in ambulance services, or refusal to admit
critically ill patients, are increasingly treated as violations of the right to treatment rather
than isolated acts of negligence. Another evolving aspect is the recognition that the right
to treatment includes access to emergency care without preconditions such as advance
payment or documentation. Judicial pronouncements emphasise that procedural
formalities cannot override the urgency of saving human life. Compensation in such
cases is not merely corrective but also serves a deterrent purpose, signalling that health
governance must prioritise patient welfare over institutional convenience. Thus,
contemporary medical negligence jurisprudence reflects a shift from individual fault-
based analysis to a rights-oriented approach, where denial of timely treatment itself can
attract constitutional scrutiny.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.freelaw.in/legalarticles/Medical-
Negligence-and-Right-to-Treatment-New-Precedents, 19-09-2025
passages.LEG-P0023:
IX. The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) marked a turning point in India’s freedom
struggle by transforming anti-colonial resistance into a mass political movement. Led by
Mahatma Gandhi, the campaign encouraged Indians to withdraw cooperation from British
institutions, including schools, courts, legislatures, and foreign goods markets. It witnessed
unprecedented participation from students, lawyers, peasants, and urban middle classes across
regions. The movement also coincided with the Khilafat agitation, reflecting attempts to forge
Hindu-Muslim political unity against colonial rule. However, the movement was abruptly
suspended following the Chauri Chaura incident in 1922, where violent clashes resulted in the
death of policemen. Despite its withdrawal, historians consider the movement crucial in
legitimising mass civil disobedience as a political tool and establishing Gandhi as the central
leader of the national movement.


Source: Bipan Chandra, India’s Struggle for Independence.
passages.LEG-P0024:
XII. The Bombay High Court has ruled that Shaadi.com, a popular matrimonial services platform, is a
well-known trademark under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, recognising its exceptional reputation,
goodwill and brand recognition in the matrimonial and matchmaking services sector. People Interactive
India Private Limited (PIIPL), contended that the defendants’ use of the getshaadi.com domain and
associated marks was deceptively similar to its registered Shaadi.com trademarks.
It argued that this not only infringed its trademark rights but also caused consumer confusion and
dilution of the distinctiveness of its mark. PITPL had adopted the Shaadi.com mark in 1996 and used it
commercially since 2000, accumulating millions of registered users, significant turnover, and extensive
advertising expenditure over the years. The Court granted a permanent injunction restraining the
defendants from using getshaadi.com or any similar mark or domain name and directed them to hand
over all infringing materials for destruction. While PIIPL had sought ?10lakh in damages, the
Court awarded %25lakh in costs to PIIPL, to be paid jointly by the defendants, with 8per cent
interest if unpaid within 12 weeks.
In India, a well-known trademark is a mark that has gained such a high level of recognition and
reputation among a substantial segment of the public who use the goods or services it represents that
the use of the same or a similar mark for other goods or services would likely be perceived as indicating
a connection with the original mark’s proprietor. This definition is codified in Section 2(1)(zg) of
the Trade Marks Act, 1999, which gives well-known marks exceptional protection compared to ordinary
trademarks.
Protection for a well-known trademark in India operateson two main fronts: the Registrar of
Trademarks can refuse registration of confusingly similar marks, and courts can act against misuse or
infringement of the well-known mark even in unrelated classes of goods or services.
To determine whether a mark is well-known, Section 11(6) of the Trade Marks Act lists multiple
factors, including public recognition, duration and geographical extent of use and promotion,
and successful enforcement history.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Unlike ordinary trademarks, well-known marks have reputational protection across the nation and
potentially beyond, and if a mark is recognised as well-known in one relevant public segment, the
Registrar must consider it well-known for registration purposes.
Source: https://ssrana.in/ip-laws/trademarks-in-india/well-known-trademarks-
india/ https://www.barandbench.com/news/why-the-bombay-high-court-recognised-shaadicom-as-
wellknown-trademark
passages.LEG-P0025:
XIV. The doctrine of caveat emptor, or "let the buyer beware," is a cornerstone of commercial law based
on the principle that the buyer must exercise their own skill and judgment when purchasing a
product. It implies that in the absence of fraud, misrepresentation, or active concealment, the
seller is under no duty to disclose defects in the goods. If a buyer examines a product and is
satisfied with its condition, they generally have no subsequent right to return it or claim damages
if they later discover a defect. This rule places the onus on the consumer to be cautious and to
protect their own rights through reasonable examination before a transaction is finalized.
However, the doctrine is not absolute and is subject to significant exceptions. It does not apply
where the buyer expressly or impliedly informs the seller of the specific purpose for which the
goods are required, relying on the seller’s expertise, or where the goods are bought by description
from a seller who deals in such items. In modern times, judicial trends have seen a shift toward
caveat venditor ("let the seller beware"), particularly in consumer protection cases where there is a
significant information asymmetry between the parties. Nevertheless, caveat emptor remains the
default rule for public auctions and many private sales of specific goods, serving as a reminder
that the law expects a basic level of diligence from every purchaser.
Source: Indian Journal of Legal Review (IJLR 2024) & Vanderbilt Law Review.
passages.LEG-P0026:
XV. South Africa says more than 50 countries have expressed support for its case at the United
Nations' top court accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in the war in Gaza. Others,
including the United States, have strongly rejected South Africa's allegation that Israel is
violating the U.N. Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
Many more have remained silent.
Genocide is a crime that involves acts committed with the intent to destroy a national, ethnic,
racial, or religious group. According to the United Nations, genocide requires a proven intent
to physically destroy a group. Cultural destruction and the intention to disperse a group are
not sufficient.
The 1948 United Nations Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of
Genocide defines genocide as any act committed with the intent to destroy a group. This
definition does not include political groups or "cultural genocide".
The key elements of the crime of genocide, as outlined in Article II of the convention, include:
+ Acts: Genocide involves specific acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in
part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. The prohibited acts include killing
members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting
conditions leading to the group's physical destruction, imposing measures to prevent births
within the group, and forcibly transferring children from the group to another.
+ Intent: The crucial element in defining genocide is the intent to destroy a protected group.
The perpetrator must have the specific intent to commit the acts mentioned above with the
purpose of annihilating the group. This distinguishes genocide from other crimes against
humanity.
The detail and technical definition is as follows:
Article I. The contracting parties confirm that genocide, whether committed in time of peace or
time of war, is a crime under international law which they undertake to prevent and punish.
Article II. In the present Convention, genocide means any of the following acts committed with
intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethical, racial or religious group as such:
(a) Killing members of the group; www.lawpreptutorial.com
(b) Causing serious bodily or mental harm to the members of the group;
(c) Deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical
destruction in whole or in part;
(d) Imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group;
(e) Forcible transferring children of the group to another group.
Article III. The following acts shall be punishable:
(a) Genocide;
(b) Conspiracy to commit genocide;
(c) Direct and Public incitement to commit genocide;
(d) Attempt to commit genocide;
(e) Complicity in genocide.
Source: https://www.euronews.com/2024/01/14/genocide-case-against-israel-where-does-the-
rest-of-the-world-stand-on-allegations?utm_source=chatgpt.com
passages.LEG-P0027:
XVI. “Deprivation (total loss) of personal liberty, which inter alia includes the right to eat or sleep when
one likes or to work or not to work as and when one pleases and several such rights sought to be
protected by the expression ‘personal liberty' in Article 21, is quite different from restriction
(which is only a partial control) of the right to move freely (which is relatively a minor right of a
citizen) as safeguarded by Article 19(1)(d). Deprivation of personal liberty has not the same
meaning as restriction of free movement in the territory of India. This is made clear when the
provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code in Chapter VIII relating to security of peace or
maintenance of public order are read. Therefore Article 19(5) cannot apply to a substantive law
depriving a citizen of personal liberty. I am unable to accept the contention that the word
‘deprivation’ includes within its scope 'restriction' when interpreting Article 21. Article 22
envisages the law of preventive detention. So does Article 246 read with Schedule Seven, List I,
Entry 9, and List III, Entry 3. Therefore, when the subject of preventive detention is specifically
dealt with in the Chapter on Fundamental Rights, I do not think it is proper to consider a
legislation permitting preventive detention as in conflict with the rights mentioned in Article
19(1). Article 19(1) does not purport to cover all aspects of liberty or of personal liberty. In that
article only certain phases of liberty are dealt with. www.lawpreptutorial.com
‘Personal liberty' would primarily mean liberty of the physical body. The rights given under Article
19(1) do not directly come under that description. They are rights which accompany the freedom or
liberty of the person. By their very nature they are freedoms of a person assumed to be in full
possession of his personal liberty. If Article 19 is considered to be the only article safeguarding
personal liberty, several well-recognised rights, as for instance, the right to eat or drink, the right
to work, play, swim and numerous other rights and activities and even the right to life will not be
deemed protected under the Constitution. I do not think that is the intention. It seems to me
improper to read Article 19 as dealing with the same subject as Article 21. Article 19 gives the
rights specified therein only to the citizens of India while Article 21 is applicable to all persons.
The word citizen is expressly defined in the Constitution to indicate only a certain section of the
inhabitants of India. Moreover, the protection given by Article 21 is very general. It is of '‘law'-
whatever that expression is interpreted to mean. The legislative restrictions on the law-making
powers of the legislature are not here prescribed in detail as in the case of the rights specified in
Article 19. In my opinion therefore Article 19 should be read as a separate complete article.”
Source: Kania CJ in AK Gopalan v. State of Madras 1950 AIR 27, 1950 SCR 88
passages.LEG-P0028:
X. Constitutional morality, though spoken of in the Constituent Assembly, remained dormant
for the rest of the last century and the first few years into the current millennium. My search
indicates that the initial discussions on constitutional morality towards the end of the first
decade of the current century started outside the discipline and forums of law, initially by a
sociologist followed by a political scientist before its entry in judicial decisions and legal


writings. This appears to be true of the discussion on constitutional morality in the West too
which gave birth to the notion in the early part of 19th century and, as is noted below, a few
hundred years before Christian era in Greece.
Let us first look at what transpired on the subject in our Constituent Assembly. Responding to
the criticism of the Draft Constitution on administrative details drawn from the Government of
India Act 1935, B.R. Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution,
agreeing that administrative details need not be incorporated in the Constitution, justified their
need in our Constitution by quoting from George Grote’s history of ancient Greece, as follows:
‘The diffusion of constitutional morality, not merely among the majority of any community but
throughout the whole, is the indispensable condition of a government at once free and
peaceable; since even any powerful and obstinate minority may render the working of a free
institution impracticable, without being strong enough to conquer ascendency for themselves.’
Following these words, which are as relevant today, as they wore at the time of making the
Constitution, Dr. Ambedkar added what seems to be prophetic in the context of current issues
that have surfaced and most clearly during the last few years in the administration of the
Constitution and laws. Therefore, I consider it absolutely necessary to quote them for the
purpose of realizing the reach of constitutional morality:
‘By constitutional morality Grote meant... a paramount reverence for the forms of the
constitution, enforcing obedience to authority and acting under and within these forms, yet
combined with the habit of open speech, of action subject only to definite legal control, and
unrestrained censure of those very authorities as to all their public acts – combined too with a
perfect confidence in the bosom of every citizen, amidst the bitterness of party contest, that
the forms of the constitution will not be less sacred in the eyes of his opponents than in his
own.’
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Observing constitutional morality”, Mahendra Pal
Singh.]
passages.LEG-P0029:
PASAGE 11
The distinction between an employee and an independent contractor remains one of the most
litigated questions in Indian labour jurisprudence. Although no single statute lays down an
exhaustive test, courts have evolved a combination of indicators: the control and supervision
test, the integration test, the economic dependence test, and, in modern settings, the
entrepreneurial/“multiple clients” test. Traditionally, the dominant factor was the employer’s
right to direct how, when, and where work must be done. A worker subject to detailed
instructions, mandatory office hours, and disciplinary oversight was more likely to be classified
as an employee. However, courts increasingly emphasise the substance of the relationship
rather than contractual labels. Merely calling someone a “consultant” or “freelancer” is
irrelevant if the actual working conditions reflect subordination. The rise of platform work, gig
services, and outsourced operations complicates this determination. A delivery rider may use
her own vehicle and enjoy flexible hours yet remain economically dependent on one platform,
subjected to algorithmic ratings and unilateral termination factors pointing toward employee-
like vulnerability. Conversely, a software architect who works project-to-project for several
clients, bears financial risk, and negotiates deliverables independently is more likely to be
treated as a contractor. Courts also consider who supplies tools, whether tax/PF deductions


are made, and whether the worker can delegate tasks to others. Misclassification carries
consequences. If a purported contractor is found to be an employee, the principal may owe
statutory benefits such as provident fund, gratuity, maternity benefits, and compliance with
working-hour norms. On the other hand, contractors normally receive only contractual
remedies unless the contract is unconscionable. The challenge lies in blended arrangements:
hybrid teams, remote-gig models, and “zero-hour” engagements where indicia point in
different directions. Indian courts adopt a “composite test,” weighing factors cumulatively. No
single factor is dispositive; the ultimate question is whether the worker is in a relationship of
subordination and economic dependence. Where evidence is evenly balanced, courts typically
tilt toward recognising employee status, emphasising labour-protective principles. The
jurisprudence thus reflects a tension between commercial flexibility and the need to prevent
disguised employment structures designed to evade welfare obligations.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://leglobal.law/countries/india/employees-vs-
independent-contractors-india/legal-framework-differentiating-employees-independent-
contractors-9/, 05-10-2025
passages.LEG-P0030:
XI. ‘Quantum meruit' is a Latin phrase meaning 'what one has earned.' In the context of contract law,
it serves as a remedy where a person has rendered services or provided materials under
circumstances that imply a promise to pay, even if an enforceable express contract was never
finalized or was later breached. The whole concept behind this solution is that the work done
should be paid for, and the other party should not be unjustly enriched by the former party's act. It
is a solution available under Indian contract law to ensure fairness when a contract is mutually
modified or deemed unenforceable due to a technical deficiency.
Recovery in quantum meruit is appropriate where the parties, which are not at fault themselves,
by their conduct, have formed a relationship that is contractual in nature. For example, if a
written agreement between an owner and a contractor is deemed unenforceable because it violates
public policy or has a technical flaw, the contractor may still recover for the reasonable value of
the labor performed. Since specific terms in an implied contract are absent, the law supplies the
missing contract price by asking what one would have to pay in the open market for the same
work. Thus, the measure of damages is defined as the reasonable market value of the materials
furnished and the labor performed.
Source: Journal of Gujarat Research Society & Law Mantra ("Doctrine of Quantum Meruit under
Indian Contract Act")
passages.LEG-P0031:
XIV. The growing debate on whether children should be allowed unrestricted access to social
media has brought child rights, parental autonomy, and state regulation into direct legal tension.
Several jurisdictions across the world have proposed or enacted minimum age requirements for
social media use, often coupled with parental consent mechanisms. The rationale behind such
regulation is grounded in mounting evidence linking excessive social media exposure to mental
health harms among children, including anxiety, cyberbullying, and addiction-like behaviour.
In India, the legal framework does not currently impose a blanket statutory age ban on social
media platforms. Instead, regulation emerges indirectly through data protection norms,
intermediary obligations, and child protection principles. The Digital Personal Data Protection
regime emphasises that children require heightened safeguards, recognising their limited
capacity to give informed consent. However, critics caution that imposing rigid age thresholds
risks paternalism and may infringe children’s evolving autonomy and freedom of expression.
A complete prohibition may also be ineffective, as children often bypass age gates through
misrepresentation. Courts examining such regulatory proposals are likely to apply a
proportionality analysis. The State must demonstrate that age-based restrictions pursue a
legitimate aim, are rationally connected to child welfare, are the least restrictive means
available, and balance benefits against harms to fundamental freedoms. Alternatives such as
parental control tools, algorithmic safeguards, and platform accountability are increasingly
viewed as less restrictive measures. The constitutional challenge lies in recognising children as
rights-bearing individuals while acknowledging their vulnerability. The legal question is not
whether children should be protected from harm, but how such protection can be achieved
without unjustifiably curtailing autonomy, expression, and access to information in the digital
age.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.livelaw.in/articles/social-media-age-
limit-for-children-analysis-514007, 20-12-2025
passages.LEG-P0032:
XII. The Punjab and Haryana High Court has directed all courts in the states of Punjab,
Haryana and UT Chandigarh to be referred to as “district courts/district judiciary/trial courts”.
In a circular uploaded on high court’s website on January 14, the high court directed that the
terms “subordinate judge/subordinate courts/lower courts” should not be used in the official
correspondence and in the high court and the district courts.
“Hon’ble the Chief Justice and Judges have been pleased to direct that henceforth, all the Courts
in the States of Punjab, Haryana and U.T. Chandigarh other than the High Court, shall be
referred to as “District Courts/District Judiciary/Trial Courts”. The terms “Subordinate
Judge/Subordinate Courts/Lower Courts” shall not be used in the official correspondence as
well as in the judicial functioning of the High Court as well as the District Courts, unless the
same is inevitable,” the circular dated December 24, 2025 read.
In 2024, a bench of Justices Abhay S Oka and Ujjal Bhuyan, had directed the registry of the
Court to not refer to the ‘Trial Courts’ as ‘Lower Courts.
“It will be appropriate if the Registry of this Court stops referring to the Trial Courts as ‘Lower
Courts’. Even the record of the Trial Court should not be referred to as Lower Court Record
(LCR). Instead, it should be referred to as the Trial Court Record (TCR),” the bench had said.
In a judgment passed last year by the division bench of Justices Oka and Augustine George
Masih, the court had reiterated its direction that the record of the Trial Court should not be
referred to as “Lower Court Record”.
“Describing any Court as a “Lower Court” is against the ethos of our Constitution,” the court
had said.
In 2024, the then Chief Justice of India (CJI) D Y Chandrachud had said district judiciary is
the “backbone of the judiciary” and thus a crucial component of the rule of law and calling it
subordinate must be stopped.
“The district judiciary is therefore called upon to shoulder tremendous responsibility and is
aptly described as the ‘backbone of the judiciary’,” Justice Chandrachud said, adding, “The
spine is the core of the nervous system. To sustain the spine of the legal system, we must stop
calling the district judiciary the ‘subordinate’ judiciary”.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Stop calling lower courts: Punjab and Haryana High
Court bars common terms, directs using district courts, trial courts”, Indian Express.]
passages.LEG-P0033:
XIII. The status of the Preamble has been one of the most debated subjects in Indian constitutional
jurisprudence, serving as the focal point for defining the relationship between the spirit and the
"letter" of the law. The Preamble to the Constitution of India records the aims and aspirations of
the people, yet its legal enforceability and its status as an integral part of the constitutional
document underwent a significant evolution through two landmark judicial pronouncements. The
first major confrontation with this issue occurred in In Re: Berubari Union (1960). The Supreme
Court was tasked with an advisory opinion regarding the transfer of certain territories to
Pakistan. During the proceedings, the role of the Preamble as a guide to legislative intent was
discussed. The Court acknowledged that the Preamble is a "key to open the mind of the makers"
and shows the general purposes for which they made the several provisions in the Constitution.
However, the Court explicitly held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.
Consequently, it was viewed as a decorative introduction that lacked substantive power. The
Court reasoned that since it is not a part of the Constitution, it cannot be regarded as a source of
any substantive power or a limitation on the powers of the government.
This restrictive view remained the law of the land until it was directly challenged and overturned
in the historic case of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). A 13-judge Bench the
largest in the history of the Court re-examined the Preamble's status while determining the scope
of Parliament's amending power under Article 368. The Court observed that the history of the
drafting of the Constitution showed that the Preamble was not just an introduction but was
actually voted upon by the Constituent Assembly, unlike the preambles of many other world
constitutions. In a monumental shift, the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is a part of the
Constitution. Justice Sikri observed that the Preamble is of extreme importance and the
Constitution should be read and interpreted in the light of the grand and noble vision expressed in
it. More importantly, the Court held that the Preamble contains the Basic Structure of the
Constitution, which is beyond the amending power of Parliament. While the Preamble itself can be
amended (as it was in 1976), such amendments cannot destroy its fundamental pillars like
secularism, democracy, or socialism.
Source: https://www.legalserviceindia.com /Legal-Articles/preamble-blueprint-of-the-indian-
constitutiona-ideals-and-aspirations /?
passages.LEG-P0034:
XIII. Trespass to land is to deliberately enter into someone's land and continue the possession on land
without permission and also without statute justification. Anyone who has the authority of land can
take legal action against the trespasser under the doctrine of torts. Trespassing to land is wrong and
against the owner's authority. Any unlawful admission on someone else's land or property can result in
trespass and the owner of the property can sue the trespasser if he can prove that he owns the
property. Even a person with wrongful possession of the land can also bring an action against the
trespasser except the real owner of the land or any person acting to be the authority of the land. It
should also be remarked that trespass of land is a wrong repressible, that is, mere entry upon land and
building under someone's authority is actionable even if no damage has been caused. This can also be
stated as injuria sine damnum, that is, infringement of a legal right without any physical damage
concerning money, comfort and so on. Trespass to land can be committed in any one or more of the
following ways: unauthorized entry to someone's land, by abusing the right of entry, and projecting
subject upon the land. Trespass by wrongful entry is the most general means of trespass in which the
defendant or some other party enters the enclosed or exclusive land or building of the plaintiff without
his authorization. The mere entry into the boundary of the land is enough for the plaintiff to be
compensated by the defendant if he sues for the same. In these trespasses intention of the defendant
does not at all matter. He will not be allowed to say that he acted under an honest but mistaken
assumption.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Source: Jadon, Viraj Singh (2022). "Trespass to Land: An Analysis." Journal of Legal Research and
Juridical Sciences, Volume 1, Issue 4, pp. 509-516. ISSN (O): 2583-0066.
passages.LEG-P0035:
PASAGE 12
 Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in India operates at the intersection of environmental
governance, administrative duty, and public accountability. Under the Environment Protection
Act, 1986, large-scale industries, infrastructure projects, mining operations, and certain
categories of manufacturing units must undergo an EIA before commencing operations. The
purpose of the EIA is not to halt development, but to ensure that development proceeds with
awareness of its ecological costs. At its core, an EIA requires the project proponent to identify
potential environmental impacts, propose mitigation strategies, and subject the proposal to
independent appraisal by an Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC). The process typically
involves four elements: screening (to determine if an EIA is required), scoping (to define the
extent of study), public consultation (where affected communities express concerns), and
appraisal (where the EAC evaluates whether the project should be granted environmental
clearance). Not all projects require a full EIA; certain activities fall under exempted categories
or are subject only to preliminary scrutiny. Even where required, the clearance is not a one-
time permission; the law envisages post-clearance monitoring, compliance reporting, and
possible suspension for violations. Recent disputes reveal recurring problems. Some project
proponents treat EIA as a procedural formality: copying baseline data, ignoring cumulative
impacts, or restricting public hearings. Others argue that delays and excessive compliance
discourage investment. Courts have held that EIA is a substantive safeguard: the duty to
assess impacts is not satisfied by filing volumes of documents, but by demonstrating genuine
environmental due diligence. A clearance obtained by concealing crucial information or
bypassing public consultation may be struck down, even after substantial investment.
Ambiguities remain, especially regarding “expansion projects,” where existing industries seek
to increase capacity. Authorities must decide whether expansions trigger fresh EIAs or only
require amendment of existing clearances. Another grey area concerns the legal status of
draft EIAs; though not final, they must still accurately disclose material facts. Ultimately, the
EIA regime is designed to balance ease of doing business with the constitutional imperative
of environmental protection. It expects accuracy, transparency, and proactive environmental
stewardshipnot mechanical compliance.


  Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.taxtmi.com/article/detailed?id=14082,
  11-04-2025
passages.LEG-P0036:
XIII. The Supreme Court, in a recent judgment, clarified the jurisdictional framework for trial of
offences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (D&C Act). The bench comprising Justice
Prashant Kumar Mishra and Justice Vipul M. Pancholi held that offences punishable under
Chapter IV of the Act must be tried by a Court not inferior to a Sessions Court, and cannot be
tried by a Magistrate. The case arose from an inspection conducted on July 22, 2014, at the
manufacturing premises of M/s SBS Biotech in Himachal Pradesh, where the Drug Inspector
alleged non-maintenance of records as mandated under Schedule M and Schedule U of the Drugs
and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. Schedule M prescribes good manufacturing practices and
documentation requirements, while Schedule U specifies particulars to be shown in manufacturing
records. A re-inspection on August 5, 2014, revealed discrepancies in manufacturing, testing, and
distribution records. Following sanction on September 15, 2016, a complaint was filed on February
27, 2017, alleging contraventions of Section 18(a)(vi) read with Rule 74, and Section 22(1)(cca)
read with Section 18-B, punishable under Section 27(d) and Section 28-A. The appellants
contended that mere non-maintenance of records falls under Section 18-B, punishable under
Section 28-A with a maximum sentence of one year, making the complaint barred by limitation as
it was filed more than two and a half years after inspection. They argued that Section 18 deals
with prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs, not record maintenance, and therefore
Section 27(d) was inapplicable. They further submitted that under Section 36-A, offences
punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, unless triable by a Special Court under

Section 36-AB, must be tried by a Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC). The Supreme Court
rejected these contentions, observing that the allegations included misuse of habit-forming drugs
and manipulation during manufacturing, thereby attracting Section 18(a)(vi), which prohibits
manufacture or sale in contravention of Chapter IV or the Rules. Since Section 27(d) prescribes
imprisonment of not less than one year and up to two years, the limitation period under Section
468 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) is three years. The complaint filed within two years
and six months was thus not time-barred. Critically, the Court held that Section 32(2) specifically
mandates that no Court inferior to a Sessions Court shall try offences punishable under Chapter
IV. This provision overrides Section 36-A, which itself excludes offences triable by Sessions Courts.
The committal to the Sessions Court was therefore upheld, and the appeal dismissed.
passages.LEG-P0037:
XII. The Supreme Court’s ruling on the protection of the Great Indian Bustard (GIB), one of
the world’s most endangered bird species, has emerged as a significant moment in India’s
evolving climate and environmental jurisprudence. The case arose from concerns that overhead
power transmission lines in arid regions of Rajasthan and Gujarat posed a fatal risk to the GIB,
which has poor frontal vision and is prone to collision. The Court initially directed that all
power lines in identified habitats be placed underground, prioritising species survival over
infrastructural convenience. However, the judgment also exposed the complex intersection
between biodiversity protection and climate action. Renewable energy projects, particularly
solar and wind installations, often rely on extensive transmission infrastructure. Critics argued
that an inflexible undergrounding mandate could severely delay India’s clean energy targets,
increase costs, and undermine climate mitigation efforts. Responding to these concerns, the
Court modified its earlier approach. It acknowledged that environmental governance cannot
operate through rigid binaries of conservation versus development. Instead, it emphasised a
principle of “informed balancing,” requiring authorities to consider ecological sensitivity,
technological feasibility, cost, and climate commitments together. The Court directed the
creation of an expert committee to assess where undergrounding is necessary and where
alternative mitigation measures, such as bird diverters- may suffice. This reflects a broader
judicial shift from absolute prohibitions to adaptive, evidence-based regulation. Importantly,
the Court recognised that climate change itself threatens biodiversity, implying that poorly
designed conservation orders may paradoxically worsen long-term environmental outcomes if
they obstruct renewable energy deployment. The ruling, therefore, reframes environmental
protection as a constitutional obligation that must be harmonised with climate goals. It signals
that courts will scrutinise executive action (or inaction) in climate matters, but will also exercise
restraint by deferring to scientific expertise where appropriate. Rather than prescribing uniform
solutions, the judgment promotes context-specific governance, reinforcing the idea that
sustainable development requires continuous calibration between competing environmental
imperatives, not categorical trade-offs.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.ceew.in/blogs/what-does-supreme-
court-ruling-on-protecting-great-indian-bustard-species-mean-for-climate-change-legislation,
23-05-2024
passages.LEG-P0038: The emergence of generative AI has posed significant doctrinal and ethical challenges to copyright law, particularly in jurisdictions governed by statutes such as the Copyright Act, 1957. Copyright protects "original works of authorship," requiring a minimal degree of creativity and, traditionally, human authorship. However, AI systems are trained on massive datasets, often scraped from the internet, which may include copyrighted works used without express authorization. A central legal issue is whether such use constitutes infringement or falls within exceptions like "fair dealing" under Section 52 of the Act. Courts have historically interpreted fair dealing narrowly, focusing on purpose, character, and market impact. While AI developers argue that training is "transformative," critics assert that large-scale, non-consensual ingestion of copyrighted material may substitute the original market or unjustly exploit creators' economic rights. Authorship presents another doctrinal challenge. Copyright law presumes a human author; hence, fully autonomous AI-generated works may fail to qualify for protection. However, where a human exercises creative control through detailed prompts, selection, arrangement, or substantial editing, the output may satisfy the originality threshold. Ethically, concerns arise regarding transparency, attribution, and bias. The opaque nature of AI training complicates identifying whose works were used and whether consent or compensation was provided. Scholars argue for a regulatory framework that ensures accountability while fostering innovation. Thus, the evolving legal landscape must reconcile statutory principles with technological realities, balancing the protection of creators with the advancement of AI.
passages.LEG-P0039:
XIV. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of
their life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. At the time
of its adoption, this provision was interpreted narrowly. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of
Madras, the Supreme Court treated “procedure established by law” as any procedure


enacted by the legislature, even if it was harsh or unfair. Under this approach, Article 21
offered limited protection against state action. This understanding changed significantly in
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India. The Court held that the “procedure” under Article 21
must be just, fair, and reasonable, and not arbitrary or oppressive. This judgment
transformed Article 21 into a dynamic and expansive guarantee, closely linked with
Articles 14 and 19. As a result, any law depriving a person of life or liberty must satisfy
standards of fairness, non-arbitrariness, and reasonableness. Over time, the Supreme Court
has interpreted the “right to life” to include more than mere animal existence. It now
encompasses the right to live with human dignity. This expansion has led to the recognition
of several unenumerated rights under Article 21, such as the right to livelihood, the right
to health, the right to privacy, and the right to a clean environment. These rights are not
explicitly mentioned in the Constitution but are considered essential to meaningful life and
liberty. Article 21 has also imposed positive obligations on the State. The Court has held
that the State must take active steps to protect life and dignity, particularly for vulnerable
groups. Thus, Article 21 has evolved from a narrowly framed protection against unlawful
detention into a foundational provision that shapes the relationship between the individual
and the State in matters affecting life, liberty, and dignity.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.scobserver.in/journal/the-right-to-
life-and-personal-liberty-under-article-21-a-timeline/, 26-05-2025
passages.LEG-P0040:
SECTION V
XVII. In criminal law, the distinction between intention, knowledge, and negligence determines not
only the quantum of punishment but the very character of the offense. Intention involves a
conscious, deliberate objective to bring about a specific consequence. Knowledge exists when
an individual is practically certain that a consequence will result from their actions, even if
that result is not their primary aim. Negligence, however, rests on the breach of a duty to take
reasonable care; harmful consequences arise because the actor failed to exercise the caution
legally expected of them in those circumstances.
The law differentiates these mental states because the moral blameworthiness is distinct. A
person who deliberately inflicts injury cannot be equated with one who inadvertently creates
risk. However, criminal negligence requires a significantly higher threshold than civil
negligence. For an act to constitute criminal negligence-such as under Section 106 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (formerly Section 304A IPC)-there must be a high degree of
disregard for human life and safety. The conduct must exhibit gross neglect or rashness, going
far beyond a mere error of judgment or ordinary carelessness.
Context is heavily determinative. Undertaking inherently dangerous activities-such as
performing complex surgery, handling hazardous substances, or operating heavy machinery-
imposes a higher standard of care because the foreseeable risks are severe. Yet, a tragic
outcome res ipsa loquitur (the thing speaks for itself) does not automatically establish criminal
liability. Courts must meticulously examine what the accused knew, what precautions were
reasonably feasible, and whether the lapse in judgment crossed the stringent threshold into
criminal culpability. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Source Inspired by Supreme Court of India precedents on medical and criminal negligence,
including Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and principles governing Sections 299, 300, and
304A of the Indian Penal Code / Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
passages.LEG-P0041:
XIV. A group of former civil servants has expressed serious concern over three recent Supreme Court
decisions related to environmental protection, warning that these rulings signal the growing
influence of “rich and powerful vested interests” over India’s ecological safeguards. In an open
letter dated December 28, the Constitutional Conduct Group (CCG) said it was deeply anguished
that the court, long considered the “last bastion” for environmental protection, appeared to be
setting aside established rules meant to protect the country’s environment. One of the key
decisions criticised is the Supreme Court’s November 20 acceptance of a new, uniform definition of
the Aravalli hill range. Prepared by a committee of eight Union government officials, the
definition restricts the Aravallis to hills rising at least 100 metres above local relief.
Environmentalists argue that this narrower definition could open large parts of the ancient hill
range to commercial activities, particularly mining. The CCG echoed these fears, warning that
such activities would weaken the Aravallis’ role as a dust barrier for Delhi, accelerate
desertification, destroy habitats, fragment ecosystems, and undermine the hills’ function as an
aquifer. The group also cautioned that increased mining would worsen already severe air pollution
in Delhi-NCR, disproportionately harming marginalised communities who work outdoors and lack
access to protective measures such as air purifiers. The Supreme Court has since taken suo motu
cognisance of the controversy and is scheduled to hear the matter. The second decision highlighted
by the CCG is the court’s November 18 order recalling its earlier May ruling, which had declared
post-facto environmental clearances for construction projects to be a “gross illegality’. While the

matter is now to be decided by a larger bench, the group urged the court to restore its earlier
stance, especially in light of worsening climate extremes and record levels of air pollution in north
India. The third concern relates to the Supreme Court’s November 22 decision preventing the
government from disbanding the Central Empowered Committee (CEC) without court approval.
The CEC, established in 2002 to monitor compliance with court orders on forests and wildlife, is
alleged by the CCG to have lost its independence and come under the influence of the Union
environment ministry. The group pointed out that a CEC official was part of the committee that
drafted the new Aravalli definition and reiterated earlier concerns about the removal of
independent members from the committee. In conclusion, the CCG warned that these decisions,
taken in quick succession, threaten both environmental conservation and citizens’ right to life. The
group urged the Supreme Court to prioritise public health over corporate interests and to uphold
established principles such as “polluter pays”, the precautionary principle, and intergenerational
equity.
Source: The Wire dated article 29 December 2025
passages.LEG-P0042:
XIII. The doctrine of separation of powers is intended to remove the abuse of power by authorities by
ensuring that no single organ of the government exercises power beyond its constitutional
mandate. This doctrine is generally based on four pillars: the Exclusivity Principle, which divides
government into three structural organs; the Functional Principle, which prevents one organ from
performing the tasks of another; the Check and Balance Principle, which mandates that organs
oversee each other to ensure actions remain within legal bounds; and the Mutuality Principle,
which encourages cooperation rather than confrontation between branches. In India, while the
doctrine is not expressly mentioned in the Constitution with "pedantic rigor,” it is recognized as a
part of the Basic Structure.
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, the Supreme Court ruled that the separation of
powers among the legislature, executive, and judiciary is a fundamental feature of the
Constitution that cannot be amended. This framework does not imply a rigid or absolute
separation, as there is some overlap; for instance, the President has certain legislative powers, and
the judiciary has the power of judicial review over executive and legislative acts. The goal of this
demarcation is to avoid the suppression of rights that occurs when power is concentrated in a
single group. By allowing each branch to specialize and providing instruments like the judicial
power to declare laws unconstitutional, the system maintains a sensible approximation of
autonomy while preventing arbitrariness.
Source: International Journal of Innovative Law Research ("Separation of Power") & JGU
Institutional Repository.
passages.LEG-P0043:
XIII. In the annals of constitutional adjudication, few maxims have resonated as powerfully as Fiat
justitia ruat caelum—let justice be done though the heavens fall. This aphorism epitomises the
judiciary's unflinching commitment to the rule of law, even when such fidelity provokes
institutional disquiet or political reprisal. The Supreme Court's recent pronouncements
whether in the validation of Parliament's power to abrogate Article 370, the insistence upon
gender equality in the Sabarimala temple entry case, or the recognition of concerns relating to
autonomy and dignity in the same-sex marriage deliberations, without granting legal
