passages.LEG-P0079:
XII. Comparative International Law studies how different countries structure and enforce legal rules
and principles in areas such as treaties, human rights, commercial law, and dispute resolution. It
involves analyzing domestic legal systems, international conventions, and customary practices to
understand similarities and differences in lawmaking, interpretation, and enforcement across
jurisdictions. This field helps policymakers, lawyers, and judges adopt best practices, harmonize
laws, and resolve cross-border disputes efficiently.
One key application is in treaty law, where countries enter agreements such as bilateral
investment treaties (BITs), extradition treaties, or trade agreements. These treaties often include
dispute resolution clauses, investor protections, or obligations to surrender fugitives.
Understanding comparative frameworks ensures that states comply with international obligations
while protecting domestic interests. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Another important area is judicial decision-making, where courts refer to international
precedents, foreign judgments, and global conventions to interpret laws and resolve disputes.
Principles like comity of nations allow domestic courts to respect foreign judicial decisions,
fostering mutual legal recognition and cooperation. Similarly, doctrines such as reciprocity and
sovereign immunity guide states in interactions with foreign nationals, foreign governments, or
international organizations.
Comparative International Law also addresses emerging issues, including cybercrime, intellectual
property, environmental regulation, and transnational commercial disputes. Courts and
legislators increasingly rely on comparative studies to craft policies that balance national
sovereignty with global obligations. The field emphasizes harmonization, predictability, and
fairness in international legal practice, enabling states to navigate conflicts of law while
maintaining domestic legal integrity.
passages.LEG-P0080:
XUII. Under Indian Contract Law, consent is considered free when it is given voluntarily, without
coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake. Section 13 of the Indian Contract
Act, 1872, defines consent and highlights its importance for the validity of a contract. A contract
entered into without free consent is voidable at the option of the aggrieved party, ensuring
fairness and protection against exploitation. Courts consider the intentions, circumstances, and
relationship between the parties to determine whether consent was genuinely free.
Coercion occurs when a person is compelled to enter into a contract by threats of injury to their
person, reputation, or property. For example, if a creditor threatens physical harm to a debtor
unless they sign an agreement, the contract would be voidable due to coercion. Undue influence
arises when one party uses a dominant position over another, such as a guardian over a ward,
employer over an employee, or a banker over a financially dependent client, to obtain consent
unfairly. In such cases, the weaker party may rescind the contract.
Fraud involves deliberate deception to induce a party to enter into a contract. Examples include
forging documents, concealing material facts, or making false promises. Misrepresentation, in
contrast, occurs when false statements are made innocently, without intent to deceive, but still
influence the other party’s consent. Mistake may relate to the subject matter, quality, or identity
of the parties and can render consent void if it affects the essence of the agreement. For instance,
selling a painting believing it to be original when it is a replica may constitute a mistake.
Courts examine all facts surrounding the agreement, including written terms, oral negotiations,
and the parties’ conduct, to decide whether consent was free. Remedies include rescission,
restitution, or damages depending on the defect in consent. Understanding free consent ensures
fairness, protects weaker parties, and upholds the integrity of contractual relations, promoting
trust and legal certainty in commercial and personal dealings.
passages.LEG-P0081:
XIII. The Constitution of India grants the Supreme Court (under Article 32) and High Courts (under Article
226) the power to issue certain prerogative orders, known as writs, for the enforcement of Fundamental
Rights and other legal rights. These writs are extraordinary remedies designed to check the abuse of
power by state authorities. The five primary writs are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari,
Prohibition, and Quo Warranto.
Habeas Corpus (meaning ‘to have the body’) is a bulwark of personal liberty. It is issued to produce a
detained person before the court to examine the legality of their detention. If the detention is found
unlawful, the person is set free. Mandamus (meaning ‘we command’) is a command issued to a public
official, corporation, or lower court, directing them to perform a public or statutory duty they have
failed or refused to perform. Certiorari (meaning ‘to be certified’) is issued by a higher court to a lower
court or tribunal to quash an order passed by it, typically for lack of jurisdiction or error of law
apparent on the record. Prohibition is a preventative writ, issued to forbid a lower court or tribunal
from proceeding in a case where it has no jurisdiction. Quo Warranto (meaning ‘by what authority’) is
directed against a person who wrongfully usurps a public office, requiring them to show the authority
under which they hold the office. The choice of writ depends on the nature of the right infringed and the
type of authority against whom relief is sought. While Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right for

enforcing other Fundamental Rights, Article 226 grants High Courts broader power to issue writs not
only for Fundamental Rights but for ‘any other purpose.’
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Maheshwari & Co., "Deciphering The Writs Under The
Indian Constitution,” Mondag (4 March 2025), available
at: https: //www.mondag.com/india/constitutional-administrative-law/1591746/deciphering-the-
writs-under-the-indian-constitution
passages.LEG-P0082:
XV. In public law and regulatory governance, delegated legislation plays a crucial role in
implementing statutory objectives while balancing administrative efficiency and
democratic accountability. Legislatures often enact broad framework statutes and delegate
rule-making powers to the executive or specialised authorities to fill in operational details.
Such delegation is considered necessary in modern governance, given the technical
complexity and evolving nature of regulation. However, this delegation is not unlimited. A
fundamental constitutional principle governing delegated legislation is that essential
legislative functions cannot be delegated. The legislature must lay down the policy,
purpose, and guiding principles of the law. Delegated authorities may only determine
details, procedures, or technical standards within this framework. If the parent statute
confers unfettered discretion without clear guidance, the delegation may be struck down
as excessive or unconstitutional. Judicial review of delegated legislation primarily focuses
on ultra vires control. A rule or regulation may be invalidated if it exceeds the scope of
authority granted by the parent statute, contradicts the statute’s objectives, or violates
constitutional provisions. Courts also examine whether delegated legislation is arbitrary,
unreasonable, or manifestly unjust, especially when it affects fundamental rights or
imposes penalties. At the same time, courts recognise that delegated legislation enjoys a
presumption of validity. Judicial intervention is cautious, particularly in areas involving
technical expertise, economic regulation, or public welfare. The role of the court is not to
assess the wisdom of the rule but to ensure that it remains within legal boundaries. Thus,


delegated legislation reflects a delicate balance: it enables flexible and responsive
governance, yet remains constrained by constitutional limits, legislative intent, and the
principles of accountability and rule of law.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.lawctopus.com/clatalogue/clat-
ug/delegated-legislation-in-administrative-law/, 24-09-2024
passages.LEG-P0083:
XII. In the law of torts, liability is typically categorized as either fault-based or no-fault. Under no-fault
liability, a defendant is held accountable for damages even in the absence of negligence or intent.
This concept is divided into two primary doctrines: Strict Liability and Absolute Liability.
Strict Liability was established in the landmark English case Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). It
dictates that if a person brings onto their land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, they
are prima facie liable for any damage caused by its escape, regardless of how much care was
taken. For this rule to apply, three essentials must be met: the defendant must bring a hazardous
substance onto their property, there must be a "non-natural" use of the land, and the substance
must actually escape the premises and cause harm.
However, Strict Liability is not an exhaustive rule and provides some specific defenses:
1. Plaintiffs Own Fault: If the damage resulted from the plaintiff's own trespassing or
negligence.

2. Act of God: Unforeseeable and uncontrollable natural disasters.
8. Volenti Non-Fit Injuria: If the dangerous substance was maintained for the mutual benefit of
both parties.
4. Act of a Stranger: If a third party over whom the defendant had no control caused the escape.
5. Statutory Authority: If the act was performed under the mandate of law.
Absolute Liability is a more stringent Indian legal doctrine evolved by the Supreme Court in M.C.
Mehta v. Union of India. Prompted by the 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy, the Court realized that the
traditional exceptions to Strict Liability allowed hazardous industries to evade accountability for
mass disasters. This rule states that an enterprise engaged in an inherently dangerous or
hazardous activity is liable for any harm resulting from an accident during that activity. Unlike
the Rylands rule, Absolute Liability is not subject to any exceptions; the defendant cannot escape
liability by claiming an Act of God or the act of a stranger. This ensures that high-risk industries
bear the full cost of any danger they introduce into society.
passages.LEG-P0084: The modern law of the sea is primarily governed by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which establishes a comprehensive framework regulating maritime zones, state rights, and navigation freedoms. Coastal states exercise varying degrees of control over different maritime zones measured from their baseline, typically the low-water line along the coast. Within territorial waters, extending up to 12 nautical miles, the coastal state enjoys full sovereignty, subject only to the right of "innocent passage" granted to foreign vessels. Passage is considered innocent so long as it is not prejudicial to the peace, good order, or security of the coastal state. Activities such as weapons exercises, spying, or fishing may render passage non-innocent. Beyond this lies the contiguous zone, extending up to 24 nautical miles, where the coastal state may enforce laws relating to customs, taxation, immigration, and sanitation.Further outward is the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), extending up to 200 nautical miles, where the coastal state has sovereign rights for the purpose of exploring, exploiting, conserving, and managing natural resources. However, other states retain freedoms of navigation and overflight in the EEZ. The high seas, lying beyond national jurisdiction, are governed by the principle of freedom of the seas. No state may validly claim sovereignty over any part of the high seas, and all states enjoy freedoms including navigation, fishing, and scientific research, subject to certain international obligations. Conflicts often arise when states attempt to extend control beyond permissible limits or when the nature of an activity such as surveillance or resource extraction blurs the distinction between lawful use and violation of coastal state rights. The resolution of such disputes depends on interpreting the balance between sovereignty and shared global commons.
passages.LEG-P0085:
IX.	The Right to Disconnect refers to an employee’s entitlement to disengage from work-related
emails, calls, and messages beyond working hours without fear of penalty. With the rise of remote
work and digital communication tools, employees often feel pressured to remain available even
during personal time. This continuous engagement disrupts work-life balance and negatively
affects mental health, family relationships, and overall well-being.
Recognizing these challenges, several countries have introduced policies supporting the Right to
Disconnect, encouraging employers to respect personal time and set clear communication
boundaries. Such measures promote healthier workplaces, improve productivity, and reduce
burnout. When employees are well-rested and mentally relaxed, they are more motivated and
efficient during working hours.www.lawpreptutorial.com
However, implementing this right requires mutual understanding between employers and
employees. Organizations must establish clear guidelines regarding after-hours communication,
while employees should use this freedom responsibly. The Right to Disconnect is not about
avoiding work, but about ensuring balance, dignity, and respect in professional life. In a fast-paced
digital world, safeguarding personal time is essential for sustainable growth and well-being.
passages.LEG-P0086:
XIV. On November 13, 2025, MeitY (India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information
Technology) notified the DPDP Rules 2025, which operationalises the DPDP Act 2023 (a.k.a.
DPDPA), the first comprehensive and full-fledged data protection and digital privacy law in
India. It replaces the previous IT (Information Technology) Rules, 2011 under the IT Act 2000.
The DPDPA introduces a rights-based, consent-led, comprehensive framework governing how
companies protect, collect, store, and process personal data. Within a phased 12–18-month
timeline, organisations operating in India (named “data fiduciaries”) must meet the Act’s core
compliance requirements. These include reporting data breaches within 72 hours,
implementing systems for express user permission, and appointing data protection officers and
consent managers.
Furthermore, the Act also aims to strengthen the rights of private individuals (referred to as
“data principals”) to control, access, erase, and correct their data. It centres on accountability,
breach reporting, security safeguards, purpose limitation, and consent, with stricter duties for
significant data fiduciaries and penalties amounting to up to INR 250 crore for non-compliance.
Additionally, it also establishes a Data Protection Board to enforce compliance while
mandating verifiable parental consent for processing children’s data.
However, the DPDPA has drawn criticism as it grants the government extensive and far-
reaching authority to access personal data without any robust independent oversight. It’s been
compared to the EU’s GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), which requires data
minimisation and strict consent, and has an independent regulator.


The DPDPA just has a government-appointed, four-person Data Protection Board, which will
oversee privacy for some 1.4 billion people, raising concerns over free speech and
compromised privacy. In fact, every successful iteration of the rules and the Act has been
criticised for granting the governing body too much control and leeway without the required
accompanying safeguards.
What’s a particularly controversial aspect of the DPDP Act is its direct impact on the RTI (Right
to Information) Act. According to RTI, citizens could seek out access to records that public
authorities held if its disclosure was for the larger interest of the public.
Under DPDPA, this public interest provision has been amended. So, even though the requested
information could possibly relate to public interest, authorities can still deny its release. This
could lead to the State possibly denying personal information outright, which citizens might
require to expose corruption and hold governing bodies accountable.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “India’s DPDP Act: Data Privacy Or Data
Surveillance?”, sify.com.]
passages.LEG-P0087:
XIV. In private law, rights are often classified as rights in rem and rights in personam. A
right in rem is a right available against the world at large for instance, ownership of
property or the right not to be physically harmed. In contrast, a right in personam binds
only specific individuals, as in contractual obligations. This distinction underlies the
traditional divide between tort and contract. Tort law typically enforces rights in rem,
protecting individuals against wrongful interference with their person, property, or
reputation. Contract law, on the other hand, arises from voluntary promises and governs
rights in personam, enforceable only between the contracting parties. Yet, this neat divide
is not always clear. For example, when a manufacturer sells a defective product, is the
liability contractual (breach of promise to the buyer) or tortious (duty of care owed to
anyone injured)? Similarly, professional negligence by doctors or lawyers blurs the line:
though the relationship is contractual, the duty breached may resemble tortious obligations
owed more broadly. Courts have thus emphasised structural analysis rather than rigid
categories. Tort liability is imposed by law, reflecting duties that exist independently of
agreement. Contractual liability arises only from consent, where parties choose their
obligations. But in practice, the same facts can trigger overlapping remedies, and judges
must balance principles of freedom of contract with the social need to hold individuals
accountable for harm. The tension illustrates a deeper policy debate: should civil liability
be primarily about compensating harm (as in tort), or enforcing bargains (as in contract)?
Understanding this divide and its exceptions is central to interpreting civil law disputes in
a principled manner.
(SOURCE [EDITED], https://lawbhoomi.com/transfer-for-the-benefit-of-unborn-person/)
passages.LEG-P0088:
PASAGE 10
The right to freedom under Articles 19–22 of the Indian Constitution forms the core of the
democratic project: it mediates the relationship between the individual and the State by
recognising liberties that enable participation, dissent, and self-expression. Yet these
freedoms are not absolute. Article 19(1) guarantees rights such as speech, assembly,
movement, residence, and profession, while Article 19(2)–(6) authorise “reasonable
restrictions” in the interests of security, public order, decency, morality, sovereignty, or to
ensure professional regulation and social welfare. The tension between liberty and regulation
is therefore structural, not exceptional. Courts routinely emphasise that restrictions must be
narrowly tailored: they must be proximate to a legitimate aim, proportionate in effect, and non-
arbitrary in application. Mere administrative discomfort or political disagreement cannot justify


curbing fundamental freedoms. The nature of restrictions varies across rights. Free speech is
particularly vulnerable to overbroad limitations justified in the name of public order. Courts
have resisted such expansions, holding that hypothetical or remote threats cannot qualify as
“reasonable restrictions.” Peaceful assemblies, too, may be regulated but not suppressed
outright; blanket prohibitions fail the test of proportionality unless accompanied by
demonstrable, imminent risks. Freedom of movement and residence is more often regulated
through statutory schemes relating to public health, criminal procedure, or national security,
but even these restrictions must meet the test of procedural fairness and necessity. The right
to life and personal liberty under Article 21 interacts closely with the freedom rights. Preventive
detention laws, for instance, are constitutionally permitted but tightly circumscribed by
procedural safeguards; courts insist that detention cannot be based on stale materials or
vague apprehensions. Similarly, custodial rights, such as the right to counsel and protection
against arbitrary arrest, serve as practical guarantees of personal liberty. Article 22 attempts
to strike a balance by allowing preventive detention while mandating disclosure of grounds,
representation before advisory boards, and time limits. Emerging debates further complicate
the landscape. Digital speech, algorithmic policing, and virtual assemblies raise questions
about whether traditional tests of “public order” or “reasonableness” remain adequate.
Scholars argue that excessive algorithmic surveillance chills freedom even without explicit
prohibitions. Ultimately, the right to freedom is best understood not as a static list of
entitlements but as an evolving equilibrium between individual autonomy and democratic
governancean equilibrium courts must continually renegotiate in light of changing
technologies, social conflicts, and state imperatives.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://blog.ipleaders.in/what-is-the-right-to-freedom/,
29-06-2022
passages.LEG-P0089:
XIII. Environmental Safeguards in India: The EPA, 1986 and the EIA Framework
India's principal legislative instrument for environmental protection is the Environment
(Protection) Act, 1986 (EPA), which empowers the Central Government to take all necessary
measures for environmental quality improvement. The Act defines environmental pollution as
the presence of any solid, liquid, or gaseous substance at concentrations harmful to the
environment, and mandates that discharge of pollutants must not exceed prescribed
regulatory standards. Under the current EPA, contravention of Section 7 or Section 8 attracts
monetary penalty under Section 14A: 21 lakh to 215 lakh, with %50,000 per day for continuing
contravention. Notably, Section 19 of the EPA permits any person — not merely government
officials — to file a complaint before a court regarding violations after giving not less than 60
days’ notice to the Central Government or authorised authority.
Complementing the EPA is the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) framework,
operationalised through the EJA Notification, 2006. EIA is a systematic process of identifying,
predicting, and mitigating the environmental effects of proposed projects before they are
undertaken. Baseline environmental data must be sufficiently representative; reliance on only
one season may distort impact prediction. EIA applicability is determined by size, capacity,
area, location, sectoral, or schedule-based thresholds, not merely investment value. Some
projects may remain outside full EIA scrutiny because of these thresholds.
The EIA process requires the project proponent to prepare an EIA report, often through
consultants. Reports are funded by project proponents themselves, creating concerns of conflict
of interest, selective reporting, and weak accountability despite the accreditation framework.
The EIA Notification mandates public consultation and appraisal by an Expert Appraisal
Committee before environmental clearance is granted. Post-clearance monitoring is essential,
but enforcement gaps, proponent-funded assessments, copy-paste reporting, and weak
accountability mechanisms have led to credibility problems in several cases. The framework
aims to balance development with environmental protection, but its effectiveness depends on
rigorous data, independent oversight, and strict adherence to procedural safeguards.
[Word Count: 312]
Source: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (as amended); EIA Notification, 2006; Environment
(Protection) Amendment Rules, 2024

X. Samariya was appointed Chief Information Commissioner on November 6, 2023, and retired upon
reaching the age of 65. Before he took charge, the post had lain vacant for a month after Y.K. Singh’s
retirement. Out of the 12 Chief Information Commissioners who have taken office since the RTI Act
came into force in 2005, only 5 assumed charge the day after their predecessors retired. The first time
the CIC was left without a chief was in August 2014 when Rajiv Mathur retired.

incumbent either attaining the age of 65 or completing his/her tenure—the government has repeatedly

laid down clear directions to ensure vacancies are filled in a timely manner.
In Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2019), the court warned that vacancies would “badly affect the
functioning of the Act, which may even amount to negating the very purpose for which this Act came
into force”.
More recently, in October 2023, the court cautioned that the RTI Act risked becoming a “dead letter” if
posts remained unfilled. This is not an isolated lapse. Vacancies have remained unfulfilled since
November 2023. Despite advertisements being issued—first in August 2024 for the eight Information
Commissioner posts, and again in May 2025 for the chief’s position—the government has failed to
complete the selection process. In January this year, the Centre told the Supreme Court that
appointments would be made by April 2025.
On September 26, 2025, the Supreme Court heard a case on the non-appointment of information
commissioners before a bench of Justices Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi. Advocate Prashant

XII. In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, the Supreme Court of India delivered a
landmark judgment on 8 April 2025, addressing the constitutional limits on the powers of a state
Governor when dealing with bills passed by a state legislature. A two-judge bench held that the
Governor lacks an unfettered veto or “pocket veto” over legislation duly adopted by the State
Assembly and emphasised that the Governor must act in accordance with constitutional
conventions and the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. The Court observed that prolonged
withholding of assent or referral of bills for presidential consideration undermines democratic
mandates and federal principles. In that context, the bench-imposed timelines directing that
Governors decide on re-enacted bills within one month and on bills reserved for the President
within three months to prevent indefinite delays that can frustrate the legislative will of elected
representatives. Utilizing its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution in the exceptional facts
of the case, the Court also declared ten pending bills as having been effectively assented to, as
they had been stalled for an unreasonable period. The judgment underscored that the Governor’s
actions must respect parliamentary democracy and not impede the functioning of state
legislatures. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Shortly after this ruling, on 13 May 2025, the President of India issued a Presidential Reference
under Article 143(1) of the Constitution to the Supreme Court, seeking its advisory opinion on 14
questions concerning the scope of Governors’ and the President’s powers under Articles 200 and
201, particularly whether the Court could lay down timelines and prescribe how these powers
should be exercised. A five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court on November 20, 2025 answered the
16th Presidential Reference the country has witnessed by opining that the judiciary cannot fetter
Governors and the President to ‘one-size-fits-all’ time-tables to dispose of State Bills or usurp their
functions by assuming ‘deemed consent’ of the proposed laws at the expiry of a court-ordered time
frame. Such a usurpation of the gubernatorial function of the Governor, and similarly of the
President’s functions, is antithetical not only to the spirit of the Constitution, but also specifically,
the doctrine of separation of powers — which is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution,
However, the court clarified that the President and Governors cannot resort to “prolonged and
evasive inaction” by sitting endlessly on State Bills awaiting their approval. This would amount to
a deliberate attempt to thwart the people’s will expressed through the proposed welfare laws
passed by State legislatures.
Source: Excerpt of State Of Tamil Nadu V. Governor of Tamil Nadu (Live Law)

XI. “Mid-term elections do not limit the plenary power of the electorate to elect representatives. The
right to vote and contest elections, while secured under Article 326, are not fundamental rights,” the
Law Ministry clarified.
The Ministry also addressed apprehensions about the federal character of the Constitution. Leaning on
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s observations during the Constituent Assembly debates, it said the Constitution
was designed to be flexible. It is federal under normal conditions and unitary during emergencies.
“Synchronisation of elections through Constitutional Amendment does not disturb this balance,” the
Ministry asserted, citing multiple Supreme Court rulings to support its position.
On the question of whether the Election Commission would wield excessive powers under the new
framework, the Ministry said the Commission already enjoys autonomy under Article 324 and has the
authority to schedule elections under Sections 14 and 15 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
“The EC will continue to exercise superintendence, direction and control over elections. In exceptional
circumstances, if polls cannot be held, the Commission may recommend deferment to the President,
who can act accordingly,” the Ministry explained.
The Ministry underscored that simultaneous elections aim to reduce the frequency of polls and
associated expenditure without compromising constitutional principles. “Technically, no Lok Sabha has
completed a full five-year term as fresh elections are held before expiry,” it observed, adding that mid-

It has further argued, citing the Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006) Supreme Court judgment, that
the right to vote, though fundamental to democracy, is not a fundamental right but a Constitutional and
a legal, statutory right. The Representation of the People Act 1951, the Law Ministry said, lays down
conditions to disqualify a voter for reasons such as “non-citizenship”, “unsoundness of mind as declared

passages.LEG-P0094:
XI.	A battery consists of a harmful, or an offensive, touching of the plaintiff's person, caused directly or
indirectly by a voluntary act of the defendant with an intention to inflict a harmful or an offensive
touching. A touching of another's person may be both offensive and harmful, or it may be merely
offensive and not inflict substantial harm. A touching which is not harmful but which is offensive to a
normal or reasonable person is a battery, and it subjects the actor to liability if the touching is not
consented to or privileged. In this type of battery, it is the insult or offensiveness of the touching that is
important and not damage in fact. A certain amount of contact with one's person must be tolerated in
decent society. But if any person uses violence against the other, to force his way in a rude manner, it
will be a battery. An offensive touching may be inflicted in many ways. Thus, forcibly pushing the
plaintiff's hat back on his head, in order to see his face and identify him, was held to be a battery. The
forcible cutting of a pauper's hair by parish officials was held to be a battery. On the other hand, merely
touching a fireman, who was engaged in directing a stream of water upon a burning house, for the
purpose of attracting his attention and giving him advice, was held not to be a battery as it was not an
act which would be offensive to a normal sense of personal dignity. The interest protected by this type
of battery is the interest in freedom from a bodily touching which is offensive to a reasonable sense of
personal dignity.
Source: Rollison, W. D. (1941). "Torts: Assault; Battery." Notre Dame Law Review, Volume 17, Issue 1,
pp. 1-18. Notre Dame Law School.
passages.LEG-P0095:
XIII. The doctrine of constructive res judicata is an important extension of the principle of res
judicata embodied under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC). While the
traditional rule of res judicata bars the re-litigation of issues that have already been directly
and substantially decided between the same parties, constructive res judicata prevents parties
from raising matters in subsequent proceedings that they “might and ought” to have raised in
earlier litigation. The doctrine is primarily incorporated through Explanation IV to Section 11
CPC and is closely connected with Order II Rule 2 of the CPC.
The rationale behind the doctrine is based upon public policy, judicial economy, and the need
to ensure finality in litigation. Courts seek to prevent parties from splitting claims or
withholding grounds strategically in order to initiate multiple rounds of litigation over the
same dispute. The principle is therefore intended to protect opposing parties from repeated
harassment and to prevent wastage of judicial time. The Supreme Court has repeatedly
emphasized that litigation must eventually attain finality, since endless challenges undermine
public confidence in the judicial process.
Recently, the Supreme Court examined the doctrine while considering a dispute concerning
property rights where a respondent attempted to claim reliefs in a later suit that could and
should have been sought in an earlier proceeding itself. The Court observed that the dispute
regarding the parties’ rights already existed at the time of the first suit, and therefore all
connected reliefs ought to have been claimed together. Since the respondent was fully aware of
the rival claim during the earlier proceedings, the subsequent suit was barred by constructive
res judicata and by the principles underlying Order II Rule 2 CPC. The Court held that parties
cannot be permitted to re-agitate issues by merely altering the form of relief sought in later
litigation.
The doctrine has also been applied beyond ordinary civil suits. In M. Nagabhushana v. State of
Karnataka (2011), the Supreme Court clarified that constructive res judicata may apply even
to writ petitions. The Court reasoned that litigants cannot repeatedly invoke constitutional
remedies on grounds that could reasonably have been urged earlier. However, courts have also

recognized that the doctrine should not be applied mechanically in exceptional situations
involving changed circumstances, continuing violations, or issues affecting personal liberty.
Thus, constructive res judicata represents a balance between two competing concerns:
ensuring fairness to litigants while also preserving certainty, consistency, and finality in
judicial proceedings. The doctrine discourages fragmented litigation and promotes efficient
administration of justice by compelling parties to present their entire case at the earliest
available opportunity.
Source: extracted with edits from https://www.livelaw.in/supreme-court/title-suit-hit-by-
constructive-res-judicata-if-plaintiff-omitted-it-in-earlier-injunction-suit-where-title-was-
disputed-supreme-court-529786

PASAGE 13
 For decades, India's labour laws were a labyrinth of over 29 central enactments, creating
confusion for employers and loopholes for exploitation. In a historic overhaul, Parliament
consolidated these into four comprehensive Labour Codes: the Code on Wages, the Code on
Social Security, the Industrial Relations Code, and the Occupational Safety, Health and
Working Conditions Code. This shift aims to balance the ease of doing business with the
protection of workers' rights in a modern economy. A pivotal change is the universalisation of
minimum wages. Previously restricted to "scheduled employments," the Code on Wages now
mandates that no employee across any sector can be paid less than the statutory minimum
wage. This creates a non-negotiable floor for income. Simultaneously, the Code on Social
Security expands the safety net beyond the traditional factory floor. It explicitly recognises "gig
workers" and "platform workers" like food delivery agents and ride-sharing drivers, granting
them access to social security schemes for the first time. This acknowledges the reality of the
gig economy, where the employer-employee relationship is often blurred. The Industrial
Relations Code introduces a significant restructuring of disputes and strikes. It mandates a
14-day notice period for strikes in all industrial establishments, not just public utility services.
This is designed to encourage dialogue and prevent abrupt work stoppages. Furthermore, it
raises the threshold for "standing orders" (rules of conduct for workmen) to apply only to
establishments with 300 or more workers, giving smaller businesses more flexibility in hiring
and firing, a move that critics argue creates a "hire and fire" regime. Finally, the Occupational
Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code streamlines safety regulations. It introduces a
single license for staffing firms and allows women to work night shifts (7 PM to 6 AM) in all
establishments, provided their consent is obtained and adequate safety measures are in
place. This provision attempts to remove legal barriers to women's employment while placing
a positive duty on the employer to ensure their safety. The overarching legal principle binding
these codes is the movement from rigid, sector-specific rules to broader, universally applicable
standards that recognise new forms of employment while attempting to streamline compliance
for industries.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from
https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2025/11/29/india-four-labour-codes-overview-
explained-scctimes/, 29-11-2025
passages.LEG-P0097:
XI. The constitutional framework of India vests in the judiciary the formidable power to issue
prerogative writs, a cornerstone of judicial review and fundamental rights enforcement.
Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution empower the Supreme Court and High Courts,
respectively, to issue writs such as Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo
Warranto. These remedies, deeply rooted in English common law, have been meticulously
adapted to serve as essential instruments for upholding the rule of law and constitutional
morality in a democratic republic. Their evolution reflects a dynamic jurisprudence that
responds to societal needs while safeguarding liberty and accountability.
Historically, writs originated as royal commands, but in India, they have transformed into
judicial orders that curtail executive and legislative excesses. Each writ serves a distinct
function: Habeas Corpus secures personal liberty against unlawful detention; Mandamus
compels public authorities to perform legal duties; Certiorari quashes orders passed without
jurisdiction; Prohibition prevents such proceedings; and Quo Warranto scrutinizes the right to
hold public office. Collectively, they form a robust mechanism for constitutional redress,
ensuring that state power is exercised within legal boundaries.
The interpretation and scope of these writs have expanded significantly through judicial
innovation. The rise of Public Interest Litigation (PIL) liberalized standing rules, allowing
courts to address systemic issues affecting communities. This development particularly
influenced Mandamus, evolving it into a tool for "continuing mandamus," where courts issue


ongoing directions and monitor compliance, especially in areas like environmental protection.
Similarly, Habeas Corpus has been broadly construed to protect not merely physical freedom
but also the right to live with dignity under Article 21. Even during periods of constitutional
strain, such as emergencies, the judiciary has navigated the suspension of rights, affirming the
resilience of writ jurisdiction as a shield against arbitrariness.
Landmark rulings, such as L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), reinforce that judicial
review via writs is a basic feature of the Constitution, immutable and inviolable. This principle
ensures that constitutional courts retain supervisory authority over tribunals, maintaining a
hierarchy of justice and preventing the ouster of fundamental safeguards. Thus, writs are not
static remedies but living instruments that adapt to contemporary challenges, balancing
individual freedoms with state authority. They embody the judiciary's role as the guardian of
the Constitution, continuously interpreting legal norms to preserve democratic values and
ensure justice remains accessible and substantive in an ever-evolving polity.
passages.LEG-P0098:
XV. In a significant ruling on personal liberty and individual autonomy, the Kerala High Court
has held that parents cannot invoke the writ of habeas corpus merely because they disapprove
of their adult daughters’ decision to join a religious congregation and lead a life of celibacy.
The case, Joju George and Ors. v. State of Kerala and Ors. (2026), was decided by a Division
Bench comprising Justice A.K. Jayasankaran Nambiar and Justice Jobin Sebastian of the
Kerala High Court.
The petition was filed by three parents alleging that their daughters, aged 21, 26 and 30, were
being illegally detained by members of a religious congregation known as the Monastery of
Holy Ruah (MHR). According to the petitioners, their daughters had joined the congregation
when it was recognised by the Archdiocese of Thrissur. However, after the Archdiocese
dissolved the congregation in 2023, the parents claimed that their daughters continued to
remain there under coercion.
The petitioners argued that parental guidance and authority over children should not be
brushed aside merely because the children had attained majority, contending that courts
should intervene where decisions taken by adult children were immature or influenced. The
Court rejected this reasoning. It noted that police enquiries revealed that the daughters
themselves signed statements affirming that they were voluntarily continuing with the
congregation. Accordingly, the Court held that parental disagreement could not justify judicial
intervention through habeas corpus.
A central theme of the judgment was individual autonomy. The Bench observed that the
choice of the alleged detenus with regard to their beliefs or the congregation that they must
join is a matter that rests exclusively within the private domain of the individual concerned,
warning that interference by the State in such matters would have a chilling effect on the
exercise of constitutional freedoms by the individual concerned. The Court cautioned that, as
"sentinels on the qui vive", this Court must tread with caution when called upon to issue writs
in the nature of Habeas Corpus alleging illegal detention.
In its concluding observation, the Bench held that the mere disgruntlement of a parent with
the decision of his adult daughter, who has chosen a life of celibacy by responding to the call of
the Divine, cannot be the basis for the issuance of a writ of Habeas Corpus. The ruling
reinforces a broader judicial trend in India protecting the autonomy of adults to make personal
choices regarding faith and lifestyle, free from parental or State coercion.
Source: https://www.barandbench.com/news/adult-daughters-free-to-choose-religious-life-
kerala-high-court-dismisses-habeas-corpus-plea-by-parents

passages.LEG-P0099: Negligence originates from the Latin term “negligentia,” meaning “failure to pick up” or “neglect.” At its core, negligence refers to carelessness or a failure to exercise the degree of care that a reasonable person would, resulting in harm to another. To establish negligence, several essential elements must be proved. First, there must be a duty of care, meaning the defendant must owe a legal obligation to act with reasonable caution toward the plaintiff. This duty arises when one person’s actions may reasonably and foreseeably affect another’s safety, and its existence depends on the relationship between the parties. Secondly, there must be a breach of duty, which occurs when the defendant fails to act as a reasonable person would under similar circumstances. The standard of care is assessed objectively by comparing the defendant’s conduct to that of an ordinarily prudent person. Another requirement is causation, meaning the breach of duty must directly result in harm to the plaintiff. Causation consists of two components. The first is actual or factual causation, commonly assessed using the “but for” test, which asks whether the harm would have occurred but for the defendant’s act. The second is legal or proximate causation, which examines whether the harm was a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the defendant’s actions. Further, the plaintiff must establish damage, demonstrating that actual injury or loss resulted from the defendant’s negligence. Foreseeability also plays an important role in negligence law, as the harm suffered must have been reasonably foreseeable at the time of the negligent act. A person generally cannot be held liable for highly unusual or remote consequences that could not reasonably have been anticipated. The law also adopts an objective standard through the reasonable person standard, which asks how an ordinarily prudent individual would have acted in the same situation. Personal limitations or characteristics of the defendant, such as carelessness or inexperience, are generally not considered relevant in determining liability. Certain defenses may also be available in negligence actions. One such defense is contributory negligence, which arises when the plaintiff contributes to his or her own harm by failing to take reasonable care for personal safety. In such situations, although the defendant may have acted negligently, the plaintiff’s own negligence may reduce or completely bar recovery of damages. Another defense is an Act of God (Vis Major), which refers to extraordinary natural events beyond human control or foresight that cannot be prevented despite reasonable care. Since such events are unforeseeable and irresistible, the defendant is generally not held liable if the harm resulted solely from them. Closely related is the concept of an inevitable accident, which refers to an event that could not have been prevented despite the exercise of reasonable care, caution, and skill. Unlike an Act of God, an inevitable accident may arise from human conduct rather than natural forces. Finally, the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur, meaning “the thing speaks for itself,” serves as a rule of evidence in negligence cases. It applies where the precise cause of an accident may be unknown, but the nature of the incident itself strongly suggests that it could not ordinarily have occurred without negligence. Source: https://www.manupatracademy.com
passages.LEG-P0100:
XVIII. In contract law, not every statement made during negotiations becomes a binding term of the
contract. A statement may be a mere representation, intended to induce the other party into
entering the agreement, or it may be a contractual promise, breach of which gives rise to
liability irrespective of fraud. The distinction depends on several factors: the importance
attached to the statement, the relative knowledge of the parties, the timing between the
statement and the contract, and whether the statement was reduced into writing. Where one
party possesses special knowledge and the other relies substantially on that assertion, the law
is more inclined to treat the statement as a term rather than casual sales talk.
This distinction has important consequences. If the statement forms part of the contract, its
falsity may amount to breach even where the maker honestly believed it to be true. If it is
merely a representation, the remedy may depend on whether the misstatement was
fraudulent, negligent, or innocent. However, the law also recognizes that exaggerated
commendation, obvious opinion, or statements not intended to be taken literally do not
ordinarily create contractual obligations. Similarly, where the representee independently
verifies the facts or expressly agrees not to rely solely on pre-contractual assertions, the legal
effect of the statement may weaken.
Courts therefore examine not merely what was said, but the commercial setting in which it
was said. The law seeks to protect genuine reliance, but it does not convert every failed
expectation into breach of contract. Much turns on whether the statement was meant to
allocate risk, and whether a reasonable person in that situation would have understood it as
contractually binding.
Source: Inspired by classic common law principles reflected in Oscar Chess Ltd v Williams,
Dick Bentley Productions Ltd v Harold Smith (Motors) Lid, and Indian Contract Act doctrines
on consent, misrepresentation, and contractual terms.
passages.LEG-P0101:
XV. Amid loud protests from the opposition, the Karnataka Legislative Assembly on December 18
passed the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025, in Belagavi. The
legislation prescribes imprisonment of one to seven years along with fines for hate crimes. For
repeat offences, imprisonment ranges from two to seven years with higher fines. The Bill covers
communication made in public through verbal, print, public, or electronic means.
While tabling the Bill, Home Minister G. Parameshwara cited a Supreme Court ruling delivered
on May 5 this year, which emphasised the need for firm action against communal hate. He noted
that hate speech had led to killings and inter-community violence, harming social harmony. The
legislation aims to protect constitutional values by addressing discrimination rooted in religion,
race, caste, gender, language, and other identities. According to Parameshwara, the objective is to
curb and prevent dissemination, publication, or promotion of hate speech that causes disharmony
or hatred against a person or group. The home minister explained that existing preventive
restrictions on provocative speech were insufficient. Alerts about potential inflammatory speech
could lead to temporary bans, but this was not a long-term solution. Therefore, a separate law was

required, as provocative speeches were often followed by violent incidents. The government is
authorised to direct the removal of hate speech material from media platforms. Hate crime under
the Bill is defined as communicating or promoting hate speech to cause disharmony, enmity, or ill-
will against individuals or groups.
The Bill makes hate speech a cognizable, non-bailable offence, and offenders can be tried by a
Judicial Magistrate First Class. For organisations, persons in charge at the time of the offence are
deemed liable.
The Congress government-initiated discussions on a hate speech law in June after a series of
communal killings in coastal Karnataka, beginning with the lynching of a Muslim man, Ashraf, in
April. Leader of the opposition R. Ashok opposed the Bill, tearing a copy in the assembly and
claiming it infringed on Article 19(1), which guarantees free expression. He argued that police
could misuse the law for political purposes, targeting journalists and opposition members. Ashok
suggested existing provisions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita were adequate. The debate
intensified after Urban Development Minister Byrathi Suresh made a remark directed at BJP
MLA Vedavyas Kamath, prompting the opposition to demand its removal from the official record.
Despite protests, Parameshwara appealed for support, and the speaker announced the Bill had
been approved through a voice vote before adjourning the House for lunch. BJP MLAs later stated
they were caught off guard by the passage without full debate. Minister for Law H.K. Patil
emphasised that the Bill had been passed and could not be discussed again. The Bill seeks to
address communal disharmony by making hate speech and hate crimes punishable under clear
statutory provisions, ensuring swift action against offenders and promoting social harmony in
Karnataka.
Source: The Wire dated Article 19» December 2025
passages.LEG-P0102:
PASAGE 15
 The Competition Commission of India’s (CCI) recent investigation into Apple’s App Store
practices has triggered a constitutional challenge that raises deeper questions about the
structure of antitrust penalties in India. The probe began after complaints alleging that Apple’s
mandatory in-app payment system and commission of up to 30% unfairly restricted
competition by raising costs for developers and forcing them to use Apple’s proprietary billing
mechanism. In 2024, the CCI’s investigation unit concluded that Apple had abused its
dominant position, describing the App Store as an “unavoidable trading partner” for developers
seeking to reach iOS users. The dispute escalated after Parliament amended Section 27(b)
of the Competition Act in 2023. Earlier, penalties could be based only on “relevant turnover,”
meaning turnover linked to the offending product or service. Following the amendment,
“turnover” is now interpreted as global turnover derived from all products and services. In
2024, the CCI’s Monetary Penalty Guidelines reinforced this shift by allowing the regulator to
rely on global turnover, especially when determining “relevant turnover” is infeasible, and to
increase penalties if necessary for deterrence. Apple contends that this regime is
unconstitutional, disproportionate, and arbitrary. It argues that penalties must be connected to


the scale of the violation within India, not tied to unrelated global revenue streams. To
demonstrate alleged absurdity, Apple analogised its situation to punishing a toy-and-stationery
seller’s entire ₹20,000 turnover for a violation limited to ₹100 worth of toys. Apple further
claims the amendment may be applied retrospectively, pointing to a recent CCI decision where
new rules were used for violations committed a decade earlier. The CCI, however, maintains
that global turnover penalties align with practices in jurisdictions such as the European Union,
where fines of up to 10% of global turnover are standard, especially for large digital platforms
whose market power extends beyond territorial borders. The underlying policy shift reflects
concerns that penalties based solely on Indian revenue may be too small to deter multinational
tech giants. The Delhi High Court must now decide whether Parliament’s decision to adopt a
global-turnover framework strikes a constitutionally acceptable balance between regulatory
deterrence and proportional punishment, or whether it impermissibly overreaches by linking
Indian violations to worldwide financial metrics.

passages.LEG-P0103: Criminal liability generally arises where an individual directly commits an offence. However, the law also recognises that a person may be held responsible even without personally carrying out the prohibited act. This principle is reflected in the law relating to abetment, which seeks to punish conduct encouraging, facilitating, or assisting the commission of an offence. The rationale is that a person who deliberately contributes to the commission of an offence may be as blameworthy as the person physically committing it. Abetment may arise in three principal ways: instigation, conspiracy, and intentional aiding. Though these concepts may overlap in certain situations, they are distinct in their legal requirements. Instigation refers to actively provoking, urging, inciting, encouraging, or stimulating another person to commit an act. Such encouragement may be express or implied and may occur through words, conduct, written communication, or even deliberate omission in certain circumstances. However, mere casual remarks, expressions of anger, or statements lacking intention to provoke commission of an offence may not amount to instigation. The focus lies upon whether the accused intended to influence or encourage another person toward committing the act. Abetment by conspiracy occurs where two or more persons agree to commit an unlawful act or agree to commit a lawful act through unlawful means, and some act or illegal omission takes place in furtherance of that agreement. Mere knowledge of an unlawful plan or passive association with conspirators does not by itself constitute conspiracy. There must ordinarily exist a meeting of minds and some step taken toward execution of the common design. Abetment by intentional aiding occurs where a person intentionally facilitates commission of an offence through acts or omissions. Aid may take various forms, including providing tools, information, transport, shelter, or any other assistance that substantially contributes to the offence. Mere presence at the scene of occurrence does not necessarily amount to aiding unless accompanied by conduct intended to facilitate commission of the offence. A person may be liable for abetment even if the principal offence ultimately differs in manner from what was originally intended, provided the consequences are a probable result of the conduct encouraged or assisted. However, where the principal offender acts independently and outside the scope of what was instigated or facilitated, liability for abetment may not arise.
passages.LEG-P0104:
XII. It's a common belief in Indian contract law that Section 32 of the Contract Act, which
deals with "contingent contracts," is the home of the modern force majeure clause. This
idea, however, may be a long-standing legal myth. A deeper look into legal history reveals
a critical distinction, borrowed from French jurist Pothier, between two types of conditions:
suspensive and resolutory. A suspensive condition (or condition precedent) is one that must
be fulfilled before a contractual obligation comes into existence. The contract is essentially
on hold, waiting for the event to happen. Section 32, which states that a contract contingent
on an event happening "cannot be enforced" unless that event happens, and becomes void
if the event becomes impossible, clearly deals with such suspensive conditions. On the
other hand, a resolutory condition (or condition subsequent) is one that extinguishes or
terminates a pre-existing, valid obligation upon the happening of a specified event. This is
the true nature of a force majeure clause. It doesn't prevent a contract from being formed;
it provides an exit ramp when an unforeseen event, like a war or natural disaster, makes
performance untenable. The original 1866 draft of the Indian Contract Act actually
contained separate provisions for these resolutory conditions, terming them "superadded
conditions" that could terminate an engagement. However, for reasons lost to history, these
clauses were omitted from the final Act of 1872. This omission suggests that Section 32,
which only covers suspensive conditions, was never intended to govern force majeure
clauses, which are fundamentally resolutory in nature.
(SOURCE              [EDITED],
https://indiacorplaw.in/2022/11/16/force-majeure-and-contingent-contracts-a-link-that-
wasnt/)

V. Inordinate delay in passing an order about the liberty of a citizen is not in tune with the constitutional mandate, the
Supreme Court observed in an order allowing anticipatory bail plea. In this case, the High Court rejected the anticipatory
bail application filed by the accused. The Supreme Court granted him ad interim protection observing that (i) it was a
cross-case arising out of the civil dispute. (ii) Prima facie there was no material to show that the provisions of Scheduled
Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, were invoked. (iii) That there was a delay of six days in
lodging the FIR. In certain minor offences, it is the right of the accused to obtain bail while the trial is pending. These are
bailable offences. On the other hand, there are more serious offences where the accused do not have a right to obtain bail;
in such cases, bail can be granted only at the court's discretion. These are non-bailable offences. Certain offences are so
serious that any police officer can investigate and arrest an accused person without obtaining a warrant from a court. For
example, murder. These are cognizable offences. In other cases, the police must wait for the order of a magistrate before
investigating and arresting the accused. These are non-cognizable offences. In certain offences, the State which conducts
the prosecution and the accused can come to an arrangement where, instead of being imprisoned, the accused can pay a
fine. These are compoundable offences. In this case, the officer fining you is compounding your offence. Of course not all
offences are compoundable; it would not be desirable that murderers should be able to compound their offences.
The CrPC also provides that certain petty offences may be tried in a summary way. In a summary trial, no sentence of
imprisonment for a term exceeding three months can be passed in any conviction. If a fine of Rs. 200 or less is imposed in
such trials, then the accused has no right to appeal. A person may submit an anticipatory bail application if they believe
they will be detained by the police for an offence for which there is no possibility of bond. Before the hearing for the grant
of regular or anticipatory bail, a short-term bail is given to the accused. Such short-term bail is called ‘interim bail’.
