passages.LEG-P0136: A seller is deemed to be an unpaid seller under certain conditions. Firstly, a seller is considered unpaid if the whole price of the goods sold has not been paid or tendered. Secondly, a seller may also be regarded as unpaid where a bill of exchange or any other negotiable instrument has been accepted as conditional payment, but the condition remains unfulfilled due to dishonour of the instrument or otherwise. An unpaid seller possesses certain rights against the goods sold. One such right is the Right of Lien. The right of lien permits an unpaid seller to retain possession of the goods until payment is made. This right may be exercised where the goods are sold without any credit terms, where the credit period has expired, or where the buyer becomes insolvent. Lien is regarded as a “particular lien,” meaning it can be exercised only by the seller and not by any assignee or creditor. The seller may exercise this right even if the goods are held as an agent or bailee of the buyer. Another important right is the Right of Stoppage in Transit. This right enables the unpaid seller to stop the goods from being delivered to the buyer and to regain possession while the goods are still in transit. However, this right becomes available only when the buyer becomes insolvent after the sale. Goods are regarded as being in transit from the time they are delivered to a carrier until the buyer or the buyer’s agent takes delivery. The unpaid seller also enjoys the Right of Resale. Where the goods are perishable in nature, the seller may resell them without providing notice to the buyer. However, where the goods are non-perishable, the seller must provide notice to the buyer and allow a reasonable period for payment before reselling them. Further, the seller may also resell where an express right of resale has been reserved in the contract itself. If the seller resells the goods without giving the required notice, the seller cannot recover damages from the buyer for losses suffered due to the resale. However, where proper notice has been given, the seller may claim damages and also retain any profit arising from the resale. It is important to distinguish between the right of lien and the right of stoppage in transit. The right of lien remains available only so long as the unpaid seller continues to retain possession of the goods. In contrast, the right of stoppage in transit arises only after the seller has parted with possession of the goods, while they are still in the course of transit. Source: https://www.defactolaw.in/post
passages.LEG-P0137:
XII. Article 21 is considered to be the heart of the Constitution, the most natural and progressive provision
of our living Constitution, the basis of our laws. The purpose of the fundamental right under Article 21
is to prevent the infringement of personal liberty and the deprivation of life except according to the
procedure laid down by law. This clearly indicates that this fundamental right has been established
against state only. The definition of the state encompasses government departments, legislative bodies,
administrative bodies, local authorities that exercise statutory powers, and so on. However, it does not
encompass non-state or private entities that do not have statutory powers. The primary purpose of
Article 21 is to ensure that the procedure laid down by law is followed prior to the deprivation of life or
personal liberty by the state. The right to life is the right to lead a life of dignity and worth. There is no
limit to the meaning of the word life. This right will be available to all the citizens of the country.
Personal liberty is the freedom from physical constraint of the person by the state. It includes all the
types of rights other than the ones laid down in Article 19 of the Constitution. The interpretation of the
right to life today is substantially different from that of 1950 when the Indian Constitution was
enforced. One of the first landmark judgments was A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras where the
Supreme Court absurdly restricted the meaning and scope of personal liberty to just freedom of the
body. The next big case that changed the way we think about the Right to Live was Maneka Gandhi v.
Union of India where the Supreme Court ruled that the word freedom in Article 21 of the Indian
Constitution has the broadest meaning and any law that is passed by the legislature should be in line
with Article 21.
Source: Roy, Shivangi (2023). "Right to Life: An Analysis on Article 21." Indian Journal of Integrated
Research in Law, Volume III, Issue VI, pp. 369-383. ISSN: 25838-0538.
passages.LEG-P0138: Constitutional democracies do not merely protect the right to speak; they create conditions under which disagreement can survive. Liberty of thought and expression is valuable not only because it protects individual autonomy but because it enables competing visions of society to coexist. Fraternity, one of the values recognised in the constitutional framework, requires citizens to acknowledge one another as equal participants despite differences in belief, ideology, faith, or social identity. It therefore accommodates disagreement and discourages enforced conformity. Throughout history, free speech has often enabled individuals and groups lacking social or political power to participate in democratic discourse. Reform movements seeking equality, dignity, and inclusion have frequently depended upon speech and expression to challenge existing structures. Therefore, dissenting opinions cannot ordinarily be suppressed merely because they disturb dominant opinion or unsettle prevailing social norms. However, constitutional protection of speech does not imply complete immunity. Freedom of expression may be subject to restrictions where expression threatens constitutionally recognised interests such as public order, decency, morality, security of the State, or the dignity of particular communities. Yet restrictions imposed upon speech must satisfy the principle of proportionality. The mere existence of disagreement or discomfort does not justify broad restrictions. Measures adopted must bear a rational connection with the objective sought and should interfere with speech only to the extent necessary. Constitutional values also distinguish between constitutional morality and popular morality. Popular morality may reflect majoritarian beliefs, customs, or social attitudes prevailing at a given time. Constitutional morality, however, derives from principles of equality, dignity, liberty, and justice embedded within the constitutional order. Constitutional rights cannot ordinarily be denied merely because a majority of people disagree with a particular belief or expression. Furthermore, threats to free expression may arise not only through direct governmental action but also through organised private conduct. If private groups use intimidation, social pressure, economic retaliation, or coordinated harassment to silence unpopular views, the practical value of free speech may become illusory. In such circumstances, the State may possess a positive obligation not merely to avoid suppressing expression itself, but also to ensure that individuals are not effectively prevented from exercising their constitutional freedoms. Finally, constitutional values are often best assessed from the standpoint of those who remain vulnerable or excluded from dominant structures. Justice and equality cannot be evaluated merely through the experiences of those who already possess social or economic privilege. Constitutionalism frequently requires attention to the perspectives of those whose voices remain unheard.
passages.LEG-P0139:
XI. In an increasingly digital India, accessing essential services often begins with a Know-
Your-Customer (KYC) check. While designed to prevent financial crimes, these digital
verification processes have inadvertently created significant barriers for Persons with
Disabilities (PwDs). Recognising this, the Supreme Court has recently expanded the scope
of Article 21, the right to life and liberty, to include the ‘right to digital access’, framing it
as a constitutional imperative. This move is anchored in the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, which mandates that all electronic media and services be
made accessible, following principles of ‘universal design’. The RPwD Act adopts a
‘social-barrier’ model, understanding disability not just as a medical impairment but as a
result of societal obstacles that prevent full participation. Current digital KYC methods,
like the Video-based Customer Identification Process (V-CIP), often exemplify these
barriers. Tasks such as eye-blinking tests, reading flashing codes, or aligning documents
for a selfie can be impossible for individuals with visual impairments or facial
disfigurements. The RBI’s rules also bar any form of ‘prompting’ or assistance during
verification, further isolating users who need help. The Supreme Court’s intervention is
based on the principle of ‘substantive equality’, which requires the state to take active
measures to ensure marginalised groups can enjoy their rights on par with others. By
directing regulators like the RBI to revise KYC norms, the Court has affirmed that digital
infrastructure is not a luxury but a fundamental part of modern life. The failure to ensure
accessibility is not merely an inconvenience; it is a denial of the right to life, dignity, and
equal participation in society.
(SOURCE             [EDITED],
https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/does-article-21-include-right-to-digital-access-
explaine d/article69580767.ece)

IV. While holding that irretrievable breakdown of a marriage can be a ground to grant a divorce by invoking powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court clarified that a party cannot file a writ petition under Article 32
of the Constitution of India and seek relief of dissolution of marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of
marriage directly from it.
The Constitution Bench approved the view taken in the judgment Poonam v. Sumit Tanwar (2010) that the parties should
not be permitted to file a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, or for that matter under Article 226 of
the Constitution of India before the High Court, and seek divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
The Writ of Habeas Corpus is issued by the Courts in those cases where a person is illegally detained. Habeas Corpus
means ‘to have the body’ and it is one of the most effective remedies available to a person detained. The Court commands
the person or authority who has detained or restrained another person to present such person before the Court. The Court
requires the detaining person to provide the grounds on which the person has been detained and if he fails to provide a
valid ground, the person who has been detained will be released by the Court immediately.
Certiorari is a Writ that can be issued when the superior court wants to decide a matter in the case itself or if there is an
excess of jurisdiction by the inferior court. This Writ can also be issued when there is a fundamental error in the procedure
followed, or in cases of violation of the principles of natural justice.
The Writ of Quo Warranto is issued by the courts against a private person when he assumes an office on which he has no
right. Quo Warranto means ‘by what authority’ and it is an effective measure to prevent people from taking over public

offices. Writ of Prohibition is not issued often and is an extraordinary remedy that a Superior Court issues to an inferior
court or tribunal for stopping them from deciding a case because these courts do not have the jurisdiction. If the court or
tribunal does not have jurisdiction and it still decides the case, it will be an invalid judgement because for an act to be
legal it should have the sanction of law.
Source: https://www.livelaw.in/supreme-court/supreme-court-writ-petition-dissolution-of-marriage-irretrievable-
breakdown-227646

passages.LEG-P0142:
XI.	The law of torts is fundamentally concerned with providing remedies for civil wrongs. Two foundational
Latin maxims distinguish between actionable and non-actionable harm. Injuria Sine Damnum refers to
a situation where there is a violation of a legal right (injuria) without the plaintiff suffering any actual,
quantifiable financial or physical loss (damnum). The infringement of the right itself is considered a
wrong, and the law provides a remedy, often nominal damages, because the right must be vindicated.
For instance, trespassing on a person's property is actionable even if no damage is caused to the
property. Conversely, Damnum Sine Injuria describes a scenario where a person suffers actual
financial loss (damnum), but this loss results from an act that does not infringe upon any of their legal
rights (injuria). In such cases, no legal remedy is available in tort, as the harm is damnum absque
injuria (damage without wrongful act). A classic example is lawful business competition that causes a
rival's profits to fall. The law recognizes that certain harms, even if real, must be borne in a competitive
society where individuals and entities exercise their lawful rights. The critical task for a court is to
determine whether the plaintiff's asserted "right" is a legally protected interest and whether the
defendant's conduct constituted a breach of a legal duty owed to the plaintiff.
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Ratanlal & Dhirajlal, The Law of Torts (26th edn,
LexisNexis 2012) 21-23.
passages.LEG-P0143:
IV.	The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 was enacted by Parliament
to curb paper leaks, impersonation, and organised cheating in public examinations. It received
the President's assent and was later brought into force on 21 June 2024, vide notification S.O.
2422(E). Although the Act was enacted before the NEET-UG 2024 controversy, it was brought
into force amid heightened public concern over paper leaks and examination malpractice,
including controversies such as NEET-UG 2024, which had shaken public confidence in the
integrity of competitive examinations.
The Act applies to examinations conducted by public examination authorities listed in its
Schedule, covering bodies such as the UPSC, SSC, Railway Recruitment Boards, banking
recruitment agencies, and the National Testing Agency. It defines "unfair means" broadly to
include the leakage of a question paper or answer key, colluding with others to effect such
leakage, and unauthorised access to or possession of a question paper or an Optical Mark
Recognition sheet, along with related acts done for monetary or wrongful gain.
On punishment, the Act distinguishes between individuals, service providers, and organised
crime. A person resorting to unfair means or committing offences under the Act may be
punished with imprisonment of not less than three years, extendable to five years, and a fine
up to ten lakh rupees. The penalties become far heavier for organised crime. Where a person
or group of persons, including an examination authority, service provider, or any other
institution, commits an organised crime, the punishment is imprisonment of not less than five
years, extendable to ten years, with a fine of not less than one crore rupees. If an institution is
involved in such an organised crime, its property is subject to attachment and forfeiture, anda
proportionate cost of the examination is recovered from it. The Act also declares offences under
it to be cognizable, non-bailable and non-compoundable.
A key protective feature is that a candidate is not liable for action under the Act and continues
to be governed by the existing administrative provisions of the concerned public examination

organisers of malpractice. Significantly, the Act is also intended to function as a model law: it
serves as a model draft that States may adopt at their discretion to prevent criminal elements

For default in payment of fines, additional imprisonment is imposed under the Bharatiya

passages.LEG-P0144: International Humanitarian Law (IHL), also referred to as the law of armed conflict or the law of war, consists of rules intended to limit the effects of armed conflict for humanitarian reasons. Rather than determining whether a war itself is lawful, IHL regulates conduct during armed conflict and seeks to balance military necessity with humanitarian considerations. Its primary objectives are to protect persons who are not, or are no longer, participating in hostilities and to restrict methods and means of warfare that cause unnecessary suffering. IHL principally applies during international and non-international armed conflicts. Among its most fundamental principles is the principle of distinction, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Attacks may lawfully be directed only against military objectives. Civilian persons and civilian objects, such as schools, hospitals, and homes, cannot ordinarily be targeted merely because incidental military advantage may arise from their destruction. Closely related is the principle of proportionality, which prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. This principle does not prohibit all civilian casualties; rather, it seeks to prevent disproportionate harm. Even where a legitimate military objective exists, military operations must not impose excessive burdens on civilians. The principle of military necessity permits only those measures necessary to achieve a legitimate military objective and not otherwise prohibited by international law. However, military necessity does not override all humanitarian obligations. Certain weapons and practices remain prohibited because they cause unnecessary suffering or fail to distinguish between military and civilian targets. Thus, military convenience cannot justify every action during war. Another important principle is humanity, which prohibits means and methods of warfare causing superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering. Torture, cruel treatment, collective punishment, and attacks directed primarily to spread terror among civilians are generally prohibited. Persons who are wounded, detained, or otherwise hors de combat (out of combat) are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of nationality or allegiance. The law also recognises the protection of medical personnel and humanitarian workers. Hospitals and medical units generally enjoy special protection because they serve humanitarian functions. However, such protection may cease if these facilities are used, outside their humanitarian purpose, for acts harmful to the enemy, though reasonable warning may be required before protection is withdrawn. Violations of serious IHL obligations may amount to war crimes. However, superior orders do not automatically excuse unlawful conduct. Individuals may bear responsibility where they knowingly participate in grave violations of humanitarian norms.
passages.LEG-P0145:
V. A Judge will pronounce a judgment of acquittal or conviction after hearing the arguments of both parties, i.e.,
the prosecution and defense, and on point of law (if any). Considering the character of the offender, the
circumstances of the case, and the nature of the offense, the Judge may decide to release the offender on
probation of good conduct. After conviction, the Judge will hear the accused and then pass a sentence. The
Judge, while passing a sentence, shall try to gather all information that influences or relates to the sentence of
the accused. The accused should be explicitly asked about what he needs to state about his sentence and whether
he wants to give any proof on his side to mitigate his sentence.


The Judge should first pass a sentence of conviction or acquittal. If the accused is convicted, he shall be heard
on the question of sentence, and only then the Court shall proceed to pass a sentence against him. This Section
provides for a bifurcated trial and specifically gives the accused person a right of pre-sentence hearing, which
may not be strictly relevant to or connected with the particular crime under inquiry but may have a bearing on
the choice of the sentence. If an accused is charged with a previous conviction and he does not admit that he has
been previously convicted with the alleged charge, the Judge, after convicting the accused, may call for
evidence of the accused of such previous conviction and shall record findings in case the accused is liable to
enhanced punishment or punishment of a different kind. The proviso to this Section mentions that such charge
shall not be read out by the Judge, nor shall the accused be asked to plead, nor shall the prosecution refer to
such previous conviction.

CrPC provides for a special procedure for determining liability to enhanced punishment as a consequence of
previous conviction. Also, prohibiting the proof of previous conviction to be given until and unless the accused
is convicted, is to prevent the accused from being prejudiced at the trial. It is required for the Court of Sessions
to try the case in accordance with the procedure for the trial of warrant-cases instituted otherwise than on a
police report before a Magistrate Court when it takes cognizance of an offense. A person shall be examined as a
prosecution witness against whom the offense is alleged to have been committed unless the Court of Session
otherwise directs. The Court has to record the reasons for it. Each trial is to be conducted in camera if the Court
thinks or if either of the parties so desires.

Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “Trial Before a Court of Session Under Criminal Procedure
Code”, https://blog.ipleaders.in/trial-before-a-cour-of-session/
passages.LEG-P0146:
XIV. The Supreme Court of India recently expressed grave concern over an emerging and what it
termed an "alarming" trend of lawyers using artificial intelligence tools to draft court petitions
often without adequate verification. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and
Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Joymalya Bagchi made these pointed remarks while hearing a
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by academician Roop Rekha Verma, which sought the
framing of guidelines governing political speeches. Although the PIL itself pertained to a different
subject matter, the bench seized the opportunity to address a pressing concern that had been
surfacing repeatedly in court filings.
"We are alarmed to reflect that some lawyers have started using AI to draft petitions. It is
absolutely uncalled for," the Chief Justice observed, reflecting the judiciary's deepening unease.
Justice Nagarathna recalled encountering a fictitious citation, a case titled "Mercy vs Mankind"
that simply does not exist in any official law report or judicial record. The Chief Justice further
noted that a similar pattern had emerged before Justice Dipankar Datta, where not one but a
series of fabricated judgments had been cited in support of legal arguments, all of which were
found to be entirely non-existent.
The court also flagged a subtler but equally concerning problem: that even where cited judgments
were genuine, petitions sometimes contained fake quotations attributed to those verdicts. This

forces judges to spend additional time verifying the accuracy of each citation creating, as Justice
Nagarathna put it, "an additional burden on the part of the judges." Justice Bagchi added to these
concerns by lamenting the visible decline in the quality of legal drafting, particularly in special
leave petitions (SLPs). He observed that many such petitions are overloaded with lengthy extracts
from previous judgments, leaving little room for original legal reasoning or structured
argumentation a hallmark of skilled advocacy.
The Supreme Court clarified that it does not oppose the use of technology in legal practice
altogether. Indeed, the Court itself has embraced AI for translating judgments into Indian
languages and for case management through machine learning tools. However, it drew a firm line:
technology may assist with research, but it cannot replace the professional responsibility of an
advocate. Every citation, quotation, and legal proposition, the bench stressed, must be verified
against authentic, authorised sources before being placed on record. A lawyer, as an officer of the
court, carries a duty of diligence that no automated tool can discharge on their behalf. Blind
reliance on Al-generated content, the Court indicated, not only misleads the judiciary but strikes
at the very integrity of legal proceedings.
Source: https://www.thehindu.com/news /national /supreme-court-flags-the-risks-of-using-ai-for-
drafting-petitions/article70644488.ece
passages.LEG-P0147: Under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the right of private defence is recognised as a natural right allowing individuals to protect their body and property against unlawful aggression. Sections 96 to 106 provide that an act done in the exercise of this right is not an offence, provided it falls within prescribed limits. The right arises when there is a reasonable apprehension of danger to body or property. It is not necessary that the offence be actually committed; the apprehension itself must be real and immediate. However, the right is preventive and not punitive-it cannot be exercised as retaliation after the danger has ceased. The extent of this right depends on the nature of the threat. In certain circumstances, the right extends to causing death, particularly where the assault reasonably causes apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, kidnapping, or wrongful confinement. However, the force used must be proportionate to the threat perceived. The law imposes clear limitations. The right cannot be exercised against acts done by public servants acting in good faith under colour of office, unless there is reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. Further, the right does not extend to situations where there is sufficient time to seek protection from public authorities.Another important limitation is that the harm caused in private defence must not be more than necessary. If the defender exceeds this limit, the protection is lost, and criminal liability may arise depending on the intention and circumstances. In assessing such cases, courts examine whether the accused acted in good faith, whether the apprehension was reasonable, and whether the response was proportionate. The law thus balances the need for self-preservation with the broader objective of preventing misuse of defensive rights.
passages.LEG-P0148:
XII. The Indian Contract Act, 1872, sharply distinguishes enforceable agreements from speculative bets. A
wagering contract is a promise to pay money upon the determination of an uncertain future event,
where the parties have no genuine interest in the event other than the stake itself. The essence is
mutual chance of gain or loss. Such agreements are expressly void under Indian law; no court will
enforce them, and money lost cannot be legally recovered. Importantly, commercial transactions like
stock market trades are not wagers if the intention is to actually deliver the shares, even if the motive
is speculative profit.www.lawpreptutorial.com
In contrast, a contingent contract is perfectly valid. It is a contract to do or not to do something,
conditional upon the happening or non-happening of a specified future uncertain event. The critical
factor separating it from a wager is the presence of a lawful interest in the event beyond the mere

payment of money. At least one party must be affected by the occurrence or non-occurrence of the event
in a way unrelated to the bet. Insurance is the prime example: the insured has an insurable interest in
the property or life, and the insurer’s obligation to pay arises only if the contingent event (like theft or
death) occurs. Other examples include contracts for sale of goods contingent on import licence approval,
or a promise to pay for a house only if it survives a flood. The enforceability depends on the nature of
the contingency and the parties' underlying interest.
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Surojit Shaw, "A guide to contingent contract and
wagering agreements," Open Legal Blog Archive (21 August 2022), available
at: https://www.openlegalblogarchive.org/2022/08/21/a-guide-to-contingent-contract-and-wagering-
agreements/
passages.LEG-P0149:
XXIV. Extortion and robbery are offences against property, but they differ in their ingredients,
degree of force, and manner of commission. Extortion is dealt with under Section 308 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Section 308 defines extortion as intentionally putting a
person in fear of injury to that person or to any other person, and thereby dishonestly inducing
the person so put in fear to deliver property, valuable security, or anything signed or sealed
which may be converted into valuable security. The essential ingredients of extortion are fear
of injury and delivery of property or valuable security.
The fear of injury may be directed against the victim himself or against any other person. The
threat must be real enough to disturb the mind of the victim and affect the voluntary nature of
his action. Mere threat of divine displeasure is not sufficient to constitute extortion. The fear
may relate to physical injury, injury to reputation, injury to character, or even fear of criminal
prosecution, whether the prosecution threatened is true or false. Where the fear relates to an
accusation of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a
term which may extend to ten years, Section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
provides aggravated punishment. Similarly, where a person is put in fear of death or grievous
hurt, the punishment may extend to ten years and fine. Delivery of property or valuable
security is also necessary for extortion. If a person merely obtains a thumb impression by force
and no property, valuable security, or signed, sealed or authenticated document capable of
being converted into valuable security is delivered, the offence of extortion is not complete.

However, if the victim is induced by fear to sign, seal, authenticate and deliver a blank paper
capable of being converted into valuable security, extortion may be complete. However,
delivery is not limited only to movable property. The terms “deliver” and “delivery” may apply
to both movable and immovable property. Therefore, compelling a person by force or fear to
give up a share in a house or landed property may also amount to extortion. Extortion is
different from theft and cheating. In theft, the property must be movable and is taken without
the consent of the victim. In extortion, the property or valuable security is delivered by the
victim, but such delivery is caused by fear of injury. In cheating, consent is obtained by
deception or fraud. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Under Section 309 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2028, in all robbery there is either theft or
extortion. Theft becomes robbery when, for the purpose of committing theft, while committing
theft, or while carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by theft, the
offender causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death,
instant hurt or instant wrongful restraint. Extortion becomes robbery when the offender is
present before the victim and puts the victim in fear of instant death, instant hurt or instant
wrongful restraint, thereby inducing delivery of the thing extorted. Robbery is punishable with
rigorous imprisonment which may extend to ten years and fine. If robbery is committed on a
highway between sunset and sunrise, imprisonment may extend to fourteen years. Under
Section 310 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, dacoity is committed when five or more
persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit robbery, or when the persons conjointly
committing or attempting robbery together with those present and aiding such commission or
attempt amount to five or more.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from
https: //epgp.inflibnet.ac.in/epgpdata/uploads/epgp_content/S000020LA/P001795/M025761
/ET/ 15137704541 7etext.pdf
passages.LEG-P0150:
XIV. The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013,
commonly known as the POSH Act, provides a comprehensive legal framework to ensure safe working
environments for women. It defines sexual harassment broadly under Section 2(n), encompassing both
physical and non-physical acts. This includes unwelcome physical contact, demands for sexual favors,
making sexually colored remarks, showing pornography, and any other unwelcome conduct of a sexual
nature. Critically, the definition covers not only explicit demands but also the creation of a hostile work
environment. The Act applies to all workplaces, organized and unorganized, in the public and private
sectors, and covers all women employees, whether regular, temporary, ad-hoc, or even apprentices and
trainees.
The Act mandates every employer with ten or more employees to constitute an Internal Complaints
Committee (ICC) at each office or branch. The ICC must have a Presiding Officer (a senior woman
employee), at least two members from amongst employees, and an external member from an NGO or
committed to social causes. The ICC is tasked with receiving complaints, initiating inquiries, and
making recommendations to the employer. For workplaces with fewer than ten employees or when the
complaint is against the employer, the Act provides for the constitution of a Local Complaints
Committee (LCC) by the District Officer. The inquiry process under the Act is confidential and must be
completed within 90 days. The ICC/LCC has the powers of a civil court for gathering evidence. If
allegations are proved, it can recommend actions ranging from a written apology and warning to
deduction of salary, withholding promotion, or even termination of the respondent's service. It can also
recommend that the employer provide counseling or other relief to the aggrieved woman. A key
provision is protection against victimization; the Act prohibits any retaliation against the complainant
or witnesses. A false or malicious complaint, however, can also be penalized. The ultimate objective is

not just redressal but also prevention, requiring employers to organize workshops, sensitization
programs, and display the penal consequences of sexual harassment.
Source: Extracted with revisions & edits from: Ministry of Women and Child Development, "Sexual
Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013," Government of
India (2018), available at: https://wed.nic.in/act/sexual-harassment-women-workplace-prevention-
prohibition-and-redressal-act-2013
passages.LEG-P0151:
XIV. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract of indemnity is a specific and crucial
arrangement defined under Section 124. It is a promise whereby one party, the indemnifier,
undertakes to protect the other, the indemnity holder, from any loss caused either by the
promisor's own conduct or by the conduct of any other person. Like all contracts, it requires
the essential elements of a valid agreement. The core of the contract is the promise to


compensate for a loss, which judicial interpretation has extended to cover losses arising not
only from human conduct but also from events or accidents.
The rights of the indemnity holder are clearly enumerated in Section 125. Once the contingent
event occurs and liability is incurred, the holder is entitled to recover all damages they are
compelled to pay in a relevant lawsuit. Furthermore, they can claim all costs of litigation,
provided they acted prudently or as per the indemnifier's directions. This extends to sums paid
under a prudent compromise of the suit, as long as the compromise did not contravene the
indemnifier's instructions. A critical operational feature is the commencement of liability. The
indemnifier's obligation arises as soon as the loss is sustained, and the holder can sue for
specific performance to be indemnified even before making the actual payment, once their
liability becomes absolute.
It is vital to distinguish indemnity from a contract of guarantee. Indemnity involves only two
parties and features a primary liability for the indemnifier. In contrast, a guarantee involves
three parties (creditor, principal debtor, surety), where the surety's liability is secondary, arising
only upon the principal debtor's default. Essentially, indemnity compensates for a potential
loss, while a guarantee ensures a duty is performed. Indemnity contracts can be express, formed
through written or oral agreement per Section 124, or implied, arising from circumstances like
agency or partnership relations. For enforcement, the indemnity holder possesses the right to
compel the indemnifier to place them in a position to meet the liability without first paying
from their own resources, underpinning the doctrine's role as a pre-emptive shield against
financial risk.
passages.LEG-P0152:
SECTION III
X.	The offences of theft, robbery and extortion come under Chapter XVII of the Indian Penal
Code, under offences Against Property. While they all involve taking property, the way they
happen and the legal elements differ significantly. In theft, the offender takes the moveable
property without the possessor’s consent. The key element is dishonest intention to take
property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent. In extortion, such
consent is wrongfully obtained by putting that person or any other person in the fear of injury.
In case of theft, the question of overpowering of will does not arise because the property is
taken out of the possession without consent, however there is overpowering of will in case of
extortion. Theft can only be committed with regard to moveable property, whereas extortion
can also be committed in case of immovable property. Robbery is an aggravated form of either
theft or extortion. Theft becomes robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in
carrying away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end, voluntarily causes or
attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death or
of instant hurt or of instant wrongful restraint. Extortion becomes robbery if the offender, at
the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits
the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant
wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear, induces
the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted.
Source: "Understanding theft, robbery, and extortion under the Indian Penal Code." Blog,
Published January 9, 2021.
passages.LEG-P0153:
XII. Fraud, as elucidated in Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, implies and involves any of the
acts mentioned below perpetrated by a contracting party or with his involvement or by his agent
with the objective of deceiving or misleading another party or his agent to enter into the
agreement. The acts which constitute fraud under this provision are as follows:- The suggestion, as
a fact, of something which is not true by someone who does not believe in its truth. The active
concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact. A promise without any intent of
carrying it out. Any other act which may mislead the other party. An act or omission which the law
specifically declares to be fraudulent. Mere silence in relation to facts which may influence the
willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud. However, if the circumstances of the
case are such that, having regard to them, it is the duty of the person keeping silent to speak, or
unless his silence, is in itself, equivalent to speech, in such circumstances the silence itself may be
deemed fraudulent. Section 17 explains fraud and mentions the acts that amount to fraud, which
are a false suggestion, active concealment, promise lacking any intention of carrying it out, any
other deceptive act, or any act declared fraudulent. In the English case, Derry vs. Peek (1889), it
was said that, “fraud” is proved when it is shown that a false representation has been made:
Knowingly, or Without belief in its truth, or Recklessly careless whether it be true or false. In
simple terms, “fraud” refers to deliberate deception perpetrated with the intent to induce another
party to act to their detriment. As far as contracts are concerned, fraud can manifest in various
forms such as false representations, concealment of facts, deceptive claims etc.
Source: Extracted with edits from https://blog.ipleaders.in/fraud-in-contracts-section-17-of-the-
indian-contract-act/
passages.LEG-P0154: Constitutional democracies ordinarily distribute governmental authority among different institutions to prevent concentration of power in a single body. This arrangement is reflected in the doctrine of separation of powers, under which legislative bodies generally enact laws, the executive implements and administers them, and the judiciary interprets and applies them. The doctrine does not necessarily require a rigid or absolute division of functions. Modern constitutional systems often permit a degree of overlap because complete separation may be impractical. Nevertheless, the central purpose remains to ensure checks and balances so that no organ exercises uncontrolled power. One of the most significant constitutional mechanisms preserving this balance is judicial review. Judicial review refers to the power of courts to examine the validity of legislative enactments and executive actions and determine whether they conform to constitutional requirements. Courts exercising judicial review do not ordinarily assess whether a law is wise, economically beneficial, or politically desirable. Rather, they examine whether constitutional limitations have been violated. Thus, disagreement with legislative policy is distinct from constitutional invalidity. At the same time, courts generally recognise that elected branches possess institutional competence in certain areas involving policy decisions, economic regulation, allocation of resources, and matters requiring specialised expertise. Therefore, judicial restraint is sometimes considered appropriate where constitutional rights are not directly threatened. However, judicial restraint does not imply judicial abdication. Courts may intervene where governmental actions are arbitrary, violate constitutional guarantees, exceed legal authority, or undermine fundamental rights. The doctrine of checks and balances recognises that constitutional organs may possess limited powers to review or influence one another. Such interaction does not necessarily destroy separation of powers. For instance, executive actions may require legislative approval, legislation may be subject to constitutional scrutiny by courts, and certain appointments or actions may involve more than one branch. Constitutional governance therefore involves both separation and controlled interaction. Another important constitutional principle is the rule of law, which requires that governmental power be exercised according to established legal principles rather than personal discretion or arbitrary preference. Under the rule of law, all individuals and institutions, including public authorities, remain accountable to law. Arbitrary exercises of power are inconsistent with constitutional governance because they undermine predictability, equality, and fairness. Constitutional adjudication also frequently involves balancing majoritarian decision-making and constitutional rights. Democratic institutions ordinarily function according to majority preference. However, constitutional systems recognise that majoritarian support alone cannot justify actions violating fundamental rights. Constitutional guarantees often exist precisely to protect individuals and minority groups from excessive exercises of governmental power.
passages.LEG-P0155:
IX.	India’s space agency, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), initiated the 24-hour countdown
on November 1, 2025, ahead of the scheduled launch of its heaviest communication satellite, CMS-03
(also known as GSAT-7R), marking a major milestone in the nation’s space and defence capabilities.
The satellite, weighing about 4,410 kg, was set to lift off on November 2, 2025 from the Satish Dhawan
Space Centre in Sriharikota, aboard the powerful LVM3-M5 (GSLV-MkIII) heavy-lift rocket. This
mission was intended to provide enhanced multi-band communication services over India and
surrounding oceanic regions, including secure voice, video, and data links critical for military and
strategic operations, especially for the Indian Navy’s maritime communication network.
In pre-launch updates, ISRO confirmed that all final preparations were complete and that “all systems
are GO” as the rocket stood ready at the Second Launch Pad. The mission was also a showcase of
indigenous launch capability, further solidifying India’s self-reliance in deploying heavy satellites from
its own soil.
Source: The Hindu. (2025, November 1). Countdown begins for launch of ISRO’s heaviest
communication satellite CMS-03 for military on November 2.)
passages.LEG-P0156: The right to freedom of religion in India is constitutionally guaranteed under Article 25 of the Constitution of India and Article 26 of the Constitution of India. While both provisions protect religious liberty, they operate in distinct yet overlapping spheres. Article 25 guarantees to all persons the freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion. However, this right is not absolute and is expressly subject to public order, morality, health, and other provisions of Part III. Additionally, the State is empowered to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political, or other secular activity associated with religious practice. Article 26, on the other hand, confers rights specifically upon religious denominations or sections thereof. These include the right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, manage their own affairs in matters of religion, own and acquire property, and administer such property in accordance with law. Like Article 25, these rights are also subject to public order, morality, and health. A crucial doctrinal development in this context is the distinction between essential religious practices and secular or non-essential activities. Courts have consistently held that only those practices which are essential and integral to a religion are protected from State interference. Conversely, activities that are merely associated with religion but are secular in nature such as administration of property or financial management may be regulated by the State. Tensions often arise where the State seeks to intervene in religious institutions on grounds of reform, equality, or public welfare. For instance, legislation aimed at ensuring social reform or opening religious institutions to all sections of society may conflict with denominational autonomy. In such cases, courts undertake a balancing exercise between individual rights under Article 25, group rights under Article 26, and broader constitutional values such as equality and social justice.
passages.LEG-P0157:
XII. Abetment is a foundational concept in criminal law that deals with the culpability of
individuals who, although may not commit the actual offence themselves, play a vital role in
facilitating or provoking its commission. Section 107 defines abetment in three distinct forms.
First, a person abets an offence if he instigates another person to do that act. Instigation
means actively suggesting, encouraging, or provoking someone to commit an offence. Mere
words can amount to instigation if they are intended to incite. Secondly, abetment also occurs
when a person engages in a conspiracy with others for committing an offence, and some act or
illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy. Mere agreement is not enough
unless followed by some act. Thirdly, a person abets by intentionally aiding the doing of an
offence. This includes providing tools, information, or facilitating the offence in any manner.

Under Section 108, an abettor is someone who abets an offence even if the offence is not
committed. Thus, abetment is complete regardless of whether the act is actually done or not.
Section 109 provides that if the abetted act is committed, and there is no specific provision for
punishment of the abettor, then the abettor is liable with the same punishment as the
principal offender.
However, a complex question arises when the act ultimately committed by the principal
offender is different from the one abetted, but is nevertheless a probable consequence of the
abetment. In such cases, the abettor can still be held liable. This principle is supported by
judicial interpretation that if the act done is the probable and natural result of the instigation,
liability attaches. Similarly, when the principal offender acts with a different intention than
what the abettor had intended, the abettor may still be held liable if the eventual act was
reasonably foreseeable. Section 113 provides that when abetment of an offence is combined
with a different intention, the abettor is liable according to the resultant offence committed.
Section 114 provides that if the abettor is present when the offence is committed, his liability
increases and he is treated as if he himself had committed the offence. Sections 115 and 116
deal with the abetment of offences not committed, prescribing punishment even when the
offence was not ultimately carried out, especially in serious offences like those punishable with
death or life imprisonment.www.lawpreptutorial.com
In conclusion, abetment is a substantive offence that punishes those who encourage, plan, or
assist in criminal acts.
Source: Extracted with revisions and edits — from https://blog.ipleaders.in/abetment-ipc/
passages.LEG-P0158:
XX. International criminal law differentiates atrocities not merely by the scale of the violence, but
by the specific intent and context of the acts. Under the Rome Statute of the International
Criminal Court (ICC), the three primary core crimes are Genocide, Crimes Against Humanity,
and War Crimes. While these categories often overlap in armed conflicts, their legal thresholds
remain distinct. The crime of genocide, originally codified in the 1948 Genocide Convention
and mirrored in Article 6 of the Rome Statute, is uniquely defined by dolus specialis-a specific
intent. To constitute genocide, acts such as killing, causing serious bodily harm, or forcibly
transferring children must be committed with the explicit "Intent to destroy, in whole or in
part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such". The destruction of political or
cultural groups does not fall under this strict definition. Crucially, the prosecution must prove
that the victims were targeted primarily because of their membership in one of the four
protected groups, not merely as a byproduct of conflict. Conversely, Crimes Against Humanity
(Article 7 of the Rome Statute) do not require the specific intent to destroy a group. Instead,
acts like murder, torture, deportation, or apartheid must be committed as part of a
"widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population". Unlike war crimes,
crimes against humanity can be prosecuted even if they occur during peacetime or are
committed by a State against its own citizens. The requirement of a "widespread or
systematic" attack ensures that isolated or random acts of violence, however heinous, do not
trigger international jurisdiction. War Crimes (Article 8) are violations of international
humanitarian law, particularly the Geneva Conventions. They are strictly contextual,
meaning they can only occur within an armed conflict, whether international or non-
international. War crimes focus on the unlawful conduct of hostilities-such as intentionally
targeting civilians, attacking hospitals, or torturing prisoners of war-irrespective of whether
the violence aims to destroy a specific ethnic group or is part of a widespread attack.
passages.LEG-P0159: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, contingent contracts are governed by Sections 31 to 36. A contingent contract is a contract to do or not do something depending on the happening or non-happening of an uncertain future event, which must be collateral to the contract. The event should not form part of the reciprocal promises themselves but must be an independent condition upon which performance depends. Such contracts are enforceable only upon the occurrence (or non-occurrence) of the specified event. Where the contract depends on the happening of an event, it cannot be enforced until the event occurs. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Importantly, the impossibility must relate to the specific event contemplated by the parties, and not merely a similar or alternative occurrence. In cases where the contract depends on the non-happening of an event within a fixed time, the contract becomes enforceable when the time expires and the event has not occurred. However, if before the expiry of the specified time, the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes enforceable immediately, as the condition of non-happening is conclusively satisfied. Conversely, where the contract depends on the happening of an event within a fixed time, and such event becomes impossible before the expiry of that time, the contract becomes void immediately. Thus, the law distinguishes carefully between (i) contracts dependent on happening, (ii) contracts dependent on non-happening, and (iii) contracts tied to a specific time frame. A crucial principle is that the event must be construed strictly as agreed between the parties. If the contract specifies the occurrence of a particular event in a particular manner (for example, destruction by fire), the occurrence of a similar result by a different cause (such as demolition) will not satisfy the condition. A wager agreement, governed by Section 30, is an agreement where two parties agree that upon the determination of an uncertain event, one shall win and the other shall lose, and neither party has any interest in that event except the stake. Such agreements are void. The essential elements of a wager include mutual chance of gain and loss, absence of control over the event, and absence of any real or commercial interest in the occurrence of the event. The distinction between a contingent contract and a wager agreement lies primarily in the presence of a legitimate interest. Where a party stands to suffer loss or derive benefit independent of the stake (for instance, due to ownership, business interest, or financial exposure), the agreement is not treated as a wager, even though it may depend on an uncertain event. Courts, therefore, look beyond form and examine the substance of the transaction, particularly whether the uncertain event is merely collateral to a genuine transaction or constitutes the sole basis of the agreement.
passages.LEG-P0160: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. It ordinarily involves three parties: the principal debtor, who is primarily liable for the debt or obligation; the creditor, to whom the obligation is owed; and the surety, who undertakes to discharge the liability if the principal debtor fails to do so. The liability of the surety is generally co- extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided by the contract. This means that the surety may be called upon to satisfy the same obligation that the principal debtor was bound to perform. Unlike ordinary contracts, consideration in a contract of guarantee may consist of any act, promise, or benefit done for the benefit of the principal debtor. It is not necessary that the surety receive direct consideration personally. However, a valid guarantee requires free consent, and if consent is obtained through misrepresentation or concealment of material facts, the guarantee may become invalid. For instance, if the creditor deliberately suppresses information regarding the financial condition or conduct of the principal debtor and such information would have influenced the surety's decision, the guarantee may be affected. Guarantees may be specific or continuing. A specific guarantee applies to a single transaction or obligation and comes to an end once that transaction is completed. A continuing guarantee, however, extends to a series of transactions and remains operative until revoked or otherwise terminated according to law. A continuing guarantee may be revoked by the surety concerning future transactions through notice to the creditor. However, such revocation does not affect transactions that have already occurred before the notice was given. Further, the death of a surety ordinarily operates as revocation of a continuing guarantee with respect to future transactions, unless there exists a contract providing otherwise. The law also recognises certain circumstances under which the surety may be discharged from liability. A surety may be discharged if the creditor and principal debtor enter into a contract varying the terms of the original agreement without the surety's consent, where the creditor releases the principal debtor, or where the creditor acts in a manner impairing the surety's eventual remedies against the principal debtor. Such discharge may occur because the surety agreed to guarantee only a specific obligation and should not be subjected to materially altered risks without consent. After satisfying the debt, the surety acquires certain rights against the principal debtor. This principle, often referred to as subrogation, permits the surety to step into the shoes of the creditor and exercise the rights that the creditor could have exercised against the principal debtor. The surety may also claim indemnification from the principal debtor for amounts rightfully paid under the guarantee.
passages.LEG-P0161:
XV. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is the definitive statute governing intestate succession
for Hindus, including Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs. It establishes a uniform and secular code,
replacing the traditional textual law of the Mitakshara and Dayabhaga schools. Its primary
objective is to systematize the rules of inheritance, bringing clarity and gender justice to the
devolution of property.

The Act's applicability extends to any person who is a Hindu by religion, in any form, including
Virashaivas and Lingayats, and to those belonging to the religions mentioned. A core feature
of the Act is the creation of a statutory hierarchy of heirs, supplanting the traditional sapinda
and gotraja systems. This hierarchy is structured into four tiers: Class I heirs, Class II heirs
(listed in an order of precedence), Agnates, and Cognates. Class I heirs, such as the widow,
mother, son, daughter, and descendants of pre-deceased children, take precedence
simultaneously, excluding all others. Only in their absence do subsequent categories inherit.

Central to the Act's operation is the concept of the coparcenary, a distinct entity within a Joint
Hindu Family comprising a common ancestor and his lineal male descendants within three
generations. The revolutionary 2005 Amendment accorded the daughter the status of a
coparcener by birth, granting her rights and liabilities equal to a son. Coparcenary property
refers to ancestral property in which each coparcener holds an undivided, birthright interest.
This contrasts with separate or self-acquired property, which an individual procures through
personal effort, free from ancestral lineage.

Upon the death of a coparcener, the mechanism of notional partition is invoked. This legal
fiction deems a partition of the coparcenary to have occurred immediately before the member's
death, crystallizing his share. This ascertained share then devolves not by survivorship to the
remaining coparceners, but by testamentary disposition or, in its absence, via intestate
succession under the Act to his own legal heirs. This intricate interplay between the law of
coparcenary and the statutory scheme of heirs ensures a structured and equitable distribution
of a Hindu's estate.
passages.LEG-P0162:
XII. Free Consent under the Indian Contract Act, 1872: Section 14 of the Indian Contract Act,
1872 provides that consent is free only when not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud,
misrepresentation, or mistake. A contract with vitiated consent is either void or voidable
depending on the cause.
Coercion under Section 15 involves threatening to commit an IPC-forbidden act or unlawfully
detaining property to compel a contract. In Chikham Amiraju v. Chikham Seshamma, a threat
to commit suicide was held to constitute coercion. Such contracts are voidable at the option of
the aggrieved party.
Undue influence under Section 16 arises where one party dominates the other's will — through
authority, fiduciary position, or the other's diminished capacity — and uses it to obtain an
unfair advantage. Once dominance is established, the burden shifts to the stronger party to
prove the transaction was not unconscionable.
Fraud under Section 17 requires a knowingly false representation made to deceive. Mere
silence is not fraud unless a duty to speak exists. Fraudulently induced contracts are voidable
and additionally ground a damages claim.
Misrepresentation under Section 18 is an honest but false assertion of fact that induces the
contract. No intent to deceive is required. Such contracts are voidable but do not independently
give rise to damages. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Under Section 20, a bilateral mistake of fact essential to the agreement renders the contract
void. A unilateral mistake under Section 22 does not ordinarily affect validity. Mistake of law
under Section 21 is no ground for avoidance.
Source: Extracted with revisions and modifications from:
K.D. Gaur, Textbook on Indian Contract Law; and relevant case law including Chikham
Amiraju v. Chikham Seshamma (1917).
passages.LEG-P0163: The law of tort recognises that a person may not always be held liable for damage merely because harm has occurred. Certain circumstances may excuse liability where the defendant demonstrates that the event occurred despite the exercise of reasonable care and caution. Two closely related yet distinct concepts in this regard are inevitable accident and Act of God (Vis Major). Although both may relieve a defendant from liability, they differ in their origin and legal requirements. An inevitable accident refers to an occurrence which could not have been prevented despite the exercise of reasonable care, caution, and skill by the defendant. The central inquiry is not whether the event caused damage, but whether a reasonable and prudent person exercising ordinary care could have avoided it. The event may arise from human conduct, mechanical failure, or unforeseen circumstances. However, the defendant cannot rely upon inevitable accident where negligence, omission, or lack of proper precautions contributed to the occurrence. Thus, a person who fails to inspect equipment, ignores warning signs, or neglects ordinary safety measures cannot later claim that the accident was inevitable. An Act of God, on the other hand, is a natural event arising exclusively from forces of nature that are so extraordinary and unforeseeable that no amount of human foresight or reasonable care could prevent the resulting damage. Examples may include unprecedented floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or violent natural disturbances. The natural event must operate independently of human intervention and must be so unusual that it could not reasonably have been anticipated. Ordinary seasonal rainfall, predictable weather conditions, or recurring natural events generally do not qualify merely because they cause harm. The distinction between these principles becomes important where natural events and human conduct combine. If a natural event merely contributes to the damage but human negligence substantially contributes to the loss, liability may still arise. Conversely, where the defendant exercised reasonable care and the damage was solely attributable to an extraordinary natural force, the defence of Act of God may succeed. The burden generally lies upon the defendant to establish facts supporting these defences. Further, where a defendant voluntarily undertakes a hazardous activity or introduces potentially dangerous things into their control, courts may closely examine whether reasonable precautions proportionate to the risk were adopted.
passages.LEG-P0164:
XXII. Fresh reports suggesting that six of the nine Lok Sabha MPs belonging to the Shiv Sena
(Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) may switch allegiance to the rival Shiv Sena faction led by
Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde have once again brought India’s anti-
defection law into focus. The development raises an important constitutional question: can
MPs who break away from their party avoid disqualification when a mere “split” is no longer
recognised as a valid defence under the Constitution? Amid the speculation, Shiv Sena (UBT)
has reportedly approached the Lok Sabha Speaker, urging that no separate faction be
recognised without taking the party’s official position into account.
The anti-defection law is contained in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India. It was
inserted to prevent elected legislators from changing political loyalty after being elected on a
party ticket. Paragraph 2(1)(a) of the Tenth Schedule provides that a member of a House may
be disqualified if he voluntarily gives up the membership of the political party on whose ticket
he was elected. Paragraph 2(1)(b) provides that a member may be disqualified if he votes or
abstains from voting in the House contrary to any direction issued by his political party, or by
any person or authority authorised by that party. Under Paragraph 2(1)(b), disqualification
may be avoided if the member had obtained prior permission from the political party before
voting or abstaining contrary to its direction. Paragraph 2(1)(b) also protects a member where
the political party condones such voting or abstention within fifteen days from the date of such
voting or abstention. Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule provides a defence based on merger.
Disqualification does not apply where the original political party merges with another political
party and not less than two-thirds of the members of the legislature party agree to such

merger. Paragraph 4 also protects members who do not accept the merger and choose to
function as a separate group, provided the requirements of merger under the Tenth Schedule
are satisfied. Before 2003, Paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule protected a “split” in a political
party if at least one-third of the legislators broke away. However, Paragraph 3 was deleted by
the Ninety-first Constitutional Amendment, which came into effect on January 1, 2004. After
the deletion of Paragraph 3, a split is no longer a constitutional defence to anti-defection
proceedings. The recognised defence is merger under Paragraph 4, subject to fulfilment of its
conditions. In Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya, the Supreme Court held that a
member may be treated as having voluntarily given up membership even without formally
resigning from the party. Such an inference may be drawn from the conduct of the member. In
Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that
the Speaker must determine which faction represents the real political party by examining the
party constitution, rules and leadership structure. The decision cannot be based only on
legislative majority. The Court also clarified that the legislature party does not have an
independent existence separate from the political party. Therefore, the political party has
primacy over the legislature party under the Tenth Schedule.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from
https://indianexpress.com/article/explained /explained-law/shiv-sena-ubt-anti-defection-law-
rebel-mp-disqualification-10747654/
passages.LEG-P0165:
XIX. The inheritance rights of children born from void or voidable marriages are mainly governed
by the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Under the Hindu
Marriage Act, Section 5 prescribes the conditions for a Hindu marriage and Section 7 deals
with ceremonies for solemnisation. Only the specific grounds stated in Sections 11 and 12
render a marriage void or voidable. Earlier, children born from such marriages suffered
serious legal and social disadvantages. However, Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act was
introduced to protect such children from the stigma of illegitimacy.
Section 16(1) provides that a child born from a void marriage shall be treated as legitimate,
even though the marriage itself is null and void. Section 16(2) similarly protects a child born
from a voidable marriage, where a decree of nullity has been passed. Thus, the law separates
the invalidity of the marriage from the status of the child. The child is not penalised merely
because the marriage of the parents is void or voidable.
However, Section 16(3) places an important limitation on property rights. It provides that such
legitimacy shall not confer upon the child any right in or to the property of any person other

than the parents. Therefore, a child from a void or voidable marriage can claim inheritance
only in the property of the parents and not in the property of any other relative.
The question then arose whether the expression “property of the parents” includes only self-
acquired property or also the parents’ share in ancestral or coparcenary property. In
Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun, the Supreme Court clarified that children born from void or
voidable marriages are entitled to inherit the property of their parents, whether self-acquired
or ancestral. The Court observed that Section 16(3) uses the word “property” broadly and does
not restrict it only to self-acquired property.
At the same time, the Supreme Court clarified that such children do not become coparceners
by birth in the Hindu Undivided Family. They cannot claim an independent right in the
coparcenary property as other coparceners may do. Their right is limited to the share that
would fall to their parent upon partition. Once that share is determined, it becomes the
property of the parent, and the child can inherit from that property.
This position balances two principles. First, the law protects innocent children from
discrimination and gives them legitimacy under Section 16. Secondly, it protects the rights of
other coparceners by ensuring that such children do not acquire rights in the property of
persons other than their parents. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The constitutional basis for this approach can also be linked with Article 39(f), which directs
that children should be given opportunities to develop in dignity, and Article 300A, which
protects property rights from deprivation except by authority of law. Thus, the present legal
position is that children from void or voidable marriages are legitimate and can inherit the
property of their parents, including the parents’ share in ancestral property, but they cannot
claim coparcenary rights by birth or inherit the property of other relatives.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://ijcrt.org/papers/IJCRT2311547.pdf
passages.LEG-P0166:
XV. The Supreme Court of India, on January 16, 2026, strongly criticised the growing and increasingly
common tendency among litigants to directly invoke Article 32 of the Constitution even in cases
where proceedings on the very same issue are already pending before a High Court. A bench
comprising Justice B.V. Nagarathna and Justice Ujjal Bhuyan took serious note of this practice
while hearing a writ petition filed under Article 32, despite the fact that an identical or
substantially similar plea was already under active consideration before the Bombay High Court.
The bench termed the petition a "gross misuse of the process of the court and of law" and
dismissed it without entertaining it on merits.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Expressing its displeasure in pointed terms, the bench observed that Article 32 was being invoked
with alarming frequency and for increasingly trivial reasons. The Court noted that litigants were
approaching the Supreme Court at even the slightest pretext — including the mere grant of an
adjournment in a High Court — rather than allowing those proceedings to reach their natural
conclusion. "Article 32 is being misused. The number of cases filed under Article 32 is
exponentially increasing. For everything, one adjournment, file Article 32 here. Especially those
surrounding Delhi are filing Article 82 petitions. What is this? It is a misuse," the bench
remarked, reflecting both frustration and constitutional concern.
Article 32 of the Constitution, which confers upon every citizen the fundamental right to approach
the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of their fundamental rights, is regarded as one of
the most important and cherished provisions in the constitutional framework. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
had famously described it as the "heart and soul of the Constitution." However, the apex court has
consistently held that this extraordinary remedy is not meant to be treated as a routine or first
resort. It is intended to be invoked only when there is a clear and demonstrated violation of
fundamental rights that warrants the direct intervention of the Supreme Court, and not as a
shortcut to bypass High Courts that are already seized of the same matter.
The Court reiterated that the appropriate constitutional remedy available before High Courts
under Article 226 — which confers a wide and expansive writ jurisdiction — must be exhausted or
at least genuinely engaged with, before a litigant seeks to invoke the Supreme Court's jurisdiction
under Article 32. By dismissing the petition, the bench sent a firm and unambiguous signal
against forum shopping and the casual erosion of the judicial hierarchy that such practices
inevitably bring about.
Source: https://lawtrend.in/supreme-court-slams-misuse-of-article-32-petitions-dismisses-plea-
filed-despite-pending-high-court-case/
passages.LEG-P0167:
XIV. Ina landmark constitutional development, the Indian Supreme Court, in MK. Ranjitsinh &
Ors. v. Union of India & Ors. (2024), recognized protection from climate change as a
fundamental right under Articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution, linking the right to life and
equality with environmental integrity. Initially concerning the endangered Great Indian
Bustard, the case expanded to address India's broader constitutional obligations to safeguard
human life, health, and equality in the context of climate change. The judgment builds upon
precedents such as Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1994) and M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath
(2000), but establishes a distinct constitutional right against climate degradation, emphasizing
the disproportionate impact on vulnerable populations including the poor, indigenous
communities, and women. The Court highlighted India's statutory framework, ranging from
the Environment Protection Act, 1986 to the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, and
constitutional directives under Articles 48A and 51A(g), underscoring the duty of the State and
citizens to protect the environment. International jurisprudence informed the reasoning,
including India's obligations under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate
Change (UNFCCC) and pronouncements by UN treaty bodies affirming that failure to mitigate
climate harm constitutes a human rights violation. Comparative references include the Dutch
Urgenda case (2015) and Held v. State (Montana, 2023), illustrating global recognition of the
right to a clean, healthful environment as an extension of human rights. The judgment
foregrounds the intersection of climate change and social justice, noting that inadequate access
to clean energy exacerbates gender inequality and health risks, particularly in rural India. By
framing environmental protection as integral to human dignity, the Court reinforces that
sustainable development, climate resilience, and clean air are inseparable from the right to

life. As observed by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, and echoed by UN Secretary-General
Anténio Guterres, safeguarding the environment is central to realizing human rights and
justice in the 21st century. This ruling situates India within a global movement recognizing
environmental protection as a fundamental human right, demanding urgent, rights-based
climate action.
Source: Extracted with edits from the case report on M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. v. Union of India &
Ors. (2024) in livelaw.in
passages.LEG-P0168:
XIII. Under the Hindu Marriage Act of 1955, the ancient sacrament of marriage is structured
within a precise legal framework. The conditions for a valid union are strict. It mandates
monogamy, rendering any subsequent marriage void. Both parties must possess the mental
capacity for valid consent and must have reached the legal age of eighteen for the bride and
twenty-one for the groom. Furthermore, the parties must not fall within the prohibited degrees
of relationship, unless permitted by custom, and cannot be sapindas—a term denoting closeness
through lineal descent or blood relation—again, unless a recognized custom allows it.
The solemnization requires customary rites and ceremonies. For many, the essential ritual is
Saptapadi, the taking of seven steps before the sacred fire. Registration, while strongly
encouraged as definitive proof, does not itself validate a marriage. The Act recognizes diverse
regional and community practices, granting legal validity to any ceremony proven to be
ancient, certain, and reasonable. For inter-religious couples or those seeking a secular
ceremony, the Special Marriage Act, 1954, provides a civil alternative. This law operates
independently of religious rites, involving a notice period and solemnization before a Marriage
Officer.


Matrimonial remedies offer avenues for redress. A marriage is void if it breaches fundamental
conditions like bigamy or sapinda rules. It is voidable for reasons such as impotency, unsound
mind, or consent obtained by force or fraud, requiring a court decree for annulment. Divorce
can be sought on specific grounds including adultery, cruelty, desertion for a continuous period
of two years, conversion to another religion, incurable unsound mind, a virulent form of leprosy
or venereal disease, renunciation of the world, or presumption of death. A simpler, non-
adversarial path is divorce by mutual consent, available after one year of separation.
Alternatives to dissolution include judicial separation, which suspends cohabitation duties
without ending the marriage, and restitution of conjugal rights, a decree to resume married life.
Throughout proceedings, courts provide critical relief. This includes alimony pendente lite for
