interim support and permanent maintenance after decree. In all decisions affecting children,
the custody and welfare of the child remains the paramount consideration for the court,
ensuring protection amidst familial breakdown. This comprehensive system balances
traditional sanctity with contemporary legal safeguards.
passages.LEG-P0169:
III. A contract is deemed complete when there is an offer and its acceptance, along with the fulfillment of other basic
requirements such as free consent, lawful consideration, and competency. However, a contract can terminate before
finality between the promisor and promisee if certain stipulations are fulfilled, known as revocation.


Revocation is the act of annulment. Section 5 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, stipulates that a contract can be revoked
any time before the communication of acceptance is made to the proposer. Once acceptance is communicated, the contract
cannot be revoked. Section 6 lays down the methods by which a revocation of a proposal can be made, and this article
elaborates on these methodologies prescribed by the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
One method is the revocation of a proposal by communication of notice, where a proposal may be revoked by the
proposer by giving notice to the offeree before it is accepted. Another method is revocation by lapse of time. If there is a
time period prescribed for acceptance, the proposal gets revoked if the acceptance is not communicated before the expiry
of the prescribed time period.
A proposal can also be revoked if the condition precedent to acceptance is not fulfilled. If the offeree fails to comply with
certain conditions before acceptance of the proposal, the proposal can revoke the offer. Death or insanity of the proposer is
another method by which a proposal can be revoked, if the fact of his death or insanity comes into the knowledge of the
offeree before the communication of acceptance.
Other methods include rejection of the proposal, death of the offeree, making a counter offer, acceptance not being made
in the mode prescribed, subsequent illegality or destruction of the subject matter of a proposal. For instance, a proposal is
revoked if a counter offer is made to it, and the acceptance of the counter offer amounts to rejection of the original offer.
Contracts are considered closed when the acceptance is communicated, and revocation has an overriding effect over the
accepted principles of communication of proposal and acceptance of proposal. The courts sometimes interfere in such
cases by modifying the contract between the parties, but it is not their duty to make the contracts for the parties. The
interpretation of law involved often leads to courts being asked to examine the validity of the revocation of a proposal,
emphasizing that revocation is a statutorily provided right of both parties.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “How revocation of proposal is made”,
https://blog.ipleaders.in/revocation-proposal-made/
passages.LEG-P0170:
X.	Under Section 2(a) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a proposal is made when one person signifies
to another his willingness to do or abstain from doing something with a view to obtaining the
other’s assent. A proposal must be definite, specific, communicated, and made with the intention of
acceptance. Once accepted, it becomes a promise and creates binding obligations; if not accepted,
no contract arises.
An invitation to offer is a preliminary communication inviting negotiations and does not create
legal obligations. Advertisements, price lists, catalogues, shop displays, and invitations to tender
are classic examples. Courts have consistently held that such communications are not offers but
invitations to treat, as seen in Pharmaceutical Products of India Ltd. v. Gwalior Chemical Works
Ltd., Fisher v. Bell, Mohanlal v. Kashiram, Harvela Investments Ltd. v. Royal Trust Co. of
Canada, and Harvey v. Facey.
Intention to create a legal relationship is an essential element of a valid contract. While
commercial agreements generally presume such intention, social or domestic arrangements do not.
In Balfour v. Balfour, a domestic promise lacked legal intention, whereas in Merritt v. Merritt, a
written agreement between separated spouses showed clear intent and consideration, making it
enforceable.
Communication of offer is necessary. In Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt, the court reiterated that
acceptance can be by performance of the required act, provided the offer is known.
Offers may be cross offers (Tinn v. Hoffman), counter-offers (Hyde v. Wrench), specific or general
(Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.). Offers may also be standing, open, or continuing, as explained
in Bengal Coal Co. v. Homee Wadia & Co. and Rajendra Kumar v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
These principles collectively govern proposal and acceptance under contract law. [Indian Contract
Act- Proposal; Word Count: 284]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://thelegalschool.in/blog/section-2-indian-
contract-act
passages.LEG-P0171:
XII. The Supreme Court’s judgment in J&K Economic Reconstruction Agency v. Rash Builders
India Private Limited revisited the distinction between the “seat” and “venue” of arbitration
and clarified how this distinction determines the supervisory jurisdiction of courts under the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The dispute arose from infrastructure contracts
executed in Jammu and Kashmir between the Jammu and Kashmir Economic Reconstruction
Agency (JKERA) and Rash Builders India Pvt. Ltd. After disagreements concerning
contractual claims, arbitration proceedings were initiated.
Initially, the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir appointed a sole arbitrator. Subsequently, by
an order dated 26 March 2016, the arbitral tribunal recorded that, with the consent of both
parties, Srinagar would be the “seat” of arbitration while New Delhi would merely function as
the “venue” for conducting hearings. The proceedings were later conducted in New Delhi for
convenience, and the arbitral award was also pronounced there.
After the award was delivered, JKERA filed a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act before the Jammu and Kashmir High Court seeking to challenge the award.
However, the High Court returned the petition on the ground that since hearings were

conducted and the award was rendered in New Delhi, courts in Delhi alone possessed
jurisdiction. JKERA challenged this conclusion before the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court observed that arbitration law consistently recognizes a distinction
between “seat” and “venue.” According to the Court, the seat of arbitration constitutes the
juridical home of the arbitration and determines which court exercises supervisory jurisdiction
over arbitral proceedings. The venue, by contrast, is merely a geographically convenient place
where hearings may be conducted. Therefore, the mere fact that hearings occur or an award is
delivered at a particular location does not automatically transfer jurisdiction to courts situated
there.
The Court emphasized that once parties expressly designate a seat of arbitration, courts at
that place alone possess exclusive jurisdiction over arbitration-related proceedings, including
challenges to arbitral awards. Such designation operates similarly to an exclusive jurisdiction
clause in commercial contracts. The Court further held that the seat remains fixed and
immutable unless the parties expressly agree to alter it later. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Applying these principles, the Supreme Court held that Srinagar remained the juridical seat
because the parties had expressly agreed to it. The Court rejected the respondent’s argument
that the award mentioning New Delhi as the “place of arbitration” changed the seat. According
to the Court, stray recitals in an arbitral award cannot override the express agreement of
parties. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and restored
JKERA’s Section 34 proceedings before the Jammu and Kashmir High Court. The judgment
reaffirmed party autonomy, certainty in arbitral procedure, and the central importance of the
juridical seat in determining court jurisdiction.
Source: https://www.verdictum.in/supreme-court /jk-economic-reconstruction-agency-v-rash-
builders-india-private-limited-2026-insc-368-seat-venue-arbitration- 1612216
passages.LEG-P0172:
XI.	Meaningful progress in reducing urban traffic congestion cannot be achieved within the current
fragmented model of municipal transport planning, in which infrastructure investment decisions
are made independently by dozens of separate local councils within each metropolitan region. The
reason is that this model creates strong incentives for each council to minimise infrastructure
expenditure within its own boundaries while directing commuter flows toward neighbouring
jurisdictions, thereby shifting the effective cost of managing peak-hour congestion onto adjacent
councils or the regional government. That is precisely the pattern demonstrated by the various
transport decentralisation experiments of the 2000s: relieve congestion on one arterial corridor and
an equally severe bottleneck emerges elsewhere. For example, when one inner-city council invested
in expanded bus rapid transit capacity, peak-hour vehicle flows simply shifted to parallel arterial
roads managed by the neighbouring council.
passages.LEG-P0173:
X. The foundational legal maxim Nemo Iudex In Causa Sua, which holds that no person shall
be a judge in their own cause, constitutes a cardinal principle of natural justice and a bedrock
requirement for the rule of law. Its primary imperative is to secure impartial adjudication, but
its profound utility lies in its equal commitment to safeguarding the perception of fairness,
thereby maintaining public confidence in the judicial system. The principle operates not merely
to root out actual bias but to eliminate any reasonable suspicion thereof, recognizing that justice
must be seen to be done.

The application of this rule encompasses several distinct yet interrelated doctrines. Bias is
categorized as either actual, requiring direct proof of prejudice, or apparent, governed by the
pervasive “reasonable suspicion” test. This objective test inquires whether a fair-minded and
informed observer, apprised of all relevant circumstances, would perceive a real possibility of
bias. Grounds giving rise to such a suspicion are well-established and include any financial or
proprietary interest in the outcome, however minimal; personal relationships suggesting
friendship or animosity; prior involvement in the same matter as an advocate or investigator;
and institutional biases where a decision-maker has pre-judged the issue. The maxim’s reach
extends beyond the traditional judiciary to all public decision-makers, including administrative
tribunals and regulators, where prior public advocacy for a specific outcome may vitiate
impartiality.

To operationalize the principle, legal systems have developed rules for judicial recusal or
disqualification, whereby a judge must—or may be required to—step aside from proceedings.
Importantly, the right to an unbiased tribunal can be waived by a party provided such waiver
is informed and unequivocal. Ultimately, this maxim is not a mere procedural technicality but
a constitutive element of a legitimate legal order. It assures citizens that decisions affecting
their rights are made by neutral arbiters, free from personal interest or preconception. In so
doing, Nemo Iudex In Causa Sua fortifies the very edifice of the rule of law, ensuring that
confidence in the system’s integrity remains unshaken.
passages.LEG-P0174:
XIII. The law of torts provides justifications or defences which, when successfully pleaded,
can absolve or mitigate a defendant’s liability, balancing the plaintiff’s right to compensation
against equitable exceptions. A foundational defence is Volenti Non Fit Injuria, which asserts
that one who voluntarily and knowingly assumes a risk cannot subsequently complain of the
harm. This applies to clear scenarios like participating in a contact sport, but courts scrutinise
the voluntariness and adequacy of consent, especially in employer-employee relationships.

Closely related is Contributory Negligence, where the plaintiff’s own failure to take reasonable
care for their safety contributes to the damage. Historically, this was a complete bar to recovery.
However, in India, through judicial evolution and statutory amendments like the Motor
Vehicles Act, courts now apportion liability using the principle of comparative negligence,
awarding damages reduced by the plaintiff’s share of fault.

Certain events negate human agency altogether. An Act of God (vis major) refers to an
overwhelming natural cause without human intervention, like an unprecedented flood, while
Inevitable Accident denotes an unexpected event despite all reasonable precautions. Both
defences succeed by proving the harm was unforeseeable and unavoidable. Justificatory
defences include the Right of Private Defence, permitting reasonable force to protect one’s


person or property from imminent threat, and Necessity, which excuses an act causing lesser
harm to prevent a greater, imminent danger—key distinctions being the source of the threat
and the absence of fault in necessity.

A complete defence is Statutory Authority, where the act complained of is expressly permitted
by law. Conversely, Mistake, whether of fact or law, is generally not a defence in tort, as
liability often hinges on the act itself, not the defendant’s subjective intent. Finally, the
procedural defence of Limitation is critical; a suit must be filed within the prescribed period
(typically one to three years from the date the wrong is discovered). Failure to do so
extinguishes the remedy, regardless of the merit of the claim, underscoring the law’s interest in
finality and diligence.
passages.LEG-P0175:
XI.	In the landmark judgment of State of UP v. Ajmal Beg, the Supreme Court of India expressed
grave concern over the "institutionalized evil" of dowry, which persists despite legal prohibitions.
The Bench observed that dowry has morphed from a voluntary practice intended for a woman's
financial independence into a mechanism for material extraction. The Court emphasized that this
practice is fundamentally at odds with the constitutional values of justice, liberty, and fraternity,
directly violating Article 14’s guarantee of equality by treating women as sources of financial gain.
The case involved the dowry death of a 20-year-old woman, married for just over a year, who was
subjected to persistent demands for a motorcycle, electronics, and cash. While the Allahabad High
Court had previously acquitted the accused—reasoning that their poverty made such demands
improbable—the Supreme Court set aside this acquittal. The Bench clarified that the Dowry
Prohibition Act makes no distinction between demands made before or after marriage and
asserted that financial status does not negate the probability of dowry harassment. Consequently,
the conviction of the husband and his mother was restored, though the Court refrained from
incarcerating the 94-year-old mother-in-law due to her age.
Significantly, the Court noted that dowry is a systemic issue prevalent across all religions in the
subcontinent. It observed that in some communities, dowry has been adopted alongside nominal
religious gifts like mehr, hollowing out the original protective purpose of such customs. To address
this social conditioning, the Court issued a series of directives, including:
Incorporating constitutional values of equality into educational curricula.
Ensuring the effective appointment and visibility of Dowry Prohibition Officers.
Sensitizing police and judicial officers to the psychological dimensions of dowry cases.
Expediting long-pending trials under Sections 304B (dowry death) and 498A (cruelty) of the IPC.
Ultimately, the Court underscored that true independence necessitates social transformation,
urging authorities to eradicate entrenched customs that undermine the dignity and financial
security of women.
Source: Extracted with edits and revision from Bar and Bench , Dowry prevailing under guise of
gifts: Supreme Court issues slew of directions to tighten law enforcement
passages.LEG-P0176:
XVI. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026 was introduced in
Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026 by Arjun Ram Meghwal, the Minister of Law, during a special
parliamentary session. It targeted Articles 81, 82, and 334A of the Constitution, addressing
two long-pending issues: the expansion of the Lok Sabha and the operationalisation of
women's reservation.
The Bill proposed that the maximum number of seats in Lok Sabha will be increased from 550
to 850, with up to 815 members from States and 35 from Union Territories. Equally
significant, it sought to amend the constitutional provision that the allocation of seats to states
in Lok Sabha will be based on the 1971 census, until the first census after 2026. Instead, the
Bill authorised Parliament to pass a law to determine when delimitation will be undertaken,
and which census will be used. Through the companion Delimitation Bill, 2026, the latest
published census — effectively the 2011 census — would govern the next delimitation.
The Bill's second principal object was to fast-track women's reservation. The 106th
Constitutional Amendment, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam): Providing 33%
reservation for women in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, came into force on 16th April 2026.
However, its actual implementation is deferred because Article 334A links it to a delimitation
exercise after the next Census (post-2027), making it unlikely to take effect before around

2034. The 131st Amendment Bill sought to delink reservation from the post-2026 census so
that the women's quota could become effective from the 2029 general elections.
The redistributive effect of using the 2011 census would be considerable. As PRS noted, Tamil
Nadu's seats will come down from 39 to 32, and Kerala from 20 to 15. Uttar Pradesh will see
an increase from 80 to 89, Bihar from 40 to 46, and Rajasthan from 25 to 30. This sparked
sharp federal concerns from southern states about diminished representation despite better
demographic performance. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The Bill ultimately failed. On 17th April 2026, with 298 votes in favour and 230 votes against
the bill, it secured a simple majority but fell short of the special majority required under
Article 368. The Opposition Leaders argued the Bill was an attack on the Constitution because
it linked women's rights to a controversial delimitation process that could alter India's
political structure. Its defeat leaves the women's quota tied to the post-2026 census timeline
and reopens the larger question of how India will balance population-based representation
with federal equity.
Source: https://prsindia.org/billtrack/the-constitution-131st-amendment-bill-2026
passages.LEG-P0177:
X.	The resignation of Justice Verma became a notable event in India’s judicial history and
sparked widespread debate on judicial accountability. Justice Verma, a senior judge of the
higher judiciary, resigned following allegations of misconduct that raised concerns about
ethical standards in the judiciary. The controversy led to strong public and institutional
scrutiny, with demands for transparency and a fair inquiry process.
The episode highlighted the challenge of balancing judicial independence with accountability
mechanisms. While internal procedures were initiated to examine the allegations, the case
exposed gaps in how complaints against judges are handled. Justice Verma’s resignation was
seen as an important moment that prevented a deeper institutional crisis but also left behind
questions about reform.
Overall, the incident became a reference point in discussions on strengthening judicial ethics
and ensuring public trust in the justice system.
passages.LEG-P0178:
XII. Muslim Succession Law in India remains primarily uncodified, deriving its authoritative
principles from religious texts: the Quran, the traditions of the Prophet (Hadith), and the
interpretative jurisprudence developed by different schools. The two major branches, Sunni
and Shia, have distinct legal frameworks, leading to variations in application while sharing core
concepts. The system is characterized by its mathematical precision and the classification of
heirs into hierarchical categories, balancing fixed divine entitlements with customary tribal
notions of agnatic succession.
The foundational element is the scheme of Fixed Shares (Quranic Heirs/Sharers). Specific
relatives are allotted ordained fractional portions of the estate. Key sharers include the spouse
(1/4 or 1/8), parents (1/6 each), and daughters (1/2 or 2/3 collectively). These shares are
calculated first. The remaining estate, if any, constitutes the residue. This residue devolves to


the Residuaries (Asabat), typically male agnatic relatives like sons, brothers, and uncles, who
inherit per capita after the sharers are satisfied. If no residuary exists, the residue may revert to
the sharers. In the absence of both sharers and residuaries, inheritance may pass to Distant
Kindred—blood relations not classified as sharers or residuaries, such as maternal siblings or
grandchildren.
A critical distinction lies in the Sunni vs. Shia rules. Sunni law prioritizes the principle of
exclusion, where a nearer relative excludes a more remote one. Shia law, conversely, follows
the principle of representation, allowing a descendant to step into the shoes of a predeceased
parent, granting inheritance rights to grandchildren. Furthermore, Shia law gives stronger rights
to uterine relations and the maternal side. Testamentary freedom is circumscribed. Through
Wasiyyat (a will), a Muslim can bequeath only up to one-third of their net estate to non-legal
heirs. Any bequest exceeding this fraction, or to a legal heir, is invalid unless the other legal
heirs consent after the testator's death. This restriction ensures the ordained shares of the
Quranic heirs are protected, embodying a blend of discretionary charity and mandatory
distributive justice within the Islamic law of inheritance.
passages.LEG-P0179:
XI.	General defences in tort law are legal principles that allow a defendant to escape liability for a
tortious act. These defences operate to protect the defendant’s legal rights where liability would
otherwise arise. While the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the tort, the defendant may avoid
liability by successfully establishing a recognised defence. The purpose of these defences is to
maintain a fair balance between the rights of the plaintiff and the defendant and to ensure that
liability is not imposed where the defendant’s conduct was justified or beyond their control.
The application of general defences depends entirely on the facts and circumstances of each case. A
defendant must clearly show that their actions fall within the scope of a particular defence. The
major general defences include volenti non fit injuria, plaintiff the wrongdoer, inevitable accident,
act of God, private defence, mistake, necessity, and statutory authority.
Volenti non fit injuria is based on consent, meaning that a person who knowingly and voluntarily
assumes a risk cannot later complain of injury arising from that risk. The defence of volenti non fit
injuria does not apply in rescue situations. The defence of plaintiff the wrongdoer, expressed in the
maxim ex turpi causa non oritur actio, bars a claim where the plaintiff's own wrongful conduct
substantially contributed to the harm. Inevitable accident applies where harm occurs despite all
reasonable care and was not foreseeable, whereas act of God refers to harm caused solely by
natural forces beyond human control.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Private defence justifies reasonable force used to protect person or property, but excessive or
unjustified force negates the defence. Mistake, even if made in good faith, is generally not a
defence in tort. Necessity allows limited interference with rights to prevent greater harm but is
narrowly applied. Statutory authority protects acts expressly or impliedly authorised by law,
though negligence in execution may still attract liability. [General Defences under Tort Law; Word
Count: 312]

torts-an-overview/
passages.LEG-P0180:
XII. The Indian Succession Act, 1925 primarily aims to consolidate the law applicable to intestate
and testamentary succession and to create clarity in situations where property devolves after
death. It mainly applies to Christians, Parsis, and persons governed by the Special Marriage
Act in certain cases. It generally does not apply to Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists, Sikhs, and
Jainas, except where specifically provided, as seen from provisions such as Sections 4, 29 and
58. Section 2 defines important terms such as will, executor, administrator, codicil and
probate. A will is the legal declaration of the intention of a testator regarding distribution of
property after death, while probate is a certified copy of a will granted by a competent court.
Domicile under Sections 4 to 19 plays a critical role in determining which law governs
succession, especially where property is located across different jurisdictions. Section 5
provides that succession to immovable property in India is governed by Indian law, while
succession to movable property is governed by the law of the domicile of the deceased. The Act
recognises domicile of origin, domicile of choice and declared domicile. It also states that a
person can have only one domicile, the domicile of origin continues until a new one is acquired,
a minor’s domicile follows that of the parent, and a married woman acquires the domicile of
her husband. Sections 20 to 22 further clarify that marriage does not automatically create
proprietary interest in the property of a spouse.
The Act also provides rules on consanguinity and kindred under Sections 23 to 28.
Consanguinity means relationship between persons descended from a common ancestor and
may be lineal or collateral. There is no distinction between paternal and maternal relations or
full blood and half blood, and posthumous children are included. Intestate succession under
Sections 29 to 49 applies where a person dies without a valid will. Property generally devolves
upon the spouse, lineal descendants and kindred. A widow gets one-third where lineal
descendants exist, one-half where only kindred exist, and the whole property where no
kindred exists. A husband has the same rights in the wife’s property.
For Parsis, Sections 50 to 56 create a separate scheme where property is divided among widow
or widower, children, parents and next-of-kin. Testamentary succession deals with wills.

Under Section 59, any major person of sound mind can make a will. A will made by fraud,
coercion or undue influence is invalid under Section 61. Section 63 requires signature by the
testator and attestation by two witnesses. Privileged wills may be made by soldiers, airmen
and mariners with relaxed formalities. Probate, letters of administration and succession
certificates under later provisions regulate estate administration and recovery of debts and
securities.
[Family Law-The Indian Succession Act, 1925; Word Count: 434]

1925/
passages.LEG-P0181:
X. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 (MWPSC Act)
provides a crucial legal shield for India's elderly, aiming to protect their dignity and well-
being. At its heart, the Act legally obligates children and relatives (who are legal heirs) to
provide financial maintenance to senior citizens (persons over 60) who are unable to
support themselves. To enforce this, the Act establishes specialised Maintenance Tribunals
at the sub-divisional level, offering a speedy and accessible forum for redressal. A
particularly potent provision of the Act safeguards the property rights of senior citizens. It
allows a senior citizen to revoke a property transfer, such as a gift deed made to a child or
relative, if the recipient fails to provide for their basic needs and physical amenities.
However, judicial interpretation has added a crucial layer to this power. In cases like
Debashish Mukherjee v. Sanjib Mukherjee, courts have held that such a revocation is only
possible if the original gift deed explicitly contains a clause or condition obligating the
recipient to maintain the senior citizen. A simple, unconditional gift cannot be revoked


under this Act, even if the recipient later neglects the donor. While the Act is a welfare
legislation, it has its limitations. For instance, the definition of "children" does not include
a son-in-law or daughter-in-law, and the maximum maintenance amount is capped at a
potentially insufficient ₹10,000. Furthermore, Section 17 of the Act controversially bars
legal representation in Tribunal proceedings. However, in a significant trend, High Courts
have read down this provision, holding that Section 30 of the Advocates Act, 1961, which
guarantees a lawyer's right to practice in all tribunals, supersedes this bar, thus allowing
for legal representation.

XVI. Unlawful Assembly under the IPC: The Constitution of India guarantees the right to
assemble peacefully and without arms under Article 19(1)(b). However, this right is not
absolute and Article 19(8) of the Constitution allows the government to impose reasonable
restrictions on the right to assemble in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, or
public order. These restrictions can include limits on the number of people who can gather, the
time and place of assembly, and the use of weapons or other dangerous objects.
Unlawful Assembly means an assembly of five or more persons with the intent to commit an
illegal act or to execute a lawful act through unlawful means. Section 141 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (IPC) deals with unlawful assembly. Whereas Section 189 of Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) deals with the same. The members of an unlawful assembly must have a
common object which falls under any of the following categories:
e To overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central or any State
Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the
exercise of the lawful power of such public servant.
e To resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process.
e Tocommit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offense.
e By means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to any person, to take or obtain
possession of any property, or to deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, or
of the use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or
to enforce any right or supposed right.
e By means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to compel any person to do what he is
not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do.

passages.LEG-P0183:
X. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a bailment creates a relationship of trust and specific
reciprocal obligations. While the bailee’s duty of care is paramount, the law concomitantly
imposes several critical duties on the bailor to ensure fairness and facilitate the purpose of the
bailment. Primarily, the bailor has a duty to disclose faults in the goods bailed, a obligation
detailed in Section 150. This duty varies significantly based on the nature of the bailment. In
a gratuitous bailment (for the sole benefit of the bailee), the bailor is bound to disclose only
known faults that could expose the bailee to an “extraordinary risk.” Conversely, in a non-
gratuitous or reward-based bailment, the standard is stricter; the bailor is liable for any defect,
whether known or unknown, which materially interferes with the intended use of the goods,
effectively implying a warranty of fitness.

Furthermore, the bailor bears financial responsibilities. As per Section 158, in a gratuitous
bailment, the bailor must repay the bailee all necessary expenses incurred for preserving or
protecting the bailed goods. This ensures the bailee is not out of pocket for acting in the
bailor’s interest. A more profound duty arises from the bailor’s title to the goods. Section 164
stipulates that if the bailor has no valid title to the goods and the bailee consequently suffers a
loss—such as being compelled to deliver the goods to the true owner—the bailor is under a
duty to indemnify the bailee for such loss. This protects an innocent bailee from the
consequences of the bailor’s defective ownership.

Finally, the bailment relationship concludes with the duty to receive back the goods upon the
fulfilment of its purpose or the expiry of its term, as implied under Section 164. A refusal to
accept the returned goods would unjustly extend the bailee’s liability and possession. Thus,


the bailor’s duties—ranging from disclosure and indemnity to acceptance—form an essential
framework that supports the bailee’s performance and upholds the equitable foundations of
the contract of bailment.
passages.LEG-P0184:
XIV. The idea of making a constitution for India did not emerge in one day. It took several years of
thinking and deliberation of the nation-makers. The leaders from the different parts of the
country had their own way of reforming the society against various kinds of societal conditions
that they were exposed to. They were also motivated by the various reformative ideologies that
had started in the international arena, such as the idea of socialism due to the Russian
revolution, the idea of ‘liberty, equality and fraternity’ from the French revolution, the practice
of parliamentary democracy persisting in Britain, etc. However, rather than simply imitating
these ideologies in the Indian context, the leaders questioned whether they will be suited to
India considering the wide diversity of people and their different ways of lives.
The need for making the Indian Constitution has stemmed from various historical, social, and
political factors. Some of the reasons are set out as follows:-
e End of British colonial rule- India was under British colonial rule for nearly 200 years.
When the national independence movement started gaining momentum, the need for a
constitution became necessary to establish a new governance framework that was not
dictated by the colonial powers.
e Unity in diversity- India is a vast country with diverse cultures, religions, languages, and
traditions. A constitution was needed to provide a common legal framework that could
accommodate this vast diversity while simultaneously ensuring unity and harmony among
its people.
e Protection of fundamental rights- One of the primary objectives of the Indian Constitution
was to safeguard the fundamental rights of its citizens. These rights include the right to
equality, freedom of speech and expression, right to life and liberty, etc. A constitution was
essential to enshrine these rights and protect them from any arbitrary encroachment by
the state.
e Establishment of a democracy- India chose to be a democratic republic after gaining
independence. Thus, to establish the principles of democracy, including free and fair
elections, separation of powers, rule of law, and checks and balances among the branches of
government, a constitution was necessary.
e Social justice and equality- It is undeniable that Indian society has always been plagued by
centuries of social discrimination based on caste, gender, and religion. The constitution was
aimed at promoting social justice and equality by outlawing discrimination, promoting
affirmative action through reservations for marginalised communities, and ensuring equal
opportunities for all citizens.
e Governance framework- The constitution provides the framework for governance by
defining the structure of the government, its powers, functions, and responsibilities. It
establishes the institutions of government, such as the legislature, executive, and judiciary,
and delineates their roles and relationships.
e Adoption of a federal system- India opted for a federal system of government where the
powers are divided between the central government and the states. The Indian

Constitution delineates this division of powers between the centre and states, as well as
the mechanisms for resolving any disputes between them.
e International recognition- A constitution was necessary for India to be recognized as a
sovereign nation in the international community and provide a legal basis for it to enter
into treaties, agreements, and diplomatic relations with other countries.
e Historical context- The struggle for independence from British rule was also a struggle for
self-determination and self-governance. Drafting a constitution was a crucial step in
realising the aspirations of the Indian people for freedom, equality, and justice.
In essence, the Indian Constitution was needed to lay down the foundational principles and
values of the newly independent nation and to provide a roadmap for its governance,
development, and progress.
Source: https://blog.ipleaders.in/making-constitution-india-detailed-analysis/#Introduction
passages.LEG-P0185:
IV. In cases of contracts, the parties themselves carve out their rights and liabilities, and it is the Indian Contract
Act that legally enforces such contracts. To effectively follow the principle of ubi Jus ibi remedium, i.e., where
there is a right, there is a remedy, the Indian Contract Act is read with the Specific Relief Act, 1963, for
remedying cases of breach of contract. In the general case of breach of contract, the person aggrieved claims the
relief of specific performance of the contract under Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act and claims
compensation under Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, alternatively or additionally. It is clear from Section
39 that a person aggrieved by an anticipatory breach of contract can either repudiate the contract or continue the
contract. If the person repudiates the contract, he will be entitled to be compensated for his loss under Section
75 of the Indian Contract. If the aggrieved party elects to continue the contract, they will become entitled to be
compensated for damages caused due to an anticipatory breach. Even if the aggrieved party allows the other
party to perform subsequently, they are entitled to compensation for any prior breaches and have no liability to
pay for the period of non-performance.
In cases of anticipatory breach where the aggrieved party elects to repudiate the contract, they are also obligated
to restore any benefits made to them till the date of repudiation under Section 64 of the Act. This includes
compensation for all performance made before the breach. If the aggrieved person elects to continue the
contract, they must compensate the breaching party for their actual performance up to the date of breach and
any continued performance thereafter. In the case of specific performance, it was held that a person guilty of


anticipatory breach cannot claim specific performance, as it is mandatory to prove readiness and willingness on
the part of the plaintiff under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act. The aggrieved party cannot claim specific
performance if it chooses to repudiate the contract but can sue for damages. If the aggrieved party chooses to
keep the contract alive and proves readiness and willingness to perform, they can claim specific performance.
Generally, a suit is filed in such cases; however, in special cases against government authorities, the High
Courts can also exercise their jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. For instance, when a
public authority, not being in a position to deliver as per the contract, demands full payment from the purchaser,
the High Court may invoke Article 226 to address the anticipatory breach.

https://blog.ipleaders.in/anticipatory-breach-of-contract/

XV. The doctrine of Absolute Liability is a seminal judicial innovation in Indian tort law,
established by the Supreme Court in the landmark 1987 case of M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India.
This ruling was delivered in the wake of the Oleum gas leak from a Delhi-based unit of Shriram
Food and Fertilizers, an incident that occurred shortly after the catastrophic Bhopal Gas
Tragedy. Recognizing the inadequacy of existing principles, the Court, under Justice Bhagwati,
consciously created a new rule distinct from the English rule of strict liability (Rylands v.
Fletcher). The Court reasoned that the old doctrine, with its numerous exceptions, was
insufficient to address the grave risks posed by modern, profit-driven hazardous industries. The
underlying rationale is that an enterprise which engages in inherently dangerous activity for
economic gain must bear the social responsibility for any harm caused, treating compensation
as a necessary cost of its business operations.
This new principle is critically distinguished from strict liability on two key grounds. First,
while strict liability requires the "escape" of a dangerous thing from the defendant's land,
absolute liability applies even if the harm occurs within the enterprise's premises, such as to
workers or visitors. Second, and most significantly, strict liability admits several exceptions
like Act of God, plaintiff's fault, or act of a third party. Absolute liability admits no exceptions
whatsoever, making the enterprise liable regardless of any supervening circumstance or fault.
As a corollary, the Court integrated the "Polluter Pays" principle, mandating that the offending
enterprise must bear the cost of remediating the damaged environment in addition to
compensating human victims.
In scope and application, the doctrine covers industries like chemical plants, fertilizer units,
nuclear installations, and hazardous waste facilities. The types of harm encompass death,
personal injury, property damage, and environmental degradation. A defining characteristic is
that no traditional defences are admissible; the defendant cannot plead that it took all
reasonable care, that the harm was caused by an Act of God or sabotage, or that the victim was
contributorily negligent. This makes absolute liability the most stringent standard, placing an
unwavering duty of safety on hazardous enterprises.
passages.LEG-P0187:
XV. Within the framework of contract law, the provision of remedies serves to address the consequences
of a breach, aiming to restore justice to the aggrieved party. The primary and most common remedy is


an award of damages, or monetary compensation. The foundational principle is to protect the innocent
party’s expectation interest—to place them, financially, in the position they would have occupied had
the contract been fully performed. Courts may alternatively award damages based on the reliance
interest (covering wasted expenditure) or the restitution interest (reclaiming a benefit conferred). This
compensation is not unlimited; it is constrained by the rules of remoteness, established in Hadley v
Baxendale, which limits recovery to losses arising naturally from the breach or those within the parties’
contemplation. Furthermore, the claimant has a duty to mitigate their loss, and damages must be proven
with reasonable certainty.
Where damages are deemed an inadequate remedy, equitable remedies may be sought. Specific
performance is a discretionary court order compelling the defaulting party to execute their precise
contractual obligations. It is typically reserved for contracts concerning unique assets, such as land or
rare goods, where monetary compensation cannot substitute the promised performance. Similarly, an
injunction—another discretionary order—commands a party to refrain from a particular action, such as
breaching a negative covenant within the contract. Crucially, both remedies are granted at the court’s
discretion and are not available as of right.
It is essential to distinguish these breach-related remedies from rescission. While not a remedy for
breach per se, rescission is available for vitiating factors like misrepresentation or undue influence. It
operates to set the contract aside ab initio (from the beginning), aiming for restitution and a return of
both parties to their pre-contractual positions. Thus, the landscape of contract remedies offers a tailored
response, from compensatory financial awards to coercive equitable orders, ensuring redress is both
practical and just in light of the breach’s nature and the subject matter of the agreement.
passages.LEG-P0188:
LEGAL REASONING

I. Article 131 of the Constitution of India provides that the Supreme Court shall have exclusive and original
jurisdiction in any dispute: The intention of the Constitution makers is that such disputes should not be
subjected to several tiers of the judicial hierarchy, but should come, for once and for all, before the highest court
of the land.
(a) between the Government of India and one or more States;
(b) between Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other;
(c) between two or more States if and in so far as the dispute involves any question (whether of law or fact) on
which the existence or extent of a legal right depends.
The dispute between the Union of India and the State cannot but be a dispute which arises out of the difference
between the Government in office at the Centre and the Government in office in the State. But there is a further
prerequisite which narrows down the ambit of the class of disputes which fall within Article 131. That
requirement is that the dispute must involve a question whether of law or fact, on which the existence or extent
of a legal right depends. It is this qualification which contains the true guide for determining whether a
particular dispute is comprehended within Art. 131. Mere wrangles between Governments have no place in the
scheme of that Article. The purpose of Art. 131 is to afford a forum for the resolution of disputes which depend
for their decision on the existence or extent of a legal right. The intention of the Constitution makers is that such
disputes should not be subjected to several tiers of the judicial hierarchy, but should come, for once and for all,
before the highest court of the land. It is only when a legal, not a mere political, issue arises touching upon the
existence or extent of a legal right that Article 131 is attracted.
In the case of Tashi Delek Gaming Solutions Ltd v State of Karnataka, the lottery agents of the States Sikkim
and Meghalaya challenged the banning of lottery games by the State of Karnataka. The Karnataka High Court
held that this dispute held the legal rights of all the three States; hence, the remedy will be under article 131
only. But the Supreme Court held otherwise and said that these agents were given the right to represent the State
Governments and hence, were private parties, thus, not coming under the jurisdiction of article 131. Such an
agent had the right to sue and be sued in his own name and thus, it would not come under this article 131.
passages.LEG-P0189:
XI. Chapter XII of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) meticulously defines and categorizes
offences against property, forming a critical pillar of India's criminal justice framework. These
provisions protect the rights of ownership and possession by penalizing various unlawful acts
of acquisition, damage, or intrusion. Central to most offences is the element of dishonest
intention—the aim to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss.
The chapter begins with foundational crimes of unlawful acquisition. Theft involves the
dishonest taking of movable property out of another's possession without consent. When this
taking is accomplished by inducing fear through threat or coercion, it becomes Extortion.
Robbery is a more severe aggregation, occurring when either theft or extortion is committed
with the added element of immediate danger, violence, or fear of injury during the act. Its most
aggravated form is Dacoity, defined as robbery committed by five or more persons conjointly.
Beyond forcible taking, the law also addresses dishonest retention. Criminal Misappropriation
occurs when a person dishonestly converts another’s movable property, which came into their


possession innocently, for their own use. Conversely, Criminal Breach of Trust involves the
misappropriation or dishonest use of property entrusted to the offender, violating a specific
fiduciary or contractual duty.
Further offences target deception and damage. Cheating entails fraudulently or dishonestly
deceiving a person to either deliver property or consent to the retention thereof, or to
intentionally induce that person to do something which causes harm. Mischief involves the
intentional causing of wrongful loss or damage to the public or any person by destroying or
diminishing the value or utility of property. Finally, the chapter covers unlawful intrusion
through Trespass, which is simply entering or remaining on another's property unlawfully. Its
aggravated forms involve trespass with intent to commit an offence or for intimidating,
insulting, or annoying the person in possession.
Collectively, these provisions create a graduated legal response, from simple unauthorized
taking to complex breaches of trust and violent group crimes, ensuring a comprehensive
safeguard for property rights in modern society.
passages.LEG-P0190:
XII. Overview of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
Dowry must be distinguished from Stridhan. Stridhan refers to property belonging to the
woman, whereas dowry refers to property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in
connection with marriage. The practice of dowry degenerated into a coercive demand, where
the groom's family expected cash, property, and other valuables as a condition of marriage.
This transformation led to widespread harassment, domestic violence, and even dowry deaths,
ultimately prompting the Indian legislature to enact the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The Act
was designed to curb the menace of dowry by criminalising its giving, taking, and demanding,
thereby providing a legal shield to women against such exploitative practices.
The Act defines dowry under Section 2 as any property or valuable security given or agreed to
be given, directly or indirectly, by one party to a marriage to the other party, or by the parents
or any other person, at or before or after the marriage, in connection with the marriage. This
definition excludes dower or mahr under Muslim personal law. However, Section 3(2) of the
Act provides a limited exception. Presents given at the time of marriage to the bride or the
bridegroom without any demand having been made in that behalf do not constitute dowry,
provided such presents are entered in a list maintained in accordance with the rules made
under the Act, are of a customary nature, and their value is not excessive having regard to the
financial status of the person by whom, or on whose behalf, such presents are given. The

satisfied."
Offences occur when dowry is exchanged, demanded, or not transferred to the bride within
three months of receipt. The Act prescribes strict punishments: under Section 3, imprisonment
of at least five years and a fine of 715,000 or the value of the dowry; Section 4 punishes dowry
demands with imprisonment of not less than six months, extendable up to two years, and fine
up to 710,000; and Section 6 separately punishes failure to transfer dowry to the woman with
imprisonment of not less than six months, extendable up to two years, or fine of %5,000 to
210,000, or both. Offences under this Act are cognizable for specified purposes, non-bailable,
and non-compoundable.www.lptedtech.com
Complaints can be filed after which the police or Dowry Prohibition Officer investigate, gather
evidence, and submit a charge sheet to the magistrate. Cognizance may be taken on the court’s
own knowledge, a police report, or a complaint by the aggrieved person, her parent/relative, or
a recognised welfare institution/organisation. The burden of proof often shifts to the accused in
cases of dowry death, particularly when a woman dies under unnatural circumstances within
seven years of marriage and there is evidence of cruelty or harassment soon before death in
connection with dowry demand. Compared to other laws, this Act focuses on prohibiting dowry
transactions, while the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita retains provisions dealing with cruelty and
dowry death. The Domestic Violence Act, 2005 also complements these laws by providing civil
remedies and protection to victims. Together, they create a strong legal framework, but
societal norms, lack of awareness, and weak enforcement continue to hinder eradication of
dowry, necessitating both legal and cultural reforms.

passages.LEG-P0191:
LEGAL REASONING

I. In a significant judgment, the Supreme Court of India has clarified the legal position regarding the transfer of title of
immovable property. The Court emphasized that the transfer of title cannot be achieved through sale agreements or
general power of attorney (GPA) alone. This decision reinforces the importance of statutory provisions in the transfer of
immovable property, particularly those outlined in the Registration Act, 1908, and the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, play a crucial role in this context. Section 17 mandates the compulsory
registration of certain documents related to immovable property. It specifies the types of documents that require
compulsory registration, ensuring legal sanctity and public record of transactions. Section 49 further strengthens this
requirement by stating that documents requiring compulsory registration, if unregistered, will not affect any immovable
property nor confer any power to adopt. Additionally, such unregistered documents cannot be received as evidence of any
transaction affecting such property. This provision safeguards against fraudulent transactions and ensures clarity in
property titles. Moreover, Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, is pivotal in understanding the legal
framework for the sale of immovable property. This section stipulates that a sale of immovable property can only be made
through a registered instrument. It clarifies that a mere agreement to sell, without proper registration, does not create any
interest or charge on such property. This legal provision is fundamental in ensuring that the transfer of property rights is
not merely based on informal agreements but is backed by a legally recognized and registered document.
The Supreme Court's decision is in line with its earlier judgments, which have consistently held that title in immovable
property can only be transferred through a registered deed. This position is not just a procedural formality but a legal
necessity to maintain clear property titles and avoid disputes. The judgment reiterates that transactions like sale
agreements or GPAs, while they may have some legal recognition, cannot by themselves result in the transfer of title if
they are not accompanied by duly registered conveyance deeds.
This ruling has far-reaching implications, particularly in real estate transactions. It underscores the need for due diligence
and adherence to statutory requirements in property dealings. The judgment serves as a reminder that while sale
agreements and GPAs are common in property transactions, they must be complemented by proper registration to
effectuate a legal transfer of title.


Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “Title Of Immovable Property Can't Be Transferred Through Sale
Agreement Or General Power Of Attorney: Supreme Court”, https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/no-transfer-of-title-of-
immovable-property-through-sale-agreement-or-general-power-of-attorney-supreme-court-242892
passages.LEG-P0192:
XI.	An agreement is a mutual understanding or arrangement between two or more parties. It
represents the meeting of minds where each party agrees to do or not do something.
Agreements can be oral, written, formal, informal, or implied by conduct. Section 2(e) of the
Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines an agreement as “every promise and every set of promises,
forming the consideration for each other.” In simple terms, when one person makes an offer
and the other accepts it, it becomes an agreement. Agreements are flexible in nature and may
be verbal, written, or implied by actions. However, not all agreements are enforceable by law.
For example, a verbal promise between friends to meet, an informal arrangement to share
expenses, or an email exchange regarding meeting details may be agreements, but they may
not create legal consequences.
A contract, on the other hand, is a legally binding agreement that the law recognises and
enforces. Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines a contract as “an agreement
enforceable by law.” A contract creates legal rights and obligations between the parties. If one
party fails to perform their part, the other party may seek legal remedies such as
compensation, specific performance, or cancellation. Examples of contracts include
employment contracts, lease agreements, sale deeds, service agreements and loan agreements.
Thus, every contract is an agreement, but every agreement is not a contract.
For an agreement to become a contract, it must satisfy certain essential elements. There must
be a lawful offer by one party and an unequivocal acceptance by the other. There must be
lawful consideration, meaning something of value such as money, goods, services, or a promise
to do or not do something. The parties must be competent to contract, meaning they must be
major, of sound mind, and not disqualified by law. Their consent must be free and genuine, not
caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake. The object must be
lawful, and the terms must be certain and capable of performance. If any of these essential
elements are absent, the agreement remains unenforceable.www.lawpreptutorial.com
The main difference between agreement and contract lies in legal enforceability. An
agreement is a wider term and may or may not create legal obligations, whereas a contract is a
narrower term and always creates enforceable rights and duties. Agreements may be informal
and may lack consideration, but contracts generally require lawful consideration, free consent,

lawful object and certainty. A simple promise to lend a bicycle may be an agreement, but a
written sale of the bicycle for 75,000 is a contract. Therefore, agreements are suitable for
informal arrangements, while contracts are necessary for transactions involving value,
duration, legal protection and remedies. [Word Count: 449]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://lawbhoomi.com/differences-between-
agreement-and-contract/
passages.LEG-P0193:
XI. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the creation of a bailment imposes a fiduciary-like
relationship upon the bailee, the party receiving the goods, charging them with several specific
and non-delegable duties central to the arrangement’s integrity. The foremost obligation,
encapsulated in Section 151, is the duty to take reasonable care of the bailed goods. The statute
mandates a uniformly high objective standard: the bailee must exercise the same level of care
as “a man of ordinary prudence” would take of his own goods of similar value and nature. This
standard applies irrespective of whether the bailment is gratuitous or for reward, and failure to
meet it results in liability for any loss, damage, or destruction.
Crucially, the bailee’s right to use the goods is strictly circumscribed by the bailment’s purpose.
Section 154 imposes a duty not to make any unauthorized use of the goods. If the bailee uses
the goods in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the bailment, they become absolutely
liable for any loss or damage occurring during such use, even if caused by an accident or
through no apparent fault. This strict liability underscores the contractual sanctity of the
bailment’s agreed purpose. Furthermore, the bailee has a duty not to mix the bailor’s goods
with their own or a third party’s goods without the bailor’s consent (Sections 155-157).
Unauthorized mixing entitles the bailor to claim compensation for any expenses incurred in
separation or, if the goods cannot be separated, for the resultant loss in value.
Upon the accomplishment of the purpose or the expiry of the stipulated time, the bailee’s duty
under Section 160 is to return, or deliver according to the bailor’s directions, the goods without
waiting for any demand. This duty reinforces the temporary and specific-purpose nature of
bailment. Finally, recognizing the bailor’s enduring ownership, Section 163 obligates the bailee
to return or account for any accretion or benefits that may have accrued from the bailed goods
during the period of bailment, such as offspring from animals or profits earned. Collectively,
these statutory duties position the bailee as a responsible custodian, legally bound to protect


the bailor’s proprietary interest and ensure the goods’ safe return, thereby balancing the benefits
derived from possession with rigorous accountability.
passages.LEG-P0194:
XIV. In a landmark development, the Supreme Court of India has held that the right to trauma
care is an integral part of the right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The
ruling, delivered in Save LIFE Foundation v. Union of India by a bench of Justices J.K.
Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar, builds upon an earlier 2025 directive in 8. Rajaseekaran
v. Union of India, where the Court ruled that access to trauma care during the golden hour is
not simply a matter of policy but a constitutional right under Article 21.
The "golden hour" refers to the first 60 minutes after a serious injury—the period when rapid
intervention can be the difference between life and death. The Court observed that a systemic

intervention, creation of a uniform framework for trauma care, building public awareness,
standardization of first aid skills and proper Good Samaritan laws are essential to protect this
right.
This jurisprudence rests on robust precedent. In Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996),
the Court held that denial of emergency care violates Article 21 and directed states to
establish referral protocols, designated hospitals, and budgetary measures, while SaveLIFE
Foundation v. Union of India (2016) gave binding force to Good Samaritan protections,
encouraging bystander assistance.
In its recent directions, the Court ordered all States and Union Territories to operationalise
within three months one helpline number '112' for emergency responses and establish
functional good samaritan grievance redressal system. It further directed that all states and
UTs that have not yet adopted the cashless treatment of road accident victims scheme, 2025 —
PM RAHAT, shall take necessary steps to fully operationalise the said schemes within a
period of three months. The Court also permitted the Centre to issue a medical rescue protocol
for trauma cases within three months, and directed all States and Union Territories to
operationalise the same within three months thereafter.
Emphasising the urgency, the Court noted that in cases of road accidents, every minute
without medical intervention significantly narrows the scope for survival, adding that the
initial response and first aid is perhaps the most crucial stage of care. States were also
directed to furnish periodic compliance reports by organising monthly meetings and uploading
the minutes on the concerned portals.
This evolving framework transforms trauma care from a matter of administrative discretion
into an enforceable fundamental right, reinforcing the State's positive obligation to protect life
through accessible, time-sensitive emergency medical care.

directs-to-integrate-emergency-helplines-into-112-implement-pm-rahat-good-samaritan-scheme-
