passages.LEG-P0196:
XIV. Judicial review of administrative action constitutes the cornerstone of India’s
constitutional framework for ensuring governmental accountability and upholding the rule of
law. As the core mechanism to check administrative excesses, it empowers constitutional courts
to scrutinize the legality, rationality, and procedural propriety of executive decisions. This
supervisory jurisdiction, inherent under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution, is not an appeal
on merits but a review of the decision-making process itself, ensuring that state power is
exercised within defined legal boundaries.

The grounds for such review are well-established. Firstly, jurisdictional error occurs when an
authority acts without jurisdiction, in excess of it, or fails to exercise a jurisdiction it possesses.
Secondly, an error of law apparent on the face of the record allows courts to intervene where a
clear legal flaw is discernible from the order itself, without delving into intricate evidence.
Thirdly, while factual findings are typically respected, courts will intervene in cases of an error
in finding of fact where the conclusion is so perverse that no reasonable person could have
arrived at it, or is based on no evidence whatsoever.

The principles of natural justice—audi alteram partem (hear the other side) and nemo judex in
causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own cause)—form a vital ground. Any decision
violating these foundational tenets of fairness, such as acting with bias or denying a reasonable
hearing, is rendered void. Furthermore, abuse or misuse of discretion is a critical check against
arbitrariness. Discretion must be exercised reasonably, for the purpose granted, without mala
fides, and considering all relevant factors; its misuse on irrelevant grounds or in a manifestly
unfair manner invites judicial correction. Finally, procedural ultra vires ensures that mandatory
statutory procedures are meticulously followed, as their breach invalidates the subsequent
action.

Thus, judicial review operates as an essential democratic safeguard. It balances administrative
efficiency with individual rights, ensuring that public power is exercised in a manner that is
neither beyond authority nor contrary to justice, thereby reinforcing constitutional governance.
passages.LEG-P0197:
XII. Indian law classifies a father’s property into two categories: ancestral property and self-acquired
property. The rights of sons and daughters vary significantly depending on this classification.
Ancestral property is joint family property inherited through four generations of male lineage and
remains undivided. Rights in such property arise by birth and not by succession after death.
A major change was introduced by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which conferred
equal coparcenary rights on daughters, placing them at par with sons. Daughters became
coparceners by birth with equal rights and liabilities, irrespective of marital status. Courts have
clarified that daughters born before 2005 or whose fathers died before the amendment can also
claim rights, provided no valid partition occurred before 20 December 2004. Married daughters
retain full coparcenary rights in ancestral property and can demand partition.
Self-acquired property refers to property acquired by the father through his own efforts or
earnings. During the father’s lifetime, sons and daughters have no rights in such property, and the
father has absolute freedom to transfer it. Rights arise only after the father’s death. If a valid will
exists, property devolves according to the will. In the absence of a will, sons and daughters inherit
equally as Class I heirs under the Hindu Succession Act.

Partition in ancestral property converts joint ownership into individual ownership, after which
each share becomes self-acquired. Adopted children enjoy the same rights as biological children.
Children born from void or voidable marriages can inherit self-acquired property but do not
automatically acquire coparcenary rights. Different personal laws apply to Muslims, Christians,
and Parsis. A father may gift property during his lifetime, subject to statutory requirements.
[Ancestral Property under Family Law; Word Count: 274]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/difference-between-
ancestral-property-and-inherited-property/
passages.LEG-P0198:
XIII. Bailable offences are those offences where the accused has a legal right to be released on bail.
Under BNSS, such offences are specifically marked as bailable in the First Schedule. These
offences are generally treated as less serious, and therefore the accused is not required to
remain in custody till the court conducts an elaborate hearing. The primary feature of a
bailable offence is that the police officer in charge can release the accused on bail after arrest
once the required bond is furnished. There is no need to wait for a court order or a complex
hearing at this stage. These offences usually involve minor harm, limited property loss,
personal disputes, or conduct having low impact on public safety.
The classification of some offences as bailable is based on the idea that unnecessary detention
should be avoided where the alleged act does not involve grave injury, severe consequences,
major threat to public order, or serious social harm. Common examples include simple hurt,
minor trespass, rash or negligent driving, obstruction in public pathways, defamation,
criminal intimidation, minor cheating, mischief causing small loss, falsification of accounts,
negligent acts likely to spread infection, and misconduct in public by intoxicated persons.
Although bailable offences are generally minor, an offence with higher punishment may
sometimes still be classified as bailable due to legislative intent or specific policy
considerations.
Non-bailable offences are more serious offences where the accused does not have a right to
bail. Release from custody depends on the discretion of the court. These offences often involve
serious violence, sexual offences, crimes against children, repeated criminal conduct, major
financial fraud, threat to national security, or significant danger to public order. In such cases,
the court examines the gravity of allegations, the nature of evidence, possibility of the accused
fleeing, past criminal record, risk of influencing witnesses, impact on society or victim, and the
need for proper investigation before granting bail.
The major difference between bailable and non-bailable offences lies in the right to bail and
the authority granting it. In bailable offences, bail is available as a matter of right and may be
granted by the police officer or the court. In non-bailable offences, bail is not a right and only

the court can grant it after judicial scrutiny. Bailable offences involve lower punishment and
limited threat, while non-bailable offences carry higher penalties and serious social impact.
Examples of non-bailable offences include waging war against the Government, counterfeiting
currency, murder, dowry death, abetment of suicide, attempt to murder, trafficking, rape,
robbery, dacoity, serious criminal breach of trust, major cheating, and cruelty against married
women. Courts may also impose conditions such as travel restrictions, regular police
reporting, or surrender of passport while granting bail in non-bailable cases.
[Word Count: 453]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https: //sheokandlegal.com/articles/difference-between-bailable-and-non-bailable-offences-in-
indian-law/
passages.LEG-P0199:
XX. The Delhi High Court’s order upholding the Central Government’s temporary blocking of
Telegram raises an important question under the Information Technology Act, 2000: whether
an entire application or platform can be blocked under Section 69A, or whether only specific
posts, messages, URLs or channels can be targeted. The dispute arose after the Ministry of
Electronics and Information Technology passed an order on June 16 blocking Telegram across
India until June 22 and disabling its message-editing feature until June 30. The order was
linked to concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination, after allegations of paper leaks
and misuse of the platform.
Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 empowers the Central Government to
block public access to information if it is necessary or expedient to do so on specified grounds,
including public order. Telegram argued that the government could have blocked specific
channels or URLs instead of restricting access to the entire app. The Central Government,
however, argued that Section 69A must be read with Section 2(1)(v) of the IT Act, which
defines “information” broadly to include data, message, text, images, sound, voice, codes,
computer programmes, software and databases. On this basis, the government submitted that
an application or platform itself may fall within the meaning of “information”.
The Delhi High Court accepted this interpretation and held that there was no reason to
exclude an application or platform from the ambit of “information” under the Act. This is
significant because the court treated the app’s software and architecture, and not merely its
user-generated content, as something capable of being blocked under Section 69A.

The procedure for blocking is governed by the Information Technology (Procedure and
Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Rule 8 ordinarily
requires a hearing before a blocking order is passed. Rule 9 allows an interim blocking
direction in cases of emergency. In such cases, the Secretary may issue an interim direction
first. The request is then placed before the committee, which gives an opportunity of hearing
and makes its recommendation, after which the Secretary passes the final order approving or
revoking the interim direction.
The court also considered whether the order was proportionate. Applying the four-part
proportionality test from Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, the court accepted the
government’s argument that channel-specific takedowns had been repeatedly ineffective
because mirror channels, bots and backup channels kept reappearing. The temporary duration
of the block was also treated as relevant in deciding that the measure was limited and least
restrictive.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from
https: //indianexpress.com/article/explained/explained-law /delhi-hc-telegram-block-section-
69a-it-act-10750367/
passages.LEG-P0200:
XIV. The 1956 Articles concerning the Law of the Sea were adopted by the International Law
Commission at its eighth session and submitted to the General Assembly as part of the
Commission’s report. The Commission considered that the law of the sea involved legal,
technical, biological, economic and political aspects, and recommended an international
conference to embody the results in conventions or other appropriate instruments. The draft
applies to the law of the sea in time of peace only, and the term “mile” means a nautical mile
of 1,852 metres. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The draft begins with the territorial sea. It states that the sovereignty of a State extends toa
belt of sea adjacent to its coast, called the territorial sea, and also extends to the air space over
it, its bed and subsoil. The Commission recognised that State practice on the breadth of
territorial sea was not uniform, but considered that international law did not permit extension
beyond twelve miles. The breadth was to be measured from the low-water line, subject to
special rules on straight baselines, bays, ports, roadsteads, islands, drying rocks, opposite
coasts, adjacent States and river mouths.

The Articles also recognise the right of innocent passage. Ships of all States may pass through
the territorial sea, but passage remains innocent only when the ship does not commit acts
prejudicial to the security of the coastal State or contrary to international law. Foreign ships
must comply with the coastal State’s transport and navigation laws. No charge may be levied
merely for passage, except for specific services rendered. The coastal State’s criminal and civil
jurisdiction over foreign ships during passage is limited, and warships may be required to give
prior authorisation or notification.
For the high seas, the draft defines them as all parts of the sea not included in the territorial
sea or internal waters. No State may validly subject any part of the high seas to its
sovereignty. Freedoms of the high seas include navigation, fishing, laying submarine cables
and pipelines, and overflight. Ships sail under the flag of one State only, and there must be a
genuine link between the ship and the flag State. The draft further deals with warship
immunity, safety of navigation, duty to render assistance, prevention of slave trade, repression
of piracy, right of visit, hot pursuit, conservation of living resources, submarine cables and
pipelines, contiguous zone control, and continental shelf rights for exploration and exploitation
of natural resources.
[International Law-United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS); Word
Count:405]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from,
hittps://legal.un.org/ilc/texts /instruments/english/draft_articles/8_1_8 2_1956.pdf
passages.LEG-P0201:
XI.	Juvenility is a legal principle that recognises that children and adolescents alleged to have
committed offences require distinct treatment from adults. The reason is that children do not
possess the same maturity, judgment, and sense of responsibility as adults. Under the
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a child means a person who has
not completed eighteen years of age at the time of the offence. The Act recognises two
important categories: a child in conflict with law, meaning a child alleged to have committed
an offence, and a child in need of care and protection, meaning a vulnerable child requiring
safeguarding. The law follows a rehabilitative and reformative approach rather than a purely
punitive one.
The JJ Act, 2015 replaced the earlier 2000 Act and came into force on 15 January 2016. It
aligns Indian juvenile law with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child,
ratified by India on 11 December 1992. The Act prioritises rehabilitation, social reintegration,
child-friendly procedures, and protection from stigma. A major feature is the special provision

for children aged 16 to 18 years alleged to have committed heinous offences. In such cases, the
Juvenile Justice Board conducts a preliminary assessment of the child’s mental and physical
capacity, understanding of consequences, and circumstances of the offence. If required, the
matter may be transferred to a Children’s Court, though safeguards such as separation from
adult offenders continue. The 2021 Amendment further strengthened accountability of Child
Welfare Committees and made certain offences under “Other Offences Against Children” non-
cognizable where punishment ranges between three and seven years.
Section 9(2) of the JJ Act is crucial because it allows a claim of juvenility to be raised at any
stage, even after final disposal of the case. If juvenility is claimed or suspected, the court must
conduct an inquiry, take evidence other than affidavits, and record a finding on age. This
ensures that a person who was a child on the date of offence is not denied the benefit of
juvenile justice merely due to delay.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Judicial decisions have reinforced this principle. In Abuzar Hossain v. State of West Bengal,
the Supreme Court held that juvenility may be raised at any stage and delay cannot defeat the
claim. In Pratap Singh v. State of Jharkhand, the Court held that the relevant date for
determining juvenility is the date of commission of the offence. In Kulai Ibrahim v. State of
Coimbatore, reformative justice was emphasised even in serious cases. Challenges remain in
age determination, overburdened Juvenile Justice Boards, weak rehabilitation infrastructure,
and social stigma. Effective juvenile justice therefore requires education, counselling,
vocational training, community support, and monitoring mechanisms to ensure true
reintegration.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/juvenile-crimes-
india/
passages.LEG-P0202:
LEGAL REASONING

I. Article 22 of the Indian Constitution outlines several rights available to an accused in the case of arrest and
detention. It mandates the duty to inform the accused of the grounds of arrest and to consult a lawyer of choice.
Additionally, it requires the police officer to present the person arrested before a magistrate within twenty-four
hours, ensuring that the individual cannot be detained beyond this period without proper judicial authority.
Under Article 22(1) and Section 41D of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), an accused person has the
right to be consulted and defended by a legal practitioner of their choice. This right is crucial, especially during
interrogation, although it does not extend throughout the entire interrogation process.
The concept of free legal aid is integral to ensuring justice for all, particularly for those who lack the economic
means to engage in legal proceedings. Article 39A of the Constitution, under the Directive Principles of State
Policy, emphasizes the state's duty to ensure justice is accessible to all citizens, thereby mandating the provision
of free legal aid. This is aimed at creating an equitable justice system where economic constraints do not hinder
access to legal recourse.
Section 54(1) of the CrPC grants the accused the right to a full-body medical examination. This examination
can be crucial in providing evidence that may either disprove the commission of an offence by the accused or
implicate someone else. However, this right is subject to the magistrate's discretion, especially if it is perceived
as a tactic to delay proceedings.
The Constitution provides a framework for the protection of individuals against arbitrary arrest and detention.
Article 22 specifically addresses these concerns, ensuring that the rights of the accused are safeguarded during
the legal process. This includes the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, the right to legal
representation, and the right to be presented before a magistrate within a specified timeframe.
An arrested individual must be informed of the reasons for their arrest. This is a fundamental right that ensures
transparency and fairness in the legal process. Additionally, the right to legal representation is critical in
safeguarding the interests of the accused, allowing them access to legal counsel to defend their case effectively.
The provisions related to arrest and detention reflect the overarching principles of justice and fairness embedded
in the Indian legal system. These provisions aim to balance the state's power to detain individuals for legal
transgressions with the fundamental rights of individuals, ensuring that the process of arrest and detention is not
abused and is conducted in a manner that respects the dignity and rights of the accused.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “Arrest of Persons Under CrPC, 1973”,
https://blog.ipleaders.in/arrest-of-a-person/#Protection_against_arrest_and_detention
passages.LEG-P0203:
VII. Copyright, a pivotal aspect of intellectual property law, bestows creators with exclusive rights over their
works. Defined by the Copyright Act, these rights extend to original literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic
works, as well as cinematograph films, sound recordings, and computer programs. The primary objective of
copyright is safeguarding creators from unauthorized reproduction or exploitation of their work.

While copyright grants exclusive rights to creators, it also imposes limitations through concepts like fair
dealing. Fair dealing, a legal doctrine, allows limited use of copyrighted work without the author's permission.
It applies to purposes such as research, private study, criticism, review, and news reporting. Although not
explicitly defined, fair dealing is interpreted by courts based on the circumstances of each case.

Legal provisions for fair dealing are found in international agreements like TRIPS and the Berne Convention,
emphasizing limitations that do not conflict with normal exploitation and do not unreasonably prejudice the
rights holder. In India, Section 52 of the Copyright Act lists standard exceptions or defences to copyright
infringement.

The doctrine of fair dealing is integral to copyright law, originating as a Doctrine of Equity. It permits the use of
copyrighted works that would otherwise be prohibited, fostering growth and creativity. The UK Copyright Act
of 1911 was the first to explicitly recognize fair dealing, providing limitations related to non-commercial
research, private study, criticism, review, and news reporting.

In India, fair dealing is governed by Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957, borrowed extensively from the UK
Copyright law. This section incorporates defences for fair dealing, such as for research, private study, criticism,
review, and reporting current events. The Copyright Amendment Act, 2012, expanded fair use to include
cinematograph films and musical works.
Fair dealing is not precisely defined in the Act but is a legal doctrine allowing limited use without permission.
The determination of whether a use is fair depends on factors like the purpose and character of use, the nature of
the copyrighted work, the amount used, and the effect on the potential market for the work.


In the United States, fair use is a concept incorporated from Justice Story's 1841 judgment, codified in the
Copyright Act of 1976. Section 107 provides for fair use purposes like criticism, comment, news reporting,
teaching, scholarship, or research. The statute outlines four factors to determine fair use: the purpose and
character of use, the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount used, and the effect on the potential market for
the work.

These factors collectively guide courts in deciding whether a particular use qualifies as fair dealing or fair use.
While fair use allows for transformative uses, the impact on the market remains a crucial consideration.
Balancing the rights of creators and users, fair dealing and fair use play crucial roles in ensuring a dynamic yet
legally protected intellectual property landscape.
passages.LEG-P0204:
XI.	Under Sections 11 and 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, persons competent to contract are
those who have attained the age of majority, are of sound mind, and are not disqualified by law. A
person attains majority at 18 years, or 21 years where a court-appointed guardian exists.
Soundness of mind requires the capacity to understand the contract and form a rational judgment
regarding its effect at the time of contracting. Any person disqualified by law, such as minors,
convicts, insolvents, alien enemies, or foreign sovereigns, is incompetent to contract.
A minor, as defined under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, is incapable of contracting. The nature of
a minor’s agreement was conclusively settled in Mohiri Bibi v. Dharmodas Ghosh, where the Privy
Council held that a minor’s agreement is void ab initio. Such an agreement creates no rights or
obligations, Sections 64 and 65 do not apply, and estoppel cannot operate against a minor even if
minority was falsely represented. A minor is generally not liable in contract or in tort arising
directly out of contract, though liability may arise for independent torts.
The doctrine of restitution, now embodied in Section 33 of the Specific Relief Act, empowers courts
to order restoration of benefits received by a minor, either when the minor seeks cancellation of an
instrument or successfully resists enforcement. However, such relief is discretionary and limited to
the extent of benefit actually received. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Certain contracts beneficial to minors are recognised. A minor may enforce a contract of marriage,
though it cannot be enforced against the minor. Apprenticeship contracts are binding under
statute, but contracts of service are not. A minor cannot be a partner, nor can they ratify a void
contract upon attaining majority, unless fresh consideration is provided.
Under Section 68, a minor’s estate is liable for necessaries supplied to them or their dependants,
provided such goods are suitable to their station in life and not already sufficiently supplied. This
liability is quasi-contractual and rests on the minor’s estate, not personal liability.
Persons of unsound mind are governed by Section 12. Capacity depends on mental condition at the
time of contracting. Temporary insanity, drunkenness, or delirium negates capacity, while lucid
intervals permit valid contracts. Finally, persons disqualified by law include alien enemies during
wartime, convicts during sentence, insolvents regarding property, and foreign sovereigns who
enjoy contractual immunity unless jurisdiction is submitted.

L	The Allahabad High Court’s decision in Anamika Tiwari and Others v. State of U.P.
reaffirmed the legal position that a wife is the absolute owner of her streedhan and cannot
ordinarily be prosecuted for criminal breach of trust in relation to property that legally belongs
to her. The dispute arose after matrimonial discord developed between the husband and wife
following their marriage in 2012. The wife had earlier lodged criminal proceedings against her
husband and his family under Sections 498-A and 323 of the Indian Penal Code and provisions
of the Dowry Prohibition Act, alleging harassment and demands for additional dowry.
Subsequently, the husband initiated a counter-complaint alleging that the wife and her
relatives had entered his house and taken away cash, jewellery, and household articles. On
the basis of these allegations, the Magistrate summoned the wife and her relatives for offences
including criminal breach of trust under Section 406 IPC.
While examining the validity of the summoning order, the High Court analysed Sections 405
and 406 IPC dealing with criminal breach of trust. The Court noted that the offence requires
entrustment of property followed by dishonest misappropriation or conversion of that property
by the person entrusted with it. However, the Court held that streedhan — consisting of gifts
and property given to a woman before, during, or after marriage — remains her exclusive
property. Since the wife herself is the absolute owner of such property, the essential
requirement of “entrustment” by the husband or his family could not exist in relation to her
own ornaments and valuables. Consequently, prosecution under Section 406 IPC against the
wife was legally unsustainable.
The Court further clarified that marriage does not transform streedhan into joint marital
property. Although a husband may, in times of financial distress, temporarily use the wife’s
streedhan, such use does not confer ownership or legal control upon him or his relatives. At
best, the husband carries a moral obligation to restore the property or its equivalent value.
The Court also criticised the Magistrate for issuing the summoning order casually without
properly examining whether the statutory ingredients of criminal breach of trust were
satisfied. Since the allegations against the wife’s relatives were similarly vague and general in
nature, the Court ultimately quashed the entire criminal proceedings.
The judgment reaffirmed broader principles repeatedly recognized by Indian courts, including
in Rashmi Kumar v. Mahesh Kumar Bhada, namely that streedhan remains the sole and
exclusive property of a woman and neither the husband nor the in-laws acquire dominion over
it merely because of marriage. The ruling also highlighted the importance of carefully
scrutinizing criminal complaints in matrimonial disputes to ensure that criminal law is not
invoked mechanically without satisfying essential legal ingredients.
Source: https://www.livelaw.in/high-court/allahabad-high-court/allahabad-hc-wife-owner-
streedhan-husband-obligation-restore-quashes-406-ipc-criminal-breach-of-trust-528393

XV. The Supreme Court of India struck down the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI's) banking ban
against cryptocurrencies on March 4, 2020, declaring the directive as disproportionate and not
applicable to any transaction pre or post judgment. A three-judge bench consisting of Justice
Rohinton Fali Nariman, Justice S. Ravindra Bhat, and Justice V. Ramasubramanian quashed
the RBI's April 6, 2018 circular (the "Crypto Circular"), which restricted banks from providing
services to businesses dealing with cryptocurrencies. The Crypto Circular provided that
"Banks shall not deal in Virtual Currencies/Cryptocurrencies ("VCs") or provide services for
facilitating any person or entity in dealing with or settling VCs. Such services include
maintaining accounts, registering, trading, settling, clearing, giving loans against virtual
tokens, accepting them as collateral, opening accounts of exchanges dealing with them and
transfer/receipt of money in accounts relating to purchase/sale of VCs. Banks which already
provide such services shall exit the relationship within three months from the date of this
circular." While imposing the ban, the RBI had stated that VCs raise concerns of consumer
protection, market integrity, and money laundering, among other risks. The Supreme Court
struck down the Crypto Circular on three principal grounds: first, there was no empirical
evidence of any harm caused by VCs or individuals and entities dealing in VCs to the RBI-
regulated entities, including banks, as set out in the Crypto Circular; second, cryptocurrencies
were not currently banned despite several committees proposing regulations and two draft
bills being discussed—the government had not been able to decide on their legality; third, the
ban was not proportionate to the risk sought to be addressed by such prohibition. The

judgment established that regulatory measures must be supported by demonstrable evidence
of harm and must maintain proportionality between the regulatory objective and the means
employed to achieve it.
Source: Internet and Mobile Association of India v. Reserve Bank of India, Writ Petition (Civil)
No. 528 of 2018, Supreme Court of India, March 4, 2020 (commonly known as the RBI
Cryptocurrency Ban case)

XIV. Patent revocation refers to the cancellation of rights granted to a patent holder, after which the
patent is treated as if it never existed. Revocation proceedings may be initiated by any person
interested, the Central Government, or by way of a counterclaim in an infringement suit before
the High Court. The objective of revocation is to prevent unjust monopolies and ensure that only
valid inventions enjoy protection.
Section 64 of the Patents Act, 1970 provides exhaustive grounds for revocation. A patent may be
revoked if the invention was already claimed in an earlier Indian patent, granted to an unentitled
person, or wrongfully obtained from the true inventor. Revocation is also possible where the
subject matter is not an “invention”, lacks novelty or inventive step, was secretly used in India
prior to filing, or is not useful. Insufficient disclosure, failure to disclose the best method, unclear
claims, false suggestions, or misrepresentation also render a patent vulnerable to revocation.
Patents covering non-patentable subject matter under Sections 3 and 4, failure to disclose the
source of biological material, anticipation by traditional knowledge, violation of Section 8 (non-

disclosure of foreign filings), breach of secrecy directions, or fraudulent amendments can equally
lead to revocation.
Apart from Section 64, post-grant opposition under Section 25(2) allows challenges within one year
of grant. Section 65 enables revocation of patents relating to atomic energy, while Section 66
empowers the Government to revoke patents prejudicial to public interest. Section 85 permits
revocation for non-working of patents after grant of a compulsory licence.
Patent revocation is crucial to balance innovation with public interest. It prevents wrongful
monopolies, protects traditional knowledge, ensures affordability and access, and maintains the
integrity of India’s patent system.
[Patent revocation; Word Count: 281]

passages.LEG-P0209:
XII. Vicarious liability, a cornerstone of tort law, operates on the principle that an employer can be held
legally responsible for the wrongful acts of an employee, even when the employer is itself without fault.
This doctrine pivots on two critical, interconnected inquiries: first, whether the tortfeasor stands in a
relationship that can trigger such imputed liability, and second, whether the act in question was
committed within the "course of employment." The latter is the most pivotal and nuanced legal test,
serving as the gateway for attributing liability from the acting employee to the controlling employer.
Determining the "course of employment" is a multifaceted analysis. A foundational principle is that an
employer remains liable for authorized acts done in unauthorized ways. This encompasses situations
where an employee fulfills a core duty but does so negligently or in direct violation of rules. For
instance, a delivery driver causing an accident while on a delivery route is acting within the course of
employment, even if they were speeding—a clear breach of company policy. The violation pertains to
the manner of performing an assigned task, not the task itself. This logic extends to distinguishing
between a mere detour, a minor deviation for which liability persists, and a frolic, a significant personal
departure that suspends liability until the employee resumes their duties. Furthermore, the nature of
prohibited acts is scrutinized. Courts distinguish between conduct rules (e.g., "drive carefully") and
scope rules (e.g., "never use the company vehicle for personal trips"). Violating the former usually
sustains vicarious liability, as the employee is still engaged in the employer's business, albeit poorly.
Violating the latter may take the employee outside the scope entirely.
The application of this test, however, is predicated on establishing the correct relationship. The classic
context is employer-employee, hinging on the employer’s right to control not just the what, but the how,
when, and where of the work. This control distinguishes an employee from an independent contractor,
for whom vicarious liability generally does not attach, as the hirer controls only the end result. Yet,


critical exceptions pierce this general rule. These include non-delegable duties, where a party (like a
hospital or landlord) bears ultimate responsibility for certain safety obligations and cannot insulate itself
by contracting out the work, and inherently dangerous activities, where the principal creates a
foreseeable risk of harm by initiating the work. Additionally, other relationships like partnerships
impose joint liability for torts in the ordinary course of business, and agency law holds principals liable
for agents acting with their authority.
Ultimately, the interplay between defining the employment relationship and scoping its boundaries
allows vicarious liability to serve its core policy goals: ensuring just compensation for victims by
linking them to a solvent defendant, and incentivizing employers to maintain rigorous standards in their
operations, thereby distributing the inevitable risks of enterprise across society as a cost of doing
business.
passages.LEG-P0210:
XIII. Bailment is defined under Section 148 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 as the delivery of
goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when
the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of
the person delivering them. The person delivering the goods is called the bailor, and the
person receiving them is called the bailee. The essence of bailment lies in transfer of
possession without transfer of ownership. Ownership remains with the bailor, while
possession is temporarily transferred to the bailee. Bailment relates only to movable property
and may arise even without a formal contract, as recognised in State of Gujarat v. Menon
Mohammad Haji Hasan.
For a valid bailment, there must be specific movable goods, delivery of goods, change of
possession, delivery for a specific purpose, and an obligation to return or dispose of the goods

as directed by the bailor. Delivery may be actual, symbolic or constructive. Mere custody does
not amount to possession, and therefore does not create bailment. In Indra Kumar v. State of
M.P., luggage placed on the roof of a bus did not create bailment due to lack of entrustment. In
Kaliaperumal Pillai v. Visalakshmi, no bailment was found where there was no effective
delivery. Bailment may be for the benefit of the bailor, bailee, or both, and may be gratuitous
or non-gratuitous.
The bailor is under a duty to disclose known faults in the goods under Section 150, bear
necessary expenses in gratuitous bailment under Section 158, and indemnify the bailee under
Sections 159 and 164. The bailee must take reasonable care under Sections 151 and 152, must
not make unauthorised use of the goods, must not mix the goods without consent, and must
return the goods after the purpose is fulfilled. Cases such as Houghland v. R.R. Low, Rampal
v. Gaurishankar, Shantilal v. Tara Chand, and Union of India v. Amar Singh explain the
standard of reasonable care.
The bailor has the right to terminate bailment, demand restoration of goods, and sue third
parties for damage. The bailee has rights to compensation, delivery according to directions,
and lien. Particular lien is recognised under Section 170, while general lien under Section 171
is available to bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys and policy brokers. A finder of goods is
treated as a bailee under Section 71 and may sell the goods under Section 169 in limited
circumstances. Bailment differs from sale because ownership is not transferred, and differs
from licence because bailment requires delivery and transfer of possession. [Indian Contracts
Act-Contract of Bailment; Word Count: 428]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/bailment-meaning-
introduction/
passages.LEG-P0211:
XIV. Protection of invention refers to the legal mechanism through which an inventor is granted
exclusive rights over their creation, preventing unauthorised making, use, sale, or distribution.
Such protection ensures recognition and financial reward for inventors while promoting innovation
and technological advancement. In India, inventions are primarily protected through patent law,
though trademarks, copyrights, industrial designs, and trade secrets may also apply depending on
the nature of the invention.
Protecting an invention is essential as it encourages innovation by assuring inventors that their
efforts will be safeguarded. Exclusive rights allow inventors to control commercial use, attract
investment, build brand value, and contribute to economic growth. Legal protection also ensures
fair recognition by preventing misuse or copying of original ideas.
Patents are the most effective method of protecting inventions. A patent is a statutory right
granted for a new invention involving an inventive step and industrial applicability, governed by
the Patents Act, 1970. Patent protection generally lasts for 20 years from the filing date. To be
patentable, an invention must be novel, non-obvious, industrially applicable, and not fall within
exclusions under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act.
The patent process involves conducting a prior art search, drafting a provisional or complete
application, filing with the Patent Office, publication, examination, response to objections, and
grant. Post-grant, annual renewal fees are mandatory to maintain validity. Failure to renew may
result in lapse of the patent. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Not all inventions are suitable for patenting. Trade secrets protect confidential business
information as long as secrecy is maintained. Trademarks safeguard brand identity, copyrights
protect creative expression such as software or manuals, and industrial designs protect the
aesthetic features of products under the Designs Act, 2000.
Patents and trade secrets may coexist only for different aspects of the same technology. Once an
invention is disclosed through a patent, it cannot be protected as a trade secret. Courts have
clarified that post-patent trade secret protection for the same disclosed information is
impermissible, though undisclosed ancillary know-how may still be protected.
Patent rights can be enforced through civil remedies such as injunctions and damages, criminal
action in limited cases, customs measures to block infringing imports, and dispute resolution
through litigation or ADR. Government initiatives like SIPP, expedited examination, PPH, and
online filing further strengthen India’s innovation ecosystem and facilitate effective protection of
inventions.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.bajajfinserv.in/types-of-intellectual-
property-protection

SECTION III
X.	The Uniform Civil Code means one country one rule in matters of personal law. Civil Code
covers laws governing personal matters such as marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption,
inheritance, succession and guardianship. Article 44 of the Constitution declares that the
State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of
India. However, Article 44 is placed under the Directive Principles of State Policy and is not
enforceable by courts. The idea is to combine different personal laws into one common law
applicable to all citizens irrespective of religion, race, caste or community. At the same time, it
has been opposed on the ground that it may affect religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26.
India is a secular and diverse country where Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis and other
communities are governed by separate personal laws. Hindus are governed by laws such as
the Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act, Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act and
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, while Muslims are governed by the Shariat
Application Act, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act and other personal law principles. This
lack of uniformity creates difficulties in matters of succession, divorce, inheritance, adoption
and maintenance, and makes it difficult for judges to apply one common standard of justice.
The Uniform Civil Code was debated in the Constituent Assembly. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, K.M.
Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar and others supported it as a step towards national unity,
secularism and social reform. However, due to strong opposition, especially from members
concerned about interference with Muslim personal law, it was placed only as a Directive
Principle. Supporters argued that religion should be separated from social relations and that
personal laws should not obstruct equality.
Uniform Civil Code is also closely linked with gender justice. Personal laws of different
communities have often placed women in an inferior position in matters of marriage, divorce,
maintenance and inheritance. Problems such as polygamy, desertion, cruelty and triple talaq
show how women may suffer under unequal personal laws. A common civil law can help
promote equality between men and women and reduce discrimination.
Goa is often cited as an example because it follows a uniform family law applicable to all
communities. The judiciary has also repeatedly discussed the need for UCC in cases such as
Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, Narasu Appa Mali and Lily Thomas. The Supreme Court has
supported the desirability of UCC, while also recognising that social acceptance and legislative
will are necessary for its implementation. [Constitutional Law-UNIFORM CIVIL CODE; Word
Count: 413]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, htips://thelawwaywithlawyers.com/uniform-
civil-code-in-india-a-constitutional-mandateoraculturalconundrum/

Passage (Q.73-Q.77): An “agent” is a person employed to do any act for another, or to represent another in dealing
        with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the “principal”. The
        contract between Principal and Agent is called ‘Contract of Agency’. Subsequent to the contract, the rights and duties
        of the principal and agent emerge. Authority of an agent can be both express and implied. According to Section 187,
        the authority is said to be express when it is given by words spoken or written. According to Section 187, authority
        is said to be implied when it is to be inferred from the facts and circumstances of the case. In carrying out the work
        of the Principal, the agent can take any legal action. That is, the agent can do any lawful thing necessary to carry out
        the work of the Principal.
        An agency relationship is built on mutual trust: the agent acts on behalf of the principal, and in return the principal
        must treat the agent fairly. The rights and duties of an agent and principal therefore move together. Indian contract
        law recognises that when an agent performs the work of the agency, the agent is generally entitled to be paid. Under
        Section 219, an agent is entitled to receive remuneration. However, Section 220 makes an important limitation: if
        the agent is guilty of misconduct in the business of the agency, the agent is not entitled to any remuneration for that
        part of the business in which the misconduct occurred. Thus, remuneration depends not only on performance, but
        also on proper conduct.
        To secure payment and reimbursement, an agent is also given protective rights. Under Section 221, in the absence
        of a contract to the contrary, an agent has a right of lien. This means the agent may retain the goods, papers, and
        other property of the principal that the agent has received, until the agent’s dues—such as commission,
        disbursements, or charges for services relating to that property—are paid or properly accounted for. The lien is
        therefore a practical safeguard, preventing a principal from taking back the property while leaving the agent unpaid.
        The principal’s responsibility is not limited to payment. Under Section 222, the principal must indemnify the agent
        against the consequences of lawful acts done by the agent in exercise of authority. Indemnity here means that the
        principal must make good the loss suffered by the agent when the agent acts lawfully within the authority given.
        Further, Section 225 protects the agent where harm is caused due to the principal’s fault: the principal must
        compensate the agent for injuries suffered because of the principal’s neglect or want of skill. In short, agency law
        ensures that an agent who acts properly is paid, protected, and reimbursed, while an agent who commits misconduct
        cannot demand reward for the tainted part of the agency work.

XIII. Current: The Telangana High Court recently held that police officers do not have the power
to detain or seize vehicles merely because the driver is found in an intoxicated condition. The
Court emphasised that while drunk driving must be prevented, seizure of the vehicle is not an
automatic or lawful consequence in such cases. The petitioner had approached the High Court
seeking release of his vehicle, which had been seized by traffic police after it was allegedly
driven by a person in an intoxicated condition. The petitioner argued that such seizure was
contrary to the law already laid down by the High Court in earlier decisions. The State
contended that the driver had prior instances of drunk driving and that the petitioner had
knowingly allowed him to use the vehicle. The Court, relying on its earlier 2021 judgment,
held that although the intoxicated person cannot be allowed to drive, the police cannot seize
the vehicle solely on that ground and directed disposal of the petition in line with established
guidelines.

The Court clarified that while traffic laws prohibit driving under the influence of alcohol, they
do not confer unrestricted power upon police authorities to seize or detain vehicles merely
because the driver is intoxicated. The primary objective of the law is to prevent unsafe driving,
not to impose additional punitive measures beyond statutory limits.
The Court laid down that where a driver is found intoxicated, the police must prevent such
person from continuing to drive. If another person accompanying the driver is sober and
possesses a valid driving licence, the vehicle should be handed over to such person. Where no
such person is available, the vehicle may be temporarily kept in safe custody. However, the
police are under a duty to release the vehicle to the owner or an authorised person upon
production of necessary documents such as the registration certificate, identity proof, and a
valid driving licence.
The Court thus balanced enforcement of road safety with protection against arbitrary exercise
of police powers, holding that seizure must be justified by law and not based on mere suspicion
or convenience. It further clarified that prior instances of drunk driving or alleged negligence
by the owner do not, by themselves, confer additional powers of seizure unless specifically
authorised by statute.
Source: https://www.livelaw.in/high-court/telangana-high-court/telangana-high-court-
police-seize-vehicle-driver-intoxicated-529649

II. In India, Article 310 of the Indian Constitution embodies the provision for the doctrine of pleasure.
According to Article 310, except for the provisions provided by the Constitution, a civil servant of the Union
works at the pleasure of the President and a civil servant under a State works at the pleasure of the Governor of
that State. This implies that the operation of the Doctrine of Pleasure can be limited by constitutional provisions.
Under the constitution, the following are excluded from the operation of this doctrine: Judges of the Supreme
Court, Judges of the High Courts, Chief Election Commissioner, and Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
Thus, this doctrine is not absolute and is subject to Constitutional provisions. Article 311 introduces significant
limitations to the Doctrine of Pleasure. It ensures that a civil servant cannot be dismissed, removed, or reduced
in rank without an inquiry where they are informed of the charges against them and given a reasonable
opportunity to defend themselves.

The doctrine of pleasure must be applied while keeping in mind the following restrictions: The contract that has
been made between the civil servants and the government may be enforceable. This doctrine of pleasure cannot
be used without sufficient cause. Article 14 states that the use of any principles or doctrines must be done on
reasonable grounds. It prohibits the exercise of a doctrine arbitrarily. Like Article 14, Article 15 also prevents
the arbitrary exercise of this doctrine of pleasure. This Article has imposed certain restrictions before their
termination from services on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. The Constitution also
states that all citizens must be treated equally without any unreasonable discrimination under Article 16.
Under certain circumstances, where the public servant is terminated from his service, it might amount to a
punishment of dismissal. One such situation can be when a person has the right to hold the post but is
terminated from his service. In that situation, his termination itself amounts to dismissal, as he had the right to
hold his office but could not as he was removed from it. The Indian legal system is in the hands of the Judiciary,
which is an independent body. The Judiciary is kept independent for fairness and justice so that it does not get
influenced by anyone while rendering justice. The doctrine of pleasure has no application in the Indian Judicial
System. It means that judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Court are exempt from the application of the
doctrine of pleasure. Not only the judges of the courts but also other categories of people such as the Indian


Audits and Accounts Department, defense personnel, Public Sector undertakings, and a few others are exempt
from this doctrine as they also cannot be removed from their offices under this doctrine of pleasure.

Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “Doctrine of pleasure”, https://blog.ipleaders.in/doctrine-of-
pleasure/
