XIII. Torts Against Property: Trespass to land is a direct, intentional interference with another's
possession of land without lawful justification. It is actionable per se — no proof of damage is
required. The tort protects possessory rights; even a person in wrongful possession may sue a
trespasser. Trespass may be committed by physical entry, placing objects on the land, or
remaining after permission is withdrawn. Mistaken belief that one owns or has permission to
enter the land is no defence.
Private nuisance is an indirect, unreasonable interference with a person's use and enjoyment
of land. Unlike trespass, damage must generally be proved. Reasonableness is assessed by
balancing the gravity of the interference, its duration, the character of the neighbourhood, and
the utility of the defendant's conduct. The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) imposes strict
liability where a person brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes, and it
does escape and cause damage. The defendant is liable even without negligence, subject to the
defences of act of God, act of a stranger, and the plaintiff's own default.
The doctrine of distress damage feasant entitles a landowner to seize and detain chattels —
animals or objects — found on his land causing damage, until compensation is paid. The right
is possessory only; the distrainor cannot sell or destroy the chattel. The right is lost once the
chattel leaves the land voluntarily.
The rule against extra-sensitive plaintiffs in property torts mirrors the general principle: a
defendant is not liable for damage that would not have occurred but for the abnormal
sensitivity of the plaintiff's property or use. Where ordinary land or property would not have
suffered the harm complained of, a defendant conducting a reasonable activity is not liable
merely because the plaintiff's particular use is unusually delicate. This principle was applied
in Robinson v. Kilvert (1889), where heat from the defendant's operations damaged the
plaintiff's unusually sensitive brown paper stored in the premises above, but would not have
affected ordinary goods; the court denied relief.
Conversion is the wrongful dealing with another's chattel in a manner inconsistent with the
owner's right to possession — including taking, destroying, selling, or retaining it without
authority. The plaintiff must have a possessory title at the time of the act. Conversion is
actionable per se and entitles the plaintiff to the full value of the chattel.
Source: Extracted with revisions and modifications from standard legal principles and case law
including Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) and Robinson v. Kilvert (1889).
passages.LEG-P0217:
SECTION III
X.	The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 is a foundational statute governing the transfer of property
between living persons in India. Its general principles provide clarity, fairness and legal certainty
in property transactions by defining the rights, obligations and limitations of parties involved.
These principles ensure orderly transfer of property, restrict arbitrary alienation, and prevent
disputes arising from uncertainty, fraud or overlapping claims. By regulating how and when
property can be transferred, the Act safeguards ownership rights and promotes transparency in
dealings.
The Act plays a vital role in economic development by enabling smooth and secure property
transactions, which are essential for investment and growth in the real estate sector. Principles
such as the rule against perpetuity, doctrine of lis pendens and fraudulent transfer protect long-
term public interest while balancing private rights. Together, these rules create predictability in
property law and contribute to stability in the property market.
The general principles of the Transfer of Property Act include transferability of property under
Section 6, which establishes that property of any kind may be transferred unless expressly
prohibited by law. Section 10 restricts absolute restraints on alienation, ensuring free circulation
of property while permitting limited restraints in specific cases. Section 13 regulates transfer to an
unborn person by requiring creation of a prior interest, while Section 14 embodies the rule against
perpetuity to prevent indefinite control over property.
Sections 19 and 21 distinguish vested and contingent interests to determine when rights accrue.
Section 25 recognises conditional transfers dependent on fulfilment of specified conditions. Section
48 lays down the doctrine of priority, giving precedence to earlier transfers. Section 41 validates
transfers by ostensible owners when the transferee acts in good faith after reasonable inquiry.
Section 43 applies estoppel, preventing transferors from denying authority once they have induced
reliance.
Section 52 incorporates the doctrine of lis pendens, making transfers during litigation subject to
the outcome of the suit. Section 53 renders fraudulent transfers voidable to protect creditors, while
Section 53A embodies the doctrine of part performance, protecting transferees who have acted on
an agreement despite lack of registration. Collectively, these principles form the backbone of
Indian property law, ensuring lawful, fair and effective transfer of property.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.kotak.bank.in/en/stories-in-
focus/loans/home-loan/transfer-of-property-act-india.html
passages.LEG-P0218:
XIII. The Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 was enacted to give Muslim women clear legal
grounds for seeking judicial divorce. Before this Act, Muslim personal law in India was mostly
governed by uncodified customs and interpretations of different Islamic schools such as
Hanafi, Shafi, Maliki, Hanbali and Shia schools. The husband had wide power to dissolve
marriage through talaq, while the wife had very limited and impractical remedies such as
talaq-i-tafweez or lian. Women deserted by their husbands, denied maintenance, or subjected
to cruelty often had no effective legal remedy. The Act was therefore introduced to remove
hardship, codify women’s right to seek divorce, clarify the law across different sects, protect
dower rights, and prevent automatic dissolution of marriage merely because of the wife’s
conversion.
The most important provision is Section 2, which gives several grounds on which a Muslim
wife may seek dissolution of marriage. If the husband’s whereabouts have not been known for
four years, the wife can seek divorce, though the decree takes effect only after six months, and
may be set aside if the husband appears and resumes marital duties. If the husband neglects
or fails to provide maintenance for two years, the wife can claim divorce, and poverty or illness
is not treated as a valid excuse. A wife may also seek dissolution if the husband is sentenced to
imprisonment for seven years or more, if he fails to perform marital obligations for three years,
or if he was impotent at the time of marriage and continues to be so. The Act also covers cases
where the husband has been insane for two years, suffers from a virulent venereal disease, or
where a girl married before fifteen repudiates the marriage before eighteen, provided the
marriage was not consummated. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Cruelty is another major ground under the Act. It includes habitual assault, making the wife’s
life miserable, associating with women of evil repute, forcing her into immoral life, disposing of
her property, obstructing her religious practice, or failing to treat co-wives equitably. Section
2(ix) also preserves other grounds recognised under Muslim law, such as lian and zihar.
Section 3 requires notice to the husband’s heirs where his whereabouts are unknown. Section 4
provides that the wife’s conversion does not automatically dissolve marriage, and Section 5

protects her right to dower or mahr even after divorce. Judicial decisions such as Satagunj v.
Rahmat, Itwari v. Asghari, Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India, and Shayara Bano v. Union of
India show that the Act is a woman-protective law aimed at fairness, dignity, and judicial
dissolution rather than unilateral hardship.
Source: Extracted with edits from indiacode.nic.in
passages.LEG-P0219:
SECTION III
X.	Administrative tribunals are quasi-judicial institutions created by statute to adjudicate
disputes relating to administrative matters. They are not regular courts, but they exercise
judicial and quasi-judicial powers in specific areas assigned by law, such as recruitment,
appointment, promotion, transfer, disciplinary proceedings, pension, retirement benefits,
taxation, labour matters and other specialised subjects. Their proceedings are treated as
judicial proceedings, and they possess powers similar to civil courts, including summoning
witnesses, receiving evidence, administering oaths, reviewing decisions and deciding matters
ex parte. Their main purpose is to ensure speedy justice, review administrative decisions,
resolve service disputes and reduce pendency before ordinary courts.
The growth of tribunalisation in India began before independence with bodies like the Income
Tax Appellate Tribunal. After independence, the expanding role of the State and increasing
administrative disputes made specialised adjudicatory bodies necessary. On _ the
recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act,
1976 inserted Part XIV-A into the Constitution, containing Articles 323A and 323B. Article
323A empowers Parliament to create administrative tribunals for disputes relating to
recruitment and conditions of service of public servants under the Union, States, local
authorities, public corporations and government-controlled bodies. Article 323B enables
Parliament and State Legislatures to create tribunals for specialised matters such as taxation,
foreign exchange, industrial disputes, land reforms, elections, rent and essential commodities.
Administrative tribunals have statutory origin, quasi-judicial nature, limited jurisdiction,
subject expertise and flexible procedure. They are not strictly bound by the Code of Civil
Procedure or the Indian Evidence Act, but they must follow principles of natural justice,
including fair hearing, absence of bias and reasoned decisions. Unlike ordinary courts, which
possess general jurisdiction and are part of the traditional judicial system, tribunals are
specialised bodies and may include administrative or technical experts.
The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 was enacted under Article 823A and provides for the
Central Administrative Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals and Joint Administrative
Tribunals. The Central Administrative Tribunal deals with service matters of Central
Government employees, civilian defence employees, members of All India Services and
employees of government-controlled authorities, excluding armed forces personnel, Supreme
Court and High Court staff, and parliamentary secretariat staff.
In S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of tribunals
as effective alternative mechanisms, while recognising judicial review as part of the basic
structure. In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, the Court held that tribunals are courts of
first instance, but their decisions remain subject to scrutiny by High Courts under Articles 226
and 227. Administrative tribunals provide speedy, expert and inexpensive justice, but

concerns remain regarding independence, uniform procedure, administrative control and
reappointment. Recent tribunal reforms and proposals for a National Tribunal Commission
aim to strengthen independence and uniformity in tribunal administration. [Word Count: 454]
Source: Extracted with edits https://prsindia.org/ and https://lawbhoomi.com/
passages.LEG-P0220:
XV. ‘Transferable property refers to property that can be legally transferred from one person to another
through recognised modes such as sale, gift, lease, mortgage or exchange. Section 6 of the Transfer
of Property Act, 1882 lays down the general rule that property of any kind may be transferred,
subject to statutory restrictions. Transferable property includes immovable property like land and
buildings, movable assets such as vehicles and machinery, intellectual property like patents and
copyrights, and financial instruments such as shares and securities.
Non-transferable property consists of interests that cannot be legally transferred due to their
personal, contingent or restricted nature. Section 6 enumerates specific exceptions to
transferability. Spes succession is, or the mere chance of an heir apparent inheriting property, is
non-transferable under Section 6(a), as affirmed in Official Assignee, Madras v. Sampath Naidu.
Similarly, the right of re-entry, easements apart from the dominant heritage, and interests
restricted to personal enjoyment cannot be transferred. Rights such as future maintenance, a mere
right to sue, public offices, salaries attached to public offices, and pensions are expressly non-
transferable.
Section 6 also prohibits transfers opposed to the nature of the interest, transfers for unlawful
objects or consideration, and transfers to legally disqualified persons. Statutory prohibitions
further restrict transfer of certain tenancy or occupancy rights, as recognised in Shanti Prasad v.
Bachchi Devi. Courts have consistently held that these restrictions preserve the purpose, dignity
and legal character of such interests. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The distinction between transferable and non-transferable property is crucial. Transferable
property offers flexibility, marketability and economic value, while non-transferable property is
protected due to its personal, public, religious or statutory character. Section 6 thus balances
freedom of transfer with legal, moral and public policy considerations, ensuring orderly and lawful
transfer of property rights. [Transferable and Non-Transferable Property; Word Count: 289]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/transferable-and-non-
transferable-property/
passages.LEG-P0221:
VII. Res means subject matter and judicata means adjudged or decided and together it means ‘a matter
adjudged’. In simpler words, the thing has been judged by the court, the issue before a court has already been
decided by another court and between the same parties. Hence, the subsequent court will dismiss the case as it
has been decided by another court. Res judicata applies to both civil and criminal legal systems. No suit which
has been directly or indirectly tried in a former suit can be tried again. The principle of res judicata seeks to
promote the fair administration of justice and honesty and to prevent the law from abuse. The principle of res
judicata applies when a litigant attempts to file a subsequent lawsuit on the same matter, after having received a
judgment in a previous case involving the same parties. In many jurisdictions, this applies not only to the
specific claims made in the first case but also to claims that could have been made during the same case. The
double jeopardy provision of the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution protects people from being put on a
second trial after the case has been judged. So the doctrine of res judicata addresses this issue and it bars any
party to retry a judgment once it has been decided. Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Court incorporates the
doctrine of res judicata also known as ‘rule of conclusiveness of judgment’. The doctrine of res judicata and res
sub judice varies in some factors such as (a). Res sub judice applies to a matter that is pending trial whereas res
judicata applies to a matter adjudicated or arbitrated and (b) Res sub judice prohibits the trial of a suit that has a
pending decision in a previous suit i.e., the suit is still not finally decided, whereas res judicata prohibits the trial
of a suit that has been decided in a former suit.
Source: https://blog.ipleaders.in/overview-on-doctrine-of-res-judicata/
passages.LEG-P0222:
XII. Capacity in tort law refers to the legal status of a person to sue or to be sued for violation of law.
Although, as a general rule, all persons may sue or be sued in tort, this is not absolute and is
subject to reasonable restrictions. Indian law largely follows English tort principles on disabilities
of parties. Parties to torts include plaintiffs (who initiate proceedings) and defendants (who
defend), and only those having the right to control proceedings or appeal are true parties; others
are privies. Proper joinder of parties is vital, as suing the wrong party or misjoinder/non-joinder
may weaken the plaintiffs case.
Certain persons face limitations in being sued or suing. Traditionally, married women could not
sue or be sued alone due to the common-law unity of spouses, but this disability was removed by
reforms like the Married Women’s Property Act, enabling independent suits. Minors can be sued
for torts like assault, defamation, fraud, etc., but may be exempt where intention or knowledge is
essential, as in Walmsey v. Humonick. Governments and municipalities may avoid liability for
acts done in discharge of sovereign functions, though liability may arise when the act is connected
with assigned duties, as in U.O.I. v. Sugrabai. A lunatic cannot be sued for acts done while not ina
stable state of mind. Alien enemies cannot be sued or sue without Central Government
permission. Corporations, having separate legal personality, can sue and be sued; however,
liability depends on whether the servant acted within authority, as illustrated in Poulton v.
London and S.W. Rly. Co. Foreign sovereigns and ambassadors enjoy immunity unless consent
and jurisdictional submission exist.
Joint tortfeasors are persons who aid, counsel, direct, or join in committing a wrongful act,
creating joint or joint-and-several responsibility. Contribution allows a tortfeasor who pays more
than his share to recover from others. Indian courts have approached English common law
cautiously; in Khushro S. Gandhi v. Guzdar, the Supreme Court held that release of all joint
tortfeasors requires full satisfaction. Joint liability commonly arises through agency, vicarious
liability, and joint action. Ex turpi causa non oritur actio bars claims arising from unlawful
conduct, subject to tests like reliance, no benefit, proportionality, inextricably linked, and public
conscience, with exceptions including public interest and victimless crimes.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/parties-in-torts-capacity-
to-sue-and-be-sued/
passages.LEG-P0223:
XII. Wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement are offences against personal liberty and
freedom of movement. Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution protects the right of citizens to move
freely throughout India, while Article 21 protects personal liberty. Criminal law gives effect to
these guarantees by punishing unlawful obstruction or detention. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023, wrongful restraint is dealt with under Section 126 and wrongful confinement
under Section 127.
Wrongful restraint occurs when a person voluntarily obstructs another person so as to prevent
that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed. The
obstruction may be physical, verbal, threatening, or created by circumstances, provided it
unlawfully prevents movement. The essence of the offence is that the victim must have a legal
right to move in that direction, and the accused must voluntarily obstruct that movement.
Mere advice, request, or moral pressure will not amount to wrongful restraint unless it
effectively prevents lawful movement.
The law also recognises an exception. If a person, in good faith, believes that he has a lawful
right to obstruct a private way over land or water, such obstruction does not amount to
wrongful restraint. However, the belief must be genuine and connected with a private way;
obstruction of a public road or obstruction without lawful basis cannot claim this protection.
Wrongful confinement is a more serious and narrower form of wrongful restraint. It occurs
when a person wrongfully restrains another in such a manner as to prevent that person from
proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits. In wrongful restraint, movement is blocked
only in one or some directions; in wrongful confinement, the person is prevented from moving
beyond a fixed boundary. Thus, all wrongful confinement involves restraint, but every
wrongful restraint is not confinement. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Actual physical force is not always necessary for wrongful confinement. Locking a person in a
room, surrounding exits with guards, threatening immediate violence if the person leaves, or

creating a reasonable fear that escape is impossible may amount to confinement. The test is
whether the person’s liberty to leave the defined area has been unlawfully curtailed.
The seriousness of wrongful confinement increases with duration and purpose. Section 127
punishes ordinary wrongful confinement, confinement for three days or more, confinement for
ten days or more, secret confinement, confinement after a writ of release has been issued, and
confinement for extortion of property, confession, or illegal compulsion. These aggravated
forms show that the law treats prolonged, secret, coercive, or extortion-based confinement
more seriously. [Word Count: 415]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://blog.ipleaders.in/wrongful-restraint-
wrongful-confinement
passages.LEG-P0224:
XIV. Remedies for torts are broadly classified into judicial remedies and extra-judicial remedies.
Judicial remedies are those granted by courts of law to an aggrieved party, while extra-judicial
remedies are those where the injured party lawfully takes action without approaching the
court. The three principal judicial remedies are damages, injunction, and specific restitution of
property. Damages are the primary remedy in tort law and consist of monetary compensation
paid to restore the plaintiff, as far as money can, to the position they would have occupied had
the tort not occurred. Different types of damages are recognised: nominal damages where a
legal right is violated without actual loss, as in Ashby v. White and Constantine v. Imperial
London Hotels Ltd.; contemptuous damages where actual harm is trivial; compensatory
damages to restore actual loss; aggravated damages for additional injury such as humiliation,
pain, and loss of self-esteem; punitive or exemplary damages to punish the defendant and
deter similar conduct; and general and special damages, where general damages flow
naturally from the wrong while special damages must be specifically proved. However, only
damage that is not too remote is compensable, and courts apply principles of remoteness as
seen in Re Polemis and Liesbosch Dredger v. SS Edison.
Another important judicial remedy is injunction, which is an equitable remedy granted at the
discretion of the court. Instead of merely awarding money, the court restrains a person from
continuing a wrongful act or directs them to perform a positive act to undo the wrong.
Injunctions may be temporary or permanent, and mandatory or prohibitory, and are governed
by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Sections 37 to 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. In
M/s Hindustan Pencils Pvt. Ltd. v. India Stationery Products, injunction was granted to
restrain trademark infringement. The third judicial remedy is specific restitution of property,
which restores goods or property wrongfully taken from the owner.
Extra-judicial remedies allow a person to protect or recover their rights without court
intervention. These include expulsion of a trespasser, re-entry on land, re-caption of goods,
abatement of nuisance, and distress damage feasant, where a person may retain cattle or
beasts that have entered and damaged their property until compensation is made. These
remedies are lawful only if exercised reasonably according to the circumstances. [Word Count:
379]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.legalbites.in/law-of-
torts /remedies-in-the-law-of-torts- 1106766
passages.LEG-P0225:
XII. A quasi-contract is a legal remedy developed by courts to prevent one party from being
unjustly enriched at the expense of another. It is called “quasi” because it is treated as if it
were a contract, even though it does not contain the usual elements of a contract such as offer,
acceptance, consideration, or mutual consent. The obligation is not created by agreement of
parties but is imposed by law to ensure fairness and justice.
The main foundation of quasi-contract is the doctrine of unjust enrichment, expressed in the
maxim “Nemo debet locupletari ex aliena jactura”, meaning no one ought to be enriched at
another’s expense. Unjust enrichment occurs when one party receives a benefit, the benefit is
received at the expense of another, and it would be unjust to retain that benefit without
restitution. Therefore, the main remedy in quasi-contract is restitution, by which the
benefiting party is required to return the benefit or compensate the aggrieved party.
Quasi-contracts have certain important features. There is an absence of agreement, as no prior
contract exists between the parties. They are imposed by law, not by the intention of the
parties. They are involuntary in nature because the obligation arises even without consent.
The benefit must also be non-gratuitous, meaning it must have been given with an expectation
of compensation. A quasi-contract creates a right against a specific person who has received
the benefit, unlike tort law where liability may operate more broadly. These obligations apply
only in specific situations recognised by law.
In India, quasi-contracts are codified under Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
Section 68 deals with necessaries supplied to a person incapable of contracting, such as a
minor or person of unsound mind, where reimbursement can be claimed from that person’s
estate. Section 69 allows reimbursement when an interested person pays money on behalf of
another. Section 70 applies where a person lawfully provides non-gratuitous goods or services
and the recipient enjoys the benefit. Section 71 imposes responsibility on a finder of goods to
take reasonable care and return them. Section 72 requires return of money paid by mistake or
under coercion.
The concept developed from English common law, especially Moses v. Macferlan, where Lord
Mansfield recognised obligations based on natural justice and equity. Indian cases such as
State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai and Hari Ram Sheth Khandsari v. Commissioner of
Sales Tax affirmed restitution for money paid by mistake. However, quasi-contracts have
limitations because there is no mutual intent, proving unjust enrichment may be complex, and
they apply only in limited situations. Unlike express contracts, which arise from agreement,
quasi-contracts arise by law to prevent unfair benefit.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://goodbrickrealty.com/quasi-contract/
passages.LEG-P0226:
XII. Peaceful settlement of disputes in international law, also known as pacific settlement of
international disputes, is a fundamental principle requiring States to resolve their
disagreements by peaceful means so that international peace, security and justice are not
endangered. Its origin can be traced to the Hague Peace Conferences of 1899 and 1907, which
produced conventions for the pacific settlement of disputes. The principle gained greater
importance after the prohibition on the use of force under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter.
Article 2(3) of the UN Charter provides that all members shall settle their international
disputes by peaceful means. This obligation was reaffirmed in the 1982 Manila Declaration on
the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.
An international dispute may be understood as a disagreement involving at least one State
and another State, international organisation, natural person, legal person, institution or
corporation from another part of the world. The Black’s Law Dictionary defines a dispute as a
conflict or controversy, especially one giving rise to legal proceedings. In international law,
peaceful settlement is treated as a continuous legal duty, where States participate as equal
units in rights. In Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua, the ICJ
recognised that parties to a dispute must seek a solution by pacific methods. However, the UN
Charter does not compel parties to adopt one fixed method. Article 33 lists peaceful methods
such as negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement and
resort to regional arrangements. If parties fail to settle the dispute, Article 37 requires them to
refer the matter to the Security Council.
Negotiation is the oldest, simplest and most common method. It involves direct discussion
between disputing parties without third-party intervention. India and Sri Lanka settled their
boundary dispute through negotiation in 1974, and the Farakka Barrage issue between India
and Bangladesh was also resolved through this method. Good offices involve a third friendly
State, individual or organisation suggesting settlement without directly participating in
discussions, as seen in the Shatt-al-Arab dispute between Iran and Iraq through the President
of Algeria. Mediation involves active participation of a neutral third party who gives
suggestions and helps parties reach settlement; the Tashkent Agreement between India and
Pakistan is an example.
Conciliation refers disputes to a commission or committee which proposes a settlement,
though its recommendations are not binding. Arbitration and judicial settlement are
adjudicative methods because they result in binding decisions. Arbitration involves a chosen
arbitrator or tribunal, while judicial settlement involves courts such as the International
Court of Justice. International disputes may be legal or political, but international law mainly
deals with legal disputes. In Nicaragua v. Honduras, the Court clarified that it concerns itself
only with legal aspects of a dispute. [Word Count: 449]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://blog.ipleaders.in/settlement-of-
disputes-in-international-law/
passages.LEG-P0227:
XIV. Bailment is a special contract recognised under Sections 148 to 171 of the Indian Contract Act,
1872. Section 148 defines bailment as delivery of goods by one person to another for some
purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned
or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The person
delivering the goods is called the bailor, and the person receiving them is called the bailee.
The essence of bailment is delivery of possession, not transfer of ownership. The bailee
receives temporary possession and must use the goods only for the agreed purpose. Bailment
may arise through express contract, implied contract, or even by operation of law, such as
where a person finds goods belonging to another and assumes responsibility over them.
Section 149 recognises that delivery may be made by doing anything which has the effect of
putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee.
The bailor has important duties. Under Section 150, the bailor must disclose faults in the
goods which are known to him and which materially interfere with their use or expose the
bailee to extraordinary risk. If the bailor fails to disclose such faults, he is responsible for
damage caused to the bailee. In gratuitous bailment, this duty applies to known faults; in non-
gratuitous bailment, the responsibility is stricter.
The bailee must take reasonable care of the goods. Section 151 requires the bailee to take as
much care of the goods as a person of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods. Under
Section 152, if such care is taken, the bailee is not responsible for loss, destruction, or
deterioration of the goods, unless there is a special contract. However, under Sections 153 and
154, unauthorised use of the goods may terminate the bailment and make the bailee liable for
loss arising from such use.
The bailee must return or deliver the goods according to the bailor’s directions when the
purpose is accomplished or the time of bailment expires. Under Section 161, if the bailee

defaults in returning the goods, he becomes responsible for any loss, destruction, or
deterioration from that time. The bailee must also return any increase or profit from the goods
under Section 163, unless agreed otherwise.
The bailee has rights too. He may claim necessary expenses in gratuitous bailment under
Section 158, compensation for defective title under Section 164, and lien under Sections 170
and 171. A pledge under Section 172 is a special form of bailment where goods are delivered as
security for debt or performance of a promise.
[Word Count: 434]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://blog.ipleaders.in/the-contract-of-
bailment/
passages.LEG-P0228:
XI.	Homicide means killing of one human being by another human being. The word comes from
Latin terms “homo”, meaning man, and “cida”, meaning to kill. However, all homicide does not
amount to murder. Section 100 of the BNS deals with culpable homicide, which includes acts
causing death but not necessarily amounting to murder. Murder is also a form of homicide, but
it is graver, more intensive, and is punished more severely. Section 101 of BNS defines murder
and explains when culpable homicide becomes murder.
The main difference between culpable homicide and murder is based on intention, knowledge,
and the degree of certainty of death. If the person committing the act has complete knowledge
that the act will, in all probability, cause death, and still deliberately commits it with free will
and intention, the act amounts to murder. In culpable homicide not amounting to murder,
there may be intention to cause death or bodily injury, but there is no certainty that death will
necessarily follow. Section 100 of BNS uses the expression “likely to cause death,” while
Section 101 of BNS uses stronger expressions such as “sufficient in the ordinary course of
nature to cause death” and “so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause
death.” www.lawpreptutorial.com
The difference can be understood through examples. If Z hates X and merely prays for X’s
death, no offence is committed because prayer does not cause death. If Z pushes X into an
eight-foot pit and X dies, it may amount to culpable homicide if Z did not know that death was
certain. But if Z ensures that X receives no food, water, or air until death, it becomes murder
because death is the natural and certain consequence.
In Nara Singh Challan v. State of Orissa, the court held that Section 100 is the genus and
Section 101 is the species. In Reg v. Govinda, the accused struck his wife and placed his foot
on her chest, resulting in death, but the act was treated as culpable homicide not amounting to
murder because death was not necessarily likely in the ordinary course. In State of A.P. v. R.
Punnayya, the Supreme Court explained three degrees of culpable homicide: murder under
Section 300, culpable homicide under Section 304 Part I, and the least grave form under
Section 304 Part II.
Confusion arises because intention and knowledge are difficult to prove. Courts examine facts,
pre-planning, grave provocation, sudden fight, fear, or private defence. Cases such as Ram
Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh, Bhagwan Singh v. State of Uttarakhand, and Macchi Singh
v. State of Rajasthan show how courts decide punishment based on the gravity, knowledge,
intention, brutality, and surrounding circumstances. [Criminal Law-Culpable Homicide and
Murder under BNS; Word Count: 443]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.legalserviceindia.com
passages.LEG-P0229:
IX.	India spent $92.1 billion on its military in 2025 according to a new report by the Stockholm
International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). That is 8.9 per cent more than what India
spent the year before.
Countries around the world spent a record $2.9 trillion on their militaries in 2025 — equal to
2.5% of the entire world's economic output. This is the eleventh consecutive year that global
military spending has increased, and the highest figure SIPRI has ever recorded since it began
tracking in 1949.
SIPRI listed the India-Pakistan clash as one of the most dangerous flashpoints of the year.
The report said India struck Pakistani air and missile bases — some of which are believed to
have nuclear-related roles — but noted that “both sides took steps to avoid escalation. The
report also pointed out that it was the first time India and Pakistan openly used cyberattacks
as part of an armed conflict. In its timeline of major events for the year, SIPRI recorded: May
7-10: India and Pakistan exchange intense cross-border fire.
International transfers of major arms reached their highest level since the end of the Cold War
during 2021-25, marking a 9.2% increase compared to 2016-20. USA, France, Russia,
Germany and China accounted for 70 per cent of export of arms. India was the second largest
recipient of major arms between 2021-25, accounting for 8.2 % in Global arms import. India is
believed to have slightly expanded its nuclear stockpile in 2025 and continued developing new
types of nuclear delivery systems. [Word Count: 253]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://indianexpress.com/article/upsc-
current-affairs /upsc-essentials/knowledge-nugget-sipri-report-2026-military-nuclear-
warheads-10736257/
passages.LEG-P0230:
XIII. A High Court is the highest judicial authority within a State or a group of States and Union
Territories, ranking below the Supreme Court of India and above all subordinate courts. High
Courts are not merely appellate bodies; they function as constitutional courts entrusted with
protecting rights, interpreting laws, supervising subordinate judiciary, and ensuring that
legislative and executive actions conform to constitutional principles.
India follows a single integrated judicial system, consisting of the Supreme Court, High Courts,
and subordinate courts. This system ensures uniform interpretation and application of both
Central and State laws across the country. Articles 214 to 231 of the Constitution, contained in
Part VI, govern the establishment, composition, jurisdiction, and administration of High Courts.
Parliament may establish a common High Court for multiple States or Union Territories, as
permitted by the Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.
Each High Court consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may
determine. Judges are appointed by the President under Article 217, following consultation with
the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High
Court. Judicial interpretation through the Second and Third Judges Cases has established the

primacy of the judiciary via the collegium system. A High Court judge must be an Indian citizen
and must have either ten years’ judicial experience or ten years’ practice as an advocate. Judges
hold office until the age of 62 and may be removed only through impeachment on grounds of
proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
High Courts exercise wide jurisdiction. Their original jurisdiction includes writ petitions, election
disputes, and certain civil and revenue matters. Under Article 226, High Courts may issue writs
not only for fundamental rights but also for other legal rights, giving them broader writ
jurisdiction than the Supreme Court. They primarily function as appellate courts in civil and
criminal matters and exercise supervisory control over subordinate courts under Article 227.
High Courts are Courts of Record, with binding precedents and contempt powers. They also
exercise judicial review over State and Central laws and executive actions. Constitutional
safeguards such as secure tenure, protected service conditions, and financial independence ensure
the autonomy and impartiality of High Courts, reinforcing their vital role in India’s constitutional
framework.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https:// https://www.sci.gov.in/

Directions (Q.53-Q.82): Read the comprehension carefully and answer the questions.
        Passage (Q.53-Q.57): Aaya Ram Gaya Ram was a phrase that became popular in Indian politics after a Haryana
        MLA Gaya Lal changed his party thrice within the same day in 1967. The anti-defection law sought to prevent such
        political defections which may be due to reward of office or other similar considerations.
        The Tenth Schedule was inserted in the Constitution in 1985. It lays down the process by which legislators may be
        disqualified on grounds of defection by the Presiding Officer of a legislature based on a petition by any other member
        of the House. A legislator is deemed to have defected if he either voluntarily gives up the membership of his party or
        disobeys the directives of the party leadership on a vote. This implies that a legislator defying (abstaining or voting
        against) the party whip on any issue can lose his membership of the House. The law applies to both Parliament and
        state assemblies.
        Legislators may change their party without the risk of disqualification in certain circumstances. The law allows a
        party to merge with or into another party provided that at least two-thirds of its legislators are in favour of the
        merger. In such a scenario, neither the members who decide to merge, nor the ones who stay with the original party
        will face disqualification.
        The anti-defection law seeks to provide a stable government by ensuring the legislators do not switch sides.
        However, this law also restricts a legislator from voting in line with his conscience, judgement and interests of his
        electorate. Such a situation impedes the oversight function of the legislature over the government, by ensuring that
        members vote based on the decisions taken by the party leadership, and not what their constituents would like them
        to vote for.
        Source: https://prsindia.org/theprsblog/the-anti-defection-law-explained?page=34&per-page=1
passages.LEG-P0232:
X.	The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) is India's primary legislation for dealing
with unlawful activities, terrorism, and threats to the sovereignty and integrity of the country.
Enacted in 1967, the Act was originally designed to prevent activities that threatened India's
unity and territorial integrity. Over the years, particularly through amendments in 2004,
2008, 2012, and 2019, it has evolved into the country's principal anti-terrorism law.
Under the UAPA, the government has the power to declare organisations as unlawful or
terrorist organizations and to take legal action against individuals involved in terrorist
activities. The 2019 amendment further expanded these powers by allowing the government to

designate individuals, and not just organisations, as terrorists. The Act also provides special
provisions for investigation, arrest, detention, and prosecution in terrorism-related cases.
Supporters of the UAPA argue that it is an essential tool for combating terrorism, insurgency,
and organised extremist activities that threaten national security. They contend that the law
enables security agencies to investigate complex terror networks and prevent attacks.
However, the Act has also been the subject of significant debate and criticism. Critics argue
that some provisions, particularly those related to arrest, detention, and bail, can potentially
affect civil liberties and may be vulnerable to misuse. As a result, the UAPA remains an
important yet controversial component of India's legal framework, reflecting the ongoing
challenge of balancing national security concerns with the protection of individual rights and
democratic freedoms.
passages.LEG-P0233:
Passage (Q.58-Q.62): Civil courts in India generally allow any person to sue to enforce a civil right, but the Code of
        Civil Procedure creates special rules when the litigant is an alien or when the dispute involves foreign States, foreign
        rulers, ambassadors, or envoys. The basic idea is to balance access to justice with concerns of sovereignty,
        diplomatic relations, and national security.
        Under Section 83 CPC, an “alien friend” (a foreign national from a country not at war with India) may sue in an Indian
        court as if they were an Indian citizen. By contrast, an “alien enemy” faces restrictions: if such a person is residing
        in India, they may sue only with the permission of the Central Government, and if they are residing in a foreign
        country, they generally cannot sue in Indian courts.
        The Code also recognises that foreign States may sometimes need to approach Indian courts. Section 84 permits a
        foreign State to sue in a competent court, especially where the suit is meant to enforce a private right vested in its
        ruler or an officer acting in a public capacity. Since a foreign ruler cannot personally appear and conduct litigation
        in India, Section 85 allows the Central Government to appoint persons to prosecute or defend suits on behalf of such
        rulers, ensuring the court knows who can validly represent them.
        However, when the suit is against a foreign ruler, ambassador, or envoy, the law is stricter. Section 86 provides that
        such a suit cannot ordinarily be instituted in a competent court without the consent of the Central Government,
        certified in writing, reflecting a limited form of sovereign/diplomatic immunity.
        These rules matter because they determine not only who may sue, but also when the judiciary must defer to
        executive certification in matters touching foreign relations.
        (Source- https://lawbhoomi.com/suits-by-aliens-and-by-or-against-foreign-rulers-ambassadors-and-envoys/)
passages.LEG-P0234:
IX.	Is the digital landscape quietly making a generation less happy? The answer, according to the
latest World Happiness Report 2026, appears to be yes. Heavy social media use seems to be
contributing to a drop in wellbeing among young people in English-speaking countries and
Western Europe, especially among girls, according to the report’s findings.
Data from Latin America show that the type of platform is crucial. Those designed to facilitate
social connections show a clear positive association with happiness, whereas those driven by
algorithmically curated content tend to demonstrate a negative association at high rates of
use. The report also found that nations in or near zones of major conflict remain at the foot of
the rankings. These rankings, according to the report, are based on a three-year average of
each population’s average assessment of their quality of life. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The global evidence makes clear that the links between social media use and our wellbeing
heavily depends on what platforms we’re using, who’s using them and how, as well as for how
long. Heavy usage is associated with much lower wellbeing, but those deliberately off social
media also appear to be missing out on some positive effects. Beyond the complexity, it is clear
that we should look as much as possible to put the ‘social’ back into social media.
The findings describe a complex global picture at a time when many countries are seeking to
implement greater legislative protections for those aged under 16 online.
