tech/health/world-happiness-report-2026-the-social-media-and-happiness-
connect /article70758644.ece
passages.LEG-P0235:
XV.	Nuisance is a civil wrong based on unlawful interference with a person’s use or enjoyment of land,
property, or a right connected with property. A person may use his own property, but such use
must not unreasonably disturb another person’s legal rights. The interference may arise through
noise, smoke, smell, vibration, obstruction, pollution, dangerous structures, or any activity that
materially affects comfort, health, safety, or property. For nuisance to be actionable, there must be
a wrongful act and substantial damage, loss, or annoyance. Mere sensitivity or ordinary
inconvenience is not enough. The law examines whether the interference is unreasonable in the
circumstances and whether an ordinary person living in that locality would be affected. Therefore,
the character of the locality, duration of interference, seriousness of harm, and reasonableness of
the defendant’s conduct are important factors. Nuisance is mainly of two kinds: public nuisance
and private nuisance. Public nuisance affects the community or a considerable section of the public.
Under Section 270 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, a person commits public nuisance when
an act or illegal omission causes common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or to persons
using a public right. Blocking a public road, polluting a public water source, or creating danger ina
public place may amount to public nuisance.
An individual can sue for public nuisance only when he suffers special damage beyond what the
general public suffers. The injury must be direct, substantial, and different in degree from the
inconvenience suffered by others. Section 91 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 also permits legal
action for public nuisance in appropriate cases. Private nuisance affects a specific person’s use or

enjoyment of land. It may involve physical injury to property or physical discomfort to the occupier.
In cases of property damage, sensible injury is usually sufficient. In cases of physical discomfort,
the interference must exceed ordinary use and affect the normal comfort of human life. The main
remedies for nuisance are injunction, damages, and abatement. Injunctions may be granted under
the Specific Relief Act, 1963 to restrain continuing or threatened nuisance. Damages compensate
the injured party for loss suffered. Abatement allows the affected person to remove the nuisance,
but only with reasonable notice and reasonable force. The recognised defences include prescription
and statutory authority. Prescription may apply when the nuisance has continued openly,
peacefully, and without interruption for the required legal period. Statutory authority may protect
an act authorised by law, provided reasonable precautions are taken. However, statutory
permission does not justify unnecessary or negligent harm. [Word Count: 423]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://blog.ipleaders.in/the-tort-of-nuisance/
passages.LEG-P0236:
XIV. The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation is an important principle of constitutional law that prevents
legislatures from indirectly doing what they are not permitted to do directly. It is often described as
a “fraud on the Constitution” because it checks attempts by legislative bodies to exceed their
constitutional authority while appearing to act within legal limits. The doctrine originates from the
Latin maxim “quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum,” which means that
what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. In India, this doctrine was adopted from
Canadian and Australian constitutional practices during British rule and later became an integral
part of constitutional jurisprudence after independence. The doctrine primarily examines the
legislative competence of Parliament and State Legislatures.
It comes into operation when a legislature enacts a law on a subject over which it has no authority,
but disguises the legislation in a manner that makes it appear valid. The courts then look beyond
the form of the law to determine its real substance and purpose. If the true nature of the legislation
reveals that the legislature has trespassed into a field outside its constitutional powers, the law
may be declared void. This doctrine is closely linked to Article 246 of the Constitution of India,
which distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States through the Union List,
State List, and Concurrent List. By applying this doctrine, courts ensure that neither Parliament
nor State Legislatures encroach upon each other’s constitutionally assigned domains.
However, the doctrine has certain limitations. It applies only to questions of legislative competence
and not to the wisdom, necessity, or motives behind a law. It is also generally inapplicable where
there are no constitutional restrictions on legislative power and does not usually extend to
subordinate legislation. The intention of the legislature, whether good or bad, is not the focus; the
only concern is whether the law falls within its constitutional authority. A significant case related
to this doctrine is R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills (1977), where the Supreme Court clarified that colourable
legislation arises when a legislature lacks the power to enact a law but attempts to create the
appearance of possessing such authority. Thus, the doctrine serves as an essential safeguard for
maintaining constitutional balance and federal governance in India.
Source: Extracted with edits from https://blog.ipleaders.in/doctrine-of-colourable-legislation/
passages.LEG-P0237:
XV. Article 22 of Constitution: Article 22 is a fundamental right of protection against arrest and
detention in certain cases. Clauses (1) and (2) of Article 22 confer four rights upon a person
who has been arrested. Firstly, he shall not be detained in custody without being informed, as
soon as may be, of the grounds of his arrest. If information is delayed, there must be some
reasonable ground justified by the circumstances. The grounds of arrest must be informed in a
language understandable by the arrestee. Secondly, he shall have the right to consult and to
be represented by a lawyer of his own choice. This right too is not lost if he is released on bail.
Thirdly, every person who has been arrested has the right to be produced before the nearest
Magistrate within 24 hours of his arrest. In computing this period of 24 hours, the time spent
on the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the Magistrate is to be excluded. This
requirement is dispensed with if the person arrested is admitted to bail. Fourthly, he is not to
be detained in custody beyond the said period of 24 hours without the authority of the court.
Even if an accused is initially illegally detained, the detention becomes lawful when
subsequently he is arrested and produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours. But where
remand orders are obtained by the police from the Magistrate or a Judge without producing
the arrested person before such Magistrate or Judge within 24 hours, Article 22(2) is violated.
An undertrial prisoner need not be arrested separately for every criminal case pending against
him. A subsequent lawful detention is not vitiated by the earlier illegal detention.
The two requirements of clause (1) of Article 22 are meant to afford the earliest opportunity to
the arrested person to remove any mistake, misapprehension or misunderstanding in the
mind of the arresting authority and also to know exactly what the accusation against him is,
so that he can exercise the second right, namely, of consulting a legal practitioner of his choice
and to be defended by him.
Source: Constitution of India by V.N.Shukla
passages.LEG-P0238:
XII. Current: The Bombay High Court recently held that recording a conference call between two
officials of Maharashtra Metro Corporation Limited (MMCL) and sharing it with another
official would not amount to “spying” under the Official Secrets Act, 1923 (OSA), since the
MMCL office does not fall within the meaning of a “prohibited place” under the Act. An FIR
was lodged against Pravin Samarth, Assistant Manager of MMCL, alleging offences under
Section 3 of the OSA and Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act. The allegation was that Samarth
recorded conference calls between senior officials and later shared them with another
employee. The prosecution claimed that this amounted to spying and unlawful disclosure of
departmental information. The High Court noted that the office of MMCL was not a
“prohibited place” and that the facts did not show any conduct prejudicial to the sovereignty,

integrity, or safety of the State. At the same time, it found that the unauthorised recording
and sharing of official communications could amount to dishonest and fraudulent interference
with computer resources and communication systems.
Section 3 of the OSA penalises acts of spying and other conduct prejudicial to the safety or
interests of the State. For the offence to be made out, the act must relate to information,
places, or communications covered by the statutory framework of the OSA, particularly where
the conduct concerns a “prohibited place” or implicates State security. Section 2(8) defines
“prohibited place” and ordinarily refers to strategic, defence, or security-sensitive locations.
The Court held that an MMCL office does not fall within this definition, and therefore Section
3 was not attracted merely because an official conversation was recorded and shared.
The Court, however, held that Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act were attracted. Section 43
imposes civil liability where a person, without permission, accesses, downloads, copies, or
extracts data from a computer, computer system, or network, or interferes with its operation.
Section 66 makes such acts punishable where they are done dishonestly or fraudulently. The
Court observed that the unauthorised recording and sharing of conference calls fell within the
scope of Section 43, and the dishonest sharing of that information with another person brought
the case within Section 66 as well.
The Court also referred to the Maharashtra Metro Rail Corporation Limited Rules, under
which employees are prohibited from communicating official information to unauthorised
persons except in accordance with authorised orders or in good faith performance of duties. On
this basis, the Court held that the applicant’s conduct was not only unethical but also
suggestive of dishonest intention.
Source: hitps://www.livelaw.in/high-court/bombay-high-court/bombay-high-court-recording-
phone-calls-officials-sharing-spying-529973
passages.LEG-P0239:
XIV. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 marked a significant shift in Indian
law by recognising that violence within the home is not merely a private or personal matter, but a
legal wrong requiring enforceable remedies. Before this legislation, women facing abuse in
domestic relationships often had to depend on limited criminal provisions, such as cruelty under
matrimonial or penal law, or pursue separate civil proceedings for residence, maintenance, or
custody. The 2005 Act changed this position by creating a specialised legal framework that treats
domestic violence as a rights-based issue connected with dignity, bodily integrity, residence, and
security within the household.
A major feature of the Act is the broad statutory meaning of domestic violence. It is not confined to
physical assault or bodily injury. The law also covers sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse,
and economic abuse. Economic abuse includes deprivation of financial resources, disposal of
household assets, denial of maintenance, and restricting access to property or necessities to which
the aggrieved woman is entitled. Because of this broad definition, conduct that may not amount to
visible physical violence can still fall within the scope of the Act if it harms the woman’s safety,
well-being, dignity, or ability to live with security.
The Act applies to an aggrieved woman who is, or has been, in a domestic relationship with the
respondent. A domestic relationship includes relationships by marriage, blood, adoption, or a
relationship in the nature of marriage, provided the parties live or have lived together in a shared
household. Therefore, the protection is not confined only to legally wedded wives; it may also
extend to mothers, sisters, widows, and women in certain non-formal domestic arrangements, if the
statutory conditions are satisfied. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Another important principle is that the Act provides mainly civil remedies, though it is supported
by criminal procedure and enforcement. The Magistrate may grant protection orders, residence
orders, monetary relief, custody orders, and compensation. The law specifically recognises a
woman’s right to reside in the shared household, irrespective of ownership or title. It also imposes

duties on police officers, Magistrates, Protection Officers, service providers, shelter homes, and
medical facilities to assist the aggrieved person. Thus, the Act reflects the legal principle that
domestic violence is not outside the concern of law, and that the State must provide immediate,
practical, and effective remedies to secure a violence-free domestic environment.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from,
https://repository.nls.ac.in/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1083&context=nlsir
passages.LEG-P0240:
XII. The doctrine of jus necessitatis, or necessity, has deep historical roots and recognises that in
certain exceptional situations, an act which would otherwise be unlawful may be justified if it
is done to prevent a greater harm. Medieval jurists such as Henry de Bracton stated that “that
which is otherwise not lawful is made lawful by necessity,” and Roman law reflected the same
idea in the maxim “Necessitas non habet legem’, meaning necessity knows no law. The
doctrine therefore developed as a legal justification for urgent acts done for survival,
preservation, or prevention of serious harm. In modern terms, jus necessitatis means a person
may do something technically illegal if it is necessary to avoid a more serious injury or danger.
A common example is breaking into a house to rescue a child trapped in a fire: the trespass is
excused because the saving of life is the higher value.

In common law, the doctrine of necessity is mainly used as a defence, especially in criminal
law, though it has also appeared in administrative and constitutional law. It is supported by
the maxims “Quod necessitas non habet legem” and “Necessitas vincit legem”, the latter
meaning necessity triumphs over law. In India, the doctrine is codified in Section 81 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860, which states that an act likely to cause harm is not an offence if it is
done without criminal intention, in good faith, and for the purpose of preventing or avoiding
other harm to person or property. This Section 81 requires two essential conditions: absence of
criminal intent and good faith, along with the idea that the harm prevented must be greater
than the harm caused. For example, destroying one house to stop a fire from spreading to an
entire neighbourhood may be justified under Section 81.
Indian courts have recognised this doctrine in cases such as Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v.
APSRTC (1958) and Election Commission of India v. Dr. Subramaniam Swamy (1996), the
latter stressing that the doctrine should apply only in cases of absolute necessity.
International cases also illustrate its limits. In Regina v. Dudley and Stephens (1884),
necessity was rejected as a defence to murder, while United States v. Holmes (1842) and Rex
v. Bourne (1938) show that it may apply under strict conditions. The doctrine, however, is
limited by requirements of proportionality, good faith, absence of alternatives, and absolute
necessity. Though criticised for possible misuse, ambiguity, and erosion of legal certainty, it
remains an important legal principle for dealing with extraordinary situations where rigid
obedience to law would produce greater injustice.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.taxmann.com/post/blog/what-
is-discharge-of-a-contract-under-indian-contract-act-1872-featuring-case-studies/
passages.LEG-P0241:
XIV. The ongoing Sabarimala reference before a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court has revived
a foundational constitutional debate on the relationship between Articles 25 and 26 and the
continued validity of the Essential Religious Practice (ERP) test. The ERP test emerged from
an obiter observation in Durgah Committee v. Syed Hussain Ali (1961), where the Court
stated that only those practices which are “essential and integral” to a religion deserve
protection under Article 26. This modified the earlier approach in Shirur Mutt (1954), where
the Court had principally distinguished between secular practices, which can be regulated,
and religious practices, which receive constitutional protection. The present reference
therefore raises a central issue: whether courts should continue identifying essential religious
practices, or whether the inquiry should only be whether a practice is religious or secular.
During the hearing, Justice BV Nagarathna suggested that once a practice is determined to be
strictly secular, everything else would fall within the religious sphere, making the ERP test
unnecessary. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, however, noted that even such a distinction
would still require the Court to evolve standards for deciding what counts as religious and
what counts as secular, thereby bringing the inquiry back to the same constitutional problem.
Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan argued that the ERP test should be abandoned
because Articles 25 and 26 themselves are clear, and that religious affairs should be
understood through the constitutional text rather than broad judicial labels. In his
submission, Article 25(1), which is expressly made “subject to the other provisions” of Part III,
should be read as subject mainly to horizontal equality provisions such as Articles 15(2), 17,
23, and 24, whereas Article 26 stands on a stronger footing because it does not contain the
same phrase.
A major interpretive issue is whether Article 26(b), which protects a denomination’s right to
manage its own affairs in matters of religion, is subject to Article 25(2)(b), which permits the
State to enact laws for social reform and temple entry for all classes and sections of Hindus.
Article 25(2)(b) permits the State to make laws for social welfare and reform, including
throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of
Hindus. Article 26(b) protects a denomination’s right to manage its own affairs in matters of
religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Sai Deepak argued that Article 26 is not
controlled by Article 25(2), and that denominational rights were deliberately insulated from
broader constitutional limitations. In contrast, Senior Advocate Gopal Subramanium argued
that Article 26 must be harmonised with Article 25(2)(a) and (b), so that denominational
temples may still be subject to reform laws opening access to excluded classes. Thus, the
reference now squarely presents two major constitutional questions: whether the ERP doctrine
should survive, and how individual religious freedom under Article 25 must be reconciled with
collective denominational autonomy under Article 26. [Word Count: 484]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.livelaw.in/top-
stories /sabarimala-reference-supreme-court-debates-essential-religious-practice-test-
denominational-rights-vs-state-reform-power-531226
passages.LEG-P0242:
XIV. In tort law, when a wrongful act is committed by more than one person, the persons involved
may be joint tortfeasors or independent tortfeasors. Joint tortfeasors are those who act
together or in furtherance of a common design, resulting in damage to another person. Their
liability is joint and several, which means that each tortfeasor is individually liable for the
entire damage and also collectively liable with the others. Independent tortfeasors, on the
other hand, act separately and without coordination. Even if their separate acts cause the
same injury, their liability arises from separate causes of action. In The Koursk, it was
observed that joint liability requires concerted action towards a common end, and mere
similarity of conduct is not enough.
The difference between independent and joint tortfeasors is important for determining
remedies. In Thompson v. London County Council, damage occurred due to separate negligent
acts of different parties, and the Court held that they were not joint tortfeasors because their
acts were independent. Similarly, in The Koursk, two ships were treated as independent
tortfeasors because there was no common design. Joint liability may arise in cases of agency,
vicarious liability, or common action. Under agency, if one person authorises another to act on
his behalf, both may be liable for torts committed within that authority. Vicarious liability
arises from relationships such as employer and employee, where one person is made liable for
the wrongful act of another. Joint liability also arises where two or more persons act together,
assist, or instigate a tort.www.lawpreptutorial.com
The doctrine of joint and several liability protects the injured party by allowing the plaintiff to
sue all tortfeasors together, sue any one of them individually, or recover the entire
compensation from any one tortfeasor. This ensures that the plaintiff is not left without
remedy if one wrongdoer is insolvent. In Arneil v. Peterson, each defendant was held liable for
the whole damage caused.
Under old English common law, once judgment was obtained against one joint tortfeasor, the
cause of action merged in that judgment, as held in Brinsmead v. Harrison. Another rule in
Merryweather v. Nixon denied contribution between tortfeasors. These rules were harsh and

were later modified by the Law Reform (Married Women and Tortfeasors) Act, 1935 and the
Civil Liability (Contribution) Act, 1978, which allowed contribution and fair apportionment. In
India, there is no complete statute on joint tortfeasors, so courts apply equity, justice, and good
conscience. In Nawal Kishore v. Rameshwar and Kushal Rao v. Babu Ram Ganapat Rao,
Indian courts rejected rigid English rules and accepted a fairer approach recognising joint and
several liability, contribution, and equitable distribution of responsibility. [Word Count: 4389]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://lawbhoomi.com/joint-and-several-
tort-feasors-in-torts/
passages.LEG-P0243:
XIV. Nuisance: The term 'nuisance' is made up of the French word 'nuire' and Latin word 'nocere'
or 'nocumentum' which in legal sense means ‘annoyance' or 'harm'. The element of unlawful
‘annoyance’ is the only thing common to all nuisances. Nuisance has been defined under two
categories - Public Nuisance and Private Nuisance. Public nuisance is a crime whereas private
nuisance is a civil wrong. To constitute the tort of nuisance, the following essentials are
required to be proved:
1. Unreasonable interference: Interference may cause damage to the plaintiff's property or
may cause personal discomfort to the plaintiff in the enjoyment of property. Every
interference is not a nuisance. To constitute nuisance, the interference should be
unreasonable. Every person must put up with some noise, some vibrations, some smell,
etc. so that members of the society can enjoy their own rights. An unreasonable activity
cannot be excused on the ground that reasonable care had been taken to prevent it from
becoming a nuisance.www.lawpreptutorial.com
2. Interference with the use of enjoyment of land: It may cause either -
(1) Injury to the property itself: An unauthorized interference with the use of the property
of another person through some object, tangible or intangible, which causes damage to
the property, is actionable as nuisance.
(2) Injury to the comfort or health of occupants of certain property: Substantial
interference with the comfort and convenience in using the premises is actionable as a
nuisance. A mere trifling or fanciful inconvenience is not enough. The rule is De
minimis non curat lex, that means that the law does not take account of very trifling
matters. The standard of comfort varies from time to time and place to place.
Inconvenience and discomfort from the point of view of a particular plaintiff is not the
test of nuisance but the test is how an average man residing in the same area would
take it.

8. Damage: Unlike trespass, which is actionable per se, actual damage is required to be
proved in an action for nuisance. In the case of public nuisance, the plaintiff can bring an
action in tort only when he proves a special damage to him. In private nuisance, although
damage is one of the essentials, the law will often presume it.
Source: Law of Torts by R. K. Bangia
passages.LEG-P0244:
XI. The Principles of Natural Justice are fundamental legal doctrines that ensure fairness,
impartiality, and reasoned decision-making in judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative
proceedings. Rooted in moral principles, Roman law, and common law traditions, they protect
individuals from arbitrary action by requiring due process in decision-making. Their historical
basis can be traced to ancient Greek and Roman thought, medieval jurists such as Henry de
Bracton, and even religious narratives that emphasised giving a person an opportunity to explain
before punishment. In modern Indian law, the Supreme Court in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief
Election Commissioner affirmed that fairness is essential in all forms of state decision-making. The
three core principles of natural justice are the hearing rule (audi alteram partem), the bias rule
(nemo judex in causa sua), and the requirement of a reasoned decision or speaking order.

The first principle, audi alteram partem, means that no person should be condemned without being
given a fair opportunity to be heard. It requires proper notice, a chance to present evidence and
arguments, the opportunity to cross-examine where necessary, and adjudication by an unbiased
authority. The second principle, nemo judex in causa sua, ensures that no one should be a judge in
their own cause. This rule guards against different forms of bias such as personal bias, pecuniary
bias, subject matter bias, departmental bias, policy notion bias, and bias due to stubbornness. The
third principle requires that every decision must be supported by reasons. A speaking order
promotes transparency, prevents arbitrariness, enables appeal or judicial review, and strengthens
accountability. These principles have become vital in administrative law, especially after Maneka
Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Supreme Court emphasised that fairness,
reasonableness, and justice are essential in procedures affecting rights and liberties.
Although natural justice is fundamental, it is not absolute and admits certain exceptions. It may be
excluded or modified in emergency situations, where immediate action is necessary for public
safety; by express statutory exclusion, where legislation validly limits procedural safeguards;
where disclosure would prejudice public interest, such as matters of national security; where
prompt action is needed; or where it is impracticable to hold a hearing or appeal. It may also be
relaxed in purely administrative matters, where no substantial legal right is affected, or where no
right of the person is infringed. Courts may also overlook procedural defects if they would have
made no difference to the outcome, or where the decision-maker acted in good faith without fault.
Even in such cases, however, these exceptions must be applied cautiously so that fairness,
transparency, and the protection of individual rights remain central to the legal process.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from,
https://www.socialresearchfoundation.com/new/publish-journal.php?editID=91 11
passages.LEG-P0245:
XVI. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act),
operationalizing Article 21A of the Constitution, mandates free and compulsory education for
all children aged 6-14 years and was enforced from April 1, 2010. The constitutional journey
toward this right began with Article 45, a non-justiciable Directive Principle directing the
State to provide free education to children up to age 14 within ten years of the Constitution's
commencement. Judicial intervention transformed this aspiration into enforceable law through
Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992), which read the right to education into Article 21,
and Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), which held that free education up to age
14 is a fundamental right. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A,
guaranteeing free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14, amended Article 45 to
provide for early childhood care for children below six years, and added Article 51A(k)
imposing a fundamental duty on parents and guardians to provide educational opportunities.
The RTE Act establishes minimum norms for school infrastructure, teacher qualifications, and
pupil-teacher ratios while prohibiting physical punishment, capitation fees, screening
procedures, and denial of admission. Critically, Section 12(1)(c) requires private unaided
schools to reserve 25% of entry-level seats (Class I or pre-primary where it exists) for children
from economically weaker and disadvantaged groups, with State reimbursement to the extent
of per-child expenditure in government schools. Educational institutions are categorized into:
government schools (fully state-funded), aided private schools (privately managed but
receiving financial aid, obligated to provide free seats proportionate to aid received), unaided
private schools (privately managed without state funding), and minority educational
institutions established and administered by linguistic or religious minorities under Article

80(1). In Society for Unaided Private Schools v. Union of India (2012), the Supreme Court
upheld the RTE Act's applicability to government, aided, and unaided non-minority private
schools while exempting unaided minority institutions. Subsequently, the five-judge
Constitution Bench in Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) held
that the RTE Act is entirely inapplicable to minority institutions—both aided and unaided—
reasoning that forcing admission of 25% children from outside the minority community would
dilute their character and infringe their Article 30(1) right to administer institutions of their
choice. This exempted minority institutions from all RTE obligations, not merely Section
12(1)(c). Recently, a two-judge Bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Manmohan
questioned the correctness of Pramati, observing that exempting minority schools may
jeopardize Article 21A rights of children studying therein. The Court emphasized that Article
80(1) minority rights and Article 21A child education rights must be harmoniously interpreted
rather than one trumping the other, and referred the question to a larger Constitution Bench
for reconsideration.
Source: extracted with edits and revision from https: //www.scobserver.in/journal/should-
certain-provisions-of-the-rte-act-apply-to-minority-educational-institutions.
passages.LEG-P0246:
XI.	Criminal trespass is defined under Section 329 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).
According to this provision, a person commits criminal trespass when they enter into or upon
property in the possession of another with the intent to commit an offence, or to intimidate,
insult, or annoy the person in possession of that property. Criminal trespass may also occur
when a person lawfully enters property but subsequently remains there unlawfully with the
intent to intimidate, insult, annoy the possessor, or commit an offence. In simple terms,
criminal trespass involves unauthorised entry into another person’s property or unlawful
remaining on the property with a wrongful intention. The essential ingredients of criminal
trespass include unlawful entry, possession of property by another person, unlawful remaining
even after lawful entry, and the presence of criminal intent. Examples include entering
someone’s private garden or farmland without permission, refusing to leave a place after being
asked to do so, or entering a fenced property without authorisation. The punishment for
criminal trespass under Section 329(3), BNS is imprisonment for up to three months, or a fine
up to %5,000, or both.
House trespass is a more serious form of criminal trespass and is defined under Section 330 of
the BNS. The concepts of house-trespass and house-breaking are dealt with in Section 330,
BNS. It occurs when criminal trespass is committed by entering or remaining in a building,
tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling, a place of worship, or a place for the custody of
property. House trespass therefore involves intrusion into private or protected spaces such as
homes, offices, religious institutions, or storage facilities. Even introducing any part of the
body, such as a hand through a window, may amount to house trespass. Examples include
breaking into someone’s house without permission, entering an office building with the
intention of committing theft, or unlawfully entering a temple, mosque, or church. The
punishment for house trespass under Section 329(4), BNS is imprisonment for up to one year,
or a fine up to 75,000, or both. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The key difference between criminal trespass and house trespass lies in the nature of the
property involved. Criminal trespass may occur on any property, including open land or fenced
areas, whereas house trespass specifically involves buildings or structures used for dwelling,
worship, or storage. Both offences require the same intent to commit an offence or to
intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor, but house trespass is treated as more serious
because it invades spaces associated with privacy and security. More aggravated forms also
exist, such as house-breaking, which is now covered under Section 330, BNS, and punishment
for lurking house-trespass or house-breaking is dealt with under Section 331, BNS. [Word
Count: 448]
