passages.LEG-P0247:
XIII. A quasi-contract is a legal remedy developed by courts to address situations where one party is
unjustly enriched at the expense of another, even though there is no formal agreement or
mutual consent between the parties. The term “quasi” comes from Latin meaning “as if,” and
therefore a quasi-contract is treated as if it were a contract despite lacking essential elements
such as offer, acceptance and consideration. Quasi-contractual obligations are imposed by law
to prevent unfair benefit and ensure that no individual gains at the expense of another. These
obligations are involuntary and arise without the intention of the parties, and their main
objective is restitution, which restores the aggrieved party to the position they were in before
the unjust enrichment occurred.
The key features of quasi-contracts include the absence of agreement between the parties, the
fact that they are imposed by law rather than created by consent, and the remedy of
restitution to compensate the party who suffered loss. The doctrine underlying quasi-contracts
is the doctrine of unjust enrichment, expressed in the maxim “Nemo debet locupletari ex
aliena jactura,” meaning no one should be enriched at another’s expense. In India, quasi-
contracts are codified under Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Section 68
deals with necessaries supplied to a person incapable of contracting, such as a minor, where
reimbursement can be claimed from the person’s property. Section 69 provides that a person
who pays money on behalf of another to protect their own interest is entitled to
reimbursement. Section 70 states that when a person lawfully provides goods or services
without intending them to be gratuitous and the other party benefits, the recipient must
compensate for the benefit. Section 71 imposes responsibility on a finder of goods to take
reasonable care and return them to the rightful owner. Section 72 provides that money paid by
mistake or under coercion must be returned.

The concept evolved from English common law and was articulated in the landmark case of
Moses v. MacFarlane (1760), where Lord Mansfield emphasised the obligation to refund
money received unjustly. Indian courts have also recognised this principle in cases such as
State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai (1964) and Hari Ram Sheth Khandsari v.
Commissioner of Sales Tax (1958), where restitution was ordered for money paid by mistake.
Unlike express contracts which are based on mutual consent and clearly defined terms, quasi-
contracts are imposed by law and apply only in limited situations to prevent unjust
enrichment. [Word Count: 413]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/contracts-and-
doctrine-of-quasi-contracts-in-india/
passages.LEG-P0248:
III. The doctrine of "Volenti Non Fit Injuria" plays a critical role. This Latin maxim, translating to "no injury is
done to one who consents,” essentially states that individuals who knowingly and willingly consent to activities
bearing inherent risks are precluded from seeking damages for any resulting injury. This principle rests on the
idea that consenting adults are aware of the risks involved and, thus, cannot hold others liable if harm occurs
during such activities.
The doctrine applies primarily to cases involving clear and informed consent, where the individual understands
the nature of the risk and voluntarily agrees to accept it. Common scenarios include sports, medical procedures,
and certain contractual agreements. In each instance, the person engaged has acknowledged and accepted the
potential for harm, negating their ability to claim compensation later.
However, the application of "Volenti Non Fit Injuria” is not absolute. Legal exceptions occur when consent is
obtained through deceptive means such as fraud, coercion, or misrepresentation, rendering the consent invalid.
Moreover, the principle does not apply if the defendant's actions were illegal or if they acted with gross
negligence exceeding what was consented to.
In sports, for example, players assume the normal risks associated with the game but do not consent to conduct
that is outside the rules and could cause unexpected harm. Similarly, patients undergoing surgery give informed
consent only for the risks disclosed to them prior to the operation, not for medical negligence or errors beyond
those risks.


Furthermore, this legal doctrine is carefully evaluated in situations involving rescuers. When the plaintiff suffers
an injury as a result of him doing an act which he knows is likely to cause harm to him but it is an act to rescue
someone, then this defence will not apply and the defendant will be held liable. Therefore, they can seek redress
for injuries sustained during the rescue.
"Volenti Non Fit Injuria” also intersects with public policy, which sometimes limits its application to ensure that
individuals are not unduly pressured into accepting risks that are unreasonable or inherently dangerous.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://www.legalserviceindia.com/legal/article-13963-volenti-
non-fit-injuria-essentials-andexceptions.html
passages.LEG-P0249:
XIV. The Supreme Court of India has established stringent safeguards for convictions based on
circumstantial evidence, where no direct eyewitness testimony exists and guilt must be inferred
from surrounding facts. In the landmark judgment of Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of
Maharashtra, the Court articulated the "Five Golden Principles" or "Panchsheel of Circumstantial
Evidence": (1) circumstances must be fully established, (2) they must be consistent only with the
guilt of the accused, (3) they must be conclusive in nature and tendency, (4) they must exclude
every possible hypothesis except guilt, and (5) there must be a complete chain of evidence with no
missing links. These principles mandate extreme judicial caution because conviction relies on
inference rather than direct observation, creating possibilities for human error, conjecture, and
suspicion masquerading as proof. The First Information Report (FIR), though not substantive
evidence, plays a crucial evidentiary role. Under Section 11 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
omissions of important facts in the FIR are relevant in judging witness veracity, as recognized in
Ram Kumar Pandey v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Omissions become particularly serious when
known accused names are absent, crucial facts appear only in later statements, or the FIR
contradicts the prosecution's subsequent narrative. In circumstantial cases, such omissions
significantly weaken the evidentiary chain. Test Identification Parades (TIP), conducted before a
Magistrate during investigation, serve to test a witness's memory and identification capacity. As
clarified in P. Sasikumar v. State, while TIP itself is not substantive evidence, dock identification

in court constitutes substantive evidence. However, when the accused is a stranger to the witness
and no TIP was conducted, dock identification becomes inherently unsafe due to memory
degradation, possible police exposure influencing recognition, and the suggestive nature of
courtroom settings. The "last seen theory" whereby guilt may be inferred if accused and deceased
were last seen together shortly before death requires extreme caution. In State of U.P. v. Satish,
the Court held that the time gap must be so minimal that third-party intervention is effectively
ruled out. This principle was consistently reiterated in Hatti Singh v. State of Haryana, Chattar
Singh v. State of Haryana, and Krishan Kumar v. State of Haryana, where the Court emphasized
that last seen evidence alone is insufficient, requires corroboration, and cannot be stretched
through conjecture or across wide time gaps. Scientific evidence including DNA analysis,
fingerprints, Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) reports, serology, and ballistics provides objective,
independent verification less prone to human bias. When scientific evidence is neutral or
exculpatory such as DNA mismatches, blood group inconsistencies, or failure to link weapons,
courts cannot ignore these findings and convict on suspicion alone. The fundamental principle,
articulated in Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh, mandates that when two views are possible
one indicating guilt and another innocence the accused must receive the benefit of doubt.
Suspicion, regardless of strength, cannot substitute proof beyond reasonable doubt, which remains
the immutable standard in criminal law.
passages.LEG-P0250:
XV. ‘The interpretation of contracts in Indian law follows a structured methodology balancing textual
fidelity with commercial realism. The literal rule serves as the foundational principle, requiring
courts to give contractual terms their plain, grammatical, and ordinary meaning. When language
is clear and unambiguous, courts will not look beyond the text, respecting party autonomy and the
principle of consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). However, the golden rule permits departure
from literal interpretation when it leads to absurd, commercially irrational, or internally
inconsistent outcomes. Courts may adjust meaning sufficiently to avoid absurdity but cannot
rewrite contractual terms to achieve fairness or commercial wisdom.
The purposive approach, borrowed from statutory interpretation, allows courts to examine the
factual matrix and commercial background surrounding the agreement, considering related
documentation, parties' conduct, and the agreement's overall structure. This approach was
articulated in Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd. v. West Bromwich Building Society, where
Lord Hoffmann established that interpretation requires objective understanding as a reasonable
person would have at the time of contracting, considering the matrix of facts available to parties
while excluding prior negotiations and subjective intentions. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The parol evidence rule, codified in Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
restricts use of external evidence to contradict clear written terms, as affirmed in Mangala
Waman Karandikar v. Prakash Damodar Ranade. This ensures the written agreement stands as
the final expression of intent. The doctrine of business efficacy permits courts to imply terms
when essential to ensure contracts deliver their intended commercial result, tested through the
officious bystander test—whether both parties would have agreed with "of course" if the term
had been suggested during negotiations. As applied in Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development
Authority v. Unity Infraprojects Ltd., this doctrine gives practical effect to contracts when written
text insufficiently conveys parties' intention, without rewriting agreements. The contra
proferentem rule resolves persistent ambiguity against the drafting party, particularly in
insurance and consumer contracts or where bargaining power is unequal.
The principle of harmonious construction requires reconciling potentially conflicting
provisions within the same contract, ensuring no clause becomes redundant and the document
operates as an internally coherent whole. Courts also apply what may be termed the principle
against disguise: where parties structure agreements to conceal true commercial nature, courts
examine substance over form, looking beyond surface terminology to reveal actual commercial
effect. This principle reflects the judicial posture that legal consequences flow from substance, not
presentation.
passages.LEG-P0251:
XII. The Special Marriage Act, 1954 is a secular law enacted by Parliament to provide a civil form
of marriage for individuals irrespective of religion or faith. The concept of a secular marriage
law in India dates back to the nineteenth century during British rule, when marriage was
largely governed by religious customs. In 1872, Sir Henry Sumner Maine introduced Act III of
1872, known as the Special Marriage Act, 1872, to allow dissenters to marry under civil law.
However, the Act required parties to declare that they did not profess any religion, making it
impractical. After independence, the Special Marriage Act, 1954 replaced the earlier law and
allowed people of any religion to marry without renouncing their faith. The Act applies to all
Indian citizens, inter-religious and inter-caste couples, Indian nationals living abroad, and
marriages between an Indian citizen and a foreign national in India. It also connects with the
Foreign Marriage Act, 1969 for citizens domiciled abroad. Marriage under the Act is civil in
nature and is treated as a legal contract solemnised before a Marriage Officer and witnesses
rather than through religious rituals.

The conditions for a valid marriage are laid down in Section 4. Neither party should have a
living spouse, both parties must have the mental capacity to give valid consent, the male must
have completed 21 years and the female 18 years, and the parties must not fall within
prohibited degrees of relationship unless permitted by custom. The procedure for marriage
begins with a notice of intended marriage under Section 5, which must be given to the
Marriage Officer of the district where one party has resided for at least thirty days. The notice
is entered and published under Section 6, and objections can be raised within thirty days
under Sections 7—8 if the conditions of Section 4 are violated. Before solemnization, the parties
and three witnesses sign a declaration under Section 11, and the marriage is solemnized
under Section 12 by a verbal declaration before the Marriage Officer. After the ceremony, a
marriage certificate under Section 13 is issued, which is conclusive proof of marriage. If the
marriage is not solemnized within three months, the notice lapses under Section 14. Existing
marriages may also be registered under Sections 15-18.
The Act also regulates legal consequences and matrimonial remedies. Under Section 19, a
Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jaina marrying under this Act is deemed to sever from the joint
family, while succession is generally governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 under
Sections 20—21A. Children born from such marriages are legitimate. Matrimonial remedies
include restitution of conjugal rights (Section 22), judicial separation (Section 23), void and
voidable marriages (Sections 24-25), and divorce (Sections 27-28) on grounds such as
adultery, cruelty, desertion, imprisonment, mental disorder, venereal disease, or
disappearance for seven years. [Word Count: 471]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in
passages.LEG-P0252:
II. In a recent Supreme Court ruling, it was determined that a Hindu couple had not legally married despite
holding a marriage certificate, as their marriage was registered under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA)
before performing the necessary wedding rituals. This decision emphasizes the requirement for fulfilling
specific ceremonial rituals to validate a marriage under the HMA, notably those outlined in Sections 7 and 5.
Section 5 of the HMA outlines the conditions for a Hindu marriage, mandating that certain conditions be met
for a marriage to be considered valid. These conditions include the requirement for neither party to have a
spouse living at the time of marriage, both parties to be of sound mind and capable of giving valid consent,
neither party suffering from mental disorders that would render them unfit for marriage and procreation, and
that the bride and groom should not fall within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits.
The distinction between marriage registration and solemnization is crucial under the HMA. Solemnization
refers to the actual marriage ceremonies required by religious practices, which are essential for a marriage to be
recognized as valid under personal laws. In contrast, registration is a formal act of record-keeping that typically
follows the solemnization of the marriage. Under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), a civil or "registered"
marriage occurs where the marriage is solemnized without traditional rituals in a registrar's office, and the
registration itself validates the marriage.
For Hindus and some Christian communities in India, marriage is considered a sacrament, necessitating specific
religious ceremonies for a valid union. Conversely, Islamic marriages are based on contractual principles,

requiring mutual consent and witnesses but not ceremonial rites. The nikahnama in Islamic traditions formalizes
the union and is generally recognized even without additional state registration.
Several states, including Karnataka and Delhi, mandate the registration of marriages, highlighting its
importance for legal recognition and administrative purposes. This registration is vital in contexts requiring
proof of marital status, such as applications for spousal visas or inheritance claims.
However, the non-registration of a marriage under the HMA does not inherently invalidate it if the required
rituals are observed. While a marriage certificate under the SMA is conclusive evidence of marriage, under the
HMA, the certificate alone is insufficient without the completion of specified rituals, per Sections 5 and 7.
Source: Extracted with edits and revision from https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/explained-law/do-
marriages-need-to-be-registered9315506/
passages.LEG-P0253:
SECTION III
X.	International Environmental Law is guided by several principles that balance State
sovereignty with the need to protect the environment. The Principle of State Sovereignty
recognises that every State is a coequal sovereign and has exclusive jurisdiction over its
territory. States are free to manage their natural resources and environmental policies, but
this freedom is not unlimited. Principle 21 of the Stockholm Declaration, 1972 and Principle 2
of the Rio Declaration, 1992 recognise the sovereign right of States to exploit their own
resources, while imposing responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction do
not cause environmental damage to other States or areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Closely connected to State sovereignty is the Principle of Good Neighborliness, based on the
maxim sic utere tuo ut alienum non laedas, meaning that one must use one’s property in a
manner that does not injure another. It requires States not to allow the use of their territory
for acts contrary to the rights of other States. The Trail Smelter case affirmed that no State
has the right to use or permit use of its territory in a manner causing serious injury to another
State by fumes, where injury is proved by clear and convincing evidence. The Lake Lanoux
case also shows the importance of good faith, consultation, and care in transboundary
environmental matters.
The Principle of Common Heritage of Mankind treats certain resources and areas beyond
national jurisdiction, particularly the deep seabed and outer space, as belonging to all
humanity. Its core elements include non-appropriation, cooperative management, equal
sharing of benefits, and preservation for future generations. It is based on a rejection of res
nullius and acceptance of res communis, though it remains controversial because it challenges
traditional ideas of sovereignty and resource allocation.
The Principle of Cooperation and Integration requires States to act collectively in conserving
and restoring the environment. Principle 24 of Stockholm and Principle 7 of Rio emphasise
cooperation, exchange of information, prior notification, consultation, emergency notification,
technology transfer, and financial assistance. The Convention on Biological Diversity also
reflects this approach. Common but Differentiated Responsibilities further recognises that all
States share environmental duties, but developed countries must bear greater responsibility
due to their historical contribution, financial capacity, and technological resources, as reflected
in the Rio Declaration, UNFCCC, and Kyoto Protocol.
Sustainable Development means development that meets present needs without compromising
future generations. It includes economic development, environmental protection, social
welfare, inter-generational equity, sustainable use, integration, cooperation, poverty
eradication, and financial assistance. The Precautionary Principle requires preventive action
even without full scientific certainty, especially where serious or irreversible harm is likely.
The Polluter Pays Principle makes the polluter bear environmental costs. Inter-Generational

Equity requires conservation of options, quality, and access for future generations.
Environmental Impact Assessment is anticipatory, participatory, and systematic, while the
Public Trust Doctrine obliges the State to protect air, water, forests, sea, and other natural
resources for public use rather than private exploitation.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/important-principles-
of-environmental-law/
passages.LEG-P0254:
XIII. The doctrine of colourable legislation is an important constitutional principle used to examine
whether a legislature has acted within the limits of its law-making power. It is based on the
maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. A legislature may appear
to make a law within its authority, but if the real substance of the law enters a field beyond its
constitutional competence, the law may be treated as colourable legislation.
In India, legislative powers are distributed mainly through Articles 245 and 246 of the
Constitution and the Seventh Schedule. Article 245(1) provides that, subject to the
Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India, and a State
Legislature may make laws for the whole or any part of that State. Article 245(2) provides that
a law made by Parliament shall not be invalid merely because it has extra-territorial
operation.
Article 246 deals with the subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures.
Article 246(1) gives Parliament exclusive power to make laws on matters in List I, known as
the Union List. Article 246(2) allows both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on
matters in List III, known as the Concurrent List. Article 246(3) gives State Legislatures
exclusive power to make laws on matters in List II, known as the State List, subject to
Parliament’s powers under clauses (1) and (2). Article 246(4) allows Parliament to legislate for
any part of India not included in a State, even on matters in the State List.
If a legislature makes a law on a subject assigned to another legislature, it acts beyond its
competence. The doctrine prevents a legislature from disguising such an encroachment by
giving the law an appearance of validity. Courts do not depend merely on the title, form, or
language of the law. They examine the true nature, object, and effect of the legislation.
If the substance of the law falls within the legislature’s field, the law is valid even if it
incidentally affects another field. However, if the substance of the law belongs to an
unauthorised field, it cannot be saved merely because its wording appears lawful.
Colourable legislation is sometimes described as a fraud on the Constitution. This does not
mean dishonest intention. In constitutional law, the focus is on legislative competence, not
personal motive. If the legislature has no power to enact a law, its intention or policy reason
cannot make the law valid. [Word Count: 409]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://lawbhoomi.com/doctrine-of-
colourable-legislation/
passages.LEG-P0255:
XIV. The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to
guardian and ward. Before this legislation, guardianship matters were governed by different
personal laws and judicial practices. The Act introduced a uniform procedural framework with
the objective of providing a judicial mechanism for appointment and declaration of guardians,
protecting the person and property of minors, regulating the powers, duties, and liabilities of
guardians, preventing misuse of a minor’s property, and ensuring that the welfare of the minor
remains the controlling consideration. The Act extends to the whole of India and applies to all
minors under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, that is, ordinarily persons below 18 years, and
covers guardians of the person, property, or both. It becomes relevant in situations such as
death of parents, custody disputes, divorce or separation, management of minor’s property,
appointment of a guardian, or removal of an existing guardian. Though it does not override
specific adoption laws, guardianship disputes may still come within its scope.
Section 4 defines the key expressions: a minor is a person who has not attained majority, a
guardian is a person having care of the person or property of a minor or both, a ward is a
minor for whom there is a guardian, and the Court generally means the District Court having
jurisdiction. The Act is divided into four chapters dealing with preliminary matters,
appointment and declaration of guardians, duties and liabilities of guardians, and
supplemental provisions. Under Section 7, the Court may appoint or declare a guardian where
necessary for the welfare of the minor. Under Section 8, applications may be made by a
proposed guardian, a relative or friend, the Collector, or any authorised person. Section 9
governs jurisdiction, Section 10 prescribes the contents of the application, and Section 12
empowers the Court to issue interim orders for production, custody, or protection of property.
The most important provision is Section 17, which makes the welfare of the minor the guiding
principle and requires the Court to consider factors such as age, sex, religion, character and
capacity of the proposed guardian, nearness of kin, wishes of a deceased parent, and even the

intelligent preference of the minor if old enough. Section 19 places restrictions on appointment
where fit natural guardians are living.
Chapter III regulates the duties, rights, and liabilities of guardians. Under Section 20, the
guardian stands in a fiduciary position toward the ward. Sections 24 to 26 deal with the
guardian of the person, who is responsible for custody, support, health, education, and cannot
remove the minor from jurisdiction without permission. Sections 27, 29, and 31 deal with
guardians of property, requiring ordinary prudence in management and court permission
before sale, mortgage, transfer, or long lease of immovable property.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawcrust.in/guardians-and-wards-
act-1890/
passages.LEG-P0256:
XIV. Article 21 of the Constitution of India, contained in Part III, guarantees that “No person shall
be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.”
Though expressed in negative language, it confers positive protection on every “person,”
including citizens and non-citizens. Initially, in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, Article 21
was interpreted narrowly, and personal liberty was confined mainly to freedom from physical
restraint. However, in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, the Supreme Court transformed its
meaning by holding that any procedure depriving life or liberty must be just, fair, and
reasonable. The Court also linked Articles 14, 19, and 21, forming the “Golden Triangle” of
equality, freedom, and personal liberty.

The scope of Article 21 has expanded to include several rights necessary for a dignified
existence. The right to live with human dignity was recognised in Francis Coralie, Bandhua
Mukti Morcha, and People’s Union for Democratic Rights, covering basic necessities, humane
work conditions, protection from exploitation, and minimum wages. The right to livelihood was
recognised in Olga Tellis, while the right to shelter was developed in Shantistar Builders and
Chameli Singh. Article 21 also includes the right to health and emergency medical care, as
held in Parmananda Katara and Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity, and the right to
reproductive choices, recognised in Suchita Srivastava.
Article 21 also protects privacy, autonomy, and personal dignity. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union
of India, a nine-judge Bench declared privacy a fundamental right, including decisional
autonomy, bodily integrity, family, marriage, sexual orientation, and data protection. Earlier
cases such as Kharak Singh, Govind, and PUCL laid the foundation for privacy, including
protection against unlawful surveillance and telephone tapping. In Navtej Singh Johar, the
Court recognised intimate relations and sexual autonomy as part of dignity under Article 21.
The Article also covers criminal justice safeguards such as protection against illegal detention,
custodial violence, handcuffing, solitary confinement, delayed execution, and public hanging.
D.K. Basu, Joginder Kumar, Sunil Batra, and Prem Shankar established safeguards for
arrested persons and prisoners. The right to free legal aid, speedy trial, fair trial, bail, and
appeal has also been recognised under Article 21. However, in Gian Kaur, the Supreme Court
held that Article 21 does not include the right to die, though passive euthanasia and the right
to die with dignity have later been recognised under strict safeguards. Article 21 further
includes the right to pollution-free air, water, and clean environment through cases such as
Subhas Kumar, M.C. Mehta, and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://indiankanoon.org/doc
passages.LEG-P0257:
XVII. Article 20 clause (1) provides that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for
violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be
subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in
force at the time of the commission of the offence.
It means that a person cannot be punished for conduct that did not constitute an offence under
the law in force when it was committed, nor can a person be subjected to a penalty greater
than the penalty prescribed at that time. This protection is generally described as the
constitutional prohibition against ex post facto criminal laws.
The said article seeks to safeguard and protect the rights of those persons who are accused of
any crime and includes citizens, non- citizens as well as corporations. Even during a National
Emergency proclaimed under Article 352, the right to move a court for enforcement of Articles
20 and 21 cannot be suspended by an order under Article 359.
Article 20(1) does not itself prohibit a later criminal law from operating retrospectively when
the later law is beneficial to the accused. However, such benefit can be applied to earlier
offences or pending proceedings only where the later law, by its terms or necessary
implication, extends to such cases. Courts have allowed beneficial later laws to operate in this
manner where the purpose of the law is reformative or rehabilitative.
Article 20(1) prohibits the imposition of enhanced penalty or punishment. But it does not bar
any reduction in the punishment. In the case of Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab, (AIR 1965 SC
444) the accused a boy of 16 yrs of age was charged against the offence of outraging the
modesty of a girl aged 7 years and house trespass. The Magistrate imposed the punishment of
rigorous imprisonment of six months and fine. In the meantime, the Probation of Offenders
Act, 1958 came into force. Section 6 required that a person below 21 years of age should not
ordinarily be sentenced to imprisonment unless the court, after considering the circumstances
of the case and the probation officer’s report, found it undesirable to deal with him under
Sections 3 or 4. The accused claimed the benefit of this reformative law. The State argued that
the later Act could not apply to an earlier offence. The Supreme Court held that beneficial
operation of the later law was not barred by Article 20(1) and remitted the sentencing issue for
proper consideration under the Probation of Offenders Act.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from hitps://www.iilsindia.com/blogs/ex-post-
facto-law/
passages.LEG-P0258:
LEGAL REASONING

I. When a perpetual injunction is granted by the judgement, it ultimately disposes of the injunction suit. It is
ordered at the time when the final judgement is given. It is a final relief injunction and is not given on an
interim basis. The granting of a perpetual injunction is defined under Section 37(2) of the Specific Relief Act,
1963. The section says that only by the decree issued after an inquiry and on hearing the merits of the case can a
perpetual injunction be granted; the defendant is thus perpetually enjoined to exercise his right or to forever
pervade his conduct, which would be in conflict with the rights of the plaintiff. According to Section 38 of the
aforesaid Act, a perpetual injunction can be granted to the plaintiff when it is necessary to avoid a breach of
duty in his favour, either specifically or by consequences, subject to the other requirements contained or as
provided for in this Section; if such obligations arise out of the contract, the court shall be directed by the
provisions and rules contained in Chapter II of the Specific Relief Act, 1963; and when the defendant invades or


attempts to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property. The plaintiff must prove the breach of the
obligation by showing the infringement of a legal right; thus, the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff. The
plaintiff must also lawfully possess the item and must prove that the defendant had no legal possession over the
item. An injunction cannot be sustained on the basis of wrongful possession against the lawful owner.

Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 deals with the Mandatory Injunction. The section doesn’t clearly
define a mandatory injunction but deals with the grant of a mandatory injunction. The section says that in order
to prevent the breach of an obligation, the court can compel the performance of certain actions at its discretion,
which it is capable of enforcing and can issue injunctions for the infringement complained of. The principle of
mandatory injunction is used to grant final relief and not interim reliefs, like in exceptional or exemplary cases
like saving life, etc. There are essentially two conditions requested for mandatory injunctions: the defendant
must be obliged to perform an act and any such breach of the obliged act must be claimed by the plaintiff; the
reliefs, as asked for, must be enforceable by the court. The principle says that the defendant must do a positive
act in order to restore the wrongful act committed by him. The complainant must present a strong case in the
court and it should be of a level higher than that of the prima facie case.

Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “Injunction: meaning, types, laws and landmark judgements”,
https://blog.ipleaders.in/injunction-all-you-need-to-know-about-it/
passages.LEG-P0259:
Passage (Q.63-Q.67): Indian consumer law treats a buyer of goods or user of services as more than a market
        participant, it treats them as a rights-holder. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 recognises six core consumer
        rights: the right to safety, right to be informed, right to choose, right to be heard, right to seek redressal, and right
        to consumer education/awareness. These rights aim to correct the information and power imbalance between
        sellers and consumers, especially in markets where advertising, packaging, and online interfaces can influence
        decisions more than actual product quality.
        Each right has a practical role. Right to Safety means the consumer’s right to be protected against the marketing of
        goods and services that are hazardous to life and property. Products and services should meet not only a consumer’s
        immediate needs but also their long-term interests. Before purchasing, consumers should insist on quality and
        warranties/guarantees, and preferably buy quality-certified items such as ISI or AGMARK marked products.
        Right to be Informed, Right to Choose, and Right to be Heard together ensure fairness in the marketplace. The Right
        to be informed means the consumer must be told the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of
        goods/services so they are protected against unfair trade practices; consumers should seek complete information
        before deciding to avoid high-pressure selling. The Right to Choose means access (wherever possible) to a variety
        of goods and services at competitive prices, and in monopoly situations, assurance of satisfactory quality and fair
        pricing, including access to basic goods and services. The Right to be Heard ensures that consumer interests receive
        due consideration at appropriate forums and includes representation in bodies formed for consumer welfare, which
        can be strengthened through non-political, non-commercial consumer organisations.
        Right to Seek Redressal means the right to fair settlement of genuine grievances and remedies against unfair trade
        practices or exploitation; even small individual complaints can have a large social impact, and consumers may take
        help from consumer organisations. Right to Consumer Education means the right to acquire knowledge and skills
        to remain an informed consumer throughout life; ignorance—especially in rural areas—often leads to exploitation,
        so awareness and exercise of rights is essential for effective consumer protection.
        Source- https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/consumer-rights?utm_source=chatgpt.com
passages.LEG-P0260:
XXI. At least seven women died after a major ammonia gas leak at a private seafood processing
unit near Periyapalayam in Tiruvallur district of Tamil Nadu. The leak occurred at Peter &
Paul Seafood Export Company, where several migrant workers from Assam, Odisha and
Jharkhand were present. Around 67 workers were taken to hospitals after complaining of
breathing difficulties and other serious symptoms. Police, fire services, revenue officials,
health officials and an NDRF team reached the spot, while the State Government constituted
an enquiry committee to examine the incident.
Industrial gas leak incidents raise important questions on the civil liability of enterprises
dealing with hazardous substances. In tort law, such liability is mainly discussed through the

principles of Strict Liability and Absolute Liability. The rule of Strict Liability was laid down
in Rylands v. Fletcher. According to this rule, a person who brings and keeps upon his land
anything likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage caused by its escape.
The first essential of Strict Liability is that the defendant must have brought a dangerous
thing upon his land. A dangerous thing means anything which is likely to cause harm if it
escapes. The second essential is non-natural use of land. The use must be special,
extraordinary, or not ordinary in the usual course of using land. The third essential is escape.
The dangerous thing must escape from the land or control of the defendant to a place outside
such control. The fourth essential is damage. The plaintiff must have suffered damage because
of the escape of the dangerous thing. The rule of Strict Liability is subject to recognised
exceptions. These exceptions include act of God, act of a stranger, plaintiff's own fault, consent
of the plaintiff, statutory authority, and common benefit.
The principle of Absolute Liability was laid down by the Supreme Court of India in M.C.
Mehta v. Union of India, also known as the Oleum Gas Leak case. The rule of Absolute
Liability applies to an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity. An
enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-
delegable duty to the community to ensure that no harm results from such activity. If harm
results from such hazardous or inherently dangerous activity, the enterprise is absolutely
liable to compensate all persons affected by the accident. The rule of Absolute Liability does
not recognise the exceptions available under Strict Liability. Therefore, the enterprise cannot
avoid liability by relying on act of God, act of a stranger, absence of negligence, reasonable
care, or statutory permission. The Supreme Court held that an enterprise engaged in
hazardous activity must bear the cost of accidents arising from such activity as part of its
social cost. The measure of compensation under Absolute Liability must have a deterrent
effect and must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://thewire.in/labour/ammonia-gas-leak-
at-seafood-processing-factory-in-tiruvallur-tamil-nadu
passages.LEG-P0261:
XIV. Right to Die with Dignity under Article 21 of the Constitution of India: Article 21 of
the Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except
according to procedure established by law. Through successive judicial interpretation, the
Supreme Court has examined whether this right extends to a choice to end one's life or to die
with dignity.
In P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994), a two-judge bench struck down Section 309 IPC,
which criminalised attempted suicide, holding that just as the right to freedom of speech
includes the right to remain silent, the right to life under Article 21 includes the right not to
live. The Court reasoned that punishing a person who has already suffered mental agony by
attempting suicide is cruel and unconstitutional.
In Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996), a five-judge Constitution Bench overruled P.
Rathinam. The Court held that the right to life under Article 21 does not include the right to
die. The Court held that the right to life does not include a right to terminate life prematurely;
the right to live with dignity extends throughout the natural course of life but does not
encompass its artificial termination. The Court upheld Sections 306 and 309 IPC as
constitutionally valid. Crucially, however, the Court also observed that the right to live with
dignity may include, for a terminally ill patient, the right to a dignified process of dying —
leaving open the door for future recognition of euthanasia.
In Aruna Ramachandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011), the Supreme Court
recognised that passive euthanasia — withdrawal or withholding of life-sustaining treatment
— may be permitted in exceptional circumstances. The Court held that active euthanasia
remained impermissible, but passive euthanasia for patients in a Persistent Vegetative State
(PVS) could be authorised by a High Court through a bench of at least two judges, following
consultation with a medical board. This decision drew on the observation in Gian Kaur that
dignified dying is part of Article 21.
In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), a five-judge Constitution Bench unequivocally
held that the right to die with dignity is an intrinsic facet of the right to life under Article 21.
The Court formalised the legality of passive euthanasia and, for the first time, recognised the
validity of Advance Medical Directives (living wills), allowing competent individuals to specify
in advance their refusal of life-prolonging treatment. The Court grounded this in individual
autonomy, bodily integrity, and self-determination as components of Article 21, and laid down
comprehensive procedural safeguards. Active euthanasia remained illegal.
In Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026), the Supreme Court applied the Common Cause
framework to permit withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition from a patient who had been in
a persistent vegetative state since 2012. The bench observed that prolonging mere biological
existence in the absence of any prospect of recovery does not serve the patient's best interests,
and that human dignity at the end of life is a legally protected value under Article 21.
Source: Extracted with revisions and modifications from constitutional principles and judicial
decisions including P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994), Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996),
Aruna Ramachandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011), Common Cause v. Union of India
(2018), and Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026).
passages.LEG-P0262:
XIII. A trademark is a mark, symbol, word, phrase, design, shape, packaging, or colour combination
that distinguishes the goods or services of one person from those of others. Under Section
2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, it must be capable of graphical representation and
capable of distinguishing goods or services. The Act was enacted to protect business goodwill,
prevent consumer deception, promote fair competition, harmonise Indian law with
international instruments such as TRIPS and the Paris Convention, and simplify registration
and enforcement. Its important features include recognition of service marks, collective marks,
multi-class applications, protection of well-known marks, and registration valid for ten years,
renewable indefinitely. The Act follows the Nice Classification, dividing trademarks into 45
classes, with Classes 1-34 for goods and Classes 35—45 for services.
Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trademark may apply for registration by
submitting the applicant’s details, a clear representation of the mark, the relevant goods or
services with class numbers, date of first use if any, and priority details where applicable. The
Registrar examines the application on formal requirements, absolute grounds under Section 9,
and relative grounds under Section 11. Absolute refusal applies where the mark lacks
distinctiveness, is descriptive, deceptive, scandalous, functional, or uses protected emblems.
Relative refusal applies where the mark is identical or deceptively similar to an earlier mark,
causes confusion, infringes a well-known mark, or is otherwise prohibited by law. If accepted,
the mark is published in the Trade Marks Journal, after which any person may file opposition
within three months, extendable by one month. Opposition is followed by counter-statement,
evidence, hearing, and decision. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Registration gives the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark, stop others from using
confusingly similar marks, assign or license it, seek customs protection, and rely on it as
prima facie evidence of ownership. Section 29 defines infringement as unauthorised use of an
identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to identical or similar goods or services in the
course of trade. Remedies include injunctions, damages, account of profits, delivery up,
destruction, Anton Piller orders, and restraining orders. Section 103 also prescribes criminal
penalties for false trademark use. Even unregistered marks are protected through passing off
under Section 27, if the plaintiff proves goodwill, misrepresentation, and likely damage. The
Act also recognises acquired distinctiveness, and regulates assignment, licensing, rectification,
restoration, and removal for non-use. After abolition of the IPAB in 2021, appeals and
rectification matters now lie directly before the High Courts. [Word Count: 413]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lexanalytico.com/

passages.LEG-P0263:
XIII. Article 32 occupies a central position in the Indian constitutional framework. During the
Constituent Assembly debates, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described it as the very heart and soul of the
Constitution, stressing that Fundamental Rights are meaningless without effective remedies.
Introduced against the backdrop of colonial denial of civil liberties, Article 32 empowers citizens to
directly approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of their Fundamental Rights.
Article 32 comprises four clauses. It grants individuals the right to move the Supreme Court for
enforcement of Fundamental Rights, empowers the Court to issue writs such as habeas corpus,
mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto, allows Parliament to confer similar powers
on other courts, and protects this right from suspension except as constitutionally permitted
during emergencies. It is a remedial fundamental right and has been recognised as part of the
basic structure of the Constitution, notably in Minerva Mills v. Union of India.
A unique feature of Article 32 is direct access to the Supreme Court without exhausting
alternative remedies. Through its writ jurisdiction, the Court protects personal liberty, ensures
performance of public duties, restrains jurisdictional excesses, quashes illegal orders, and prevents
unlawful occupation of public offices. However, writ jurisdiction is discretionary and subject to
limitations such as locus standi, availability of alternative remedies, delay, and res judicata.
Article 32 applies only to Fundamental Rights and generally not to private disputes.
The scope of Article 32 expanded through Public Interest Litigation, allowing public-spirited
individuals to approach the Court on behalf of marginalised groups, as recognised in S.P. Gupta v.
Union of India. Compared to Article 226, Article 32 is narrower in scope but stronger as a
guaranteed right. Despite suspension of Article 32 during emergencies under Article 359, core
rights under Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable. Overall, Article 32 serves as a dynamic
instrument of constitutional justice and judicial review. [Article 32 under Indian Constitutional
Framework; Word Count: 307]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://theamikusqriae.com/
passages.LEG-P0264:
XI.	In a significant decision on the scope of compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the
Supreme Court considered whether injuries caused by the fall of a roadside tree branch on a
stationary autorickshaw could be treated as an accident “arising out of the use of a motor
vehicle”. The claimant was travelling in an autorickshaw in Bengaluru when heavy rain forced
him to stop by the roadside. While the vehicle was standing under an old tree, a branch fell on
it and caused grievous injuries, including permanent paraplegia.
The main provision considered was Section 165 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. This section
empowers the State Government to constitute Motor Accident Claims Tribunals for deciding
compensation claims arising from accidents involving death, bodily injury, or damage to third-
party property. However, the accident must arise out of the use of a motor vehicle. Therefore,
the Tribunal’s jurisdiction depends not merely on the presence of a vehicle, but on a real
connection between the injury and the use of that vehicle. Section 166 of the Act provides the
procedural route for filing an application for compensation in such cases. A claim under this
section must relate to an accident of the kind described in Section 165. Hence, where the
injury is caused by an external event having no proximate connection with the vehicle’s
movement, operation, condition, or use, Section 166 may not be the proper remedy. The Court
acknowledged that the expression “use of a motor vehicle” has been interpreted broadly. It can
include cases where the vehicle is stationary and not moving. Similarly, the phrase “arising
out of” is wider than “caused by” and does not always require a direct causal connection. Still,
the Court clarified that some proximate and meaningful connection with the vehicle must
exist. In the present case, the autorickshaw merely happened to be the place where the
claimant was sitting. The injury was caused by the falling branch, not by the vehicle.

Section 147 of the Act, dealing with compulsory third-party insurance, is also relevant because
an insurer’s statutory liability generally arises where death or bodily injury is caused by, or
arises out of, the use of a motor vehicle in a public place. If the vehicle has no causal role, the
insurer cannot be treated as liable merely because the injured person was inside an insured
vehicle. Section 168 empowers the Claims Tribunal to determine the amount of compensation
and specify the person or persons who must pay it. This provision becomes relevant only after
the case falls within the Motor Vehicles Act. It cannot itself create liability where the
statutory requirement of a motor-vehicle accident is absent.
Section 164, which deals with fixed compensation on a no-fault basis for death or grievous
hurt, is useful as a comparison. Even under this beneficial provision, the injury must be due to
an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle. Therefore, the requirement of a motor-
vehicle nexus remains central. The Court also considered the defence of act of God or vis
major. A sudden fall of a tree branch during heavy rain may, depending on the facts, be an
unforeseen natural occurrence beyond reasonable anticipation. Municipal bodies have a duty
to maintain roadside trees, but they cannot be expected to inspect every branch constantly or
remove every branch merely because it may fall someday. [Word Count: 560]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from
https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/06/16/falling-tree-branch-not-a-motor-vehicle-
accident-sc/
passages.LEG-P0265:
XV. Malicious prosecution under the law of tort means the wrongful institution of legal
proceedings, usually criminal, against a person without reasonable and probable cause and
with a malicious intention. The iPleaders article explains that Black’s Law Dictionary defines
it as a legal proceeding initiated without probable cause and with harmful intent, and the
Supreme Court in West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray (2006) described it
as misuse of the legal system to harm another person without valid justification. The article
also distinguishes malicious prosecution from abuse of process and abuse of power. Malicious
prosecution concerns the wrongful starting of proceedings at the very beginning, whereas
abuse of process refers to misuse of a legal process after it has been properly initiated, and
abuse of power concerns misuse of official authority outside the courtroom context.

The article identifies five essential elements that a plaintiff must prove in an action for
malicious prosecution: prosecution by the defendant, absence of reasonable and probable cause,
malice, termination of proceedings in favour of the plaintiff, and damage suffered by the
plaintiff. “Prosecution” is used in a wider sense than a trial and can include criminal
proceedings by way of appeal or revision, though the article notes that mere proceedings before
a police officer have been held not to amount to prosecution, while the position regarding
quasi-judicial authorities has been treated differently in different cases. Absence of reasonable
and probable cause means the prosecution had no justified basis. Malice does not necessarily
mean personal spite; it may also mean any improper purpose, such as gaining a collateral
advantage. Proceedings must have terminated in favour of the plaintiff, which generally
means there is no judicial determination of guilt, and the plaintiff must show actual damage,
which the article groups into damage to reputation, person, or property. The burden of proving
all these essentials lies on the plaintiff.
The article further notes that earlier courts were reluctant to recognise malicious civil
proceedings, but later decisions accepted that malicious abuse of civil proceedings may also be
actionable if bad intention, absence of reasonable cause, favourable termination, and resulting
harm are proved. As for remedies, the article says that the aggrieved person may file a suit for
damages, including compensation for injury to reputation and recovery of legal costs, and in
appropriate cases may also seek constitutional relief under Articles 32 or 226. The principal
defences available to a defendant are the presence of reasonable grounds and proof of good
faith, that is, showing that the proceedings were started honestly and not to misuse the legal
system.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://www.ijfmr.com/
passages.LEG-P0266:
XII. The 42nd Amendment of the Constitution of India, enacted in 1976 during the Emergency, is
one of the most far-reaching constitutional amendments in Indian history and is often
described as the “Mini-Constitution.” Its background lies in the political turbulence of the
1970s, particularly after the Golaknath case (1967), which intensified conflict between the
judiciary and the executive over Parliament’s amending power. The Allahabad High Court
judgment against Prime Minister Indira Gandhi for election malpractice further deepened the
crisis. After the declaration of Emergency on 25 June 1975, the government acquired
extraordinary powers and introduced several constitutional changes, of which the 42nd
Amendment was the most comprehensive. Its objectives were to strengthen executive power,
curtail judicial review, enhance Parliament’s authority, centralise administration, and reshape
the Constitution in line with the government’s political and ideological agenda.
The amendment introduced sweeping changes across the Constitution. In the Preamble, it
added the words “Socialist” and “Secular” and changed “unity of the nation” to “unity and

integrity of the nation.” It expanded the Directive Principles of State Policy by inserting
Articles 39A, 43A, and 48A, dealing with free legal aid, workers’ participation in management,
and environmental protection, and amended Article 39(f) for child welfare. It also inserted Part
IV-A, introducing Fundamental Duties of citizens. In the Seventh Schedule, subjects such as
education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and
administration of justice were shifted from the State List to the Concurrent List, increasing
central control. It formalised the rule that the President must act on the advice of the Cabinet,
inserted Article 257A to allow deployment of central forces in states, abolished quorum
requirements in legislatures, and extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
from five years to six years. The amendment also altered emergency provisions, allowed
national emergency to apply to the whole or part of India, extended the duration of President’s
Rule, restricted High Courts’ jurisdiction, required a seven-judge bench with a two-thirds
majority in certain constitutional cases, inserted Part XIV-A with Articles 323A and 323B for
tribunals, and expanded the operation of Article 358 for suspension of Article 19 rights during
emergencies.
The amendment faced strong criticism for weakening democracy, federalism, and judicial
independence. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down
important parts of the amendment, especially provisions that gave Parliament unlimited
amending power and curtailed judicial review, and reaffirmed the Basic Structure Doctrine.
After the Emergency, the 43rd and 44th Amendments reversed many of its excesses. Thus, the
42nd Amendment remains a landmark example of both constitutional overreach and the
resilience of judicial review in India.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/42nd-amendment-of-
indian-constitution/
passages.LEG-P0267:
VI. The Transfer of Property Act, enacted on July 1, 1882, governs property transactions in India, stipulating
clear provisions for the conditions and constituents of valid transfers. The Act primarily aims to define and
amend the law regarding property transfers by acts between parties, excluding transfers by operation of law. The
essence of a ‘transfer of property’ involves an act where one person conveys property to one or more individuals
or to himself and others. The term ‘person’ includes individuals, groups of individuals, associations, or
companies, and ‘transfer’ is broadly defined in relation to the term "convey," indicating the process of
transferring something to another party.
For a transfer to be deemed valid under the Act, several essential criteria must be met. Firstly, as per Section 5
of the Act, the transfer must occur between two or more living persons, necessitating that both the transferor and
the transferee be alive at the time of the transfer. This ensures that the property cannot be transferred to or by
deceased persons, making the act of conveyance a strictly inter vivos transaction.
Additionally, the property in question must be legally transferable. Section 6 outlines certain properties that are
inherently non-transferable, which includes exceptions such as spes successionis (the chance of an heir
succeeding), easements, right of re-entry, interests restricted to personal enjoyment, and the mere right to sue,
among others. For instance, rights that are purely personal or attached to a future maintenance cannot be
transferred. Also, stipends such as military pensions and political pensions are specified as non-transferable
under this section.
Specific instances of non-transferable property rights include the right of re-entry, which cannot be transferred
separate from the property it concerns, and stipends or pensions, which are personal to the receiver and thus
non-transferable. The prohibition against transferring a mere right to sue underscores the personal nature of
such claims, which are designed to redress personal grievances rather than transferable property rights.

Furthermore, the Act specifies that any transfer intended for unlawful purposes, or those that are inherently
fraudulent, immoral, or opposed to public policy, are void. This includes transfers for purposes that are
forbidden by law or involve or imply injury to another person or property, ensuring that property transactions
adhere to legal and ethical standards.
Section 7 of the Transfer of Property Act delineates who is competent to transfer property. To validly transfer
property, a person must be the owner or legally authorized to make the transfer. This authority may be personal,
derived from agency, or granted by law or court order. Competency requires that the person be of majority age
and sound mind, and not disqualified by any law to which they are subject.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://blog.ipleaders.in/necessities-transfer-transfer-property-
act-1882/
passages.LEG-P0268:
III. Article 352 of the Constitution provides for the provision of National Emergency which can be applied if
any extraordinary situation arises that may threaten the security, peace, stability and governance of the country.
Whenever any of the following grounds occur, an emergency can be imposed: War, External aggression; or
Internal rebellion. Article 352 provides that if the President is ‘satisfied’ on the grounds that the security of India
is threatened due to outside aggression or armed rebellion, he can issue a proclamation to that effect regarding
the whole of India or a part thereof. However, sub-clause (3) states that when a piece of written advice is given
by the Union Cabinet then only the President can make such a proclamation. Such a proclamation must be
placed before each house of the Parliament and must be approved within one month of the declaration of the
proclamation otherwise it will expire.
Furthermore, it is not necessary that for the proclamation of National Emergency, external aggression or armed
rebellion should actually happen. Even if there is a possibility that such a situation can arise, a National
Emergency can be proclaimed. If the situation improves then the President can revoke the emergency through
another proclamation. The President may make a Proclamation of Emergency in respect of the whole India or
any part of India, as required.
If approved by both Houses of Parliament, then National Emergency can continue for 6 months and it can be
renewed by approval of Parliament after every 6 months. But if the dissolution of Lok Sabha takes place in that
6 months and resolution for renewal of National Emergency is under consideration then emergency exists till 30
days from the first sitting of newly elected LS provided that it is approved by Rajya Sabha.
According to Article 353, the Union can use its executive power to the extent of giving directions to the State
relating to the manner in which the executive powers shall be exercised by the State. As per Article 353(b), the
Union Parliament can make laws relating to the matters in the State List. According to Article 354, the
distribution of revenue between the Union and the State can be altered by the Centre. As per Article 358, during
a National Emergency, the fundamental rights under Article 19 shall be suspended. However, in any case, the
fundamental rights under Article 20 and Article 21 will not be affected.

passages.LEG-P0269:
XI.	Belligerent occupation refers to a situation in which the armed forces of one state seize and
administer control over the territory of another sovereign state during armed conflict or its
aftermath. The control is not meant to be permanent; rather, it is provisional and continues
only for the period of military necessity or until the conflict is resolved. A territory is
considered under belligerent occupation when it is under the effective control of a hostile
army, meaning there must be actual administration and “boots on the ground,” and when the
control is temporary in character rather than an annexation. The occupying power is bound by
international law and must protect the rights and welfare of the civilian population.
Belligerent occupation is therefore distinct from annexation or colonialism, because
sovereignty is not lawfully transferred to the occupier.
The legal framework of belligerent occupation is primarily found in the Hague Conventions of
1907, the Geneva Conventions of 1949, especially the Fourth Geneva Convention, and
customary international law. Article 42 of the Fourth Hague Convention states that a territory
is occupied when it is actually placed under the authority of a hostile army, while Article 43
obliges the occupying power to restore and maintain public order and safety and to respect the
existing laws of the occupied territory as far as possible. The Fourth Geneva Convention adds
humanitarian protections, especially for civilians, including the prohibition on forced transfer
or deportation under Article 49. The law emphasises that occupation is only an interim
arrangement and must not become a method of permanently displacing sovereignty. Scholars
such as Eyal Benvenisti have explained that the modern law of occupation rests on the
principle of the inalienability of sovereignty, meaning that military control cannot lawfully
extinguish the sovereign rights of the occupied state.
History provides several illustrations of belligerent occupation. After the First World War, the
Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) governed parts of the Middle East from

1917 to 1920 as a temporary regime. After the Second World War, Allied-occupied Germany
(1945-1949) was administered militarily until sovereignty could be gradually restored. In the
contemporary era, one of the most debated examples is the Israeli control over Palestinian
territories, which the United Nations has characterised as belligerent occupation. UN Security
Council Resolutions 242 and 338 support the principle of “Land for Peace,” under which
territorial withdrawal is linked to peace and recognition. At the same time, modern conflicts
involving non-state actors, fragmented authority, insurgency, cyber means, and hybrid
warfare have made the traditional idea of occupation harder to apply, requiring continued re-
examination of how international law defines and regulates effective control over territory.

https://opil.cuplaw.com/display/10.1093/law:epil/ 9780199231690/law-9780199231690-
e359

SECTION III
X.	Marriage in India, in layman’s language, is a union of two persons of opposite sex. Through
religious ceremonies, two different persons of opposite sex unite and start living together as
husband and wife. The concept of marriage is to establish a relationship between husband and
wife.
According to Hindu law, marriage is a sacrament, while according to Muslim law, marriage is
a contract. Thus, different religions have different concepts about marriage. However, one
thing is common: it is the right of every person, irrespective of religion, to marry a person of
one’s own choice and lead a happy life.
The Constitution of India guarantees the Right to Life under Article 21, and this article also
encompasses the right to marry. Therefore, the right to marry a person of one’s own choice is
an integral part of Article 21 of the Constitution of India. One of the earliest cases dealing with
this issue was Lata Singh v. State of UP, concerning an inter-caste marriage. The Supreme
Court held that since the petitioner was a major, she was at liberty to marry whoever she
wanted, and no law bars inter-caste marriage.
Though the right to marry is a fundamental right of every person irrespective of gender, it is
not an absolute right. This means it is subject to certain conditions. For example, a minor, i.e.,
a person who has not completed 18 years of age, can be restricted from marrying. In India
under Hindu law, for marriage a girl should have completed 18 years of age and boy should
have completed 21 years of age.
Further, Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 provides that “all agreements are
contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful
consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.” If
these essential conditions are fulfilled, an agreement becomes a valid contract.
After entering into a valid contract, the parties are bound by contractual relationships.
However, there are certain exceptional cases in which, even if an agreement complies with all
the essentials of a valid contract, it becomes void. One such agreement is an agreement in
restraint of marriage.

XII. Mens rea means the guilty mental state that ordinarily accompanies a criminal act. This
article explains it through the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea: an act does not
make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty. It notes that mens rea was not always
treated as an ingredient of crime; in earlier periods, punishment could follow even without
proof of intention. Over time, especially from the seventeenth century onward, criminal law
came to recognise that blameworthy conduct usually requires both a wrongful act and a
blameworthy state of mind. In India, this idea entered criminal law through English influence
and became reflected across the Indian Penal Code, even though the phrase “mens rea” itself is
not expressly used in the Code. The article points out that many IPC offences use words such
as “voluntarily,” “dishonestly,” “knowingly,” and “fraudulently,” which embody the idea of a
guilty mind.
The passage identifies four main forms of mens rea: intention, knowledge, recklessness, and
negligence. Intention refers to a deliberate mental decision to bring about a consequence;
knowledge refers to awareness of facts and likely consequences; recklessness means foreseeing
a risk but proceeding with indifference to it; and negligence is failure to exercise the degree of
care that a prudent person would have used in the circumstances. It also emphasises that
mens rea is usually essential in criminal law unless a statute expressly or by necessary
implication excludes it. The Supreme Court decisions discussed, such as Ravule Hariprasada
Rao v. State and State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George, support the principle that guilty
mind is generally presumed to be a component of criminal liability unless legislation clearly
rules it out.
Another key point in the article is the need for concurrence of mens rea and actus reus: the
guilty mind and the wrongful act must exist together for criminal liability in the ordinary case.

Mere intention without the act, or the act without the corresponding guilty state of mind, will
not usually be enough. At the same time, it notes important exceptions, especially strict
liability offences, where proof of mens rea is not required. Examples listed include criminal
libel, public nuisance, contempt of court, kidnapping/abduction, bigamy, rape, sale of obscene
books, and certain statutory offences under laws such as the Essential Commodities Act and
the Motor Vehicles Act. The overall conclusion of the article is that mens rea remains a
foundational idea in criminal law, but its role depends on the language, structure, and purpose
of the particular offence.

know-about-mens-rea/

        that their social advancement has historically lagged behind. Hence the communities which had the privilege of
        being considered genuine at that time, certainly have made a lot of progress both in the social as well as an

        The main implication of the EWS reservation is that Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution now stand amended,
        empowering the state to provide a maximum of 10 per cent reservation for the economically weaker sections of the
        society excluding the SCs, STs and the OBS-NCL (non-creamy layer). To avail this EWS reservation, an individual

        reservation, i.e., a ceiling of fifty percent. This was first clearly defined in the case of M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
        wherein the court realised that the constitution-makers did assume the fact the caste reservation policy would not

passages.LEG-P0273:
VI. According to Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, “when, at the desire of the promisor, the
promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to
do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the
promise.” In the following definition, a promisor is the party that performs a promise and a promisee is the
party to which a promise is made.

Essential elements of consideration:

1. The consideration must move at the desire of the promisor – The definition of consideration under the
Indian Contract Act, 1872, starts with “when, at the desire of the promisor....”, which clearly specifies that any
act or abstinence or promise by the promisee should act at the desire of the promisor. It means that any act or
abstinence done voluntarily or without the desire of the promisor is not a valid consideration in the eyes of the
law.
2. The consideration may move from the promisee to any other person or a third party – As long as there
is no objection by the promisor, the consideration may move to any other person or proceed from any other
person than the promisee. In simple words, it states that it is not a mandate that only the promisee should grant
the consideration; it can also be provided by any other person. The doctrine of privity of consideration is, thus,
not applicable in India.

3. The consideration must not be unlawful – It's very obvious that any act, abstinence or promise made that is
considered illegal in the eyes of the law is not a valid consideration. Also, if there is an involvement of any
injury to a person or property of another person or is immoral in nature, it makes the consideration invalid under
the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Such considerations make the contract void. For example, if you promise a
person to pay Rs. 10,000 for selling drugs at his workplace, such consideration will not be valid.
4. The consideration must not be physically impossible – A consideration that is not physically possible to be
performed or carried out is considered invalid. A decision should always be something that is capable of being


performed or carried out. For example, X makes a promise to Z to pay Rs. 1,00,000 if Z runs 100 km in 1
minute. Here, it is impossible to perform the said task. Thus, such considerations that are physically impossible
to perform are deemed invalid.

5. The consideration may not be adequate – While entering into a contract, consideration is something that is
to be mutually decided by the parties to that contract. When the question of adequacy of consideration arises
while enforcing the contract, the court is not concerned with the adequacy of consideration in it. In simple
words, the court has nothing to do with the question of whether the consideration in the contract is adequate or
not.

Source: https://blog.ipleaders.in/consideration-in-contract-law/

IV. One of the significant factors of a valid contract is free consent. Both the parties involved in the contract
must enter into the contract with consent and under no force. Various factors damage the free consent of either
party. One such factor is "mistake", which involves a mistake of fact and mistake of law. A mistake of fact arises
when a person does any act but misunderstood some fact that negates an element of the crime. A mistake of fact
as a defense applies to various crimes. If the criminal defendant can prove that he does the act due to a mistake
of fact or misunderstood some fact that negates an element of the crime. In general, the mistake of law is no
defense to the violation of the law. It is presumed that all people know and understand the law of the land,
except minors, lunatics or insane. There are few other rare exceptions to this rule.

A mistake of fact can be an exception in reducing or eliminating the liability of the person. A person cannot
escape his liability for intentional mistakes. A criminal defendant can argue that he never intended to commit
the crime and the criminal act occurred as a result of the mistake of fact as per the situation or
misunderstanding. Such exception is only allowed when there's a mistake of fact, but the mistake of law is not
considered as a defence. When a person commits any tort and asks for the defence that he does not know the
law, that does is considered as a defence. Court thinks that every person knows the law of the country that's why
the mistake of law is not considered as a defence in IPC as well as in tort. The mistake of law is not considered
