passages.LEG-P0275:
II. A recent rule in company law has generated concerns and criticism regarding the requirement for
independent directors (IDs) to clear an online proficiency test conducted by the Indian Institute of Corporate
Affairs (IICA). This rule mandates that existing IDs and individuals aspiring to become IDs must pass the self-
assessment test within a year of their inclusion in the IICA's maintained data. To recognize the standing and
experience of individuals, the rule exempts directors or key managerial personnel who have worked in these
roles for at least ten years in listed or unlisted companies. While there is no limit on the number of attempts to
clear the test, a minimum aggregate score of 60% is necessary.
At first glance, this move seems reasonable. The rule introduces the concept of passing a test to formally qualify
and demonstrate the expected qualifications for individuals aspiring to be IDs, which is already provided by the
Companies Act, 2013. The existing regulations under the Companies Act outline certain qualifications for IDs,
including their experience and knowledge in relevant fields such as finance, law, management, sales, marketing,
administration, research, corporate governance, and technical operations related to the company's business.
Additionally, IDs are obligated by law to regularly update and refresh their skills, knowledge, and familiarity
with the company. Thus, the Companies Act already requires a minimum set of qualifications for IDs. However,
despite these provisions, some concerns have emerged.
Certain industry bodies, chambers, and even IDs themselves are contemplating recommending to the Ministry
of Corporate Affairs that this rule be reconsidered. Their concern stems from the belief that it is inappropriate to
expect IDs, who are often individuals of reputation, standing, and experience, and who meet the legal eligibility
criteria for ID appointments, to undergo and pass a technical test to establish their eligibility. They argue that
this requirement could undermine their status and position.
Critics point out that the Companies Act already has stringent eligibility criteria for IDs, as it states that only
individuals considered by the board of directors to possess integrity, relevant expertise, and experience should
be appointed as IDs. According to them, this requirement is sufficient to ensure suitable individuals are selected,
rendering an additional test unnecessary. Hence, their view is that this rule should be revoked. While this
argument is intriguing, there is no inherent issue with passing a test to establish proficiency. Another argument
raised is that no such test requirement exists for other directors, so why should it be imposed on IDs. While it is
true that other directors are not required to pass such a test, it cannot be denied that the roles, duties, and
responsibilities of IDs are significantly greater than those of other directors. It is prudent for IDs to establish
their eligibility by passing a simple test. In fact, IDs and their conduct play critical roles in adhering to corporate
governance norms.
The new rule in company law regarding the proficiency test for IDs has sparked concerns and criticism. While
some argue that IDs should not be required to undergo such a test, considering their reputation and eligibility
under the existing law, others believe that passing the test is a reasonable way to establish proficiency. IDs hold
crucial positions in corporate governance, and the test can help ensure their qualifications and capabilities align


with their responsibilities. Ultimately, the debate continues regarding whether the rule should be maintained or
reconsidered.
Source: https://taxguru.in/company-law/independent-director-section1496-companies-act-2013.html

V. Rape is defined in section 375 of IPC: "A man is said to commit "rape" if he— (a) penetrates his penis, to
any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other
person; or (b) inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body, not being the penis, into the vagina, the
urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (c) manipulates any part of
the body of a woman so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of body of such
woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (d) applies his mouth to the vagina, anus, urethra
of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person..."

The definition of rape has changed to include non-penile penetration, although it remains gender-specific when
committed against a female. The new definition, which raises the age of consent to 18, is crucial since it now
considers any type of penetration under the Section with a female under the age of 18 to be rape. If the woman
was still under the age of 18 and over the age of 15, it would not have been considered rape in a married context
as long as the agreement was given under Exception 2 of the provision. Exception 2 of section 375 provides that
Sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his wife, the wife not being under fifteen years of age, is not
rape.

passages.LEG-P0277:
XII. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, designates offences against the state’s very existence as its
most severe crimes, encapsulated in Chapter VI. At its apex lies Section 121, which
criminalizes the act of waging, attempting to wage, or abetting the waging of war against the
Government of India. This provision targets not mere disorder but collective violence of a
political character aimed at overthrowing the government or coercing it by force. The essence
of "waging war" distinguishes it from riots or isolated rebellions; it requires an assembly with
a public, general purpose and a force sufficient to challenge the state’s sovereignty. An
illustrative example is an armed insurrection to seize a government arsenal with the goal of
subverting constitutional authority. Given its gravity, the punishment is extraordinarily
stringent: death or imprisonment for life, coupled with a fine and mandatory forfeiture of
property.

Recognizing that the gravest threats often begin in secret, the law proactively targets conspiracy
through Section 121A. This section penalizes the very agreement to commit offences under
Section 121, criminalizing the planning stage before any overt act of violence materializes. The
key ingredient is a conspiracy between two or more persons either to wage war or to deprive
India of its sovereignty. Thus, the state need not wait for an uprising; the plot itself is punishable
by imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and a fine.

Further along the continuum of preparation, Section 122 addresses the tangible steps taken
towards this end. It punishes collecting arms, ammunition, or otherwise preparing to wage war,
provided such acts are done with the specific intention of using them against the state. This
moves beyond conspiracy into actionable preparation, meriting a similarly severe punishment
of life imprisonment or up to ten years, and a fine.

Finally, Section 123 casts a wide net by criminalizing the concealment of a design to wage war.
An individual who, knowing of such a treasonous design, actively conceals it with the intent
to facilitate its execution, becomes complicit. This offence underscores the legal duty not to
aid such plots through silence or deception, punishable by imprisonment up to ten years and a
fine.

Collectively, these sections form a formidable legal bulwark. They protect state stability by
addressing the entire spectrum of treasonous activity—from the ultimate act of war, through
its conspiracy and preparation, down to its intentional concealment—ensuring that both action
and treacherous intent are met with the full force of the law.
passages.LEG-P0278:
SECTION III
xX.	A contract of indemnity is a contract of protection by which one party undertakes to save the
other from loss. Halsbury describes indemnity as a contract, express or implied, to keep a
person indemnified against loss, independent of whether a third person makes default. Black’s
Law Dictionary also explains indemnity as a right by which the entire loss is shifted from one
who is only technically or secondarily liable to another who is primarily responsible. The
Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines it in Section 124 as a contract by which one party promises
to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of
any other person. The person giving the indemnity is the indemnifier, and the person
protected is the indemnity-holder or indemnified. The contract may be express or implied, as
seen in Adamson v. Jarvis, Secretary of State v. Bank of India Ltd., and Starkey v. Bank of
England, where courts recognised implied promises of indemnity from the circumstances and
conduct of parties.
The essential features of a contract of indemnity are that it must be a valid contract under the
Indian Contract Act, its main object must be protection from loss, its terms may be express or
implied, and it involves only two parties, unlike a contract of guarantee. It is contingent in
nature because liability arises on the happening of a specified event causing loss. Insurance
contracts are generally contracts of indemnity except life insurance, because life insurance
does not depend on proof of an actual quantified loss. As held in New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
v. State Trading Corporation of India, almost all insurance other than life and personal
accident insurance are contracts of indemnity. A third party cannot sue the indemnifier
because of the doctrine of privity, as observed in National Petroleum Company v. Popat Lal
Mulji.
Section 125 sets out the rights of the indemnity-holder. He may recover all damages he is
compelled to pay in a suit to which the indemnity applies, all costs incurred in bringing or
defending such a suit if he acted prudently and within authority, and all sums paid under a
reasonable compromise made in good faith. The indemnifier, though not expressly given rights
in the Act, enjoys subrogation rights after making payment. In Gajanan Moreshwar v.
Moreshwar Madan, the Bombay High Court held that once the indemnified’s liability becomes
absolute, the indemnifier must fulfil the promise without waiting for actual payment. This
modern rule departs from the old English view that actual loss must first be suffered. Cases
like Osman Jamal and Sons Ltd. v. Gopal Purushottam and The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
v. State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. support the principle that indemnity becomes
enforceable as soon as liability becomes absolute. However, indemnity will not cover unlawful
or intentional wrongful acts, as shown in Sheikh Meherulla v. Sariatulla and Geismar v. Sun
Alliance and London Insurance Ltd. Thus, contracts of indemnity remain an important legal
device for risk allocation, financial security, and protection against liability.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from,
http://student.manupatra.com/Academic/Abk/Law-of-Contract-and-Specific-
Relief/Chapter9.htm
passages.LEG-P0279:
XII. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, meticulously defines offences but also incorporates
essential General Defences (Sections 76-106) that absolve or mitigate liability by negating the
requisite mens rea or justifying the act. These defences are fundamental to a just criminal
jurisprudence, recognizing that not every harmful act constitutes a crime. A key defence is
Mistake of Fact, where a person acting under a genuine and reasonable mistaken belief of fact
is excused, as it negatives criminal intention. Similarly, acts performed by judges or officers
pursuant to Judicial and Executive Acts are protected when done in good faith under court
orders or legal authority.

The IPC excuses harm caused by an Accident (Sec. 80)—a purely unfortunate event occurring
despite ordinary care and without criminal intent. Conversely, the defence of Necessity (Sec.
81) justifies an act done to prevent greater harm, provided the act was necessary and the harm
caused was proportionate. The law also prescribes exemptions based on capacity. Infancy
completely exempts a child below seven and conditionally those between seven and twelve, if
lacking maturity of understanding. Insanity (Sec. 84) is a complete defence, adhering to the
M’Naghten Rules, requiring proof that the accused, due to unsoundness of mind, was incapable
of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong.

Intoxication (Sec. 85-86) provides a nuanced defence. Involuntary intoxication can excuse if it
renders the person incapable of forming intent. However, voluntary intoxication is generally
no defence, except potentially for proving the absence of a specific intent in certain crimes. A
vital justificatory defence is the Right of Private Defence (Sec. 96-106), which empowers
individuals to protect their own or another’s body and property against imminent unlawful
aggression, subject to the cardinal principle of proportionality. Furthermore, Consent can be a
defence, but only if it is free, informed, and given by a competent person, and never for acts
intended or known to cause grievous hurt or death. Finally, the law disregards Trivial Acts (Sec.
95) causing harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain.


Collectively, these defences ensure the penal code punishes only blameworthy conduct,
balancing societal protection with individual justice.
passages.LEG-P0280:
XI.	The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 was enacted to ensure that Muslims
in India are governed by Islamic law in personal matters instead of inconsistent regional or
tribal customs. Before 1937, courts often relied on local usage rather than Quranic principles,
which created uncertainty and diluted uniform application of Muslim personal law. In
response to demands from Muslim scholars and leaders, the British Indian legislature passed
this Act, making Shariat the rule of decision in specified matters. The Act was therefore a
major reform measure, as it gave legal recognition to Islamic personal law within the Indian
legal framework and aimed to preserve the religious and cultural identity of Muslims while
replacing contrary customs.
The Act is short but legally important. Section 1 gives its title and extends it to the whole of
India, later fully extended through subsequent amendments. Section 2 is the heart of the Act.
It begins with the overriding phrase “notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary”
and provides that in matters such as intestate succession, special property of females,
marriage, dissolution of marriage including talaq, ila, zihar, lian, khula and mubaraat,
maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts, trust properties and wakfs, the rule of
decision for Muslims shall be Muslim Personal Law (Shariat). However, agricultural land is
excluded, which has often been criticised because this exclusion affected inheritance rights,
particularly of Muslim women, in agricultural property.
Section 3 gives a Muslim person the option to make a declaration for extending the application
of Shariat to additional matters not automatically covered under Section 2, such as adoption,
wills and legacies, provided the person is Muslim, competent to contract under Section 11 of
the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and resident within the territories to which the Act applies.
Such declaration, once accepted, binds not only the declarant but also minor children and
descendants. Section 4 empowers the State Government to frame procedural rules regarding
declarations, prescribed authorities, form, and fees, and these rules must be published and
laid before the State Legislature. Section 5 was later repealed by the Dissolution of Muslim
Marriages Act, 1939, and Section 6 repeals earlier inconsistent regional laws to secure
uniformity.
Judicial interpretation has further shaped the Act’s significance. In Shah Bano Begum v.
Mohd. Ahmed Khan (1985), the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman could

claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, highlighting the interaction between personal
law and secular law. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Court declared triple talaq
unconstitutional, holding that it was not protected as an essential religious practice. In
Sameena Begum v. Union of India (2018), issues such as polygamy and nikah halala were
questioned, reflecting the continuing constitutional debate on reform, equality, and gender
justice within Muslim personal law. [Word Count: 460]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/the-muslim-
personal-law-shariat-act-1937/
passages.LEG-P0281:
XII. Treaties are one of the principal sources of international law and are recognised under Article
88(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice along with custom, general principles,
and judicial decisions and teachings of highly qualified publicists. They are formal written
agreements by which States bind themselves in matters of international responsibility,
cooperation, organisation, trade, security, and rights. The modern law governing treaties is
primarily contained in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969, which came into
force on 27 January 1980. Article 2(1)(a) of the Convention defines a treaty as an international
agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law,
whether contained in one or more related instruments and whatever its designation. The
binding basis of treaty law is the principle of pacta sunt servanda, recognised in Article 26,
which requires every treaty in force to be performed in good faith. Although, as a rule, only
signatory or ratifying States are bound, the North Sea Continental Shelf Cases recognised
that some treaties may have a norm-creating character. States may also enter reservations
under Article 2(1)(d), but reservations cannot defeat the object and purpose of the treaty.
Treaties may broadly be classified as law-making treaties and contractual treaties. Law-
making treaties are generally multilateral and create general binding norms, often in fields
such as human rights, maritime law, international mandates, tribunals, and waterways. They
resemble legislation and impose duties independent of private bargains. Contractual treaties,
on the other hand, are usually bilateral or limited in scope, and are based on mutual benefit,
such as trade, alliance, or conveyance agreements. The Vienna Convention governs the
making of treaties through stages such as adoption, authentication, expression of consent,
ratification, accession, and reservations. Ratification reflects approval, while accession refers
to becoming a party after the minimum ratification requirement has been met. Under Articles
34 to 37, third States are generally neither bound nor benefited by a treaty without their
consent, though customary international law may eventually make some treaty rules binding
more broadly.
The Convention also regulates invalidity, suspension, and termination. Under Articles 46 to
58, a treaty may be invalidated for conflict with domestic law regarding competence, error,
fraud, corruption, coercion, or conflict with jus cogens, that is, peremptory norms such as
genocide, piracy, apartheid, or torture. A treaty may terminate by withdrawal, breach,
impossibility of performance, conclusion of a later treaty on the same subject, fundamental
change of circumstances, or emergence of a new jus cogens norm. Thus, treaties remain a
central instrument of international law because they create legal certainty, regulate inter-
State conduct, and promote peace, order, and cooperation in the international system. [Word
Count: 434]

V. A geographical indication (GI) is a sign used on products that have a specific geographical origin and possess
qualities or a reputation that are due to that origin. In order to function as a GI, a sign must identify a product as
originating in a given place. In addition, the qualities, characteristics or reputation of the product should be
essentially due to the place of origin. Since the qualities depend on the geographical place of production, there
is a clear link between the product and its original place of production.
As per section 2 (e) of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, the
definition is as follows:
(e) "geographical indication", in relation to goods, means an indication which identifies such goods as
agricultural goods, natural goods or manufactured goods as originating, or manufactured in the territory of a
country, or a region or locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of such
goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and in case where such goods are manufactured goods
one of the activities of either the production or of processing or preparation of the goods concerned takes place
in such territory, region or locality, as the case may be.
Section 2 (f) states: "goods" means any agricultural, natural or manufactured goods or any goods of handicraft
or of industry and includes food stuff.
Section 2 (k) "producer", in relation to goods, means any person who: (i) if such goods are agricultural goods,
produces the goods and includes the person who processes or packages such goods; (ii) if such goods are natural
goods, exploits the goods; (iii) if such goods are handicraft or industrial goods, makes or manufactures the
goods, and includes any person who trades or deals in such production, exploitation, making or manufacturing,
as the case may be, of the goods.
A geographical indication must be registered by a producer with the registrar of Geographical indications after
paying the mandatory fee. The registration of a geographical indication shall be for a period of ten years, but
may be renewed from time to time according to section 18. As per section 20, no person shall be entitled to
institute any proceeding to prevent, or to recover damages for, the infringement of an unregistered or lapsed


geographical indication. There can be infringement action in registered GI under section 21 and 22. There will
be penalty as fine and imprisonment if false geographical indication is applied.

%20in%20a%20given%20place.

VI. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 recognises acid attack victims as a category of persons entitled to
statutory protection, rehabilitation, and disability-related benefits. In Shaheen Malik v. Union of India & Anr. (2025),
the Supreme Court invoked its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to hold that the expression "acid attack
victim" must receive a purposive and beneficial interpretation. The Court held that the expression includes not only
persons disfigured by the throwing of acid but also persons who are forcibly made to consume acid and those who suffer
internal injuries caused by acid or similar corrosive substances, notwithstanding the absence of visible external
disfigurement. The Court directed that this interpretation shall operate retrospectively from the commencement of the
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 and urged the Union Government to suitably amend the Schedule appended
to the Act so as to remove the existing statutory lacuna. The Court observed that the legislative objective of the Act is to


protect every person who suffers disability as a consequence of an acid attack, irrespective of the manner in which the
injury is inflicted.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 criminalises voluntarily causing injury by throwing, administering, or otherwise using
acid or any corrosive or burning substance. The offence includes causing permanent or partial damage, deformity,
maiming, disfigurement, disability, internal injuries, burn injuries, or rendering a person into a permanent vegetative state.
The offence is cognizable and non-bailable and is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than ten years, which
may extend to imprisonment for life, together with a mandatory fine that is just, reasonable, and payable directly to the
victim for medical treatment and related expenses. Attempt to commit an acid attack constitutes a separate cognizable and
non-bailable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than five years but which may extend to seven
years, together with fine. A public servant who intentionally fails to record information relating to an acid attack commits
a cognizable and non-compoundable offence punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than six months
but which may extend to two years, in addition to fine.
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 guarantees immediate and free medical treatment to every acid attack
survivor. Every public and private hospital is under a statutory obligation to provide prompt treatment without delay or
refusal and must immediately inform the police upon admitting such victim. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita
further provides for a statutory Victim Compensation Scheme under which acid attack survivors are entitled to
compensation independent of, and in addition to, any fine or compensation imposed upon the offender by a criminal court.
Acid attack survivors are also entitled to financial assistance under governmental rehabilitation schemes and to free legal
aid through the District Legal Services Authorities, State Legal Services Authorities, and the National Legal Services
Authority irrespective of their economic status.
Acid attack has been recognised as a specified disability under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
Consequently, acid attack survivors are entitled to all statutory rights, reservations, rehabilitation measures, social security
benefits, and welfare schemes available to persons with disabilities. In Parivartan Kendra v. Union of India (2013), the
Supreme Court directed strict regulation of the manufacture, sale, and distribution of acid and held that the authorities
responsible for regulating its sale must ensure effective implementation of the regulatory framework. The statutory
framework governing acid attacks must therefore be interpreted in a manner that advances the constitutional values of
dignity, equality, rehabilitation, access to justice, and effective protection of victims.

VI. The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, is a comprehensive piece of legislation that governs the admissibility and
relevancy of evidence in the Indian court system. The Act is divided into three parts: Part 1 deals with the
relevancy of facts, Part 2 covers types of evidence and when each is preferred, and Part 3 focuses on issues such
as the burden of proof and estoppel. For this excerpt, we will delve into the Doctrine of Estoppel as outlined in
Section 115 and 116 of the Act, which provides numerous legal principles that can be tested in various
hypothetical scenarios.
Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act defines the doctrine of Estoppel. It states, "When one person has, by his
declaration, act or omission, intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true by his
act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed, in any suit or proceeding between
himself and such person or his representative, to deny the truth of that thing".
   1. Principle of Representation: A representation must be made by one person to another. This
      representation must concern an existing fact and be conveyed in a manner that makes the other person
      believe it to be true.
   2. Principle of Reliance: The person to whom the representation is made must act upon their belief of its
      truthfulness. If this person suffers a loss due to their reliance on the representation, the doctrine of
      estoppel may apply.
   3. Principle of Consistency: One cannot contradict, deny or declare to be false a previous statement made
      by them in court. For example, if a person accepts their liability to make payment under an arbitration
      award, they cannot later challenge the award.
   4. Principle of Legitimacy: A person is bound by their previous statements and cannot challenge facts
      they've previously accepted. In Shammim Beg v. Najmunnissa Begum, the husband could not challenge
      the legitimacy of a child he had accepted as his own.


Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act extends the doctrine of estoppel to specific circumstances involving
tenancies and licenses. This section prohibits a tenant or licensee from denying the title of the landlord or
licensor during the continuance of the tenancy or license.
   5. Principle of Tenancy: No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant, shall,
      during the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny that the landlord of such tenant had, at the
      beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable property.
   6. Principle of License: No person who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in
      possession thereof, shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time
      when such license was given.
These principles are interrelated and form the bedrock of the Doctrine of Estoppel in Indian law, ensuring that
individuals cannot benefit from their own deceit or contradiction in legal proceedings.
[Source with edits revision made from: https://lawctopus.com/clatalogue/clat-pg/notes-on-introduction-to-
indian-evidence-act/]

III. Right to Freedom to practice religion under Article 25 and 26 of Part III of the Indian Constitution is subject
to public morality, public order and public health. The rights under Articles 25 & 26 are not absolute or
unfettered but subject to legislation by the State limiting or regulating any activity, economic, financial, political
or secular which are associated with the religious behalf, faith, practice or custom and they are also subject to
social reform by suitable legislation. Article 25 gives individual right to freely profess, profess and practice their
religion while Article 26 gives every religious group a right to establish and maintain institutions for religious
and charitable purposes, manage its affairs, properties as per the law. Within the Constitution of India, these are
two impulses that may, at times, come into conflict with one another. The first impulse recognizes that India is a
pluralist and diverse nation, where groups and communities — whether religious or cultural — have always
played an important role in society. Following up on this impulse, the Constitution recognizes both the freedom
of religion as an individual right (Article 25), as well as the right of religious denominations to manage their
own affairs in matters of religion (Article 26). The second impulse, on the other hand, recognises that while
community can be a source of solidarity at the best of times, it can also be a terrain of oppression and exclusion.

The Constitution, therefore, expressly provides for the possibility that there may be times when members of
religious and cultural communities may need to be protected from authoritarian and oppressive social practices.
Thus, both Articles 25 and 26 are subject to public order, morality, and health; and further, Article 25 is also
subject to other fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, and to the state’s power to bring in social
reform laws.

Over the years, the Supreme Court has attempted to strike the balance by carving out a jurisprudence that
virtually allows it to sit in theological judgment over different practices. It has done this by recognizing that it is
only those practices that are “essential” to religion that enjoy constitutional protection. Any other ritual is seen
as secular and amenable to the state's interference. The legislature does not efface a religion altogether, by doing
away with its basic or essential doctrines or practices. Essential religious practices test puts its faith in practices
that bear a very intense and proximate connection to the basic tenants of religion, or are rather integral to the


religion, and any activity would be redundancy if it does not bear such a close connection with the religion
(including practices which may be superstitious) and that may be deemed extraneous. By following this
principle, the concept of social reforms was inherited by the Indian Constitution under Article 25(2)(b) without
impairing the freedom of religion.

Source: https://www.barandbench.com/columns/the-supreme-court-urgently-reconsider-jurisprudence-
religious-freedom

XI.	In the law of torts, liability generally arises when a person causes harm to another through a
wrongful act or omission. However, not all damage results in legal responsibility. There are
situations where harm is caused without any human fault, purely due to natural forces beyond
control. In such cases, the law recognizes a defence known as the Act of God, also referred to as
Vis Major. This doctrine plays an important role in determining the limits of liability,
especially in cases involving natural disasters such as floods, earthquakes, storms, and
lightning. It reflects the principle that individuals should not be held responsible for events
that are entirely outside human foresight and control.
An Act of God refers to an extraordinary natural event caused exclusively by natural forces,
which is unpredictable, unforeseeable, and unavoidable despite reasonable care. The term Vis
Major is derived from Latin, meaning “superior force,” and both expressions are used

interchangeably in tort law. The essence of this defence is that when damage is caused solely
by natural forces, without any human intervention or negligence, the defendant cannot be held
liable.
For the defence of Act of God to succeed, certain essential conditions must be fulfilled. First,
the event must arise purely due to natural forces such as earthquakes, floods, cyclones, or
lightning, and if human involvement contributes to the damage, the defence fails. Secondly,
the event must be extraordinary and not something expected under ordinary circumstances,
which means predictable events like normal seasonal rainfall do not qualify. Thirdly, the event
must be unforeseeable so that a reasonable person could not have anticipated it through
ordinary knowledge or scientific means. Lastly, the event must be inevitable and unavoidable
despite the exercise of reasonable care and precautions.
A significant distinction exists between an Act of God and negligence. If damage is caused
entirely due to natural forces, liability does not arise. However, where a natural event
combines with human negligence, liability may still be imposed. For example, destruction
caused by an unprecedented flood may qualify as an Act of God, but if defective construction or
lack of maintenance contributed to the damage, the defendant may remain liable.
The doctrine also acts as an exception to the rule of strict liability. Under strict liability, a
person may be held liable even without negligence, but the defence of Act of God operates
where the harm is caused solely by natural forces that could neither be anticipated nor
controlled. Thus, even strict liability has limits when confronted with extraordinary natural
events. Courts have repeatedly emphasized that: (1) the natural event must be exceptional and
unprecedented; (2) there must be no human contribution to the damage; and (3) reasonable
care and precautions must have been exercised. If these conditions are not satisfied, the
defence is rejected.
The defence of Act of God is applied cautiously and is subject to several limitations. Firstly,
with advancements in science and technology, many natural events can now be predicted, and
therefore, if an event is foreseeable, the defence may not apply. Secondly, individuals and
authorities are expected to take reasonable precautions against known risks, and failure to do
so may result in liability. Thirdly, even minimal human negligence can defeat the defence
because the event must be entirely natural in origin. Lastly, modern courts have adopted
stricter standards due to improved disaster forecasting, better infrastructure planning, and
increased expectations of safety.
Although primarily a concept in tort law, Act of God is also relevant in contract law through
force majeure clauses. These clauses excuse parties from performing contractual obligations
when extraordinary natural events occur, although the extent of protection depends upon the
wording of the contract. The principle underlying this defence is reflected in the legal maxim
“Actus Dei nemini facit injuriam,” meaning that an act of God injures no one in the eyes of the
law. Ultimately, the doctrine of Act of God represents an important limitation on liability by

ensuring that individuals are not unfairly held responsible for damage caused entirely by
forces beyond human control, while also preventing negligence from escaping accountability
under the guise of natural events.
Source: https://www.freelaw.in/legalarticles /Act-of-God-Vis-Major-in-Tort-Law-Scope-and-
Limitations

III. The constitutional promise of an independent judiciary depends not merely upon the decisions rendered by
courts but equally upon the manner in which judges are appointed. The process of judicial appointments has,
therefore, remained one of the most debated constitutional questions in India, engaging issues of judicial
independence, executive accountability, separation of powers, and the Basic Structure Doctrine. Through a
series of landmark constitutional decisions, the Supreme Court has progressively shaped the law governing
appointments to the higher judiciary, ultimately establishing the Collegium System as the prevailing
constitutional mechanism. The appointment of judges to the Supreme Court is governed primarily by Article
124 of the Constitution, which embodies the constitutional principles of judicial independence, institutional
consultation, and constitutional checks and balances. Under Article 124(2), every Judge of the Supreme Court is
appointed by the President of India by warrant under his hand and seal in accordance with the constitutional
procedure. A person shall be qualified for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court if he or she is a citizen
of India and has either served for at least five years as a Judge of one or more High Courts in succession, or has
practised for at least ten years as an advocate of one or more High Courts in succession, or is, in the opinion of
the President, a distinguished jurist. Every Judge of the Supreme Court holds office until attaining the age of
sixty-five years, may resign by writing addressed to the President, or may be removed only through the
constitutional procedure prescribed under Article 124(4) on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
The sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court is determined by Parliament, and appointments are made against
sanctioned vacancies in accordance with the constitutional framework.

The constitutional interpretation of the expression "consultation" under Article 124(2) has undergone significant
judicial evolution through the Three Judges Cases, which collectively constitute the foundation of the present
Collegium System. In S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case, 1981), the Supreme Court held that
consultation with the Chief Justice of India did not imply concurrence, and the executive possessed primacy in
judicial appointments. The Court interpreted consultation as an exchange of views rather than binding advice,
thereby recognising executive supremacy. This position was fundamentally altered in Supreme Court
Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Second Judges Case, 1993), wherein a nine-judge Bench


overruled the earlier decision and held that the Chief Justice of India's opinion, formed collectively after
consulting the two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court, would enjoy primacy. The Court held that judicial
independence forms part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution and that appointments must remain insulated
from executive influence by giving institutional primacy to the judiciary. It further clarified that the opinion of
the Chief Justice is not an individual opinion but an institutional opinion formed through collective consultation.

The scope and functioning of the Collegium System were further clarified in the Special Reference No. 1 of
1998 (Third Judges Case) rendered under Article 143 pursuant to a Presidential Reference. The Supreme Court
held that the expression "consultation" under Article 124(2) requires consultation with a plurality of judges, and
not merely the individual opinion of the Chief Justice of India. Accordingly, the Collegium for appointments to
the Supreme Court consists of the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court.
The Court further held that where two members of the Collegium express adverse opinions regarding a
proposed candidate, the recommendation ordinarily should not be forwarded. The Collegium's views must be
recorded in writing, and the Chief Justice forwards the recommendation to the President along with the opinions
of all members consulted. Although the executive may return a recommendation for reconsideration, if the
Collegium reiterates the recommendation upon reconsideration, the President is constitutionally bound to accept
it.

The constitutional position underwent a temporary transformation through the Constitution (Ninety-Ninth
Amendment) Act, 2014 and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014, which substituted the
Collegium System with the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC). The amendment inserted
Articles 124A, 124B and 124C, and amended Articles 124(2), 127 and 128, providing that appointments would
be made by the President on the recommendation of the NJAC. The Commission comprised the Chief Justice of
India, two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court, the Union Minister for Law and Justice, and two eminent
persons nominated by a committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India, and the Leader
of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015),
popularly known as the Fourth Judges Case, the Supreme Court declared both the Ninety-Ninth Constitutional
Amendment and the NJAC Act unconstitutional. The Court held that judicial independence and the separation
of powers constitute integral features of the Basic Structure Doctrine, and that the inclusion of executive and
non-judicial members in the appointment process diluted the institutional independence of the judiciary.
Consequently, the Collegium System, as evolved through the Second and Third Judges Cases, stood revived and
continues to govern appointments to the higher judiciary.

The constitutional framework governing appointments also incorporates the Memorandum of Procedure (MoP),
evolved through judicial decisions and executive consultation, which regulates the process of identification,
evaluation, consultation, recommendation, reconsideration, and appointment of judges. The Collegium assesses
merit, integrity, judicial competence, seniority, professional ability, suitability, regional representation, diversity,
and institutional requirements while making recommendations. Although seniority remains the governing
principle for the appointment of the Chief Justice of India, appointments to the Supreme Court also recognise
considerations relating to gender representation and diversity consistent with constitutional values. The recent
appointments of Justice Sheel Nagu, Justice Shree Chandrashekhar, Justice Sanjeev Sachdeva, Justice Arun
Palli, and Senior Advocate V. Mohana have brought the Supreme Court closer to its sanctioned strength of 38
judges, while also increasing the representation of women on the Bench.


Sources: LiveLaw – Five New Judges Take Oath in Supreme Court, Court Moves Closer to Full Strength

XI.	Section 504 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) proscribes intentional insult with intent to
provoke breach of public peace. In Fiona Shrikhande v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme
Court delineated three essential ingredients constituting the offence under Section 504 IPC:
(a) intentional insult; (b) the insult must be of such nature as to give provocation to the person
insulted; and (c) the accused must intend or know that such provocation would cause another
to break the public peace or commit any other offence. The intentional insult must be of
sufficient degree to provoke a person to break public peace or commit another offence. Mere
abusive language, absent the requisite provocative element and mental state, does not ipso
facto satisfy Section 504. Significantly, the Supreme Court clarified that verbatim reproduction
of offending words in the complaint is not mandated. Rather, the Magistrate must read the
complaint holistically and determine prima facie whether intentional insult coupled with
provocative potential exists. Background facts, circumstances, the occasion, the manner of
utterance, the addressee, temporal context, and the accused's conduct constitute relevant
considerations in evaluating complaints under Section 504 IPC. As articulated in B.V. Ram
Kumar v. State of Telangana, if the Magistrate, upon reading the complaint as a whole,
concludes prima facie that an intentional insult was made with capacity to provoke breach of
public peace or commission of another offence, the complaint falls within Section 504's ambit.
Critically, Section 504 operates as an inchoate offence—it does not require proof that public
peace was actually broken or that another offence was in fact committed. The statutory focus
rests on the tendency and likelihood of provocation leading to such consequences, not
accomplished disturbance. The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) provides procedural
mechanisms governing private complaints alleging offences like Section 504. Section 200 CrPC
mandates examination of the complainant and witnesses on oath, forming the foundational
step in complaint cases. Section 202 CrPC permits postponement of process issuance where the
Magistrate considers it necessary to conduct a preliminary inquiry or investigation to verify
whether sufficient grounds exist to proceed. This provision operates as an optional safeguard
against mechanical process issuance. Where complaints fail to disclose essential ingredients or
constitute abuse of process, the High Court may exercise inherent jurisdiction under Section
482 CrPC to quash proceedings. This power ensures prevention of unjust continuation of
proceedings and secures justice, distinguishing it from appellate re-appreciation under Section
3897 CrPC or compounding under Section 320 CrPC. Section 504 IPC must be distinguished
from Section 506 IPC (criminal intimidation), which addresses threats intended to cause alarm
or compel action or inaction, rather than provocative insults aimed at breaching public peace.
The two provisions protect distinct legal interests and operate on different factual matrices.
Source: Extracted with edits and revision from judgement delivered by Mehta, J. in B.V. Ram
Kumar v. State of Telangana, (2025) 3 SCC 475
passages.LEG-P0289:
V. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, as amended in 2021, regulates the conditions under which
pregnancies may be lawfully terminated in India. The Act recognises the reproductive autonomy of women


while prescribing statutory safeguards based upon the stage of pregnancy and the opinion of qualified medical
professionals. As a general rule, a pregnancy may be terminated up to twenty weeks of gestation, provided the
conditions prescribed under the Act are fulfilled and the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner is
obtained. For pregnancies between twenty and twenty-four weeks, termination is permissible only for specified
categories of women, including survivors of rape, sexual assault or incest, minors, women whose marital status
changes due to widowhood or divorce during pregnancy, women with physical disabilities recognised under the
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, mentally ill women including women with mental retardation,
women carrying foetuses suffering from substantial abnormalities likely to be incompatible with life or likely to
result in serious physical or mental disability, and women whose pregnancies occur in humanitarian, disaster or
emergency situations declared by the Government. Termination during this period requires the opinion of not
less than two Registered Medical Practitioners.

The Act imposes stricter conditions once the pregnancy exceeds twenty-four weeks. Termination beyond this
stage is ordinarily prohibited and is permissible only where it is immediately necessary to save the life of the
pregnant woman or where substantial foetal abnormalities are diagnosed in accordance with the statutory
procedure. In cases involving substantial foetal abnormalities after twenty-four weeks, the opinion of the State-
level Medical Board is mandatory. The Act further permits termination of pregnancy on the ground of failure of
any contraceptive method or device, and this ground is available equally to both married and unmarried women.
Thus, while the Act recognises reproductive choice, it subjects such choice to different procedural requirements
depending upon the duration of pregnancy.

The Act also prescribes the places where pregnancy may be lawfully terminated. No termination may be carried
out except in a hospital established or maintained by the Government or at a place specifically approved for the
purposes of the Act by the Government or by a duly constituted District Level Committee. Such Committee is
required to consist of not less than three and not more than five members, with the Chief Medical Officer or
District Health Officer serving as its Chairperson. To ensure confidentiality, Section 5A prohibits a Registered
Medical Practitioner from disclosing the identity or other particulars of a woman whose pregnancy has been
terminated under the Act, except where disclosure is authorised by law. The Act also grants protection to
Registered Medical Practitioners acting in good faith by providing that no civil or criminal proceedings shall lie
against them for any act done or intended to be done in accordance with the Act.

The constitutional validity and operation of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act have repeatedly come
before constitutional courts. The Supreme Court has observed that the statutory scheme permits termination of
pregnancies beyond twenty-four weeks where substantial foetal abnormalities exist but does not ordinarily
extend similar protection to pregnancies resulting from rape or incest involving minor girls. The Court has
therefore indicated that the legislative framework may require reconsideration to remove the statutory time limit
in cases involving pregnancies of minor rape victims. The issue highlights the interaction between statutory
restrictions and constitutional guarantees of dignity, bodily autonomy and reproductive choice.

Indian constitutional jurisprudence has consistently recognised that a woman's decision whether to continue or
terminate a pregnancy forms part of the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the
Constitution. The constitutional protection extends to decisional autonomy, bodily integrity, privacy and the
freedom to determine whether to enter motherhood. Judicial decisions have emphasised that compelling a
woman to continue a pregnancy arising from rape may infringe her dignity and personal liberty by forcing her


to endure continuing physical and psychological trauma. Constitutional courts have therefore interpreted the
Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act in a manner that seeks to balance legislative safeguards with the
fundamental rights of women while ensuring that the statutory requirements governing gestational limits,
medical opinions, approved medical facilities and confidentiality are strictly complied with.

Source: https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/amend-law-to-remove-time-limit-for-termination-of-pregnancy-
ofminor-rape-victim-supreme-court-to-centre-532351

XIII. In India the law on this subject is mentioned under Section 84 of IPC, the provisions are same
as mentioned in McNaughten case held by House Of Lords. By the way Section 84 use a more
comprehensive term unsoundness of mind rather than the word insanity.
Essential ingredients of Section 84 of Indian Penal Code (IPC):
1. Act must be done by a person of unsound mind.
2. Such person was unsound at the time of committing the act.
8. Such incapacity should be of unsoundness of mind of the accused.
4. Such person was not capable to know the nature of the act or the act he was doing was
either wrong or contrary to law.
Distinction between Legal Insanity and Medical Insanity:
It is important to note that insanity plays a vital role in criminal law and it is legal sense is to
be understood rather than medical sense in order to claim defense under IPC. Legal insanity is
narrower than medical insanity because some illness which are termed as insanity according
to medical science but it cannot fulfil the criteria of Legal Insanity in order to get the defense
under IPC.
Medical Insanity: According to medical science, unsoundness of mind or insanity is a type of
disease which messes with mental faculty of a person. This disease in brain or nervous system
leads to working of one or two functions of brain in an abnormal way or these functions of
brain do not function at all because of the disease in brain. There are four kinds of person
which are categorised into unsound mind and these are as follows:
1. Idiot: A person who is non-sane since his/her birth without any lucid intervals.
2. Lunatic: Lunatic is a type of person who is triggered of mental disorder only for certain
period. Lunacy is acquired insanity but idiocy is a natural insanity.
8. Non Compos Mentis (not of sound mind) by illness: This type of person do not know what
he/she is doing and prolonged disease cause fits of delirium and under such fits the person
is not able to identify what is right or wrong.
4. One who is under intoxication, so much so as to completely be devoid of his cognitive
abilities
Legal Insanity: Legal conception of the insanity is different from the Medical conception of
the insanity, not every kind of insanity is made excusable in the eyes of Law. Section 84 of IPC
cannot be invoked unless it is established that the accused was suffering from legal insanity at

the time of commission of act. To invoke the benefit of Section 84 of the IPC it must be proved
that unsoundness of mind was of such a degree which should be capable to fulfil any one of the
test laid down under this section and they are:
1. The accused was either incapable of knowing the nature of the act; or
2. The accused was not capable of understanding that what he was doing was either wrong or
contrary to Law.
However, in the case of Bapu Gujarat Singh v. State of Rajasthan, it was held that the words
“either” & “or” shall be read as the term “And”, and thus in the later part of the section, mere

passages.LEG-P0291:
IV. The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, commonly known as the anti-defection law, lays down the
circumstances in which a member of a legislature incurs disqualification on the ground of defection. A member
elected on the ticket of a political party is liable to be disqualified if the member voluntarily gives up the
membership of that political party or votes, or abstains from voting, contrary to any direction issued by the
political party without prior permission, unless such action is condoned by the political party within fifteen
days. The expression "voluntarily giving up membership" is not confined to formal resignation and may be
inferred from the conduct of the member. An independently elected member incurs disqualification upon joining
any political party after the election, while a nominated member incurs disqualification if the member joins a
political party after the expiry of six months from the date of taking a seat in the House. Any question relating to
disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is decided by the Speaker or the Chairman of the House, whose
decision remains subject to judicial review.

The Constitution recognises only one exception to disqualification on the ground of defection, namely a valid
merger under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule. A member shall not be disqualified if the original political
party merges with another political party and the member acts in accordance with such merger. A member who
does not accept a valid merger is also protected from disqualification and is entitled to continue functioning as a
separate group within the House. However, constitutional protection is available only when the merger satisfies
all the conditions prescribed under Paragraph 4.
For the purposes of the Tenth Schedule, the "original political party" and the "legislature party" are distinct legal
entities. The original political party refers to the parent political organisation, whereas the legislature party
consists only of the members of that political party in a particular House. The legislature party derives its
existence and authority from the original political party and cannot function independently in matters
concerning merger. Consequently, the decision to merge must originate from the original political party. A
legislature party cannot independently initiate, declare, or create a merger with another political party, and any
such attempt does not satisfy the constitutional requirements governing mergers.

Paragraph 4(2) provides that a merger shall be deemed to have taken place only if not less than two-thirds of the
members of the legislature party concerned have agreed to such merger. The requirement of a two-thirds
majority is mandatory but is not, by itself, sufficient to constitute a valid merger. Such approval acquires legal
effect only after the original political party has resolved to merge with another political party. Therefore, a valid
merger requires the coexistence of two conditions: a merger of the original political party and the approval of
not less than two-thirds of the members of the corresponding legislature party. Failure to satisfy either condition

renders the constitutional exception inapplicable and attracts the ordinary provisions relating to disqualification
under the anti-defection law.

The constitutional position regarding mergers was strengthened by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment)
Act, 2003, which omitted the earlier provision recognising splits by one-third of the members of a legislature
party. Following the amendment, the Constitution recognises only mergers supported by not less than two-thirds
of the members of the legislature party, thereby preventing legislators from circumventing the anti-defection
law through smaller breakaway groups.
Judicial interpretation has consistently affirmed the primacy of the original political party under the Tenth
Schedule. In Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that voluntary relinquishment of
party membership may be inferred from the conduct of a member and does not require a formal resignation. In
Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya (2007), the Court rejected the "two hats theory" and held that
legislators cannot simultaneously claim an independent constitutional identity separate from the original
political party. More recently, in Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (2023), the
Supreme Court reaffirmed that a legislature party cannot function independently of the original political party in
matters relating to party leadership, organisational authority, or constitutional recognition. The constitutional
scheme, therefore, recognises the original political party as the primary legal entity under the Tenth Schedule,
while the legislature party functions only as its legislative manifestation. Accordingly, protection from
disqualification on the ground of merger is available only upon strict compliance with the constitutional
requirements prescribed under Paragraph 4.
Source: https://www.livelaw.in/articles/is-raghav-chaddhas-merger-with-bjp-a-valid-defence-under-
antidefection-law-531690

SECTION III
XI.	Common Intention and Common Object under BNS: Sections 3(5) and 190 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) are the two principal doctrines of constructive or joint
criminal liability. Both provisions impose criminal liability on each member of a group for an
act committed by any member, but they differ substantially in their requirements and
operation.
Section 3(5) BNS provides that when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance
of the common intention of all, each person is liable as if the act were done by him alone.
Section 3(5) is not a substantive offence but a rule of joint liability that operates in conjunction
with another penal provision. Its essential ingredients are: (i) a criminal act done by several
persons; (ii) existence of a common intention shared by all; and (iii) participation in the act in
furtherance of that common intention. Mahbub Shah v. Emperor emphasised that common
intention implies prior concert and is distinct from similar intention, which is merely a
simultaneous inclination of several persons acting independently. However, such a meeting of
minds need not involve lengthy premeditation and may crystallise on the spot in response to
developing circumstances.
Active participation in the criminal act is a necessary element of Section 3(5). Mere presence at
the scene is insufficient to attract liability. However, participation need not take the form of
direct physical commission of the offence; assistance, instigation, or facilitation at the scene in
furtherance of the pre-arranged plan suffices. In Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor
(1925), the Privy Council held that an accused who stood guard outside a post office while his
associates entered and killed the postmaster during a robbery was jointly liable for murder
under Section 3(5), since he was present and participating in furtherance of the common plan
even though he did not personally fire the shot. The principle that "the act of one is the act of
all" applies where participation in furtherance of the plan is established.
Section 190 BNS operates on a different basis. It provides that every member of an unlawful
assembly is guilty of any offence committed by any member of that assembly in prosecution of
the common object, or of such offences as the members knew were likely to be committed in
prosecution of that object. An unlawful assembly is defined under Section 189 BNS as an
assembly of five or more persons sharing a common object of one of the enumerated kinds.
Section 190 does not require proof of a prior meeting of minds; membership in the unlawful
assembly at the time the offence is committed is sufficient to attract vicarious liability. In Lalji
v. State of U.P. (1989), the Supreme Court held that the crucial inquiry is whether the accused
was a member of the unlawful assembly at the relevant time and whether the offence was
committed in prosecution of the common object or with knowledge that it was likely to be
committed.

Section 190 contains two distinct limbs: (i) liability for offences committed in prosecution of the
common object; and (ii) liability for offences which members knew were likely to be committed.
The Supreme Court in Mizaji v. State of U.P. (1959) clarified that knowledge under the second
limb must be of the likelihood of the specific offence, assessed objectively from the
circumstances — not a vague awareness of possible disorder.
A critical distinction between Sections 3(5) and 190 is that the former requires active
participation while the latter imposes liability on the basis of membership alone. Under
Section 190, if the number of members of the unlawful assembly is reduced below five owing to
acquittals, the remaining accused cannot be convicted under Section 190 unless Section 3(5)
independently applies. The Supreme Court in Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab (1963) held that
Section 190 cannot be applied where fewer than five persons are found to have shared the
common object. Sections 3(5) and 190 are not mutually exclusive; courts have recognised that
Section 3(5) may be applied in place of Section 190 where evidence establishes common
intention, provided the accused suffered no prejudice in their defence.
Source: Extracted with revisions and modifications from:
Ratanlal & Dhirajlal, The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Commentary)

Which of the following authorities is NOT correctly matched with its enabling
       environmental legislation?

State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) - The Water (Prevention & Control of
              Pollution) Act, 1974

questions.questionText:
A tribunal passed an award in favour of Mahima. Dev, the opposing party, files a challenge
under Section 34 after 4 months, stating that the arbitrator ignored a crucial witness. Will his
challenge be entertained?
options: Yes, arbitrators must hear all witnesses.
No, the challenge is time barred.
Yes, because it’s against public policy.
No, because only Supreme Court can hear such matters.
questions.solution: The passage provides that an arbitral award may be challenged within 3 months from the date of receipt of the award, extendable by an additional 30 days if sufficient cause is shown. Beyond this period, the challenge is barred by limitation.

questions.questionText:
A German software company accuses an Indian firm of infringing intellectual property rights by
copying its code. Both firms present national laws, EU directives, and Indian judicial precedents to
resolve the dispute. Which comparative approach is being applied in this scenario?
options: Legal transplants, copying foreign law verbatim into domestic statutes.
Lex mercatoria, applying commercial customs to intellectual property disputes.
Comparative analysis, studying foreign precedents for domestic decision-making.
Customary international law, automatically binding private firms across borders.
questions.solution: Option (a): Incorrect. Legal transplants require formal adoption, not mere reference. Option (b): Incorrect. Lex mercatoria governs trade, not IP law. Option (c): Correct. Comparative study helps interpret foreign precedents for domestic cases. Option (d): Incorrect. Customary international law binds states, not private entities. Reference: "Comparative International Law involves analyzing domestic systems and international conventions."

questions.questionText:
A tribunal passed an award in favour of Lakshmi, but it was later found that the arbitrator
had accepted bribes from the opposing party. Can the award be set aside?
options: Yes, because an award induced by fraud or corruption is against public policy.
No, arbitration awards are final.
No, unless criminal charges are filed.
Yes, but only if both parties agree.
questions.solution: The passage states that an arbitral award may be set aside if it is contrary to the public policy of India. Awards induced by fraud, corruption, bribery, or conduct violating fundamental fairness fall within this category.

questions.questionText:
A rule requires all job applicants to clear a physical endurance test designed for
combat roles, even though the job is purely clerical. Which equality concern does this
situation most clearly raise?
options: Violation of formal equality only
Violation of substantive equality due to unequal impact
No equality issue since the rule applies uniformly
Both A and B

questions.questionText:
Ravi, a small shopkeeper, signed a lease agreement under threat from a local gang demanding
payment or facing violence. The lease caused him financial hardship, and he seeks to challenge it.
Which element of free consent is primarily violated here?
options: Undue influence, arising from dominant position over the party.
Coercion, involving threats to person or property.
Misrepresentation, due to false statements made innocently.
Mistake, concerning the subject matter of the contract.
questions.solution: Option (a): Incorrect. Undue influence involves a dominant position, not threats. Option (b): Correct. Coercion occurs when consent is obtained through threats or pressure. Option (c): Incorrect. Misrepresentation involves false statements, not threats. Option (d): Incorrect. Mistake concerns errors affecting the essence of the contract. Reference: "Coercion occurs when a person is compelled to enter into a contract by threats of injury to their person, reputation, or property."

questions.questionText:
Arjun tells Karan: "If it rains this afternoon, you pay me 25,000. If it doesn't rain, I pay you
nothing." It rains. Is this arrangement a wagering agreement?
options: Yes, because both parties agreed to the terms
No, because the amount is too small for consideration
No, because only one party can win.
Yes, because rain is an uncertain future event
questions.solution: because the passage explicitly states such one-sided arrangements are NOT wagering contracts due to lack of mutual risk.

questions.questionText:
Mohammed Shami discovers that a person with forged educational certificates has been appointed as
the Head Coach of the National Cricket Academy, a public post. Shami wants to challenge this
appointment. Which writ will question the validity of the coach’s claim to that public office?
options: Certiorari to cancel the appointment letter.
Mandamus to appoint a qualified person.
Habeas Corpus for public safety concerns.
Quo Warranto against the appointee.
questions.solution: This is the precise function of Quo Warranto — to challenge a person's legal right to continue in a substantive public office.

questions.questionText:
Rahul purchased a car after the dealer deliberately concealed that it had been involved in an
accident. Rahul discovered the truth after taking delivery and seeks to rescind the contract. Which
element of free consent is primarily affected here?
options: Coercion, involving threats to person or property.
Mistake, concerning the identity of the car.
Undue influence, due to dominant position over buyer.
Fraud, involving deliberate deception to induce agreement.
questions.solution: Option (a): Incorrect. No threats or pressure were involved in this case. Option (b): Incorrect. The issue is not a mistake but intentional deception. Option (c): Incorrect. No dominant position was exploited to gain consent. Option (d): Correct. Fraud occurs when one party intentionally deceives another to obtain consent. Reference: "Fraud involves deliberate deception to induce a party to enter into a contract." 77. Answer: C

questions.questionText:
A ministry issues rules fixing penalties that are not mentioned anywhere in the parent
statute, which only authorised procedural regulations. Based on the passage, what is the
most logical outcome?
options: The rules are valid because penalties improve enforcement.
Courts cannot review delegated legislation once notified.
The rules are valid due to presumption of constitutionality.
The rules may be struck down as ultra vires the parent statute.

questions.questionText:
The Supreme Court initially directed the undergrounding of all power lines in GIB
        habitats, but later modified its stance. Which rationale best explains this shift?
options:
The Court concluded that biodiversity protection must always yield to economic
      growth.

The Court recognised that rigid conservation measures could undermine climate
      mitigation goals.

The Court accepted that renewable energy projects are immune from environmental
      scrutiny.
Both A and C.

questions.questionText:
Why did the Indian Supreme Court evolve the doctrine of Absolute Liability in the MC.
Mehta case?
options: To simplify the definition of "non-natural use" of land.
To allow defendants to use the "Act of a Stranger" defence more effectively.
To ensure hazardous industries do not escape liability using traditional defence.
To replace all fault-based liability categories with no-fault liability.
questions.solution: The text states the Court realized traditional exceptions allowed industries to "evade accountability," thus ensuring industries "bear the full cost." Incorrect: (A), (B), and (D) are not mentioned as the rationale in the passage.

questions.questionText: State Y intercepts a foreign ship 20 nautical miles from its coast on suspicion of tax evasion. Which is the best legal justification?
options: State Y has full sovereignty over the area and may act freely.
The action is invalid because the area lies outside territorial waters.
The action is justified under the powers available in the contiguous zone.
The action is valid only if approved by an international body.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The action is justified under the powers available in the contiguous zone. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
X filed a suit against Y for partition of ancestral property. The suit was decreed by a competent
court and became final. Later, Z, who is the legal heir and privy of Y, files a fresh suit against X
claiming the same property on the same grounds. Can Z's suit proceed?
options: Yes, because Z was not a party to the original litigation
No, but only if X proves that Z is a legal heir
Yes, because legal heirs always have independent property rights
No, because res judicata binds the privies of the parties
questions.solution: , as the passage clearly states that res judicata operates between parties and their privies; Z, being the legal heir of Y, is bound by the final judgment.

questions.questionText: What was the key legal disagreement between the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court?
options: Whether the accused were identified correctly
Whether the acts amounted to preparation or attempt
Whether POCSO applied to minors
Whether trial courts can frame rape charges
questions.solution: The central dispute was classification of the conduct — the High Court treated it as preparation while the Supreme Court held it amounted to attempt. A is incorrect because identity of accused was not the issue.

questions.questionText:
Why do courts resist allowing every economic loss from market fluctuation or

Because doing so would undermine freedom of contract by imposing duties

Because tort and contract are structurally identical, making dual remedies

Because economic losses are never compensable in law, whether in tort or
      contract.

questions.questionText:
In which of the following situations would the writ of Mandamus, which is issued to compel the
performance of a public legal duty, NOT be maintainable under constitutional law principles?
options: A public authority refuses to perform a statutory duty
A government officer refuses to act on a statutory application
The President refuses to exercise a discretionary constitutional function
A licensing authority refuses renewal contrary to rules mentioned in a statute
questions.solution: Mandamus lies to compel performance of a public legal duty that is mandatory in nature. It does not lie to compel exercise of a discretionary function because courts cannot dictate how discretion is to be exercised, only that it must be exercised.

questions.questionText:
Which of the following best explains the conceptual difference between a
        contractual duty and a tortious duty?
options:

Both are essentially voluntary, since one can avoid liability by choosing not to
      enter into relationships that might create duties.

Tort duties apply only when parties are in a prior contractual relationship, while
      contractual duties apply against the world.

Tort and contract duties are identical in structure but differ only in the remedies
      available.

options: That judicial review is not part of the Basic Structure.
That Parliament can override judgments by reenacting laws.

That judicial review is part of the Basic Structure and Parliament cannot override

That judicial review is only applicable to executive actions.

questions.questionText:

questions.questionText: A foreign corporation begins oil drilling operations 150 nautical miles from the coast of State Z without its permission. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The activity is lawful as it occurs beyond territorial waters.

The activity is permissible under freedom of the high seas.
The activity is valid if it does not interfere with navigation.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The activity violates State Z's sovereign rights over natural resources in the EEZ. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

Completely void ab initio and cannot be revived under any circumstances by

questions.questionText:

reports as highlighted in the passage?

Reports are prepared by consultants who are not independently accredited by any

Reports are funded by project proponents themselves, creating concerns of conflict of

The EIA Notification, 2006 does not require any public consultation before environmental

Post-clearance monitoring is conducted exclusively by the project proponent without any
external oversight.
questions.solution: The passage highlights that reports are funded by project proponents themselves, creating concerns of conflict of interest, selective reporting, and weak accountability despite the accreditation framework. This is the core credibility issue identified.

questions.questionText:

Article 142 powers
Separation of Powers
questions.solution: The five-judge bench specifically stated that usurping the function of the Governor by assuming deemed consent is antithetical to the Doctrine of Separation of Powers, which is part of the Basic Structure. The Court held that the judiciary cannot perform the legislative/executive function of giving assent.

questions.questionText:
According to the passage, what is the primary distinction between the "retrospective" and
"retroactive" application of a law?
options:
Retrospective application only affects future events, while retroactive application changes past
laws.

Retrospective application changes the legal consequences of past acts, while retroactive
application imposes new burdens on a continuing state of affairs that began in the past.

Retrospective application is permitted under Article 20(1), whereas retroactive application is
strictly prohibited.

There is no distinction; both terms refer to criminalizing an act that was legal when it was
committed.
questions.solution: Why Option B is Correct: Option B accurately summarizes the definitions provided in the text. It captures the essence that retrospective application changes the legality or consequences of a completed past act (e.g., making a past legal act a crime), whereas retroactive application is a "middle ground" that applies to a situation that started in the past but is still ongoing (a "continuing state of affairs").

questions.questionText:

questions.questionText:

questions.questionText:

Credible material established that the daughters were being confined and their signed
