questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: C may be justified, as house-breaking at night can create a reasonable apprehension of serious harm justifying even death. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Vaishali was born as a trans-woman and she lived her life as a female and also identified as one. One
day in college she was subjected to physical abuse for being a trans-woman. She filed an FIR against
the perpetrators under the law, and requested for them to be imprisoned for 2 years i.e., the maximum
punishment under the said law. Decide.
options: The perpetrators can be punished under The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.
The perpetrators can be punished under the Bhartiya Nyay Sanhita, 2023 only.
The perpetrators will be punished only if Vaishali submits her identity certificate.
The perpetrators cannot be punished.
questions.solution: A is the correct answer as the Act provides that causing harm to a transgender person attracts punishment of imprisonment ranging from six months up to two years, along with a fine. In this case, Vaishali is a trans-woman who was subjected to physical abuse because of her gender identity.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statement is not correct regarding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
options:
Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is a comprehensive, house-to-house verification process to
update and verify electoral rolls.

SIR is legally backed by section 21(3) of the Representation of People Act, 1950 and Article 324
(1) of the constitution.
The Election Commission of India conducts SIR before every general election.
The objective of SIR is to remove ineligible or duplicate voters, including illegal immigrants.
questions.solution: The Election Commission of India conducts SIR before every general election is not correct because The Election Commission of India (ECI) doesn't conduct a "SIR" (Special Intensive Revision) on a fixed schedule or time interval. The ECI conducts SIRs as needed, often in preparation for elections, to update and purify electoral rolls.

questions.questionText:
During the early functioning of the Constituent Assembly, several members expressed
concerns regarding the future nature of the Indian State, the source of constitutional
authority, the structure of governance, and the ideals that the Constitution should ultimately
embody. In order to provide philosophical direction and a common constitutional vision to the
Assembly amidst these uncertainties, a landmark resolution was introduced which later
became the basis of the Preamble to the Constitution of India.
Which of the following correctly identifies the resolution and the leader associated with
introducing it in the Constituent Assembly?
options: Objectives Resolution — Jawaharlal Nehru
National Sovereignty Resolution — Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Constitutional Ideals Resolution — Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
Democratic Governance Resolution — Rajendra Prasad
questions.solution: The Objectives Resolution was introduced by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent Assembly on 13 December 1946. It laid down the guiding principles and philosophy that would shape the Constitution of India and later became the foundation of the Preamble.

questions.questionText:
A delivery company's van has a mechanical failure because the company skipped maintenance,
leading to an accident. Simultaneously, the driver was also speeding. The passage mentions both
direct and vicarious liability. Which of the following is true?
options: The company can only be held liable for the driver's speeding
The company can only be held liable for the poor maintenance
The company can be held liable under both types of liability
All of the above statements are correct regarding the legal position
questions.solution: , as the passage distinguishes between direct liability for the employer's own negligence and vicarious liability for the employee's acts.

questions.questionText:
Global Tech, a major electronics manufacturer, enters into an agreement with Speed Logistics, a
delivery company, to handle all logistics for their new product launch. A month before the product
launch, Speed Logistics experiences significant operational issues that might prevent them from meeting
their contractual obligations. Despite these challenges, Speed Logistics does not repudiate the contract
and informs Global Tech of their intention to fulfill their duties, albeit with potential delays. If Speed
Logistics keeps the contract alive and proves readiness and willingness to perform, can they claim specific
performance from Global Tech to uphold the terms of their partnership?
options: Yes, because they informed Global Tech about potential delays.
No, because they anticipated operational issues.
Yes, because if the aggrieved party chooses to keep the contract alive, they can claim specific performance.
No, because specific performance is not applicable in-service contracts.

questions.questionText:
Kunal files for a patent on a new agricultural drone component. Two years later, he claims the
protection will last forever as long as he keeps selling the product, because “it’s my invention.” A
competitor replies that patent protection has a fixed term from filing, after which exclusivity ends
even if the inventor keeps using it.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Patent protection generally lasts for 20 years from the filing date, even if the inventor keeps
selling the product.

Patent protection lasts as long as the invention remains profitable, because exclusivity
depends on market success.

Patent protection lasts forever once granted, because statutory rights cannot expire without
consent of the inventor.

Patent protection lasts only 10 years, because technology changes quickly and law presumes
early public release.
questions.solution: The reference line explicitly states that a patent “generally lasts for 20 years from the filing date.” This directly refutes Kunal’s “forever” claim and explains that the right is time-bound even if commercial use continues. The inventor’s continued selling does not extend the statutory term beyond what the law provides.

questions.questionText:
Dev obtains a granted patent but forgets to pay the annual renewal fee for two consecutive years.
He later discovers competitors freely selling the invention and files a suit claiming his patent still
protects him because the grant once issued cannot “die.” The competitor argues the patent lapsed
due to non-renewal and cannot be enforced as an existing right. Which statement is most
accurate?
options:
The patent remains valid forever once granted, because renewal fees are optional and only
affect damages.

The patent remains enforceable if Dev proves he intended to renew and the omission was
accidental.

Post-grant, annual renewal fees are mandatory to maintain validity, and failure to renew may
result in lapse.

The patent can lapse only if a court cancels it, because administrative non-payment cannot
affect legal rights.
questions.solution: The reference line directly applies: renewal fees are mandatory, and failure to pay may result in lapse. If the patent lapses, Dev’s claim of continuing enforceability becomes weak because the legal mechanism for maintaining validity was not complied with.

questions.questionText:
In a coastal district, the Electoral Registration Officer deletes names of several women from
the electoral roll after receiving a complaint that they married into another caste community
and “should vote elsewhere.” The women still reside in the same constituency and have valid
documents. The officer says deletion is needed to preserve “community purity” and prevent
local tension. The women seek restoration, claiming the deletions are discriminatory.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Officer may exclude because local custom controls rolls, and caste based screening
preserves community harmony during elections in villages lawfully.

Exclusion is unlawful because only Election Commission can decide roll entries, and
officers have no power to revise them ever.

Officer must exclude because voter rolls are privileges, and state may choose eligible
groups to avoid fraudulent entries at will.

Exclusion is unlawful because it prohibits exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds of
religion, race, caste, or sex for citizens.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “prohibits exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste, or sex,” which is the precise constitutional bar stated in the reference line. Since the deletion is based on caste-linked marriage and targets women, it falls within the prohibited grounds.

questions.questionText:
Rohan discovers that his colleague, Amit, has been secretly recording private office
       conversations. Rohan approaches Amit and says, "Give me ₹50,000, or I will send these
       recordings to the management and ruin your career." Amit, fearing professional ruin,
       hands over the money. What is the most accurate legal characterization of Rohan's
       conduct based on the provided passage?
options:
Rohan has committed theft, as he dishonestly took movable property (money) from
Amit's possession without his true consent.

Rohan has committed extortion, as he intentionally induced fear in Amit by
threatening to cause harm to his reputation to dishonestly obtain the money.

Rohan has committed robbery, because the threat of ruining Amit's career amounts to
putting Amit in fear of injury during the act of taking the property.

Rohan's conduct is legally permissible, as he was rightfully exposing Amit's
wrongdoing and the payment was a voluntary settlement between them.

questions.questionText:
Farhan leases a small shop to Nitin for running a lawful pharmacy. Nitin then agrees to “transfer”
his lease rights to a person who is legally disqualified from holding such premises under local
rules, to hide that person’s involvement. Farhan objects, saying the transfer is barred because it is
being made to a disqualified person and for an unlawful arrangement. Nitin argues that any
transfer is valid if parties consent.
Which option is most accurate?
options:
Nitin is correct because consent of the parties always overrides restrictions on the identity of
the transferee.

Nitin is correct because lease rights are always transferable, regardless of unlawful object or
legal disqualification.

Farhan is correct only if he proves the pharmacy business itself was illegal, otherwise the
transfer must stand.
Farhan is correct because Section 6 prohibits transfers to legally disqualified persons.
questions.solution: The reference line directly matches the facts: the transfer is alleged to be for an unlawful arrangement and to a legally disqualified person. Since Section 6 “prohibits” such transfers, Farhan’s objection is supported by the stated principle.

questions.questionText:
Four employees approach the Central Administrative Tribunal together: a Central
Government clerk challenging pension denial, an Army combat soldier challenging field
posting, a High Court registry employee challenging promotion, and a parliamentary
secretariat employee challenging disciplinary action. The tribunal must decide whose claim
falls within its service jurisdiction under the passage. The clerk argues that Central
Government civilian service matters are covered, while others fall within excluded categories.
Which claimant has the strongest jurisdictional basis?
options: Army combat soldier because all defence-related service matters fall within CAT.
High Court registry employee because court staff are ordinary service employees.
Central Government clerk because civilian government service matters are covered.
Parliamentary secretariat employee because legislative staff are always included.
questions.solution: This option directly follows the reference line because Central Government employees fall within the Central Administrative Tribunal’s service jurisdiction. The clerk’s pension dispute is therefore the strongest fit among the four claimants.

questions.questionText:
Mehul, who suffers from severe psychosis, throws a stone at a passer-by during an episode when
he is completely disoriented and unable to understand his actions. The injured passer-by sues
Mehul in tort for battery. Mehul’s family argues he cannot be sued for acts done while he was not
in a stable state of mind, though they express sympathy. The plaintiff argues injury should be
compensable regardless.
Which option is most accurate?
options:
The plaintiff must succeed because tort liability is automatic once harm is proved, regardless
of mental stability.

Mehul cannot be sued because a lunatic cannot be sued for acts done while not in a stable state
of mind.

The plaintiff must succeed because intention is irrelevant in battery and mental illness never
excuses liability.

Mehul cannot be sued only if the episode was witnessed by a doctor; otherwise the claim must
proceed.
questions.solution: The reference line directly applies: “A lunatic cannot be sued for acts done while not in a stable state of mind.” Since the facts state Mehul acted during a severe episode with no understanding, the disability aligns with the principle.

questions.questionText:
Ms. Anita plants a Yew tree (a poisonous plant) on her land. The branches of the tree grow over
the fence into her neighbour's yard. The neighbour’s horse eats the leaves and dies. Anita argues
she is not liable because she didn't "bring" the leaves to the neighbour; the horse reached for them.
Is Anita liable under Strict Liability?
options: No, because there was no "escape" of the substance.
Yes, because the overhanging branches constitute an "escape" of a hazardous substance.
No, because planting a tree is a "natural use" of land.
Yes, but only if Anita knew the leaves were poisonous.
questions.solution: In legal terms, "escape" occurs when a substance moves from the defendant's area of control to an area outside it. Overhanging branches entering a neighbour’s airspace constitute an escape.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): A quasi-contractual obligation may arise even where there is no prior
agreement or consent between the parties.
Reason (R): Such obligations are imposed by law, are involuntary in nature, and require that
the benefit be non-gratuitous with an expectation of compensation.
options: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Assertion (A) is true because the reference line clearly states that quasi- contracts involve an “absence of agreement” and arise even where no prior contract exists between the parties. Reason (R) is also true because the same reference line explains that such obligations are “imposed by law,” are “involuntary,” and require a “non-gratuitous” benefit given with expectation of compensation.

questions.questionText:
A senior citizen gifted a property to his nephew (who is also his legal heir)
      through a gift deed that contained a specific clause: "The recipient of this
      property is obligated to provide for the monthly medical and living expenses of
      the donor." After a year, the nephew stops providing for the senior citizen. Based
      on the passage, what is the senior citizen's strongest remedy under the MWPSC
      Act?
options:
He can file for monthly maintenance up to a maximum of ₹10,000 from his
    nephew.

He can approach the Tribunal to revoke the gift deed, as the transfer was
    explicitly conditional on his maintenance.

He must file a civil suit for breach of contract, as the Maintenance Tribunal does
       not have the power to enforce specific clauses in a gift deed.

He can only file a complaint for punishment under the Act for neglect, but
       cannot revoke the deed or claim maintenance.

questions.questionText:
Parliament creates one tribunal to handle recruitment, promotion, pension, and disciplinary
disputes of public servants. Separately, a State Legislature creates another tribunal to decide
disputes involving taxation, land reforms, rent control, and essential commodities. A litigant
argues that both bodies must have exactly the same constitutional source and subject matter
because all tribunals are identical. The State argues that the constitutional scheme permits
service tribunals and specialised-subject tribunals under distinct heads.
Which response is legally strongest?
options: Litigant succeeds because every tribunal must decide only public-servant service disputes.
Litigant succeeds because taxation and land reform cannot be tribunalised at all.
State fails because specialised tribunals must always be ordinary civil courts.
State succeeds because service and specialised tribunals arise under distinct provisions.
questions.solution: This option accurately captures the reference line’s distinction between service tribunals and specialised-subject tribunals. The two bodies need not have identical subject matter because the constitutional scheme recognises separate tribunal categories.

questions.questionText:
Sara, aged 16 years and 4 months, is alleged to have participated in a planned acid attack
causing permanent injury. The investigating agency demands that she be immediately sent for
adult-style trial because the offence is heinous. Her lawyer objects, saying the Board cannot
transfer her merely on the label of the offence and must first examine her mental capacity,
physical capacity, understanding of consequences, and surrounding circumstances.
What should the Board do before deciding the next step?
options:
Transfer her immediately because every heinous allegation against a sixteen-year-old
requires adult-style trial.
Discharge her automatically because no child can face proceedings for a heinous offence.

Conduct assessment of mental and physical capacity, consequences understood, and offence
circumstances.
Decide only from police papers because personal assessment of the child is unnecessary.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “mental and physical capacity,” “understanding of consequences,” ? and “circumstances of the offence.” These are the required components of the preliminary assessment before deciding whether further special procedure is warranted.

questions.questionText:
Two neighbouring States dispute responsibility for pollution in a shared lake. State X agrees
to one meeting, then refuses further discussion and says State Y must first accept X’s superior
historical status in the region. State Y insists that peaceful settlement is not a one-time
courtesy and that both States must participate as equal legal units while seeking a solution.
State X argues that stronger States may decide when talks end.
Which answer best applies?
options: State X succeeds because powerful States may end settlement efforts unilaterally.
State X succeeds because one meeting fully satisfies all peaceful settlement duties.

State Y succeeds because equality between States is irrelevant during environmental
disputes.
State Y succeeds because peaceful settlement is a continuous duty among equal States.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “continuous legal duty” and “equal units in rights,” matching the reference line. State Y’s insistence on continued good-faith engagement and equal participation is consistent with the stated principle.

questions.questionText:
Facts: Mr. Z and Ms. Y have been married for five years. Three years into the marriage, Mr. Z’s
parents demand a luxury car from Ms. Y’s family, claiming it is a "social expectation" for a
successful son-in-law. The family argues this cannot be "dowry" because the marriage was already
settled and completed years ago. Based on the Supreme Court’s clarification in the passage, is this
demand considered dowry?
options:
No, because the Dowry Prohibition Act only covers demands made at the time of or before the
wedding.
Yes, because the Act does not distinguish between demands made before or after the marriage.

No, because "social expectations" and "gifts" are exempt from the definition of dowry under the
new judgment.
Yes, but only if the demand is linked to a specific religious custom like Mehr.
questions.solution: Why (b) is correct: The passage explicitly states that the timing of the demand (pre- marriage vs. post-marriage) does not change its legal status as dowry.

questions.questionText:
Leo contracted to buy a standard, mass-manufactured sedan from a dealership for £20,000.
    The dealership later breached the contract by selling the car to another customer. Leo could
    have immediately purchased an identical model from another dealer for £21,000 but chose to
    wait six months, during which prices rose to £23,000. He now sues for his loss. What is the
    likely outcome regarding damages?
options:
Leo will recover the full £3,000 difference as his loss was directly and foreseeably
             caused by the dealership's clear breach of contract.

Leo will recover £1,000, as he had a duty to mitigate his loss by buying the
             immediately available identical car.

The court may order specific performance to compel the dealership to source an
             equivalent new vehicle for Leo at the original price.

No damages are owed because the loss was not reasonably foreseeable to the
             dealership at the time the contract was formed.

questions.questionText: M agreed to provide transport to N knowing that N intended to commit burglary at a warehouse. M drove N to the warehouse and waited nearby so that N could escape quickly after the offence. Which option most appropriately follows?
options: M may be liable for intentional aiding because his conduct substantially facilitated the offence.
M may only be liable if he personally entered the warehouse.
M cannot be liable because transport services are legally neutral acts.
M committed only conspiracy because aiding requires supply of weapons.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: M cannot be liable because transport services are legally neutral acts. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Shalini’s father is alive but elderly. Shalini’s cousin, who expects to inherit as an heir apparent,
signs an agreement “selling” his expected future share in the father’s property to a financier for
immediate cash. After the father later changes his plans, the financier sues Shalini’s cousin for
specific enforcement of the “sale.” The cousin argues that he sold only a chance, not an existing
property interest.
Which option is most accurate?
options:
The financier will succeed because an heir apparent’s expected inheritance is treated as
valuable property that can be sold.

The financier will succeed because future inheritance becomes transferable once money
consideration is paid.

The cousin will succeed because the mere chance of an heir apparent inheriting property is
non-transferable.

The cousin will succeed only if he proves the financier knew the father was likely to change his
plans later.
questions.solution: The reference line directly covers the situation: the cousin attempted to transfer only an expected inheritance, i.e., a “mere chance.” Since spes successionis is stated to be non- transferable, the cousin’s defence is likely to succeed against enforcement. Option (da) Incorrect: The prohibition is not based on the financier’s knowledge or the father’s future choices; it arises from the very nature of what was attempted to be transferred.

questions.questionText:
Kavya owns expensive lighting equipment kept in a locked studio. She agrees to let Rohan use
the equipment for a wedding shoot. Instead of physically handing over each item, Kavya gives
Rohan the studio access code, disables her own lock, and instructs the security guard to allow
only Rohan to remove the equipment. Before Rohan removes anything, a dispute arises, and
Kavya claims there was no delivery because the goods were not handed over physically. Is
Kavya’s claim correct?
options: Yes, because delivery under bailment requires physical handing over of each movable item.
Yes, because Rohan had permission to enter but had not yet removed the goods.
No, because Kavya’s acts placed the goods in Rohan’s effective possession.
No, because intention creates bailment even before possession is affected.
questions.solution: Kavya did acts that gave Rohan effective possession of the lighting equipment. The passage explains that delivery may be made by doing anything that places the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, even without manual transfer.

questions.questionText:
A factory owner locks an injured worker inside a sealed storeroom overnight to “teach him
discipline,” despite knowing the room has no ventilation, no water, and dangerous chemical
fumes. He refuses repeated requests from staff to open the door. By morning, the worker dies
from suffocation and toxic exposure. The owner argues that he never physically struck the
worker and only intended confinement. The prosecution argues that he knowingly created
conditions where death would, in all probability, result.
What is the strongest conclusion?
options:
It amounts to murder because he knowingly and deliberately caused conditions where
death was probable.

It is only wrongful confinement because absence of direct physical assault prevents murder
liability.
It is only negligence because he did not expressly say that he wanted the worker dead.

It is no offence because workplace discipline excuses confinement causing unintended
death.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “knowledge,” “in all probability cause death,” and “deliberately,” matching the reference line. The owner knew the storeroom conditions were fatal and still intentionally kept the worker locked inside, making the act fall on the murder side of the distinction.

questions.questionText:
A district court appoints Nirmal as guardian of a 12-year-old ward’s immovable property.
Nirmal later mortgages part of the ward’s land to raise money for repairs to another property
belonging to the ward. He obtains written approval from the ward’s maternal uncle, a local
welfare officer, and two village elders, but does not seek permission from the court that
appointed him. When the mortgage is questioned, Nirmal argues that these approvals were
sufficient because responsible persons had considered the ward’s interest. Is this argument
legally sustainable?
options:
Yes, because a guardian may execute transactions that are necessary, reasonable, and
proper for managing the ward’s estate.

Yes, because approvals from family elders and a welfare officer sufficiently protect the
ward under parens patriae.

No, because a court-appointed guardian cannot mortgage the ward’s immovable property
without prior court permission.

No, because repairing another property can not amount to a necessary or clearly
advantageous transaction for the ward.
questions.solution: it directly applies Section 29 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890. A court-appointed guardian is statutorily barred from mortgaging the ward’s immovable property unless prior permission of the court is obtained.

questions.questionText:
A journalist publishes a critical report on a sitting minister. The High Court in that State initiates
contempt proceedings and also notes that its earlier judgment on a similar issue binds all
subordinate courts. The journalist argues the High Court is not a Court of Record, so it cannot
punish for contempt and its decisions are only persuasive. Another lawyer claims High Court
decisions bind subordinate courts and contempt powers follow from record status.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
High Court rulings are never binding, and contempt can be punished only by the Supreme
Court.

High Courts are Courts of Record with binding precedents and contempt powers and exercise
judicial review.

High Courts are Courts of Record but do not have contempt powers and cannot enforce their
own authority.

High Courts can punish contempt only when the State legislature passes a law specifically
authorising such punishment.
questions.solution: The reference line directly confirms that High Courts are “Courts of Record” and that this includes “binding precedents and contempt powers,” along with judicial review. Therefore, the journalist’s objection that the High Court lacks contempt power and binding authority is inconsistent with this stated principle.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The legal doctrine of contribution was developed to allow a joint tortfeasor to
recover proportionate damages from other wrongdoers.
Reason (R): The traditional rule of joint and several liability often unfairly forced a single
tortfeasor to bear the entire financial burden.
options: The Assertion (A) is completely true, but the Reason (R) is factually false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and (R) perfectly explains (A).
The Assertion (A) is factually false, but the Reason (R) is completely true.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but (R) does not explain (A).
questions.solution: The Assertion accurately describes the doctrine of contribution, and the Reason correctly provides the exact historical imbalance that led to its creation.

questions.questionText:
The "Progressive Alliance Party" (PAP) has 90 MPs in the Lok Sabha. Following ideological differences regarding
        foreign policy and economic reforms, a faction led by senior leader Ramesh Kumar decides to break away and form
        a new political party called "National Progress Forum" (NPF). Out of the 90 PAP MPs, 65 declare their support for
        Ramesh Kumar and join the NPF, while the remaining 25 MPs choose to stay with the original PAP under its founding
        leader Meena Sharma. Both factions claim to be the legitimate continuation of the party's ideology. The 25 MPs who
        stayed with PAP file a disqualification petition against the 65 MPs who joined NPF, arguing they have defected by
        voluntarily giving up PAP membership. Based on the passage, will the 65 MPs who joined the National Progress
        Forum face disqualification?
options:
Yes, because they voluntarily gave up their membership of PAP to join NPF, which constitutes defection under
            the first ground mentioned in the Tenth Schedule.

No, since 65 out of 90 MPs (more than two-thirds) quit PAP and joined the NPF

1

Yes, because the passage only permits mergers between two existing parties, not the creation of a new party,
            which is what happened when NPF was formed.

No, because as long as the government remains stable and does not fall, individual legislators can freely change
            their party affiliation without risk of disqualification.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, since 65 out of 90 MPs (more than two-thirds) quit PAP and joined the NPF 1. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
During the period of National Emergency under Article 352, the President can suspend
       the right to move any court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article
       19 and others. However, which writ remains maintainable even during such suspension
       to challenge a detention order?
options:
Habeas Corpus, but only if the detention is not under a law providing for
              preventive detention.

Habeas Corpus, because the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21
              cannot be suspended.

Mandamus, to compel the detaining authority to follow the procedure
              established by law.

None of the above; all writs for enforcement of suspended rights become
              infructuous.

questions.questionText:
Match List I with List IT:
List I	List IT
A. Kidnapping from lawful guardianship 1. Force or deceit is essential
B. Abduction	2. Guardian's consent is central
C. Kidnapping from India	8. Taking a person beyond India's limits
D. Minor's consent	4. Legally irrelevant
Options:
questions.solution: A — 2 (guardian consent is central) B — 1 (force or deceit essential) C > 8 (beyond territorial limits of India) D — 4 (minor's consent irrelevant)

questions.questionText:
During elections, the three-member Commission considers whether to suspend a recognised
party’s symbol for repeated Model Code violations. Two Election Commissioners vote to
suspend; the Chief Election Commissioner dissents and issues a press note stating his view
will “override” the majority because he heads the body. The party relies on the press note and
challenges the suspension as invalid, claiming the majority decision cannot stand.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Decision stands because decisions are taken by majority, and the Chief Election
Commissioner has no overriding power over the others.

Decision fails because Chief Election Commissioner is chair, so his dissent nullifies any
majority view automatically every time in law.

Decision stands only if unanimous, because electoral fairness requires consensus, and split
votes show bias and invalidity always for citizens.

Decision fails because dissent triggers judicial review immediately, and courts may
substitute their preference for the minority opinion right away.
questions.solution: The option directly reproduces “decisions are taken by majority” and “no overriding power,” exactly matching the reference line. Where two members support suspension, the majority decision governs, and the CEC’s press note cannot legally “override” the majority.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The current legal position of the Money Laundering Act may be viewed as
discriminatory under Article 14 of the Indian Constitution.
Reasoning (R): The law effectively creates two different classes of people—those who spent their
"proceeds of crime" before the law was notified and those who retained them—treating the latter
as offenders while the former remain beyond the reach of the Act.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.solution: Why Option (a) is Correct: Assertion (A) is True: The passage specifically raises the question of whether the PMLA creates an "unfair advantage." In Indian Constitutional law, if a law treats people in similar situations differently without a valid reason, it is considered discriminatory under Article 14. Reasoning (R) is True: This is the factual basis for the doubt.

questions.questionText:
Karan leaves his laptop with a service centre to replace the keyboard. The service centre
accepts the device, gives him a token, and tells him to collect it after inspection. Later, the
centre argues that because it never bought the laptop, it cannot be treated as bailee. Karan
says the person delivering the laptop is the bailor, and the person receiving it for repair is the
bailee.
Which identification is legally accurate?
options: Karan is bailee and service centre is bailor because centre controls repair process.
Service centre is bailee and Karan is bailor because Karan delivered the laptop.
Both are bailors because neither side intended permanent ownership transfer.
Neither is bailee because electronic goods cannot be subject of bailment.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line’s distinction between the person delivering goods and the person receiving them. Since Karan delivered the laptop and the service centre received it for a repair purpose, Karan is the bailor and the service centre is the bailee.

questions.questionText:
A group of 20 people, all of whom are unarmed, gather outside a government hospital to
protest against the depleting service towards patients. The group sits on a hunger strike in
front of the emergency ward, thereby obstructing ambulances and patients from entering the
ward. The hospital management called the police, who then started to disband the group.
Which is the most legally accurate statement?
options: The police action is a valid exercise of power, as it falls under reasonable restrictions.

The police cannot disperse the assembly, as it is peaceful and unarmed, and therefore,
protected by Article 19(1)(b) of the Constitution.

The group is protected by their fundamental right to protest, and blocking the path to the
emergency ward is not an issue of public order.

The police must wait for a violent act to occur before they can legally issue a dispersal
order for a peaceful assembly.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: Option A is correct because the disruption of the emergency services by blocking the path to the ward qualifies as an obstruction to public order. Hence, the police or any legal authority can curb the right to protest, as per the reasonable restrictions of Article 19(3).

questions.questionText:
A farmer's cattle strayed onto a neighbour's field, grazed on crops, and were seized by the
neighbour before they wandered off. The neighbour refused to return the cattle until the
farmer paid for the crop damage. The farmer argued the seizure was unlawful as the cattle
had caused no substantial harm.
options:
The seizure is unlawful; distress damage feasant requires the distrainor to first obtain a
court order before detaining another's animals.

The seizure is unlawful because the cattle were animals capable of independent movement;
the doctrine applies only to inanimate objects.

The seizure is lawful; distress damage feasant entitles a landowner to detain chattels
causing damage until compensation is paid.

The neighbour may detain the cattle only for 24 hours after which statutory provisions
require their return irrespective of compensation.
questions.solution: The doctrine applies to animals as much as inanimate objects and does not require damage to reach a specific threshold. Any damage caused while the chattel is on the land suffices to trigger the right of detention.

questions.questionText:
The passage describes how India historically addressed witness protection through ‘scattered
provisions' before the Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 was introduced. Which of the following
best explains why a piecemeal statutory approach was insufficient to ensure effective witness
protection in India, based on the passage?
options:
Because the Indian Evidence Act and IPC lacked penal provisions entirely, and without
punishments for threatening witnesses, accused persons had no incentive to refrain from
intimidation.

Because India's federal structure made policing a State subject, preventing Parliament
from enacting a uniform national law, and high-profile cases exposed the absence of a
cohesive protection mechanism.

Because scattered provisions like Section 282 BNS focused only on criminalising threats
but did not provide physical protection, relocation, or identity change, leaving witnesses
practically unprotected despite legal remedies on paper.

Because the Law Commission's recommendations were binding on Parliament and its non-
implementation amounted to a constitutional violation of Article 21.
questions.solution: The passage directly states that since policing and public order are state subjects, consensus could not be reached on a uniform national law, and that high-profile cases exposed this gap. Option B captures both elements accurately.

questions.questionText:
Vikram, aged 17, is alleged to have committed a heinous offence after months of planning.
After a proper preliminary assessment, the Board decides that the case should go before the
special forum empowered to try such matters. The prosecution asks that Vikram be lodged
with adult undertrial prisoners because the matter is no longer before the Board. His counsel
argues that transfer does not erase juvenile safeguards, especially separation from adult
offenders.
Which position is correct?
options:
Adult custody is mandatory once the matter leaves the Board after preliminary
assessment.
Adult custody is allowed because safeguards end once serious offence allegations are made.

Separate treatment continues only if prosecution consents after the transfer order is
passed.
Transfer may occur, but safeguards like separation from adult offenders continue to apply.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “matter may be transferred” and “safeguards such as separation from adult offenders continue,” matching the reference line. Vikram may face proceedings before the Children’s Court, but he cannot be treated exactly like adult prisoners for custody.

questions.questionText:
Rohit, his father Mahesh, and his grandfather jointly hold an undivided family house that has
come down through the family for decades. Rohit demands that Mahesh sell the entire house to
fund a business, claiming he has a “share” even while Mahesh is alive. Mahesh refuses, saying
Rohit has no present right until Mahesh dies. Rohit files a claim asserting a birth-based right.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Rohit can claim a present share because rights in such undivided joint family property arise by
birth, not after death.

Mahesh can deny Rohit any interest because children get rights only by succession once the
father dies.

Rohit can claim only if the property was purchased by Mahesh from his personal earnings and
not inherited.

Mahesh can sell freely because undivided joint family property is treated like self-earned
property of the father.
questions.solution: The reference line directly states that ancestral property remains undivided joint family property and that “rights arise by birth and not by succession after death.” Since the house is described as inherited through generations and still undivided, Rohit’s claim to a present interest is conceptually rooted in birth-based rights rather than waiting for Mahesh’s death. Hence,

questions.questionText:
The FSSAI decides to lower the permissible limit of a certain preservative in milk. A group of
milk producers challenges this in court, arguing that the FSSAI’s decision is “too strict” and
will hurt business. They ask the Court to replace the FSSAI's limit with a more “reasonable”
one suggested by their own private consultants. Based on the passage, what is the legal
standard for the Court's response?
options:
The Court should substitute the limit because it has the power to manage technical
domains to ensure business interests are protected.

The Court should defer to the FSSAI because it is a multidisciplinary, specialized body
entrusted with supervising these specific standards.

The Court should intervene because any change in standards by a statutory body is an
“exceptional case” under the West Bengal case’s precedent.

The Court should intervene because the producers' consultant reports constitute “empirical
data” that proves the FSSAI is acting incorrectly.
questions.solution: Option B is correct because the passage states that the FSSAI is a “specialised, multidisciplinary body” and that courts “ordinarily defer to the expertise of the regulator” in technical domains. Option A is incorrect the passage explicitly states the Court “cannot be expanded to assume supervisory or managerial control...

questions.questionText:
Arjun and his friends illegally enter a closed railway yard at night to shoot a music video. Warning
boards clearly state “No Entry-High Voltage.” Arjun climbs a stationary coach, touches an exposed
cable, and suffers an electric shock. He sues the railway authority for failing to secure the area.
The authority argues his own wrongdoing bars the claim.
Which option best fits?
options:
Arjun will succeed because the railway must guarantee safety even to illegal entrants and
cannot rely on his conduct.

Arjun will likely be barred because his own wrongful conduct substantially contributed to the
harm he suffered.

Arjun will succeed because warning boards create liability by proving the railway knew injury
could occur.

Arjun will be barred only if the railway proves it had zero duty to prevent foreseeable injury in
restricted zones.
questions.solution: The reference line applies because Arjun’s wrongdoing trespassing into a closed high-voltage yard to shoot a video directly and substantially contributed to the harm. The injury is not an innocent accident but a foreseeable result of illegal and risky conduct, which supports barring his claim.

questions.questionText:
The passage describes the Mediation Act, 2023 asrepresenting"a decisive policy shift towards
institutionalized alternative dispute resolution." Which evidence from the passage most strongly
supports this characterization of a fundamental policy shift rather than mere technical amendment?
options: The Act received Presidential assent and was implemented in phases starting October 2023

The Act placed mediation on equal statutory footing with arbitration and recognized online
mediation
The Third Schedule of the Act substituted both Exception 1 and Exception 2 to Section 28
Various High Courts had adopted divergent approaches before the Act's enactment
questions.solution: Why B is correct: This option captures the substantive policy dimensions of the reform. Placing mediation "on equal statutory footing with arbitration" represents a fundamental policy decision to treat mediation as comparably important to arbitration, which has been promoted for decades.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The defeat of the 131st Amendment Bill effectively preserves the status quo
under which women's reservation may not take effect before approximately 2034.
Reason (R): The 106th Amendment's Article 334A ties operationalisation of reservation to a
delimitation exercise after the post-2027 census.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Ais true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Inspector Rao arrests David for assault. While in custody, David confesses, "I hit him with an
iron rod and threw it in the municipal garbage bin." However, an hour before David's
confession, a sanitation worker had already found the exact iron rod and handed it over to
Inspector Rao. The prosecution seeks to admit David's statement in court. What is the legal
next step for the judge?
options:
Reject the statement solely because a Magistrate was not physically present during
David's confession.

Admit the portion about throwing the rod in the bin, as it proves David's knowledge of the
weapon.

Reject the entire statement because the physical fact was not discovered as a direct
consequence of David's disclosure.

Admit the entire confession because the earlier discovery of the iron rod perfectly
corroborates David's story.
questions.solution: the passage mandates the fact must be "previously unknown" and discovered as a "direct consequence" of the disclosure, which fails here.

questions.questionText:
A citizen reads five separate newspaper articles detailing severe food poisoning incidents at
different restaurants in their city over a single month. Alarmed, they file a PIL under Article
82 in the Supreme Court, seeking to dismantle the local food regulatory authority and install a
court-monitored task force, arguing that these reports prove a collapse of the regulatory
framework. Will the Supreme Court entertain this PIL?
options:
Yes, because five incidents in one month constitute clear empirical data of systemic failure
requiring immediate judicial intervention to protect public health.

Yes, because the right to safe food is a fundamental right, and the Court must assume
supervisory control when any statutory body fails.

No, because mere reliance on unverified newspaper reports about isolated instances is
insufficient to demonstrate a systemic failure in the regulatory mechanism.

No, because the Supreme Court under Article 32 can never issue directions to specialized
statutory authorities like food safety boards under any circumstances.
questions.solution: Option C is correct because the passage clearly establishes that isolated instances of non-compliance and unverified materials like newspaper reports do not prove a systemic failure or justify sweeping judicial directions like creating task forces. Option A is incorrect because five incidents reported in a newspaper are classified as “isolated or stray instances” and “unverified material,” not the empirical data required to prove a systemic collapse.

questions.questionText:
Gita holds occupancy rights in agricultural land under a local tenancy statute that restricts
transfer without government permission. She “sells” these occupancy rights to a trader through a
simple agreement and takes full payment. Later, the trader sues for possession, claiming that
occupancy rights are like ordinary property and can always be sold. Gita argues that statutory
prohibitions restrict such transfers.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
The trader will succeed because once consideration is paid, even restricted tenancy or
occupancy rights become transferable.

The trader will succeed because statutory restrictions apply only to ownership rights, not to
occupancy or tenancy rights.

Gita will succeed only if she proves the trader acted dishonestly, otherwise the transfer must
be enforced.

Gita will succeed because statutory prohibitions further restrict transfer of certain tenancy or
occupancy rights.
questions.solution: The reference line directly supports Gita: “Statutory prohibitions further restrict transfer of certain tenancy or occupancy rights.” Since her occupancy rights are restricted by a tenancy statute, the attempted sale without required permission is likely unenforceable.

questions.questionText:
Nisha enters into a written agreement to buy a small plot from Raj and pays most of the price. Raj
hands over possession and Nisha builds a boundary wall and a room, living there openly for
months. However, the agreement is not registered. Later, Raj tries to evict her, arguing that
without registration she has no protection and must vacate immediately.
Which statement best reflects the legal position?
options:
Nisha is protected because part performance, protects a transferee who has acted on an
agreement despite a lack of registration.

Nisha is not protected because any unregistered agreement is void and cannot be relied upon
for any purpose.

Nisha is protected only if she completes full payment and also gets the agreement notarised by
a magistrate.

Nisha is not protected because possession given under an agreement can always be revoked at
will by the owner who has given the possession.
questions.solution: The reference line states that Section 53A protects transferees who have “acted on an agreement despite lack of registration.” Nisha paid consideration, took possession, and made construction clear acts in reliance so Raj cannot simply evict her by using non-registration as a weapon after benefiting from the arrangement.

questions.questionText:
In 2019, the Ministry of Finance establishes an expert committee to examine cryptocurrency
regulation. The committee recommends a complete ban on private cryptocurrencies through
legislation. However, by March 2020, when the Supreme Court strikes down the RBI Crypto
Circular, Parliament has not enacted any law banning cryptocurrencies. A cryptocurrency
exchange challenges a subsequent RBI directive in 2021 that again restricts banking services
to crypto businesses, arguing that the 2020 Supreme Court judgment bars any such regulatory
action. Which legal position is most sound based on the passage?
options:
The 2020 judgment permanently bars RBI from any future regulation of cryptocurrency-
banking relationships under any circumstances whatsoever

The 2020 judgment struck down the specific 2018 circular for lack of evidence, but does not
prevent fresh regulation

The RBI can reissue identical restrictions because regulatory bodies have inherent power
to protect financial stability and market integrity

The judgment requires Parliament to legislate on cryptocurrencies before RBI can issue
any directives affecting banking services to crypto entities
questions.solution: The passage indicates the Supreme Court struck down the specific April 6, 2018 Crypto Circular on the grounds that (1) there was no empirical evidence of harm, (2) cryptocurrencies were not banned, and (3) the ban was disproportionate. These are context-specific findings about that particular circular, not a permanent bar on all regulation.

questions.questionText:
A private firm engaged by an examination authority to print question papers conspires with a
coaching centre, and together they leak the paper for money to a network of aspirants spread
across three States. On these facts, the conduct is most likely to be treated as —
options:
an individual offence punishable with three to five years and a fine up to ten lakh rupees,
and nothing graver.

no offence at all, because the candidates who purchased the paper cannot be prosecuted
under the Act.

merely a service-provider lapse punishable only by debarment from conducting future
examinations.
an organised crime carrying five to ten years and a fine of at least one crore rupees.
questions.solution: A firm, a coaching centre, and a network acting together for wrongful monetary gain across States is a group furthering a shared interest — the definition of organised crime — attracting five to ten years and a minimum one-crore fine. (a) understates it as an individual offence; (b) is wrong because the organisers (not the candidates) are squarely liable; (c) wrongly treats a serious conspiracy as a mere debarment-only lapse.

questions.questionText:
In 2012, Kunal’s father died leaving an undivided family agricultural land that had been inherited
for generations. Kunal’s married sister, Pooja, asks for an equal share, saying she is a coparcener
by birth and marriage does not reduce her rights. Kunal argues that daughters do not get
coparcenary rights once married and that only sons can demand partition.
Which option best reflects the legal position?
options:
Kunal is correct because marriage ends a daughter’s coparcenary status and removes her right
to demand partition.

Pooja is correct because married daughters retain full coparcenary rights in ancestral property
and can demand partition.

Kunal is correct because coparcenary rights were limited to unmarried daughters and never
extended to married daughters.

Pooja is correct only if her father left a will giving her a share, otherwise she cannot claim
partition rights.
questions.solution: The reference line uses clear wording “Married daughters retain full coparcenary rights and can demand partition.” Pooja’s claim aligns with this exact position because the property is described as ancestral and undivided and her marital status cannot be used to deny her partition demand.

questions.questionText:
P files a writ petition challenging a government notification on procedural grounds. The
petition is dismissed. Later, P files another writ petition challenging the same notification on
constitutional grounds that existed and were known during the first petition. Which of the
following best reflects the reasoning in the passage?
options:
The second writ petition is maintainable because constitutional grounds can never be
barred.
The second petition is maintainable because writ jurisdiction is discretionary.

Constructive res judicata applies only to civil suits under the CPC and never to writ
petitions. The petition is not barred.

The second writ petition may be barred because constructive res judicata may apply to writ
proceedings as well.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The second writ petition may be barred because constructive res judicata may apply to writ proceedings as well. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Rukhsana’s husband repeatedly prevents her from attending religious observances, sells her
jewellery without consent, and often tells relatives that she should be forced into
“entertaining” his business associates. He rarely assaults her physically, so his family argues
that cruelty under the Act requires severe beating only. Rukhsana seeks dissolution, relying on
conduct that makes her life miserable, interferes with religious practice, and disposes of her
property.
Which statement best captures the legal position?
options:
Cruelty is unavailable because only repeated physical assault can constitute cruelty under
this law.

Cruelty is unavailable because selling wife’s property is financial conduct, not matrimonial
conduct.

Cruelty may apply because it includes obstructing religion, disposing property, and
immoral pressure.
Cruelty may apply only if husband admits each act before relatives and court witnesses.
questions.solution: This option directly connects to the passage’s cruelty ground by using conduct such as obstructing religion, disposing property, and immoral pressure. Since cruelty is a major ground under the Act, Rukhsana’s facts strongly support a claim for dissolution.

questions.questionText:
The Sultan of Brunara, a small Middle Eastern monarchy, owns extensive property in Mumbai that was purchased
        decades ago as a personal investment. A local builder has allegedly encroached upon part of this property and
        constructed an unauthorized structure. The Sultan wishes to file a suit for recovery of possession and demolition of
        the unauthorized construction. However, the Sultan cannot personally appear in India due to diplomatic protocol
        and security concerns. His private secretary contacts an Indian law firm to initiate proceedings. Based on the
        passage, how can the Sultan's interests be represented in the Indian court proceedings?
options:
The Sultan must personally appear before the court at least once to establish standing, after which his lawyers
            can represent him in subsequent hearings.

The Central Government may appoint persons to prosecute or defend suits on behalf of foreign rulers, ensuring
            the court knows who can validly represent them.

The private secretary can directly represent the Sultan without any formal appointment, as any agent of a
            foreign ruler has automatic standing in Indian courts.

The Indian law firm can represent the Sultan by filing a power of attorney signed by the Sultan, following the
            same procedure applicable to any Indian litigant.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The Central Government may appoint persons to prosecute or defend suits on behalf of foreign rulers, ensuring the court knows who can validly represent them. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Anil bailed his cow to Bala for care during a year. During this period, the cow
           gave birth to a calf. Bala kept the calf and used its milk for himself. Anil now
           demands the calf and a share of the milk profits.
options:
Bala can rightfully retain the calf and milk as a fair reward for his year of labor and
expenses incurred in maintaining and caring for the cow.

Bala must return the cow but may keep the calf as it was not part of the original
bailment agreement and resulted from his efforts.

Bala is required to return the cow and may keep the calf, but he must pay Anil for the
value of any milk consumed, as that constitutes use of the bailed property.

Bala must return the cow, the calf, and account for benefits like milk, as accretions
from the bailed goods belong to the bailor.

questions.questionText:
Consider that in the above question, Himesh offered to pay off the amount that Bharat owed Chandni
in case Bharat wasn’t able to, and Bharat and Chandni accepted. What would be the nature of such a
contract?
options:
It would be a contract of indemnity as Himesh offered to make good some losses that Bharat might
suffer in case he didn’t make the payment.

It would be a contract of guarantee as there are three parties, the primary basis for considering a
contract as that of guarantee.
It is a contract of indemnity as the liability that is sought to be covered might not even arise.
It is a contract of guarantee as there is an existing debt that Himesh has sought to discharge.
questions.solution: In this situation, Bharat already owes Chandni %2 lakhs. This is an existing and definite liability.

questions.questionText:
Ritika is accused of a serious financial fraud involving forged documents and multiple victims.
She offers to surrender her passport and report weekly to the police. The prosecution opposes
bail, alleging risk of witness influence and destruction of records. Ritika says the police officer
should immediately release her because conditions can control risk. The prosecution says that
in non-bailable offences, only the court can decide after examining relevant factors.
Which answer best reflects the law?
options: Ritika must be released by police because conditions replace judicial scrutiny.
Ritika must be released because non-bailable offences still give bail as right.
Ritika’s release depends only on whether victims agree to compromise.
Ritika’s release depends on court discretion after scrutiny of relevant risks.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line by recognising that only the court can grant bail after judicial scrutiny in non-bailable offences. The court may consider passport surrender, reporting, witness risk, and evidence concerns before deciding.

questions.questionText:
A Public Interest Litigation is filed seeking the Supreme Court's intervention to immediately
cancel all infrastructure projects in a coastal state, alleging that they "may" harm marine
ecology. No concrete evidence or expert report is presented, but the petitioners invoke Fiat
justitia ruat caelum, urging the Court to halt all activity "in the interest of justice and
environmental preservation." The government contends that the projects are duly approved
under environmental laws. Which of the following most accurately analyses whether the
doctrine applies?
options:
The maxim directly applies, since judicial conscience must prevail even in the absence of
factual substantiation or evidence

Applying the maxim here would amount to judicial restraint, as courts must defer to
executive expertise on technical matters

The doctrine cannot be invoked, as doing so would convert moral idealism into
unwarranted interference beyond evidentiary limits

The maxim applies partially, since environmental protection is part of basic structure and
must override administrative decisions
questions.solution: The passage describes Fiat justitia ruat caelum as "justice, anchored in constitutional principle" being rendered based on law, not arbitrary intervention. The maxim demands fidelity to constitutional adjudication, which requires evidentiary basis and legal principles.

questions.questionText:
During a wedding dispute, Imran suddenly sees his brother being beaten by three men. In
panic, he picks up an iron rod and strikes one attacker once on the head. The attacker dies.
Evidence shows no earlier enmity, no weapon brought from home, and no repeated blows, but
the prosecution argues that a head injury proves intention to murder. The defence claims the
act occurred in fear, sudden fight, and possible defence of another.
How should the court approach classification?
options:
Treat it as murder because death by head injury always proves intention beyond further
factual inquiry.

Examine circumstances like sudden fight, fear, provocation, private defence, and absence
of pre-planning.

Treat it as no offence because panic and fear automatically excuse every death-causing
assault.

Ignore surrounding facts because intention and knowledge are presumed whenever a
person dies.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference factors such as sudden fight, fear, provocation, private defence, and absence of pre-planning. Since Imran acted during an unexpected assault on his brother, without earlier enmity or repeated blows, the court must assess these circumstances before deciding the exact homicide category.

questions.questionText:
Sana seeks dissolution after her husband, Imran, is sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment for
a serious offence. His family argues that she must wait until he actually completes several
years in jail, because a sentence alone cannot affect marriage. Sana also states that even
before imprisonment, he had refused marital responsibilities for more than three years. The
family says imprisonment and marital neglect are moral issues, not legal grounds.
Which statement is legally strongest?
options:
Sana cannot seek dissolution because imprisonment never affects marital status without
husband’s consent.

Sana must wait until release because only completed imprisonment supports any divorce
claim.

Sana must prove cruelty separately because imprisonment and marital neglect are
insufficient grounds.

Sana may seek dissolution if husband is sentenced seven years or fails obligations three
years.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “sentenced... seven years or more” and “fails to perform marital obligations for three years,” matching the reference line.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): In offences punishable up to seven years, arrest is not automatic and must be
based on necessity, recorded reasons, and judicial scrutiny rather than routine police power.
Reason (R): Trap cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act are treated differently
because immediate arrest may be necessary to preserve evidence.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
questions.solution: The assertion is true because the core principle is that arrest must not be routine; it must be justified by necessity with recorded reasons and judicial scrutiny. The reason is also true because trap cases are treated differently due to evidence-preservation needs.

questions.questionText:
Sunil is a 37-year-old transgender. He was actively employed as a labourer under a govt. scheme. He
used to face a lot of backlash and harassment in his village by his relatives and others for his biological
differences. This made him fall into severe depression over the course of a few years. He was having
suicidal thoughts and even tried to commit suicide, however he survived. An NGO for mental health
wrote a letter to the government to provide him with therapy and medication if needed for free.
options: The government would provide him therapy free of cost.
The government would not provide him therapy free of cost.
Sunil would first require an identity certificate.
The National Council for Transgender Persons should provide him therapy.
questions.solution: Option B is correct as the NGO has requested that therapy and medication be provided free of cost. While mental healthcare clearly falls within the broad idea of healthcare services, the statute does not impose a clear legal obligation on the government to provide such services free of cost.

questions.questionText:
A contractor stores construction material in different places during a road-widening project. In one
case, pipes are left across a public road, making passage dangerous for residents, commuters,
school vehicles, and pedestrians using the road. In another case, a generator shakes the wall of one
adjoining shop. In a third case, smoke enters one neighbour’s balcony. In a fourth case, leaking
water stains one tenant’s ceiling. Which situation is closest to public nuisance rather than private
nuisance?
options: Pipes obstruct a public road and create danger for persons using that public route.
Generator vibration affects one neighbouring shop and disturbs its ordinary business display.
Smoke enters one adjoining balcony and interferes with that occupier’s residential comfort.
Water leakage stains one tenant’s ceiling and affects that tenant’s use of the premises.
questions.solution: the obstruction affects persons using a public route, including residents, commuters, school vehicles, and pedestrians. The passage distinguishes public nuisance by its effect on the community or a considerable section of the public.

questions.questionText:
Mira owns Flat 4B, while Neel owns Flat 4C in the same building. A contractor hired by Mira
mistakenly renovates Neel’s balcony, installing new tiles and safety railings. Neel watches the
work for two days, knows it is being done at another person’s expense, and later refuses
payment, saying he never signed any contract. Mira demands compensation because Neel has
retained a valuable benefit without paying.
How should the claim be assessed?
options: Neel need not pay because no written agreement existed between him and Mira.
Neel need not pay because benefit without request can never create legal obligation.

Neel may compensate because quasi-contract prevents unjust enrichment at another’s
expense.
Neel must pay double because every mistaken benefit creates punitive civil liability.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “quasi-contract,” » « “unjust enrichment,” and “at another’s expense,” matching the reference line. Neel received a valuable renovation paid for by Mira and knowingly retained it, making compensation consistent with the purpose of quasi- contract.

questions.questionText:
Jasprit Bumrah files a petition under Article 32 in the Supreme Court, arguing that a new state law
which mandates prior police permission for any sportsman’s public event violates his Fundamental
Right to peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b). Which of the following is the most accurate
description of his petition’s basis?
options: He is seeking a writ because High Courts refused to hear him.
He is enforcing a Fundamental Right via a constitutional remedy.
He is seeking an appeal against a High Court’s writ order.
He is asking for a writ for a purpose other than a Fundamental Right.
questions.solution: Article 32 provides the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. This is the direct and correct basis.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation is primarily concerned with the legislative
competence of a law rather than the motive or wisdom behind its enactment.
Reason (R): The doctrine becomes applicable only when a legislature, lacking constitutional
authority over a subject, disguises its law to appear as if it falls within its legislative domain,
requiring courts to examine the true substance of the legislation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
Ais false, but R is true.
questions.solution: A Correct Both statements accurately reflect the passage. The Assertion correctly states that the doctrine focuses on legislative competence, not motive or wisdom.

questions.questionText:
The respondent before the Supreme Court argued that since the arbitral award mentioned
New Delhi as the "place of arbitration," the seat had effectively shifted from Srinagar to New
Delhi. Which of the following best characterises the Supreme Court's response to this
argument?
options:
The Court accepted the argument, holding that the place mentioned in the arbitral award
becomes the effective seat of arbitration.

The Court partially accepted the argument, holding that New Delhi became a concurrent
seat along with Srinagar.

The Court rejected the argument, holding that the place where the award is pronounced
automatically becomes the seat of arbitration.

The Court rejected the argument, holding that stray recitals in an arbitral award cannot
override the express agreement of parties regarding the seat.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The Court rejected the argument, holding that stray recitals in an arbitral award cannot override the express agreement of parties regarding the seat. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Riya owns a bakery and asks Dev to design a logo for her new outlet. Dev says he will prepare
three logo samples within ten days if Riya pays 215,000 after approval. Riya replies, “Agreed,
send the samples as discussed.” Dev prepares the designs, but Riya later says there was no
agreement because they never signed a formal document. Dev argues that each side made a
promise forming consideration for the other.
Which statement is most accurate?
options: No agreement exists because only signed documents create promises between parties.
No agreement exists because logo design cannot form contractual consideration.
An agreement exists because reciprocal promises formed consideration for each other.
An agreement exists only if payment was made before Dev started work.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line because Dev’s promise to design logos and Riya’s promise to pay %15,000 form consideration for each other. These reciprocal promises satisfy the basic idea of an agreement under the passage.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Sobhraj, an undertrial prisoner, is in custody for a series of bank robberies. The police
receive information that he is also responsible for two previously unsolved murders. The
police, without a new arrest or a separate remand order, begin to interrogate him about the
murders. The lawyer for Mr. Sobhraj objects, arguing that the police must arrest him again for
the new charges. What should the police do?
options:
The police should arrest him again for the murder charges because they are separate and
more serious crimes.

The police should seek a separate remand order for the murder cases to legally extend his
detention.

The police do not need to arrest him again, as an undertrial prisoner does not need to be
arrested separately.

The police cannot interrogate him for a crime that he has not been formally charged with
in court.
questions.solution: An undertrial prisoner does not need to be arrested separately for every pending criminal case. The seriousness of the crime does not change this principle; thus, option A is incorrect.

questions.questionText:
Riya, aged 16, is persuaded and encouraged by her neighbour Aman to accompany him to
another city without informing her parents. Aman neither threatens nor deceives her, but he
actively induces her to leave home. Riya’s parents had not consented to her leaving.
Which of the following is the most appropriate legal conclusion based on the passage?
options:
Aman is guilty of kidnapping from lawful guardianship because guardian consent is
absent.
Aman is guilty of abduction because Riya moved from one place to another.
Aman is guilty of both kidnapping and abduction.
Aman is guilty of neither offence because Riya consented.
questions.solution: Option A (Correct): The passage clearly states that guardian consent is decisive. Since Riya is a minor and parental consent was absent, kidnapping from lawful guardianship is established Option B (Incorrect): Abduction requires force or deceitful means, neither of which is present.

questions.questionText:
A chemical factory located near a river discharges untreated industrial waste into the water body,
causing contamination of drinking water and damage to crops in nearby villages. The pollution
results in health problems among residents and loss of livelihood for farmers. The Supreme Court
directs the factory to bear the full cost of cleaning the river, compensating affected villagers, and
restoring the damaged environment, regardless of whether the factory had obtained prior
government permissions. Which legal principle is the Supreme Court most likely applying in this
situation?
options: Polluter Pays Principle
Absolute Liability
Public Trust Doctrine
Sustainable Development
questions.solution: The Polluter Pays Principle requires that the party responsible for causing environmental damage must bear the cost of remedying that damage. In the given situation, the Court orders the factory to pay for: Cleaning the polluted river, Compensating affected villagers, Restoring environmental damage.

questions.questionText:
Meera is the natural guardian of her 14-year-old son, Rahul, who owns an undeveloped and
undivided share in a piece of agricultural land. Facing a severe financial crisis due to Rahul’s
sudden, urgent medical emergency and pending school fees, Meera decides to liquidate this
asset. She sells a small portion of this undivided share to a local buyer at the exact market
price. The village elders formally approve the sale, and every rupee is directly used to pay the
hospital and the school. No prior permission of the court is obtained because Meera believed
the clear benefit to her son justified the quick sale. Can this sale transaction be legally
justified solely on the ground that it was necessary and beneficial to the minor?
options:
Yes, because a natural guardian has the legal authority to manage a minor's estate and
can convert an unproductive asset into usable funds for the child's urgent welfare.

Yes, because the combination of fair market value, local village approval, and the actual
use of money proves that the best interest of the child was fully protected.

No, because the law strictly requires prior court permission for transferring a minor's
immovable property, which cannot be bypassed even for genuine welfare reasons.

No, because any transfer of a minor's immovable property executed without prior judicial
approval is void from the beginning and has no legal effect.
questions.solution: the passage explicitly provides that a natural guardian cannot sell or transfer any part of the minor’s immovable property without prior permission of the court. Even though the Shephali Chakraborty case notes that converting an undeveloped, undivided share into usable funds can be a genuine benefit, such a realistic evaluation must be made by the court before the sale, making the unilateral transaction legally unjustified.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): On the facts of the passage, the dissolution of the congregation by the
Archdiocese in 2023 was immaterial to the maintainability of the writ.
Reason (R): The Court's conclusion rested on the voluntariness of the daughters' continuance
rather than on the institutional status of the congregation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Ais true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
