questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
An employee at the Maharashtra Metro Corporation (MMCL) discovers a digital file on the
office server containing the blueprint of the city’s upcoming metro expansion. He copies this
file onto a personal USB drive to study it at home to improve his technical knowledge. He does
not show it to anyone else. Does his act of copying the file attract liability under the IT Act?
options:
No, because the IT Act only penalizes the “sharing” or “disclosure” of information to third
parties, not the act of copying for personal study.

Yes, because Section 43 imposes liability on anyone who, without permission, copies or
extracts data from a computer system or network.

No, because the employee belongs to the organization and therefore has implied
permission to access and copy any file on the office server.

Yes, because copying blueprints of public infrastructure is considered “spying” under the
Official Secrets Act, regardless of where the office is located.
questions.solution: Option B is correct because the passage explicitly states that Section 43 of the IT Act is attracted when a person, “without permission, accesses, downloads, copies, or extracts data.” The employee’s motive does not negate the fact that the act of copying was unauthorized. Option A is incorrect because the text clarifies that the scope of Section 43 includes the mere act of copying or extracting data, not just sharing it.

questions.questionText:
Rupa, married for eight years, is repeatedly slapped and threatened at home when she
questions unexplained withdrawals from the joint account. One evening, her husband locks
her in a room, takes her phone, and warns she will be thrown out if she approaches anyone.
When Rupa goes to the police station, the duty officer refuses to record anything, saying "these
are private family issues." Rupa seeks immediate protection and residence-related relief
through a Magistrate.
What position best fits the framework described?
options:
Home disputes remain private matters; courts intervene only after criminal conviction, so
immediate civil relief is unavailable.

Violence within the home is a legal wrong requiring enforceable remedies, not merely a
private matter.

The law addresses only public violence; domestic incidents must be handled by family
elders, not courts.

A Magistrate can grant protection or residence relief only after the police formally register
a complaint; an FIR must first be filed by the aggrieved woman.
questions.solution: This option directly uses "violence within the home," "legal wrong," and "enforceable remedies," tracking the reference line's words. It explains why the police officer's dismissal of Rupa's complaint as a "family issue" is inconsistent with the rights-based remedial approach the Act creates.

questions.questionText: B sold shares of the company to W. B also delivered the share certificates along with transfer deed. To pay for the shares, W issued a cheque to B. When B went to encash, the cheque bounced. B decided to exercise his right to lien. As per the passage, choose the correct option.
options: B cannot exercise his right to lien as he has already transferred the possession of shares.
B cannot exerciser his right to lien as shares are movable objects.
B can exercise his right to lien as W has not satisfied the payment against the buying of shares.
B can exercise his right to lien as a compensation for the bouncing of cheque.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: B cannot exercise his right to lien as he has already transferred the possession of shares. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Ramesh executes a written gift deed transferring his farmhouse to his friend Vinay. Vinay argues
that any property can be transferred in law if the parties agree and the document is registered.
Ramesh’s brother objects, saying some transfers are barred by law even if both parties consent.
The dispute is only about whether the law allows transfer in general, not about stamp duty or
registration.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Any property of any kind may be transferred, but only subject to statutory restrictions
recognised by law.

No property can ever be transferred unless a court first grants permission for that specific
transfer.

Any property becomes transferable if it is registered, because registration cures all legal
restrictions.

Property can be transferred only if it is immovable; movable and intangible rights are never
transferable.
questions.solution: The reference line states the “general rule” that “property of any kind may be transferred,” but clearly qualifies it by adding “subject to statutory restrictions.” This captures why consent and registration alone cannot override legal bars: transferability exists, but only within the limits set by law.

questions.questionText:
Nazia’s husband, Arif, left home after a family dispute and his whereabouts remained
unknown for four years. Nazia filed for dissolution, and the court granted a decree on that
ground. Four months after the decree, Arif returned with proof of identity and offered to
resume marital duties sincerely. Nazia objects that the decree became final immediately and
cannot be disturbed once pronounced. Arif says the law gives a limited window before the
decree becomes effective.
What should the court consider?
options:
Decree becomes final immediately because four-year absence alone permanently ends the
marriage.

Decree is invalid because unknown whereabouts can never support judicial dissolution of
marriage.

Decree takes effect after six months and may be set aside if husband appears and resumes
duties.

Decree depends only on wife’s consent after return, because husband’s readiness is legally
irrelevant.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “takes effect only after six months,” “set aside,” and “appears and resumes marital duties,” matching the reference line. Since Arif returned within four months and offered to resume duties, the court must consider whether the decree can be set aside.

questions.questionText: L was a renowned godman in the region. He received tons of gold and other valuable kinds in donation. M, a person who lived in the same region, was an ardent follower of L. One day he came to know about L’s secret drug dealing activities. M threatened L to share with him half of the donations, otherwise he would expose his indiscretions. Decide whether this would amount to extortion?
options: This not a case of extortion because L was indeed involved in drug trafficking.
This is a case of extortion by L, as he fools his followers into believing him as a godman.
This is a case of extortion because M threatened L for dishonest inducement.
This is not a case of extortion because sharing of donations would not amount to dishonest inducement.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: This is a case of extortion because M threatened L for dishonest inducement. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Seema, aged 17, signs an agreement to sell her inherited plot to a neighbour for 78 lakhs and takes
an advance. Later, her family refuses to complete the sale, and the neighbour sues to enforce the
agreement. The neighbour argues Seema appeared mature and willingly accepted the advance, so
the agreement should bind her. Seema argues the agreement is void from the start.
What is the most accurate view?
options:
The neighbour succeeds because an advance payment creates binding obligations even if one
party is a minor.

Seema succeeds only if she proves she did not understand the contract terms at the time of
signing.

The neighbour succeeds because the agreement can be enforced once Seema turns 18 without
any new bargain.

Seema succeeds because a minor’s agreement is void ab initio and creates no rights or
obligations.
questions.solution: The reference line directly supports Seema’s position: the agreement is void from the beginning, and it creates no enforceable obligations. Since the contract itself is void ab initio, the neighbour cannot compel performance based on it.

questions.questionText: P acted as surety for a debt owed by Q to Bank A. After Q defaulted, P paid the entire amount to the bank and subsequently sought recovery from Q. Which principle most directly supports P's claim?
options: Novation because the original contract has automatically ended.
Co-extensive liability because both parties are equally liable forever.
Subrogation because the surety steps into the creditor's position after payment.
Continuing guarantee because the liability survives indefinitely.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Subrogation because the surety steps into the creditor's position after payment. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Aakash is hit by a speeding bike outside a mall. His phone shatters, he suffers a fractured
wrist, and he misses two weeks of work. The biker admits fault but offers only a casual
apology and refuses to pay anything. Aakash wants a legal remedy that restores him, as far as
money can, to the position he would have occupied if the accident had not occurred. He files a
civil claim seeking an appropriate court-granted relief.
Which remedy best fits that objective on these facts?
options:
Award damages, because monetary compensation paid to restore the plaintiff, as far as
money can, to position before.

Grant injunction, because equitable restraint is primary remedy, and money cannot ever
address bodily injury or loss alone.

Order specific restitution, because returning the vehicle restores everything, and courts
never award money for tort injuries now.

Allow self-help abatement, because extra-judicial action replaces court relief, and
compensation is unnecessary when harm occurred here later.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “monetary compensation” and “restore the plaintiff, as far as money can,” matching the reference line. Aakash’s losses include injury, broken property, and lost wages, which are classically addressed through compensation.

questions.questionText:
John Doe, recently convicted for burglary, is being considered for enhanced sentencing due to an
undisclosed previous conviction for a similar crime. The prosecution, eager to secure a harsher penalty,


introduces evidence of the prior conviction during the initial phase of the trial in an attempt to sway the
jury’s perception of John's character. The Judge allows this evidence to be presented before the
conviction. Was this action by the Judge lawful?
options:
No, because previous convictions should only be considered after the initial conviction to prevent
prejudicing the jury.
Yes, because the prosecution has the right to introduce all relevant evidence.
No, because previous convictions are not admissible during civil proceedings.
Yes, because the Judge has discretion over what evidence is presented during the trial.

questions.questionText:
Meera is repeatedly called “worthless” by her husband, who also threatens to leak private photos to
her employer if she does not comply with his demands. He isolates her from friends and locks away
her documents so she cannot travel for work. Meera is never beaten, so her in-laws claim “there is
no violence” and that her complaint is merely emotional. Meera argues the statute’s concept of
domestic violence is intentionally broad and can include non-physical conduct that destroys safety
and dignity.
Which conclusion best fits?
options:
Yes, because broad statutory meaning of domestic violence can cover non-physical conduct that
harms safety, well-being, or dignity.

No, because domestic violence requires physical assault only; insults and threats are rude but
never legal wrongs here.

Yes, because any unpleasant talk inside home automatically becomes domestic violence,
regardless of impact on her life always alone.

No, because civil remedies apply only after criminal conviction; without police charge-sheet, the
court cannot act at this stage.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “broad statutory meaning of domestic violence,” aligning with the reference line, and correctly recognises that non-physical conduct may still qualify. Meera’s threats, humiliation, and coercive control can harm safety and dignity even without assault, which is precisely why the meaning is broad.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): A transfer of property that seeks to postpone vesting of ownership for an indefinite
period is invalid in law.
Reason (R): The law restricts such transfers to prevent property from being tied up under
prolonged control beyond permissible limits.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion states that transfers postponing vesting for an indefinite period are invalid, which directly reflects the rule against perpetuity. The reason explains why such transfers are restricted namely, to prevent prolonged or indefinite control over property.

questions.questionText:
Meena, a key witness in a high-profile organised crime case, receives a credible threat to her
life from the accused. A Threat Analysis Report (TAR) prepared by senior police officials
confirms a direct threat to her life and that of her family members. Under the Witness
Protection Scheme, 2018, which category of threat applies, and what protection measures may
be provided?
options:
Category A applies because it covers threats to life of witness or family, and measures such
as relocation, change of identity, and video conferencing with concealed identity may be
provided.

Category C applies because the threat is from an organised crime syndicate, and only
moderate protection measures such as regular police patrolling are available.

No category applies until the accused is convicted, as the Scheme is available only post-
conviction.

Category B applies, and the only available measure is in-camera proceedings without any
change of identity or relocation.
questions.solution: The passage states that Category A covers threats to life of witness or family and provides measures such as relocation, change of identity, and video conferencing with concealed identity. Since the TAR confirms a direct threat to Meena's life, Category A applies.

questions.questionText:
A State Legislature enacts a law that is within its legislative competence but is found to be unwise
and inefficient by the public. A petitioner challenges the law in the High Court solely on the
grounds that it is a bad policy. Based on the narrow parameters mentioned in the passage, how is
the Court likely to rule?
options: The Court will strike it down because it has the power to review any legislative action.
The Court will strike it down as an administrative error.

The Court will replace the law with a more efficient version using its power as an ultimate
arbiter.
The Court will uphold it, as review is limited to constitutional validity, not policy wisdom.
questions.solution: The passage emphasizes that judicial review of legislative action operates within narrower parameters and requires specific grounds such as a violation of fundamental rights or constitutional distribution of powers. Incorrect Options:

questions.questionText:
Consider four objectives. Which combination correctly identifies all and only the principal
objects of the 131st Amendment Bill as set out in the passage?
(c) Increase the Lok Sabha's maximum strength
(ii) Delink women's reservation from the post-2026 census
(iii) Confer on Parliament the power to determine, by law, which census governs delimitation
(iv) Raise the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha
options: (i), (i) and (iv) only
Gi), (iii) and (iv) only
(i) and (iv) only
(i), Gi) and (iii) only
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: (i), Gi) and (iii) only. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
At an informal social gathering organised by the firm, Mr. Rohan, a manager, approached Ms.
Tanya, a subordinate. While speaking closely to her ear, he placed a hand on her back and
made a polite comment about how good her outfit was. Ms. Tanya felt deeply uncomfortable
during this interaction and subsequently avoided Mr. Rohan for the rest of the evening. The
company has a clear policy against unwelcome conduct in the workplace. Does this incident
constitute sexual harassment?
options:
Yes, but only if Ms. Tanya had immediately confronted Mr. Rohan and clearly
communicated her discomfort at the time of the incident.

No, because the facts do not explicitly state that any sexually explicit words were used by
Mr. Rohan during the interaction.

Yes, because even though the comments were not explicitly sexual, the unwelcome
physical contact and conduct can contribute to a hostile work environment.

No, because the incident occurred at an informal social gathering organised by the firm,
and such settings fall entirely outside the statutory definition of a workplace.
questions.solution: The passage defines sexual harassment broadly to include unwelcome physical conduct and hostile work environments — it does not restrict harassment to explicitly sexual words or acts. Option C correctly identifies that unwelcome physical contact, even when accompanied by a polite remark, can constitute sexual harassment under the Act.

questions.questionText:
SparkleTea Pvt. Ltd., established in 2015, sells premium tea blends in India. Over the past seven
years, it has conducted extensive marketing campaigns on social media, TV, and print, reaching
millions of consumers across India. SparkleTea has also won multiple awards for product quality.
Recently, a new company, SparkleTeaWorld, started selling tea products with a similar name and
branding in the same markets. SparkleTea Pvt. Ltd. wants to challenge the new company, claiming
that its brand is awell-known trademark and the new company is attempting to trade on its
reputation.
Based on the facts and the legal principles governing well-known trademarks as per the passage
would SparkleTea Pvt. Ltd.’s mark likely qualify as a well-known trademark?
options:
Yes, because it hasa strong reputation, extensive advertising, and recognition among
a substantial segment of consumers.
No, because the company has been operating for less than ten years.
No, because only marks registered in multiple classes can be considered well-known.

Yes, because the new company is using a similar name, which automatically makes SparkleTea
well-known.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because it hasa strong reputation, extensive advertising, and recognition among a substantial segment of consumers. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Ritika gives her diamond necklace to a jewellery repair shop for polishing before a family
ceremony. The shopkeeper issues a receipt and promises to return it after two days. Before the
return date, he claims that because the necklace remained owned by Ritika, no bailment arose
and he had only a casual obligation to keep it safely. Ritika argues that possession was
transferred for a specific purpose and the necklace had to be returned after polishing.
Which statement best applies?
options:
Bailment arose because goods were delivered for a purpose and had to be returned
afterward.

Bailment failed because ownership remained with Ritika and never passed to the
shopkeeper.

Bailment failed because jewellery repair requires sale, not temporary delivery of movable
goods.

Bailment arose only if Ritika permanently transferred ownership along with physical
possession.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line because Ritika delivered movable goods to the shopkeeper for a specific purpose, namely polishing, and the shopkeeper was bound to return them once that purpose was completed. Bailment does not require permanent transfer of ownership; it requires delivery of possession for a purpose and an obligation to return or dispose of the goods as directed.

questions.questionText: X and Y agreed to intimidate Z by threatening him verbally to withdraw a civil complaint. However, without informing X, Y later independently assaulted Z causing severe injuries. Which option is most appropriate?
options: X automatically becomes liable for every act committed by Y.
X may not be liable for the assault if it fell outside the scope of the original agreement.
X becomes liable because conspiracy makes all future conduct attributable.
X becomes liable because any offence arising later becomes a probable consequence.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: X may not be liable for the assault if it fell outside the scope of the original agreement. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A husband files criminal proceedings against his wife’s relatives alleging that they helped her
remove ornaments and household items from the matrimonial house. However, the complaint
contains only broad allegations without specifying individual acts by each relative. Applying
the passage, which of the following is consistent with the Court’s reasoning?
options: All relatives must necessarily face trial because they are named in the complaint.
General and non-specific allegations may justify quashing of proceedings.
Criminal law presumes collective liability in matrimonial disputes.

Relatives become automatically liable if they are present at the matrimonial home.

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
questions.solution: Option A — Incorrect. Merely naming individuals in a complaint is insufficient.

questions.questionText:
At 2 a.m., Anaya hears screams from a neighbour’s locked house and sees smoke pouring from
a window. She breaks the latch, enters immediately, and carries a child outside before
firefighters arrive. The owner later files a complaint for unlawful entry and damage to the
lock, insisting Anaya should have waited for police. Anaya pleads necessity, saying the entry
was only to avoid a serious danger and save life.
How should her defence be assessed?
options:
Defence fails because trespass can never be excused, even to rescue life, so unlawful entry
remains punishable.

Defence succeeds because a person may do something technically illegal if necessary to
avoid a more serious injury or danger.

Defence fails because necessity applies only when property is protected, not when human
life is involved, so rescue is irrelevant.

Defence succeeds only if owner consented beforehand, because permission converts entry
into lawful act, and necessity does not matter here.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “technically illegal,” “necessary,” and “avoid a more serious injury or danger.” Anaya’s act was a trespass-like entry, but it was aimed at preventing a greater harm loss of life during an urgent emergency. That is the precise situation the reference line describes.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): A religious denomination has a constitutional right to manage its own affairs
in matters of religion.
Reason (R): This right is expressly made subject to public order, morality and health, so
regulation may be justified when those limits are implicated.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Assertion (A) is true because the reference line recognises a denomination’s right to manage its own religious affairs. Reason (R) is also true because the same reference line makes that right “subject to public order, morality and health.” However, R functions as a constraint, not the explanation for A’s existence.

questions.questionText:
After losing his criminal appeal, Farhan files an application claiming that he was 17 years old
on the date of the offence. He produces school admission records and municipal birth records.
The State objects that the case has already reached final disposal and that juvenility cannot be
reopened after such delay. Farhan argues that the law permits juvenility claims at any stage
and requires proper age inquiry if the claim is raised or suspected.
What should the court do?
options: Reject the claim because juvenility must be raised only before trial begins.
Reject the claim because final disposal permanently bars any later age inquiry.
Conduct inquiry because juvenility may be raised at any stage, even after final disposal.
Conduct inquiry only if prosecution first admits the birth records as genuine.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “raised at any stage” and “even after final disposal,” matching the reference line. Since Farhan has produced age-related records, the court should not reject the claim merely on delay and must proceed according to the required inquiry process.

questions.questionText:
State X claims control only over the water column of its territorial sea but argues that aircraft
may freely conduct surveillance overhead and foreign companies may drill the seabed below it
without permission. A foreign corporation relies on this argument and begins exploratory
seabed activity within the belt adjacent to State X’s coast. State X later objects, saying its
sovereignty over territorial sea also covers the air space, bed, and subsoil.
Which view is legally correct?
options:
Corporation succeeds because territorial sea sovereignty covers water only, not seabed or
airspace.

Corporation succeeds because drilling below sea level never affects coastal State
sovereignty.
State X succeeds only over airspace, while seabed remains open for foreign exploitation.
State X succeeds because sovereignty extends to air space, seabed, and subsoil too.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “air space,” “bed,” and “subsoil,” matching the reference line. State X’s territorial sea sovereignty therefore extends vertically above and below the adjacent belt of sea.

questions.questionText: P operated a tourist boating service on a river known for periodic seasonal rainfall. Weather authorities issued warnings three days in advance predicting unusually strong storms and dangerous water conditions. Despite this, P continued operations without reducing capacity or taking additional safety measures. During a severe storm, several boats overturned causing injuries to passengers. P argues that the storm was a natural occurrence and therefore an Act of God. Which of the following is most appropriate?
options: P may succeed because any event involving natural forces automatically constitutes an Act of God.
P may not succeed because predictable natural conditions combined with inadequate precautions may defeat the defence.
P may succeed because negligence becomes irrelevant whenever nature contributes to harm.
P may succeed because storms and floods always constitute extraordinary events.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: P may not succeed because predictable natural conditions combined with inadequate precautions may defeat the defence. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
During a raid, Sub-Inspector Meena seizes a laptop suspected to contain evidence of financial
fraud. She documents the seizure but does not ensure audio-video recording of the search and
seizure process. Under which framework would her procedure be deficient, and why?
options:
Under CrPC only, because Section 102 specifically mandates audio-video recording for all
types of seized property.

Under BNSS only, because Section 105 BNSS introduces audio-video recording of search
and seizure, unlike CrPC.

Under both CrPC and BNSS, since both statutes equally require audio-video recording for
all categories of seized items.

Under neither statute, since audio-video recording requirements apply only when the
seized item is presented before a sessions court.
questions.solution: The passage states that Section 105 BNSS introduces audio-video recording of search and seizure. Her procedure may be deficient under BNSS if the search and seizure process was not audio-video recorded as required.

questions.questionText:
Two days before nomination closes for a state election, a sudden flood destroys bridges and blocks access
to the district headquarters. The election authority announces a one-day extension of the filing deadline
so candidates from cut-off villages can submit papers. A rival challenges the extension as unlawful and
argues that statutory timelines cannot be altered. The authority replies that the decision was compelled
by necessity and that the doctrine should operate only where absolute necessity exists.
Which conclusion best applies this limitation?
options:
Upheld because necessity always excuses illegality, and courts never review emergency choices once
officials claim public interest.

Struck because necessity applies only to criminal cases, and election administration cannot ever use
necessity for procedural changes.

Upheld because necessity knows no law, so statutory deadlines may be ignored whenever there is
inconvenience or delay in logistics.

Upheld only where absolute necessity exists, so extraordinary flood justifying limited extension fits
necessity’s strict threshold.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “absolute necessity” and applies the strict threshold to an extraordinary flood that blocks access and prevents compliance. A limited, targeted extension can fit the doctrine only if the situation truly leaves no practical alternative, matching the passage’s limitation.

questions.questionText:
In a high-profile organised crime case, the accused was released on bail with a condition that
he would not contact or threaten any witness. Two weeks later, the complainant received
credible reports that the accused had intimidated three key witnesses. The complainant filed
an application for cancellation of bail. The Sessions Court, however, dismissed the application,
directing the complainant to seek relief exclusively under the Witness Protection Scheme,
2018 instead. Was the Sessions Court's approach legally correct?
options:
Yes, because bail cancellation is a drastic remedy that should be avoided when alternative
protective mechanisms like the Witness Protection Scheme are available.

Yes, because the Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 is specifically designed to address
witness intimidation by accused persons, making it the appropriate and sufficient remedy
in such cases.

No, because the Witness Protection Scheme only applies to witnesses in cases involving
organised crime, and therefore the complainant had no remedy under that Scheme at all.

No, because the Witness Protection Scheme is a curative measure addressing threats after
they arise, while bail cancellation is a preventive judicial remedy for breach of bail
conditions, and the two are not interchangeable.
S-20, Nandkishore Parikh Marg, Bapu Nagar, JAIPUR Ph. 7240060099 | www.lptedtech.com	28

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
questions.solution: The passage, drawing from Phireram v. State of U.P.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements based on the principles provided in the passage:
I. A single, isolated act of torture by a state official against a civilian during peacetime can
be prosecuted as a Crime Against Humanity.
II. A government ordering the mass deportation of its own citizens during peacetime can be
prosecuted for Crimes Against Humanity if the attack is widespread.
III. Intentionally targeting a hospital during peacetime constitutes a War Crime under Article
8.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
options: Only IT is correct.
All of the above are correct.
Only I and II are correct.
Only I and III are correct.
questions.solution: Statement II perfectly aligns with the text, which allows Crimes Against Humanity to be charged during peacetime by a State against its own citizens if widespread.

questions.questionText:
Raghav contracts to deliver 500 branded chairs to Meera’s café on 10 June against full payment on
delivery. On 10 June, Raghav brings the chairs in a truck, shows the invoice, and asks Meera to
accept delivery and pay. Meera, angry over a minor delay in earlier messages, refuses to open the
gate and says she will “never take delivery.” Two weeks later, Meera sues alleging non-delivery.
What is the legal effect of Raghav’s tender?
options:
The contract continues because refusal does not matter, and the seller must keep offering
performance until the buyer accepts delivery.

A valid tender has the same effect as performance, so the seller is discharged and the buyer
cannot claim non-delivery thereafter.

Tender is irrelevant unless goods are deposited in court, so seller remains bound and must
perform again later on request.

The buyer’s refusal cancels the contract automatically, so both parties lose all rights and no
remedy survives.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference words “valid tender” and “same effect as performance,” aligning with Raghav’s offered delivery and Meera’s refusal. Once tender is valid and refused, Raghav is treated as having done what the contract required, so Meera cannot later allege non-delivery as a breach by him.

questions.questionText:
Raghav is accused in a non-bailable economic offence involving forged invoices and diversion of
company funds. He applies for bail, arguing that he has cooperated with investigation and is
willing to appear whenever required. The prosecution opposes release, saying he may travel
abroad or avoid questioning. The court considers granting bail but proposes conditions
requiring weekly police reporting, surrender of passport, and prior permission before leaving
the city.
Which conclusion is most accurate?
options: Bail cannot be granted because courts cannot impose conditions in non-bailable cases.
Bail may be granted with conditions such as reporting and passport surrender.
Bail must be granted unconditionally once the accused offers cooperation.
Bail must be refused because travel concerns can never be controlled by conditions.
questions.solution: This option directly matches the reference line. Since the prosecution fears foreign travel and non-cooperation, the court may address those concerns through conditions such as passport surrender, weekly reporting, and travel restrictions while granting bail.

questions.questionText:
A start-up receives an invoice for 78 lakh from a software vendor and pays it promptly. A week
later, its accounts team discovers that the invoice had already been paid the previous month
by automatic transfer, and the second payment was made due to a clerical mistake. The
vendor admits receiving both payments but refuses refund, saying the company should have
been careful before paying. The start-up seeks return of the duplicate amount.
Which conclusion is correct?
options: Vendor may retain money because payer’s negligence bars recovery of mistaken payments.

Vendor may retain money because duplicate payments become valid once accepted by
recipient.
Vendor must refund only if a separate written repayment agreement was signed later.
Vendor must return money because money paid by mistake is required to be returned.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “money paid by mistake” and “required to be returned,” matching the reference line. The second payment was a clerical duplicate, so the vendor must return it under the restitutionary principle.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): An Election Commissioner cannot continue in office after attaining the age of
65 years, even if six years from the date of appointment are not yet completed.
Reason (R): Commissioners hold office for six years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is
earlier, and enjoy status and salary equivalent to Supreme Court Judges.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion is true because the tenure rule is expressly limited by the phrase “six years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.” This means that even if the six-year term has not ended, the Commissioner must demit office on attaining 65 years. The reason is also true and directly explains the assertion because it contains the exact tenure formula that resolves the issue.

questions.questionText: R entered into a contract with S to sell 100 bags of rice. S failed to pay the price on the agreed date. R, after giving due notice to S, resold the goods to T at a lower price due to a fall in market value. Later, R sued S for the loss incurred on resale. Decide whether R is entitled to recover the loss.
options: R cannot recover the loss because once goods are resold, the original contract comes to an end.
R can recover the loss because he exercised his right of resale after giving notice to S.
R cannot recover the loss because resale is only allowed when goods are perishable.
R can recover the loss only if S expressly agreed to such resale at the time of contract.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: R can recover the loss because he exercised his right of resale after giving notice to S. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Four creators — Ayaan, Tara, Neha, and Kabir — sign a written agreement to run a paid online course business for
        one year. The agreement fixes the term as one year, but does not mention what happens after that. After the year
        ends, the creators continue selling the same course, collecting subscription revenue, and splitting profits in the same
        ratio. They do not sign any renewal document, and they still have no clause explaining how the partnership will end.
        According to the passage, after the fixed term ends, the partnership is best treated as:
options: A partnership at will after the end of the term, since it continued beyond the fixed period without fresh terms.

Automatically dissolved at the end of the term, because the partnership was formed for a fixed period and
            renewal needs a new contract.

A specific partnership, because the partners are continuing only the same single course venture they originally
            set out to complete.

A partnership at will only if the partners explicitly agree in writing that the fixed-term partnership will convert
            into an at-will partnership.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: A partnership at will after the end of the term, since it continued beyond the fixed period without fresh terms. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Nikhil is arrested for simple hurt, classified as bailable. His brother reaches the police station
with the required bond and identity documents. The officer says he has no authority to release
Nikhil and that only the Magistrate can consider bail after production the next day. Nikhil’s
family argues that in a bailable offence, the police officer in charge may release the accused
once the required bond is furnished.
Which conclusion is correct?
options: Release must be refused because police never grant bail after arrest.
Release must be refused because every accused must first face court.
Release may be granted because the police officer can act after bond.
Release may be granted only if the Magistrate records detailed reasons.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line because Nikhil is arrested for a bailable offence and the required bond is ready. The police officer in charge can release him at that stage.

questions.questionText:
Sara is arrested at night for a bailable offence involving minor public nuisance. She
immediately offers to furnish the required bond, but the police station staff say she must
remain in custody until morning because a court order is always necessary. Sara argues that
no complex hearing or prior court order is required at this stage for a bailable offence. The
officer says custody is safer until the Magistrate opens.
Which view is legally sound?
options: Sara must wait because every bail release requires a prior court order.
Sara must wait because night arrest suspends bailable offence safeguards.
Sara need not wait because court order is unnecessary at this stage.
Sara need not wait only if the complainant signs the bond too.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line by stating that a court order is not necessary at this stage. Sara’s position is legally sound because the offence is bailable and the required bond is being furnished.

questions.questionText:
Nikhil is arrested in 2026 for a murder committed in 2024. School records show that he was 17
years and 7 months old on the date of the offence, but 19 years old when arrested. The
prosecution argues that his age at arrest should control because the system is now dealing
with an adult. Nikhil argues that the decisive date is when the offence was committed.
Which conclusion is most legally defensible?
options:
Age at arrest controls because criminal process begins only when the accused is
apprehended.

Age at charge-sheet controls because prosecution formally begins after investigation is
completed.

Age at conviction controls because punishment is decided only after guilt is finally
established.
Age at offence controls because juvenility is determined by date of commission of offence.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “date of commission of offence,” matching the reference line. Since Nikhil was below eighteen on the date of the murder, his claim must be assessed on that basis even though he was nineteen at arrest.

questions.questionText:
A storm damages the common boundary wall between two warehouses. Without waiting for
formal signatures, warehouse owner Ira hires workers to rebuild the wall after informing
neighbouring owner Sohan that she expects him to pay half because both properties are
protected. Sohan watches the repairs, uses the rebuilt wall for his security cameras, and later
refuses to contribute, saying he never accepted an offer. Ira claims the work was lawful, non-
gratuitous, and beneficial to him.
What follows?
options:
Sohan need not pay because silence during repairs always defeats compensation claims by
other party.

Sohan may compensate because lawful non-gratuitous services benefited him and he
enjoyed them.
Sohan need not pay because boundary walls benefit land, not owners personally.
Sohan must pay punitive damages because refusal after benefit is always fraudulent.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “lawful,” “non-gratuitous services,” “benefited,” and “enjoyed,” matching the reference line. Ira informed Sohan that contribution was expected, and Sohan used the rebuilt wall, making compensation consistent with the principle.

questions.questionText:
Samay, an 18-year-old citizen of India, residing in the State of Uttar Pradesh, is a notorious boy. He often
commits petty offences like theft of things that are not much in value. He had never been caught before, and always
used to get away with whatever he stole. One day, however, he tried stealing a diamond necklace and was caught by
the police. The police lodged an FIR and he was brought before the magistrate to hear his case under the penal
provision of section 378 of IPC. Samay applies for bail. Decide if bail can be granted.
options: It is Samay's right to be granted bail.
It is a bailable offence and therefore, he must get bail.
Bail is at the discretion of the magistrate.
Bail cannot be granted at all.
questions.solution: The passage distinguishes bailable offences, where bail is a matter of right, from non-bailable offences, where bail is granted only at the discretion of the court. Theft under the relevant penal provision is treated as a non-bailable offence for the purposes of this question. Accordingly, Samay is not entitled to bail as a matter of right, and the Magistrate must decide whether bail should be granted based on the circumstances. Therefore, Option C is correct. Why other options are incorrect: A. This is incorrect because bail is not an absolute right in non-bailable offences.

questions.questionText:
Two rival cab companies separately instruct their drivers to park near a railway station exit
during peak hours. Neither company communicates with the other. On a busy evening, drivers
from both companies block the exit, causing a passenger to miss a train and suffer loss. The
passenger argues that because both companies behaved similarly and caused the same
inconvenience, they must be treated as joint tortfeasors. The companies argue that similar
conduct alone does not prove concerted action.
Which legal assessment is most accurate?
options: Joint liability arises because both companies followed similar parking behaviour.
Joint liability arises because the passenger suffered one practical inconvenience.
Joint liability fails because similarity alone is not concerted common action.
Joint liability fails only if neither company had any commercial motive.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line. The two cab companies acted similarly, but there is no communication, agreement, or common plan between them.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the distinction between Theft and Extortion
based on the passage:
I. Theft involves taking property without consent, whereas Extortion involves obtaining
consent wrongfully through fear.
II. Theft can be committed regarding both moveable and immovable property, while Extortion
is limited to moveable property.
III. In Extortion, there is an overpowering of the victim's will, which is absent in Theft.
IV. Theft becomes Robbery only if death or hurt is caused, whereas Extortion becomes Robbery
merely by being in the presence of the victim.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: Iand III only
I, II and III only
I and IV only
I and IV only
questions.solution: Statement I is correct per the passage ("without the possessor’s consent" s "consent is wrongfully obtained"). Statement III is correct ("overpowering of will does not arise [in theft]...

questions.questionText: C promotes a skincare product claiming it is "dermatologically tested and completely safe," without verifying the claim. The product later causes harm to users. Which of the following best reflects the legal position?
options: C is not liable since the claim was provided by the brand.
C is liable only if it is proven that the brand intended to deceive consumers.
C may be liable for failing to exercise due diligence before making the claim.
C is liable only if they personally manufactured the product.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: C may be liable for failing to exercise due diligence before making the claim. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Country Alpha's government systematically rounds up and executes thousands of members of
the opposition 'Blue Political Party' during peacetime to ensure no future political resistance.
Which of the following international crimes is the government most likely liable for under the
Rome Statute?
options: War Crimes, since the targeted execution of civilians is an unlawful act of hostility.

None of the above, because political groups are completely excluded from the Rome
Statute.
Crimes Against Humanity, as it involves a systematic attack against a civilian population.
Genocide, because the government intended to completely destroy a distinct group.
questions.solution: , while political groups are excluded from Genocide, a systematic execution campaign against them easily meets the threshold for Crimes Against Humanity, which applies to "any civilian population" during peacetime.

questions.questionText:
Mr. A owns a small, aesthetic coffee shop in a quiet residential area. His neighbor, Ms. B, a
professional musician, begins practicing her drums for half an hour a day in a soundproofed
studio in her basement. Despite the soundproofing, the barely perceptible vibrations from the
drums are felt by Mr. A in his shop.. The vibrations are not loud enough to disturb his
customers, and no tangible damage has been done to the building itself. Mr. A claims this is a
nuisance. Decide on your understanding of the passage, the most legally sound option.
options:
Yes, because any interference with the enjoyment of one's property gives one a right to
claim the tort of nuisance.
Yes, because the interference is a result of a continuous unreasonable activity.
No, because the interference is minor and trifling nature.
No, because Ms. B has taken reasonable care by soundproofing her studio.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because the interference is minor and trifling nature. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Rohan pays the overdue electricity charges of a banquet hall because the power company
threatens disconnection during his daughter’s wedding reception being hosted there. The hall
owner had promised to clear the bill but failed to do so. After the event, the owner refuses
reimbursement, saying Rohan acted for his own convenience. Rohan argues the owner’s
liability was discharged using Rohan’s money, and retaining that benefit without repayment
would be unjust.
What is the strongest view?
options:
Rohan can recover because owner received benefit at Rohan’s expense and unjustly retains
it.
Rohan cannot recover because he also benefited by saving his daughter’s reception.
Rohan cannot recover because payments to utilities never create restitutionary claims.
Rohan can recover only if the hall owner signed a written promise afterward.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “received benefit, » «, at Rohan’s expense,” and “unjustly retains,” matching the reference line. The hall owner’s outstanding liability was cleared using Rohan’s money, so refusing reimbursement may amount to unjust retention of a benefit.

questions.questionText:
The Central Empowered Committee (CEC), established by the Supreme Court in 2002 to monitor
compliance with environmental laws, had its composition altered by the government. The
committee now includes only retired bureaucrats, as the two independent members were removed.
A CEC official was also part of the eight-member government committee that drafted the new
definition of the Aravalli hill range. Former civil servants and environmental groups have raised
concerns and filed a petition requesting that the CEC be reconstituted with both government and
non-government experts, ensuring it functions as an independent monitor.
Why is the composition of the CEC being challenged in the petition?
options: Because the committee includes too many scientists instead of bureaucrats.
Because the committee now lacks independent members and may be biased.
Because the committee was not formed through a parliamentary process.
Because the committee has no legal authority to monitor environmental matters.
questions.solution: The challenge is based on the loss of impartiality: removing independent members and including only government-appointed bureaucrats compromises the CEC’s role as an independent monitor. Options A, C, and D are incorrect because the concern is about independence and bias, not the number of scientists, parliamentary procedure, or legal authority.

questions.questionText:
State Q plants a floating military platform in a part of the ocean lying outside all territorial
seas and internal waters. It announces that the surrounding fifty nautical miles are now
under its exclusive sovereignty and that all ships must seek permission to navigate there.
Several States protest, arguing that the area is high seas and cannot be subjected to State
sovereignty. State Q claims occupation of the platform gives it sovereign title over the
surrounding sea.
Which position is strongest?
options:
State Q succeeds because physical occupation creates sovereignty over high seas
immediately.
Protesters succeed because no State may validly subject high seas to sovereignty.

State Q succeeds because military platforms convert high seas into internal waters
automatically.
Protesters fail because navigation freedom exists only inside territorial sea and ports.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “no State” and “subject high seas to sovereignty,” matching the reference line. Since the claimed area lies beyond territorial sea and internal waters, State Q cannot validly declare exclusive sovereign control over it.

questions.questionText:
Sana builds a machine learning tool and wants a patent. During review, she learns that novelty
and industrial usability alone are not enough; the invention must also be non-obvious and must
not fall under certain exclusions. Sana argues that because her tool works in factories, it must
automatically qualify for protection. The examiner disagrees, citing additional requirements.
Which statement best reflects the correct standard?
options:
The invention must be novel, non-obvious, industrially applicable, and must not fall within
exclusions.

The invention is patentable if it is useful in business, regardless of whether it is obvious to
experts.

The invention is patentable if it is new and profitable, because profitability proves inventive
step automatically.

The invention is patentable if it is described well, even if it falls within excluded categories of
subject matter.
questions.solution: The reference line sets out a cumulative test: the invention must be “novel, non-obvious, industrially applicable,” and also must not fall within exclusions. Sana’s reliance only on factory use addresses industrial applicability but ignores non-obviousness and exclusions.

questions.questionText:
Based on the passage, what is the underlying judicial principle that justifies the imposition of the
death penalty in cases involving systematic sexual abuse of multiple children, despite general
judicial reluctance to award capital punishment?
options:
The doctrine of proportionality requires that the severity of the punishment must be strictly
calculated based on the total number of victims involved.

Crimes of exceptional heinousness and scale that demonstrate no possibility of offender
reformation and threaten society's most vulnerable warrant the ultimate deterrent.

All sexual offences against children under the POCSO Act automatically qualify for enhanced
sentencing including the death penalty regardless of the specific facts.

The "rarest of rare" doctrine mandates the death penalty whenever physical injuries are
medically documented during the investigation of sexual assault cases.
questions.solution: The passage states that the death penalty was imposed because the crime was of "such an exceptional and heinous nature that it leaves no room for reformation, necessitating the ultimate judicial deterrent to meet the ends of justice." This reflects the Supreme Court's "rarest of rare" doctrine, which requires exceptional circumstances including the nature, scale, and impact of the crime, combined with the impossibility of reformation. Option (A) is incorrect because the passage does not suggest

questions.questionText:
A professional council proposes to cancel Dr. Leena’s registration based on two written
statements from unnamed complainants alleging misconduct during consultations. Leena
receives only a brief summary of allegations and is told she cannot cross-examine the
complainants because it would “discourage reporting.” The council insists written statements
are enough and that Leena may submit a written defence. Leena argues that credibility is
central and that without testing the statements, the process is unfair.
What is the best legal assessment?
options:
Decision valid because anonymous statements suffice, and cross-examination is never
required; written summaries satisfy hearing requirements for fairness.

Decision invalid only if biased; denial of cross-examination cannot matter since committee
offered appeal and counselling afterwards.

Decision flawed because it requires proper notice, a chance to present evidence and
arguments, and cross-examine where necessary, before decision.

Decision valid because misconduct is serious, so procedures may be relaxed; hearing is
optional in purely administrative matters like this.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: This option directly uses “proper notice,” » 6 “chance to present evidence and arguments,” and “cross-examine where necessary,” tracking the reference line’s words closely. The facts show limited disclosure and denial of cross-examination where credibility is pivotal, so the process is flawed under the stated fairness requirements.

questions.questionText:
In recent years, as geopolitical tensions increased in the region, the Indian government began
seriously considering the implementation of compulsory military service. The proposal suggested that all
able-bodied citizens, upon reaching the age of 18, would be required to undergo a specific period of
military training and service, typically ranging from one to two years. This is in conflict with
Fundamental Rights & DPSP. It was implemented by the Parliament of India and military training is
compulsorily imposed on every citizen above eighteen years of age citing Article 51A being a compulsory
part of the Indian Constitution. Is the law enforcing Fundamental Duties valid?
options: Yes, because there can be no laws made to give effect to Fundamental Duties.
No, because the law enforcing Fundamental Duties is not in consonance with Fundamental Rights and DPSP.
Yes, because Fundamental Duties are made compulsory for governance.
No, because there has to be sanction of the President for the same.

questions.questionText:
A files a suit against B seeking declaration of title over a property but does not seek possession
despite knowing that B is occupying the property. After losing the first suit, A files another
suit seeking possession on the basis of the same title dispute. Applying the doctrine discussed
in the passage, which of the following is most accurate?
options: The second suit is maintainable because possession and title are separate remedies.

The second suit is barred because A ought to have claimed all connected reliefs in the first
suit itself.

The second suit is maintainable because constructive res judicata applies only to defenses
and not reliefs.
The second suit is barred only if the first court expressly decided the issue of possession.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The second suit is barred because A ought to have claimed all connected reliefs in the first suit itself. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Ranjan Sharma is an MLA belonging to the "Bharatiya Jan Morcha" (BJM), a national political party, in the Madhya
        Pradesh Legislative Assembly. During a crucial vote on a state electricity amendment bill, Ranjan defies the party
        whip issued by the BJM state unit and votes against the bill, arguing that it would harm farmers in his constituency.
        The bill passes with a slim majority. Arvind Tiwari, also a BJM MLA but serving in the Uttar Pradesh Legislative
        Assembly, is outraged by Ranjan's defiance. Arvind believes that Ranjan's vote has damaged the party's national
        image and set a bad precedent for party discipline across states. Arvind approaches the Speaker of the Madhya
        Pradesh Legislative Assembly and files a disqualification petition against Ranjan under the Tenth Schedule, arguing
        that as a fellow BJM legislator (even from another state), he has standing to seek disqualification of any BJM member
        who defies the party whip anywhere in the country. Based on the passage, is Arvind's disqualification petition
        against Ranjan maintainable?
options:
Yes, because the Tenth Schedule applies uniformly to all legislators belonging to the same national political
            party, and any party member from any state can file a petition to enforce party discipline across state
            boundaries.

Yes, because Ranjan's defiance of the party whip affects the BJM's national reputation, and the Tenth Schedule
            protects the interests of political parties at the national level, not just individual state assemblies.

No, because Arvind is a member of the Uttar Pradesh Assembly, not the Madhya Pradesh Assembly where
            Ranjan serves.

No, because only the national president of the BJM party has the authority to file disqualification petitions
            against state-level MLAs who defy party whips, not individual legislators from other states.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because Arvind is a member of the Uttar Pradesh Assembly, not the Madhya Pradesh Assembly where Ranjan serves. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
The National River Protection Board, a statutory body, has a strict legal mandate to inspect
riverside factories annually. Relying on official government logs, an activist proves the Board
has entirely halted all inspections for five consecutive years without justification. The activist
seeks a writ of mandamus from the Supreme Court compelling the Board to resume these
inspections. Decide how the Court should respond.
options:
The Court will refuse, as issuing such a writ would amount to substituting the statutory
machinery with routine judicial management.

The Court will refuse, because specialized regulatory domains are completely immune
from judicial intervention under Article 32.

The Court will agree, because there is a clear legal duty coupled with a demonstrable
failure in its discharge by the statutory body.

The Court will agree, because fundamental rights empower the judiciary to actively
supervise and manage all environmental statutory authorities.
questions.solution: Option C is correct because a writ of mandamus specifically requires two elements according to the text: a clear legal duty and a demonstrable failure to discharge it. The statutory mandate to inspect annually (duty) and the official logs proving a five-year halt satisfy these conditions.

questions.questionText:
Kavita is the natural guardian of her 17-year-old son, Rohan. She signs a three-year lease
agreement to rent out a commercial shop inherited by Rohan to a local business owner. The
monthly rent is fair, and the tenant agrees to handle all property maintenance. However,
because Rohan will turn 18 next year, this three-year lease is scheduled to run for about two
years after he reaches adulthood. Is prior court permission required for this lease?
options:
Yes, because the lease is scheduled to remain in effect for more than one year after the
minor reaches adulthood.

Yes, because court approval must be secured whenever a lease agreement impacts the
minor's future control of the property.

No, because the total duration of the lease is under five years and stays within the
permitted statutory timeline.

No, because securing a fair market rent and structural maintenance terms fulfills the
guardian's duty to protect the estate.
questions.solution: the passage sets up two distinct restrictions on a guardian's power to lease a minor's immovable property. A lease requires prior court permission if it either exceeds five years total or extends beyond one year after the minor turns 18.

questions.questionText:
According to the passage, which Constitutional Amendment Act inserted Article 21A
guaranteeing the right to free and compulsory education for children, and what is the specific
age group covered by this fundamental right as enacted?
options:
The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A covering children aged
6-14 years for free compulsory education

The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A covering children aged
6-18 years for free compulsory education

The 98rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005 inserted Article 21A covering children aged
6-14 years for free compulsory education

The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A covering children up to
14 years for free compulsory education
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states: "The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted: Article 21A: Right to free and compulsory education for all children aged 6-14." This directly answers both parts of the question—the amendment number (86th, 2002) and the precise age range (6-14 years). Option (D) is the close distractor stating "up to 14 years" rather than "aged 6-14," which could be interpreted as starting from birth rather than age 6.

questions.questionText:
A courier company stores high-value parcels in a locked warehouse. Late at night, Sameer
enters the warehouse without permission and starts checking boxes, hoping to find expensive
electronics. He is caught before removing any parcel. Sameer argues it is not “house trespass”
because the place is not a home and no one lives there. The prosecution claims the structure is
protected.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
It is house trespass because any entry into any building is house trespass even without
intent to commit offence there.

It is only criminal trespass because warehouses are not dwellings worship places or
custody places, so house trespass fails here.

No trespass because an unlocked door implies consent, and criminal intent cannot create
liability when entry is permitted at all.

It is house trespass because he entered a building used for the custody of property with
criminal intent at night.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “building used for the custody of property,” and the facts show entry with theft-oriented intent, satisfying the structure-plus-intent combination. The space need not be a dwelling; custody-of-property structures are expressly covered.

questions.questionText:
A courier mistakenly delivers Arjun’s sealed carton of premium paint cans worth 240,000 to
Bhanu’s workshop instead of Arjun’s. Bhanu notices the delivery slip bears another name but
uses the paint for a paid project, earning profit. When Arjun traces the consignment, Bhanu
refuses to pay, arguing there was no contract with Arjun and he never “ordered” anything.
Arjun sues to recover the value, claiming Bhanu should not keep a benefit gained by mistake.
What outcome best follows?
options:
Arjun loses because no contract existed, so Bhanu may keep the paint despite Arjun’s
mistaken delivery claim under law alone.

Arjun wins only if Bhanu signed acceptance, because quasi-contracts require mutual
consent and consideration just like ordinary contracts always here.

Arjun wins because quasi-contract remedies apply when one party is unjustly enriched at
another’s expense without formal agreement between them.

Arjun loses because restitution is granted only for physical goods supplied as necessaries,
not for commercial deliveries mistaken or not.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “unjustly enriched without formal agreement,” matching the reference line’s core trigger. Bhanu gained a benefit at Arjun’s expense without a real contract, so restitution can be imposed to prevent unfair enrichment.

questions.questionText:
Joseph, aged 19, owns self-acquired property and executes a will while undergoing treatment
for fever. The doctor certifies that at the time of execution he understood the nature of the
document, the property involved, and the persons who would benefit. His uncle challenges the
will, arguing that only persons above 21 can make wills and that any illness automatically
destroys testamentary capacity. Joseph’s sister argues that majority and sound mind at the
time of making the will are sufficient.
Which view is correct?
options: The will is invalid because every testator must be at least twenty-one years old.
The will is invalid because any medical illness automatically removes soundness of mind.
The will may be valid because any major person of sound mind can make a will.
The will may be valid only if all close relatives consent before its execution.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “major person of sound mind,” matching the reference line. Since Joseph is nineteen and appears to have understood the nature and effect of the will when executing it, the will may be valid.

questions.questionText:
The passage relies on two distinct precedents pre-dating the present ruling. Which option
accurately distinguishes the specific contribution of each precedent to the trauma-care
framework described?
options:
Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) gave binding force to Good Samaritan
protections, while SaveLIFE Foundation (2016) directed states to establish referral
protocols and designated hospitals

Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) held that denial of emergency care violates
Article 21 and directed referral protocols, while SaveLIFE Foundation (2016) gave binding
force to Good Samaritan protections

Both precedents dealt exclusively with Good Samaritan protections and neither addressed
referral protocols

S. Rajaseekaran (2025) was the first ruling to connect any aspect of trauma care to Article
21, with no earlier precedent doing so
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) held that denial of emergency care violates Article 21 and directed referral protocols, while SaveLIFE Foundation (2016) gave binding force to Good Samaritan protections. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A State Government enacts a statute restricting public assemblies and processions in the
interest of maintaining "public tranquillity." The legislation is challenged before the Supreme
Court for violating the citizens' right to peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b). Despite
massive public support for the law, the Court strikes it down, holding that "the preservation of
constitutional freedoms cannot be contingent upon public convenience or majority
endorsement." Which of the following most accurately reflects the judicial philosophy guiding
this verdict?
options:
The Court subordinated constitutional rights to societal expediency, thereby reinforcing
the doctrine of judicial restraint in matters

The Court's reasoning is consistent with Fiat justitia ruat caelum, as it prioritised
constitutional justice despite political upheaval

The Court declined to weigh competing social interests, thus exhibiting an instance of
judicial abdication rather than assertiveness

The decision manifests majoritarian constitutionalism, emphasising that public order must
prevail over judicial idealism and theory
questions.solution: The Court struck down the law despite "massive public support," holding that constitutional freedoms cannot depend on "majority endorsement." This mirrors the passage's description of Fiat justitia ruat caelum: "justice, anchored in constitutional principle, must be rendered irrespective of political tempests or societal disquietude" and constitutional morality prevailing "over transient majoritarian impulses." The Court prioritized constitutional rights over public convenience, exactly as the m

questions.questionText:
A municipal officer seizes a truck carrying perishable goods during an investigation and places
it in a guarded public warehouse. No written contract is signed between the truck owner and
the department. While the goods are in official custody, the warehouse staff carelessly leaves
them exposed to rain. The department argues that no bailment can arise without a formal
agreement. The owner says bailment may arise even without formal contract if goods are
delivered or held in circumstances creating possession and duty.
Which view is stronger?
options:
Department succeeds because bailment always requires a signed written contract between
parties.

Department succeeds because official seizure can never create responsibility for movable
goods.

Owner fails because bailment applies only to private commercial transactions, not custody
by authorities.

Owner succeeds because bailment may arise without formal contract in proper
circumstances.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line’s idea that bailment may arise without a formal contract. The truck and goods are movable property, and the department’s custody may create bailment-like obligations even in the absence of a signed agreement.

questions.questionText:
Rajat and Aman are professional boxers who have competed in the national boxing league for over
five years, gaining a reputation for their intense rivalry. During the championship match, the tension
escalated significantly. In the third round, while the referee was momentarily distracted, Rajat, feeling
overwhelmed by Aman's superior technique, grabbed a wooden stick that was part of the event's
decoration near the ring and struck Aman, causing a severe injury. Aman, unable to continue, lost the
match as a result. After recovering, Aman decided to sue Rajat for damages due to the injury sustained
during the match. Rajat argues that Aman, as a professional boxer, consented to the risks inherent in
boxing. Will Aman succeed in his legal claim for damages?
options:
Yes, because Aman consented to the normal risks associated with boxing, not to being hit with a foreign
object, which is outside the rules of the sport.

No, because by participating in a professional boxing match, Aman consented to all forms of physical
contact, regardless of their nature.

No, because the use of the stick could be seen as part of the competitive strategy inherent in such a high-
stakes sports environment.

Yes, because the wooden stick caused unexpected harm, which should legally be considered within the
normal scope of the boxing match.

questions.questionText:
An advocate with nine years of practice applies for appointment as a High Court judge, claiming
her academic record and social work should compensate for the shortfall. Separately, a judicial
officer with ten years of experience applies but is 63 years old at the time of proposed
appointment. Both argue eligibility should be relaxed because of shortages in the judiciary. Which
statement is most accurate?
options:
Both are eligible because merit and shortage can replace formal experience and age
requirements.

The advocate is eligible but the judicial officer is not because only advocates, not judges, can be
appointed.

The judicial officer is eligible but the advocate is not because experience can be less than ten
years if achievements are strong.

Neither fits the stated conditions because a judge must meet the ten-year requirement and
hold office only until 62.
questions.solution: The reference line clearly requires ten years’ experience and states that judges “hold office until the age of 62.” The advocate fails the ten-year practice condition, and the 63-year- old cannot hold office beyond 62 as per the stated tenure rule.

questions.questionText:
Vikram is charged with murdering taxi driver Amar. Witness Deepak, who never met Vikram
before, saw someone near the crime scene but no TIP was conducted. At trial, Deepak identifies
Vikram. Additionally: Vikram's mobile tower location places him at the scene; blood group O-
positive found in Vikram's car matches victim's blood group (37% population share). Based on the
passage, what conclusion is legally sound?
options:
Conviction is unsustainable because dock identification of a stranger without TIP is unsafe,
and a common blood group cannot exclude alternative hypotheses.

Conviction is sustainable because mobile tower location data combined with a matching blood
group creates sufficient corroboration for the dock identification.

Conviction is unsustainable solely because the prosecution failed to conduct DNA testing,
thereby violating the mandatory requirement for conclusive scientific evidence.

Conviction is sustainable because the presence of the victim’s blood in the car is objective
scientific evidence that legally compensates for identification defects.
questions.solution: Here, conviction genuinely cannot be sustained due to multiple evidentiary defects. The passage explicitly states: "when the accused is a stranger to the witness and no TIP was conducted, dock identification becomes inherently unsafe." Second, the blood group evidence is not "conclusive'—shared by 37% of the population, it fails to "exclude every possible hypothesis except guilt" as required by Sharad Birdhichand Sarda.

questions.questionText:
Suppose the government argues that the Preamble can be amended to reflect changing social
values, and this amendment passes. What is the most likely judicial outcome according to the
passage?
options: The amendment would be valid if it changes only non-core aspects.
The amendment would be valid because the Preamble is not part of the Constitution.
The amendment would be invalid if it destroys the Basic Structure.

The amendment would be invalid because preamble cannot be amended as it forms the part of
basic structure.
questions.solution: Kesavananda established that while the Preamble can be amended, its Basic Structure pillars cannot be destroyed. Incorrect Options:

questions.questionText:
Imran is accused of a non-violent offence punishable up to seven years. The IO believes Imran
is involved but does not write any reasons for arrest and does not consider whether arrest is
necessary to prevent tampering, absconding, or further offence. The IO simply states in the
diary: “Arrested as offence is serious.” Imran argues that even if the IO had reason to believe
involvement, arrest still requires recorded reasons showing why arrest is necessary on
statutory grounds.
What is the best legal position?
options:
Arrest lawful because seriousness alone satisfies necessity, and recording reasons is
optional when police suspect involvement in offence.

Arrest lawful because once reason to believe exists, arrest must follow, and writing reasons
