would only delay investigation for police today.

Arrest unlawful because for offences up to seven years, arrest needs reason to believe plus
recorded reasons showing why arrest is necessary.

Arrest unlawful because police can never arrest in offences up to seven years, and must
always issue summons instead of arresting them.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “reason to believe” and “recorded reasons showing why arrest is necessary,” mirroring the reference line. Since the IO recorded only “serious offence” without necessity grounds, the arrest violates the required standard.

questions.questionText:
A patentee obtains a patent for a mechanical device but describes the invention in vague terms
and does not disclose the best method of performing it. A competitor argues that the disclosure is
insufficient and misleading, making it impossible for a skilled person to work the invention
properly. The patentee responds that once the patent is granted, disclosure defects cannot be used
to cancel it.
Which option is most accurate?
options:
The competitor is correct because insufficient disclosure and failure to disclose the best method
render a patent vulnerable to revocation.

The patentee is correct because disclosure issues can be raised only at filing, not after the
patent is granted.

The competitor is correct only if it also proves the invention lacks novelty, since disclosure
defects alone cannot matter in patent revocation.

The patentee is correct because unclear claims can be corrected later, so they can never
support cancellation.
questions.solution: The reference line explicitly lists “insufficient disclosure” and “failure to disclose the best method” as defects that “render a patent vulnerable to revocation.” Since the scenario alleges exactly these shortcomings, the competitor’s revocation argument coheres with the stated principle.

questions.questionText:
Four law students make the following observations:
Student I: "Strict liability and absolute liability are identical because both dispense with proof
of negligence."
Student II: "Absolute liability was developed because strict liability's exceptions could
inadequately protect victims of industrial disasters."
Student III: "An enterprise engaged in hazardous activities can avoid liability under absolute
liability if the accident was caused by an act of God."
Student IV: "Absolute liability imposes a higher responsibility on hazardous enterprises than
strict liability."
Which student(s) present the most legally sound understanding based on the passage?
options: Student I only
Students IT and III only
Students II and IV only
Students I, II and IV only
questions.solution: Option (C): Student II correctly identifies the rationale behind the development of absolute liability. Student IV correctly recognizes its stricter nature.

questions.questionText:
Arjun’s father, acting as his natural guardian, sold a portion of Arjun’s inherited land when
Arjun was 16 years old, without obtaining prior court permission. The purchaser later leased
the land to a company, which built a warehouse on it. When Arjun turned 18, he did not
immediately challenge the sale, but his uncle, who had no legal claim through Arjun, argued
before the revenue authority that the sale was void from the beginning and that the
purchaser’s lease should not be recognised. What is the strongest argument against the uncle’s
objection?
options:
The objection fails because the transfer is voidable, not void, and remains binding until
challenged by Arjun or a person claiming through him.

The objection fails because later commercial use of the land may show that the transfer
ultimately benefited the minor’s estate.

The objection fails because every family member loses the right to question a guardian’s
transfer once the minor attains majority.

The objection fails because a natural guardian may perform all reasonable acts necessary
for protecting the minor’s property.
ii
questions.solution: it applies Section 8(3) as stated in the passage. The transfer made without prior court permission is not void from the beginning; it is only voidable at the instance of the minor or a person claiming through the minor.

questions.questionText:
Parul, an experienced mountain climber, decides to participate in an expedition organized by Apex
Adventures. The expedition involves climbing a notoriously difficult peak known as "The Phantom.”
Parul is informed by the Apex Adventures’ team that the expedition has a 90% success rate and is guided
by professional climbers with decades of experience. Relying on this information, Parul signs a consent
form acknowledging the risks of mountain climbing, including possible injury or death. However, she
later discovers that the actual success rate is only 60% and the guides are relatively inexperienced
climbers. During the climb, Parul suffers a serious fall due to inadequate guidance. She now wants to sue
Apex Adventures for damages. Will she succeed?
options: Yes, because the nature of the activity inherently includes the risk of injury or death.
Yes, because the consent she provided was based on misinformation provided by Apex Adventures.
No, because she signed a consent form acknowledging the risks involved in mountain climbing.

No, because mountain climbing is an activity that inherently involves high risks, regardless of the guide's
experience.

questions.questionText: State Y identifies an enemy weapons storage facility in a crowded residential area. Military experts estimate that attacking it would eliminate a moderate military threat but would likely destroy hundreds of surrounding homes and cause severe civilian casualties. Which principle most directly governs the legality of the decision?
options: Humanity alone, because civilian casualties are always prohibited.
Distinction alone, because civilian objects can never be located near military objectives.
Proportionality, because civilian harm must not be excessive compared to anticipated military advantage.
Military necessity, because military objectives automatically override civilian concerns.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Proportionality, because civilian harm must not be excessive compared to anticipated military advantage. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Read the following statements carefully based on the principles laid down in the AK Gopalan
case and the passage provided:
1. Article 21 of the Constitution protects the personal liberty of every person in India, not just
citizens, and includes rights such as the freedom to eat, sleep, work, and conduct one’s
personal affairs, making it narrower than the freedoms guaranteed under Article 19(1).
2. The freedoms specified under Article 19(1), such as freedom of movement, residence, and
occupation, are available to all persons in India and can be invoked by non-citizens as well.
8. Kania CJ emphasized that “deprivation” of personal liberty under Article 21 is not the same as
“restriction” under Article 19(1), which only deals with certain phases of liberty for citizens,
and therefore, not all restrictions under Article 19 amount to deprivation under Article 21.
4. Article 21 prescribes detailed limitations on the law-making powers of the legislature, similar
to the detailed restrictions found under Article 19(1) for citizen rights.
Based on the passage, how many of the above statements are true?
questions.solution: False: Article 21 is broader, not narrower, than the freedoms in Article 19(1). The passage explicitly says: “Article 19 gives the rights specified therein only to the citizens of India while Article 21 is applicable to all persons...

questions.questionText:
The Municipal Corporation of City X is legally required under the SWM Rules to establish a bio-
methanation facility to process wet waste. The facility costs 12 crore. The municipality has only
%2 crore in its budget and cannot proceed without external financing. A carbon credit consultant
proposes that the municipality can earn CCC certificates under the CCTS by projecting methane
emission reductions, and the anticipated carbon credit revenue of 210 crore would make the
project financially viable. The municipality proceeds with the project solely because carbon credit
revenue bridges the funding gap. Subsequently, the BEE rejects the carbon credit application
citing the regulatory surplus doctrine. Based on the passage, which argument would most strongly
support the municipality's appeal against BEE's rejection?
options:
Rule 8 of the SWM Rules explicitly encourages local bodies to generate carbon credits, thereby
creating a legally recognized exemption from the regulatory surplus doctrine for all waste
management activities

The bio-methanation facility, though legally mandated, would not have been implemented
without carbon credit revenue, demonstrating that credits overcome a financial barrier and
enable compliance rather than reward pre-existing compliance

Voluntary carbon markets like Verra and Gold Standard accept barrier-based additionality,
and since CCTS allows voluntary participation, the municipality should be permitted to apply
Verra's standards instead of CCTS eligibility criteria

The CCTS prohibits double counting between carbon credits and RECs but explicitly allows
concurrent earning of carbon credits and Green Credits, indicating regulatory flexibility that
should extend to mandated activities
questions.solution: The passage explains barrier analysis as a pathway: "if a municipality faces prohibitive costs for a mandated project (such as a 210 crore bio-methanation plant) that becomes financially viable only through carbon credit revenue, the credits overcome implementation barriers despite legal mandate... the carbon credits aren't rewarding compliance but making this compliance financially possible." This directly applies to City X's situation where the project is mandated but financially impossible wi

questions.questionText:
PQR Industries contracts with ABC Logistics: "ABC shall transport 1000 tons monthly for 25 per
kg. Payment within 30 days of delivery." After six months, a new government regulation mandates
additional safety documentation increasing ABC's costs by 40%. ABC demands 27 per kg citing
increased costs. PQR refuses, stating the contract clearly specifies 5 per kg with no escalation
clause. Based on the passage, what is the correct legal position?
options:
Courts may apply the golden rule to adjust the %5 rate to ?7 because literal enforcement
creates commercially irrational outcome for ABC

The doctrine of business efficacy permits implying a cost escalation term to make the contract
workable under changed circumstances

The literal rule requires enforcement of %5 per kg as clearly stated, because courts cannot
rewrite contracts to address commercial inconvenience

The purposive approach allows considering the regulatory change as part of the factual matrix
justifying rate adjustment
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states in Union of India v. Jindal Rail Infrastructure Ltd.

questions.questionText:
Neeraj and Farah submit their civil marriage notice and it is displayed publicly. Farah’s
cousin objects on day 40, alleging Neeraj already has a living spouse. The cousin insists the
Officer must halt the process because bigamy is a serious issue. Neeraj argues the objection is
too late and cannot be entertained at this stage. The Officer is unsure whether to accept a
delayed objection.
How should the Officer treat it?
options:
Objection must be heard, because any person may object at any time, and delay never
matters when marriage validity is questioned by law always.

Objection must be heard, because thirty days is only a guideline, and officers must reopen
notice whenever relatives complain later in every case today.

Objection is time-barred, because objections can be raised within thirty days if conditions
are violated, so a forty-day objection need not proceed further here.

Objection is barred, because only parties can object, and third parties have no right to
raise objections regardless of timing under this process ever.
questions.solution: The correct option directly uses “objections within thirty days” and links it to a violation claim. Since the objection arrives on day 40, it falls outside the stated window, so the Officer need not proceed on that late objection.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Sharma, the owner of a private clinic, accidentally left a file containing highly sensitive patient data in a
café. This file included detailed medical records and personal information of various patients, including a famous
actress. Mr. Roy, a journalist known for his investigative reporting, found the file. Recognizing the potential
impact, he published an article revealing the actress's confidential medical history, arguing that it was in the public
interest. The actress, distressed by this invasion of privacy, sued both Mr. Sharma for negligence in handling her
medical records and Mr. Roy for the unauthorized publication of her private information. In the context of the law
of torts, who is more likely to be held liable for constituting a tort against the actress?
options: Mr. Sharma, for negligently handling sensitive patient data.
Mr. Roy, for the unauthorized publication of confidential information.
Both, as Mr. Sharma's negligence and Mr. Roy's publication collectively led to the breach of privacy.
Neither, as Mr. Sharma's action was unintentional, and Mr. Roy acted in the perceived public interest.
questions.solution: A tort is constituted when there is an act or omission that infringes a legal right and gives rise to a legal remedy. In this case, the actress's legal right to privacy and confidentiality is directly violated by Mr. Roy, who knowingly published her confidential medical information without authorization. Although Mr. Sharma acted negligently by leaving the file unattended, the passage emphasizes that tortious liability primarily arises from the infringement of a legal right. Mr. Roy's deliberate publication is the direct act that violates the actress's legal right, making him more likely to be held liable in tort. Why other options are incorrect:

questions.questionText:
A landlord threatened his tenant that unless the tenant signed a lease renewal at triple the
original rent, he would file a false criminal complaint against the tenant's son. The tenant
signed under this threat and later sought to avoid the contract on grounds of coercion.
options:
The contract is void, not voidable, because coercion involves a threat of criminal action
which renders the consent entirely absent rather than merely defective.

This constitutes coercion as threatening to file a false complaint to compel consent amounts
to threatening a forbidden act; the contract is voidable at the tenant's option.

Since the tenant had an option to refuse and approach the courts, the threat does not
constitute coercion; free consent requires only that no physical force was used.

This is not coercion under Section 15 as threatening a criminal complaint does not
constitute an act forbidden by the IPC; coercion requires physical compulsion to be present.
questions.solution: A threat to file a false case to compel contract falls squarely within Section 15. The resulting contract is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so obtained.

questions.questionText: A State law mandates that all temples, irrespective of denomination, must allow entry to all classes of persons, including historically excluded groups. A religious denomination challenges this law claiming violation of its right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion. Which is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The law is valid as Article 25 permits State intervention for social reform, even if it affects denominational practices.
The law is invalid as denominational rights under Article 26 are absolute.
The law is invalid unless it is proven that exclusion is not an essential religious practice.
The law is valid only if the denomination consents to such reform.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The law is valid as Article 25 permits State intervention for social reform, even if it affects denominational practices. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Imran and Hina, a Muslim couple in Mumbai, had a grand wedding ceremony performed according
to Islamic rites, attended by a large gathering of family and friends. However, in the flurry of the
wedding activities, they overlooked the formal signing of the nikahnama. The marriage included all
customary rituals and was publicly acknowledged by the community. A year later, Hina needs to provide
proof of her marriage to Imran to apply for a joint home loan. When they realize the nikahnama was
never signed, they present wedding photographs and testimony from witnesses who attended the
marriage. Can Imran and Hina successfully prove their marital status for the home loan application
based on the evidence provided, despite the absence of a signed nikahnama?
options:
Yes, because the public ceremony and witness testimonies establish their marriage under Islamic customs,
which should be recognized legally.
No, because registration of marriage in Islamic law is mandatory.

Yes, because the extensive wedding rituals performed are sufficient to validate the marriage legally, even

without a written contract.

No, because Islamic law strictly requires a signed nikahnama to validate a marriage, and without it, the
marriage is not legally recognized for official purposes.

questions.questionText:
Argument: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) should be allowed to file writ petitions before High
Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution, even though it is an investigative agency created by
statute.
Which of the following statements, if true, would most strengthen the above argument?
options:
The statute establishing the ED expressly authorises it to initiate legal proceedings and sue in its
own name.

Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs only for the enforcement of fundamental rights of
citizens.
Investigative agencies frequently challenge judicial inquiries before constitutional courts.
State Governments have opposed the ED’s participation in writ proceedings in several cases.
questions.solution: Most strengthens the argument The argument is that the ED should be allowed to file writ petitions under Article 226. The reference line indicates that explicit statutory power to sue is decisive for recognising an entity as a juristic person.

questions.questionText:
In 2025, the President appoints a new Election Commissioner after receiving
recommendations from the Prime Minister and a Union Minister nominated by him. The
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha is not consulted despite being in office. A public-
interest petitioner challenges the appointment process as incomplete and claims the
appointment is void. The Union argues the President’s appointment power is independent and
committee procedure is only directory.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Appointment is valid because President appoints independently, and any committee is
advisory only; omission of one member cannot matter legally here today.

Appointment is valid because PM’s minister can replace Opposition Leader, and selection
committee may be two-member for convenience always in practice too.

Appointment is invalid because it needs recommendation of selection committee: Prime
Minister, Lok Sabha Opposition Leader, and Minister nominated by Prime Minister.

Appointment is invalid because Commissioners are chosen only by High Court, so
President lacks power even with a committee at all ever.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference committee composition Prime Minister, Lok Sabha Opposition Leader, and a Minister nominated by the Prime Minister showing why bypassing the Opposition Leader makes the recommendation incomplete. Because the reference line ties appointment to that committee’s recommendation, skipping a required participant creates a strong procedural defect.

questions.questionText:
Parul obtains a valid state license to operate a metal-polishing unit next to Princy’s established
coaching centre. To save on initial setup costs, Parul chooses not to install the recommended rubber
vibration-absorbers under her heavy machinery. When the unit functions, frequent vibrations
shake Princy’s classroom boards and a chemical smell enters the windows, causing significant
discomfort to the students and disrupting classes. Princy sues Parul for private nuisance. Parul
argues that her state license provides her with complete statutory authority to operate the unit.
Will Princy’s suit succeed?
options:
Yes, because a state license only governs regulatory compliance and can never be pleaded as a
defense against an action for private nuisance.

Yes, because statutory authority does not shield an authorized activity if the defendant fails to
take reasonable precautions and causes unnecessary harm.

No, because an activity authorized by a valid legal license is protected by law against claims
based on ordinary personal discomfort.

No, because private nuisance requires an actual physical trespass or direct entry of foreign
objects onto the plaintiff's leased premises.
questions.solution: . The passage explains that while statutory authority protects legally authorized acts, it is conditional upon taking "reasonable precautions" and does not justify "unnecessary or negligent harm." By intentionally skipping the installation of recommended vibration-absorbers to save costs, Parul failed to take reasonable precautions, rendering her defense invalid under the passage.

questions.questionText: A purchases a smartphone through an e-commerce platform. Before completing the purchase, A is required to click "I Agree" to a set of terms and conditions, which include a clause stating that the platform shall not be liable for any defects in the product. The product delivered is defective, and the seller refuses replacement. Which of the following is the most legally sound conclusion?
options: The clause excluding liability may be challenged as an unfair contract term despite A's acceptance through click-wrap.
A is bound by the clause since clicking "I Agree" conclusively proves informed consent.
The contract is void as electronic agreements cannot exclude liability.
The platform cannot be held liable under any circumstance once terms are accepted.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The clause excluding liability may be challenged as an unfair contract term despite A's acceptance through click-wrap. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Rohan Mehta is the Managing Director of Galaxy Bank. On April 10, 2018, Galaxy Bank
allowed "CoinTech Pvt. Ltd.", a company engaged in facilitating crypto-to-crypto exchanges, to
open a current account. At this time, the RBI Circular dated April 6, 2018 had already been
issued, and the bank continued maintaining this account until August 2018. During an RBI
inspection in September 2018, this account relationship was discovered. Did Galaxy Bank
violate the Crypto Circular during the period it was in force (before being struck down in
2020)?
options:
Yes, since the Crypto Circular explicitly prohibited banks from opening or maintaining
accounts for entities dealing with VCs

No, because CoinTech only exchanged one cryptocurrency for another and did not deal with
INR fiat currency transactions

Yes, because the Circular required banks to exit pre-existing VC-related relationships
within three months, and CoinTech’s account fell under this category

No, because the Supreme Court eventually struck down the Crypto Circular in 2020,
nullifying its retrospective effect completely
questions.solution: The passage quotes the Crypto Circular as prohibiting banks from "opening accounts of exchanges dealing with them [VCs]" and states banks must "not deal in Virtual Currencies... or provide services for facilitating any person or entity in dealing with or settling VCs." Opening an account for CoinTech on April 10, 2018 (after the April 6 circular) directly violated this prohibition.

questions.questionText:
The State Government passed a temporary Executive Order stating that to reduce accidents
during a festival month, police are encouraged to seize the vehicles of all drunk drivers for 48
hours to act as a deterrent. A driver challenged the seizure of his car under this Order. Based
on the High Court’s logic, would this Executive Order be considered a valid basis for seizure?
options:
Yes, because the Court acknowledged that drunk driving must be prevented and
deterrents are a lawful way to achieve road safety.

Yes, because the State has the power to impose additional punitive measures whenever it
deems it necessary for public interest.

No, because the Court held that road safety laws only apply to the condition of the driver
and never to the status of the vehicle itself.

No, because the Court held that seizure must be “specifically authorised by statute”, and
an executive order is not a substitute for statutory authorization.
questions.solution: Option D is correct because the passage emphasizes that seizure must be “justified by law” and specifically “authorised by statute”. It cautions against “additional punitive measures beyond statutory limits.” An executive order trying to expand these powers would likely fail this test.

questions.questionText:
After multiple citizens are hospitalised, a food-safety officer seals a restaurant immediately,
citing “urgent risk of contamination.” The owner complains that no prior notice or hearing was
given, and argues that livelihood is affected. The authority responds that the decision was
taken to prevent further harm and that a hearing can be provided later after the risk is
contained. The owner challenges the closure solely on the ground of lack of prior hearing.
How should a court most plausibly approach this?
options:
Action valid because natural justice may be excluded in emergency situations where
immediate action is necessary for public safety now.

Action invalid because no person should be condemned without fair opportunity to be
heard, even when prompt action is needed.

Action valid only if reasons were published; hearing can be skipped permanently if
authority believes closure benefits public interest alone.

Action invalid because statutory exclusion is impossible; fairness is absolute and admits no
exceptions in any proceedings.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “excluded or modified in emergency situations” and “immediate action is necessary for public safety,” matching the reference line’s wording. Where imminent public harm is alleged, the law may permit urgent action first, with fairness accommodated through prompt post-decision procedures.

questions.questionText:
A technology company, Tech Gen, enters a contract with Data Solutions to provide cloud storage
services. Three months before the end of the fiscal year, Tech Gen receives a better offer from another
provider and notifies Data Solutions of their intention not to renew the contract and to reduce their
current usage significantly in anticipation of the switch. Data Solutions claims damages for the expected
loss in revenue for the remaining three months. Can Tech Gen be held liable for damages caused by this
anticipatory breach?
options: Yes, because Tech Gen used less storage than originally contracted for.
No, because the contract was near its end anyway.
Yes, because they will become entitled to be compensated for damages.
No, because anticipatory breach applies to completely terminated contracts.

questions.questionText:
Aman agrees to buy antique furniture from Bhavya for 72 lakh. Later, it is discovered that
Aman is a minor, the furniture is actually prohibited wildlife material, and Bhavya induced
the deal by hiding that fact. Aman refuses to proceed. Bhavya says an agreement exists
because there was price, subject matter, and acceptance. Aman argues that even if an
agreement exists, it cannot become enforceable when essential elements such as competence,
lawful object, and genuine consent are absent.
Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The agreement is enforceable because price and acceptance are always enough.
The agreement is enforceable because illegality affects only criminal liability.
The agreement is enforceable unless Bhavya voluntarily releases Aman.
The agreement remains unenforceable because essential elements are absent.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line. Aman’s minority, unlawful subject matter, and affected consent show absence of essential elements, so the agreement cannot be converted into an enforceable contract.

questions.questionText:
A trekking group is trapped when a sudden landslide blocks the only marked trail and an avalanche
warning is issued. To reach safety before nightfall, the guide cuts a locked fence and leads hikers
through a private orchard, trampling saplings and breaking irrigation pipes. The owner files a complaint
for trespass and damage. The guide claims necessity but evidence shows an alternative public route
existed, though it would take two extra hours.
How should the necessity defence be assessed under the stated limits?
options:
Defence succeeds because any emergency automatically justifies illegality, and proportionality or
alternatives do not matter once danger exists.

Defence fails because necessity never applies outside murder, so property damage and trespass can
never be excused in law.

Defence succeeds only if proportionality, good faith, absence of alternatives, and absolute necessity
are shown, so evidence matters.

Defence fails because rescuers must wait for police permission, and self-help is never allowed even to
prevent serious harm.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference line's four conditions — proportionality, good faith, absence of alternatives, and absolute necessity — and correctly makes the outcome dependent on evidence. Here, an alternative public route existed.

questions.questionText:
A university’s anti-ragging committee receives an anonymous email alleging that Aarav
threatened a junior in a hostel corridor. Without issuing any show-cause notice, it suspends
Aarav the same day, seals his hostel room, and later circulates a one-line order stating
“misconduct proved.” Aarav claims he was never informed of the allegation’s specifics, was not
allowed to present his version, and could not test the junior’s statement. The university argues
swift action was needed to “send a message.”
What is the strongest legal assessment?
options:
Decision valid because emergency discipline permits action, and later appeal suffices; prior
notice and hearing are not required always here.

Decision invalid because no person should be condemned without a fair opportunity to be
heard after proper notice given first.

Decision valid because reasons were recorded internally, and speaking order alone satisfies
fairness even when the person was absent from the process.

Decision invalid only if authority was biased; lack of hearing matters little when evidence
is strong and undisputed on record.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “no person should be condemned” and “fair opportunity to be heard,” and it connects them to the missing notice and chance to respond. Aarav was punished without being heard, so the core fairness requirement is violated on these facts.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): In India, different religious communities are governed by separate personal
laws in matters such as marriage, succession, adoption, divorce, and maintenance.
Reason (R): This lack of uniformity creates difficulties in applying one common standard of
justice in personal-law disputes.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Assertion (A) is true because the reference line clearly states that Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis and other communities are governed by separate personal laws. Reason (R) is also true because the passage says this lack of uniformity creates difficulties in succession, divorce, inheritance, adoption and maintenance, and makes judicial application of one common standard difficult.

questions.questionText: Commander R authorises use of a weapon causing severe and prolonged suffering to combatants even after they become incapable of fighting. He argues that the weapon is useful because it discourages resistance among enemy forces. Which option best applies?
options: The conduct may violate the principle of humanity because unnecessary suffering cannot be justified merely by strategic convenience.
The conduct is lawful because any measure increasing military success satisfies military necessity.
The conduct is lawful because combatants possess no legal protection.
The conduct is permissible because IHL only protects civilians.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The conduct may violate the principle of humanity because unnecessary suffering cannot be justified merely by strategic convenience. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Vaibhav enters a gated colony to meet his friend. The security supervisor wrongly believes
that Vaibhav has entered without permission. He closes all the exit gates and does not permit
Vaibhav to leave the colony premises. Vaibhav is allowed to walk inside the colony park, sit
near the guard room, and use the internal pathways, but he is not permitted to cross the
colony gate for two hours. Which offence is most appropriately made out?
options:
Wrongful restraint, because Vaibhav’s movement was blocked only towards one exit but
not inside the premises.

Wrongful confinement, because Vaibhav was prevented from proceeding beyond the
colony’s fixed boundary.

No offence, because Vaibhav could still move freely within the park and internal colony
pathways.

No confinement, because the supervisor did not lock Vaibhav inside any room or enclosed
chamber.
questions.solution: Vaibhav was allowed internal movement but was prevented from going beyond the colony limits. The passage explains that confinement arises when a person is prevented from moving beyond a fixed boundary.

questions.questionText:
A company files a patent disclosing its full formula for a chemical coating. After publication, it
tells employees to treat the same formula as a “trade secret” and threatens them for sharing it
externally, claiming trade secret law still protects it. A former employee argues that once disclosed
through the patent route, the same disclosed information cannot be protected as a trade secret,
though separate internal know-how might be.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Patent disclosure destroys all confidentiality claims, including undisclosed internal know-how,
even if never published.

Patent disclosure strengthens trade secret protection, because publication proves ownership
and makes secrecy unnecessary.

The same information can be both patent and trade secret forever, because exclusivity always
overrides disclosure.

Once disclosed through a patent, the same disclosed information cannot be protected as a trade
secret, though ancillary know-how may still be protected.
questions.solution: The reference line directly resolves the dispute: once an invention is disclosed through a patent, it “cannot be protected as a trade secret,” but “undisclosed ancillary know-how may still be protected.” The former employee’s distinction between disclosed formula and separate internal know-how matches the exact structure of the reference line.

questions.questionText:
Ms. Rina, a senior manager at Innovate HR Solutions, has been consistently subjecting Ms.
Kavya, a team leader, to unwelcome conduct. This includes making comments about Ms.
Kavya's body, sending inappropriate memes through work chat, and frequently invading her
personal space during team discussions. Ms. Kavya reports this to the Internal Committee,
alleging sexual harassment under the POSH Act. Ms. Rina argues that the complaint is not
valid, as the Act is specifically designed to protect women from harassment by men, not from
other women. Decide.
options:
The IC must dismiss the complaint, as the legislative intent of the POSH Act was
exclusively to address gender-based power dynamics where the perpetrator is male and the
victim is female.

The IC has the authority and duty to proceed with the inquiry, as the POSH Act's broad
definition of sexual harassment is not restricted to male perpetrators alone.

The IC can proceed only if Ms. Kavya proves that the conduct was explicitly sexual in
nature, since non-explicit conduct between same-gender individuals falls outside the
POSH Act's coverage.

The IC should advise Ms. Kavya to file a complaint under general workplace misconduct
policies instead, since the POSH Act's definition of sexual harassment is ambiguous in
same-sex contexts.
questions.solution: The passage states that the Act defines sexual harassment broadly to include unwelcome physical, verbal, or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature and hostile work environments, without restricting the identity of the perpetrator by gender. Option B correctly recognises that the Act's definition is conduct-focused, not gender-of-perpetrator-focused.

questions.questionText:
Two States agree to submit a river-navigation dispute to an arbitral tribunal after
negotiations fail. The tribunal hears evidence and issues an award allocating navigation
rights. One State later rejects the result, saying arbitration is only a friendly recommendation
like conciliation and need not be followed. The other State argues that arbitration and judicial
settlement are adjudicative methods because they produce binding decisions.
Which statement best applies?
options: The award is non-binding because arbitration is identical to conciliation.
The award is binding because arbitration is an adjudicative method.
The award is non-binding because only mediation creates legal finality.
The award is binding only if both States approve it again afterward.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line by treating arbitration as an adjudicative method resulting in a binding decision. Once the States submitted the dispute to arbitration, the award cannot be dismissed as a mere friendly suggestion.

questions.questionText:
'Z-Chem Ltd.', a large industrial enterprise, manufactures hazardous pesticides. A disgruntled ex-
employee sneaks into the facility at night and sabotages a valve, causing poisonous gas to leak
into the nearby village, causing several deaths. Z-Chem Ltd. argues they are not liable as the leak
was caused by the "Act of a Stranger."
Is Z-Chem Ltd. liable for the damages?
options: No, because the sabotage was an "Act of a Stranger" over whom the company had no control.

Yes, because under Absolute Liability, an enterprise engaged in hazardous activity has no
exceptions.
No, because the company did not "bring" the danger to the village; the stranger did.
Yes, but only if the villagers can prove the company was negligent in their security.
questions.solution: Since 'Z-Chem Ltd.' is an enterprise engaged in an inherently dangerous/hazardous activity, the doctrine of Absolute Liability (M.C. Mehta case) applies.

questions.questionText:
The Bansal family runs a popular family restaurant in Indore under the name “Bansal Da Dhaba.” It is managed as a
        Family business. The eldest member decides the menu and finances, while younger members handle billing and
        delivery tie-ups.
        For the last two years, the family has been splitting the restaurant’s earnings in fixed proportions. They also created
        an internal Google Sheet titled “Partner Profit Split” and sometimes introduce family members to suppliers as
        “partners,” to negotiate better credit. However, there is no separate partnership deed or contract among them
        stating that they are partners, and they continue to describe the restaurant as a “family business.” According to the
        passage, which statement is the most accurate?
options:
They are partners because they call each other partners and maintain a “partner profit split” record to share
            earnings.

They are not partners as such, because partnership arises from contract, not status, and HUF members running
            a family business are excluded.

They are partners because they share profits in fixed proportions and one member manages the business on
            behalf of all.

They are not partners because a partnership can exist only if the business is registered under a “company name”
            with authorities.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: They are not partners as such, because partnership arises from contract, not status, and HUF members running a family business are excluded. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
State A permits a copper smelting company to operate near its border with State B. For
several months, toxic fumes drift into State B, damaging crops, forests, and livestock in nearby
villages. State A argues that it has exclusive control over industries within its own territory
and that State B cannot question its domestic environmental policy. State B produces scientific
reports showing serious injury caused by the fumes.
Which conclusion best reflects the applicable international environmental rule?
options:
State A succeeds because territorial control allows unrestricted industrial activity within
its borders.

State A succeeds because foreign environmental harm is irrelevant if industry remains
domestic.

State B succeeds because serious injury by fumes cannot be permitted from State A’s
territory.

State B succeeds because any minor cross-border discomfort automatically creates strict
responsibility.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference idea that no State may use or permit its territory to cause serious injury to another State by fumes. Since State B proves serious injury through scientific reports, the rule applies against State A’s unrestricted sovereignty claim.

questions.questionText:
State M and State N dispute fishing rights in an offshore zone. State M says the dispute must
go only to judicial settlement before an international court, and all negotiations are legally
useless. State N says the Charter requires peaceful settlement but does not force parties to
adopt one single method; parties may choose negotiation, mediation, arbitration, or other
peaceful processes. State M refuses any non-judicial path.
Which statement is most accurate?
options: State N is correct because no single fixed method is compulsory.
State M is correct because all disputes must go only to courts.
State M is correct because negotiation has no value in international law.
State N is correct because parties cannot choose between peaceful methods.
questions.solution: This option directly follows the reference line because the Charter requires peaceful settlement but does not compel one fixed method. State N may therefore propose negotiation, mediation, arbitration, or another peaceful method instead of accepting only judicial settlement.

questions.questionText:
Shalini’s partner never hits her, but he constantly humiliates her in front of relatives, monitors her
phone, and threatens to throw her out at night if she speaks to her parents. He also forces her to
sleep in the kitchen and denies her access to the bedroom, saying she is “not worthy.” When she
seeks relief, the respondent argues that without visible physical injuries the law cannot intervene.
Shalini argues that the harm is about dignity, residence, and security in the household.
What is the most defensible view?
options:
Relief denied because without bruises there is no legally cognisable harm, so dignity and
residence concerns are irrelevant.

Relief granted because any marital dispute is a rights issue, and courts must intervene to
protect feelings always at once.

Relief granted because the framework treats domestic violence as rights-based, linked with
dignity, bodily integrity, residence, and security at home.

Relief denied because only divorce courts can address residence and money issues, and criminal
courts handle assaults alone.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “rights-based” and the exact cluster “dignity, bodily integrity, residence, and security,” mirroring the reference line. Shalini’s facts target dignity and household security, fitting that rights-based framing.

questions.questionText:
Parliament enacts the “Island Public Health and Local Markets Regulation Act” for an island
territory that is part of India but is not included in any State. The Act regulates local
hospitals, small markets, and sanitation boards in that territory. Traders challenge the Act,
arguing that public health and markets are matters ordinarily connected with the State List,
and that Parliament should not interfere with local democratic choices. The Union defends the
law by saying that the territory is not part of any State. Is the challenge likely to succeed?
options:
Yes, because Parliament cannot legislate on State List matters merely by citing territorial
convenience.

Yes, because local democratic concerns reduce Parliament’s competence over internal
market regulation.
No, because Parliament may legislate for such territory even on matters in the State List.

No, because Parliament’s welfare purpose can validate any law affecting local
administration.
questions.solution: the territory is described as part of India but not included in any State. The passage states that Parliament can legislate for such a territory even on State List matters.

questions.questionText:
Under the Right to Information Act, 2005, the appointment of the Chief Information
        Commissioner and Information Commissioners is made by the President based on the
        recommendation of a committee. Which of the following correctly constitutes this committee?
options:
The Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Speaker of Lok Sabha, and the Minister of Law and
        Justice.

A sitting Supreme Court Judge (Chairperson), the Cabinet Secretary, and the Leader of
        Opposition in Lok Sabha.

The Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Chief Justice of India, and the Leader of Opposition in
        Lok Sabha.

The Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and a Union
        Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.

questions.questionText:
Ramesh filed a suit against Suresh claiming ownership of a plot of land. The competent civil court,
after hearing both parties and examining evidence, dismissed Ramesh's claim and held that
Suresh is the rightful owner. The judgment became final. Two years later, Ramesh files another
suit against Suresh claiming the same plot on the same grounds. What will be the outcome?
options: The second suit is entertained because Ramesh has legal rights
The second suit is allowed if Ramesh pays higher court fees
The second suit is barred by the principle of res judicata
The second suit is heard only if Suresh gives prior consent
questions.solution: , as all conditions for res judicata are satisfied: identical parties (Ramesh and Suresh), same issue (ownership of the same plot), final judgment by competent court, making the second suit barred.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): A guardian of the person is responsible for the minor’s custody, support, health, and
education, and cannot remove the minor from jurisdiction without permission.
Reason (R): Sections 24 to 26 deal with the guardian of the person, who is responsible for custody,
support, health, education, and cannot remove the minor from jurisdiction without permission.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion correctly states the scope of responsibilities of a guardian of the person and includes the restriction on removing the minor from jurisdiction without permission. The reason is also true because it restates the same statutory principle and directly explains why the assertion holds.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): High Courts in India are able to function independently and impartially as
constitutional courts, even when faced with political or administrative pressures, because judges
are institutionally insulated from external influence.
Reason (R): Constitutional safeguards such as secure tenure, protected service conditions, and
financial independence ensure the autonomy and impartiality of High Courts, reinforcing their
vital role in India’s constitutional framework.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion states that High Courts can function independently and impartially because judges are insulated from external influence. The reason directly identifies how this insulation is created: through “secure tenure, protected service conditions, and financial independence,” which “ensure the autonomy and impartiality of High Courts.” ” The reason therefore both restates and explains the institutional basis for the independence claimed in the assertion, exactly in line with the reference li

questions.questionText:
A nurse employed by a private hospital administers the wrong dosage of medication due to
personal negligence, severely injuring a patient. The patient sues the hospital and is awarded
%6 lakhs. The hospital pays 74 lakhs to the patient and immediately files a claim for indemnity
against the nurse for the remaining 22 lakhs still owed to the patient. Can the hospital's
indemnity claim succeed at this stage?
options: No, because indemnity can only be claimed after the plaintiff has been fully compensated.

Yes, because the hospital is only secondarily liable and the nurse's personal negligence
makes her primarily responsible

Yes, because contractual employment relationships allow indemnity claims at any stage of
proceedings

No, because nurses cannot be held liable for clinical errors made during the course of
employment
questions.solution: The passage explicitly requires full plaintiff compensation before either contribution or indemnity can be invoked. Since %2 lakhs remains unpaid to the patient, the hospital's claim is premature.

questions.questionText: Two friends, T and R went in a shop. The skylight of the shop was broken and not repaired. A portion of the glass fell and hit T, causing him injuries on the head. R, when saw the glass falling on T, clutched his arm to pull him aside, in the process, R injured his hand, and amplified the injury in his already fractured wrist. Decide whether R can claim compensation for negligence?
options: R cannot claim compensation for negligence because he knew the risk and danger of helping T.
R can claim compensation for negligence only for the actions that were consequent to the negligence of the shop.
R cannot claim compensation because the glass fell on T.
R can claim compensation because he also sustained severe injury.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: R can claim compensation for negligence only for the actions that were consequent to the negligence of the shop. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A municipal authority launches a compulsory “citizen transparency portal” requiring residents
to publicly disclose medical history, marital status, sexual orientation, biometric details, and
family relationships. The authority claims public disclosure helps efficient governance and
removes secrecy. A resident challenges the scheme, arguing that privacy includes decisional
autonomy, bodily integrity, family, marriage, sexual orientation, and data protection. The
authority replies that privacy is not expressly written in Article 21 and therefore cannot be
enforced.
Which conclusion is most accurate?
options:
Resident fails because privacy is not expressly mentioned and therefore cannot be
fundamental.

Resident fails because data disclosure for governance always defeats personal autonomy
claims.
Resident succeeds only if the information is collected by police rather than municipality.

Resident succeeds because privacy includes autonomy, bodily integrity, family, sexuality,
and data protection.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “autonomy,” “bodily integrity,” “family,” ” «& “sexual orientation,” and “data protection,” matching the reference line. A public portal forcing disclosure of such intimate information strongly engages the privacy right under Article 21.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The State’s objection in Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab was accepted because
the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 was an ex post facto law and therefore could not apply to
the accused.
Reason (R): Article 20(1) prohibits the retrospective application of a later law when that law
is beneficial to the accused and serves a reformative purpose.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
A is false and R is false.
questions.solution: The assertion is false because the State’s objection was rejected by the Apex Court. The reason is also false because the passage provides that a beneficial ex post facto law does not fall under the prohibition of Article 20(1).

questions.questionText:
Dev ties his rival to a chair in an abandoned shed and leaves him there for thirty minutes
intending to frighten him, but returns and releases him safely. Later, in another incident, Dev
locks the same rival in an airtight metal container in summer heat, knowing there is no air
supply and rescue is impossible, causing death. In deciding whether the second act is murder
rather than lesser culpable homicide, what distinction should the court emphasise?
options:
Whether the victim was Dev’s rival, because personal rivalry alone decides murder
classification.

Whether Dev later regretted the act, because remorse converts murder into lesser
homicide.

Whether the act occurred indoors, because closed places automatically create murder
liability.
Whether intention, knowledge, and certainty of death show the graver offence of murder.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “intention, knowledge, and degree of certainty of death,” matching the reference line. Locking a person in an airtight container with no possible air supply strongly supports the graver classification because death is highly certain.

questions.questionText:
A State Government issues an executive order that provides special educational grants only to
students who belong to a specific religious denomination, citing Article 30. A petitioner challenges
this, claiming it violates the secular nature of the Republic. Which set of Articles mentioned in the
passage would the petitioner most likely rely upon to prove discrimination?
options: Articles 51-A and 44
Articles 14, 15, and 16
Articles 25 and 26
Articles 29 and 30
questions.solution: The passage states that Articles 14, 15, and 16 prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion and ensure equality before the law and equal opportunity. While 29 and 30 protect minorities, 14-16 are the primary tools against state-sponsored discrimination.

questions.questionText:
Farhan agrees to build a website for Sana by 1 March for %2,00,000. He misses the deadline and
stops responding for three weeks, and Sana emails that she will claim losses for the delay. In April,
Farhan returns and offers a new “replacement agreement” with a later delivery date and a reduced
price, stating it “replaces the old deal entirely.” Sana signs to get the site urgently, but later sues
for damages for the earlier delay.
How should the April document be treated?
options:
It is novation because any later replacement agreement automatically wipes out prior breach,
ending all damages claims.

It is not novation, yet breach rights vanish whenever parties sign new terms, even after default,
without express waiver.

It is novation only if the court approves, so without filing suit the new contract cannot
substitute the old one.

Novation must occur before breach, so a post-breach rewrite cannot substitute the old contract
unless parties settle expressly in writing.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference idea that novation “must occur before breach,” applying it to a post-breach “replacement agreement.” After breach, the old contract cannot be said to be substituted by novation in the strict sense; at best, there must be an express settlement/waiver of accrued claims.

questions.questionText:
In a legal dispute over the ownership of a commercial property, Meena presented an unregistered power of
attorney (POA) from Raj, claiming that it granted her the authority to sell the property on his behalf. The POA
was comprehensive and detailed Raj's intent to delegate his selling rights to Meena. However, Raj's legal team
argued that the POA was not valid for the purpose of transferring property rights. They contended that the
Registration Act, 1908, and the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, required certain formalities for such transactions,
which were not met. Meena's legal team countered that the POA, though unregistered, represented Raj's clear
intention and should be considered valid. What argument should be given the most weight in deciding the validity
of the POA for the purpose of transferring property rights?
options: The POA was comprehensive and detailed Raj's intent.
The POA was unregistered and thus does not fulfill the statutory requirements.
The POA, representing Raj's intention, should be sufficient for legal purposes.
The POA was not required to be registered as it was for commercial property.

questions.questionText:
Harsh guarantees payment to Saurabh, a tea-dealer, to the amount of Rs. 10,000, for any tea he may
from time to time supply to Neelam. One day, Saurabh supplies Neelam with tea to the value of Rs.
20,000. Neelam fails to pay. Is Harsh liable to pay Saurabh any amount in this situation?
options: No, as Harsh’s guarantee was only one-time.
No, as Harsh is not responsible for Neelam’s failure to pay.
Yes, Harsh is liable to pay Saurabh an amount to the extent of Rs 10,000.
Yes, Harsh being the surety has to pay Saurabh any loss he suffers due to failure on Neelam’s part.
questions.solution: C is the correct answer as Harsh has guaranteed payment to Saurabh up to a fixed amount of Rs. 10,000 for any tea that Saurabh may supply to Neelam from time to time.

questions.questionText:
A dam owned by State R suddenly releases contaminated water into a river flowing toward
State S. Instead of informing State S, State R waits several days, fearing diplomatic
embarrassment. State S suffers preventable damage to fisheries because emergency
precautions were not taken. State R argues each State handles environmental incidents
independently within its territory. State S argues that States must act collectively, including
through information exchange, prior notification, consultation, and emergency notification.
Which conclusion is strongest?
options:
State S succeeds because cooperation requires collective action in conserving and restoring
the environment.

State R succeeds because territorial sovereignty excludes duties of consultation and
emergency notification.

State S succeeds because environmental cooperation applies only after formal
compensation proceedings begin.

State R succeeds because embarrassment is sufficient reason to delay transboundary
environmental information.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: This option directly uses “act collectively” and “conserving and restoring the environment,” matching the reference line. State R’s silence prevented coordinated mitigation and undermined the cooperative approach required in transboundary environmental matters.

questions.questionText:
A person signed a surety agreement believing, due to his own misreading, that he was signing
a guarantee for Rs. 10,000 when the document stated Rs. 1,00,000. No one misled him. He
later sought to avoid the contract claiming unilateral mistake.
options:
The contract is voidable at the option of the disadvantaged party under Section 22 as
unilateral mistake vitiates consent when it relates to the amount — a fundamental term.

The contract is void under Section 20 as the party was clearly mistaken about the essential
terms of the agreement.

The contract is valid as unilateral mistake does not ordinarily affect the validity of the
contract; no other party caused or contributed to the mistake.

The contract is void because any mistake relating to the monetary value of an obligation,
however caused, is a mistake of fact essential to the agreement under Section 20.
questions.solution: A self-induced misreading by one party, without any contribution from the other, is a classic unilateral mistake governed by Section 22, which denies relief. The contract binds both parties on its actual terms.

questions.questionText:
The CEO of a private software firm records a board meeting without informing the other
directors and shares the audio with a competitor to “get back” at the board for a low bonus. He
argues he is not liable under the Official Secrets Act. Is his argument valid and consistent
with the High Court's reasoning?
options:
No, because sharing confidential corporate information with a competitor is an act of
“spying” that harms the economic interests of the country.

No, because any unauthorized recording of a professional conversation is automatically
classified as a threat to national sovereignty.

Yes, because a private software firm’s office does not fall within the definition of a
“prohibited place” as it is not a strategic or defense-sensitive location.

Yes, because the Official Secrets Act only applies to junior-level employees and does not
cover senior executives like a CEO.
questions.solution: Option C is correct because the Court’s primary reason for quashing the OSA charges was that the MMCL office was not a “prohibited place”. A private software office, like the Metro office, lacks the “strategic, defence, or security-sensitive” nature required by Section 2(8).

questions.questionText:
Lara, an artist, discovers that a local gallery is displaying a sculpture she claims was stolen from her
studio. Lara asserts she has the original purchase receipts and creation documentation proving her
ownership. The gallery, however, claims they purchased the sculpture legally from a third party, unaware
of its history. Lara sues to reclaim her sculpture, arguing that her documentation proves her lawful
possession and the gallery's lack of legal title. Should the court grant the injunction to return the
sculpture to Lara if she has able to prove her lawful ownership?
options: No, the gallery purchased the sculpture from a third party.
Yes, Lara provides original purchase receipts and creation documentation for the sculpture.
No, the gallery acted in good faith and checked the third party's credibility.
No, the gallery has already sold the sculpture to another buyer.

questions.questionText:
The making of the Indian Constitution was a long and detailed process involving debates,
committee discussions, drafting stages, and deliberations on governance, rights, and federal
structure. The Constituent Assembly held numerous sessions before finally adopting the
Constitution of India.
How much time did the Constituent Assembly take to complete the framing of the Constitution
of India?
options: 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days
2 years, 9 months, and 12 days
8 years, 2 months, and 15 days
1 year, 11 months, and 26 days
questions.solution: The Constituent Assembly took exactly 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days to complete the framing of the Constitution of India. The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946, and the Constitution was finally adopted on 26 November 1949.

questions.questionText:
During a festival, Farid stands outside a temple office room where donation cash is counted.
Through a half-open window, he pushes his hand inside to knock papers off the table and
frighten the clerk, shouting insults. He does not enter the room fully. Farid claims there is no
“house trespass” because he never stepped inside, and the temple is a public place. The clerk
alleges protected intrusion.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
No offence because full body entry is required and touching a window frame cannot satisfy
entry element in law ever.

Even introducing any part of the body such as a hand through a window may amount to
house trespass here.

House trespass because standing near a window equals entry even without introducing
any part of the body into premises inside.

Only criminal trespass because the structure is public worship so house trespass applies
only to private dwellings with residents always.
questions.solution: The option directly reproduces the reference words “hand through a window” and “may amount to house trespass,” matching the precise factual mechanism used. Since the act involves intrusion into a protected structure space, the “partial body” entry is enough to meet the entry/remaining element.

questions.questionText:
Asha owns a catering business and offers to supply meals for Kabir’s office seminar for
80,000. Kabir replies, “I accept, provided you also include flower decoration and photography
within the same price.” Asha does not agree to these added services. Kabir later claims that a
contract was formed because he responded to the offer and promised payment. Asha argues
that there was no unequivocal acceptance of her original offer, and the added conditions
changed the proposal.
Which statement best applies?
options: A contract formed because Kabir mentioned payment and responded to Asha’s offer.
No contract formed because acceptance was conditional, not unequivocal and exact.
A contract formed because added services never affect contractual acceptance.
No contract formed only because catering services lack lawful consideration.
questions.solution: This option directly applies the requirement of “unequivocal acceptance.” Kabir’s reply imposed additional conditions and changed the scope of Asha’s offer, so it cannot be treated as a clear acceptance of the original proposal.

questions.questionText: Following intense close-quarters combat, an enemy unit exhausts its ammunition and surrenders to a State military force. The soldiers are disarmed, restrained, and transported to a field detention facility. The commanding officer orders physical coercion and restricted food rations for all detainees. He justifies the orders on two grounds: first, that the detainees possess time-sensitive operational intelligence; and second, that because they were active combatants until moments before capture, full hors de combat protections have not yet been triggered. Which option most appropriately follows from the passage?
options: The treatment may be permissible because detainees who were active combatants retain combatant status for the period immediately following capture, and measures proportionate to the urgency of obtaining operational intelligence may be justified by military necessity.

The treatment is unlawful because persons who are hors de combat by reason of surrender are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of their prior combatant status, the intelligence value they may possess, or any military necessity invoked by the captor.

The treatment may be lawful to the extent that restricting food rations in a field detention facility constitutes a logistical measure rather than prohibited inhumane treatment, even if physical coercion would separately violate IHL.

The treatment is unlawful, though primarily because the physical coercion violates hors de combat protections; the restriction of rations may warrant separate evaluation and could potentially be justifiable on logistical rather than punitive grounds.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The treatment is unlawful because persons who are hors de combat by reason of surrender are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of their prior combatant status, the intelligence value they may possess…. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Raghav lives in a remote village where "AquaPure" is the only company supplying Filtered drinking water. No other
        brand is available within 50 kilometers. AquaPure charges ₹80 for a 20-liter water can, while the same quantity
        costs ₹30-40 in nearby towns where multiple brands compete. Raghav complains to a consumer forum arguing that
        his Right to Choose is being violated because he has no alternatives and is being charged unfairly. AquaPure defends
        itself by stating that the Right to Choose only means access to variety, and since they are the only supplier, the right
        does not apply. Based on the passage, is Raghav's complaint regarding Right to Choose valid?
options:
No, because the Right to Choose means access to variety of goods at competitive prices, and since Raghav has
             no variety available, this right cannot be invoked in his situation.


1

Yes, because the Right to Choose includes, in monopoly situations, assurance of satisfactory quality and fair
            pricing, including access to basic goods like drinking water.

No, because the passage states that the Right to Choose applies "wherever possible," implying that in remote
            areas without alternatives, consumers cannot claim this right.

Yes, because AquaPure is violating the Right to Seek Redressal by refusing to lower its prices despite customer
            complaints.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because the Right to Choose includes, in monopoly situations, assurance of satisfactory quality and fair pricing, including access to basic goods like drinking water. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Chetan wants to steal a car. He tells his friend Dilip about his plan. Dilip agrees to the plan
and says he will act as a lookout. A week later, Chetan successfully steals the car, but Dilip
reached late at the scene and by then the theft was committed so Dilip didn’t do anything and
went back to Chetan’s house. Did Dilip abet the crime?
options:
Yes, because his agreement alone is sufficient for the offence of criminal conspiracy and to
prove his criminal intent, which makes him an abettor.

Yes, even though he was not present during the crime, he later went to Chetan’s house,
this shows his malicious intent.
No, because he was not physically present at the scene of the crime.

No, because although he agreed to the conspiracy, he did not commit any act or illegal
omission in pursuance of the conspiracy.
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states: “Mere agreement is not enough unless followed by some act.” Dilip agreed, but no act or illegal omission took place in pursuance of the conspiracy. Why (a) is incorrect: This directly contradicts the line in the passage about mere agreement being insufficient.

questions.questionText: A State government issues an executive order prohibiting a peaceful assembly organised by a minority religious group. The government's stated justification is threefold: the group's publicly expressed theological positions are deeply offensive to the convictions of the majority community; multiple surveys show that over 80% of citizens support the prohibition; and in a functioning democracy, elected officials are obligated to reflect the will of the majority. No credible evidence of threatened violence, specific public disorder, or any concrete harm attributable to the assembly has been placed on record. A petition challenging the prohibition is filed. Which option most appropriately applies the passage?
options: The prohibition may be constitutionally defensible because democratic systems are fundamentally premised on majority preferences, and elected officials who respond to overwhelming public sentiment in regulating public assemblies are exercising their democratic mandate within permissible bounds.

The prohibition raises constitutional concerns because constitutional guarantees protecting individual and minority rights exist precisely to safeguard them from excessive majoritarian exercises of governmental power, and public disapproval of beliefs alone cannot justify restricting a peaceful assembly.

The prohibition is justified because the responsibility of elected governments to maintain social cohesion and respond to the deeply held sensitivities of the majority community necessarily includes authority to restrict assemblies that cause widespread public offence, even in the absence of immediate disorder.

The prohibition is problematic because while majoritarian preferences legitimately guide governance in most areas, constitutional rights cannot be overridden solely by popular disapproval particularly when no demonstrable public order threat has been established though the outcome might differ where a genuine and proximate security risk is shown.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The prohibition raises constitutional concerns because constitutional guarantees protecting individual and minority rights exist precisely to safeguard them from excessive majoritarian exercises of…. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A maritime dispute arises between two States after fishing boats are detained near a
contested zone. One State proposes enquiry by a fact-finding panel, followed by mediation if
facts remain disputed. The other State says only military escort or economic blockade can
resolve the matter quickly, and peaceful procedures have no recognised legal basis. The first
State relies on the Charter’s list of peaceful methods, including enquiry, mediation,
conciliation, arbitration and judicial settlement.
Which option best reflects the correct legal position?
options: Military escort is preferred because peaceful methods lack legal recognition.
Economic blockade is required because fact-finding is not a settlement method.
Enquiry and mediation are recognised peaceful methods under Article 33.
Judicial settlement alone is recognised, while other peaceful processes are excluded.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line by identifying enquiry and mediation as recognised peaceful methods under Article 33. The first State’s proposal therefore fits the Charter-based approach to pacific dispute settlement.

questions.questionText:
Parliament enacts the National Digital Security Act, 2027 to regulate online platforms. The Act
requires all social media companies to store user data on servers located within India, comply with
government cybersecurity standards, and submit periodic security audits. Several technology
companies challenge the law, arguing that the real objective of Parliament is to increase
governmental control over private digital communications rather than cybersecurity. They contend
that the law is therefore a colourable exercise of legislative power.
Assume that Parliament unquestionably possesses constitutional authority to legislate on digital
communications and cybersecurity.
Which of the following is the most appropriate constitutional conclusion?
options: The Act is colourable legislation because its actual objective differs from its stated objective.

The Act is colourable legislation because courts may invalidate any law enacted with an
ulterior motive.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation is unlikely to apply because Parliament possesses
legislative competence.

The Act is automatically unconstitutional because governmental control over communications
violates the doctrine.
questions.solution: The doctrine applies when a legislature lacks authority and attempts to achieve indirectly what it cannot do directly. Here, Parliament unquestionably has competence over the subject matter.

questions.questionText:
Dev owned a small chemical-polishing unit in an industrial lane and kept barrels of a volatile
solvent inside a locked storage room. During routine operations, fumes from one barrel leaked
inside the same storage room and injured a technician who had entered the room to inspect
the barrel. The fumes did not pass into any neighbouring premises, public road, or area
outside Dev’s control. A nearby shopkeeper, who heard about the leak but suffered no physical
injury or property damage, also sought compensation under the rule of Strict Liability.
Consider the following statements:
I. The solvent may be treated as a dangerous thing if it is likely to cause harm if it escapes.
II. Strict Liability may be imposed even when the dangerous thing remains within the
defendant’s land and control.
III. The use may be non-natural if it is special, extraordinary, or not ordinary in the usual
course of using land.
IV. A plaintiff may succeed under Strict Liability even without suffering damage from the
escape of the dangerous thing.
Which of the following statements are false?
options: I and III only
II and IV only
I, Il and IV only
II, II and IV only
questions.solution: Statement II is false because the passage requires the dangerous thing to escape from the land or control of the defendant to a place outside such control. Statement IV is false because the plaintiff must have suffered damage because of the escape of the dangerous thing.

questions.questionText:
A news channel plays a 7-second song clip during its coverage of a political rally.
         The rally itself is not connected to the song, and the clip is included mainly for
         dramatic effect.
Applying the reasoning in the passage, how is a court most likely to treat this?
options: It qualifies as fair dealing since the duration is very short.

It is infringement since the use is unrelated to reporting the event and adds no
       transformative purpose.
It qualifies as de minimis because the clip is trivial in length.
It is permissible since the channel is engaged in news reporting.

questions.questionText:
