A pedestrian is injured when a delivery van suddenly stops without warning and, seconds
later, a cyclist independently swerves onto the pavement to avoid a pothole. The van driver
and cyclist had no prior communication, no shared plan, and no relationship with each other.
Their separate acts together worsened the pedestrian’s injury. The pedestrian argues they
should be treated as joint tortfeasors merely because the final injury was one. Both defendants
say their liability, if any, arises separately.
Which answer best applies?
options: They are joint tortfeasors because the pedestrian ultimately suffered one combined injury.
They are joint tortfeasors because both acts occurred near the same location.
They are independent tortfeasors because separate acts may still cause one injury.

They are independent tortfeasors because they acted separately without coordination.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reasoning given in the passage because the van driver and cyclist acted separately and without coordination. Even if their acts contributed to one injury, their liability would arise independently rather than as joint tortfeasors.

questions.questionText:
A new fintech company, "QuickLoan," develops a KYC process that uses an
       advanced AI to analyze a user's facial muscle movements to detect liveness. This
       method becomes the sole way to get a loan through their app. A person with facial
       paralysis due to a medical condition is repeatedly rejected by the AI. The
       company argues that its system is not a "social barrier" but a necessary security
       measure to prevent fraud. Based on the passage, why is the company's argument
       flawed?
options:
Because the RBI’s rules explicitly prohibit the use of AI in KYC verification,
  making the company's entire process illegal from the outset.

Because under the ‘social-barrier’ model, a system that fails to account for physical
  impairments and prevents a person with a disability from accessing a service is
  precisely the kind of obstacle the law seeks to remove.

Because the company failed to offer the alternative of an in-person verification,
  which is the only legally acceptable accommodation for PwDs.

Because any digital KYC process that does not include an eye-blinking test is
  automatically considered non-compliant with universal design principles.

questions.questionText:
Priya is selling her bakery business to Arjun. During negotiations, Priya casually mentioned
over coffee, three months before the contract was signed: “The oven equipment is fairly new
and works without any issues.’ When the formal written contract was eventually drafted and
signed, it made no mention of the condition of the equipment whatsoever. Within weeks of
taking over, Arjun discovered the oven had a chronic heating fault that required expensive
repair. Arjun seeks to rely on Priya's earlier statement as a contractual term. Which of the
following most accurately states the legal position?
options:
The statement is definitely a contractual term because it was specific, factual, and directly
related to the subject matter of the contract.

The timing of the statement and its omission from the written contract are factors that
weigh against treating it as a contractual term.

Since the statement was made before the contract, it automatically qualifies as a pre-
contractual representation giving rise to full contractual liability.

Arjun can claim breach of contract because any statement made by a seller about the
subject matter of sale is always treated as a guarantee.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The timing of the statement and its omission from the written contract are factors that weigh against treating it as a contractual term. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A competent adult suffering from a terminal illness executed a written Advance Medical
Directive specifying that she did not wish to be placed on mechanical ventilation in the event
she lost capacity. A year later, she was hospitalised, lost the ability to communicate, and
doctors proposed ventilator support. The hospital sought legal clarity on whether the directive
was binding and whether withholding treatment in compliance with it would expose doctors to
criminal liability.
options:
Advance Medical Directives are merely advisory; doctors are not bound by them and must
administer all possible treatments in the patient's clinical interest.

A directive refusing ventilator support is invalid because passive euthanasia always
requires fresh judicial approval at the time of withdrawal of treatment.

A validly executed Advance Medical Directive is legally binding; doctors who act in
compliance with it and follow prescribed safeguards are protected from criminal liability.

Advance Medical Directives are binding only on family members and not on treating
doctors, who remain independently bound by their professional duty to preserve life.
questions.solution: A properly executed Advance Medical Directive is legally binding. Doctors who honour it in accordance with the procedural safeguards laid down in Common Cause act within the law and are protected from criminal liability for withholding life-sustaining treatment.

questions.questionText:
A State Law Commission proposes a draft “Family Relations Code” dealing only with property
partition among brothers and sisters. It excludes marriage, divorce, adoption, maintenance,
guardianship, and succession, arguing that a civil code is limited to inheritance disputes.
Several groups object, saying a civil code in personal-law matters must cover a wider set of
family relations, not merely one property issue. The Commission asks which subjects
ordinarily fall within such a civil code.
Which formulation is most accurate?
options:
It covers marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption, inheritance, succession, and
guardianship.

It covers only inheritance and succession, because marriage and divorce remain purely
religious affairs.

It covers only criminal punishment for family disputes, not civil personal-law
relationships.

It covers only property partition, because adoption and guardianship are outside personal
law.
questions.solution: This option directly reproduces the reference line by including marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption, inheritance, succession, and guardianship. The Commission’s draft is too narrow if it treats a civil code as limited only to property partition or inheritance disputes.

questions.questionText:
A suit is filed between siblings over ownership of a disputed farmhouse. While the case is pending,
one sibling sells the farmhouse to an outside buyer who claims he paid market value and acted
honestly. Later, the court decides the seller had no right to the farmhouse. The buyer argues his
purchase should stand because he was not a party to the suit and did not cause the dispute. Which
statement is most accurate?
options:
The buyer is protected because transfers during disputes are free and clear if the buyer pays
market value in good faith.

The buyer is protected because only parties to the lawsuit are bound, and outsiders are never
affected by the judgment.

The buyer is not protected because transfers during litigation are subject to the outcome of the
suit.

The buyer is not protected only if the seller expressly warned him about the lawsuit, otherwise
the transfer remains valid.
questions.solution: The reference line states that transfers during litigation are “subject to the outcome of the suit.” Since the court later held the seller had no right, the buyer’s purchase cannot rise above the seller’s defeated claim and is bound by the judgment’s outcome.

questions.questionText:
Fifteen-year-old Arjun punches a classmate during a school fight, causing a broken nose. The
injured student sues Arjun in tort for assault. Arjun argues he is a minor, so he cannot be sued at
all. The plaintiff responds that age does not create blanket immunity in tort for physical attacks.
Which option best states the correct position?
options:
Arjun cannot be sued because minors are always immune from tort claims, including assault
and battery.
Arjun can be sued because minors can be sued for torts such as assault, defamation, fraud, etc.

Arjun cannot be sued unless the plaintiff proves Arjun was above 16 at the time of the
incident.

Arjun can be sued only if the plaintiff first sues the school, because minors must be sued
through institutions.
questions.solution: The reference line directly states that minors can be sued for torts such as assault. Since the claim is for a physical attack, Arjun’s minority does not automatically protect him from being sued for assault.

questions.questionText:
In a cheating case punishable up to seven years, the IO decides not to arrest the accused and
instead continues investigation. The IO neither forwards the non-arrest decision to the
Magistrate within two weeks nor seeks any extension from the Superintendent of Police. After
one month, the complainant alleges the IO is shielding the accused and demands immediate
arrest for “inaction.” The accused argues that the non-arrest decision is permissible but must
be forwarded within the prescribed time, with extension only for recorded reasons.
What is the strongest legal view?
options:
IO must forward non-arrest decision to Magistrate within two weeks, extendable by SP for
recorded reasons.

IO can keep non-arrest decision secret until chargesheet because forwarding to Magistrate
is optional and only needed after arrest.

IO must always arrest if no forwarding done, because delay automatically converts non-
arrest into illegal favour and mandates custody.

IO cannot avoid arrest in any cognizable case, so forwarding rule is meaningless and arrest
must happen immediately always.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “forwarded... within two weeks” and “extendable...

questions.questionText:
Deepak, an experienced construction worker, is employed by BuildRight Ltd. to work on a high-rise
construction project. Due to a tight project deadline, the company pressures Deepak to work overtime on
a scaffold system known to have safety issues, despite Deepak's reservations. The company assures him
that all safety measures are in place and requires him to sign a waiver acknowledging the risk of potential
falls and injuries. During his overtime shift, the scaffold collapses due to the unaddressed safety issues,
and Deepak is seriously injured. Deepak decides to sue BuildRight Ltd. for negligence and unsafe work
conditions. Will he succeed?
options:
No, because working on scaffolds inherently involves risk, which Deepak accepted as part of his
employment contract.

No, because Deepak signed a waiver accepting all risks associated with his construction duties, including
potential equipment failure.

Yes, because forcing Deepak to work under known unsafe conditions violates public policy and renders the
waiver he signed irrelevant.

Yes, because the company failed to properly inspect and maintain the scaffold, which is an independent
violation of workplace safety regulations.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Alok, a wealthy businessman, executes a will stating: "I bequeath my
        Mumbai farmhouse to my dear friend, Brijesh, for his lifetime. After Brijesh's
        death, the farmhouse shall be enjoyed by his eldest son for his lifetime, and
        thereafter, the absolute ownership shall pass to Brijesh's eldest grandson." At the
        time of the will, Brijesh has one son, Chetan, but no grandson. The transfer is
        challenged after Alok's death. What is the legal validity of this transfer?
options:
The entire transfer is valid because it creates a prior life interest for Brijesh and
      Chetan, who are living, before transferring to the unborn grandson.

The transfer to Brijesh and Chetan is valid, but the transfer to the unborn
      grandson is void because it attempts to create a successive life interest for a person
      not in existence.

The transfer to the unborn grandson is void because the law does not permit
      transfers to be made through a will, only through an immediate gift.

The transfer is void because the ultimate beneficiary (the grandson) is not given
      the absolute interest immediately after the first life interest holder (Brijesh).

questions.questionText:
A licensing officer personally drafts a complaint alleging that trader Imran violated storage norms.
The same officer then chairs the hearing, refuses Imran’s request to submit documents, and issues
a one-line refusal: “Licence cancelled for public interest.” Imran challenges the decision as unfair,
saying he was not properly heard, the decision-maker was interested in the outcome, and no
reasons were provided.
Which option best captures the set of safeguards implicated by these defects?
options:
Only speaking order required; hearing and bias rules are optional, so decision stands if brief
reasons are recorded.

Three principles are hearing rule, bias rule, and reasoned decision; all were breached when
same officer judged and no reasons were given.

Only bias matters; absence of hearing and reasons is cured by internal review, so no natural
justice violation exists here.

Only hearing rule applies to criminal trials; administrative permits may be denied silently, and
decision-makers may have interests disclosed later.
questions.solution: This option directly reproduces the reference line’s trio “hearing rule, bias rule, and reasoned decision” and applies it to the facts: no fair chance to present material, the complainant chaired the decision, and the order gave no reasons. Those defects map onto each core principle, making this the best statement.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Administrative tribunals are considered useful because they provide speedy,
expert and inexpensive justice in specialised disputes.
Reason (R): Recent tribunal reforms and proposals for a National Tribunal Commission seek
to address concerns relating to independence and uniformity in tribunal administration.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Both statements are independently supported by the reference line. The assertion deals with the advantages of tribunals, while the reason deals with institutional concerns and reform proposals.

questions.questionText:
Rohan and Anita, an interfaith couple from different states in India, decide to marry under the
Special Marriage Act (SMA), 1954, to avoid the traditional rituals tied to their respective religions. They
submit a notice of intended marriage to the marriage registrar of Delhi, where they both currently reside.
However, due to unforeseen circumstances including work commitments and travel restrictions, they fail
to appear before the registrar within the stipulated 30 days following the notice period to solemnize the
marriage. Instead, they have a simple exchange of vows in a private ceremony attended by friends,
believing it to be a sufficient formality under the SMA. A few months later, when applying for a joint
home loan, they present their private ceremony photographs and an affidavit stating their marriage, but
the bank requests an official marriage certificate issued by the registrar. Is Rohan and Anita's marriage
legally valid under the Special Marriage Act, considering they did not solemnize it in the registrar’s office
within the required time frame?
options:
Yes, because their private ceremony and affidavit are sufficient proof under the SMA since they had initially
filed a notice with the registrar.

No, because under the SMA, the marriage must be solemnized in the presence of a marriage officer and
witnesses within the specified time frame after filing the notice.

Yes, because their interfaith status allows flexibility in how they fulfill the SMA requirements, making any
form of vow exchange legally binding.

No, because the marriage requires traditional rituals for validation, which they skipped, making the marriage
invalid under the SMA.

questions.questionText:
Aarav gives his vintage motorcycle to Bhavesh, a mechanic, for three days so that Bhavesh can
test the engine and identify its defects. Aarav explicitly instructs Bhavesh that once the defect
is identified, Bhavesh must either return the motorcycle to Aarav or deliver it directly to a
third-party specialist, but the transfer to the specialist can only happen if Aarav gives a
separate approval later. Bhavesh subsequently argues that a valid contract of bailment was
never created because Aarav’s instructions left the final disposal of the motorcycle entirely
unsettled and conditional upon a future approval. Is Bhavesh’s argument legally sustainable?
options:
Yes, because a contract of bailment cannot be legally sustained when the final disposal of
the goods depends entirely on a future, unsettled approval.

Yes, because Aarav's conditional instruction to send the motorcycle to a third-party
specialist prevents a definitive, immediate obligation to return the goods to the original
bailor.

No, because the motorcycle was delivered for a specific testing purpose with clear
directions regarding its return or conditional further disposal.

No, because the later approval requirement delayed disposal and gave Bhavesh discretion
to choose the next course after testing.
questions.solution: it accurately applies the definition of bailment provided in the passage. Aarav delivered the motorcycle for a specific purpose, namely engine testing, and gave explicit instructions regarding its eventual return or conditional disposal.

questions.questionText:
A vacancy arises in a High Court. A political leader claims the State Governor can directly appoint
a judge, because the judge will serve within the State. Another person claims the President
appoints but can do so alone without any consultations. A third person says the consultations are
only “symbolic” and have no practical weight due to later judicial interpretation.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
The Governor appoints High Court judges because the High Court primarily deals with State
matters.

The President appoints High Court judges without needing any consultation with
constitutional authorities.

The President appoints High Court judges after consultation, with judicial primacy established
through the collegium system.

High Court judges are appointed by State legislatures through a resolution, and the President
only issues a notification without consultation.
questions.solution: The reference line exactly describes the appointment mechanism Presidential appointment under Article 217, mandatory consultation with specified authorities, and “judicial primacy” through the collegium system. This directly resolves all three competing claims.

questions.questionText:
At midnight, Pawan climbs over a locked gate into Amina’s fenced farm. He does not damage
crops or steal anything. Instead, he shouts insults about Amina’s family and stays for ten
minutes to “humiliate her” before leaving. Pawan argues that since nothing was taken, the
matter is only a civil trespass. Amina claims the entry itself was criminal due to the intention.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Criminal Trespass as he enters into or upon property in the possession of another with
intent to intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor.

Not trespass because, without theft or violence entry onto farmland is harmless and only
invites civil suit for damages alone.

House trespass because farmland is treated as a place for custody of property so any entry
becomes house trespass automatically.

Not trespass because the land was vacant and owner absent; possession requires physical
presence not legal control at night always.
questions.solution: The correct option directly lifts “enter into or upon property in the possession of another” and “intent to intimidate, insult, or annoy,” matching the facts: Pawan entered fenced land and did so to insult/humiliate. Theft is not mandatory; the intent to insult/annoy is an independent trigger for criminal trespass.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Mediation is a peaceful method of dispute settlement in which a neutral third
party actively participates and assists the parties in reaching a settlement.
Reason (R): The Tashkent Agreement between India and Pakistan is cited as an example of
mediation in international dispute settlement.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Assertion (A) is true because mediation involves a neutral third party who actively participates, gives suggestions, and helps parties reach settlement. Reason (R) is also true because the Tashkent Agreement is cited as an example.

questions.questionText:
Aarohi invents a compact water-purification cartridge and files for legal protection. A rival
company begins manufacturing identical cartridges and selling them online without permission.
Aarohi demands they stop, arguing her protection allows her to control who can make and sell the
product. The rival replies that “ideas are free” and that unless Aarohi proves actual losses, they
can continue selling.
Which statement best reflects Aarohi’s legal position?
options:
Aarohi’s protection grants exclusive rights, preventing unauthorised making, use, sale, or
distribution of her invention.

Aarohi’s protection only gives moral recognition, so competitors may freely sell unless a
criminal case is filed.

Aarohi’s protection blocks only physical copying, but online sales and imports are outside its
legal scope.

Aarohi’s protection operates only after a court awards damages, so she cannot stop sales until
then.
questions.solution: The reference line directly states that protection grants “exclusive rights” and prevents “unauthorised making, use, sale, or distribution.” Since the rival is manufacturing and selling identical cartridges without permission, Aarohi’s claim aligns precisely with the exclusive-control idea embedded in the reference line. The need to show losses may affect damages, but does not negate exclusivity against unauthorised commercial exploitation.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following two situations involving individuals formally accused of crimes and in
active police custody:
Situation I: Anita states, "I poisoned my husband's tea, and the remaining poison is kept on
the top kitchen shelf." The police recover the poison from the shelf based on this.
Situation II: Vikram states, "I murdered my partner." Later that day, the police, using their
own independent investigative tracking, find the murder weapon in Vikram's car.
Based strictly on the passage, which of the following conclusions is legally sound?
options:
Both Anita's full confession and Vikram's statement are admissible because physical
evidence was ultimately found in both cases.

Only Anita's statement regarding the location of the poison is admissible, while Vikram's
statement is completely inadmissible.

Anita's entire statement is admissible under the doctrine of confirmation by subsequent
events, but Vikram's statement is not.

Neither statement is admissible because confessions made without a Magistrate present
are absolutely barred by evidence law.
questions.solution: Anita's statement directly caused a discovery (allowing partial admission), whereas Vikram's discovery was independent, making his confession completely barred.

questions.questionText: A person is prohibited by law from performing a religious ritual in a public place due to concerns of public health during a pandemic. The person challenges this restriction under Article 25. Which is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The restriction is invalid as Article 25 guarantees absolute freedom of religion.
The restriction is valid as Article 25 is subject to public order, morality, and health.
The restriction is invalid unless the ritual is proven to be non-essential.
The restriction is valid only if applied to all religions equally.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The restriction is valid as Article 25 is subject to public order, morality, and health. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A granted patent is challenged 14 months after grant by a rival company through a mechanism
that is available only for a limited period after grant. The patentee argues that this route is time-
barred now, but the challenger insists this method remains available indefinitely. The rival does
not rely on a separate revocation petition at this stage and wants to proceed only through the
time-limited post-grant route.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
The challenger is correct because post-grant challenges can be filed at any time after grant
without any limitation period.

The patentee is correct because post-grant opposition allows challenges only within one year of
grant.

The challenger is correct because any delay is cured if the patent is alleged to harm public
interest and affordability.

The patentee is correct only if it proves the challenger is not a “person interested” and lacks
standing to object.
questions.solution: The reference line explicitly states that post-grant opposition “allows challenges within one year of grant.” Since the challenge is filed 14 months after grant, it falls outside the stated one-year window, supporting the patentee’s time-bar objection.

questions.questionText:
While engaging in a contract for the construction of a new office building, ConstructCo anticipates
that the material costs will rise due to market rumours, which could jeopardise the completion of the
project. Prior to any rise in costs, ConstructCo notifies the client, Office Corp, that it cannot proceed
under the original terms. If Office Corp decides to respond to this anticipatory breach, is it legally
justified in repudiating the contract and claiming damages under the Indian Contract Act?
options: Yes, because they can repudiate the contract and claim damages as allowed by the Act.
No, because they must first allow ConstructCo to adjust the terms of the contract.

Yes, because ConstructCo should be allowed to renegotiate the contract due to unforeseen economic
changes.
No, because ConstructCo has not yet failed to perform any of the contractual terms.

questions.questionText:
Nisha manufactures a product and is sued for patent infringement before the High Court. She
believes the patent is invalid because similar technology was publicly known earlier. Instead of
filing a separate challenge elsewhere, she wants the invalidity issue to be decided within the same
infringement case. The patentee objects, arguing she must start an independent revocation case
only.
What is the most accurate view?
options:
The patentee is correct because invalidity cannot be raised in an infringement suit and must
be filed only as a separate case.

Nisha is correct because revocation can be initiated only by the Central Government or a
patent office, not by defendants.

Nisha is correct because revocation may be initiated by way of a counterclaim in an
infringement suit before the High Court.

The patentee is correct because only “any person interested” can challenge validity, and an
accused infringer is never interested.
questions.solution: The reference line directly supports Nisha’s approach by stating that revocation proceedings may be initiated “by way of a counterclaim in an infringement suit before the High Court.” Since she is already before the High Court in an infringement case, she can raise validity through that counterclaim route.

questions.questionText: A enters into an agreement with B stating that A will pay B Rs.10,00,000 if B's warehouse is destroyed by fire within the next 12 months. The agreement also records that B has stored high-value goods in the warehouse and would suffer severe financial loss if such destruction occurs. After 6 months, the warehouse is compulsorily acquired by the government and demolished for public use. Which of the following is the most legally accurate conclusion?
options: The agreement becomes void as the specified event (fire) has become impossible before the expiry of time.
The agreement remains enforceable since destruction has occurred, even though by a different cause.
The agreement is a wager since neither party controls the event of fire.
The agreement becomes enforceable immediately upon destruction of the warehouse irrespective of the cause.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The agreement becomes void as the specified event (fire) has become impossible before the expiry of time. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Sunrise Public School is a private unaided school in Delhi. Its management argues that since
Fundamental Rights are enforceable only against the State, they are not bound by the
Supreme Court's directions on menstrual hygiene infrastructure. Based on the passage, is this
argument valid?
options:
Yes, the argument is valid because Fundamental Rights operate vertically and private
institutions cannot be held liable under Articles 21 or 21A.

No, the argument is invalid because Articles 21 and 21A can extend to private educational
institutions, making them liable to comply with MHM directions.

Yes, the argument is valid because only government-aided private schools are covered
under the judgment, and unaided schools remain exempt from these obligations.

No, the argument is invalid, but only because private schools voluntarily accepted State
funding and thereby assumed constitutional obligations.
EC-22A, First Floor, Opp. Steel Bhawan, Shastri Circle, JODHPUR (M) 76659 44999 | www.lptedtech.com	31

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states that ‘Articles 21 and 21A can extend to private educational institutions’ and that the Court directed States/UTs to ensure compliance by every school, whether government-run or privately managed. Option B reflects this correctly.

questions.questionText:
Vivek, a well-known artist, offers to sell one of his paintings to a gallery, with the acceptance deadline set for
July 15th. Unfortunately, Vivek suffers a mental breakdown and is declared legally insane on July 10th, a fact that
comes to the gallery's knowledge on the same day. The gallery, however, had already sent a letter of acceptance on
July 9th, which reaches Vivek's legal guardian on July 12th. Can the gallery enforce the contract for the purchase
of the painting?
options: Yes, because the gallery sent the acceptance before Vivek's insanity was declared.
No, because Vivek was declared legally insane before the acceptance reached his guardian.
Yes, because the gallery was unaware of Vivek's condition when they sent the acceptance.
No, because the contract is automatically void due to Vivek's insanity.

questions.questionText:
The Ambassador of the Republic of Verdania to India allegedly failed to pay ₹45 lakh to an Indian interior design
        firm that renovated his official residence in New Delhi. Despite multiple reminders and promises to pay, the
        Ambassador has avoided settling the dues for over two years. The interior design firm, having exhausted all informal
        remedies, wishes to file a civil suit for recovery of money against the Ambassador. The firm's lawyer advises that
        this is not a straightforward case. Based on the passage, can the interior design firm directly institute a suit against
        the Ambassador?
options:
No, because a suit against a foreign ambassador cannot ordinarily be instituted without the consent of the
            Central Government, certified in writing.

Yes, because the debt arose from a private commercial transaction for interior design services, which falls
            outside the scope of diplomatic immunity recognized under Indian law.

Yes, because ambassadors only have immunity for their official diplomatic functions, and personal debts like
            interior design payments are not covered by any immunity provisions.

No, because foreign ambassadors are completely immune from all legal proceedings in India, and no suit can
            ever be filed against them under any circumstances.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because a suit against a foreign ambassador cannot ordinarily be instituted without the consent of the Central Government, certified in writing. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Rahul, an artist, creates a series of paintings inspired by famous literary works and exhibits them in a
local gallery without seeking permission from the authors or copyright holders. He believes that his
artistic interpretation is transformative and falls under fair use. In the context of the passage on
copyright and fair dealing, evaluate the situation and answer the following question: Considering Rahul's
situation, which legal concept might he argue to justify the exhibition of his paintings without seeking
permission?
options:
The Doctrine of Fair Dealing provides a broad exemption for artists to freely use and interpret copyrighted
works for creative expression.

The Copyright Act explicitly allows artists to reproduce and exhibit works inspired by copyrighted material
without seeking permission, given that it is for artistic purposes.

Rahul could argue the Transformative Use Doctrine, which permits artists to create derivative works without
infringing on copyright, as long as the new work adds significant value and purpose.

Artists are entirely exempt from copyright laws when their works are displayed in galleries for public
viewing, and no permissions are required.

questions.questionText:
Raghav joins a paid “extreme zipline” event at an adventure park in Rishikesh. Before
participating, he signs a printed form stating he understands the risk of injury and still wishes to
proceed. During the ride, the harness is properly fitted, but Raghav twists mid-air to film a reel,
slips awkwardly, and fractures his arm. He sues the park for damages.
Which statement best reflects the likely outcome?
options:
Raghav will succeed because any injury at a paid adventure park automatically makes the
organiser liable, regardless of prior consent.

Raghav will likely fail because he knowingly and voluntarily assumed the specific risk
associated with the activity.

Raghav will succeed because signing a standard form can never amount to voluntary
acceptance of physical risk.

Raghav will likely fail because the park’s duty ends once customers enter the ride area,
irrespective of safety measures.
questions.solution: The reference line squarely applies because Raghav knew the activity carried risk, signed a form acknowledging it, and voluntarily chose to proceed. Where the harm flows from a risk that the participant accepted as part of the activity, the law generally prevents him from later complaining as if the risk was forced upon him.

questions.questionText:
Priyank purchases a residential apartment located directly above a long-established spice
market. For over twenty-five years, a neighbouring shop has ground mild spices for two hours
every afternoon openly and without any complaints. Recently, however, the shop switches to
grinding highly pungent industrial chili peppers without upgrading its ventilation filters.
While other ordinary residents in the building now experience severe coughing fits and
watering eyes due to the intensified fumes, Priyank, who has a rare respiratory sensitivity is
completely bedridden. Priyank sues the shop owner for private nuisance. The owner argues
that the suit must fail because the shop has a prescriptive right to grind spices in an
established market locality. Will Priyank's suit succeed?
options:
Yes, because the defense of prescription cannot protect a fundamental change in an
activity that creates a new, more serious harm affecting ordinary persons in that locality.

Yes, because a plaintiff's rare and severe health vulnerability takes legal precedence over
the historical commercial character of a locality.

No, because the shop has openly and peacefully ground spices for the required legal period,
giving it an absolute prescriptive right over the property's environmental impact.

No, because by voluntarily purchasing an apartment located directly above a pre-existing
spice market, Priyank legally accepted the locality's inherent discomforts.
questions.solution: . The passage states that the seriousness of harm and unreasonableness are critical factors in determining nuisance, and prescription only applies when "the nuisance" (the specific interference) has continued uninterrupted for the legal period.

questions.questionText:
A startup selling home cleaning services applies to register the mark “BEST CLEANING
SERVICES” for its services. The applicant argues that customers like straightforward words
and that registration should be granted because no one else has complained yet. The Registrar
objects that the phrase is descriptive and lacks distinctiveness, and therefore cannot be
registered as a trademark in the ordinary way. The applicant says descriptive marks should
be allowed because they are common and useful.
Which statement best matches the absolute refusal idea?
options:
Refusal justified because absolute refusal applies where the mark lacks distinctiveness or
is descriptive, even if applicant likes clarity.

Refusal unjustified because descriptive phrases must be registered to help consumers
understand services and improve market transparency always.

Refusal unjustified because absolute grounds apply only to scandalous or deceptive marks,
not to descriptive words in service marks.

Refusal justified only if there is earlier mark conflict, because descriptiveness is a relative
ground and not an absolute one today.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “lacks distinctiveness” and “descriptive,” matching the reference line. “BEST CLEANING SERVICES” describes the nature/quality of the service rather than indicating source, so the absolute grounds logic supports refusal.

questions.questionText:
The State Government of "Alpha" is led by a party whose manifesto explicitly promotes the
establishment of a state-funded religious university dedicated exclusively to one faith. After a
major religious monument of a minority group is damaged by a mob, the Chief Minister holds a
press conference praising the "zeal" of the protesters. The Union Government moves to dismiss the
State Government, citing a failure of constitutional machinery. According to the passage, which of
the following best supports the Union’s decision?
options:
Secularism is a part of the basic structure, and a Ministry’s actions and manifestos can
demonstrate a failure to uphold it.

The mere existence of a religious manifesto is enough to dismiss a government, even if no
violence occurs.
Article 25 allows the state to prioritize the religion of the majority to maintain public order.

Any disturbance involving loss of life automatically signifies a failure of constitutional
machinery.
questions.solution: The passage highlights the argument that secularism is part of the basic structure and soul of the Constitution and that a political plank or the conduct of leaders (like exhortations or lack of regret) can be seen as concrete proof of an intent that violates this principle. Incorrect Options:

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Under the framework described, trauma care has become an enforceable
fundamental right rather than a matter of administrative discretion.
Reason (R): The passage states that the right to trauma care is an integral part of the right
to life under Article 21.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Ais true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
During naval deployment, Commander Arif suffers a serious injury while his ship is engaged
in emergency operations at sea. Believing he may not survive, he orally declares before two
fellow officers that his savings and medals should go to his widowed mother. No formal
written will is prepared, and the declaration does not satisfy ordinary attestation
requirements. After Arifs death, his cousin objects that every will must follow ordinary
formalities, regardless of military or maritime circumstances.
Which statement best applies?
options:
The declaration is invalid because oral wishes can never operate as testamentary
directions.

The declaration may be valid because mariners can make privileged wills with relaxed
formalities.

The declaration is invalid because relaxed formalities apply only to civilians during
emergencies.

The declaration may be valid only if all relatives later approve the testamentary
arrangement.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “mariners” and “relaxed formalities,” matching the reference line. Since Arif was serving at sea during emergency operations, his declaration may fall within the privileged-will category, subject to proof of the statement and surrounding circumstances.

questions.questionText:
An internal audit of a national medical device regulator is leaked, conclusively proving that
85% of devices approved last year bypassed mandatory safety protocols due to widespread
corruption by officials. A health NGO files a PIL under Article 32, submitting this audit as
evidence, and requests the Supreme Court to intervene and issue appropriate directions to the
dysfunctional regulatory mechanism. Will the Court intervene?
options:
Yes, because the internal audit provides clear, reliable evidence of systemic failure and
mala fide action within the statutory regulator.

Yes, because the Supreme Court's primary role under Article 32 is to assume managerial
control over all technical domains to prevent public harm.

No, because courts must always defer to the expertise of a statutory regulator, regardless
of the level of dysfunction or corruption shown.

No, because extraordinary powers must only be exercised by the High Courts, and the
Supreme Court cannot substitute its judgment for a statutory body.
questions.solution: Option A is correct because the scenario provides an official internal audit, which can be considered a reliable source of material, showing 85% non-compliance due to corruption. This meets the threshold of “clear evidence of arbitrariness, mala fide action, or systemic failure” required for the Court to intervene and substitute its judgment.

questions.questionText:
A municipal tender committee awards a road-repair contract to Firm Z. Later, it is discovered
that the committee chair’s spouse owns shares in Firm Z, and the chair never disclosed this
interest. The chair argues that the price was lowest and the decision was unanimous, so his
presence made “no difference.” A rival bidder challenges the award, claiming the decision was
tainted because the chair participated in evaluation and signing.
How should the challenge be assessed?
options:
Award stands because bias is presumed harmless, and professionalism ensures neutrality;
prior acquaintance with bidder cannot disqualify decision-maker.

Award stands because hearing was offered, so impartiality is satisfied; financial interest
does not matter if disclosures were made publicly.

Award invalid because no one should be a judge in their own cause, and pecuniary bias
taints decision.

Award invalid only if reasons missing; bias rule applies only to courts, not to tender
committees in administration.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “no one should be a judge in their own cause,” mirroring the reference line. A spouse’s financial interest is a classic form of pecuniary bias, and participation in evaluation and signing makes the taint real, not hypothetical.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Under the "Golden Triangle" doctrine, a law that is procedurally perfect may still
be declared unconstitutional under Article 21.
Reason (R): Article 14 acts as a restrictive filter that prohibits the State from creating any
classification among individuals when drafting procedures for personal liberty.
Select the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct, but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect, but (R) is correct.
questions.solution: The Assertion is true because a law might follow all procedures but still be "unfair" or "unreasonable." However, the Reason is false. Article 14 does not prohibit classification; it only prohibits unreasonable classification.

questions.questionText:
PIPL argues that recognition of Shaadi.com as a well-known trademark justifies refusal of registration
and restraint against the use of deceptively similar marks, even when such marks are used for services
outside the matrimonial sector.
Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen PIIPL’s argument?
options:
Evidence showing that PIIPL has consistently invested heavily in nationwide advertising and
promotion of Shaadi.com over several years, resulting in widespread public recognition

Proof that the defendants registered the domain getshaadi.com after PIIPL adopted the Shaadi.com
mark

Data indicating that the defendants’ services cater to a niche audience distinct from Shaadi.com’s
primary users
Showing that the defendants did not obtain prior permission from PIIPL before adopting the mark
questions.solution: Option A directly supports the well-known trademark criteria under Section 11(6) mentioned in the passage—specifically public recognition, duration, and extent of promotion, which are decisive in granting broader protection beyond class limitations Option B only shows priority in adoption, which helps infringement claims but does not by itself justify well-known status or cross-class protection. Option C weakens the argument by suggesting absence of confusion.

questions.questionText:
Nandini’s husband stops her from using the ATM card linked to her salary account, takes her
jewellery and sells it to “recover his expenses,” and refuses to give her money for medicines
unless she signs over her scooter. He also tells her parents that he will not provide any
maintenance because she is “useless.” When Nandini seeks relief, the respondent argues this
is only “budget discipline,” not violence. Nandini claims the conduct is economic abuse
recognised by the framework.
Which option fits best?
options:
No, because controlling household spending is normal finance management; denying
purchases cannot be treated as domestic violence ever.

Yes, Economic abuse includes deprivation of financial resources, denial of maintenance,
and restricting access to property or necessities by the partner.

No, because only physical injury matters; cutting money access is civil dispute and outside
protective remedies always.

Yes, because any quarrel about expenses is economic abuse, so every financial
disagreement triggers orders automatically now for her.
questions.solution: This option directly uses key words from the reference line—“deprivation of financial resources,” “denial of maintenance,” and “restricting access to property or necessities.” Nandini’s blocked salary access, sale of jewellery, and maintenance denial fit that description.

questions.questionText:
During a constitutionally proclaimed emergency, a detainee files a petition before the Supreme
Court complaining that he was forced to confess and was kept in solitary confinement without
basic safeguards. The State claims the right to move the Court for enforcement of rights is
suspended, so the petition must be dismissed. The detainee argues that some core rights remain
enforceable despite such suspension.
Which option is most accurate?
options:
The State is correct because once suspended, no fundamental protection can be enforced during
an emergency.

The detainee is correct because despite suspension of Article 32 during emergencies, core
rights under Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable.

The State is correct because enforceable rights during emergencies are limited only to property
rights and not to liberty concerns.

The detainee is correct only if Parliament passes a special resolution restoring all remedies for
every Fundamental Right.
questions.solution: The reference line’s exact wording supports the detainee’s position: even if the general right to move the Court is curtailed, “core rights under Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable.” Claims like forced confession and unlawful deprivation of personal liberty align with those core protections.

questions.questionText:
Mrs. Gupta, a 75-year-old senior citizen, is neglected by her son but is financially
        supported by her daughter-in-law, who is a successful entrepreneur. Mrs. Gupta is
        unable to maintain herself from her own resources. She wishes to file a
        maintenance claim. Against whom can she file a claim under the provisions of the
        MWPSC Act as described in the passage?
options:
She can file a claim against both her son and her daughter-in-law, as they are
      both part of her immediate family.

She can file a claim only against her son, as the Act's definition of "children"
      does not include a daughter-in-law.

She can file a claim only against her daughter-in-law, as she is the earning
    member of the family and has the means to provide support.

She cannot file a claim against anyone, as she is already receiving financial
    support, even if it is from her daughter-in-law.

questions.questionText:
Rajesh and his wife Meena operated a tutorial center in Jaipur between 2015 and 2022. The CBI
investigation revealed that they systematically sexually assaulted 28 male students aged between
4 and 12 years by offering them free computer game access and mobile phones. Medical
examination confirmed physical injuries on 15 victims, and several victims required psychiatric
treatment. Rajesh and Meena were convicted under the POCSO Act for aggravated penetrative
sexual assault, use of children for pornography, and criminal conspiracy. The prosecution argues
for the death penalty. Based on the principles in the passage, which factor would most strongly
support the imposition of the death penalty under the "rarest of rare" doctrine?
options:
The presence of medical evidence confirming physical injuries and the long-term clinical need
for psychiatric rehabilitation of the victims.

The systematic nature of the crimes spanning seven years with a large number of victims,
combined with extreme moral depravity.

The calculated use of modern technology and electronic gifts as a specific modus operandi to
lure and groom vulnerable children.

The conviction under multiple sections of the POCSO Act including criminal conspiracy and
the organized nature of the tutorial centre.
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states that the death penalty was justified on the basis of "unparalleled depravity and systemic nature of their crimes" and "the sheer scale of victimization across multiple districts, combined with the extreme moral turpitude." The systematic operation over seven years with 28 victims mirrors the factual matrix in the passage (33 victims over ten years). Option (A) is incorrect because physical injuries alone, while serious, were not cited as the primary basis for the "r

questions.questionText:
In a bustling urban area called "Cityville," a group of concerned citizens decided to organize a
peaceful protest to raise awareness about environmental conservation. The citizens were advocating for
the preservation of a small park owned by the government located in the heart of the city, which was
under threat of being converted into a commercial complex by a private real estate developer. The police
arrived in the peaceful march which then turned into a violent protest. Several benches of the park were
broken by some hoodlums. Can the government enforce Article 51A against the hoodlums in Court?
options: Yes, because there can be cases under Article 51A of the Constitution.
No, because Fundamental Duties are not enforceable.
Yes, because there can be enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32.
No, because Fundamental Duties are persuasive in nature.
questions.solution: The passage clearly states that the Fundamental Duties contained in Article 51A are not enforceable in courts. Although citizens are expected to safeguard public property and abjure violence, these duties by themselves cannot be directly enforced through legal proceedings unless supported by a valid law enacted in consonance with Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy. Why other options are incorrect: A: Article 51A itself is not directly enforceable in courts. C: Article 32 provides remedies for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, not

questions.questionText:
Aman sells a residential plot to Bhavna through a registered sale deed. In the deed, Aman adds a
clause stating Bhavna “shall never sell, gift, or mortgage this plot to anyone, at any time,” and if
she does, the property will automatically revert to Aman. Bhavna later plans to sell the plot due to
financial stress and challenges the clause as invalid.
Which statement best reflects the legal position?
options:
The clause is valid because a seller can permanently control later transfers to protect family
sentiment and legacy.

The clause is invalid because Section 10 restricts absolute restraints on alienation, ensuring
free circulation of property.

The clause is valid because restrictions on sale are always enforceable if written in a registered
document.

The clause is invalid only if Bhavna proves Aman acted with fraud or coercion while inserting
the restriction clause.
questions.solution: The reference line directly states that Section 10 “restricts absolute restraints on alienation,” which matches the clause that Bhavna can never sell, gift, or mortgage at any time. Since the restriction is absolute and not a limited restraint, it conflicts with the rule ensuring free circulation.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Gupta agreed to sell a piece of land to Ms. Singh. They drafted a sale deed, and Mr. Gupta received the full
payment from Ms. Singh. However, before the sale deed could be registered, Mr. Gupta passed away unexpectedly.
His only heir, his son Mr. Amit Gupta, discovered the unregistered sale deed while settling his father's estate.
Acknowledging the agreement, Amit registered the sale deed in his name and then after few days claimed that the
land was his, refusing to acknowledge Ms. Singh's rights to the property, arguing that the registration was a mere
formality and didn't actually indicate an intention to transfer the property to Ms. Singh. Can Ms. Singh legally
enforce her claim to the land based on the sale deed which was registered posthumously in the name of Mr. Amit
Gupta?
options: Yes, because the sale deed was ultimately registered, even if posthumously.
No, because the original seller, Mr. Gupta, did not register the deed before his death.
Yes, but only if she can prove that the payment was made to Mr. Gupta before his death.
No, because Amit's registration of the deed in his name indicates his ownership.

questions.questionText:
A popular online game called Fable 5 allowed users to install third-party “quest mods” created
by independent developers. One such mod, ShadowRoute, contained executable code which,
when installed, automatically generated false in-game alerts that resembled real government
emergency messages and redirected players to external pages carrying fabricated public-order
warnings. After several users shared screenshots of these alerts outside the game, local panic
spread in two districts. The Central Government directed blocking of public access to the
ShadowRoute code repository and its compiled plug-in under Section 69A of the Information
Technology Act, 2000. The developer argued that Section 69A could cover messages, posts or
images, but not code written for a game mod because code is only a technical instruction and
not “information”. Is the developer’s argument correct?
options:
Yes, because code inside a gaming mod is a technical instruction and cannot be treated as
public information.

Yes, because Section 69A applies to messages and images, but not to software used inside
games.

No, because Section 2(1)(v) defines information broadly to include codes, computer
programmes and software.

No, because any game mod causing public panic can be blocked without examining
whether it is information.
questions.solution: The passage provides that “information” is broadly defined to include codes, computer programmes and software. Since ShadowRoute consists of executable code and a compiled plug-in, it can fall within the meaning of information for the purpose of Section 69A.

questions.questionText:
A chemical unit located near a village releases untreated effluents into a stream used for
drinking water and irrigation. Villagers complain of skin infections, crop loss, and
contaminated groundwater. The factory argues that environmental regulation is only a
statutory matter and cannot become a fundamental-right claim. The villagers file a petition
claiming that Article 21 includes the right to pollution-free water and a clean environment.
Which legal position is strongest?
options:
Villagers succeed because Article 21 includes pollution-free air, water, and clean
environment.

Factory succeeds because environmental harm can never affect life or personal liberty
rights.
Villagers succeed only if every resident proves identical medical injury from the pollution.

Factory succeeds because clean environment depends only on policy, not constitutional
protection.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “pollution-free air, water, and clean environment,” matching the reference line. Contamination of a village stream used for drinking and irrigation directly affects life, health, and dignified existence under Article 21.

questions.questionText:
Neha is arrested for an offence punishable up to seven years. The IO produces her before the
Magistrate within 24 hours but submits only the FIR and a short remand note with no
checklist and no written reasons showing necessity of arrest. The Magistrate mechanically
grants custody for 7 days without asking for the statutory materials. Neha challenges the
remand order and argues that the Magistrate must scrutinise the checklist and recorded
reasons rather than act as a rubber stamp.
What is the best legal view?
options:
Remand valid because Magistrate need not scrutinise arrest materials; police discretion is
sufficient and court cannot question it.

Remand invalid because officer must prepare checklist and record reasons, and Magistrate
must scrutinise these materials on production.

Remand valid because once FIR exists, custody must be granted, and checklist is internal
police paperwork with no legal value.

Remand invalid only if accused proves innocence, because scrutiny duty arises only after
trial and not at remand stage.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: This option directly uses “prepare a checklist,” ” «6 “record reasons,” and “Magistrate must scrutinise,” matching the reference line. Since both steps were skipped, the remand is procedurally vulnerable and appears mechanical.

questions.questionText: The legislature of State X enacts a law requiring all print and digital news publications to submit content relating to public policy, national security, or electoral matters to a Government Media Review Board at least five days before publication. The Board is empowered to withhold approval if it determines the content poses a risk to 'social stability.' The government argues that the measure represents a legitimate exercise of legislative authority over media regulation, is supported by a large majority of citizens in opinion surveys, and that elected institutions are constitutionally competent to define permissible limits on public discourse. A petition challenging the law alleges violation of fundamental rights. Which of the following most appropriately follows from the passage?
options: The law may withstand challenge because prior regulatory frameworks for media content fall within the institutional competence of elected legislatures, and courts should ordinarily exercise restraint where legislation reflects majority preference and no explicit constitutional violation is demonstrated on the face of the law.

Courts may appropriately examine the law because judicial review permits scrutiny of whether legislative enactments conform to constitutional requirements, and majority support for a measure does not itself determine its constitutional validity.

The law should be upheld because democratic institutions operating according to majority preferences represent the primary source of constitutional legitimacy, and courts lack the institutional expertise to assess the national security and social stability considerations that underlie the measure.

The law raises serious constitutional concerns because requiring prior government approval of publications may implicate fundamental rights, and the passage establishes that majoritarian support alone cannot justify restrictions on rights that constitutional guarantees exist to protect.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The law raises serious constitutional concerns because requiring prior government approval of publications may implicate fundamental rights, and the passage establishes that majoritarian support alone cannot…. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Father Ramesh bought a Pune flat in 2018 solely from his salary income and registered it in his
own name. In 2024, while Ramesh is alive and healthy, his son and daughter demand an
immediate share, insisting that children have an automatic right in all property of a father.
Ramesh refuses and proposes to gift the flat to a charity. The children sue to restrain him.
Which is the most accurate view?
options:
The children will succeed because sons and daughters have an enforceable right during the
father’s lifetime in all property he owns.

The children will fail because during the father’s lifetime, sons and daughters have no rights in
self-acquired property.

The children will succeed because once a property is registered, it becomes joint family
property and creates birth-based rights.

The children will fail only if Ramesh proves he had no intention to benefit them, otherwise an
equal share is mandatory.
questions.solution: The facts match the reference line exactly: Ramesh bought the flat from salary income, i.e., through his “own efforts or earnings,” making it self-acquired. The reference line then states that children have “no rights” during the father’s lifetime, so their attempt to restrain him fails.

questions.questionText:
After the sudden death of both parents, 16-year-old Nisha begins living with her maternal
aunt. Nisha’s paternal uncle files an application in the District Court seeking to be declared
guardian of Nisha’s person and property, alleging the aunt is “too lenient.” The aunt objects,
stating Nisha is settled with her and the uncle mostly wants control of a small inherited plot.
Nisha, who is mature and articulate, tells the judge she prefers to remain with her aunt.
How should the court approach the decision?
options:
The court must appoint the paternal uncle because nearer male kin always prevails and
the minor’s preference is irrelevant.

Court should decide by welfare of the minor as controlling consideration, considering
kinship, capacity, and the minor’s intelligent preference too.

The court must appoint the person who filed first, because guardianship is procedural and
priority depends on filing time.

Court should deny all applications because death of parents automatically makes the State
the guardian, leaving relatives without standing to apply.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “welfare of the minor” and “intelligent preference,” matching the reference line’s core language. It also captures the balancing nature of the court’s inquiry capacity, nearness of kin, and the minor’s own reasoned preference rather than a single rigid factor.

questions.questionText:
During a sudden roadside quarrel, Kunal stabs Arjun once in the thigh with a small knife to
stop him from chasing him. The wound unexpectedly cuts a major artery, and Arjun dies
before medical help arrives. Evidence shows Kunal did not aim at the chest, neck, or abdomen,
and witnesses confirm that he ran away immediately after one blow. The prosecution alleges
murder, while the defence argues there may be intention to cause injury but not certainty that
death would necessarily follow.
Which answer best fits?
options: It is murder because every intentional stab leading to death has certainty of death.

It may be culpable homicide because injury was intended but death was not necessarily
certain.
It is no offence because only one blow was given during a sudden quarrel.
It is only civil wrong because death happened unexpectedly after a minor injury.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “intention to cause bodily injury” and “no certainty that death will necessarily follow,” matching the reference line. The single thigh stab may show intention to injure, but the facts may not prove the higher certainty required for murder.

questions.questionText:
XYZ Corp enters into a contract with ABC Ltd. for the delivery of specialised machinery by June 1st.
On May 15th, XYZ Corp informed ABC Ltd. that due to unforeseen improvements in their production
process, they no longer require the machinery as originally planned and intend to repudiate the contract.
ABC Ltd., which had not yet started manufacturing or procuring any components for the machinery,
faces no financial loss due to the cancellation. Is XYZ Corp required to compensate ABC Ltd. for any loss
under the Indian Contract Act?
options: Yes, because the contract was repudiated before the agreed date of performance.
No, because the contract does not specify penalties for early termination.
Yes, because repudiation automatically triggers compensation regardless of actual loss.
No, because compensation under Section 75 is contingent upon the non-breaching party suffering a loss.

questions.questionText:
Y was doing the job of a Court usher, and her primary responsibilities included making sure that the
lawyers and defendants were present at the time of the hearing. A high-ranked judge of the Supreme
Court, Justice XYZ is going to hear a case of sexual harassment at the workplace against himself. Based
on the principles of natural justice, is this action of such an esteemed judge valid, or is it in violation of
the principles of natural justice?
options: It is a violation because of the rule nemo judex in causa sua.
It is a violation of the rule of audi alteram partem.
It is a violation of the rule of reasoned decisions.
It is not a violation at all.
questions.solution: The maxim nemo judex in causa sua means that no person should be a judge in his own cause. If Justice XYZ hears a sexual harassment case against himself, he is deciding his own case, which is a direct violation of the rule against bias and therefore contrary to the principles of natural justice. Why other options are incorrect: B: The issue is not the denial of an opportunity to be heard under audi alteram partem. C: The problem arises before any reasoned decision is made; it concerns judicial bias, not reasoning.

options:
Conviction is unsustainable because dock identification without a prior TIP is inherently
unsafe under the P. Sasikumar rule regardless of other corroborative evidence.

Conviction is sustainable because the 20-minute gap satisfies the last seen theory, fingerprints
are scientific evidence, and TIP is only required for strangers.

Conviction is unsustainable because the last seen theory requires independent corroboration
and cannot stand alone as the sole basis for conviction in this case.

Conviction is sustainable because fingerprints constitute conclusive scientific evidence which
legally overrides any procedural defects regarding the witness identification.
questions.solution: This is a trap question where multiple facts suggest problems, but conviction is actually sustainable. First, regarding TIP: the passage states dock identification "becomes inherently unsafe" only "when the accused is a stranger to the witness"—the question doesn't state Ajay was a stranger, suggesting they were known to each other (given the debt relationship), making TIP requirement inapplicable.

questions.questionText:
Dr. Anita is a well-regarded surgeon specializing in advanced neurosurgical procedures. Her patient,
Mr. Sharma, requires surgery for a rare brain tumor. Before the operation, Dr. Anita informs Mr.
Sharma of the specific risks associated with the surgery, such as potential loss of vision and memory
based on his tumor’s location. Mr. Sharma signs an informed consent form acknowledging these risks.
During the surgery, a technical error occurs with the surgical equipment, leading to an unintended nerve

damage that causes paralysis in Mr. Sharma's left arm, a risk not discussed prior to the surgery. Mr.
Sharma decides to sue the hospital and Dr. Anita for negligence. Will he succeed?
options: Yes, because any injury during surgery is grounds for a negligence claim, regardless of informed consent.
No, because Mr. Sharma had signed an informed consent form acknowledging the risks of surgery.

No, because nerve damage is a known risk in any surgical procedure, regardless of whether it was
specifically disclosed.

Yes, because the paralysis was not a disclosed risk, and the injury was due to a technical error, not an
inherent surgical risk.

questions.questionText:
A chemical plant stores hazardous materials on its premises. During a routine
           inspection, a safety officer employed by the plant is injured due to a sudden leak
           within the plant boundary. The plant owner argues that since the leak did not
           escape the premises, strict liability does not apply. Under Indian law, based on the
           doctrine established in M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India, is the plant owner liable?
options:
Yes, because absolute liability applies even if the harm occurs within the enterprise's
premises, such as to workers.

No, because strict liability requires escape from the land, and since the harm occurred
within the premises, there is no liability under that rule.

No, because the safety officer assumed the risk by working in a hazardous
environment and cannot claim compensation from the owner.

Yes, but only if it can be proven with evidence that the plant was negligent in
maintaining safety standards.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is not correct as per the passage?
options:
A compensation claim cannot rest only on the beneficial nature of the provision if the
injury is not meaningfully linked to the vehicle’s use.

A vehicle may still be regarded as being used even when it is temporarily stopped,
depending on the connection between the vehicle and the injury.

A sudden natural event, such as the unexpected fall of a branch during heavy rain, may be
relevant where it could not reasonably have been anticipated.

An insurer may be made liable once the injured person is inside an insured vehicle in a
public place, even if the vehicle had no role in the injury.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: An insurer may be made liable once the injured person is inside an insured vehicle in a public place, even if the vehicle had no role in the injury. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Sameer and Ms. Tara, employees of Global Tech Solutions but from different departments,
attended an employer-organised team celebration/client-networking event held off-site on a
weekend. Mr. Sameer repeatedly made unwelcome romantic advances toward Ms. Tara,
including attempts to hold her hand, despite her clear discomfort and visible efforts to avoid
him. Ms. Tara felt distressed, particularly given that she would have to continue interacting
with Mr. Sameer at work. She subsequently filed a sexual harassment complaint with the
company's IC, alleging that the behaviour created a hostile environment. Is Ms. Tara's
complaint maintainable before the IC?
options:
No, unless the event was a company-sponsored or employer-organised event, as only such
occasions would fall within the extended definition of a workplace.

Yes, if the off-site event has a sufficient workplace nexus, such as being employer-
organised, work-related, or arising out of/during employment. A purely private event may
not automatically fall within POSH.

No, because the incident took place at a purely private social event entirely unrelated to
work, which cannot be brought within the scope of the statutory workplace definition.

Yes, but only if the conduct was explicitly sexual and severe in nature, as the off-site
location becomes legally irrelevant only when the behaviour meets a heightened threshold
of severity.
questions.solution: Maintainability depends on whether the event had _ sufficient workplace/employment nexus. The passage states that the POSH Act's coverage is extensive and includes places visited by an employee arising out of or during the course of employment.

questions.questionText:
Vikram Singh is an MLA belonging to the "Lok Shakti Party" (LSP), which is the ruling party in Rajasthan with 112
        MLAs in the 200-member assembly. During the state budget session in March 2025, the LSP issues a three-line whip
        directing all its members to vote in favor of the budget. Vikram, representing a drought-affected constituency, is
        deeply opposed to certain provisions in the budget that cut allocations for drought relief and irrigation projects.
        Despite his reservations, the party leadership refuses to modify the budget. Vikram decides to vote against the
        budget, following what he believes to be his conscience and the interests of his constituents. The budget passes with
        105 votes in favor. Immediately after the vote, another LSP MLA files a disqualification petition against Vikram with
        the Speaker, citing violation of the party whip. Based on the passage, is Vikram likely to face disqualification under
        the Tenth Schedule?
options:
No, because Vikram voted based on his conscience and the interests of his electorate, which the passage
            recognizes as important considerations for legislators.

Yes, because a legislator is deemed to have defected if he disobeys the directives of the party leadership on a
            vote, and defying the party whip can lead to loss of House membership.

No, because the budget ultimately passed, so Vikram's dissenting vote did not cause the government to fall or
            destabilize governance.

Yes, but only if at least two-thirds of LSP MLAs vote to expel Vikram from the party, following the same threshold
            required for party mergers.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because a legislator is deemed to have defected if he disobeys the directives of the party leadership on a vote, and defying the party whip can lead to loss of House membership. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Riya is detained by local police for four days without being produced before a magistrate, and her
family is not told her whereabouts. Her brother wants the quickest judicial remedy and plans to
file directly before the highest court, without first going to the High Court or approaching any
lower forum. The State argues he must exhaust alternative remedies before approaching that
court.
Which option is most accurate?
options:
The State is correct because citizens must first approach lower courts, and only then can they
seek enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

Riya’s brother is correct because Article 32 empowers citizens to directly approach the
Supreme Court for enforcement of their Fundamental Rights.

The State is correct because detention matters are private disputes between individuals and
cannot be raised as constitutional grievances.

Riya’s brother is correct only if Parliament has separately authorised such petitions for
detention cases by a special law.
questions.solution: The reference line directly supports the brother’s approach because he is seeking enforcement of a Fundamental Right and Article 32 expressly “empowers citizens to directly approach the Supreme Court” for that purpose. The State’s objection does not negate this basic entitlement to move the Court.

questions.questionText:
Priya is tried for killing colleague Ravi. They left office together at 6 PM; Ravi's body found at 6:40
PM in a park 1.5 km away; Priya's dupatta near body; park security confirms no other person
present between 6-7 PM. However, FIR omits Priya's name despite family knowing they left
together, and fingerprints on Ravi's phone don't match Priya. What evaluation is most
appropriate?
options:
Conviction sustainable because 40-minute gap satisfies last seen theory, security rules out
third party, and dupatta provides physical linkage despite FIR omission and fingerprint
mismatch

Conviction unsustainable because FIR omission of known suspect is serious, 40-minute gap
allows intervention, and exculpatory fingerprint evidence cannot be ignored

Conviction sustainable based on last seen theory alone as security testimony eliminates third-
party hypothesis

Conviction unsustainable because exculpatory scientific evidence always defeats
circumstantial evidence
questions.solution: Multiple fatal defects exist. First, FIR omission: the passage emphasizes omissions are "particularly serious when known accused names are absent"—here Priya was known to have left with Ravi but wasn't mentioned.

questions.questionText:
A company registered in India entered into a contractual relationship with a company registered in
Europe for outsourcing-related work for a period of 6 years, at a fixed price. There was a force majeure
clause in the contract. Due to some unforeseeable circumstances in India, the Indian Company failed to
