rights, superseding High Court jurisdiction

Highlight the constitutional significance of the provision, in contrast to the manner in which it
is increasingly being casually and indiscriminately invoked by litigants for routine matters

Suggest that since Article 32 is constitutionally sacrosanct, any restriction placed by the
Supreme Court on its invocation would amount to an unconstitutional curtailment of a
fundamental right
questions.solution: is correct because the reference to Ambedkar's quote is placed immediately after describing Article 32 as "one of the most important and cherished provisions," and is followed by the Court's concern about its casual misuse — creating a deliberate contrast between the provision's intended gravitas and its trivialised invocation in practice.

questions.questionText:
A contractor engaged for a public sanitation project makes workers clean toxic drains without
gloves, masks, or safe drinking water. Workers are paid far below the minimum wage and
threatened with dismissal if they complain. The contractor argues that Article 21 only protects
bare animal existence and physical survival, not workplace dignity or minimum working
conditions. The workers claim that dignified life includes humane work conditions, protection
from exploitation, and minimum wages.
Which view best follows?
options:
Contractor succeeds because Article 21 protects only survival and excludes workplace
conditions.

Contractor succeeds because wage disputes are purely contractual and outside
constitutional concern.

Workers succeed because dignity includes humane work conditions, exploitation protection,
and minimum wages.
Workers succeed only if they prove permanent physical injury from every working day.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “humane work conditions,” ” «, “protection from exploitation,” and “minimum wages,” matching the reference line. The workers’ claim is not merely about better employment terms; it concerns dignified existence protected under Article 21.

questions.questionText:
Sheetal runs an auction shop on Marine Drive. Mukul is an entrepreneur who asks her friend Sheetal
to auction off some goods that the former has smuggled in from Bangladesh. Sheetal ran all the usual
checks on the goods and was reasonably confident that the goods were genuine. She auctioned off the
goods and then the anomaly was detected and the new owners sued Sheetal.
options: Sheetal is liable because she should have checked in a better way and not cheated her customers.
Sheetal is not liable because she had performed all the checks and was reasonable in her approach.
Sheetal is not liable because she sold off the goods under a genuine mistake.
Both (B) and (C).
questions.solution: Sheetal exercised reasonable care by conducting the usual checks and honestly believed that the goods were genuine. Her actions were based on a reasonable and honest mistake of fact rather than intentional misconduct. Therefore, she should not be held liable. Why other options are incorrect: A: The facts indicate that Sheetal took reasonable precautions and did not intentionally deceive anyone. B: This is correct but incomplete because the reason for non-liability is her reasonable mistake of fact.

questions.questionText:
During a period of National Emergency in India, which of the following statements is correct
regarding the suspension of fundamental rights?
options: All fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution, including Article 20 and Article 21, are suspended.
Only the fundamental rights related to freedom of speech and expression (Article 19) are suspended.
Fundamental rights under Article 20 and Article 21 remain unaffected during a National Emergency.
Fundamental rights are suspended indefinitely until the President revokes the National Emergency.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Criminal trespass and house trespass both require the intention to commit an
offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the person in possession of the property.
Reason (R): House trespass is treated as a more serious offence because it involves intrusion
into spaces associated with privacy and security such as dwellings or protected structures.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion correctly states that both criminal trespass and house trespass require the same intention namely the intention to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor. The reason is also true because house trespass is treated as more serious due to invasion of spaces connected with privacy and security.

questions.questionText:
Kritika and Adil plan a civil marriage. They currently work in City A but want the ceremony
in City B because their friends live there. Neither of them has lived in City B, but they submit
the marriage notice there to speed up the process. The Marriage Officer in City B accepts the
notice and posts it publicly. A neighbour later complains that the notice should not have been
accepted in that district at all.
How should the validity of the notice be assessed?
options:
Notice was defective, because notice of intended marriage must be given where one party
has resided for at least thirty days before filing.

Notice was proper, because parties may file notice in any district of India, and residence
requirements apply only after solemnisation stage begins later.

Notice was defective, because parties must give notice only in the capital city, and district
officers cannot accept such notices anywhere at all.

Notice was proper, because thirty-day residence is needed only for witnesses, and the
couple’s travel bookings satisfy the requirement in law today fully.
questions.solution: The correct option directly uses “notice of intended marriage” and “resided for at least thirty days,” which is the controlling condition in the reference line. Since neither party resided in City B, acceptance of notice there is defective on this rule.

questions.questionText:
A dispute arises where individual devotees claim a right of access to a temple practice, while
the denomination claims autonomy to manage religious affairs as a collective body. The State
also has a reform law aimed at inclusion and temple entry. The court must decide how to
reconcile individual religious freedom with denominational autonomy and also whether it
should continue using a doctrine that filters protection to “essential” practices. What
statement best describes what the reference “squarely presents,” as per the passage?
options:
The reference presents only one question: how to classify a practice as religious or secular;
all other issues are settled already today.

The reference presents only one question: whether reform laws always override
denominational autonomy; ERP debate is irrelevant now.

The reference presents two questions: whether ERP should survive, and how individual
religious freedom must be reconciled with denominational autonomy.

The reference presents two questions: whether courts should avoid all review, and whether
all customs become law if long followed by a community today.
fad.
OP dS se ae
questions.solution: This option directly uses “ERP doctrine should survive” and “reconciled with collective denominational autonomy,” matching the reference line’s words. It correctly captures the two-fold structure of the issues presented by the reference.

questions.questionText:
A telecom company updates its KYC process for issuing new SIM cards. The
        new process requires users to take a selfie while blinking their left eye, a measure
        designed to prevent spoofing with static photos. An acid-attack survivor, whose
        left eyelid was permanently damaged, is unable to complete the process. The
        company's defense is that their process is compliant with the law because it is a
        security feature, not a barrier. Why is this defence weak?
options:
Because the RPwD Act mandates that all KYC processes must be identical for
   every user.

Because the RBI has explicitly banned eye-blinking tests in its Master Directions
   on KYC.

Because the Supreme Court has ruled that any digital barrier, even if designed for
   security, that excludes PwDs violates the principle of substantive equality.

Because the law requires companies to provide a human assistant to help users
   who face difficulties with automated processes.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Bhattacharya, a seasoned finance professional, has never served as a director or in a key
managerial role in a company. With over 15 years of experience in the finance sector and having
consulted for multiple firms on financial strategy, he aspires to serve as an Independent Director. He is
aware of the new rule requiring a proficiency test but is unsure about its applicability to his situation.
Would Mr. Bhattacharya be required to take the online proficiency test conducted by the Indian Institute
of Corporate Affairs (IICA) to qualify as an Independent Director?
options: Yes, because he has never served as a director or in a key managerial role in a company.
No, because he has over 15 years of experience in the finance sector.
Yes, because the Companies Act, 2013 requires a proficiency test for Independent Directors.
No, because his experience in financial consulting exempts him from the test.

questions.questionText:
A warehouse employee, tasked with moving inventory using a forklift, operates it recklessly
        in violation of strict company safety protocols and causes extensive property damage. The
        injured party sues the warehouse company. How is the company's vicarious liability likely to
        be resolved?
options:
The company is not liable because the employee's willful violation of safety rules takes the
        act outside the scope of employment entirely.

Liability would depend on whether the company had previously disciplined this specific
        employee for similar safety violations.

The employer is only responsible if it was directly negligent in maintaining the forklift, not
        for the employee's reckless operation.

The company is liable because the employee was performing an authorized core duty, albeit
        in a negligent and prohibited manner.

questions.questionText:
"TechSolutions," an IT firm, wants to assign a critical project to Ms. Rao, a senior
       engineer, which would require her to work from 8 PM to 4 AM. Ms. Rao is willing to take
       the shift. However, the company's HR policy strictly prohibits women from working after
       7 PM to avoid legal liability. Based on the Occupational Safety Code, identify the
       correct statement regarding the company's policy.
options:
The policy is valid because the law strictly forbids women from working night shifts to
ensure their safety.

The policy is invalid because the Code mandates that all women must be given night
shifts to ensure gender equality in the workplace.

The policy is valid because the Code gives the employer absolute discretion to decide
shift timings for all employees.

The policy is invalid because the Code allows women to work night shifts in all
establishments, provided the employer obtains their consent and ensures adequate safety
measures.

questions.questionText:
Justice Dhananjay, a judicial magistrate in one of the districts of Nagpur, passes a judgment regarding the
enforcement of the fundamental rights of an aggrieved citizen. The citizen had filed a petition against Tata Motors
Private Limited, alleging that they had committed a gross violation of fundamental rights. The High Court of
Bombay took suo moto cognizance of this case and held that the district court had exceeded its jurisdiction. Decide
the validity of the judgment.
options: The High Court judgment is invalid because the district court did not exceed its jurisdiction.
The district court is correct because it is a matter of fundamental rights and any court can hear the same.
The High Court is valid in taking up suo moto cognizance because it is a matter of fundamental rights.
No case stands because matters of fundamental rights violations can only be invoked by the State.

questions.questionText:
Daniel, a Christian businessman, dies leaving commercial property and bank deposits in India
without executing a valid will. His widow claims that succession should be governed under the
Indian Succession Act. Daniel’s brother argues that Indian succession rules are meant
uniformly for all Indians, including Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis, Buddhists, Sikhs
and Jainas, without any distinction. Another relative argues that the Act mainly applies to
Christians, Parsis, and certain persons governed by civil marriage law.
Which statement best reflects the correct position?
options:
The Act applies equally to every religious community without exceptions or personal-law
distinctions.

The Act applies only to Hindus and Muslims because they form the main succession
categories.
The Act mainly applies to Christians, Parsis, and certain Special Marriage Act cases.

The Act never applies to Christians because they follow only uncodified customary
succession rules.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “Christians, Parsis, and persons governed by the Special Marriage Act in certain cases.” Since Daniel is a Christian who died without a valid will, the Act’s applicability is correctly identified through this principle. Hence,

questions.questionText:
A company director circulates an investment memorandum stating that a newly discovered
technology has already received regulatory approval. At the time of making the statement, the
director has not verified the information and has no basis for believing it to be true. Nevertheless,
he proceeds to make the representation because he assumes the approval "probably exists."
Applying the principle laid down in Derry v. Peek (1889), which of the following factors most
strongly supports a finding of fraud?
options: The director genuinely believed the statement to be true, although it later proved inaccurate.
The investors suffered substantial financial loss after relying on the statement.
The representation was made recklessly without caring whether it was true or false.
The representation was made during the course of a commercial transaction.
questions.solution: Option C is correct because the facts indicate that the director had no basis for believing the statement to be true and made the representation without verifying its accuracy. He proceeded merely on an assumption that approval "probably existed." This demonstrates reckless disregard for the truth of the statement.

questions.questionText:
A government-contracted demolition team uses controlled explosives to legally
       demolish an old building. The planned implosion causes minor vibration damage to
       the foundation of a nearby shop, despite all safety protocols being followed. The shop
       owner sues the demolition company.
options:
The company is not liable as the act was done under Statutory Authority with due
       care.

The company is liable because it caused damage, and mistake in execution is no
       defence.
The company is liable as the shop owner's property rights were violated.
The company is not liable if the shop owner cannot prove intentional harm.

questions.questionText:
Ritu pays her college fee online, but the payment gateway shows “failed.” She immediately
pays again. Two days later, her bank statement shows both payments were successful and the
college received double the fee. The college refuses to refund, arguing the money was credited
“in good faith” and fees are non-refundable once received. Ritu demands restitution, saying the
extra payment was purely accidental and the college cannot retain a windfall.
What is the strongest conclusion?
options:
Return is barred because payments through banking systems are final, and mistakes are
the payer’s risk in law always alone.

Return is required because money paid by mistake or under coercion must be returned,
even if the payee acted innocently.

Return is required only if payer proves fraud, because innocent recipients can keep
mistaken money until a court convicts them.

Return is barred because quasi-contracts apply only to goods, not to money transfers, and
banks never refund overpayments today here.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “money paid by mistake... must be returned,” reflecting the exact reference line.

questions.questionText:
Rajiv, an Independent Director (ID), was appointed to the board of XYZ Corp. one month before the
enactment of the new rule requiring IDs to clear an online proficiency test conducted by the Indian

Institute of Corporate Affairs (IICA). He had been in a key managerial position for 8 years prior to his
appointment as an ID. The board has now requested Rajiv to take the test in accordance with the new
rule. Rajiv, on the other hand, argues that since he was appointed before the introduction of the rule, he
should be exempted. Is Rajiv required to take the proficiency test as per the new rule?
options: No, because he was appointed before the rule was introduced.
No, because he has been in a key managerial position for more than 5 years.
Yes, because he has not completed ten years in a directorial or key managerial role.
Yes, because the new rule applies retrospectively to all existing IDs.

questions.questionText:
Ramesh is arrested by the police on suspicion of theft. The police, due to a misunderstanding,
believe that he is a wanted criminal named in an FIR. The police verify his identity and
confirm that he is not the person they were looking for. However, by this time, he has been in
custody for 22 hours. The police decide to produce him before a Magistrate, hoping to get a
remand order, but Ramesh's lawyer argues that the police had a "misunderstanding" and the
initial arrest was invalid. Decide the most legally accurate option.
options:
The arrest is invalid because it was based on a misunderstanding, and therefore Mr.
Kumar must be released.

The detention is unlawful because the police did not have a valid reason to arrest Mr.
Kumar, and the arrest was not for a crime.

Even if the arrest was based on a misunderstanding, the detention becomes lawful when
he is produced before the Magistrate within 24 hours.

The police violated Article 22 by delaying the verification of his identity, and this
constitutes an unreasonable delay in informing him of the grounds of his arrest.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Even if the arrest was based on a misunderstanding, the detention becomes lawful when he is produced before the Magistrate within 24 hours. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Rohit checks into a private resort and later disputes an additional bill raised by the manager.
The manager does not lock Rohit’s room, but places two guards near the only staircase and lift.
The guards tell Rohit that if he tries to leave before paying, he will be “handled outside the
cameras.” Rohit remains inside the room for six hours, though he is given food and allowed to
call his lawyer. Has wrongful confinement likely occurred?
options:
Yes, because guarded exits and threatened violence created a reasonable fear that leaving
the defined area was not possible.

Yes, because the manager linked Rohit’s departure to settlement of the disputed bill, and
Rohit remained in the room until the issue was resolved.

No, because the room was not locked and Rohit was neither physically touched nor directly
chained by the guards.

No, because the resort gave food and phone access, which shows that personal liberty was
not substantially curtailed.
questions.solution: the passage explains that actual physical force is not essential. Guarding the only exits and threatening violence if Rohit leaves creates a reasonable fear that escape is not possible, even though the room itself is not locked.

questions.questionText:
During a campus quiz on constitutional history, Meenal reads an old Preamble poster showing
only “Sovereign Democratic Republic” and the phrase “unity of the nation.” Her friend shows a
newer pocket Constitution, printed after the Emergency-era “Mini-Constitution,” containing
extra descriptive words and a different unity phrase. Meenal is confused because both
documents look official. She must choose one option that precisely and directly reflects the
textual edit made in 1976.
Which Preamble modification should she select?
options:
It removed “Sovereign” and “Democratic” and inserted “Federal” and “Presidential”,
claiming Emergency required a stronger central identity in Preamble for national stability.

It inserted a new clause making elections optional during Emergency and changed “We,
the People” to “We, the Parliament” in Preamble textually.

It added the words “Socialist” and “Secular” and changed “unity of the nation” to “unity
and integrity of the nation” in Preamble.

It deleted the Preamble entirely, shifting all ideals into Directive Principles, arguing
judges often misused the opening words to block reforms earlier.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “Socialist,” “Secular,” and “unity and integrity of the nation,” matching the precise textual modification stated. It explains why an older printing lacks those words and why a post-1976 printing contains them.

questions.questionText:
Exception 2 of section 375 provides that Sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his wife, the
wife not being under fifteen years of age, is not rape. Ananya, a 25-year-old woman, was married to
Raunak, aged 32 years. They did not have a happy married life, and Ananya was often forced into a lot of
decisions. Some of these included forced sexual intercourse. Can Raunak be held guilty of the rape of
Ananya?
options: Raunak cannot be held guilty because his acts were done in the past.
He cannot be held guilty because they are married.
He cannot be guilty under section 375's exception 2.
Both (b) and (c).
questions.solution: The passage reproduces Exception 2 to Section 375, which states that sexual intercourse by a man with his wife, provided she is not under 15 years of age, is not rape. Since Ananya is 25 years old and legally married to Raunak, he is protected by this marital exception under the passage. @CLAT_OWNER Why other options are incorrect: A: Whether the acts occurred in the past is irrelevant. B: Marriage is the reason for the exception, but this option is incomplete because the

questions.questionText:
The Constitution places "Agriculture" in the State List and "Inter-State Trade and Commerce" in
the Union List. Concerned about food security, Parliament enacts the National Agricultural Supply
Stabilisation Act, 2026. The Act is stated to regulate the movement of agricultural products across
state borders. However, its provisions require farmers to obtain cultivation permits from a Central
Authority, prescribe the crops that may be grown in particular districts, regulate irrigation
practices on private farms, and authorize the Central Authority to inspect agricultural lands.
Parliament argues that these measures are necessary to ensure a stable national supply chain and
therefore fall within its power over inter-State trade.
The State of Z challenges the Act, alleging that Parliament has used its power over inter-State
trade as a device to assume control over agriculture. The Union responds that the Act's objective is
national market regulation and that courts cannot question legislative wisdom.
Which of the following is the most constitutionally sound conclusion?
options:
The Act is valid because whenever a law is connected to a Union List subject, courts cannot
examine its practical effect.

The Act is valid because legislative motive is irrelevant, and therefore any challenge based on
colourable legislation must fail.

The Act may be struck down if the court finds that, in substance, Parliament is regulating
agriculture under the guise of regulating inter-State trade.

The Act must be upheld because food security is a matter of national importance and
automatically overrides the distribution of legislative powers.
questions.solution: This option correctly applies the doctrine. The court would examine the substance over form of the legislation.

questions.questionText:
A messaging platform, CityLink, was being used to circulate false messages that a particular
religious group had attacked several shops in a busy market area. Within a few hours, local
clashes began and police reported that the same messages were being forwarded through
multiple public groups. Treating the situation as urgent, the Secretary issued an interim
direction blocking access to the platform in the affected region for three days. CityLink was
not heard before the interim direction, but the request was later placed before the statutory
committee. The committee gave a hearing and made its recommendation, after which the
Secretary passed the final order approving the interim block. CityLink challenged the order
only on the ground that no hearing was given before the interim direction. Is CityLink’s
challenge likely to succeed on this ground?
options:
Yes, because Rule 8 ordinarily requires that the affected platform must be given a hearing
before any blocking order is passed by the competent authority.

Yes, because a later committee hearing cannot support or validate an interim direction
that was issued first during an urgent situation.

No, because Rule 9 permits interim blocking in emergencies, followed by hearing,
committee recommendation and final order by the Secretary.

No, because emergency blocking can be issued whenever public messages create
administrative inconvenience or practical difficulty for government authorities.
questions.solution: The passage states that Rule 9 allows an interim blocking direction in cases of emergency. It further provides that the Secretary may issue an interim direction first, after which the request is placed before the committee, the committee gives an opportunity of hearing and makes its recommendation, and the Secretary passes the final order.

questions.questionText:
After heavy rains damage a town, Palak converts the rear portion of her residential house into
a free community kitchen for displaced families. To cook on a large scale, she uses a diesel
generator and an industrial exhaust fan late into the night. The smoke and vibration
repeatedly enter Payal’s adjoining house, disturbing her sleep, worsening her father’s
breathing difficulty, and making ordinary use of the house uncomfortable. Payal files a suit for
nuisance. Palak argues that her activity cannot be considered a nuisance because it is a
temporary, charitable effort necessary for public welfare. Will Palak's defence succeed?
options:
Yes, because the activity serves public welfare and the disturbance arises from the
compassionate and morally necessary use of property.

Yes, because temporary disaster relief work reduces the gravity of the interference and
should be treated differently from an ordinary private commercial activity.

No, because a socially beneficial use of property may still constitute a nuisance if it
unreasonably disturbs another person’s legal rights to enjoy their property.

No, because any charitable activities becomes a public nuisance once smoke and vibration
affect a neighbour's health and safety.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: it balances Palak’s right to use her property with Payal’s right not to suffer unreasonable interference. The facts show smoke, vibration, disturbed sleep, and worsened breathing in the adjoining house, which directly connect with the use and enjoyment of property.

questions.questionText:
Rahul and five associates, armed with rifles, forcefully occupy a district magistrate's
        office. They broadcast a video declaring their aim to overthrow the central government
        and establish a new regime from that very building. Police surround the office and arrest
        them after a brief standoff. For what most serious offence are they likely to be charged?
options:
They are likely to be charged with waging war against the Government of
                India under Section 121, due to their collective armed action with a political
                purpose of overthrowing the state.

They are likely to be charged with criminal trespass and unlawful assembly for
                disrupting government work and causing public terror.

They are likely to be charged with sedition for making statements intended to
             bring the government into hatred and contempt among the public.

They are likely to be charged with conspiracy to wage war under Section
             121A, as they had an agreement but did not successfully execute their plan to
             its final conclusion.

questions.questionText:
A warehouse owner signs a written lease with a trader for five years, specifying rent, security
deposit, duration, maintenance obligations, and consequences of breach. The trader later
refuses to pay rent and says the document is merely an agreement, not a contract, because
both words mean exactly the same thing. The warehouse owner argues that the arrangement
is enforceable by law and therefore qualifies as a contract.
Which statement correctly captures the distinction?
options: It is only an agreement because leases cannot create enforceable obligations.
It is a contract because it is an agreement enforceable by law.
It is not a contract unless both parties avoid all future disputes.
It is not an agreement because written terms make it too formal.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line because the lease is not merely a casual understanding; it contains definite terms and is intended to be legally enforceable. Therefore, it can properly be treated as a contract.

questions.questionText:
Isha (Hindu) and Daniel (Christian), both Indian citizens, approach the local Marriage Officer
to marry under a civil process because their families oppose a church or temple ceremony. The
Officer agrees to accept their forms but insists they must first sign an affidavit declaring they
“do not profess any religion,” failing which the marriage will not be processed. Isha and Daniel
refuse, saying they want a civil marriage without changing faith.
How should their request be treated?
options:
Refuse registration because parties must declare they do not profess any religion, and
interfaith couples cannot use this civil route at all.

Allow registration, because people of any religion may marry without renouncing their
faith, and refusal on that ground is improper.

Refuse registration, because only same-faith couples can marry under this Act, and
different religions must follow their personal rites only now always.

Allow registration only after both parties convert to one religion, because conversion
supplies a common faith and removes legal objections for marriage.
questions.solution: The correct option directly uses the reference words “any religion” and “without renouncing their faith,” and applies them to the Officer’s refusal. The Officer cannot insist on a renunciation affidavit as a condition for a civil marriage under this regime.

questions.questionText:
An employee at MMCL accidentally leaves his recorder on during a meeting. He later realizes
he has a recording of a senior official admitting to a clerical error. He shares it with his
supervisor to correct the error, believing he is acting in the company's best interest. The
management files a case under Section 66 of the IT Act. Will the charge hold?
options:
Yes, because any recording made without the explicit permission of the parties involved is
“dishonest” under the IT Act.

Yes, because the Maharashtra Metro Rail Corporation Rules prohibit the communication
of official information to any person.

No, because Section 66 requires the act to be done “dishonestly or fraudulently,” and acting
in “good faith” to correct an error may negate this.

No, because the IT Act only applies to external hackers and not to internal employees who
have authorized access to the office.
questions.solution: Option C is correct because the passage notes that Section 66 makes acts punishable only when done “dishonestly or fraudulently.” It also highlights that communication in “good faith performance of duties” is an exception under the service rules, suggesting that a helpful, non-deceptive motive would not meet the “dishonest” threshold. Option A is incorrect because while it might be a civil violation under Section 43, Section 66 (the criminal part) specifically requires a dishonest or fraudulent

questions.questionText:
Suresh, a resident living near an industrial unit operated by Arvind Industries, notices that
the unit has been discharging untreated effluents into a nearby river for the past 14 months,
causing severe pollution and health issues in the village. He wishes to take legal action. Under
the current EPA framework, which of the following is the most accurate statement?
options:
Suresh cannot file any complaint because only government officials have locus standi
under the EPA.

Suresh may file a complaint only after giving not less than 60 days’ notice under Section
19. The penalty should be framed under the current EPA monetary penalty structure
(Section 14A).

Suresh can directly approach the court under Section 19, and Arvind Industries may face
imprisonment of up to seven years for the continuing violation.

Suresh must first approach the State Pollution Control Board, and only if it fails to act can
he file a complaint in court.
questions.solution: Section 19 allows any person to file a complaint but only after giving not less than 60 days’ notice. Under the current EPA (post-amendment), the applicable consequence for Section 7 discharge violations is monetary penalty under Section 14A, not automatic imprisonment.

questions.questionText:
Which of the following principles is most centrally affirmed by the Supreme Court's ruling as
described in the passage?
options:
Article 32 protects the constitutional right to enforce fundamental rights, though this
protection may be suspended by presidential order during a proclaimed national emergency
under Article 359.

While litigants ordinarily need not exhaust all available administrative remedies before
approaching a constitutional court, some statutory exhaustion requirements may apply in
specific procedural contexts.

The Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction, though constitutionally guaranteed, should be
exercised consistently with judicial hierarchy and ordinarily cannot be invoked to bypass High
Courts already handling the same substantive matter.

High Courts exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 and the Supreme Court under Article 32
possess distinct but complementary jurisdictional power, though litigants seeking fundamental
rights enforcement may generally approach either forum as their initial recourse.
questions.solution: is correct because the passage's central message is that while Article 82 is constitutionally guaranteed, it must be exercised responsibly and in a manner that respects the judicial hierarchy — particularly when a High Court is already hearing the same matter. The Court's dismissal of the petition and its strong remarks about misuse together affirm this principle of hierarchical judicial discipline.

questions.questionText:
A transfer deed states: “This house is transferred to Arjun immediately, but if Arjun clears a bank
loan within one year, he will keep it permanently; otherwise, the transfer will not take effect.”
Arjun takes possession and claims ownership from day one. The transferor’s heirs argue Arjun’s
right is uncertain until the condition is met, so he cannot claim a vested right immediately.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Arjun’s right is vested immediately because every transfer creates an immediate, absolute
right regardless of any condition.

Arjun’s right is contingent only if the condition is illegal; if it is legal, the right is always
vested.

Arjun’s right is vested only if the condition is waived in writing, otherwise no legal interest can
exist at all.
Arjun’s right is contingent because rights accrue only after the specified condition is fulfilled.
questions.solution: The reference line supports the analysis that the distinction between vested and contingent interests determines when rights accrue. Since the deed ties permanent keeping of the property to clearing a loan within a year, Arjun’s entitlement is dependent on fulfilling a condition, making the right contingent until the condition is satisfied.

questions.questionText:
A startup, "QuickReach," connects freelance plumbers and electricians with customers
     through a mobile app. The workers choose their own hours and use their own tools.
     QuickReach argues it is merely a technology aggregator and not an employer, hence it
     has no obligation to provide any benefits to these workers. Based on the passage, which
     of the following is the most logical legal outcome under the new framework?
options:
QuickReach is exempt because freelance workers are independent contractors and do
not fall under the definition of "employee" in any labour code.

QuickReach will be required to provide access to social security schemes, as the new
Code explicitly recognizes "gig and platform workers" and extends benefits to them despite
the blurred employer-employee relationship.

QuickReach is liable to pay minimum wages but not social security, as the Code on
Wages applies to all sectors, but social security is restricted to factory workers.

QuickReach is exempt because the Code on Social Security only applies to traditional
industries with fixed working hours.

questions.questionText:
During the Emergency period, a journalist writes that the government reshaped constitutional
machinery to ensure uninterrupted rule, including changes affecting the President,
legislatures, and security deployment in states. Years later, a civics student reads this article
and is asked to identify which specific package of changes the 1976 amendment actually
introduced. The student must choose an option that matches the amendment’s operational
tweaks rather than its general political narrative.
Which change should the student attribute to that amendment?
options:
It reduced Lok Sabha term to four years, restored quorum rules, and barred central forces
from entering states without prior written consent.

It mandated the President act independently of the Cabinet, removed Article 257A, and
required two-thirds quorum for every sitting always in legislatures.

It extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies from five years to six years
and abolished quorum requirements together.

It kept five-year terms but introduced proportional representation, banning Cabinet advice
to the President and ending any emergency deployment powers in states.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “extended the term... from five years to six years” and “abolished quorum requirements,” both appearing in the reference line.

questions.questionText:
Anamika and Bijoy got into a contractual relationship for the supply of tender coconuts for a period
of one year at a fixed price. There was also a force majeure clause in their contract. 6 months into the
contract, the prices of tender coconuts increased to an extent, and due to the increase in prices, strikes
were being held. Owing to this situation, Bijoy was unable to procure tender coconuts for Anamika and
asked for the frustration of the contract under the force majeure (hereinafter referred to as FM) clause.
Decide.
options: FM clause can be applied here because he is unable to procure goods.
FM clause cannot be applied because it is merely a commercial hardship.
FM clause can be applied because strikes were being held.
FM clause can be applied because tender coconuts are perishable goods.
questions.solution: The passage explains that a force majeure clause applies only to unforeseen events that make contractual performance impossible or impractical, not merely more @CLAT_OWNER expensive or commercially burdensome. A rise in prices and the resulting commercial difficulty do not amount to force majeure. Courts have consistently held that increased cost or reduced profitability is insufficient to excuse contractual obligations. Why other options are incorrect: A: Mere inability to procure goods due to higher prices does not constitute force majeure.

questions.questionText:
Six months after marriage, a bride dies under unnatural circumstances in her matrimonial
home. Investigations reveal that shortly before her death she was subjected to harassment and
dowry demands by her husband and in-laws. A case under Section 304B of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita (Dowry Death) is registered. In this situation, what would be the next legal
step regarding the burden of proof?
options:
The prosecution must independently prove beyond reasonable doubt that the death was
directly caused by the accused through harassment and dowry demands, as no
presumption operates in favour of the State.

Once foundational facts are shown, especially cruelty or harassment soon before death in
connection with dowry demand, the court may draw the statutory presumption, which the
accused may rebut.

The accused must prove the actual cause of death and present a defence to rebut the legal
presumption that arises against them on account of the circumstances of the death.

It would be entirely at the court's discretion to determine whether to rely on evidence
presented by the prosecution or the defence first, based on the facts of the case.
questions.solution: The passage states that the burden of proof often shifts to the accused in cases of dowry death when a woman dies under unnatural circumstances within seven years of marriage and there is evidence of cruelty or harassment soon before death in connection with dowry demand. Option B correctly captures the statutory presumption and that it is rebuttable once foundational facts are proved.

questions.questionText:
Meera purchases a "herbal weight loss supplement" from a health store. The packaging prominently displays "100%
        Natural" and "Clinically Proven Results" but does not mention the exact quantity of active ingredients, potential side
        effects, or the standard/grade of herbs used. After consuming the supplement for two weeks, Meera experiences
        severe digestive issues. Upon investigation, she discovers that the product contains synthetic additives not
        mentioned on the label. Meera files a complaint claiming violation of her consumer rights. The company argues that
        they provided sufficient information by stating the product was "natural" and "clinically proven." Based on the
        passage, which consumer right has been primarily violated?
options: Right to Safety, because the supplement caused digestive issues which are hazardous to Meera's health.

Right to Consumer Education, because Meera was ignorant about herbal supplements and should have educated
            herself before purchasing.

Right to be Informed, because the consumer must be told the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and
            price of goods to be protected against unfair trade practices.
Right to be Heard, because Meera's complaint is not being taken seriously by the company.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Right to be Informed, because the consumer must be told the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of goods to be protected against unfair trade practices. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Vikram, a Hindu by religion, married Anjali in a traditional ceremony attended by friends and family
five years ago. However, they never registered their marriage legally. Recently, their relationship
deteriorated, and they have been living separately for the last two years, although they have not legally
divorced. Vikram meets Priya, and after a year of dating, they decide to marry. Assuming his first
marriage is not legally recognized due to the lack of registration, Vikram marries Priya in a ceremony
that is both traditionally conducted and legally registered. Is Vikram’s marriage to Priya valid under the
Hindu Marriage Act (HMA)?
options:
Yes, because the first marriage with Anjali was not registered, it is not recognized legally, allowing Vikram to
marry Priya validly.

No, because under the HMA, Vikram is still considered married to Anjali since Hindu marriages do not
require registration to be valid.

Yes, because Vikram has been separated from Anjali for more than two years, which implies a de facto
divorce under common law principles.

No, because the separation from Anjali does not constitute a legal divorce, and Vikram’s marital status with
Anjali still exists.

questions.questionText:
A landowner granted a licence to a contractor to enter his land and lay pipes. The contractor
completed the work but remained on the land for three additional days to store surplus
equipment, without the landowner's permission. The landowner sued in trespass.
options:
The contractor is liable for trespass from the moment his continued presence exceeded the
scope of the licence; permission once withdrawn or expired does not immunise subsequent
occupation.

The contractor is not liable; having originally entered with permission, his continued
presence cannot constitute trespass as the initial licence covers the entire period of the
project's practical completion.

The contractor is liable only in contract for breach of the licence terms, not in tort; trespass
requires entry without any prior permission and does not apply where the initial presence
was authorised.

The landowner must first demand the contractor's departure and allow a reasonable period
before trespass is constituted; mere overstay without a formal notice does not amount to
trespass.
questions.solution: Once the authorised purpose was complete, the contractor's licence terminated. His continued presence without fresh permission constituted trespass, regardless of the fact that his original entry was lawful.

questions.questionText:
Nisha purchases a new pressure cooker from "KitchenMart," a popular online marketplace. The product does not
        carry any ISI certification mark. After using it twice, the cooker's safety valve malfunctions during cooking, causing
        steam burns to Nisha's hands. She later discovers that the manufacturer had received multiple complaints about the
        same defect but continued selling the product without any warning label or recall. Nisha approaches a consumer
        forum claiming that her Right to Safety has been violated. KitchenMart argues that since Nisha purchased the
        product voluntarily without checking for certification marks, she assumed the risk and cannot claim any consumer
        rights. Based on the passage, is Nisha's claim regarding violation of Right to Safety likely to succeed?
options:
Yes, because the Right to Safety means the consumer's right to be protected against marketing of goods that are
            hazardous to life and property, and the defective pressure cooker caused burns to Nisha.

No, because Nisha failed to insist on quality-certified items such as ISI marked products before purchasing, as
            the passage advises consumers should do.

Yes, because KitchenMart is an online marketplace, and the passage specifically states that online interfaces
            influence decisions more than actual product quality.

No, because the Right to Safety only applies to services that are hazardous, not to goods like pressure cookers
            which are physical products.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because the Right to Safety means the consumer's right to be protected against marketing of goods that are hazardous to life and property, and the defective pressure cooker caused burns to Nisha. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Parliament enacts the “Overseas Financial Fraud Prevention Act” to punish Indian citizens
and India-registered companies that operate fraudulent investment schemes from foreign
countries but target investors residing in India. The Act also requires such companies to
disclose foreign bank accounts connected with the scheme. A company incorporated in India
but operating from Singapore challenges the Act, arguing that Parliament cannot make a law
having extra-territorial operation. Is the challenge likely to succeed?
options:
Yes, because Parliament’s legislative competence is confined to matters occurring within
the territory of India.

Yes, because a Parliamentary law operating beyond India falls outside the scope of Article
245.

No, because a law made by Parliament does not become invalid on the ground that it has
extra-territorial operation.

No, because Parliament may legislate with respect to matters outside India whenever such
legislation affects persons connected with India.
questions.solution: the challenge is based on the fact that the law has extra- territorial operation. Article 245(2) expressly provides that a law made by Parliament does not become invalid on that ground.

questions.questionText:
Meera is prosecuted for poisoning her husband Suresh. Evidence shows: property dispute worth %5
crore; Meera purchased pesticide three days before death; Suresh died after consuming food
prepared by Meera. The FIR filed by Suresh's brother mentions only "sudden death after dinner"
without naming Meera or mentioning the property dispute. These facts emerged during trial.
Based on the passage, what is the appropriate legal conclusion?
options:
Conviction unsustainable because omission of Meera's name and property dispute from FIR
are serious credibility issues under Section 11 Evidence Act, significantly weakening the
circumstantial chain

Conviction sustainable because FIR is not substantive evidence, and omissions are only
relevant if the FIR directly contradicts the trial testimony

Conviction sustainable if circumstances of motive, pesticide purchase, and opportunity to
poison form a complete chain, as FIR omissions affect credibility but don't destroy proved
circumstances

Conviction unsustainable because crucial facts appearing for the first time at trial always
render prosecution case unreliable in circumstantial evidence cases
questions.solution: This is a deceptive question where FIR omissions appear fatal but aren't necessarily so. While the passage states FIR omissions "are relevant in judging witness veracity" and become "particularly serious when known accused names are absent," it doesn't state omissions automatically make conviction impossible.

questions.questionText: A popular fitness influencer promotes a protein supplement on social media, claiming it leads to "guaranteed muscle gain within 2 weeks." The influencer has been paid by the brand but does not disclose this fact. A consumer purchases the product relying on the endorsement but sees no results. Which of the following is the most legally sound conclusion?
options: Both the influencer and the brand may be liable, as the endorsement is misleading and lacks disclosure of material connection.
Only the brand is liable, as influencers merely act as intermediaries in advertising.
Only the influencer is liable, since the claim originated from their account.
Neither party is liable, as consumers are expected to exercise independent judgment.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Both the influencer and the brand may be liable, as the endorsement is misleading and lacks disclosure of material connection. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): If a person pushes another into an eight-foot pit and death follows, the act may
amount to culpable homicide if the person did not know that death was certain.
Reason (R): Every act causing death must necessarily be treated as murder because death,
once caused, is always the natural and certain consequence of the act.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Assertion (A) accurately reflects the reference line because a push into an eight-foot pit causing death may be culpable homicide if the accused did not know death was certain. Reason (R) is false because death-causing acts are not always murder; murder arises where death is the natural and certain consequence, such as deliberate deprivation of food, water, or air until death.

questions.questionText:
Two neighbouring States face administrative difficulties and propose having one common High
Court to hear matters from both States and a nearby Union Territory. A local lawyer objects,
claiming each State must have a separate High Court and Parliament has no power to create a
shared court arrangement. Another lawyer argues that the Constitution allows Parliament to
establish such a common High Court.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
A common High Court is impossible because each State must constitutionally have a separate
High Court.

A common High Court is possible because Articles 214 to 231 govern High Courts and
Parliament may establish a common High Court.

Acommon High Court is possible only if the Supreme Court first approves it through a judicial
order.

A common High Court is impossible unless both States pass identical laws creating the court
by themselves without the interference of Parliament.
questions.solution: The reference line directly supports this: Articles 214 to 231 govern High Courts, and Parliament “may establish a common High Court.” Therefore, the lawyer's objection that Parliament lacks power is inconsistent with the stated constitutional principle. Hence, Option

questions.questionText:
Two experienced wrestlers, A and B, sign a detailed agreement. Under its terms, they agree to
wrestle each other in a public exhibition match on a specific date. The agreement has three
distinct clauses: (i) both will participate in the match; (ii) if either party fails to appear, that
party must pay the other a fixed sum of %5,000 as a penalty; and (iii) the winner of the
wrestling match will receive the entire gate money collected from ticket sales, estimated at
around 21,00,000. B fails to appear, and A sues to enforce the penalty clause (clause ii). B
defends, arguing the entire agreement is a wagering contract, and therefore void under
Section 30 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
options:
The agreement is a wagering contract because the payment to the winner is contingent on
an uncertain future event (who will win), and therefore the entire contract is void.

The agreement is not a wagering contract because the wrestling match is a game of skill
and physical strength, and the winner receives a prize, which is a legitimate incentive.

The agreement is a wagering contract, but the penalty clause (clause ii) can be severed and
enforced as it does not depend on the match's outcome.

The agreement is not a wagering contract for the winner's prize, which comes from public
gate money, not the loser's pocket, and the penalty clause is a separate, enforceable
contract.
questions.solution: This captures the two-fold reasoning of the court: 1. No Mutual Stake: The prize (gate money) is provided by the public, not the losing wrestler.

questions.questionText:
After a civil ceremony, Rohan and Salma receive a marriage certificate and move abroad. Two
years later, Rohan’s father files a suit claiming the marriage is invalid because there were no
religious rites and the family never consented. Salma produces the certificate and says it ends
the dispute. The father argues documents can be challenged like any other evidence and
insists the court must re-examine whether a “real marriage” occurred.
What weight should the certificate carry?
options:
Certificate is weak because family can rebut it by proving no religious rituals occurred, so
the civil record loses all effect now.

Certificate controls because marriage certificate issued after ceremony is conclusive proof
of marriage, so absence of rituals cannot defeat it here today.

Certificate is irrelevant because only customary ceremonies create marriage, and
documents issued by officers are merely supportive evidence, not final at all.

Certificate is conclusive only if witnesses later testify, and without testimony the
certificate cannot prove marriage in any case at all today.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “marriage certificate” and “conclusive proof of marriage,” which is the decisive phrase in the reference line. Once issued after the civil ceremony, the certificate defeats a later challenge based only on absence of religious rites.

questions.questionText:
A consumer advocacy group called "JanAdhikar" files a public interest complaint before the National Consumer
        Disputes Redressal Commission regarding misleading advertisements by a major telecom company. The telecom
        company objects, arguing that JanAdhikar is a registered NGO with political affiliations to an opposition party and
        therefore lacks standing to represent consumer interests. JanAdhikar counters that any organization working for
        consumer welfare can represent consumer interests. Based on the passage, does the telecom company's objection
        regarding JanAdhikar's political affiliation have merit?
options:
No, because the Right to be Heard allows any organization to represent consumers at appropriate forums,
            regardless of their political or commercial affiliations.

Yes, because the passage states that consumer representation should be strengthened through non-political,
            non-commercial consumer organisations.

No, because the Right to Seek Redressal allows consumers to take help from any consumer organisation without
            restrictions.

Yes, because the passage specifically prohibits political parties from filing complaints on behalf of consumers
            under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because the passage states that consumer representation should be strengthened through non-political, non-commercial consumer organisations. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Enraged by the company’s executive decision on wages, Rahim and his colleagues decide to go
over to the headquarters of the company located in the capital city for a peaceful protest. They
decide to sit in small groups of 7-10 people across the neighbourhood, where the headquarters
office is located to protest. When company officials attempted to engage with the group, a
physical altercation broke out and the group collectively threatened the officials to concede.
What is the status of the group now?
options:
This is an unlawful assembly, as the number of individuals in the group exceeds the legal
limit for a peaceful protest.
This is a protest under Article 19, as their intent was to only hold a peaceful protest.

This is an unlawful assembly, as the object of the group has changed with the use of
criminal force.
This is not an unlawful assembly, as the fight broke out due to the company official.
questions.solution: An unlawful assembly consists of five or more persons with the common object. The common object can change over time, thus also changing the nature of the group.

questions.questionText:
A, an accused, has allegedly murdered a girl living in the same locality as him. A is young, aged only 23 years
old and is yet to make a good career out of his life. While the proceedings for the murder case go on, it becomes
very evident that A has committed the murder. To save his future career prospects, the State, playing the role of the
prosecution, and A, the accused, come into an agreement that if A pays compensation worth rupees 1 lakh, he will
not be imprisoned and will be granted bail. Decide the validity of such an agreement.
options: It is valid because the State and the accused can come to an agreement that the accused pay fine.
It is valid because the State and the accused can agree that the accused pay a penalty as a form of compensation.
It is invalid because murder cannot be a compoundable offence.
It is invalid because the State cannot take decisions.
questions.solution: The passage clearly states that although certain offences may be compounded through an agreement between the prosecution and the accused, murder is not a compoundable offence. Public policy and the seriousness of the offence prevent parties from avoiding criminal liability merely by paying compensation. Consequently, the agreement between the State and A is legally invalid. Therefore, Option C is correct. Why other options are incorrect: A. This is incorrect because the ability to compound offences does not extend to murder. B. This is incorrect because compensation cannot replace criminal punishment for a non-

questions.questionText: A, a moneylender, had been demanding repayment of his money from B for several weeks. One evening, A forcibly stopped B on a deserted road, caught hold of his collar, and pointed a knife at his chest saying, “Give me Rs. 50,000 right now, or I will stab you.” Terrified, B called his friend C on the phone and asked him to immediately bring Rs. 50,000 to the spot. Within minutes, C arrived and handed over the money to A in B’s presence, after which A fled. From the options below choose the correct answer.
options: This is extortion because there is an element of dishonest inducement.
This is robbery because there was immediate transfer of valuable under threat.
This is extortion because there was threat and fear.
This is robbery because there was a threat of killing.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: This is robbery because there was immediate transfer of valuable under threat. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): A wife cannot ordinarily be prosecuted under Section 406 IPC for taking away
her own streedhan.
Reason (R): The offence of criminal breach of trust requires entrustment of property followed
by dishonest misappropriation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct Explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct Explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
Ais false, but R is true.
questions.solution: Option A — Correct. Both statements are true, and the Reason directly explains the Assertion.

questions.questionText:
The Union Government passes legislation requiring all new residential constructions to
mandatorily incorporate renewable energy infrastructure, citing its constitutional obligation to
protect the environment and ensure the right to life under Articles 21 and 48A. Builders
challenge the law as an unreasonable restriction on their right to carry on business. The
Government defends the mandate as flowing directly from the State's constitutional duty
recognized in M.K. Ranjitsinh. Which assessment is most legally sound?
options:
The law is unconstitutional because imposing construction mandates on private builders
exceeds the State's environmental protection powers under Articles 48A and 21 of the
Constitution.

The law is a valid exercise of State power since the passage confirms the State bears
constitutional duty to protect the environment, and reasonable regulatory mandates serve
that recognized obligation directly.

The law is invalid because M.K. Ranjitsinh only created rights against climate harm, not
affirmative legislative power to impose infrastructure obligations on private construction
activity.

The law requires mandatory referral to a constitutional bench before enforcement, since
any legislation touching fundamental rights under Article 21 must receive prior judicial
validation.
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states the judgment underscored "the duty of the State" to protect the environment and highlighted India's "statutory framework, ranging from the Environment Protection Act, 1986 to the Energy Conservation Act, 2001" as instruments through which the State discharges this obligation. Legislation mandating renewable energy infrastructure in new constructions is a direct exercise of this recognized State duty, making it a constitutionally grounded regulatory measure.

questions.questionText:
Sunita Devi is an MLA in the Bihar Legislative Assembly belonging to the "Samajwadi Janata Party" (SJP). She defies
        the party whip during a vote on a resolution condemning the central government's agricultural policies. Mohan Lal,
        an SJP member serving as a Rajya Sabha MP from Bihar, files a disqualification petition against Sunita before the
        Speaker of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. Based on the passage, is Mohan Lal's petition against Sunita
        maintainable?
options:
Yes, because Mohan Lal is an elected representative from Bihar and belongs to the same party as Sunita, giving
            him sufficient interest in maintaining party discipline in the state.

Yes, because only a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly qualifies as “any other member of the House” for
            petitions against its MLAs.


1

Yes, because the Tenth Schedule applies to both Parliament and state assemblies, and therefore members from
            either House can file petitions against legislators in any other House.

No, because only a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly qualifies as “any other member of the House” for
            petitions against its MLAs..
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because only a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly qualifies as “any other member of the House” for petitions against its MLAs. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
State X begins large-scale lithium mining in a mountain region close to State Y’s river basin. It
claims that, as a sovereign State, it may exploit its natural resources without seeking outside
permission. However, untreated mining waste begins flowing into State Y’s drinking water
sources. State Y complains that sovereignty does not allow a State to cause environmental
damage beyond its jurisdiction. State X argues that resource exploitation is entirely an
internal matter.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
State X has resource rights, but must ensure activities do not damage other States or areas
beyond jurisdiction.

State X has absolute freedom because sovereignty removes every environmental duty
toward neighbouring States.

State Y cannot object unless State X voluntarily signs a separate compensation agreement
first.

State Y can stop all mining because neighbouring States control each other’s resource
policies.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “sovereign right,” “exploit their own resources,” and “ensure... do not cause environmental damage to other States,” matching the reference line.

questions.questionText:
A software company, "CodeCraft," signs a five-year contract to provide
      maintenance services to a bank. The contract contains a clause: "In the event of a
      nationwide internet shutdown lasting more than 30 consecutive days, this contract
      shall automatically stand terminated." Two years into the contract, such a
      shutdown occurs. CodeCraft stops services, and the bank sues for breach. How
      would the passage's legal framework describe the termination clause?
options:
It is a suspensive condition under Section 32, as the obligation to perform is
    contingent on the internet being available.

It is a resolutory condition, as it extinguishes a pre-existing contractual
    obligation upon the happening of a specified future event.

It is an invalid clause because it was omitted from the final version of the
    Contract Act and therefore has no legal basis.

It is a classic force majeure clause governed by Section 32, which makes the
    contract void upon the event becoming impossible.

questions.questionText:
The power of Parliament to frame its own rules of procedure for conducting business is
        derived from which Article, and what is the key verb used that indicates this is a discretionary
        power?
options: Article 105, which uses the word "shall"
Article 118, which uses the word "shall"
Article 105, which uses the word "may"
Article 118, which uses the word "may"

questions.questionText:
During a rapidly spreading warehouse fire, Ritu, the site supervisor, orders workers to pull down a
neighbour's wooden shed to create a firebreak. The shed is destroyed, but the fire stops and a dense
residential lane is saved. The shed-owner lodges a complaint alleging intentional destruction of
property. Ritu argues she acted in good faith, without any criminal intention, and solely to prevent
much greater harm to nearby homes and people.
Which outcome best follows on these facts?
options:
Defence fails because the act was deliberate and targeted at another's property; even if the
result was beneficial, intentional destruction cannot be excused without the owner's prior
consent.

Defence fails because destroying property is always criminal mischief, and necessity never
excuses deliberate destruction of another's house.

Defence succeeds only if the act was done without criminal intention, in good faith, and to
prevent other harm.

Defence fails because the harm caused must equal or exceed the harm prevented before
necessity can apply, and here only one shed was lost against a neighbourhood saved.
questions.solution: This option directly uses "without criminal intention" and "in good faith" and links the act to preventing “other harm," tracking the reference line's wording. These three conditions form the conjunctive test under Section 81 — all must be satisfied together.

questions.questionText:
Aaliya’s husband, Sameer, has not provided any maintenance for two years. During this
period, Aaliya borrowed money from relatives for food, rent, and medical expenses. Sameer
argues that his business failed and he was ill for several months, so his inability to maintain
her should excuse him. Aaliya seeks dissolution, contending that prolonged non-maintenance
itself gives her a legal ground and that poverty or illness cannot defeat it.
Which result best follows?
options:
Aaliya can claim divorce because two-year maintenance failure is enough, and poverty or
illness is no valid excuse.

Aaliya cannot claim divorce because poverty and illness always excuse non-maintenance by
husband in tough times.
Aaliya can claim divorce only if Sameer deliberately spent money on another woman.

Aaliya cannot claim divorce unless she proves physical cruelty along with non-
maintenance.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “fails to provide maintenance for two years” and “poverty or illness is not treated as a valid excuse,” matching the reference line. Sameer’s business failure or illness does not defeat Aaliya’s statutory ground if two years of non- maintenance is established.

questions.questionText:
A start-up signs an indemnity clause promising to protect its CFO against any penalty the
regulators may impose for an internal compliance failure. A whistleblower complaint is filed,
but no notice has been issued and no penalty proceedings have begun. The CFO demands
immediate payment into escrow, saying the indemnity is "for protection" and uncertainty is
enough. The company refuses, saying the indemnity obligation is triggered only if a specified
loss event actually happens.
How should the timing of liability be understood?
options:
The indemnifier must pay immediately because indemnity is absolute, and contingency is
irrelevant once promise is signed, even if no loss event occurs.

The indemnifier must pay immediately because liability arises whenever the indemnity-
holder feels insecure, so court orders pre-emptive reimbursement to avoid future disputes.

Indemnifier need not pay yet because no regulatory notice has been issued and no penalty
proceedings have begun, so the specified loss event that would trigger the indemnity
obligation has not occurred.

Indemnifier pays only when liability arises on the happening of a specified event causing
loss, so payment is premature before the specified loss event occurs.
questions.solution: The option directly uses "liability arises on the happening of a specified event causing loss," mirroring the reference line. Because no penalty event has occurred yet, demanding immediate payment is premature under the stated contingent logic.

questions.questionText:
An electrician, Nikhil, is called to “Flat 12” by a client, but the building has two Flat 12s in
different towers. He lawfully enters the wrong Flat 12, repairs dangerous wiring, and replaces
a burnt switchboard. The occupant, Tara, watches silently, knows she did not call him, and
later uses the safe wiring daily. When Nikhil discovers the error and asks for charges, Tara
refuses, saying she never consented and no contract exists.
How should Nikhil’s compensation claim be decided?
options:
He cannot claim because no contract existed, so any benefit received is free unless the
recipient promised payment beforehand clearly.

He can claim because any work done on another’s property automatically creates a debt,
even if meant as a gift.

He cannot claim because mistake about identity bars recovery, and restitution applies only
when the recipient demanded the service directly.

He can claim because he lawfully provided services without intending them gratuitous and
the recipient benefited, so must compensate him.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “lawfully provided services,” » 6, “without intending them gratuitous,” and “recipient benefited,” mirroring the reference line. Tara accepted the benefit while knowing it was not meant as a gift, so compensation is due to prevent unjust enrichment.

questions.questionText:
ABC Industries operates a manufacturing facility in Maharashtra with a floor area of 25,000
square meters and generates 80 kg of waste per day. The company installs a bio-methanation
plant to process its wet waste on-site as mandated under the SWM Rules and additionally uses
12% RDF in place of solid fuel, whereas the legal requirement at the time of implementation is
only 6%. ABC Industries applies for carbon credits under the CCTS for both activities. Based on
the passage, which of the following conclusions is most accurate regarding ABC Industries'
eligibility for carbon credits?
options:
ABC Industries cannot claim credits for either activity because both bio-methanation and RDF
usage are mandated under the SWM Rules, and the CCTS regulatory surplus doctrine bars
credits for legally mandated activities

ABC Industries can claim credits for the entire 12% RDF usage because using any RDF
demonstrates environmental commitment beyond business-as-usual scenarios

ABC Industries can claim credits only for the 6% additional RDF usage (12% minus 6%
mandated) because this portion exceeds minimum legal requirements and demonstrates
additionality

ABC Industries can claim credits for both activities because Rule 8 explicitly encourages
carbon credit generation, creating a special exemption from CCTS additionality requirements
questions.solution: The passage states that "projects exceeding minimum requirements can demonstrate additionality" and specifically provides the example: "if industrial units are required to use 6% RDF but voluntarily use 20%, that additional 14% demonstrates they're doing more than legally necessary." ABC Industries uses 12% RDF when only 6% is mandated, so the additional 6% exceeds legal requirements and qualifies for credits. However, ABC's floor area (25,000 sq m) triggers EBWGR obligations under Rule 6 (floor

questions.questionText:
Kavya is convicted for entering a neighbour’s private garden at night to annoy him and
refusing to leave when asked. The court labels it “criminal trespass” and sentences her to six
months’ imprisonment without any fine. Kavya appeals, arguing the sentence exceeds the
maximum punishment for this offence. The State argues the court can impose higher custody
to deter such behaviour.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Sentence is illegal because imprisonment up to one month applies so six months cannot
stand; court must reduce it today.

Sentence is valid because imprisonment up to one year applies so six months is within
limit for criminal trespass here.

Sentence is valid because imprisonment up to three years applies so six months is well
within court’s power today clearly.

Punishment is imprisonment for up to three months, or a fine up to 25,000, or both, so six
months illegal.
questions.solution: The option directly reproduces the reference words “imprisonment for up to three months” and “fine up to %5,000, or both.” Since Kavya received six months, it exceeds the stated maximum and is therefore illegal on the punishment ceiling described.

questions.questionText:
Priya runs a successful online business from her home, selling artisanal handicrafts. Her neighbour, Vikram,
starts a construction project that involves loud machinery, significantly disrupting Priya's business operations. The
noise makes it difficult for Priya to communicate with her clients and concentrate on her work. Priya sues Vikram
for nuisance, claiming that his construction project is causing her business losses. Vikram argues that he has all the
necessary permits and is conducting construction only during legally allowed hours. Considering the principles of


tort law, especially the concepts of 'Damnum Sine Injuria’ and ‘Injuria Sine Damnum', which statement best
applies to this case?
options: Priya can claim damages, as Vikram’s construction is disrupting her business.
Priya cannot claim damages, as Vikram is exercising his legal rights.
Priya can claim damages, as she has a legal right to a noise-free environment.
Priya cannot claim damages, as she does not have a legal right to business profits.
questions.solution: The passage explains the doctrine of Damnum Sine Injuria, which means actual damage without the violation of a legal right is not actionable in tort. Vikram possesses the necessary permits and carries out construction during legally permitted hours. Although Priya suffers financial loss because of the construction noise, there is no indication that Vikram has violated any legal right belonging to Priya. Like the defendant in Mayor & Co. of Bradford v. Pickles, Vikram is merely exercising his lawful rights. Therefore, Option B is correct. Why other options are incorrect:
