questions.questionText:
A registered brand “SUNLITE” sells soaps. A small shop begins selling soaps under
“SUNLITE” with identical packaging and claims it is “just a tribute” and that customers can
check the seller name printed in tiny letters. The proprietor sues for infringement, alleging
unauthorised use of an identical or deceptively similar mark for identical goods in the course
of trade. The shop argues that it is not infringement because it did not copy the full logo and
did not intend deception.
Which statement best captures the infringement rule?
options:
Not infringement because intention is required, and without intent to deceive, identical
mark use cannot be stopped under law.

Infringement because unauthorised use of identical or deceptively similar mark for
identical goods in course of trade is covered.

Not infringement because only unregistered marks can sue, and registration prevents civil
remedies and forces criminal complaint only.

Infringement only if goods are different; if goods are identical, the law assumes consumers
will not be confused at all.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “unauthorised use,” “identical or deceptively similar mark,” “identical goods,” and “course of trade,” matching the reference line’s wording. Selling soaps under the same mark for the same goods fits the definition.

questions.questionText:
Motu and Patlu are childhood friends. One day, Motu approached Patlu to ask for a sum of Rs.
40,000 to pay his mother’s urgent medical bills. Patlu without a thought, transferred him the
money. Motu promises to return the money soon. However, a month passes, and Motu keeps
making excuses. Upon learning what had happened, Patlu’s 5 sisters reach Motu’s tea stall
with weapons to threaten him to return the money. Decide which is the most suitable
statement:
options: This is not an unlawful assembly, as no criminal act has been committed against Ram.

This is an unlawful assembly, as entering Motu’s shop with ill intention constituted
mischief.

This is not an unlawful assembly, as the sisters are trying to recover the money that is
legally owed by Motu.

This is an unlawful assembly, as the sisters are trying to enforce a right by a show of
criminal force.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: This is an unlawful assembly, as the sisters are trying to enforce a right by a show of criminal force. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Samar and Nandini exchange garlands in a private temple ritual with families present and
then start living together as “husband and wife.” Months later, they seek legal recognition
under a civil marriage route because they want a formal certificate for a visa application. They
never appeared before any Marriage Officer, and no civil declaration was made before
witnesses. Nandini argues the religious ceremony should be treated as sufficient since both
consented and the community recognises them.
What is the best legal conclusion?
options:
Valid under this Act, because any customary ceremony between consenting adults creates
a civil marriage, even without appearing before officers or witnesses today too.

Valid under this Act, because registration later cures any defect, and solemnisation rules
are optional when families already performed rites publicly for their marriage.

Not valid under this Act, because the Act requires renouncing religion first, and a religious
ceremony proves they failed that requirement before civil marriage.

Not valid under this Act, because it is a legal contract solemnised before a Marriage Officer
and witnesses, rather than religious rituals alone here.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “legal contract,” » & “solemnised before a Marriage Officer and witnesses,” and “rather than religious rituals,” mirroring the reference line. Without civil solemnisation before the Officer and witnesses, the claim under this civil route cannot succeed.

questions.questionText:
A fertilizer factory accidentally releases toxic waste into a nearby river, causing
           extensive environmental damage and health issues for local residents. The factory
           is found liable under the absolute liability doctrine. What additional obligation
           does the factory have under the integrated "Polluter Pays" principle?
options:
The factory must only compensate the victims for personal injuries and property
damage.

The factory must pay fines to the government but has no duty to remediate the
environment under any circumstances.

The factory can avoid further liability if it demonstrates that the release was due to an
act of a third party.

The factory must bear the cost of cleaning up and restoring the damaged river
environment in addition to compensating victims.

questions.questionText:
Karan is stopped by the traffic police at a midnight checkpoint. A breathalyzer test confirms
he is intoxicated. Karan is alone in his car. The police officer, citing that Karan is a “repeat
offender” with three previous drunk driving tickets, immediately calls a tow truck to seize the
vehicle and take it to the police station for a minimum of 15 days. Based on the High Court’s
ruling, is the officer’s action lawful?
options:
Yes, because the primary objective of the law is to punish repeat offenders and prevent
them from endangering public safety again.

Yes, because the officer has the authority to keep the vehicle in safe custody if no sober
person is available to take it.

No, because prior instances of drunk driving do not confer additional powers of seizure
unless specifically authorized by a statute.

No, because the police are never allowed to prevent an intoxicated person from driving if
they are the sole owner of the vehicle.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: Option C is correct because the passage explicitly states that “prior instances of drunk driving... do not, by themselves, confer additional powers of seizure unless specifically authorised by statute.” While the police can prevent the person from driving, they cannot use “repeat offense” as a justification for an automatic seizure.

questions.questionText:
State M’s army occupies a border region of State N and then issues a proclamation declaring the region
“permanently annexed.” M replaces local flags, issues new passports, and claims N has “lost sovereignty
forever.” N’s government protests that the occupation is only temporary control and that sovereignty
cannot be legally extinguished by force. M argues that its proclamation and administrative integration
prove a lawful transfer of title.
Which statement best reflects the passage’s treatment of sovereignty?
options:
Annexation decree transfers sovereignty, so occupation ends and occupier gains lawful title, even if
troops still patrol the streets.

Sovereignty is not lawfully transferred, so occupier must withdraw within twenty-four hours and
every administrative act becomes void automatically.

Sovereignty is not lawfully transferred, so territory remains occupied and annexation claims lack
legal effect under international law during conflict still.

Sovereignty transfers if locals vote, so annexation becomes lawful once occupier conducts
referendum and issues new passports to residents there afterward.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “sovereignty is not lawfully transferred,” matching the reference line, and correctly concludes annexation claims lack legal effect while occupation continues. It preserves the distinction between temporary control and lawful sovereignty transfer.

questions.questionText:
A law enacted by Parliament substantially restricts freedom of speech on grounds beyond public
order as a ground. Upon challenge, the Judiciary examines the law and declares it
unconstitutional. Upon examination the court also finds that such restrictions in the legislation
are unrelated to the scope of reasonable restrictions. This judicial intervention most accurately
reflects which principle emphasized in the passage?
options: The authority of the Legislature to determine the scope of fundamental rights.
The supremacy of constitutional law ensured through judicial review.
The power of the Executive to balance rights with public interest.
The doctrine of separation of powers limiting judicial interference.
questions.solution: The passage emphasizes that judicial review embodies the supremacy of law, allowing courts to examine the actions of the Legislature, Executive, and even the Judiciary itself to ensure they conform to the Constitution. By declaring the law unconstitutional, the court exercises this power to protect fundamental rights and uphold constitutional values, which directly reflects the principle of judicial review rather than parliamentary or executive supremacy.

questions.questionText:
Seventeen-year-old Aarav, who lives alone while studying in another city, falls seriously ill
and is admitted to a nearby private hospital. Since Aarav cannot legally enter into binding
contracts, the hospital provides essential medical treatment and medicines without obtaining
any formal agreement. After recovery, Aarav refuses to pay the hospital bill, arguing that he is
a minor and therefore not legally bound by any contract. The hospital then approaches the
court seeking recovery of the treatment expenses.
How should the court decide?
options:
The hospital cannot recover any amount because a minor is completely incapable of
entering any legal obligation under any circumstances.

The hospital can recover the expenses because necessaries supplied to a minor allow
reimbursement to be claimed from the minor’s property.

The hospital cannot recover the expenses because treatment provided without a prior
agreement is presumed to be voluntary assistance.

The hospital can recover the expenses only if the minor had expressly promised to repay
the amount after receiving treatment.
questions.solution: The law recognises that essential goods or services such as food, shelter, or medical treatment may be supplied to persons incapable of contracting, including minors. In such cases, the supplier can recover the reasonable value of those necessaries from the minor’s property, even though no formal contract exists.

questions.questionText:
After occupying a province, State Q dissolves the local courts, cancels the entire criminal code, and
introduces Q’s domestic laws in a new language. Local police are disbanded and replaced with Q’s
military police. Crime spikes, and Q argues the changes are necessary for “efficiency” and long-
term governance. The occupied state claims Q must maintain order while preserving the local legal
framework as far as possible.
Which statement best reflects the occupier’s obligation described in the passage?
options:
Occupier must maintain public order and safety but may suspend all existing laws completely
replacing courts whenever it prefers for security reasons during control.

Occupier must restore and maintain public order and safety while respecting existing laws as
far as possible so wholesale replacement breaches duty.

Occupier may freely rewrite all laws to suit its policy because military authority includes
permanent legislative sovereignty during control of territory without limits.

Occupier owes only humanitarian aid so public order and existing laws are irrelevant;
administrative chaos is acceptable during occupation on grounds of necessity alone.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “restore and maintain public order and safety” and “respect the existing laws... as far as possible,” matching the reference line’s core language.

questions.questionText:
Meera, a member of the State Legislative Assembly, was elected on the ticket of Naitik Vikas
Party. The party president had authorised its Chief Whip to issue voting directions in the
House. Before a no-confidence motion, the Chief Whip directed all party members to vote
against the motion. Meera disagreed and obtained written approval from the chairperson of
her district unit, who was politically influential but had not been authorised by the party to
permit contrary voting in the House. She then voted in favour of the motion. Naitik Vikas
Party initiated disqualification proceedings. Can Meera avoid disqualification?
options:
Yes, because she obtained written approval before voting, and Paragraph 2(1)(b) protects
members who act with prior permission.

Yes, because the approval came from a party functionary before the vote, and she may
argue that such approval should be treated as prior permission, even though the Chief
Whip had issued a contrary direction.

No, because she voted contrary to a direction issued by an authorised party authority
without valid prior permission from the political party or an authorised person.

No, because any vote on a no-confidence motion contrary to the party’s position results in
disqualification irrespective of permission.
questions.solution: Meera voted contrary to the direction issued by the authorised Chief Whip. Although she obtained written approval from the district chairperson, that chairperson had not been authorised by the party to permit contrary voting in the House.

questions.questionText:
In response to the new rule requiring independent directors (IDs) to clear an online proficiency test,
the Association of Corporate Entities (ACE) decides to file a lawsuit challenging the rule's validity. ACE
argues that the rule undermines the prestige and dignity of IDs who, by virtue of their experience and
stature, already satisfy the statutory eligibility criteria. Furthermore, ACE argues that the rule is
unnecessary and redundant because the Companies Act already imposes stringent eligibility
requirements for IDs. In light of the given scenario, would ACE's lawsuit against the new rule be
justified?
options:
Yes, because the new rule is demeaning to the status of independent directors who have already proven their
expertise through years of experience.

No, because while the rule may seem redundant, it provides an additional layer of assurance that IDs are
equipped to fulfil their duties effectively.

Yes, because the Companies Act already imposes sufficient eligibility criteria for IDs, making the rule
unnecessary.

No, because the rule provides an objective measure of an ID's proficiency, which cannot be fully determined
based on reputation or experience alone.

questions.questionText:
A enters into an agreement with B, a 19-year-old Hindu male, promising to pay him a monthly
allowance on the condition that B will not marry until he attains the age of 21. B agrees to the
condition and begins receiving payments under the agreement. However, at the age of 20, B
decides to marry, and A stops the payments, claiming that B has violated a valid contractual
condition.
In light of the principles discussed in the passage, what is the correct legal position?
options:
The agreement is valid because it restrains marriage only up to the legally permissible age
for marriage under personal law, and thus does not impose an unlawful restriction.

The agreement is void because B is a major, and any restriction on marriage after
attaining 18 years of age is legally impermissible.

The agreement is void because all agreements in restraint of marriage are invalid,
irrespective of the duration or purpose of restraint.

The agreement is voidable at B’s option since he has attained majority and can choose
whether to be bound by such conditions.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The agreement is valid because it restrains marriage only up to the legally permissible age for marriage under personal law, and thus does not impose an unlawful restriction. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Saira lives with her husband in a home registered solely in her mother-in-law's name. After a
dispute, the husband changes the locks, leaves Saira's clothes outside, and says she has "no
right" because she has no title documents. The mother-in-law supports the eviction and
threatens police action for trespass if Saira returns. Saira seeks an order allowing her to
return and live there safely, arguing that her residence right does not depend on ownership.
Which statement best matches the described right?
options:
She cannot stay because only the legal owner may decide residence, and without title she
must leave immediately.

She may stay only if her mother-in-law permits, because shared household rights always
depend on consent of the titleholder.

She has a right to reside in the shared household, irrespective of ownership or title, so
eviction order fails.

She may stay only if she first obtains a divorce decree, since residence orders under the Act
are available solely to women whose marriages have been legally dissolved by a competent
court.
questions.solution: This option directly uses "right to reside in the shared household" and "irrespective of ownership or title," matching the reference line's exact words. The house qualifies as a shared household because Saira and her husband lived together in it within a domestic relationship.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Verma has worked in an unlisted company, TechVentures, for the last 15 years as a key
managerial personnel. Recently, he has decided to become an Independent Director (ID) and wishes to
understand if he is required to clear the proficiency test conducted by the Indian Institute of Corporate
Affairs (IICA). Given Mr. Verma's circumstances, is he exempt from clearing the proficiency test as per
the new company law?
options: YES, because he is a key managerial personnel and the rule exempts all managerial personnel from the test.
YES, because he has served as a key managerial personnel in an unlisted company for more than ten years.
NO, because the rule applies to all individuals aspiring to become IDs, regardless of their past experience.
NO, because he works for an unlisted company and the rule only exempts personnel from listed companies.

questions.questionText:
A State legislature passes a detailed Education Code and claims exclusive authority over
schooling policy. Within months, Parliament enacts a national Education Standards Act and
says it can co-legislate because the subject now sits in a shared list. The State challenges the
Centre’s competence, arguing education was historically state-controlled. A constitutional
historian explains that a 1976 amendment shifted several subjects to expand central control.
Which described shift best directly supports Parliament’s claim of concurrent competence?
options:
It shifted defence and foreign affairs into the State List, giving states primary control and
reducing Parliament’s reach over national policy choices.

It abolished the Concurrent List entirely, forcing every subject to be either Union or State,
and forbidding overlapping legislation thereafter by design.

It moved police and public order to the Union List, permitting central takeover of daily law
enforcement and local peacekeeping functions directly.

It shifted education, forests, and administration of justice from the State List to the
Concurrent List, increasing central control over them.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “shifted... from the State List to the Concurrent List” and includes “education,” matching the reference line’s core movement.

questions.questionText:
A National Emergency has been proclaimed in India due to a perceived threat of armed rebellion. The
President has issued a proclamation under Article 352 of the Constitution. The emergency has been
approved by both Houses of Parliament and is currently in effect. As a result of the emergency, certain
provisions and rights have been suspended. A and B, during this National Emergency. A is a journalist
who has been critical of the government's policies and has written articles exposing corruption within the
administration. B is a student activist who has been actively participating in peaceful protests advocating
for social justice and equality. Both A and B are concerned about the impact of the National Emergency
on their rights and freedoms. During the National Emergency, which fundamental rights will not be
affected according to the provisions of the Indian Constitution?
options: Freedom of speech and expression (Article 19).
Right to peaceful assembly and association (Article 20).
Right to protection from arrest and detention (Article 21).
Both (B) and (C).
questions.solution: The passage specifically states that during a National Emergency, the rights under Articles 20 and 21 remain unaffected. Therefore, the rights represented by Options B (Article 20) and C (Article 21) continue to enjoy constitutional protection even while Article 19 is suspended. Why other options are incorrect: A: Freedom of speech and expression forms part of Article 19, which is suspended during a National Emergency under Article 358. B: Although Article 20 remains protected, this option is incomplete because Article 21 is also

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The Central Government may, in a proper case, block access to an entire
application under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, instead of limiting
itself only to particular posts, messages, URLs or channels.
Reason (R): Section 69A must be read with Section 2(1)(v), which defines “information”
broadly to include computer programmes, software and databases.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.solution: The assertion is correct because the passage explains that an application or platform itself may fall within the meaning of “information”. The reason is also correct because this conclusion comes from reading Section 69A with the broad definition of “information” under Section 2(1)(v), which includes computer programmes, software and databases.

questions.questionText:
An environmental group seeks a Writ of Mandamus against the FSSAI. They present a
specific statutory rule from the Food Safety Act that requires the FSSAI to publish an annual
“Contaminant Report” every January. It is now August, and the report has not been published.
The FSSAI argues that they have been busy with other safety drives. How does the principle
regarding Mandamus apply here?
options:
The Writ should be refused because the Court cannot issue a Mandamus based on a single
instance of a missed deadline.

The Writ should be issued because any delay by a statutory body automatically constitutes
a “systemic failure” requiring a National Task Force.

The Writ should be refused because the FSSAI is a specialized body, and the Court must
defer to its decision on when to prioritize its work.

The Writ should be issued because there is a clear, non-discretionary legal duty that the
authority has demonstrably failed to perform.
questions.solution: Option D is correct because the passage defines Mandamus as applicable when there is a “clear legal duty” and a “demonstrable failure in its discharge”. A specific statutory requirement to publish a report by a certain date is a clear duty.

questions.questionText:
Arjun, an accused in a robbery case, was released on bail. His bail conditions required him not
to threaten or contact any witness. After release, Arjun relocated to another city and made no
contact with witnesses. However, one of the witnesses, Kavita, began receiving anonymous
threatening calls from an unknown number. Kavita approached the court seeking both bail
cancellation of Arjun and protection under the Witness Protection Scheme. The court found no
direct evidence linking Arjun to the calls. Which of the following represents the most legally
sound course of action for the court, based on the passage?
options:
The court should cancel Arjun's bail immediately, since any threat to a witness during the
bail period is automatically attributable to the accused, making bail cancellation the
appropriate and sufficient remedy.

The court should dismiss both applications since the Witness Protection Scheme is only
applicable once the accused is convicted, and bail cancellation requires a formal FIR
against the accused for the new offence.

The court should grant Kavita protection under the Witness Protection Scheme since
threats have materialised, but should not cancel bail without evidence of Arjun's direct
involvement in breaching bail conditions.

The court should refer the matter to the Law Commission of India for fresh
recommendations, since the Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 does not cover threats
originating from unidentified persons.
questions.solution: The passage clarifies that the Witness Protection Scheme is a curative measure activated when threats materialise — which they have for Kavita. Bail cancellation, however, requires evidence of the accused breaching bail conditions.

questions.questionText:
Priya is a Class 9 student in a government school in rural Rajasthan. Her school has no
functional girls' toilet and provides no sanitary products. She frequently misses school during
menstruation due to discomfort and shame. Based on the passage, which of the following best
describes the legal position?
options:
Priya's situation involves only a social and hygiene issue and does not attract any
constitutional provision under the given framework.

The school's failure violates Article 21, as the denial of MHM infrastructure causes
humiliation, health risk, and loss of dignity to Priya.

Priya's rights under Article 21A are violated, but Article 21 cannot be invoked since she is
not facing a direct threat to her physical life.

Only Article 14 is violated in Priya's case, since the school treats boys and girls differently
by not providing separate facilities.
questions.solution: The passage states that denial of MHM infrastructure 'cause[s] humiliation, health risks, and loss of dignity,' which are violations of Article 21. Option B correctly identifies this.

questions.questionText:
The Legislature of State X enacts the “Public Order and Online Accountability Act,” stating
that its purpose is to maintain public order and prevent unrest caused by misleading online
content. The Act requires every social media platform operating anywhere in India to obtain a
licence from State X if its posts are accessible to users in State X. It also empowers State X
authorities to suspend accounts of users located in other States if their posts are likely to
affect public sentiment in State X. The State defends the law as a reasonable restriction
necessary to balance free expression with public order. A platform headquartered and
operating mainly outside State X challenges the Act as colourable legislation. Which
conclusion is most appropriate?
options:
The law is valid because public order justifies a reasonable restriction on online expression
affecting State X residents.

The law is valid because the title and stated object show that State X is acting within its
public-order concern.

The law may be invalid because constitutional balancing cannot save a law whose real
substance enters a field beyond competence.

The law may be invalid if the platform proves that State X acted with dishonest political or
personal motive.
questions.solution: the passage provides that a law may appear to be within authority, but if its real substance goes beyond constitutional competence, it may be treated as colourable legislation. Constitutional balancing or reasonable-restriction language cannot cure a basic lack of legislative competence.

questions.questionText:
State R occupies a border strip and orders all civilians living near the frontier to board buses to
“temporary camps” far away. Families are told they cannot return until “security conditions improve,”
with no date provided. R claims relocation is necessary to build a buffer zone and prevent attacks. A
human rights group argues the measure unlawfully transfers civilians and threatens permanent
displacement. R argues the move is administrative and not punitive.
Which statement best fits the humanitarian protection described in the passage?
options:
Forced transfer of civilians is prohibited so relocating residents for security corridor violates
humanitarian protections of occupation law very clearly.

Forced transfer of civilians is prohibited but relocation becomes lawful if consent is presumed from
silence and compensation offered in law.

Forced transfer is lawful if occupier offers compensation so security relocation with payment
complies with humanitarian duties in law.

Forced transfer is lawful when civilians are moved within same territory so only deportation abroad
is prohibited by law.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “prohibition on forced transfer or deportation,” matching the reference line, and applies it to forced mass relocation into camps with indefinite return. The measure is a forced transfer of civilians, which is precisely what the humanitarian protection forbids.

questions.questionText:
Alpha Ltd. and Beta Corp. execute a service agreement stating: "Beta shall provide technical
support for 10 lakh monthly." The contract contains no termination clause. After 18 months,
Alpha terminates citing "changed business needs." Beta sues for breach. Alpha argues no
termination clause exists, so either party may exit anytime. Based on the passage, which principle
would most appropriately govern this dispute?
options:
The literal rule requiring plain meaning of express terms, under which absence of termination
clause permits unilateral exit

The doctrine of business efficacy permitting implication of reasonable notice term to make the
contract commercially workable

The parol evidence rule preventing introduction of evidence about parties’ understanding of
termination rights

The contra proferentem rule interpreting the ambiguity against Alpha as the party asserting
termination rights
questions.solution: The passage states the doctrine of business efficacy "permits courts to imply terms when essential to ensure contracts deliver their intended commercial result." A service contract providing monthly payment for ongoing technical support necessarily implies some mechanism for termination—complete absence would create commercial absurdity. The officious bystander test applies: if asked during negotiations whether either party could terminate without notice, both would likely have said "of course n

questions.questionText:
A supplier entered into a contract with a company for supply of raw materials. During
negotiations, the company’s agent stated that “the company’s standard payment cycle is
30 days, and all suppliers are paid within that period.” Relying on this statement, the
supplier agreed to the contract. However, the written agreement provided for a 90-day
payment period, which the supplier did not notice at the time of signing. The agent
genuinely believed the statement to be true but was mistaken.
The supplier later sought to avoid the contract on the ground of misrepresentation.
options:
The statement constitutes fraud under Section 17 as any incorrect statement inducing a
contract amounts to fraud irrespective of intent; the supplier may therefore rescind the
contract and additionally claim damages for the loss suffered.

The contract is valid because the supplier had the opportunity to read the written
agreement and is bound by its terms; a party who fails to exercise due diligence at the time
of signing cannot subsequently seek avoidance on grounds of misrepresentation.

The statement constitutes misrepresentation under Section 18 as an honest but false
assertion of fact that induced the contract; the contract is voidable at the supplier's option
since the agent's genuine belief does not cure the falsity of the representation.

The statement is merely an expression of opinion regarding business practice and does not
amount to any representation of fact; no actionable misrepresentation arises where the
party merely describes a general commercial practice without asserting it as a contractual
term.
questions.solution: The agent made a false statement of an existing fact — the company’s standard payment practice — which induced the supplier to contract. Even though made honestly, it constitutes misrepresentation under Section 18, rendering the contract voidable.

questions.questionText:
Before the Constituent Assembly of India was finally established, the British Government
introduced several constitutional proposals to address the growing demand for Indian self-
governance. Some of these proposals were rejected by Indian political leadership, while others
ultimately laid the foundation for the making of the Indian Constitution.
Which of the following correctly identifies the plan that was rejected and the plan that
eventually provided for the establishment of the Constituent Assembly of India?
options: Wavell Plan — Cabinet Mission Plan
Cripps Mission Plan — Cabinet Mission Plan
August Offer — Simon Commission Plan
Cabinet Mission Plan — Cripps Mission Plan
questions.solution: The Cripps Mission Plan of 1942 proposed the idea of a Constituent Assembly, but it was rejected by major Indian political groups, particularly the Indian National Congress, mainly because the proposals did not provide immediate self-government and allowed provinces the option to separate from the Union. Later, the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 successfully provided the framework for the establishment and composition of the Constituent Assembly of India.

questions.questionText:
Harish Rana suffered severe brain injuries in 2012 and had been in a persistent vegetative
state for over a decade, sustained solely by clinically assisted nutrition. His family, unable to
bear his prolonged suffering, approached the Supreme Court seeking permission to withdraw
nutritional support, relying on the Common Cause framework. The hospital contended that
nutritional support was not a medical intervention and therefore could not be withdrawn
under passive euthanasia guidelines.
options:
Clinically assisted nutrition is basic care, not a medical intervention; withdrawing it
constitutes active euthanasia and remains impermissible regardless of the patient's
condition.

Passive euthanasia under Common Cause is limited to withdrawal of mechanical
ventilation and does not extend to nutritional support; food and water constitute a
fundamental entitlement courts cannot authorise withdrawal of.

Withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition from a patient in a persistent vegetative state
falls within permissible passive euthanasia, as prolonging existence without dignity does
not serve the patient's best interests.

Withdrawal of any life-sustaining care requires an advance medical directive from the
patient; in the absence of a living will, the family's consent alone is insufficient to permit
withdrawal.
questions.solution: The Court in Harish Rana extended the Common Cause framework to cover clinically assisted nutrition, holding that sustaining a patient in a vegetative state without recovery prospects serves no purpose consistent with human dignity under Article 21. Withdrawal was permitted upon satisfaction of procedural safeguards.

questions.questionText:
Gopal finds a neighbour’s cattle repeatedly entering his field and damaging crops. In anger, he
captures the cattle, ties them in a shed, and refuses to release them unless the neighbour pays
a very high amount. When the neighbour comes to negotiate, Gopal pushes him and threatens
to keep the cattle for weeks. The neighbour complains that this is unlawful self-help. Gopal
argues he can retain the cattle until compensation is made.
When is such self-help legally permissible?
options:
It is lawful only if exercised reasonably according to the circumstances, so excessive force
or demands defeat it.

It is lawful whenever property is invaded, because self-help remedies are absolute rights
and need no restraint ever.

It is lawful only after police permission, because extra-judicial acts are illegal unless
authorised by magistrate order first.

It is unlawful because courts alone may grant remedies, and private detention of cattle is
always a crime.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “lawful only if exercised reasonably according to the circumstances,” mirroring the reference line. Self-help may exist, but it is constrained by reasonableness, so excessive force, threats, and ransom-like demands defeat legality.

questions.questionText:
Farida, a teacher, was falsely prosecuted for cheating in an exam on a complaint by a rival
colleague. She was arrested at school, suspended for three months, and local newspapers
reported the allegation. The criminal court later discharged her without any finding of guilt.
Farida files a tort suit and must show actual damage rather than relying on hurt feelings
alone. She claims her reputation suffered, her liberty was restrained, and she spent money on
legal defence.
Which description best captures the kinds of damage recognised for this tort?
options:
Damage may be to reputation, person, or property, so arrest humiliation, medical stress,
and legal fees can satisfy actual damage.

Damage is presumed from acquittal alone, so the plaintiff need not show any injury to
reputation, person, or property.

Only physical injury counts as damage, so reputational harm and litigation costs are
irrelevant to malicious prosecution actions in tort.

Only property loss counts as damage, so arrest and stigma cannot be considered even if
proceedings ended favourably for plaintiff.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference categories “reputation, person, or property,” and fits Farida’s losses: stigma and news reporting affect reputation, arrest affects person/liberty, and legal expenses affect property/financial position. It therefore matches the recognised heads of actual damage described in the passage.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate answer. Statement I: In our country, a certain section of people have been particularly
        denounced to such an extent that their social advancement has historically lagged behind. For the upliftment of such
        a section of people the concept of reservation was announced. To ensure that reservation doesn’t produce inequality
        in society, a ceiling of 50% was introduced which can breach under exceptional circumstances only.
        Statement II: EWS provides reservation to the general category in education as well as in government jobs with
        certain essential requisites to be fulfilled. Even if the 50% ceiling of the reservation is breached by the introduction
        of EWS, it can’t be held unconstitutional.
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is partially correct but Statement II is partially incorrect.

Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.


1
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct. 1. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Megha runs a shop on rent in a building owned by Dev. Dev stops paying municipal dues, and
the municipality issues an attachment notice stating the entire building may be sealed, which
would shut Megha’s shop and ruin her inventory. To prevent sealing, Megha pays %75,000 of
Dev’s arrears directly to the municipality and obtains a receipt in Dev’s name. Dev later
refuses to reimburse, saying Megha paid “voluntarily” and no contract exists.
How should Megha’s reimbursement claim be assessed?
options:
Megha can recover because a person who pays money on behalf of another to protect their
own interest is entitled.

Megha cannot recover because she acted voluntarily, and voluntary payments never create
obligations unless the debtor expressly requested payment first.

Megha can recover because any tenant paying landlord dues becomes owner of the
property and may keep possession forever thereafter.

Megha cannot recover because only courts can order reimbursement, and private claims
fail when no written contract exists at all.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “pays money on behalf of another to protect their own interest” and “entitled,” which fits Megha’s payment to avoid sealing. She paid to protect her own shop interest but discharged Dev’s liability, so reimbursement is justified by the stated rule.

questions.questionText:
Tina is walking down the street one day when he passes Anjali's house and happens to see his lost cat,
Minny, sitting in the living room window. Tina goes over to the window, forces it open, reaches inside, and
takes Fudgy out. Further, in the jurisdiction where Tina lives, it is considered a crime of theft to remove
any item from another person's house without the person’s consent, whether that item belongs to them or
not. Tina was not aware of this law. Decide which of the following statements is true?
options: Tina is not liable because the cat belonged to her.
Tina is liable because mistake of law does not serve as a valid defense.
Tina is not liable because she was not aware of the law.
Both (A) and (C).
questions.solution: Tina was unaware that removing property from another person's house without consent constituted theft even if the property belonged to her. Her ignorance concerns the law, not the facts. The passage clearly states that mistake of law is generally no defence because everyone is presumed to know the law. Why other options are incorrect: A: Ownership of the cat does not excuse violation of the criminal law as described in the jurisdiction. C: Ignorance of the law does not exempt a person from criminal liability.

questions.questionText:
A beverage company tries to register the single colour “deep orange” for its fruit drink bottles,
claiming customers recognise the colour alone as its brand. The application includes a colour
swatch and description, but no word or logo. The examiner objects that a trademark must be
capable of graphical representation and capable of distinguishing goods. The company argues
the swatch is graphical and that the colour distinguishes its product in the market.
Which statement best reflects the legal requirement at the application stage?
options:
Registration must fail because colours can never be trademarks, and the Act recognises
only words and logos for registration always.

Registration may proceed only if the mark is capable of graphical representation and
capable of distinguishing goods or services.

Registration must fail because single-colour marks are always functional, so
distinctiveness is irrelevant and refusal is mandatory.

Registration must fail because a trademark must be spoken aloud, and a colour cannot be
pronounced or described in law today.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “capable of graphical representation” and “capable of distinguishing,” matching the reference line. A colour swatch can satisfy graphical representation, and the key legal question is whether it distinguishes the goods in trade.

questions.questionText:
A guardian of property, Suresh, wants to sell the minor ward’s agricultural land because he
believes land prices will fall soon. He executes a sale deed to a third party without approaching
the court, saying it is “urgent business judgment.” The purchaser argues he paid fair market
value and therefore the sale should stand. The minor’s mother challenges the sale, claiming
court oversight is mandatory before sale of a ward’s immovable property.
How should this dispute be approached?
options:
Court permission required before sale or transfer of minor’s immovable property, so sale
without permission breaches the guardian’s limit.

No permission required if price is fair, because fairness of consideration automatically
validates any guardian sale of land on behalf of minors.

Permission is required only for movable property, because immovable property is stable
and guardians are presumed competent to sell freely.

No permission required if guardian believes it benefits ward, because subjective belief
overrides procedural safeguards for property transfers entirely.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “court permission before sale, mortgage, transfer” and “immovable property,” which mirrors the reference line. Even if the price is fair, the statutory safeguard focuses on prior permission to prevent misuse and ensure welfare-centered oversight.

questions.questionText:
A bank guarantees a borrower’s liability to a vendor and receives a separate indemnity from
the borrower promising to protect the bank against that vendor claim. The vendor sues the
bank, and the court passes a final decree making the bank’s liability fixed and enforceable.
Before the bank actually pays the vendor, it demands that the borrower deposit the decree
amount under the indemnity. The borrower argues indemnity is payable only after the bank
actually pays.
Who has the stronger position on timing?
options:
The indemnifier can wait until indemnity-holder actually pays, because indemnity is
enforceable only after real loss is suffered, not earlier in any case ever.

The indemnifier must pay only if third party sues him directly, because indemnity cannot
be claimed by holder until privity is removed fully.

The indemnifier must pay when liability is contingent, because mere apprehension is
enough, and the indemnity-holder may demand advance payment before any claim arises.

Once the indemnified’s liability becomes absolute, the indemnifier must fulfil the promise
without waiting for actual payment, so the indemnity-holder can claim immediately.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference words “liability becomes absolute” and “without waiting for actual payment,” maintaining exact correlation. Once the decree fixes liability, the indemnifier’s obligation matures under this modern approach, allowing the bank to claim the amount before paying out.

questions.questionText: X guaranteed a single loan transaction between Y and Bank B. After repayment of the loan, Bank B granted another independent loan to Y and attempted to enforce X's guarantee for the second loan as well. Which option is most appropriate?
options: X remains liable because every guarantee automatically extends to future transactions.
X remains liable because sureties continue until expressly discharged.
X may not be liable because a specific guarantee ordinarily applies only to a particular transaction.
X remains liable because the principal debtor remained the same.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: X may not be liable because a specific guarantee ordinarily applies only to a particular transaction. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
During a period of National Emergency in India, A, a member of the Union Cabinet, advises the
President to issue a proclamation based on the grounds of internal rebellion. The President subsequently
issues the proclamation for the whole of India. However, B, a member of the Rajya Sabha, argues that
such a proclamation is not valid since there is no actual occurrence of internal rebellion at the time.
Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A's advice to the President is sufficient for the proclamation of a National Emergency.
B's argument is valid, and the proclamation is not valid without the actual occurrence of internal rebellion.

The President can issue a proclamation for a National Emergency based on the possibility of internal
rebellion, even if it has not yet occurred.
The President's proclamation can only be issued for a part of India and not for the whole country.

questions.questionText:
A finance company held a charge over a debtor's car. A third party, believing the car to be the
debtor's free asset, purchased it from the debtor. The finance company sued the third party for
conversion.
options:
The third party is liable only for the depreciated value of the car at the time of his
purchase, not its full market value, as he derived no wrongful benefit.

The third party is not liable for conversion as he purchased in good faith without
knowledge of the charge; bona fide purchase for value is a complete defence to conversion.

The finance company cannot sue in conversion as it did not have physical possession of the
car at the time of the alleged conversion; conversion requires prior actual possession by the
plaintiff.

The third party is liable for conversion; dealing with another's chattel in a manner
inconsistent with the owner's right to possession constitutes conversion regardless of good
faith.
questions.solution: Purchasing a chattel from a person who had no authority to sell it constitutes a dealing inconsistent with the finance company's superior possessory title, satisfying the elements of conversion regardless of the buyer's knowledge.

questions.questionText:
Karan bailed his car to Leela for her to drive to a meeting 10 km away. Leela
           instead used the car for a road trip of 500 km, during which the car was damaged
           in a hail storm. Karan seeks compensation from Leela for the damage.
options:
Leela is not liable because the hail storm was an unforeseeable act of nature and she
did not cause the damage through her own direct negligence.

Leela is liable only if it can be proven that her driving was reckless and that
recklessness made the hail damage worse than it otherwise would have been.

Leela is liable for the damage as she used the car in an unauthorized manner, making
her responsible for any loss during that use.

Leela must pay, but only for the extra wear and tear from the long trip, not for the hail
damage which was entirely accidental.

questions.questionText:
Arvind, a practising advocate, is preparing a writ petition challenging a government notification.
Pressed for time, he uses an AI tool to draft the petition and directly copies the citations generated
by it without cross-checking them against any official law report. One of the cited cases turns out
to be entirely fictitious. When the matter comes up before the bench, the judge is compelled to
spend additional time verifying the citations. Which of the following most accurately describes
Arvind's conduct in light of the passage?
options:
Arvind's conduct is permissible since the Supreme Court has expressly endorsed AI tools for
legal research and petition drafting by advocates in practice.

Arvind violated his professional duty as an officer of the court by placing unverified AI-
generated citations on record without authenticating them against authorised sources.

Arvind's conduct is procedurally irregular but does not breach any legal obligation since no
formal guidelines.

Arvind is only liable to the extent that the fictitious citation was actually relied upon by the
court in its final order, and no professional obligation is breached merely by the inclusion of an
unverified citation in a petition
questions.solution: is correct because the facts of the scenario directly mirror the concern raised by the Supreme Court in the passage — "A lawyer, as an officer of the court, carries a duty of diligence that no automated tool can discharge on their behalf. Blind reliance on AI-generated content...not only misleads the judiciary but strikes at the very integrity of legal proceedings.” Arvind's failure to verify the Al-generated citations before placing them on record is a clear breach of this duty.

questions.questionText:
Raj, a 25-year-old man, enters into an agreement with his uncle, who promises to transfer a
substantial portion of his property to Raj on the condition that Raj will not marry for the next
10 years. Raj willingly agrees to this condition and accepts the agreement without any coercion
or undue influence. However, after 2 years, Raj decides to marry. His uncle refuses to transfer
the property, claiming that Raj has violated the terms of a valid contract.
In light of the above passage, what is the correct legal position?
options:
The agreement is void because it imposes a restriction on Raj’s right to marry, which is an
agreement in restraint of marriage even if other contract conditions are satisfied.

The agreement is valid since Raj entered into it voluntarily with free consent and full
capacity, and therefore he is bound to comply with its terms.

The agreement is valid in law, but Raj’s decision to marry amounts to a breach, making
him liable to compensate his uncle for non-performance of the condition.

The agreement is voidable at Raj’s discretion because he later chose to exercise his
personal right to marry, which overrides prior commitments.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The agreement is void because it imposes a restriction on Raj’s right to marry, which is an agreement in restraint of marriage even if other contract conditions are satisfied. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Anjali, who is blind, attempts to open a new bank account using the bank's V-CIP
        application. The app requires her to align her Aadhaar card perfectly within a
        frame on the screen and then read a randomly generated code that flashes for 30
        seconds. The app has no screen-reader support or audio cues to help her with
        alignment. After several failed attempts, the bank rejects her application, citing a
        "technical failure" and asks her to visit a branch in person. Which of the
        following is the strongest legal argument Anjali can make?
options:
The bank's V-CIP application violates her right to digital access under Article
   21 because it fails to follow ‘universal design’ principles, creating a social barrier to
   an essential service.

The bank is liable for discrimination because it did not provide a human
   prompter to assist her, which is a mandatory requirement under the RBI's Master
   Directions.

The bank's request for her to visit the branch in person is a reasonable
  alternative and therefore does not violate her rights.

The bank has not violated any law because the RPwD Act only applies to
  government services, not to private banking applications.

questions.questionText:
A collector offers to sell an antique coin to Y for %5 lakh. The collector is aware that a leading
auction house recently authenticated the coin as a rare historical artifact worth nearly 750 lakh.
During negotiations, Y specifically asks whether there is any information known to the collector
that could materially affect the coin's value. The collector remains silent and proceeds with the
sale. Later, Y discovers the auction-house report and seeks to avoid the contract on the ground of
fraud.
Which of the following most accurately reflects the legal position?
options:
The collector's silence cannot amount to fraud because mere silence regarding facts affecting
willingness to contract is never fraudulent.

The collector's silence may amount to fraud because, once directly questioned on a material
fact, the circumstances created a duty to speak.

The collector's silence amounts to fraud only if the coin was ultimately sold for less than its
market value.

The collector's silence constitutes active concealment because withholding material information
may itself amount to deception.
questions.solution: Option B is correct because although mere silence ordinarily does not amount to fraud, the passage recognises an important exception. Where the circumstances create a duty to disclose material information, silence may itself become fraudulent.

questions.questionText:
Aarav bailed his vintage watch to Bina for safekeeping while he traveled. Bina
           placed the watch in a drawer in her home, which was later damaged when a pipe
           burst unexpectedly, flooding the room. Aarav claims Bina is liable for not taking
           enough care. What is the correct legal position?
options:
Bina is not liable if she took the care a prudent person would take with their own
similar goods, even if an accident occurred.

Bina is absolutely liable for any loss or damage that happens while the goods are in
her possession, irrespective of the circumstances or her caution.

Bina would only be responsible if her own intentional or grossly negligent action
caused the pipe to burst, which is not the case here.

Bina is liable because she failed to take extraordinary care to protect the watch from
all possible risks, including unpredictable accidents like pipe bursts.

questions.questionText:
Radhika marries Amit in Delhi. Before the wedding, Amit's parents allegedly demanded 210
lakh and a luxury car as a condition for proceeding with the marriage. Radhika's father, under
pressure, fulfilled the demand. Six months later, Radhika confides in her close friend Neha
that she continues to face harassment for additional dowry. Neha, disturbed by the situation,
discusses it with Radhika's uncle, who also witnessed the original demands. Who among them
is legally entitled to lodge a complaint under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961?
options:
Only Radhika and her parents, because only those who are directly affected by the dowry
demand and harassment are recognised as competent complainants under the Act.

Only Radhika's father and uncle, because the Act restricts the right to file complaints to
close family members of the bride who were present at or aware of the original demand.

Only the police or the Dowry Prohibition Officer, as they are the designated authorities
who must formally initiate legal action upon receiving information about a dowry offence.
questions.solution: The passage states that cognizance may be taken on the court’s own knowledge, a police report, or a complaint by the aggrieved person, her parent/relative, or a recognised welfare institution/organisation. Option C correctly identifies the statutory complainants.

questions.questionText:
Ramesh runs a street-food cart and publicly criticises the local licensing officer on social media.
The officer, without filing any case or approaching any court, cancels Ramesh’s vending licence
the next morning and orders municipal staff to seize his cart, saying it is “punishment for
disrespect.” Ramesh later learns that no notice or hearing was given and no proceedings were
initiated. He considers a tort action and must identify whether the wrong is about starting
proceedings, misusing process later, or misusing official authority outside court.
How should this conduct be classified?
options:
It is wrongful institution at the beginning, because a baseless case was instituted without
cause solely to harm the target.

It is misuse of legal process after properly initiated, because court steps were exploited
later to pressure settlement and silence criticism.

It is misuse of official authority outside the courtroom context, because power was used
administratively to punish the person without proceedings.

It is neither, because official decisions and court tactics can never be questioned in tort,
whatever the motive behind them.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “misuse of official authority outside courtroom context,” matching the reference line’s description of abuse of power. Since the officer punished Ramesh through official administrative action without invoking court proceedings, this classification is the best fit.

questions.questionText:
Dev owned a walled botanical garden attached to his farmhouse, where he grew rare
poisonous shrubs for private research and display. At the entrance and on the boundary wall,
he placed boards stating: “Some shrubs inside are poisonous. Keep away.” One afternoon, four
children saw bright fruits growing inside the garden. To look more closely, they climbed over
the wall, entered the garden without Dev’s permission, plucked and ate some fruits from the
shrubs, and fell unconscious. Their parents sued Dev under the rule of Strict Liability, arguing
that poisonous shrubs were dangerous things kept on his land and that the children had
suffered damage. Is Dev strictly liable?
options:
Yes, because poisonous shrubs are dangerous things, their cultivation is special use of
land, and the children suffered damage.

Yes, because Dev knew the shrubs were poisonous and the warning boards show that harm
from them was reasonably foreseeable.

No, because the dangerous thing did not escape from Dev’s land or control to a place
outside such control

No, because the children ignored the warning boards, and a written warning by itself
removes Strict Liability.
questions.solution: The passage provides that the dangerous thing must escape from the land or control of the defendant to a place outside such control. In this case, the poisonous shrubs and fruits remained inside Dev’s walled garden.

questions.questionText:
In a boxing match, Rahul and Sanjay agree to fight according to the rules. During the
       match, Rahul punches Sanjay, causing a minor bruise. Sanjay had consented to
       participate in the match. Is Rahul criminally liable for causing hurt?
options:
He is liable only if Rahul clearly violated the established rules of boxing during the
       punch and intended to cause injury beyond the sport.

He is not liable because boxing is a legal sport recognized by the government where
       participants assume all inherent risks involved.

He is liable because consent to physical injury is never a valid defence under the IPC
       for any kind of hurt caused to another person.

He is not liable as Sanjay's consent to a lawful sporting activity validly excuses the
       injury, provided it was within the rules and not intended to cause grievous hurt or
       death.

questions.questionText:
The family of a patient who had been in an irreversible coma for eight years petitioned the High
Court seeking authorisation for active euthanasia — specifically, the administration of a lethal
drug by a physician — arguing it was more humane than the prolonged withdrawal of nutrition and
hydration permitted under passive euthanasia. The family relied on the Common Cause judgment
and submitted that the constitutional right to die with dignity recognised in that case must
logically extend to active euthanasia as the more immediate and less distressing method of ending
life.
The High Court must determine whether active euthanasia is permissible under the constitutional
and legal framework as it currently stands in India.
options:
Active euthanasia is permissible where authorised by a High Court following procedural
safeguards applicable to passive euthanasia, since both involve a physician causing death and
the distinction between them is ethically arbitrary.

Active euthanasia is permissible under Common Cause where the patient has been in an
irreversible coma for a prolonged period, as the "best interests" standard permits the most
humane available option.

Active euthanasia remains impermissible under Indian law; the Supreme Court in both Aruna
Shanbaug and Common Cause expressly confined permissible euthanasia to passive euthanasia
and has not recognised active euthanasia.

The distinction between active and passive euthanasia is not legally recognised in India; once a
court authorises termination of life on grounds of dignity, the method is a clinical matter left to
the treating physician.
questions.solution: The Supreme Court in Aruna Ramachandra Shanbaug (2011) and Common Cause (2018) both expressly held that active euthanasia — the deliberate administration of a lethal substance to end life — remains impermissible in India. Only passive euthanasia, consisting of the withdrawal or withholding of life-sustaining treatment, has received judicial recognition.

questions.questionText:
"Global Events" contracts with a famous singer, Aria, for a concert on December
      31st. The contract includes a clause stating, "This agreement is conditional upon
      the issuance of all necessary public performance licenses by the city authorities
      by December 1st." Due to an administrative backlog, the city fails to issue the
      licenses by the deadline. Global Events informs Aria that there is no contract.
      Aria argues that the company should have ensured the licenses were obtained and
      is in breach. What is the most accurate legal analysis of the situation based on the
      passage?
options:
A valid contract exists, and Global Events is in breach because the license
    clause is a resolutory condition that only extinguishes the contract after it has been
    formed.

No enforceable contract was ever formed because the issuance of licenses was
    a suspensive condition (condition precedent) that was not met, and Section 32
    would render the agreement unenforceable.

The contract is valid, and the license clause is a force majeure provision that
    excuses performance, meaning neither party can sue the other.

The contract is void from the beginning because the failure to obtain a license
    makes the object of the contract illegal.

questions.questionText:
An applicant files a trademark application for “PURE MILK” for dairy products. The form is
properly filled, class is correctly mentioned, and representation is clear. The Registrar issues
an examination report raising objections that the mark is descriptive and lacks
distinctiveness, and also notes a similar earlier mark “PUREMIIK’” exists for dairy goods. The
applicant argues the Registrar should check only paperwork and not examine similarity or
distinctiveness at this stage.
What is the correct position?
options:
Registrar examines only formal requirements, and cannot consider distinctiveness or
similarity until after opposition is filed later.

Registrar examines only earlier marks, because absolute grounds do not apply unless
someone complains through opposition proceedings.

Registrar examines formal requirements, absolute grounds, and relative grounds, so both
descriptiveness and similarity can be raised.

Registrar examines only use evidence and market surveys, and cannot raise legal
objections based on Sections 9 and 11 now.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “formal requirements,” » & “absolute grounds,” and “relative grounds,” matching the reference line. “PURE MILK” can trigger absolute objection (descriptive) and relative objection (similar earlier mark), so both can be raised in examination.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): A person is regarded as of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract only if,
at the time of the agreement, they are capable of understanding its terms and forming a rational
judgment about how it will affect their interests.
Reason (R): Soundness of mind requires the capacity to understand the contract and form a
rational judgment regarding its effect at the time of contracting.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion states that a person is of sound mind for contracting only if they can understand the agreement and rationally judge its impact at the time of making it. The reason restates the legal test in almost identical terms: soundness of mind “requires the capacity to understand the contract and form a rational judgment regarding its effect at the time of contracting.” Since the reason not only is true but directly explains why the assertion is correct, this option accurately captures the r

questions.questionText:
A group of citizens challenges the felling of trees in a public park for construction of a metro
station. The authorities argue it's for public transportation, which will reduce carbon emissions
in the long term. Which of the following assessments is legally correct?
options:
The principle in M.K. Ranjitsinh directly applies as any felling of trees violates the right to
a healthy environment

Since the project aims at sustainable mobility and achieves net reduction in emissions, it
will be permitted under the principle.

The Court will strike down the project under Article 48A as it violates the constitutional
directive on environmental protection

The project violates equality under Article 14 since it affects only certain localities and not
others uniformly
questions.solution: The passage emphasizes that M.K. Ranjitsinh frames environmental protection within "sustainable development, climate resilience" as integral to the right to life.

questions.questionText:
The Lok Chetna Party had 15 MPs in the Lok Sabha. Six MPs wrote to the Speaker stating
that they had lost confidence in the party president, would sit separately in the House, and
would support the rival National Front in future parliamentary proceedings. They did not
formally resign from Lok Chetna Party. They argued that since they were more than one-third
of the party’s MPs, their group should be treated as a valid split. They also claimed that their
conduct could not amount to voluntarily giving up membership because they had not
submitted resignation letters. No merger of the original political party with another political
party had taken place.
Consider the following statements:
I. The six MPs can claim protection as a split because they constitute more than one-third of
the legislature party.
Il. The six MPs may be treated as having voluntarily given up membership even without
formally resigning from the party.
III. The Speaker may decide which faction represents the real political party only by
comparing the strength of MPs in each faction.
IV. The recognised defence after deletion of Paragraph 3 is merger under Paragraph 4, subject
to fulfilment of its conditions.
Which of the above statements are false?
options: Iand III only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
questions.solution: Statement I is false because, after deletion of Paragraph 3, a split is no longer a constitutional defence to anti-defection proceedings, even if the breakaway group is more than one- third. Statement III is false because the Speaker’s decision cannot be based only on legislative majority.

questions.questionText:
The Jan Shakti Party had 30 MLAs in a State Assembly. Twenty MLAs announced that the
“legislature party” had merged with the Rashtriya Vikas Party and requested the Speaker to
recognise them as the real Jan Shakti Party because they formed a clear legislative majority.
However, the Jan Shakti Party’s national president and working committee rejected the
merger and produced the party constitution, rules and leadership records showing that no
decision to merge had been taken by the original political party. Ten MLAs refused to join the
twenty MLAs and claimed that even if there was a merger, they were protected because they
had chosen to function as a separate group. What should the Speaker do under the Tenth
Schedule?
options:
Recognise the twenty MLAs as the real political party because their legislative majority
satisfies the merger defence under Paragraph 4.

Recognise the ten MLAs as a protected separate group because Paragraph 4 protects
members who do not accept a claimed merger.

Examine the party constitution, rules and leadership structure, because the real political
party cannot be determined only by legislative majority.

Treat the twenty MLAs as protected from disqualification because the deletion of split does
not affect a two-thirds legislative merger.
questions.solution: This option correctly applies the passage. The Speaker cannot decide the real political party only by looking at which faction has more MLAs.

questions.questionText:
The owner of a factory, Mr. K, operates heavy machinery that produces a continuous humming
sound and slight vibrations. This is a private nuisance to the neighboring resident, Ms. L.
However, the factory is a major employer in the town and a significant contributor to the local
economy. Mr. K argues that his factory is essential for public good and therefore, Ms. L must
tolerate the interference. In a lawsuit for private nuisance, how would a court likely evaluate
this claim?
options:
The court would rule in favor of Mr. K, as the public benefit of the factory outweighs the
private discomfort of Ms. L.

The court would rule in favor of Ms. L, as the passage states that an unreasonable activity
cannot be excused on the ground that reasonable care had been taken to prevent it from
becoming a nuisance.

The court would rule in favor of Ms. L because she has suffered personal discomfort, and
the factory's public utility is not a defense in a private nuisance action.

The court would dismiss the case because Ms. L must prove a special, distinct damage to
her beyond what other neighbors might experience, as this is a public nuisance.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The court would rule in favor of Ms. L because she has suffered personal discomfort, and the factory's public utility is not a defense in a private nuisance action. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
To celebrate ‘Pride’ month, an NGO called ‘Hum Sab’ decided to organise a rally in their city
open to only members associated with the NGO. On the day of the rally, all members
(approximate 100) wore an ID tag and took part in the rally. Suddenly, an individual was seen
crossing the road to join the rally and seen lighting a car on fire. Soon, chaos ensued, and the
rally was dispersed by the authorities. The municipal corporation is now blaming the NGO for
all the damage to life and property caused, as they organised the rally, thus leading to an
unlawful assembly. Decide:
options:
Yes, this was an unlawful assembly, because despite the initial celebration, the act of
vandalism changed the object of the rally.

No, this was not an unlawful assembly, because the individual was not a member of the
NGO, and his actions cannot be associated with the group.

Yes, this was an unlawful assembly, because as the organisers, the NGO was supposed to
exercise care and safety, which they failed to do.

No, this was not an unlawful assembly, as after the car blew up, the rally was dispersed,
thus, there is no criterion of common object to hurt or damage life and property.
questions.solution: Option A is partially correct because there is no doubt that the nature of the rally changed with the criminal act of vandalism, but it was only caused by one individual, thus failing to be qualified for an unlawful assembly. To make an assembly unlawful, there should be a common object between all the members.

questions.questionText:
A dispute arises where an old regional regulation allows a custom-based divorce practice
differing from Shariat principles. A party argues the regional law still applies because it
predates 1937 and has not been expressly repealed in local statutes. The other party argues
the Act was designed to secure uniformity and therefore repeals earlier inconsistent regional
laws, making Shariat the rule of decision in listed matters.
Which statement best reflects the Act’s effect on inconsistent older laws?
options:
Earlier inconsistent regional laws are repealed to secure uniformity, so local regulations
contrary to the Act cannot continue in force.

Earlier inconsistent regional laws survive because they are older, and later Acts cannot
override local traditions without explicit state consent always.

Earlier inconsistent regional laws survive unless courts declare them unconstitutional,
because statutory repeal requires constitutional litigation, not ordinary application.

Earlier inconsistent regional laws survive for marriage only, because uniformity applies
only to inheritance and trusts, not to divorce matters here.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “repeals earlier inconsistent regional laws” and “secure uniformity,” matching the reference line exactly. Therefore, an inconsistent old regional regulation cannot be relied on to displace the uniform rule the Act sought to enforce.

questions.questionText:
A 17-year-old boy, Kabir, inherits a shop and his neighbour is appointed to manage it until
Kabir reaches majority. Kabir later challenges the appointment and says he is “almost an
adult,” so the Act should not apply. The neighbour argues Kabir is still legally a minor and
therefore Kabir is a ward and must be protected. The petition is filed in the local District
Court.
Which statement best matches the Act’s key definitions and forum?
options:
A minor is anyone below sixteen, a guardian is only a property custodian, a ward is any
child, and the Court means the family court.

A minor includes anyone below twenty-one, a guardian must be a parent only, a ward must
be an orphan, and the Court means the High Court.

A minor is a person who has not attained majority; a guardian cares for the person or
property; a ward is a minor with a guardian; and the Court means the District Court.

Minor is person below eighteen only by police rules, guardian is employer, ward is tenant,
and Court means revenue officer in district.
questions.solution: The option directly reproduces the reference terms “minor not attained majority,” ” “guardian having care of person or property,” » &, “ward is minor for whom there is a guardian,” and “Court... District Court.” This matches Kabir’s age, the neighbour’s management role, and the forum chosen.

questions.questionText:
Ravi, a freelance photographer, offers to sell his vintage camera to Kiran, a camera enthusiast, with the
stipulation that Kiran must first enroll in a specific photography course by June 15th and provide evidence of
enrollment as a condition precedent to acceptance. Kiran communicates his acceptance on June 10th but enrolls in
the course and provides proof of enrollment only on June 20th. Meanwhile, Ravi, having not received proof of
enrollment by the 15th, sells the camera to another buyer on June 18th. Considering the principles of the Indian
Contract Act, 1872, what is the legal status of the contract between Ravi and Kiran?
options: The contract is valid because Kiran communicated his acceptance within the offer's timeframe.
The contract is invalid because Kiran failed to fulfill the condition precedent before communicating acceptance.
The contract is valid because Ravi should have waited for Kiran's proof of enrollment before selling to another buyer.
The contract is invalid because Ravi is free to sell his camera to another buyer at any time.

questions.questionText:
The State Legislature of "Pradesh" passes the Welfare of Farmers Bill in January. The Governor
holds the Bill for four months without comment. In May, the State Assembly re-passes the exact
same Bill and sends it back to the Governor. It is now July (two months later), and the Governor
has still not signed it, claiming he needs more time to study the "federal implications." Based
purely on the Supreme Court’s ruling on April 8, 2025, which of the following is the correct legal
consequence?
options:
The Court can declare the Bill effectively assented to as the Governor exceeded the one-month
timeline for re-enacted bills.
