The Governor has the "pocket veto" power to hold the Bill indefinitely if the federal
implications are serious.

The Bill is automatically considered "void" because the Governor did not give assent within the
first month of the initial passing.

The Governor must refer the Bill to the President within three months, and until then, the
Court cannot intervene.
questions.solution: The April Bench rejected the pocket veto, ruling that Governors cannot indefinitely delay bills and must decide on re-enacted legislation within one month. To protect the legislative will, the Court utilized Article 142 to grant "deemed assent" to bills stalled beyond this reasonable period.

questions.questionText:
A municipal corporation election is announced in State X. After reports of booth capturing, a
citizen group writes to the national Commission seeking countermanding and re-poll, citing its
expertise and national role. The national Commission replies that local body elections are
outside its mandate and advises approaching the State authority. The group files a petition
claiming the national Commission must administer every election in India to ensure
uniformity.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Commission must intervene because municipal elections affect democracy, and Article 324
powers extend to every electoral body nationwide without exception.

Commission does not conduct elections to Panchayats and Municipalities, because separate
State Election Commissions exist for those bodies in India.

Commission must act because it administers all elections, and any local poll is part of
parliamentary process too always here.

Commission cannot act because municipal polls are civil matters, and only civil courts
supervise them, not election bodies at all.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the key reference words “does not conduct elections to Panchayats and Municipalities” and “separate State Election Commissions exist.” That directly answers the petition’s uniformity argument and supports the national Commission’s refusal as consistent with constitutional design.

questions.questionText:
Vikram, a wealthy individual, has a large personal collection of licensed firearms and
       ammunition. During a trial, evidence emerges showing he recently purchased
       additional rifles and grenades. When questioned, he states he collected these new
       items specifically for a planned uprising to liberate a region from Indian control next
       year. What is the strongest applicable charge based on his stated intention?
options:
He can only be charged under the Arms Act for unauthorized possession of
              certain items, as his stated plan is a future possibility and not an immediate act
              of war.

He can be charged under Section 122 for collecting arms with the specific
              intention of using them to wage war against the Government of India.

He can be charged under Section 121 for waging war, as the purchase of
              weapons with this intention constitutes the first overt act of the war itself.

He cannot be charged yet, as he only has a personal intention and has not
              conspired with another person, which is necessary for any offence related to
              war.

questions.questionText:
Which of the following statements most accurately captures the author's primary
      argument regarding Section 32 of the Indian Contract Act?
options:
Section 32 is a flawed and poorly drafted provision that has created unnecessary
    confusion in Indian contract law.

Section 32 has been correctly interpreted by Indian courts for over a century to
    include both suspensive and resolutory conditions.

Section 32 has been historically misinterpreted to govern force majeure clauses,
    when its text and drafting history show it only applies to suspensive conditions that
    precede the formation of an obligation.

The omission of resolutory conditions from the final Act was a deliberate
    legislative choice to strengthen the principle of strict liability in contracts.

questions.questionText:
A businessman, Mr. Molya is arrested for a white-collar crime. The police produces him before
a Magistrate within 24 hours. During the hearing, his lawyer finds out that the police's
internal records show his arrest time as 12:00 AM, but he was actually taken into custody at
11:59 PM on the previous day. This means that at the time of the hearing, he had been in
police custody for 24 hours and one minute, a minute over the legal limit. What is the legality
of the detention?
options:
The detention is illegal because the police violated the 24-hour limit, even if only by one
minute.

The detention is lawful because the police produced him before the Magistrate and the one-
minute violation is too trifling for the law to take into account.

The detention is illegal because the police intentionally altered the arrest time to meet the
24-hour deadline.

The detention is lawful because a minor margin of difference is allowed in the calculation
of the 24-hour period.
questions.solution: Option A is correct because the right under Article 22(2) is a strict rule that states a person cannot be detained beyond 24 hours without court authority. A one-minute violation is a violation, nonetheless.

questions.questionText:
A hospital hires a cleaning company, an independent contractor, to maintain sterile conditions
        in its operating rooms. Due to the cleaning company employee's negligent sterilization, a
        patient develops a serious infection. The patient sues the hospital. What is the hospital's likely
        liability?
options:
The hospital is directly liable because it has a non-delegable duty to ensure a safe
        environment for its patients.

The hospital is not vicariously liable as it properly delegated the task to a specialized
        independent contractor.

The hospital is only liable if it can be proven it was careless in selecting that specific cleaning
        company from available alternatives.

Vicarious liability attaches because the cleaning staff was integral to the hospital's core
        function of providing patient care.

questions.questionText:
Rekha is travelling in an insured city bus on a permitted route. During a lawful halt at a
traffic signal, the driver keeps the bus stationary with the doors closed. A dispute between two
groups breaks out on the roadside, and an unknown person throws a stone at the other group.
The stone misses its target, enters the bus through an open window, and injures Rekha. The
bus had no defect, did not strike anyone or anything, and its movement, operation or condition
did not contribute to the stone being thrown. Rekha files a claim against the bus insurer,
arguing that she was injured while travelling in an insured motor vehicle in a public place. Is
the insurer liable under the stated principles?
options:
Yes, because Rekha was a passenger in an insured bus during a halt in the course of public
transport.

Yes, because the injury occurred inside the bus while it was being used on a permitted
public route.

No, because insurer liability arises only when the vehicle collides with another person or
object.
No, because the injury resulted from an external act without any causal role of the bus.
questions.solution: the stone was thrown by an unknown person during a roadside dispute, and the bus had no role in causing or contributing to that act. The passage requires that the injury be caused by, or arise out of, the use of the vehicle; mere presence inside the insured bus is insufficient.

questions.questionText:
After a divorce, both parents are alive but dispute custody and education decisions for their 9-
year-old child. The father claims the mother is unfit and seeks a court declaration appointing
him as guardian of the person, while the mother says she already has custody and no
“appointment” is needed because both are natural parents. The court is asked to intervene
formally to settle authority and reduce conflict.
Under what condition can the court appoint or declare a guardian in such a situation?
options:
The court may appoint a guardian only when relatives consent unanimously, because
courts cannot interfere in parental disputes without family agreement.

The court may appoint a guardian only if both parents die, because living parents always
bar the court from making any declaration.

The court may appoint a guardian only if the minor owns property, because guardianship
of the person is private and courts cannot decide it.

Court may appoint or declare a guardian where necessary for the welfare of the minor,
even if parents dispute custody and control.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “appoint or declare a guardian” and “necessary for the welfare of the minor,” which is the exact test in the reference line. Custody conflict and authority disputes can make a formal declaration necessary to protect welfare, especially to ensure stable decisions.

questions.questionText:
An elderly widow, Maria, initially plans to divide her estate equally among her three children.
Her eldest son locks her in a room for several hours, threatens to stop her medical care, and
forces her to sign a new will leaving everything to him. Two neighbours later confirm that
Maria was frightened and signed only to avoid further harm. After her death, the son seeks
probate of the new will. The other children challenge it.
Which conclusion best follows?
options: The will is valid because Maria physically signed the document before her death.
The will is valid because unequal distribution among children is always legally permitted.
The will is valid unless Maria filed a police complaint before her death.
The will is invalid because fraud, coercion or undue influence invalidates a will.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “fraud, coercion or undue influence” and “invalid,” matching the reference line. Maria’s confinement, threats, and fear indicate coercive pressure, making the new will vulnerable to invalidation.

questions.questionText:
A denominational temple follows a long-standing rule excluding a particular group from
entering the inner sanctum during certain months. The trustees defend it as “integral” to
worship, while petitioners argue it is a social exclusion and not a religious necessity. The court
must decide what the right constitutional inquiry should be: should judges identify whether
the practice is “essential and integral,” or should they only ask whether the practice is
religious (protected) or strictly secular (regulable) without ranking essentials?
Which approach best matches the reference issue?
options:
Court should decide only popularity of practice, because common acceptance proves
legality and ends constitutional inquiry fully.

Court should apply only criminal-law standards, because religious disputes are non-
justiciable and cannot be reviewed today.

Court should decide whether to identify essential religious practices or only determine if
the practice is religious or secular.

Court should defer to trustees always, because denominational autonomy excludes any
judicial examination of practices completely today.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the words “essential religious practices” and “religious or secular,” which are the exact alternatives posed in the reference line. It captures the methodological choice the court must resolve in such disputes.

questions.questionText:
Anant is a 29-year-old resident of Nagpur. He has been facing financial issues lately, and therefore, he
is being forced to resort to unfair means. He recently made some money by drug peddling. However, he
was caught by the police while peddling. His case is now being heard in the court by Justice Swami Roy,
who is a relative of Anant. Is this a violation of the principles of natural justice?
options: This is a violation of the principle of audi alteram partem.
This is a violation of the bias rule.
This is not a violation because the judge is not an immediate family member.
This is not a violation because Anant was facing financial issues.
questions.solution: One of the fundamental principles of natural justice is nemo judex in causa sua, which requires that no one should be a judge in a matter where there is a likelihood of bias. Since Justice Swami Roy is related to Anant, there exists a reasonable apprehension of bias, making the proceedings inconsistent with this principle. Why other options are incorrect: A: Audi alteram partem concerns the right to be heard, which is not the issue here. C: The passage does not distinguish between immediate and distant relatives; any reasonable likelihood of bias is sufficient.

questions.questionText:
Prakash, a school teacher in Kerala, was convicted under the POCSO Act for committing
aggravated penetrative sexual assault against one 8-year-old boy on a single occasion in 2024. The
victim suffered severe psychological trauma and required prolonged counselling. Medical evidence
confirmed injuries. Prakash has no prior criminal record. The prosecution seeks the death penalty,
citing the heinous nature of the crime and the victim's tender age. Based on the reasoning in the
passage, what would be the most appropriate conclusion regarding the death penalty in Prakash's
case?
options:
Death penalty is warranted because the victim's tender age and psychological trauma make it
a "rarest of rare" case.

Death penalty is not warranted because a single incident, despite being heinous, lacks the
systemic scale and multi-victim depravity.

Death penalty is warranted because all aggravated penetrative sexual assaults under POCSO
automatically qualify as "rarest of rare."

Death penalty is not warranted because the accused is a first-time offender whose lack of
criminal history prevents such a classification.
questions.solution: The passage emphasizes that the death penalty was imposed due to the "sheer scale of this victimization" involving 33 victims over ten years across multiple districts, reflecting "systemic nature" and "unparalleled depravity." A single incident, however heinous, does not meet the threshold of systematic, large-scale victimization that characterized the case in the passage.

questions.questionText:
A tourist collapses unconscious outside a private clinic. The doctor provides emergency
treatment and medicines, documenting everything, and the tourist later fully recovers. After
regaining consciousness, the tourist refuses to pay anything, saying “I never asked you, never
agreed, and never intended to enter any contract.” The doctor claims it is unfair for the tourist
to keep the benefit without compensating the clinic. The tourist argues absence of intention
defeats any liability.
What legal conclusion best fits these facts?
options:
No liability because without intention of parties there can be no obligation, and courts
never impose contract-like duties at all.

Liability arises because every benefit received creates a criminal offence, and restitution is
ordered as punishment for enrichment always here.

Liability may arise because obligations are involuntary and aim at restitution, restoring
the aggrieved party to position before enrichment occurred.

No liability because quasi-contract requires written offer and acceptance, so emergency
services are presumed gratuitous unless signed in advance today.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “obligations are involuntary” and “objective is restitution restores the aggrieved party,” matching the reference line. Emergency treatment confers a clear benefit, and restitution prevents the tourist from being enriched at the clinic’s expense without fairness.

questions.questionText:
Sanjay, a well-known real estate developer, enters into an agreement to buy a large plot of land from
Mr. Gupta. The land is crucial for Sanjay's planned residential project. Included in the agreement is a
clause that Sanjay also acquires the "right to sue" any third parties that Mr. Gupta is currently in
litigation with over a boundary dispute affecting the plot. Believing this to enhance the value of his
purchase, Sanjay proceeds with the deal. However, when Sanjay attempts to initiate legal proceedings
against the third parties as the new owner, he finds out that the mere "right to sue” for a personal claim
such as a boundary dispute is inherently non-transferable under the law. Sanjay decides to sue Mr. Gupta
for the invalidity of part of their agreement and demands a reduction in the purchase price or a rescission
of the contract. Can Sanjay successfully claim a reduction in the purchase price or rescind the contract
based on the invalid transfer of the "right to sue"?
options:
Yes, because the inclusion of a non-transferable right invalidates the entire agreement, allowing Sanjay to
rescind the contract.

No, because Sanjay should have known that legal rights associated with personal claims cannot be
transferred, and his lack of due diligence does not constitute grounds for contract rescission or price adjustment.

Yes, because transferring such a right is illegal, and thus the entire contract is void as it includes an illegal
term.

No, because the "right to sue" is a mere expectancy and considered inherently non-transferable under Section
6, thus not affecting the validity of the other terms of the agreement.

questions.questionText:
Shah Rukh Khan's seaside bungalow, "Mannat," has enjoyed an open, picturesque view of the Arabian
Sea for decades. The Municipal Corporation, acting under a valid town planning permit, approves the
construction of a large public hospital on a vacant plot directly in front of Mannat. The construction
completely blocks the sea view, significantly reducing the property's market value. Shah Rukh
challenges this in court. Based on the principles in the passage, what is the most likely outcome?
options: He will win, as his right to a scenic view is a legally protected property interest.
He will lose, as the hospital serves a greater public benefit than his private view.
He will lose, as he suffers only financial loss with no right being violated.
He will win, but only to receive compensation for the drop in his property's value.
questions.solution: The financial loss (reduced value) is damnum. The lawful construction violated no legal right of Shah Rukh (injuria), making it Damnum Sine Injuria.

questions.questionText:
States A and B sign a document titled “Green Shipping Protocol,” setting binding emission
caps for their state-owned shipping fleets. The protocol is in writing, signed by authorised
representatives, and states disputes will be resolved under international law. Later, State A
argues the instrument is not a treaty because it is called a “protocol,” not a “treaty,” and
therefore it is not legally binding. State B sues before an international tribunal claiming it is a
treaty regardless of name.
Which position best follows?
options:
Not a treaty because only documents named “treaty” count; protocols and memoranda are
political and non-binding always.

It is a treaty because an international agreement in written form governed by
international law is a treaty whatever its designation.

Not a treaty because treaties must be one single instrument only; a protocol is not a treaty
if it has annexures.

It is a treaty only if registered at the UN; without registration it remains unenforceable
and purely voluntary between States.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “international agreement,” » &, “written form,” » “governed by international law,” and “whatever its designation,” matching the reference line. Since the protocol is a written inter-state agreement governed by international law, it fits the treaty definition despite its label.

questions.questionText:
Dr. Aarav, a leading researcher in biotechnology, receives a substantial stipend from the government
for his pioneering work in genetic engineering. The stipend is specifically awarded to support his research
and personal expenses while he completes his groundbreaking project. Due to financial difficulties, Dr.
Aarav decides to assign half of his future stipend payments to his colleague, Dr. Priya, in exchange for an
immediate lump sum payment to cover his urgent expenses. Dr. Priya agrees, hoping the stipend support
will help further her own research in a related field. However, upon reviewing the agreement, the
government refuses to redirect the payments to Dr. Priya, citing the personal nature of the stipend. Is the
government's refusal to transfer part of Dr. Aarav's stipend to Dr. Priya legally justified?
options: Yes, because the stipend is personal to Dr. Aarav and non-transferable as it is inherently non-transferable.

No, because the agreement between Dr. Aarav and Dr. Priya to share the stipend payments constitutes a
binding contract under the Contract Act.

Yes, because stipends are generally considered as income and are taxable, therefore, they cannot be assigned
to another individual.

No, because Dr. Priya's involvement in a related field of research justifies the transfer of stipend benefits to
support the broader research initiative.

questions.questionText:
A agreed to sell a specific parcel of land to B for construction of a warehouse. Both parties
believed that the land measured 10,000 square feet, based on an old survey map relied upon
during negotiations. After execution of the agreement, it was discovered through an official re-
survey that the land actually measured only 6,000 square feet, substantially reducing its
suitability for the intended purpose. B sought to avoid the contract on the ground of mistake.
The question is whether the agreement is affected by mistake under the Indian Contract Act,
1872.
options:
The contract is valid because the mistake relates only to the quantity of the land, which
does not affect the validity of the agreement unless expressly made a condition of the
contract.

The contract is voidable at B’s option because the mistake materially affected the value of
the subject matter, and any such mistake renders the contract voidable.

The contract is void as both parties were under a bilateral mistake of fact essential to the
agreement ie., the identity and extent of the subject matter.

The contract is valid because a mistake as to area is a unilateral mistake, and only one
party can rely on it to avoid the contract.
questions.solution: Both parties entered into the agreement under a shared mistake regarding the extent of the land, which directly affects its identity and utility. This is a mistake of fact essential to the agreement, rendering the contract void under Section 20.

questions.questionText:
In the fertile plains of the northern Indian subcontinent, the region encompassing parts of India and
Pakistan, Basmati rice has been cultivated for centuries. This aromatic, long-grain rice is famous for its
unique flavor, aroma, and texture, which are attributed to the specific geographical area's soil, climate,
and traditional cultivation methods. Over the years, there has been an increasing number of instances
where rice producers from outside the designated region have been falsely labeling their rice as
"Basmati." These counterfeit products are often grown in regions outside the recognized Basmati
cultivation areas and do not possess the unique characteristics of genuine Basmati rice. “Bharat Rice”
takes the rice from the farmers and packages them for sale. They decide to apply for geographical
indication of the basmati variety of rice. Will they succeed in light of the passage?
options: Yes, because they have fulfilled the criteria of section 2 (e) of the GI Act 1999.

No, because Bharat Rice did not manufacture or produce the good which makes them ineligible as a
producer.
Yes, because the definition of producer includes entities packaging the agricultural good.
No, because they have not met the requirements under section 2 (f) of the 1999 Act.

questions.questionText:
Meera boards a registered private mini-bus from Jaipur to Ajmer. The bus has a valid permit
for the route and a current fitness certificate, but its rear door has been loosely tied with a
rope for several days because the latch is not functioning properly. Also, this defect was not
reflected in the certificate. During the journey, the conductor asks Meera to stand near that
door because the front portion is crowded. While the bus is taking a sharp turn at moderate
speed, the rope snaps, the rear door opens, and Meera falls onto the road, suffering serious
injuries. The owner argues that there was no collision with another vehicle, that the bus was
not being driven rashly, and that the bus was otherwise registered, permitted and certified for
use on the route. Meera files an application under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act. Is the
claim maintainable before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal?
options:
Yes, because the injury had a real connection with the vehicle’s movement, condition and
use during the journey.

Yes, because Meera was travelling in a registered and permitted motor vehicle when she
suffered bodily injury.

No, because the fall was caused by a door defect rather than by collision, rash driving or
external impact.

No, because the immediate cause was the snapped rope and not the mechanical operation
of the bus.
questions.solution: Meera’s injury is connected with the mini-bus being used for transport, its movement during the turn, and the unsafe condition of its rear door. The passage requires a real connection between the injury and the use of the motor vehicle, and that connection is present here.

questions.questionText:
Kavita’s petition under Article 32 challenges a departmental order from 2015 that she says
violated her Fundamental Rights. However, she filed it only in 2026 without explaining the long
delay. The State argues that even if a right is claimed, the Court may refuse relief due to
discretionary limits, including delay. Kavita insists the Court must hear it because it involves
Fundamental Rights.
What is the most accurate view?
options:
Kavita is correct because writ relief must be granted whenever a Fundamental Right is
alleged, regardless of delay.

The State is correct only if it proves the petition is about a private dispute and not about any
Fundamental Rights.

Kavita is correct because once the Supreme Court is approached, it cannot consider delay as it
applies only to civil suits.

The State is correct because the writ jurisdiction under Article 32 is discretionary and subject
to limitations such as delay.
questions.solution: The reference line precisely addresses the situation by listing “delay” as a limitation and stating the jurisdiction is “discretionary.” A long unexplained gap from 2015 to 2026 gives the Court a clear basis to decline relief even if a Fundamental Right is asserted.

questions.questionText:
Inspector Surya got reliable information from his source that Amish, a local politician is carrying out
the illegal prostitution in Tilak Nagar area. He raided the said place to catch Amish red handed. However,
when he reached the place, Amish was not there and Surya arrested Satyam believing him to Amish.
Decide whether Inspector can be held liable for the offence of wrongful confinement?
options: Inspector can be held liable for the offence of wrongful confinement.
Inspector cannot be held liable for any offence as he arrested Satyam by mistake of fact.
Inspector can be held liable as Mistake of fact is not an exception under IPC.
Both (A) and (C).

questions.questionText:
A plaintiff stored unusually fragile orchids in a greenhouse adjacent to the defendant's
brickworks. The defendant's operations produced ordinary levels of smoke that would not have
harmed standard plants. The orchids were damaged. The plaintiff sued in nuisance.
options:
The plaintiff succeeds because nuisance protects any use of land including specialised
agricultural activity regardless of its sensitivity.

The plaintiff fails; a defendant conducting a reasonable activity is not liable in nuisance
merely because the plaintiff's use of land is abnormally sensitive.

The plaintiff succeeds because the defendant is strictly liable for all consequences of
operations adjacent to residential or agricultural land.

The defendant is liable because proximity to a known horticultural use imposes a duty to
eliminate all emissions regardless of their effect on standard uses.
questions.solution: As established in Robinson v. Kilvert, where ordinary goods would not have been damaged by the defendant's operations, a plaintiff cannot recover merely because his unusually sensitive property suffers harm.

questions.questionText:
Suppose in the above question that Chameli asked Amit if she could borrow Bhola for a month.
She promised that she would pay Bhola for his services and that, if she was not satisfied with his
services, she would fire him. Amit agreed and asked Bhola to follow Chameli’s directions. While
working for Chameli, Bhola met with an accident. Decide:
options: Amit is liable, as he was the master of Bhola and Bhola was following Amit’s instructions.
Chameli is liable, as she was the master of Bhola for that month.
Chameli is not liable, as Bhola was working as an independent contractor.
Both A and C.
questions.solution: Chameli pays Bhola, controls him, and can fire him (control test satisfied) applying the borrowed servant rule and making Chameli liable. Option A incorrect: Control shifted to Chameli, so Amit is not primary master during that period.

questions.questionText:
Farah reports that her husband repeatedly forces sexual acts against her will, calls her
abusive names daily, and blocks her access to household money unless she “behaves.” He
argues that only physical beating matters and that her complaint mixes “private marital
issues” with finances. Farah seeks protection and monetary relief and claims that the statute
recognises multiple forms of domestic violence beyond bodily injury.
Which statement best reflects the scope described?
options:
Only physical assault counts; sexual coercion and constant insults are private issues and
cannot attract protective orders.

Only sexual coercion counts; verbal humiliation and financial restriction are irrelevant
unless bruises appear and injuries are proven in court.

Economic restriction is not covered; money disputes are civil, and only physical injury can
trigger relief under law.

It covers sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse, and economic abuse, so each conduct
can be addressed even together.
questions.solution: This option directly reproduces “covers sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse, and economic abuse,” mirroring the reference line. Farah’s allegations fit all three categories, so the scope described supports addressing the combined conduct.

questions.questionText:
Aman and Jia file their civil marriage notice and complete the public display stage. They then
postpone the ceremony due to an overseas assignment and return after four months asking the
Officer to solemnise the marriage on the basis of the earlier notice. The Officer refuses and
says they must start again. Aman argues the notice was already accepted and should remain
valid until used. Jia argues delays should be condoned because both parties still consent.
What is the correct procedural result?
options:
No fresh notice needed, because once notice is filed it remains valid until marriage occurs,
even after several months delay in this process.

No fresh notice needed, because three months rule applies only to objections, and delay
merely extends time for solemnisation automatically by law today.

Fresh notice needed, because parties must always renounce religion before marriage, and
delay proves they failed to renounce timely here under this Act.

Fresh notice needed, because if marriage is not solemnized within three months, the notice
lapses and cannot support later ceremony at all now.
questions.solution: The correct option directly uses “not solemnized within three months” and “notice lapses,” tracking the reference line exactly. Since Aman and Jia returned after four months, the earlier notice cannot support solemnisation and a fresh notice is required.

questions.questionText:
Meera is walking home when a thief snatches her purse and runs. Meera chases him
       and hits him with her umbrella, causing a minor bruise. The thief falls and drops the
       purse. Is Meera criminally liable for causing hurt to the thief?
options:
She is liable because she used force after the snatching was complete and the
       immediate threat had arguably ceased.

She is not liable as she was exercising her right of private defence of property against
       an imminent unlawful aggression, and the force used was proportionate.

She is liable only if the thief requires substantial medical attention for the bruise and
       it is proved she intended to cause harm.

She is not liable because the thief was committing a crime and therefore deserves to
       be punished for his actions by any means.

questions.questionText:
An artist, commonly known by his stage name as Raffy in India, is arrested for painting
graffiti on a public building. At the time of his arrest, a senior police officer verbally informs
him of the charge but, seeing that the artist speaks only in a regional dialect not common in
the area, hands him a written document in Hindi, which Raffy cannot read. The police,
however, produces him before a Magistrate within 24 hours. Has the police fulfilled its
obligation under Article 22?
options:
Yes, because they verbally informed him of the grounds and also provided a written
document, thus fulfilling the requirement.

No, because the information was not provided in a language that the accused could
understand, thereby defeating the purpose of the right.

Yes, because the artist was produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours, which is the
primary requirement for a lawful arrest.

No, because the police should have given him a lawyer to explain the grounds of his arrest
at the time of arrest.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because the information was not provided in a language that the accused could understand, thereby defeating the purpose of the right. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A shipping company enters into an indemnity arrangement with a port operator to cover losses
arising from mishandling of containers. A container owner, whose goods are damaged, directly
sues the port operator’s indemnifier for compensation, arguing the indemnity “shifts the entire
loss” and therefore the owner should recover from the party backing the risk. The indemnifier
objects that the owner is not a party to the indemnity. The container owner insists the
indemnity exists for his benefit.
Which view best fits the privity position?
options:
Cargo owner can sue indemnifier directly, because indemnity shifts the entire loss and
privity never blocks enforcement when third parties suffer harm.

Cargo owner can sue indemnifier only if he proves malice, because indemnity resembles
tort and requires wrongful intent before courts grant recovery.

Cargo owner cannot sue indemnifier because of the doctrine of privity, so only the
indemnity-holder may enforce the promise against him directly.

Cargo owner cannot sue indemnifier because indemnity is void without court registration,
so absence of stamp and filing defeats enforcement by anyone.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the words “cannot sue” and “doctrine of privity,” matching the reference line’s core statement. Because the container owner is a third party to the indemnity arrangement, he lacks the contractual standing to sue the indemnifier; the indemnity- holder must enforce it.

questions.questionText:
Ravi is named in an FIR for a workplace scuffle allegedly causing simple injuries, punishable
up to seven years. The Investigating Officer arrests Ravi immediately after the FIR, saying
“registration itself proves a cognizable offence.” No statements are recorded from witnesses,
CCTV is not checked, and medical reports are not collected before arrest. Ravi challenges the
arrest, arguing the officer must first collect evidence and test whether a prima facie cognizable
offence is made out.
What is the strongest view?
options:
Arrest valid because a complaint alone is enough to justify arrest, and evidence collection
can happen after custody begins.

Arrest invalid because police cannot arrest merely on the basis of complaint/FIR and must
assess necessity under Section 41 CrPC.

Arrest valid because offences up to seven years always require immediate arrest, and
Section 41 safeguards apply only above seven years.

Arrest invalid only if Magistrate refuses remand later, because police may arrest first and
justify later with reasons afterwards.
questions.solution: The option closely tracks the reference wording: “must first collect evidence” “determine prima facie,” and “complaint alone not enough.” Since the IO arrested without basic verification steps, the arrest fails the stated procedural threshold.

questions.questionText:
Ananya owned a large artificial water tank on her farm to supply water to a private flower-
processing unit. The tank was not part of ordinary agricultural irrigation and was built at an
elevated level. One night, Vihaan, a trespasser who had no connection with Ananya or her
workers, cut the lock and opened the outlet valve to damage the property. Water rushed out of
the tank, crossed into the neighbouring field of Kunal, and destroyed his harvested crops.
Kunal sued Ananya under the rule of Strict Liability. Is Ananya strictly liable?
options:
Yes, because Ananya brought and kept a dangerous thing upon her land, it escaped from
her control, and Kunal suffered damage.

Yes, because the elevated tank was a non-natural use of land, and the damage followed
from the escape of water outside her control.

No, because although the essential elements of Strict Liability are present, the damage
was caused by the act of a stranger.

No, because the water tank supplied a private flower-processing unit, and such use may be
treated as common benefit.
questions.solution: This option correctly balances the rule and the exception. The facts may satisfy the core elements of Strict Liability because a dangerous thing was kept for non-natural use, escaped from Ananya’s control, and caused damage to Kunal.

questions.questionText:
Vidya, a bookseller agreed to sell a copy of a Tolkien novel that was signed by the late author. The
buyer Siya was precisely interested in buying the book as that contains Tolkien's signature. Vidya is
aware that with this authentic signature, the book fetches a very high price. Later it is discovered that the
signature was actually forged and neither the seller nor the buyer knew about the forgery. Based on the
situation, decide which of the following statements is true?
options: Siya can sue Vidya for fraud because she made a mistake of law.
Siya cannot sue Vidya for fraud and she has to keep the book.
Siya cannot sue Vidya for fraud, but she has the right to return the money and get her money back.
Siya can sue Vidya because she made a mistake of fact, which cannot be used as defense.

questions.questionText:
Lily agrees to sell her vintage car to Max for Rs. 1000. Both parties sign a contract agreeing to the
sale. However, after the transaction is completed, Max realizes that similar vintage cars in the market are
selling for much higher prices, around Rs. 50,000. Max feels that Rs. 1000 is inadequate as consideration
for the vintage car and decides to take legal action. Based on the facts of the case provided, which party is
liable regarding the adequacy of consideration in the contract?
options: Lily, because she agreed to sell the vintage car for an inadequate amount.
Max, because he willingly entered into the contract knowing the agreed-upon price.
Both Lily and Max, as they should have mutually agreed upon a fair price for the vintage car.
Neither Lily nor Max, as the court does not concern itself with the adequacy of consideration in contracts.

questions.questionText:
A fleet owner, Mr. Gupta, sends his driver to pick up a delivery. The driver is caught drunk at
a checkpoint. Since the driver is alone, the police move the car to the station. Two hours later,
Mr. Gupta arrives at the station with his ID, the truck's RC, and his own valid licence. The
police refuse to release the truck, stating that Mr. Gupta is liable for “knowingly allowing” an
intoxicated driver to use his vehicle. Can Mr. Gupta legally demand the release of the vehicle?
options:
No, because the state has a valid contention that the owner is responsible for the driver's
intoxicated state.

No, because the police have “unrestricted power” to detain vehicles to ensure that owners
conduct better background checks on drivers.

Yes, because the police are under a duty to release the vehicle to the owner upon
production of the registration certificate and identity proof.

Yes, because the High Court held that drunk driving is no longer an offense that allows
police to stop a vehicle.
questions.solution: Option C is correct because the passage states that the police are under a duty to release the vehicle to the owner... upon production of necessary documents.

questions.questionText:
Rajesh and Sunita enter a partnership deed drafted by Rajesh stating: "Profits split 60:40; Rajesh
handles all client relations; Sunita manages accounts." After three years, Sunita claims equal
profit-sharing, producing evidence that for three years they actually divided profits equally and
both handled clients jointly. Rajesh opposes, citing the written deed. Which principle from the
passage most directly governs admissibility of Sunita's conduct evidence?
options:
The parol evidence rule bars Sunita's evidence as it contradicts clear written terms of profit-
sharing and role allocation

The purposive approach permits examining parties’ actual conduct to understand true
commercial arrangement despite written terms

The literal rule requires enforcement of the 60:40 split as plainly stated, regardless of
subsequent conduct

The principle against disguise allows examining substance over form to reveal the
partnership's actual profit-sharing arrangement
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The purposive approach permits examining parties’ actual conduct to understand true commercial arrangement despite written terms. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A resort owner signs a written “indemnity clause” with a wedding organiser, stating the
organiser will protect the owner against claims arising during the wedding. The organiser
hires an outside caterer. A guest slips on spilled oil near the buffet, sues the resort owner, and
the owner faces a damages claim. The organiser argues the clause covers only the organiser’s
own conduct, not the caterer’s negligence. The owner seeks reimbursement under the
indemnity clause.
What legal position best fits the indemnity definition?
options:
The clause applies only to the promisor’s own acts, so losses from any other person’s
conduct fall outside indemnity, leaving the owner to defend alone.

The clause applies because it covers loss caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or
by the conduct of any other person, including the caterer.

The clause fails because indemnity requires three parties, so without a separate guarantor,
no one can shift liability for injuries to owner here.

Clause applies only after owner pays damages, so until payment is made, indemnifier owes
nothing even if liability is already clear in court.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the words “loss caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of any other person,” exactly matching the reference line. Because the caterer is “any other person,” the organiser’s indemnity can extend to that source of loss if the clause applies to the wedding event.

questions.questionText:
Raghav, a natural guardian, owns no personal income and manages his 13-year-old daughter’s
unused shop. To prevent deterioration of the premises, he gives the shop on a four-year lease,
uses the rent for repairs and property tax, and ensures that the lease ends before she attains
majority. No court permission is taken. Which application of the principle is most appropriate?
options:
The lease is impermissible because every lease of minor’s immovable property needs prior
permission.

The lease may be valid because it protects the estate and does not cross the restricted
duration.

The lease is impermissible because earning rent reflects the guardian’s convenience rather
than minor’s welfare.

The lease may be valid because temporary possession is unrelated to minor’s immovable
property.
questions.solution: the facts show estate protection, use of rent for repairs, and a lease that ends before majority. The passage permits necessary, reasonable, and proper acts for protecting and managing the minor’s estate.

questions.questionText:
A public-spirited lawyer files a petition seeking clean drinking water for a remote tribal hamlet,
attaching reports showing repeated illness and administrative neglect. None of the affected
villagers can travel to court, and the State objects that only the directly affected persons can
approach the Supreme Court. The lawyer argues he can approach on their behalf because the
affected group is marginalised and unable to litigate.
Which option is most accurate?
options:
The State is correct because only a directly injured person can move the Supreme Court, and
outsiders have no standing.

The lawyer is correct because Article 32 expanded through Public Interest Litigation, allowing
individuals on behalf of marginalised groups.

The State is correct because Article 32 cannot be used for any welfare issue and is limited
strictly to property and contract disputes.

The lawyer is correct only if the villagers first sign individual affidavits and personally appear
before the Supreme Court.
questions.solution: The reference line exactly states that Article 32 expanded through PIL, “allowing public-spirited individuals to approach the Court on behalf of marginalised groups.” The lawyer’s petition fits this rationale because the hamlet is remote, affected persons are unable to litigate, and the grievance concerns a serious rights-linked deprivation.

questions.questionText:
The Municipal Street Trade Rules provided that a licensed street-vending stall could be
operated only by the licence-holder and could not be transferred, leased or commercially
assigned to another person. Ramesh held such a licence for a busy market location but wanted
to move abroad for two years. He entered into an agreement with Ishaan under which Ishaan
would run the stall, pay Ramesh a fixed monthly amount, and continue using Ramesh’s licence
number on all municipal records. The agreement stated that “ownership of the licence remains
with Ramesh” and that Ishaan was merely “assisting in daily operations.” After six months,
Ishaan stopped paying the monthly amount. Ramesh sued to recover the unpaid amount. Is
the agreement enforceable?
options:
Yes, because the licence was not formally transferred and Ramesh remained the recorded
licence-holder in municipal records.

Yes, because Ishaan received the benefit of operating the stall and promised monthly
payment as consideration.

No, because the agreement indirectly achieved through contract what the law did not
permit directly

No, because the agreement would be void only if the municipal authority first cancelled the
vending licence.
questions.solution: The passage explains that the object is unlawful if it defeats the provisions of law, and parties cannot indirectly achieve through contract what the law does not permit directly. Since the Rules prohibited transfer, lease or commercial assignment of the licence, the agreement allowing Ishaan to run the stall under Ramesh’s licence is not enforceable.

questions.questionText:
Manav was born from a marriage that was later declared void under the Hindu Marriage Act.
His father, Ramesh, was a member of a Hindu Undivided Family with Ramesh’s father, elder
brother and nephew. After Ramesh’s death, Manav files a claim stating that because Section
16 treats him as legitimate, he must be treated as a coparcener by birth and should receive an
independent share in the entire coparcenary property along with Ramesh’s brother and
nephew. In the alternative, he claims at least the share that would have fallen to Ramesh if a
partition had taken place. Ramesh’s brother argues that Manav cannot claim anything from
ancestral property because his parents’ marriage was void. Which of the following is correct?
options:
Manav can claim an independent coparcenary share because legitimacy places him with
other coparceners.

Manav can claim the entire HUF property because ancestral property is included within
parental property.

Manav can inherit Ramesh’s determined share, but cannot claim coparcenary rights by
birth.

Manav can inherit only Ramesh’s self-acquired property, not any share in ancestral
property.
questions.solution: it applies both sides of the rule. Manav cannot claim coparcenary rights by birth, but he is not excluded from ancestral property altogether.

questions.questionText:
Four contractors jointly agree to demolish a building wall without safety barricades, despite
knowing pedestrians use the lane. The wall collapses and injures a passer-by. One contractor
becomes insolvent, while another has sufficient assets. The injured passer-by sues only the
solvent contractor for the whole compensation. The contractor argues he can be liable only for
one-fourth of the loss because three others were also involved. The passer-by claims he may
recover the full amount from any one of them.
Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The passer-by may recover the entire compensation from any one joint wrongdoer.
The passer-by may recover only one-fourth because liability is always divided equally.
The contractor escapes liability because another contractor has become insolvent.
The contractor is liable only if all four are sued in the same proceeding.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line because joint and several liability protects the injured party by allowing recovery of the entire compensation from any one tortfeasor. The solvent contractor may later seek contribution, but the injured passer-by need not bear the insolvency risk.

questions.questionText:
Tech Solutions Ltd. and Client Corp. sign a software development contract titled "Service Level
Agreement for Consultancy Services." The agreement specifies monthly fees, deliverables, and
performance metrics but contains no clause transferring intellectual property rights in developed
software. After project completion, Client claims ownership of source code. Tech Solutions refuses,
stating no IP transfer clause exists. Client argues the agreement's commercial purpose necessarily
includes IP transfer. Which principle determines this dispute?
options:
The literal rule requiring that absence of IP transfer clause means no transfer occurs, as
contracts mean what they expressly say

The doctrine of business efficacy permitting implication of IP transfer term because software
development contracts necessarily include such transfer

The principle against disguise allowing courts to examine substance over title to determine the
agreement actually transfers IP despite silence

The purposive approach requiring consideration of industry practice where software
development always includes IP transfer to client
questions.solution: The passage emphasizes that "courts will not create rights that the text does not grant," drawing from the Supreme Court's reasoning that "there could be no tenancy in the absence of a clause of transfer of exclusive possession." Similarly, there can be no IP transfer without an express clause granting it. IP rights are property interests requiring explicit transfer— their absence cannot be filled through implication.

questions.questionText:
A 14-year-old ward, Arman, owns a small apartment inherited from his mother. His current
guardian, a distant cousin, begins negotiating a quick sale and tells neighbours he will “finalise it
this week.” Arman’s school principal learns this and informs the court that Arman is being
pressured to sign papers. A relative files an urgent request asking the court to immediately stop
any sale and to secure the property documents until a full guardianship inquiry is completed. The
guardian argues nothing can be done until final appointment proceedings end.
What can the court do at this stage?
options:
Court may issue interim orders for custody or protection of property so documents and
possession can be secured immediately to prevent misuse.

The court cannot pass any interim order because guardianship disputes require a full trial first,
and urgent directions are barred by law.

Court may only punish the guardian criminally, because civil courts cannot interfere with
property negotiations unless fraud is already proved fully.

The court must allow the sale because guardians have absolute property powers, and minors’
property can be disposed of without court supervision.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference words “interim orders” and “custody or protection of property,” which fits an urgent situation where there is risk of dissipation of a minor’s asset. Interim protection is designed precisely to preserve the ward’s property until the court completes a fuller inquiry.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the new labour framework:
Statement I: A trade union in a private shoe manufacturing factory (non-public utility) acts
illegally if it initiates a strike immediately after a dispute arises with the management, without
providing any prior warning.
Statement II: The Industrial Relations Code has expanded the requirement of a mandatory
14-day notice period for strikes to encompass all industrial establishments, moving beyond
the earlier limitation to only public utility services.
Based on the passage, determine the relationship between the two statements:
options:
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, and Statement II provides the legal
justification for the conclusion in Statement I.

Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, but Statement II is unrelated to Statement
I.

Statement I is incorrect because private factories retain the right to strike without notice,
while Statement II is correct.

Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect as the notice period applies only to
factories with over 300 workers.

questions.questionText: Y contracted with Z to sell 50 kg of grain on a stipulated day and destination. Z paid 30% of the total price before the delivery and promised to pay the reminder after the reminder. Meanwhile Y heard that Z has contracted someone else for the same consignment, therefore Y delivered only 50% of the grain to Z, and asked to him to pay in full, to get the rest 50%. Z did not reply to Y’s proposal. Decide whether Y could exercise right to lien in this case.
options: Y cannot exercise this right because he was already paid half of the amount.
Y cannot exercise this right because he already parted with 50% of the grains.
Y can exercise this right on the reminder 50% of the grains.
Y can exercise this right on the grain he has delivered to Z.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Y can exercise this right on the reminder 50% of the grains. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Rohit and Sanya have been living together for three years and are now planning to marry formally
under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Sanya has a diagnosed genetic condition that typically does not
impair her daily activities but can lead to significant cognitive impairments during periods of extreme
stress, which are rare but severe. Their psychiatrist has noted that while the condition is mostly
manageable with preventive measures, it can render Sanya temporarily unfit during these extreme
episodes. They seek to understand if Sanya's condition could legally impact their marriage under the
HMA, considering they now wish to perform the necessary ceremonial rituals. Which of the following is
most accurate concerning their situation under the HMA?
options:
Their marriage would be invalid because Sanya's condition, although occasional, could still impact her
fitness during extreme stress, violating the continuous fitness required under the HMA.

Their marriage would be invalid because the condition might render Sanya temporarily unfit during stressful
periods, violating the HMA requirements.

Their marriage would be valid as long as Sanya is capable of giving valid consent at the time of the
ceremony, despite her condition.

Their marriage would be invalid since any mental disorder, even intermittent, precludes a valid marriage
under the HMA.

questions.questionText:
X and Y have lived separately for several years, exchanged serious allegations, failed
mediation repeatedly, and no possibility of reconciliation exists. The Supreme Court dissolves
their marriage under Article 142 despite procedural complications. Which principle from the
passage best justifies this action?
options: Article 142 can be used whenever parties mutually request divorce.

Article 142 permits the Court to do complete justice where the marriage is emotionally
dead and beyond salvation.
Article 142 overrides every statutory safeguard under matrimonial law.
Article 142 can only be exercised after criminal proceedings are quashed.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Article 142 permits the Court to do complete justice where the marriage is emotionally dead and beyond salvation. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Gian operates a private music school in a residential locality. He teaches the drums and
electric guitar for ten hours every day. Shizuka, a neighbour who works from home and has an
infant child, sues Gian for the tort of private nuisance due to the constant, loud noise. Which
of the following is the most accurate statement regarding Gian's liability?
options:
Gian is not liable because he has a right to use the property for his profession, provided he
takes reasonable care.

Gian is not liable to Shizuka because the law does not protect people who are abnormally
sensitive.
Gian is liable because Gian’s act constitutes an unreasonable and substantial interference.

Gian is liable only if Shizuka can prove actual physical damage to her house caused by the
sound vibrations.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Gian is liable because Gian’s act constitutes an unreasonable and substantial interference. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A constitutional challenge was raised against Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption
        Act, 1988. In a split verdict, the two-judge Supreme Court bench delivered differing opinions
        on its validity. What was the core point of disagreement between Justice Nagarathna and
        Justice Viswanathan?
options:
Justice Nagarathna held the provision was unconstitutional for violating Article 21, while
        Justice Viswanathan argued it was necessary to protect privacy.

Justice Nagarathna held the provision was unconstitutional for violating Article 14, while
        Justice Viswanathan argued it should be upheld if sanction power lies with an independent
        authority.

Justice Nagarathna held the provision was valid but needed amendment, while Justice
        Viswanathan argued it was wholly unconstitutional.

Both justices agreed the provision was unconstitutional but differed on which constitutional
       article it violated.

questions.questionText:
The call to decriminalise defamation creates a direct legal tension between two
           fundamental rights. A proponent of decriminalisation would argue that the current
           law disproportionately infringes one right, while its defender would cite the
           protection of the other. Which two constitutional articles are central to this legal
           debate?
options:
Article 19 (Freedom of Speech and Expression) and Article 21 (Right to Life and
Personal Liberty).
Article 14 (Right to Equality) and Article 15 (Prohibition of Discrimination).

Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) and Article 226 (Power of High
Courts).

Article 25 (Freedom of Religion) and Article 26 (Freedom to Manage Religious
Affairs).

questions.questionText:
A municipal fire brigade, while responding to a fire, drives through a narrow lane and accidentally
damages parked scooters due to emergency manoeuvring. Scooter owners sue the municipality for
negligence. The municipality argues that the brigade was performing a core public emergency
function and should not be liable merely for consequences of carrying out that function. The
owners argue the municipality is always liable like a private actor.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
The owners must succeed because governments and municipalities can never avoid tort
liability for any act.

The municipality must succeed because any public service automatically gives total immunity
for all harm caused.

The owners must succeed because once property is damaged, liability is strict regardless of the
nature of the function.

The municipality may avoid liability for acts done in discharge of sovereign functions, though
liability may arise for assigned duties.
questions.solution: The reference line directly states the governing idea: governments and municipalities may avoid liability for sovereign functions, but may be liable where the act is connected with assigned duties. Since the fire response is presented as an emergency public function, this option best reflects the legal position.

questions.questionText:
A museum mistakenly receives a rare sculpture from a shipping company meant for another
gallery. The museum displays it for a month, attracting unusually high-ticket sales, and
refuses to return it until the true owner sues. The owner seeks return of the sculpture and
compensation for benefit enjoyed from its display. The museum argues that because no
contract existed, only an apology is required. Which remedy best reflects quasi-contractual
principle?
options: No remedy is available because the museum never promised to return or compensate.
Only apology is available because mistaken benefit creates moral duty, not legal duty.

Restitution applies because benefiting party must return benefit or compensate aggrieved
party.

Criminal punishment is automatic because every mistaken receipt becomes theft by law by
that person.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “return benefit” and “compensate aggrieved party,” matching the reference line. Since the museum enjoyed the sculpture and increased ticket revenue, restitution is the remedy most aligned with quasi-contract.

questions.questionText:
XYZ Bank's loan agreement with Mohan states: "Borrower shall repay principal with 12% interest
annually. Default triggers penal interest at prevailing market rates." After Mohan defaults, the
Bank charges 24% penal interest (current market rate). Mohan argues "prevailing market rates" is
ambiguous and should mean rates at loan origination (8%). The loan agreement was drafted
entirely by XYZ Bank using its standard format. Based on the passage, which interpretive
principle resolves this ambiguity?
options:
The literal rule requiring "prevailing market rates" to mean rates at the time of interpretation,
supporting 24%

The golden rule permitting departure from literal meaning because 24% creates commercially
irrational outcome

The contra proferentem rule interpreting the ambiguity against XYZ Bank as the drafting
party, favoring 8%

The doctrine of business efficacy implying a cap on penal interest to make the contract
commercially reasonable
questions.solution: The passage states the contra proferentem rule "resolves persistent ambiguity against the drafting party, particularly in... contracts...

questions.questionText:
Argument: A promise by one party to cover another party’s legal costs in case a third person takes
legal action against them amounts to a contract of indemnity and not a contract of guarantee.
Which of the following, if true, would most strongly strengthen the above argument?
options:
The Indian Contract Act defines a contract of indemnity as a promise to save another from loss
caused by the conduct of any person, and legal costs arising from a lawsuit are a form of such loss.

A contract of guarantee always requires the consent of the creditor in addition to the debtor and the
surety.

In most commercial transactions, parties prefer contracts of indemnity over contracts of guarantee
because they are simpler to draft.

In a contract of guarantee, the surety promises to pay an existing debt of a third party, and not
expenses like legal costs arising from a possible future lawsuit.
questions.solution: most strongly strengthens this argument because it directly links legal costs to the definition of indemnity given in the passage. The passage states that a contract of indemnity involves a promise to save another from loss caused by the conduct of any person.

questions.questionText:
State J signs a bilateral “Security Cooperation Treaty” with State K that includes a clause
permitting “interrogation methods involving torture” for intelligence gathering. Years later, J
tries to withdraw from the clause, claiming it is invalid from the start because it conflicts with
a peremptory norm. K argues the treaty was freely signed and therefore binding under pacta
sunt servanda. J argues treaty consent cannot validate a clause that conflicts with jus cogens
norms like torture.
Which statement best matches the invalidity ground described?
options:
Clause can be invalidated because a treaty may be invalidated for conflict with jus cogens
norms such as torture.

Clause cannot be invalidated because pacta sunt servanda makes every clause binding
once signed, even if it permits torture today.

Clause can be invalidated only if domestic law forbids it, because international law cannot
override consent between sovereign States ever.

Clause cannot be invalidated because jus cogens applies only to custom, not to treaties,
and treaty clauses cannot be voided on that basis.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “may be invalidated” and “conflict with jus cogens... torture,” matching the reference line’s invalidity ground.

questions.questionText:
In a scenario where Aarav, accused of financial misconduct, is undergoing an interrogation, he
exercises his right to have a lawyer present. However, the police limit the lawyer's involvement,
permitting their presence only during specific segments of the interrogation, claiming that legal
representation is not necessary at all times. Aarav's lawyer argues that this selective allowance violates
Aarav's rights. Assessing the nuances of this situation, which of the following statements is most
accurate?
options:
The limitation of the lawyer's presence is valid, as continuous legal representation is not a requirement
during interrogation.

The selective allowance of the lawyer's presence is invalid, as it violates the accused's right to consistent
legal representation.

The police's decision is valid, as they have the authority to determine the necessity of legal representation
during interrogation.

The selective allowance is invalid, as the right to legal representation implies uninterrupted presence during
the entire interrogation.

questions.questionText:
A human rights treaty contains a core obligation to prohibit torture. State E ratifies the treaty
but enters a reservation stating: “We reserve the right to use physical coercion in interrogation
where domestic security requires it.” Other States object, arguing the reservation defeats the
treaty’s object and purpose. State E claims reservations are always permitted because
sovereignty allows States to accept only what they like. A dispute arises on whether such a
reservation is legally acceptable under treaty principles.
Which statement best fits?
options:
Reservation valid because any reservation is allowed, and no reservation can be questioned
once ratification happens under treaty law.

Reservation invalid because reservations cannot defeat the object and purpose of the
treaty, especially when undermining core obligations.

Reservation valid because security reservations are automatically superior to treaty
obligations, and object-and-purpose limits never apply in law.

Reservation invalid because reservations are not recognised in treaty law, and every
ratifying state must accept all clauses without exception.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “cannot defeat the object and purpose of the treaty,” matching the reference line. A reservation permitting conduct that the treaty centrally prohibits would undermine the treaty’s core purpose, so it is inconsistent with the stated limit.

questions.questionText:
In 2023, Meera, a director of a pharmaceutical company, was accused of distributing medicines
without maintaining a mandatory batch register. At that time, the offence was punishable
with a maximum fine of %2 lakh. In 2025, before the judgment in her case, the law was
amended to impose imprisonment up to three years and a maximum fine of 725 lakh for the
same offence. The prosecution accepts that the act occurred in 2023 but argues that the
amended penalty should apply because Meera is being convicted only after the amendment
and because public health offences require stricter deterrence. Can the court impose the 2025
punishment on Meera?
options:
Yes, because the conviction is being recorded after the amendment and the offence
concerns public health regulation.

No, because Article 20(1) prevents conviction itself once the punishment is changed before
judgment.

Yes, because the act was already an offence in 2023 and the later law only changes the
sentencing range.

No, because the later punishment is greater than the penalty available under the law in
force in 2023.
questions.solution: The passage provides that no person shall be subjected to a greater penalty than what could have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of commission. In 2023, the maximum punishment was only a 22 lakh fine, so the 2025 imprisonment and enhanced fine cannot be imposed for that earlier act.

questions.questionText:
A newspaper editor publishes a harsh, false article accusing a citizen of corruption, believing the
allegation to be true because a source told him so. The citizen sues and also seeks criminal action,
and the editor argues he lacked any guilty mind because he honestly believed the claim and had no
intention to harm. The complainant replies that certain offences do not require proof of mens rea
and are treated as strict liability in law.
Which statement best reflects the passage’s point about exceptions?
options:
The editor must be acquitted because mens rea is always essential, and honest belief
automatically defeats every criminal offence in all cases.

The editor may still face liability because strict liability offences exist where proof of mens rea
is not required, as it is an exception.

The editor must be acquitted because strict liability applies only to traffic violations, and never
to publication-related offences in criminal law.

The editor must be acquitted because civil suits are the only remedy for publications, and
criminal law never recognises any publication offence.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference words “strict liability offences” and “proof of mens rea is not required,” matching the passage’s exception framework. It answers the editor’s argument by noting that even absent guilty mind, certain offences may still impose liability depending on the offence structure.

questions.questionText:
Rohit and a contractor are in a billing dispute about renovation work. To force Rohit to pay
immediately, the contractor files a criminal complaint alleging Rohit stole tools, even though
the contractor’s real aim is to secure a quick settlement and threaten Rohit’s reputation. The
case is later withdrawn after Rohit pays part of the bill, and Rohit sues for malicious
prosecution, arguing the complaint was used for an improper purpose rather than justice.
In assessing malice, what interpretation best matches the passage?
options:
Malice requires personal spite alone, so unless the builder hated the owner personally, the
element fails even if the complaint aimed to pressure payment.

Malice is irrelevant if the case ends in acquittal, because favourable termination
automatically proves improper purpose and replaces the malice requirement.

Malice may mean an improper purpose, such as gaining a collateral advantage, so filing a
complaint to force payment can satisfy the malice requirement.

Malice exists whenever the police investigate, because starting any complaint shows
hostility, and courts presume malicious intention from litigation.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “improper purpose” and “collateral advantage,” tracking the reference line’s language. Using criminal process to force settlement in a civil billing dispute can evidence malice because the purpose is collateral, not legitimate prosecution.

questions.questionText:
A citizen files a petition in the High Court complaining that a private neighbour has breached a
purely private contract and asks the High Court to issue a constitutional writ to recover money.
The neighbour argues that writ jurisdiction is meant for rights protections and public law issues,
not for enforcing private contractual disputes between two individuals. The citizen claims the
Supreme Court alone has writ power, so the High Court should still entertain because it is
“closer.”
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
The High Court has broader writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court because it may issue
writs for fundamental rights and other legal rights.

The High Court cannot issue writs at all because writ powers belong only to the Supreme
Court.

The High Court may issue writs only for private contract enforcement, not for rights against
public authorities.

The High Court’s writ jurisdiction is narrower than the Supreme Court because it cannot
address non-fundamental legal rights.
questions.solution: The reference line expressly states High Courts have “broader writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court” because they may issue writs not only for fundamental rights but also “other legal rights.” This directly corrects the citizen’s misconception that only the Supreme Court has writ power and clarifies the High Court’s wider scope in principle. Hence,

questions.questionText:
A Hindu temple managed by a religious denomination is open to the general public and follows
a rule that bars one class of Hindu devotees from carrying offerings into the sanctum. The
State enacts a “Temple Entry Reform Act” stating that all Hindus, regardless of class or
section, must be allowed to enter and perform offerings in public temples. The denomination
challenges the Act as interference with its religious affairs.
How should the court assess the State’s law on these facts?
options:
The exclusion rule prevails because denominational management in matters of religion
cannot be overridden by a State temple-entry reform law.

The reform law prevails because any social-reform statute automatically overrides
denominational autonomy, regardless of public character or temple type.

The exclusion rule prevails because constitutional protection covers worship only, and
cannot compel entry rights for every class and section.

The reform law can prevail because it allows throwing open Hindu religious institutions of
a public character to all classes and sections.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character” and “all classes and sections,” mirroring the reference line’s words. On these facts, the Act aligns with that textual reform permission, making this the most defensible view.

questions.questionText:
“BOMBAY BITES” is an unregistered snack brand used for five years in local markets. A new
seller begins using “BOMBAY BYTEZ” with similar colour scheme and claims no infringement
exists because the older brand is unregistered. The older seller sues, arguing passing off
protects unregistered marks if goodwill exists and misrepresentation causes likely damage.
The defendant argues that without registration, no protection exists under any law.
Which statement best matches the protection available?
options:
Protection available because unregistered marks can be protected through passing off if
goodwill, misrepresentation, and likely damage are shown.

No protection because passing off is available only for registered marks, and registration is
mandatory to sue for any remedy.

Protection available only if Registrar issues certificate first, because passing off requires
prior administrative recognition before court can act.

No protection because Section 27 blocks all actions relating to unregistered marks,
including passing off, so suit must fail entirely.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “protected through passing off” and the three requirements “goodwill, misrepresentation, and likely damage,” matching the reference line. Therefore, lack of registration does not bar protection if these elements are proved.

questions.questionText:
A hazardous chemical enterprise transports highly explosive chemicals as part of its business.
Unknown outsiders sabotage the containers, causing an explosion that injures several
villagers. The villagers sue the enterprise. Applying the doctrine of absolute liability, which
conclusion is most consistent with the passage?
options:
The company is liable because stranger intervention is not a defence under absolute
liability.

The company is not liable because terrorists are strangers which is a defence under strict
liability.
The company is liable only if negligence is proved.
The company is liable only if the explosives escaped from company-owned land.
questions.solution: Option (A): Absolute liability excludes the defence of act of a stranger. Incorrect Options:

questions.questionText:
A monastery runs an educational trust and charges fees for lodging, claiming it is part of its
spiritual mission. The State regulates the fee structure, and the monastery challenges the
regulation as interference in religious affairs. The State argues fee management is a secular
activity linked to administration, while the monastery claims it is part of its faith. The court
considers whether to use an approach that separates secular practices (regulable) from
religious practices (protected), or instead to ask whether the specific practice is “essential and
integral” to religion.
Which statement best reflects the passage’s description of the earlier approach?
options:
Earlier approach distinguished secular practices that can be regulated from religious
