practices that receive constitutional protection.

Earlier approach required courts to treat every practice as essential, so all matters were
protected and regulation was impossible always.

Earlier approach required courts to defer to government policy, so religious practices were
regulable whenever public interest was claimed.

Earlier approach rejected all distinction, so secular and religious practices were treated
identically and received the same protection.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: This option directly uses “distinguished between secular practices, which can be regulated, and religious practices, which receive constitutional protection,” matching the reference line’s words. In the scenario, fee regulation turns on whether the activity is secular administration or religious practice.

questions.questionText:
A Muslim woman makes a valid declaration under the Act extending Shariat to wills and
legacies. Years later, her minor son becomes involved in a dispute about a legacy left by his
grandfather. Relatives argue the declaration binds only the woman personally and cannot
affect minors or descendants, so customary rules should still apply to the child’s legacy
dispute. The woman argues that once the declaration is accepted, its effect extends to her
minor children and descendants as well.
Which statement best matches the passage?
options:
Declaration binds only declarant, so minors and descendants are free to choose custom and
cannot be bound by parent’s declaration.

Declaration binds only the declarant’s spouse, because only marital unit is covered;
children and descendants are excluded always.

Declaration binds declarant plus minor children and descendants, so accepted declaration
extends its effect beyond the individual alone.

Declaration binds only after minors attain majority, because legal effect is suspended until
children can consent at age eighteen.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “binds... minor children and descendants,” mirroring the reference line’s exact words.

questions.questionText:
A State government issues rules prescribing the authority, form, and fee for making
declarations under Section 3. A citizen challenges the rules, arguing the government has no
power to regulate declarations and that such matters must be left to courts. The State replies
it can frame procedural rules regarding declarations and must publish them and lay them
before the State Legislature for oversight.
Which statement best matches the Act’s description?
options:
State cannot frame rules because declarations are religious matters, and governments
cannot regulate them through any notified rules today.

State can frame procedural rules regarding declarations, prescribed authorities, form, and
fees, and such rules must be published and laid.

State can frame rules only if Parliament approves each declaration; otherwise rules are
invalid and cannot control any declaration filing.

State can frame rules, but it need not publish or lay them, because declaration rules are
purely internal administrative circulars.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “frame procedural rules,” » “prescribed authorities, form, and fees,” and “published and laid,” matching the reference line’s wording. It captures both the power and the procedural safeguards of publication and legislative laying.

questions.questionText:
A legislative committee studies complaints from women across different communities. One
complaint concerns unilateral divorce without meaningful hearing, another concerns desertion
without effective maintenance, and another concerns unequal treatment where a husband’s
second marriage is socially accepted while the wife has no similar protection. The committee
proposes a common civil law for marriage, divorce, and maintenance to reduce gender-based
disadvantages while preserving essential religious worship.
Which response best applies the principle?
options:
The proposal is invalid because personal-law inequality can never justify common civil
reform for family matters.

The proposal is unnecessary because desertion and cruelty affect only private morality, not
legal equality.

The proposal is justified because common civil law may promote gender equality and
reduce discrimination.

The proposal is excessive because equality between spouses is irrelevant when customs are
long-standing.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference idea that “common civil law” can “promote equality” and “reduce discrimination.” The committee’s proposal addresses unequal treatment in marriage, divorce, and maintenance, which are precisely the areas where women may suffer under unequal personal laws. Option (da) Incorrect: Long-standing custom does not by itself make gender inequality legally acceptable.

questions.questionText:
PIIPL successfully establishes that Shaadi.com is a well-known trademark under the Trade Marks Act,
1999. Subsequently, a third party applies for registration of the mark “ShaadiPlus” for services that are
not directly related to matrimonial matchmaking. The applicant argues that the relevant public for
such services does not overlap with Shaadi.com’s user base and that the mark has not been used in the
matrimonial sector.
Based solely on the legal principles discussed in the passage, which of the following is the most legally
sustainable conclusion?
options:
The application must be allowed because well-known trademark protection applies only within the
class in which the mark is registered

The application may be refused since recognition of a mark as well-known allows action against
confusingly similar marks even in unrelated classes of goods or services

The application must be allowed unless PIIPL proves actual consumer confusion and quantifiable
loss

The application must be refused only if the applicant intended to deceive consumers of matrimonial
services
questions.solution: Option A This reflects the rule applicable to ordinary trademarks, not well-known trademarks. The passage clearly distinguishes well-known marks by granting them protection beyond class limitations.

questions.questionText:
Nisha is accused by a shop owner of switching a costly watch with a duplicate. The shop owner
asks her to wait until the police arrive. The front exit is left open, but two employees stand
near it and repeatedly say that if she steps out, they will “break her phone and drag her back.”
Nisha remains seated for two hours. The owner later argues that no confinement occurred
because no one touched her and the exit was technically open. Is this argument legally
sustainable?
options:
Yes, because an open exit prevents wrongful confinement unless the victim is locked inside
a space or subjected to continuous physical restraint.

Yes, because remaining in a commercial establishment during a theft dispute constitutes a
voluntary stay rather than an unlawful curtailment of liberty.

No, because a shop owner's suspicion of theft automatically invalidates the requirement to
prove that the victim's physical movement was restricted.

No, because the deployment of employees combined with threats of immediate force can
cause a reasonable apprehension that leaving the area is impossible.
questions.solution: Is correct because the passage provides that surrounding exits or threatening immediate violence if a person leaves can create a reasonable fear that escape is impossible, thereby satisfying the legal test for wrongful confinement despite an unlocked door.

questions.questionText:
In acriminal law exam, a student writes that culpable homicide and murder are two unrelated
offences with no conceptual overlap. Another student writes that murder is a graver form
within the broader category of culpable homicide, and every murder is culpable homicide
though not every culpable homicide is murder. The examiner asks which answer better
reflects the relationship between the two provisions as explained by courts.
Which response is most accurate?
options:
They are unrelated offences because murder and culpable homicide share no common legal
foundation.

They are identical offences because every culpable homicide must receive the same
punishment as murder.
Section 299 is the genus and Section 300 is the species within that broader category.

Section 300 is broader because every death-causing act automatically becomes murder
first.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “Section 299 is the genus” and “Section 300 is the species.” It accurately captures the doctrinal relationship that culpable homicide is broader, while murder is its graver and more specific form.

questions.questionText:
The Supreme Court's observation that "those surrounding Delhi are filing Article 32 petitions"
most likely reflects:
options:
A finding by the bench that litigants residing in or near Delhi are geographically advantaged
in approaching the Supreme Court, and that this advantage is being systematically exploited
to bypass High Courts located in other states

A concern that litigants who have easy physical access to the Supreme Court in New Delhi are
more likely to file Article 32 petitions as a matter of convenience, rather than pursuing
appropriate remedies before their respective High Courts

A formal direction issued by the bench restricting litigants from the Delhi National Capital
Region from filing Article 32 petitions without prior leave of the Supreme Court

An observation that the High Courts located in and around Delhi are overburdened and
dysfunctional, compelling litigants to bypass them and directly approach the Supreme Court
for timely relief
questions.solution: is correct because the bench's remark is best understood as a practical observation about how geographical proximity to the Supreme Court in New Delhi incentivises litigants to file Article 32 petitions out of convenience, rather than as a reflection of any genuine or urgent fundamental rights violation. The remark underscores the casual, convenience-driven misuse of the provision that the Court was lamenting.

questions.questionText:
A Magistrate issues a summoning order against a wife for criminal breach of trust merely on
the basis of a complaint alleging that she removed jewellery from the matrimonial home,
without examining whether the jewellery constituted her streedhan. Applying the passage, the
High Court is most likely to:
options: Uphold the order because factual disputes cannot be examined at the summoning stage.
Set aside the order for failure to examine the essential ingredients of Section 406 IPC.
Direct the wife to return the jewellery before considering the legality of the proceedings.
Hold that matrimonial disputes automatically require criminal trial.
questions.solution: Option A — Incorrect. Although courts generally exercise caution at the summoning stage, they must still ensure that the basic ingredients of the alleged offence are disclosed.

questions.questionText:
The Mullaperiyar dam issue is a longstanding dispute between two Indian states - Kerala and Tamil
Nadu. The dam is located in Kerala's Idukki district on the Periyar river. There have been fresh disputes
on sharing of Cauvery water between Tamil Nadu and Kerala and the formation of the Cauvery Water
Management Authority. In recent years, increasing water scarcity, a rapid rise in urban and rural
demands for freshwater, and contentious political dynamics have further exacerbated the problem.
Owing to continuous interstate water dispute, the state of Kerala decided to file a petition in the High
Court of Kerala.
options:
The State of Kerala can file a petition in the High Court of Kerala as the Mullaperiyar dam is situated in
Kerala and hence, the jurisdiction lies with the High Court of Kerala.

The State of Kerala cannot file a petition in the High Court of Kerala as it does not have Original Jurisdiction
over it since the original jurisdiction for the dispute between the states lie with the Supreme Court.

River water disputes being important disputes between two or more States and/or the Union, should be heard
by a more competent court.

The State of Kerala should directly file a petition in the Supreme Court as it is the highest judicial court and
can solve the dispute efficiently.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): An employer will never be liable for intentional torts committed by employees.
Reason (R): Employers are generally not held liable for intentional torts, but may be liable if they
knew or should have known about the employee’s propensity.
options: Ais true, R is true and R is the correct explanation
Ais true, R is true but R is not the correct explanation
Ais true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.solution: The assertion uses the word “never,” which makes it absolute. The passage clearly creates an exception where employers may still be liable if they knew or should have known about the employee’s propensity.

questions.questionText:
Sahil buys a life policy naming his mother as beneficiary. After Sahil’s death, the insurer
refuses to pay, arguing the family has not produced bills or evidence of an “actual quantified
loss” and therefore the policy functions like indemnity, requiring strict proof of financial
damage. The mother replies that the policy pays a fixed sum on the covered event and does not
depend on proving monetary loss. The insurer insists all insurance is indemnity and that loss
quantification is mandatory.
Which conclusion best follows?
options:
Insurer cannot demand proof of quantified loss, because life insurance does not depend on
proof of an actual quantified loss, and pays on death.

Insurer can demand proof of quantified loss, because all insurance is indemnity, and
claimant must show actual monetary damage before any payout is allowed.

Insurer can deny payout because indemnity arises only after liability becomes absolute, so
without court decree of loss, the policy remains unenforceable.

Insurer must reimburse only medical expenses, because life policies cover only proved
hospital bills, and do not pay any fixed sum upon death.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: The option directly uses “life insurance does not depend on proof of an actual quantified loss,” which is the exact language of the reference line. It correctly separates life insurance from indemnity logic and shows why the insurer’s “show bills” demand is misplaced.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The practice of dowry is considered a direct violation of Article 14 of the Indian
Constitution.
Reasoning (R): The dowry system reinforces structural discrimination by treating women as
tools for financial extraction, thereby undermining the principle of equality.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.solution: is correct: The Assertion is true as the Court explicitly links dowry to a violation of Article 14. The Reasoning is also true and provides the specific legal logic (structural discrimination/financial extraction) used by the Court to justify why dowry violates the right to equality.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): If a disgruntled trespasser sabotages a large industrial pesticide plant causing a
gas leak, the plant owner will be held liable for all resulting damages, even if they had
implemented state-of-the-art security.
Reason (R): The landmark English case Rylands v. Fletcher established that a defendant
is prima facie liable if a hazardous substance brought onto their land escapes and causes mischief.
Select the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct, but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect, but (R) is correct.
questions.solution: 1. Analysis of Assertion (A): The assertion describes a "large industrial pesticide plant" (an enterprise) dealing with a gas leak caused by a "trespasser" (Act of a Stranger).

questions.questionText:
A franchise agreement between FastFood Ltd. (franchisor) and Ramesh (franchisee) contains two
clauses: Clause 5 states "Franchisee has exclusive rights in Delhi territory"; Clause 12 states
"Franchisor may appoint additional franchisees at its sole discretion in any territory." After
FastFood appoints another franchisee in Delhi, Ramesh sues for breach. FastFood cites Clause 12.
Based on the passage, which interpretive principle should the court apply?
options:
The literal rule of interpretation requiring the enforcement of Clause 12 as it provides a
clearer and more specific grant of discretionary power

The principle of harmonious construction requiring interpretation of both clauses so each
retains meaning without rendering either redundant.

The contra proferentem rule which mandates that any internal conflict or ambiguity be
interpreted against FastFood as the drafting party.

The parol evidence rule which prevents the court from examining extrinsic evidence to
determine which specific clause governs territorial rights.
questions.solution: The passage states the principle of harmonious construction requires "reconciling potentially conflicting provisions within the same contract, ensuring no clause becomes redundant and the document operates as an internally coherent whole." The court must interpret Clauses 5 and 12 so both have effect—for example, reading "any territory" in Clause 12 as excluding territories where exclusive rights have been granted under Clause 5. The passage notes this principle "finds equal relevance in contrac

questions.questionText:
A city hires a licensed, independent demolition contractor to tear down an old building. The
        contract specifies the safety standards but the city does not control the daily methods. The
        contractor's negligence causes debris to damage a neighboring store. The store owner sues the
        city. What is the probable result?
options:
General vicarious liability applies because the city hired the contractor and ultimately
        benefited from the completion of the work.

The city is vicariously liable because demolition is an inherently dangerous activity creating a
        foreseeable risk.

The city is not vicariously liable as the contractor is independent, and there was no non-
        delegable duty or negligence in selection.

The city is only directly liable if it failed to properly verify the contractor's license and
        insurance before hiring them.

questions.questionText:
Parliament enacts the “Coastal Examination Integrity Act” after reports of organised cheating
networks operating in selected coastal districts. The Act applies only to five coastal districts
across three States and not to the rest of India. Several petitioners argue that since
examination malpractice is a national concern, Parliament could either legislate for the whole
country or not legislate at all. They claim that a central law limited to only a few districts is
invalid merely because it does not apply uniformly across India. Which outcome best follows
from the passage?
options:
The law is invalid, because Parliament must apply national laws uniformly across the
whole territory of India.

The challenge fails on this ground because Parliament may make laws for the whole or any
part of India.

The law is invalid, because Parliament requires State approval before applying laws to
selected districts.

The challenge fails because Article 245(2) removes all territorial limits from Parliament’s
law-making power.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: the challenge is based only on limited territorial application. The passage clearly permits Parliament to legislate for the whole or any part of India.

questions.questionText:
Match the following judicial developments with their correct implications under
Article 21:
List I (Judicial Development):
1. A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
2. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
3. Expansion of “right to life” jurisprudence
4. Reading Article 21 with Articles 14 and 19
List II (Implication)
1. Procedure must be just, fair, and reasonable
2. Narrow interpretation of “procedure established by law”


3. Recognition of rights such as health, livelihood, and environment
4. Requirement of non-arbitrariness and reasonableness in State action

Choose the correct option:

The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 complements the Dowry
Prohibition Act by providing civil remedies to women facing domestic violence, including
dowry-related harassment. As noted in the passage, such civil remedies include protection
orders, residence orders, monetary relief, and compensation to address the harm suffered.
Which of the following is an order that a court could never pass under the PWDVA, given its
nature as a civil remedy statute?
options:
An order directing the respondent to cease all communication with and harassment of the
aggrieved woman, enforceable as a protection order under the statute.

An order granting the aggrieved woman the right to continue residing in the shared
household, regardless of whether she holds any ownership title over the property.

An order sentencing the respondent to three years of imprisonment as a primary remedy
for dowry-related harassment under the civil provisions of the PWDVA.

An order awarding financial compensation to the aggrieved woman for the mental torture
and emotional distress caused by domestic violence and dowry-related harassment.
questions.solution: The passage explicitly characterises the PWDVA as a statute providing civil remedies — protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, and compensation. A criminal sentence of imprisonment is not a civil remedy and falls entirely outside the scope of what a civil remedy statute can order.

questions.questionText:
The picturesque town of Kanchipuram, located in the southern state of Tamil Nadu, India, is
renowned for its centuries-old tradition of weaving by handloom exquisite silk sarees known as
"Kanchipuram Silk Sarees." Bhagyashree sarees situated in the town of Kanchipuram buys these sarees
from the weavers and sells these sarees in their retail store. They decide to apply for the registration of
these sarees as geographical indication. Can they do so in accordance with the definition of good and
producer from the passage?
options: Yes, because it is handicraft which is traded by Bhagyashree sarees.
No, because they are neither agricultural or natural or industrial good under section 2 (f).
Yes, because it is an industrial good being manufactured by Bhagyashree sarees.
No, because Bhagyshree sarees did not manufacture the good under section 2 (k).
questions.solution: Under Section 2(f), handicraft goods are expressly included within the definition of "goods." Further, Section 2(k) provides that in relation to handicraft or industrial goods, a "producer" includes not only the manufacturer but also any person who trades or deals in such goods. Since Bhagyashree Sarees purchases and trades in Kanchipuram Silk Sarees, it qualifies as a producer for the purposes of the Act and may apply for GI registration. Why other options are incorrect: B: Handicraft goods are expressly included within the statutory definition of goods.

questions.questionText:
Two companies enter into a contract specifying Hyderabad as the seat of arbitration. After
hearings are completed, the parties informally discuss preferring Kolkata, but no express
modification to the arbitration agreement is recorded.”, No written amendment is made to the
arbitration agreement. Subsequently, one party files a Section 34 petition in Kolkata.
Applying the reasoning of the Supreme Court, which of the following statements is most
accurate?
options:
The Kolkata courts can entertain the petition because the parties orally agreed to shift
jurisdiction.

The Hyderabad courts retain exclusive jurisdiction because the seat, once designated,
remains fixed and immutable unless the parties expressly agree to alter it.

Both Kolkata and Hyderabad courts can simultaneously exercise jurisdiction since the
parties orally agreed.

Neither court can exercise jurisdiction, and the matter must be referred back to the
arbitrator.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The Hyderabad courts retain exclusive jurisdiction because the seat, once designated, remains fixed and immutable unless the parties expressly agree to alter it. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A Parsi woman, Leena, was domiciled in Singapore at the time of her death. She owned an
apartment in Mumbai, jewellery kept in Singapore, and shares in a foreign company. Her
nephew argues that all her property must follow Singapore law because that was her domicile.
Her sister argues that Indian law governs the Mumbai apartment, while movable property
follows the law of Leena’s domicile. The dispute turns on how succession law treats immovable
and movable property differently.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Singapore law governs both immovable and movable property because domicile controls
every asset.
Indian law governs every asset because one property item is located within India.

Indian law governs only movable property, while domicile controls Indian immovable
property.

Indian law governs Indian immovable property, while domicile law governs movable
property.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line by distinguishing Indian immovable property from movable property. Therefore, Leena’s Mumbai apartment would follow Indian law, while her jewellery and foreign shares would be governed by the law of her domicile.

questions.questionText:
Mehul was admitted to a private de-addiction centre where another inmate, acting at the instigation of a staff
member, secretly mixed a highly corrosive substance into his liquid medication. Mehul survived after prolonged
treatment but suffered irreversible damage to his food pipe and respiratory tract due to severe internal burns.
Since he did not suffer any visible burns or facial disfigurement, the authorities rejected his application for benefits
available to acid attack victims under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Mehul challenged the
decision before the High Court. Decide the case.
options:
The court should dismiss the claim because benefits under the Act are available only where acid causes visible external
disfigurement.

The court should allow the claim because victims suffering internal injuries caused by corrosive substances can also
fall within the category of acid attack victims.

The court should reject the claim because injuries sustained through ingestion of a corrosive substance do not qualify
as an acid attack under the Act.

The court should allow the claim because every person injured by a hazardous chemical automatically qualifies as an
acid attack victim irrespective of the nature of the assault.

questions.questionText:
A large crowd of protestors, angry about a new law, clashes with police. They set
       vehicles on fire, damage a police station, and chant slogans demanding the resignation
       of the current Prime Minister. The protest turns violent, but there is no evidence they
       aimed to seize state power or overthrow the constitutional order. Can this be
       prosecuted as waging war under Section 121?
options:
No, this cannot be prosecuted as waging war because the crowd had no
               organized weapons or clear military-style strategy, which are essential to
               constitute the act of waging war.

Yes, this can be prosecuted as waging war because the violence was collective
               and targeted a police station, a key symbol of state authority, alongside the
               demand for a leader's resignation.

No, this cannot be prosecuted as waging war. While violent, the acts appear to
               be a riot with the object of protesting a policy, not a rebellion with the political
               purpose of overthrowing the government.

Yes, this can be prosecuted as waging war under Section 121 because any
               large-scale violence that challenges public order inherently threatens the state's
               stability and sovereignty.

questions.questionText:
Rohan marries Kavita in a Hindu ceremony while his earlier marriage with Neha is still
legally subsisting. Kavita is unaware of the earlier marriage. Two years later, a court declares
the marriage between Rohan and Kavita null and void under the Hindu Marriage Act. Their
son, Aarav, was born before the declaration. Rohan’s brother argues that since the marriage
itself was void from the beginning, Aarav must also be treated as illegitimate for family-law
purposes. Is this argument correct?
options:
Yes, because a child’s legal status follows the validity of the parents’ marriage under
Sections 5 and 7.

Yes, because once a marriage is declared null and void, no legal protection can arise from
that marriage.

No, because a child born from a void marriage shall be treated as legitimate despite the
marriage being null and void.

No, because the court declaration converts the void marriage into a valid marriage for the
child’s benefit.
questions.solution: Aarav was born from a void marriage, and Section 16(1) protects such a child from illegitimacy. The marriage between Rohan and Kavita may be null and void, but the child is not penalised merely because the parents’ marriage is void.

questions.questionText:
Rina is appointed guardian of her nephew Dev (a minor) and is given control over Dev’s rental
income. Rina starts depositing the rent into her personal account and uses it to fund her own
business expansion, promising that she will “repay later with profit.” Dev’s grandmother challenges
this conduct and seeks the court’s intervention, arguing that a guardian must not treat the ward’s
money as personal capital. Rina argues she is “family” and acted in Dev’s best interest by investing.
What is the best legal view?
options:
Guardian stands in a fiduciary position toward the ward, so personal use of the ward’s funds
breaches the duty even if repayment is promised.

Guardian is like an owner of the ward’s income, so using it for personal business is allowed as
long as some benefit is intended.

Guardian owes only moral duties, not legal ones, so court cannot intervene unless the guardian
admits dishonesty in writing first.

A guardian may freely invest the ward’s money in any venture without constraints, because
family relationships remove fiduciary duties altogether.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “fiduciary position toward the ward,” matching the reference line. A fiduciary cannot mix the ward’s assets with personal business interests or treat the ward’s money as private capital, because fiduciary duty demands loyalty and avoidance of conflict.

questions.questionText:
A student writes the following note after reading Section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act,
2019:
“A person can be treated as a consumer only when the entire consideration has been paid by
him personally. A user of goods or a beneficiary of services cannot claim consumer status
unless he was also the person who paid the price.”
Which of the following is the best correction of the student’s statement?
options:
Consideration may be paid, promised, partly paid or deferred, and an approved user or
beneficiary may also be included.

Consideration may be deferred only in goods transactions, while approved beneficiaries are
included only in service complaints.

Consideration may be partly promised only where the buyer personally uses the goods or
services without another beneficiary.

Consideration may be treated as valid only after delivery, while approved use only
supports compensation after purchase.
questions.solution: The passage provides that consideration may be paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or deferred. It also includes a user of goods or beneficiary of services where such use or benefit is with the approval of the buyer or hirer.

questions.questionText:
Ramesh is a purchasing agent for a pharmaceutical company, authorized to procure raw materials from approved
        suppliers. Acting within his authority, Ramesh places an order worth ₹25 lakh with a government-approved supplier
        for chemical compounds. After delivery and payment, the government suddenly bans the chemical compound due
        to newly discovered health hazards. The pharmaceutical company refuses to reimburse Ramesh for the ₹25 lakh,
        arguing that he should have anticipated the regulatory ban and that the loss is his responsibility since he made the
        purchasing decision. Based on the passage, is the pharmaceutical company liable to indemnify Ramesh for the ₹25
        lakh?
options:
No, because indemnity under the passage is meant for harm like injury, not for losses from purchase
            transactions.

No, because the government ban was an unforeseeable event, and principals are only required to indemnify
            agents for losses arising from foreseeable consequences of authorized acts.

Yes, because the agent acted lawfully within authority, and the law requires the principal to make good the
            consequences.

1

Yes, but only for 50% of the loss, as the passage implies that risks of authorized transactions should be shared
            equally between principal and agent.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because the agent acted lawfully within authority, and the law requires the principal to make good the consequences. 1. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Aman discovered that Bharat had once used a forged experience certificate while applying for
a private job. Aman met Bharat and said that he would send the documents to Bharat’s
employer and also file a criminal complaint unless Bharat transferred 73 lakh to Aman’s
brother within two hours. Bharat knew that the allegation was partly true, but he feared loss
of reputation and possible prosecution. He transferred the money to Aman’s brother. Aman
later argued that no extortion was committed because he did not threaten physical injury and
the money was not delivered directly to him. Has Aman committed extortion?
options:
Yes, because fear of injury may include injury to reputation or fear of criminal prosecution,
and Bharat delivered property due to that fear.

Yes, because any threat to file a complaint becomes extortion once the threatened person
decides to avoid public embarrassment.

No, because the allegation against Bharat was partly true and fear of prosecution can
amount to extortion only when the case is false.

No, because the money was transferred to Aman’s brother and not delivered directly to
Aman after the threat was made.
questions.solution: The passage explains that fear of injury may relate not only to physical injury but also to injury to reputation or fear of criminal prosecution, whether the prosecution threatened is true or false. Bharat transferred money because Aman intentionally put him in such fear.

questions.questionText:
Meera, a college student, was arrested on suspicion of cyber fraud at 8:00 p.m. The police informed
her that she was being taken into custody but did not clearly explain the grounds of her arrest. She
repeatedly requested to contact her lawyer, but the investigating officer delayed access, stating that legal
consultation would only be allowed after the initial questioning was completed. Meera was produced
before a magistrate within twenty-four hours. She later challenged the legality of the police's actions,
arguing that her constitutional rights had been violated. Based on the legal principles discussed in the
passage, which of the following statements is most accurate?
options:
Since Meera was produced before the magistrate within twenty-four hours, the police's failure to inform her
of the grounds of arrest and denial of access to a lawyer are legally immaterial.

Meera's constitutional rights were violated because Article 22 requires that an arrested person be informed of
the grounds of arrest and be allowed to consult a legal practitioner of her choice.

The police acted lawfully because they have complete discretion to postpone legal consultation until
interrogation is concluded.

Meera cannot challenge the arrest because procedural safeguards apply only after formal charges have been
filed.

questions.questionText:
Hiroshi, a Japanese businessman, operates a successful import-export company in Chennai. He leases a warehouse
        from an Indian landlord, Venkatesh. After a dispute over lease renewal terms, Venkatesh illegally locks the
        warehouse, preventing Hiroshi from accessing his goods worth ₹3 crore. Hiroshi wishes to immediately file a civil
        suit for mandatory injunction to regain access and for damages. Venkatesh argues that as a foreign national, Hiroshi
        must obtain special permission from the Government before approaching any Indian court. Based on the passage,
        is Venkatesh's argument regarding Hiroshi's right to sue correct?
options:
Yes, because all foreign nationals, regardless of their country's relationship with India, must obtain Central
             Government permission before filing any civil suit in Indian courts.

Yes, because the passage states that foreign nationals can only file suits in Indian courts if the Central
             Government appoints persons to represent them under Section 85.

No, because an "alien friend" from a country not at war with India may sue in an Indian court as if they were an
             Indian citizen under Section 83 CPC.

No, because Hiroshi has been conducting business in India, which automatically grants him Indian citizenship
             for litigation purposes regardless of his actual nationality.


1
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because an "alien friend" from a country not at war with India may sue in an Indian court as if they were an Indian citizen under Section 83 CPC. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Three event organisers plan to block a rival organiser’s exhibition by arranging volunteers to
remove signboards, cut the temporary lighting wires, and stop visitors at the entrance. Each
organiser performs a different part of the plan, but all had discussed the objective the previous
night. The exhibition suffers financial loss. One organiser argues that he only removed
signboards and did not personally cut wires or stop visitors. The rival organiser claims all
three acted together toward a common wrongful objective.
Which conclusion is most accurate?
options: They are independent actors because each person performed a different physical act.
They are joint tortfeasors because they acted together under a common design.
They are not liable together because only the wire-cutting directly caused damage.
They are liable together only if all three repeated the same wrongful act.
questions.solution: This option directly follows the reference line because the organisers acted together and in furtherance of a common design to obstruct the rival exhibition. Their coordinated plan resulted in financial damage, making the conclusion of joint tortfeasorship legally appropriate.

questions.questionText:
A technologically advanced State claims exclusive ownership over a mineral-rich part of the
deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction. It grants mining licences to its corporations and
refuses to share environmental data or economic benefits, arguing that first discovery creates
ownership. Several developing States object, saying resources of this nature belong to all
humanity and require cooperative management and benefit sharing.
Which conclusion best reflects the relevant environmental-law principle?
options:
Advanced State succeeds because first discovery gives permanent ownership over all
unoccupied global resources.

Objecting States succeed because seabed resources are treated as belonging to all
humanity.

Advanced State succeeds because technology gives superior title over resources beyond
national territory.

Objecting States succeed because benefit sharing applies only to rivers within national
borders.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “seabed” and “belonging to all humanity,” matching the reference line. The claim of exclusive ownership over deep seabed minerals conflicts with the idea that such resources require treatment as part of the common heritage of mankind.

questions.questionText:
Thanjavur Art Plates are known for their historical and cultural significance, dating back to the
Chola dynasty in the 9th century. The craft has been nurtured and refined by generations of artisans in
Thanjavur, who have preserved and passed on their intricate skills to their descendants. These art plates
are made using traditional materials and techniques, including the casting of metal alloys, detailed hand
sculpting, and the application of gold foil. Each plate is a masterpiece, taking weeks or even months to
complete. In recent years, there has been concern regarding the misrepresentation and imitation of
Thanjavur Art Plates by producers from outside the region, leading to a loss of income for local artisans
and diminishing their cultural significance. The Producers’ Association decide to apply for a
Geographical Indication (GI) in 2010 to protect and promote the unique identity and heritage of
Thanjavur Art Plates. They apply for the registration with the requisite fee and the registration is
granted. The renewal is neglected by them. When Vishnu is visiting a place in the north in 2021, he sees
replica of these plates. He, being a trader of such plates, files for infringement of the GI. Will he succeed
in light of the passage?
options: Yes, because there can be infringement action for a registered GI under section 21 and 22.
No, because this kind of product is not included in the definition of good under section 2 (f).
Yes, because the product is included as a good with unique characteristics under section 2 (e).
No, because the registration has surpassed the time period with no renewal.

questions.questionText:
Akash and Akanksha are 17 and 16 years old respectively and are living in the State of Uttar Pradesh,
a State that is known to condemn relationships between any unmarried couple. Being very close to each
other, Akash and Akanksha decide to have sexual intercourse one day. Some neighbours, on coming to
know about this, file a charge of rape against Akash. Is he liable for rape?
options: He is liable because he should not have had sexual intercourse with Akanksha as it is against his morals.
He is liable because the people of Uttar Pradesh will condemn it.
He is liable because Akanksha is below 18 years of age.
He is not liable.
questions.solution: The passage clearly states that after the amendment to Section 375 IPC, any form of penetration with a female below 18 years of age amounts to rape, irrespective of her consent. Since Akanksha is only 16 years old, Akash's act falls within the definition of rape. The social views of Uttar Pradesh are legally irrelevant. Why other options are incorrect: A: Criminal liability is based on law, not personal morals. B: Public opinion or social condemnation does not determine criminal liability. D: Incorrect because consent of a girl below 18 is not legally valid for the purpose of Section

questions.questionText:
A municipal regulation requires residents to remain indoors after 10 PM unless they obtain
special permission from local authorities. A citizen claims that this regulation deprives them of
personal liberty under Article 21.
Applying the reasoning in the passage, which interpretation is most consistent?
options: The regulation amounts to restriction of movement under Article 19 rather than Article 21.
The regulation is unconstitutional because Article 21 protects all forms of liberty.
The regulation automatically amounts to deprivation of personal liberty.

The regulation cannot be challenged under the Constitution.
7:44 @	Bil 64.
€	Balance & History	;
Your Accounts
Total Balance: $11.03	(1 of 2 accounts)
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The regulation amounts to restriction of movement under Article 19 rather than Article 21. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A courier company instructs its delivery rider to deliver parcels within office hours using a
company vehicle. While rushing to complete assigned deliveries, the rider negligently hits a
pedestrian. The company argues that only the rider touched the vehicle controls and therefore
only he can be liable. The pedestrian says the rider was acting in the course of employment
and the employer may also be responsible for the wrongful act.
Which conclusion best follows?
options: The company escapes liability because only the rider physically caused the accident.
The company escapes liability because employment never affects tort responsibility.
The company may be liable only if it personally instructed negligent driving.
The company may be liable because employers can answer for employees’ wrongful acts.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line because vicarious liability may arise where one person is made liable for another’s wrongful act due to the employer-employee relationship. The rider was using a company vehicle for assigned deliveries, making employer liability arguable.

questions.questionText: R repeatedly told S that his business rival had ruined his reputation and that "a lesson should be taught so severe that he never dares interfere again." Over several weeks, R continuously encouraged S to confront the rival and praised violent retaliation as the only meaningful response. Eventually, S assaulted the rival. Which of the following is most appropriate?
options: R may be liable for abetment by instigation because repeated conduct intended to encourage the offence may amount to active provocation.
R cannot be liable because he did not physically participate in the assault.
R may only be liable if he supplied weapons used in the assault.
R cannot be liable because expressions of opinion can never constitute instigation.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: R may be liable for abetment by instigation because repeated conduct intended to encourage the offence may amount to active provocation. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A 18-year-old child is found repeatedly stealing packaged food from a supermarket and is later
discovered to be living under a flyover after being abandoned by relatives. The store owner
demands that the child be publicly punished to deter other children. A child-rights worker
argues that the matter should be handled through counselling, education support, shelter
linkage, and reintegration measures rather than adult-style punishment.
Which approach best reflects the governing principle?
options:
Public punishment is proper because repeated conduct removes the child from juvenile
protection.

Adult-style deterrence is proper because property offences require exemplary punishment
for children.

Reformative handling is proper because juvenile law follows rehabilitation rather than
purely punitive response.

Criminal trial is mandatory because poverty and abandonment cannot affect treatment of
child offenders.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “rehabilitation” and “rather than purely punitive response,” matching the reference line. The facts involve a young child, repeated petty misconduct, and visible care-and-protection concerns, making counselling, shelter support, and reintegration more aligned with juvenile justice.

questions.questionText:
A enters into an agreement with B, under which A promises to pay B a monthly allowance on
the condition that B does not marry until the age of 25. At the time of entering into the
agreement, B is 16 years old. B accepts the condition and begins receiving payments. After
attaining the age of 19, B decides to marry, and A stops the payments, claiming that B has
violated the agreement.
In light of the above passage and principles of law, what is the correct legal position?
options:
The entire agreement is void from the beginning because it restrains marriage, and no part
of it can be enforced at any stage.

The agreement is valid only until B attains the age of 18, after which it becomes void as it
restrains the marriage of a major.

The agreement is fully valid until the age of 25, as B had voluntarily consented to the
condition at the time of entering into the agreement.

The agreement is voidable at the option of B upon attaining majority, and remains valid
unless B expressly repudiates it.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The agreement is valid only until B attains the age of 18, after which it becomes void as it restrains the marriage of a major. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A person obtains a license from another person to use their vacant land for parking his car. The
license is for a period of six months and the person pays a monthly fee to the licensor. After three months,
the licensor sells the land to a third party, who wants to construct a building on it. The third party asks
the person to vacate the land and stop parking his car there. The person refuses and files a suit for
injunction against the third party, claiming that the original licensor had no valid title of ownership. Can
the person invoke the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the third party?
options:
Yes, because he made a representation of an existing fact (that he had a license to use the land) to the third
party, who acted upon it and bought the land, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

Yes, because he made a representation of a future fact (that he would use the land for parking his car) to the
licensor, who acted upon it and granted him the license, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he did not make any representation to the licensor or the third party, but only obtained a license
from the licensor, who was not a party to the suit, and he cannot be estopped by a third party.

No, because he obtained a license from the licensor to use their immovable property, and then relied on it to
claim some right or interest in the property, and he cannot be estopped by his own reliance.

questions.questionText:
Assume that after the earlier incident, Ananya converted her private flower-processing unit
into a large fragrance-extraction enterprise, where highly volatile chemical vapours were used
under pressure to extract oil from flowers. The activity required specialised storage chambers
and carried a known risk of toxic exposure if vapours leaked. Ananya appointed an
independent contractor to maintain the chambers and argued that all safety inspections had
been outsourced to that contractor. One night, due to a defect in a chamber maintained by the
contractor, toxic vapours escaped from the unit and affected workers inside the unit as well as
residents of the nearby village, including Kunal’s family. Ananya argued that she was not
liable because the defect was caused by the contractor, she had not personally acted
negligently, and similar defences would have been available under Strict Liability. Is Ananya
absolutely liable?
options:
Yes, because the enterprise carried on a hazardous activity, owed an absolute and non-
delegable duty, and harm resulted from that activity.

Yes, because the enterprise carried on a hazardous activity, but only the workers directly
present inside the unit can be compensated.

No, because the defect arose from the contractor’s maintenance, and liability can be
avoided by delegating safety inspection.

No, because absence of personal negligence and contractor fault remain available as
exceptions to Absolute Liability.
questions.solution: The passage provides that an enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. Here, Ananya’s fragrance-extraction enterprise used volatile chemical vapours under pressure, and harm resulted from that hazardous activity.

questions.questionText:
A new religion, Asatru, has this practice of the first child in each family being sent to a religious school
to learn the practices of Asatrus. The religious school demands that all entrants join the school at the age
of 5 and stay there till they complete their education by the age of 25. Post this, the student would be
allotted one of the schools Asatru runs where the student should be attached to till the age of 60,
whereupon the student should retire to the Himalayas. Students should dedicate their lives to Asatru and
disown their own families. Supreme Court receives a petition from adherents of Asatru requesting that
this practice be banned. Decide which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Supreme Court cannot interfere as Article 26 explicitly states guarantees the rights of religions.
The Supreme Court cannot intervene as this is an essential tenet of religion Asatru.
The Supreme Court cannot intervene as Article 25 protects the rights of any individual to follow any religion.

The Supreme Court can intervene in order to protect young children from being oppressed and excluded
from normal life.

questions.questionText:
W and Z signed a tenancy agreement in which Z agreed to pay the electricity charges in addition to
the agreed-upon rent. Later, Z refused to pay the electricity bills, alleging that he had recently been laid
off. Because W was a friend, he did not pressure him and instead gave him some time to arrange for the
money. After six months, W became irritated and demanded that Z either pay the electricity bill or vacate
the flat. Because the arrangement was for 10 months, Z proceeded to court and sued W for breach of
contract. Because the verdict was in W's favour, Z decided to file a lawsuit in a different state's high
court. What do you have to say about Z's course of action?
options:
Z made the right choice because, when justice isn't served in one high court, a person has the right to file a
claim in another high court.
Z faulted in his judgment since in such circumstances, the Supreme Court should be promptly appealed to.
Given that the res judicata principle will invalidate Z's action, he did not make the right decision.

Since such frivolous disagreements between friends are not intended to be brought before a judge, Z has not
made the right choice.

questions.questionText:
Two security guards jointly agree to teach a shopkeeper “a lesson” after an argument. One
holds the shopkeeper back while the other breaks the glass counter and damages stored goods.
Both guards later argue that the person who restrained the shopkeeper should not be liable for
the broken counter because he did not personally damage the property. The shopkeeper argues
that both acted together and each is responsible for the entire damage caused by the
coordinated wrongful act.
Which statement is correct?
options: Each may be liable for the entire damage because liability is joint and several.
Each is liable only for the exact physical act personally performed by him.
The restraining guard escapes liability because property damage was done by another.
Both escape joint liability unless they broke the same counter together.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line by recognising that each joint tortfeasor may be individually liable for the entire damage and collectively liable with others. Since both guards acted together in a coordinated wrongful plan, each may bear full responsibility.

questions.questionText:
Suresh owned a licensed textile shop and also secretly operated an illegal betting counter from
the back room of the same premises. He entered into one written agreement with Mehul, an
accountant, under which Mehul had to maintain accounts for the textile shop and also conceal
the betting-counter collections from official records. The agreement promised Mehul one
consolidated monthly fee of %75,000 and did not divide the fee between the lawful accounts
work and the unlawful concealment work. After two months, Suresh refused to pay Mehul.
Assertion (A): Mehul cannot enforce the agreement even for the textile-shop accounts work,
because the lawful and unlawful parts were combined under one inseparable fee.
Reason (R): If any part of a single consideration for one or more objects is unlawful, the
agreement is void.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.solution: Assertion is true because Mehul was promised one consolidated fee for both lawful accounting work and unlawful concealment of betting-counter collections. Reason is also true because the passage provides that if any part of a single consideration for one or more objects is unlawful, the agreement is void.

questions.questionText:
A patient's family executed a living will on her behalf claiming she had orally authorised them
to do so. The patient subsequently recovered partial consciousness but could not communicate.
The hospital refused to treat the living will as valid. The family argued that Common Cause
does not require the patient to personally execute the directive and that their authorisation
suffices.
options:
A living will may be executed by an immediate family member on behalf of a patient, as
they are the most appropriate persons to speak to the patient's best interests under the
"best interests" principle.

An Advance Medical Directive must be executed by the individual personally while
competent; a directive executed by a family member in their place is invalid under the
Common Cause framework.

Since the patient recovered partial consciousness, the living will — whether valid or not —
is superseded by the patient's current condition and cannot guide treatment decisions at
this stage.
questions.solution: An Advance Medical Directive is an exercise of personal autonomy and must be executed by the individual herself while mentally competent. The entire basis of its legal validity — self-determination and bodily integrity — requires that the will expressed is the patient's own, not a surrogate's.

questions.questionText:
A 15-year-old child, Aaron, was born in India while both parents were domiciled in India.
Later, his father permanently shifted to Canada and clearly acquired Canadian domicile.
Aaron continued studying in India, and relatives argued that he independently retained
Indian domicile because he personally preferred living in India. A dispute arises over
succession to Aaron’s movable assets after his death.
Which principle best applies to determine the domicile issue?
options: Aaron’s domicile follows the parent, and one person can have only one domicile.

Aaron may keep two domiciles because residence and personal preference both operate
together.
Aaron’s domicile is fixed permanently at birth and can never follow parental change.
Aaron’s domicile depends only on school location, not on the parent’s domicile.
questions.solution: This option directly uses two parts of the reference line: a person can have only one domicile, and a minor’s domicile follows that of the parent. Since Aaron is a minor, his personal preference or school location cannot independently create a separate domicile contrary to the relevant parental domicile.

questions.questionText:
On a foggy highway, Dev suddenly sees a school bus stopped ahead and a child running into his lane. To
avoid hitting the child, Dev swerves into a parked delivery van, causing costly damage and minor injury
to his passenger. The van owner files a complaint, alleging Dev knowingly caused harm to property. Dev
pleads necessity, saying he acted in good faith, without criminal intent, and that the harm prevented
was far greater than the harm caused.
How should the court evaluate his defence?
options:
Defence fails because any harmful act is an offence, and preventing harm can never justify causing
harm to property here.

The defence succeeds because Section 81 requires absence of criminal intent and good faith, and the
harm prevented must exceed harm caused.

Defence succeeds because intention to save someone automatically excuses any damage, even if
alternatives existed and the risk was avoidable.

Defence fails because good faith is irrelevant, and only the actor’s personal fear matters, not
proportionality of harms.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “absence of criminal intent and good faith” and the proportionality idea that “harm prevented must exceed harm caused,” matching the reference line’s language. Dev’s defence turns on whether he acted in good faith, without criminal intention, and whether the avoided harm (death/serious injury) outweighed the caused harm (property damage/minor injury).

questions.questionText:
Ms. Sharma has been an independent director at 'TechFlow Ltd.", a listed company, for the past 12
years. Recently, she was notified about the new rule that requires IDs to clear an online proficiency test
conducted by the IICA. Given her long-standing role in the company, she was surprised and contacted
the legal team for advice. In this context, should Ms. Sharma be required to take the proficiency test as
per the new rule?
options:
Yes, because as an Independent Director, Ms. Sharma is obligated to regularly update and refresh her skills,
knowledge, and familiarity with the company, which the proficiency test seeks to establish.

No, because Ms. Sharma, as a director, has served for more than ten years in a listed company, making her
exempt from the test under the new rule.

Yes, because the proficiency test aims to demonstrate the expected qualifications for individuals aspiring to
be IDs, which Ms. Sharma must prove despite her experience.

No, because Ms. Sharma, as an existing ID, has already demonstrated her proficiency and capabilities
through her past work, making the test unnecessary for her.

questions.questionText:
Sita, a 16-year-old schoolgirl, playfully threw a small pebble at her classmate and best friend
Geeta during lunch break in the school courtyard, intending it as harmless jest as they had done
many times before without incident. However, this time the pebble struck Geeta's eye, causing
retinal detachment resulting in permanent partial blindness. There was no prior enmity, quarrel,
or malicious intent whatsoever between the two friends. Decide Sita's criminal liability under IPC
for causing grievous hurt.
options:
Sita is not criminally liable since she possessed no intention to cause hurt or injury to her
friend

Sita is liable under strict liability principles as grievous hurt was caused regardless of mental
state of the accused

Sita may be liable for voluntarily causing grievous hurt as the act was voluntary and hurt was
a foreseeable consequence

Sita's liability is confined exclusively to civil damages under tort law and does not attract
criminal prosecution in this case
questions.solution: This tests understanding of voluntary acts with foreseeable consequences. While Sita lacked intention to cause grievous hurt specifically, the passage framework requires examining whether the consequence was foreseeable from a voluntary act.

questions.questionText:
A, a 15-year-old girl living in Nagpur, has a friend, B, who is 23 years old in actuality but has
concealed his age to make A believe that he is only 18 years old. Actually, A and B met online and A has
never seen B in real life. They decide to meet up one day. B called her to a secluded place, and she
followed because she trusted him. One thing led to another and B inserted his body part into A's vagina.
A refused continuously, but he did not stop. Although there was no penile penetration, A was extremely
traumatised by this event. She files a charge of rape against B. Decide.
options: B is liable for rape because he inserted his body part into A's vagina.
B is not liable because there was no penal penetration.
B is liable because he concealed his age.
B is not liable because there was implied consent by following him to the secluded place.
questions.solution: The passage states that the amended definition of rape includes the insertion of any object or any part of the body, other than the penis, into the vagina, urethra, or anus of a woman. It further explains that any penetration involving a female below 18 years of age amounts to rape. In this case, A is 15 years old, continuously refused the act, and B inserted a body part into her vagina. Therefore, B is liable for rape under Section 375. Why other options are incorrect: B: The passage explicitly states that rape is no longer limited to penile penetration. C: Concealing his age may amount to deception, but it is not the legal basis for rape under

questions.questionText:
Rohan, an experienced trekker, signed a detailed waiver before joining a guided
       mountain expedition, acknowledging risks like avalanches. During the trek, a sudden,
       unprecedented avalanche, which no forecast predicted, swept him away, causing severe
       injury. He sues the tour company for negligence.
options:
The tour company would likely be held liable as the waiver cannot cover gross
       negligence.

The tour company would likely be liable because an avalanche is never considered a
       natural risk.

The tour company would likely not be liable as Rohan voluntarily assumed the known
       risks of trekking.

The tour company would likely not be liable because the avalanche was an
       unforeseeable Act of God.

questions.questionText:
Meera leaves an antique wooden chest with Nikhil, a professional storage operator, for two
months while her house is renovated. Nikhil keeps the chest in the same humidity-controlled
room where he stores his own expensive furniture, checks the room daily, and maintains
security records. During an unexpected internal wiring spark, the sprinkler system damages
the chest. Meera argues that Nikhil must compensate her because the chest deteriorated while
it was in his possession.
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Nikhil’s duty is to take the level of care that an ordinarily prudent person
would take of his own goods.
Statement B: Nikhil becomes liable merely because the chest deteriorated while it was in his
custody.
Statement C: The comparison is with reasonable ordinary care, not with perfect protection
against every mishap.
Which of the above statements is correct?
options: Statements A and C are correct, while Statement B applies an excessive standard.
Statements A and B are correct, while Statement C reduces the bailee’s duty.
Statements B and C are correct, while Statement A ignores professional storage.
Statement A alone is correct, while Statements B and C excuse deterioration.
questions.solution: the passage states that the bailee’s duty is measured by the care of a person of ordinary prudence dealing with his own goods. Nikhil stored the chest with precautions similar to those used for his own valuable furniture, and the standard is reasonable care, not faultless preservation.

questions.questionText:
A person rents a shop from another person for a period of one year. The rent agreement mentions that
the landlord has a valid title to the shop and that the tenant will not dispute it during the tenancy. After
six months, the tenant learns that the landlord has mortgaged the shop to a bank and that the bank has
initiated foreclosure proceedings against the landlord. The tenant stops paying rent and files a suit for
injunction against the landlord and the bank, claiming that he has a better title to the shop than the
owner. Can the tenant invoke the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the landlord and the bank from evicting
him?
options:
Yes, because he made a representation of an existing fact (that he agreed to the landlord's title) to the
landlord, who acted upon it and leased him the shop, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

Yes, because he made a representation of a future fact (that he would not dispute the landlord's title) to the
landlord, who acted upon it and leased him the shop, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he did not make any representation to the bank, but only to the landlord, who was not a party to
the suit, and he cannot be estopped by a third party.

No, because he accepted a fact (that the landlord had a title to the shop) in his rent agreement, and then tried
to deny it during the continuance of the tenancy, and he cannot be estopped by his own acceptance.

questions.questionText:
A severe and unprecedented flood struck a town, causing extensive damage to nearby houses
and commercial establishments. Ravi owned a large warehouse near the riverbank, where he
stored heavy construction material. During the flood, a boundary wall of the warehouse
collapsed, and the material was washed into neighbouring properties, causing substantial
damage. An investigation later revealed that the wall had not been repaired for several years
despite visible structural cracks and repeated warnings from local authorities.
In light of the above passage, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
Ravi can successfully use the defence of Act of God because floods are natural events
entirely beyond human control and foresight.

Ravi will not be liable because the damage was primarily caused by an extraordinary
natural disaster rather than any intentional act on his part.

Ravi cannot claim the defence of Act of God because negligent maintenance of the
boundary wall contributed to the damage caused during the flood.

Ravi can avoid liability under strict liability since natural disasters automatically exempt
all persons from legal responsibility.
questions.solution: The defence of Act of God applies only where the damage is caused exclusively by natural forces without any human contribution or negligence. In the present case, although the flood was a natural event, Ravi failed to maintain the warehouse wall despite visible cracks and prior warnings.

questions.questionText:
Neha wanted to obtain a large bank loan against her warehouse. The bank required an
independent valuation report before sanctioning the loan. Neha entered into an agreement
with Varun, a registered valuer, under which Varun would prepare a valuation report showing
the warehouse to be worth 28 crore, although both knew its approximate value was only %3
crore. The agreement described Varun’s fee as “professional charges for documentation
support.” Varun prepared and submitted the inflated report, but Neha later refused to pay the
fee. Varun sued Neha for his professional charges, arguing that he had performed the agreed
service. Is Varun’s claim enforceable?
options:
Yes, because Varun prepared the report and Neha received the benefit of the promised
documentation service.

Yes, because the bank was not a party to the agreement and Neha had voluntarily agreed
to pay Varun’s fee.

No, because the agreement is unenforceable only if the bank proves actual financial loss
from the report.

No, because the object or consideration of the agreement was fraudulent and therefore
unlawful under Section 23.
questions.solution: The passage states that Section 23 declares an agreement void where the object or consideration is fraudulent. Since Neha and Varun agreed to create a knowingly inflated valuation report to support a loan application, the object of the agreement was fraudulent.

questions.questionText:
A women’s rights group challenges different personal-law rules that allow easier divorce rights
to husbands than wives and unequal maintenance outcomes after desertion. The group argues
that a common civil framework may reduce discrimination in marriage and divorce and
support women’s dignity and equality. Opponents respond that uniformity has no connection
with women’s rights and concerns only administrative convenience.
Which statement best reflects the principle in the passage?
options:
Uniform civil rules concern only administrative convenience and have no link with
women’s equality.
Uniform civil rules are linked only with criminal reforms, not family-law discrimination.
Uniform civil rules may be discussed only for inheritance, not marriage or maintenance.
Uniform civil rules are closely linked with gender justice in personal-law matters.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “closely linked with gender justice,” matching the reference line. Unequal divorce and maintenance rules are precisely the kind of personal-law concerns through which the gender-justice argument becomes relevant.

questions.questionText:
Amit gratuitously lends his vintage motorcycle to Bela for a weekend trip. Amit is
       aware that the motorcycle's front brake cable is severely worn and may fail, but he
       does not inform Bela. During the trip, the front brake fails on a steep hill, causing an
       accident and significant damage to the motorcycle. Bela seeks compensation from
       Amit for the repair costs. Is Amit liable?
options:
The liability should be apportioned between both parties since Bela also assumed
           some risk by using an old vehicle.

Amit is not liable for the damages because the bailment was entirely for Bela's
           benefit with no payment involved.

Amit is liable because he failed to disclose a known fault posing an extraordinary
           risk in a gratuitous bailment.

Amit would only be held liable if Bela could successfully prove in court that Amit
           had prior knowledge of the specific mechanical fault.

questions.questionText:
A person represents themselves as the landlord of an immovable property and leases it to another
person for a period of one year. The rent agreement mentions that the landlord has a valid title to the
property and that the tenant will not dispute it during the tenancy. The tenant pays rent and occupies the
property as per the agreement. After six months, the landlord informs the tenant that he has sold the
property to a third party and asks him to vacate it within one month. The tenant refuses and files a suit
for injunction against the landlord and the third party, claiming that he has a right to continue his
tenancy till its expiry. Can the landlord invoke the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the tenant from
claiming his tenancy rights?
options:
Yes, because he made a representation of an existing fact (that he was the landlord of the property) to the
tenant, who acted upon it and rented the property, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

Yes, because he made a representation of a future fact (that he would sell the property to a third party) to the
tenant, who acted upon it and rented the property, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he did not make any representation to the tenant, but only represented himself as the landlord of
the property, who was not a party to the suit, and he cannot be estopped by a third party.

No, because he represented himself as the landlord of an immovable property and leased it to another person,
who paid rent and occupied the property, and then he tried to deny his title or possession, and others cannot be
estopped by his representation.

questions.questionText: R and T entered into a contract whereby R agreed to sell metallic rods to T for a specified price. T paid the entire purchase price in advance before dispatch of the goods. While the goods were being transported to T’s factory, T inspected the shipment upon arrival and found that the rods were of inferior quality and therefore rejected the order. Decide whether R has the right of stoppage in transit.
options: R does not have the right to stoppage in transit because the goods were not of the stipulated quality.
R does not have the right to stoppage in transit because he has already been paid in full.
R does have the right to stoppage in transit because T refused to accept the delivery.
R does have the right to stoppage in transit because it is a right available to every seller
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: R does not have the right to stoppage in transit because he has already been paid in full. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Which of the following situations is most analogous to the conduct that the Supreme Court
criticised in the passage?
options:
A litigant who files a fresh writ petition before the Supreme Court under Article 32 after their
petition under Article 226 before the High Court has already been finally decided and
dismissed on merits

A litigant who directly approaches the Supreme Court under Article 32 seeking enforcement of
a fundamental right, without having filed any prior petition before any High Court on the
same issue

A litigant who files a petition under Article 32 before the Supreme Court on the same issue for
which their petition is already pending and has not yet been decided by the High Court

A litigant who withdraws their pending petition before the High Court under Article 226 and
thereafter approaches the Supreme Court under Article 32 on the same matter with the court's
permission
questions.solution: is correct because it directly mirrors the factual situation in the passage — the petitioner approached the Supreme Court under Article 32 while a similar matter was already pending and actively being heard by the Bombay High Court. This is precisely the conduct the bench described as a "gross misuse of the process of the court and of law."

questions.questionText:
Following her release after being acquitted in a high-profile case, Kavita, a renowned activist, decides
to file a lawsuit against the government for wrongful imprisonment and defamation. She seeks free legal
aid, citing her financial difficulties. However, the legal aid organization is hesitant, given her high public
profile and previous legal history. Kavita argues that her case is genuine and falls within the parameters
of legal aid eligibility. Which of the following statements most accurately reflects the legal aid
organization's position in this scenario?
options:
Yes, they can refuse legal aid as Kavita's high public profile and previous legal history may impact the
perception of her case.

No, they cannot refuse legal aid because Kavita has a right to legal aid regardless of her public profile or
previous legal history.

Yes, they can refuse legal aid if they believe Kavita's case does not have merit or falls outside the scope of
their assistance.
No, they cannot refuse legal aid as previous legal history and public profile are not valid grounds for denial.

questions.questionText:
After a shipwreck, four survivors drift for days without food or rescue, facing extreme starvation.
Believing all will die, two survivors agree to kill the weakest member and consume his body to
