survive. They are rescued the next morning and prosecuted for intentional killing. They claim
necessity: the act was the only way to avoid the greater harm of everyone dying. Assuming these
facts are proved, which legal position best matches the passage principle on necessity?
options:
Defence succeeds because necessity triumphs over law, so killing one to save others is lawful
when survival is at stake.

Defence fails because necessity was rejected as a defence to murder, so intentional killing
cannot be justified by survival claims.

Defence succeeds because absence of alternatives always excuses homicide, and courts must
prefer utilitarian outcomes over legal prohibitions.

Defence fails only if killing was malicious, so if done in good faith and fairly, murder becomes
excusable necessity.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “rejected as a defence to murder” and applies them to intentional killing for survival. Under the passage’s principle, necessity does not justify murder even in desperate conditions, making the defence unavailable on these facts.

questions.questionText:
A person is accused of murdering his wife. In his statement to the police, he confesses that he killed
her in a fit of rage after finding out that she was having an affair. He also gives details of the time, place
and mode of the murder. However, in his trial, he retracts his confession and pleads not guilty. He claims
that he was tortured and coerced by the police to make a false confession. He also produces an alibi
witness who testifies that he was with him at the time of the murder. Can the person invoke the doctrine
of estoppel to prevent the prosecution from using his confession as evidence against him?
options:
Yes, because he made a representation of an existing fact (that he killed his wife) to the police, who acted
upon it and arrested him, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he made a statement in court that contradicted, denied or declared to be false his previous
statement to the police, and he cannot be estopped by his own statement.

Yes, because he made a statement in court that was consistent with his innocence and supported by an alibi

witness, and he cannot be estopped by his previous statement to the police.

No, because he did not make any statement in court, but only retracted his previous statement to the police,
and he cannot be estopped by a retraction.

questions.questionText:
Assume that the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO), a statutory investigative body under
central law, files a writ petition before a High Court challenging a State Government’s order that
allegedly interferes with its investigation. The State objects, arguing that the SFIO cannot file a writ
petition under Article 226 as it is only an investigative agency.
Based on the reasoning adopted by the High Court in the passage, which of the following is
the most appropriate conclusion?
options:
The writ petition is not maintainable because investigative agencies cannot seek remedies under
Article 226.
The writ petition is maintainable only if the fundamental rights of accused persons are violated.

The writ petition is maintainable because the SFIO performs statutory functions and may be
treated as a juristic entity.

The writ petition is not maintainable because Article 226 is available only against investigative
agencies, not to them.
questions.solution: This option correctly applies the High Court’s reasoning. Just as the ED was allowed to file a writ due to its juristic status and statutory functions, the SFIO can also be treated similarly.

questions.questionText:
A foreign national residing in India is denied permission to practice a profession under a state law.
They claim that their personal liberty under Article 21 has been violated. The state argues that
Article 19(1) rights are only for citizens, so the law is valid. Based on the above case, which of the
following is correct?
options: Article 21 applies to all persons, so the foreign national can challenge the law.
Only citizens are protected under Article 21, so the foreign national has no claim.
Article 19(1) rights are broader than Article 21, so citizenship is irrelevant.
Preventive detention laws override Article 21 for foreign nationals.
questions.solution: Principle from the case: Kania CJ emphasized: “Article 19 gives the rights specified therein only to the citizens of India while Article 21 is applicable to all persons.” This means personal liberty under Article 21 is not restricted to citizens; any person in India, including a foreign national, can invoke it.

questions.questionText:
A construction company indemnifies its architect against litigation arising from design
allegations. A client sues the architect and demands damages. The architect, acting on legal
advice, enters a settlement that is reasonable in the circumstances and made in good faith,
avoiding a larger exposure. The indemnifier refuses reimbursement, arguing that only court-
decreed damages are covered and settlements are “voluntary.” The architect claims indemnity
includes certain payments made by compromise.
Which claim most directly fits the indemnity-holder’s recovery rights?
options:
The indemnity-holder may recover only court-awarded damages, and cannot claim
compromise amounts, even if settlement was reasonable, because no decree exists.

The indemnity-holder may recover costs only, because indemnity covers litigation
expenses, but compromise sums are personal choices and remain unpaid by indemnifier
alone.

The indemnity-holder may recover all sums paid under a reasonable compromise made in
good faith, if compromise was within authority and prudent too.

The indemnity-holder may recover compromise sums only if indemnifier signed the
settlement deed, because good faith alone never permits reimbursement in law.
questions.solution: The correct option directly uses the reference phrase “all sums paid under a reasonable compromise made in good faith,” giving exact word-level correlation. It also preserves the prudence/authority condition, aligning with how indemnity-holder recovery is structured.

questions.questionText:
Ramu, a 19-year-old college student, was racing his friend Shyam on motorcycles through a
residential street at 9 PM where children often play. Ramu knew hitting someone was possible but
assumed his riding skills, honed over two years, would allow him to maneuver safely. While
overtaking a parked vehicle at high speed, Ramu struck a 7-year-old child who had suddenly run
onto the road. The child died instantly. Decide Ramu's criminal liability under IPC.
options:
Ramu is liable for murder as he was consciously racing at high speed in a residential area
knowing children were present

Ramu is not criminally liable as he did not intend to kill the child and the child's sudden
appearance was unforeseeable

Ramu is liable for culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to knowledge of risk and
reckless disregard

Ramu is liable only for rash and negligent driving causing death under Section 304A as racing
constitutes traffic violation
questions.solution: The passage establishes that culpable homicide requires "either intention to cause death or knowledge that the act is imminently likely to cause death." Ramu had knowledge—he "knew hitting someone was possible" while racing in a residential area where "children often play." questions.questionText:
During a cricket match in a public park, batsman Suresh hits a ball very hard. The ball
       deflects off a tree and hits a spectator, Vikas, causing a fracture. Suresh had no
       intention to hit Vikas and was playing with ordinary care. Is Suresh criminally liable
       for causing hurt?
options:
He is liable because his action directly caused grievous hurt to Vikas and he did not
       take all possible precautions.

He is not liable if he apologizes to Vikas for the unfortunate accident and offers to pay
       for medical compensation.

He is not liable under Sec. 80 as the injury was caused by accident in doing a lawful
       act with ordinary care and without criminal intent.

He is liable because he should have chosen a safer, designated place to play and
       ensured complete spectator safety beforehand.

questions.questionText:
Ram lives in a scheduled tribe locality. He got his admission to NLUO under the EWS reservation category. However,
        while pursuing his course, his father, a police inspector, got an increment of fifty percent in his salary. After knowing
        about Ram’s father's increment, his friend complained to the administration about his ineligibility under the EWS
        reservation policy. In the record of the University, it was found that Ram’s father's salary was Rs. 6 lakh annually.
        Decide whether the Ram admission in NLUO is valid or not under the EWS category?
options:
Ram's admission to NLUO under the EWS category is not valid as people only from the general category can
            avail of the benefits of EWS reservation scheme.

Ram's admission to NLUO under the EWS category is not valid as he belongs to Scheduled Tribe and thus, he
            can’t get the benefits of EWS reservation policy.

Ram's admission to NLUO under EWS is valid as all the essentials have been fulfilled by him which are required
            to take admission.

Ram's admission to NLUO is valid as he is fulfilling all the essentials and his father's current income is less than
            the limit of Rs. Eight lakh.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Ram's admission to NLUO under EWS is valid as all the essentials have been fulfilled by him which are required to take admission. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A recognised consumer association received complaints from 160 buyers who had purchased
the same “exam-success tablet package” through an online platform run by EdNova Digital
Pvt. Ltd. The package was advertised as including recorded classes, doubt-solving access and
study tablets. Several buyers alleged that the tablets were defective and the doubt-solving
access was never activated. EdNova argued that the association could not file the complaint
because the buyers had purchased the package individually through an online platform and
because only the persons who directly paid for the package could approach the Commission.
Can the recognised consumer association file the complaint?
options:
Yes, because a recognised consumer association may file a complaint for consumers having
the same interest, including online purchases.

Yes, because any consumer association may file a complaint where several buyers
purchased goods through the same online platform.

No, because online buyers must file individual complaints unless the Central Government
or State Government takes up the matter.

No, because Section 35 gives standing to individual consumers but does not extend it to
platform-based collective claims.
questions.solution: The passage provides that a recognised consumer association may file a complaint before the appropriate Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. It also recognises that modern consumer markets include purchases through online platforms.

questions.questionText:
Viktor, a Russian national, has been living in New Delhi for the past five years on a valid work visa. He entered into
        a business partnership with an Indian entrepreneur, Ramesh, to establish a chain of restaurants. Following a bitter
        dispute, Ramesh allegedly misappropriated ₹2 crore from the partnership funds. Viktor wishes to file a civil suit
        against Ramesh for recovery of money and breach of contract. However, due to escalating tensions between India
        and Russia over a territorial dispute, the two countries have formally declared war on each other last month. Viktor's
        lawyer advises him that his status has now changed under Indian civil procedure law, affecting his right to sue.
        Based on the passage, can Viktor institute a civil suit against Ramesh in an Indian court?
options:
Yes, because Viktor has been residing in India for five years and holds a valid work visa, which grants him the
            same rights as an Indian citizen regardless of war status.

No, because an alien enemy residing in a foreign country generally cannot sue in Indian courts, and the
            declaration of war automatically terminates Viktor's residence status.

Yes, but only with the permission of the Central Government, because an alien enemy residing in India may sue
            only with such permission under Section 83 CPC.

No, because Section 86 CPC prohibits all suits by foreign nationals against Indian citizens without the written
            consent of the Central Government certified in writing.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, but only with the permission of the Central Government, because an alien enemy residing in India may sue only with such permission under Section 83 CPC. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A climate treaty negotiation involves several coastal and island States vulnerable to rising sea
levels. Developed State P argues that all States should bear exactly equal financial and
technological burdens because every State shares environmental duties. Developing State Q
agrees that duties are shared, but argues that richer industrialised States must take greater
responsibility due to historical emissions, financial strength, and access to technology.
Which formulation best reflects the relevant principle?
options: State P is correct because shared duties always mean identical burdens for every country.
State P is correct because historical contribution is irrelevant to environmental obligations.

State Q is correct because developed States bear greater responsibility due to history,
finance, and technology.

State Q is correct because developing States alone must finance adaptation in vulnerable
regions.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “developed States,” ” 6 “greater responsibility,” “historical contribution,” “financial capacity,” and “technological resources,” matching the reference line. It captures the balance between shared environmental duties and differentiated burdens.

questions.questionText:
In the context of Article 22 and Section 41D of the CrPC, consider a scenario where Karan, accused of
theft, is denied the right to a lawyer during his interrogation. Karan later learns that his lawyer was
trying to reach him but was not permitted by the police. Following his release, Karan wants to take legal
action against the police for this denial. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action
for Karan based on the legal provisions mentioned in the passage?
options:
Karan cannot take legal action as the police have the authority to deny a lawyer during interrogation to
ensure the interrogation is not influenced.

Karan can file a complaint for the violation of his constitutional rights, as the denial of a lawyer during
interrogation is against Article 22(1) and Section 41D of the CrPC.

Karan should seek compensation for emotional distress, as the denial of a lawyer does not directly relate to


legal procedural violations.
Karan should take no action as the police's decision is final and cannot be contested in court.

questions.questionText:
Two incidents occur on the same night. First, Ritu climbs into a neighbour’s open backyard to
shout abuses and leave after five minutes. Second, she walks into the neighbour’s locked store-
room attached to the house and searches drawers to “annoy the owner.” Ritu argues both are
the same offence because intention is identical. The owner says the law treats the store-room
intrusion as more serious because of the space invaded.
Which statement best explains the distinction?
options:
The key difference lies in the nature of the property involved: open land suits criminal
trespass, buildings suit house trespass.

The key difference lies in the nature of the property involved: buildings suit criminal
trespass, open land suits house trespass.

Key difference lies in intent since both apply to any property if annoyance exists, making
building irrelevant always in law.

Key difference lies in ownership since house trespass needs owner possession, but criminal
trespass needs tenant possession only under law.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “key difference nature of the property involved,” and correctly maps open land to criminal trespass and protected structures to house trespass. This explains why identical intent can still produce different offences based on the nature of the invaded space.

questions.questionText:
A transport company negligently crashes into Leena’s delivery van, delaying her shipment by
three days. Because of the delay, Leena loses a routine delivery fee. Separately, during those
three days, a rare overseas market crash occurs, and Leena claims she also lost a speculative
export profit that she “might have earned” if the van had not been delayed. She sues for both
the delivery fee and the speculative export profit.
Which loss is least likely to be compensable?
options:
All losses recoverable, because defendant takes victim as found, and remoteness never
limits damages in tort law today.

Only physical repair costs recoverable, because courts never compensate economic loss,
even if directly caused by negligence here.

All claimed profits recoverable, because once breach occurs, every subsequent financial
consequence is presumed foreseeable by law always.

Exclude the market-crash losses, because only damage that is not too remote is
compensable under tort principles here.
questions.solution: The option directly uses “only damage that is not too remote is compensable,” tracking the reference line. The speculative export profit linked to a rare market crash is a classic remote claim compared to the direct delivery fee loss.

questions.questionText:
Two days before polling, a candidate’s nomination is rejected by the Returning Officer for an
alleged mismatch in her affidavit. She files a writ petition seeking an immediate order to
accept her nomination and postpone polling in that constituency. The High Court is asked to
decide before polling day to avoid “irreparable harm.” The election schedule is already notified
and campaigning is underway. The State argues the challenge must wait until the election is
over.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
The court should decline because it bars judicial interference during the election process
except by election petitions after completion of elections.

The court may intervene because nomination rejection violates natural justice, and
constitutional rights allow immediate writ relief despite ongoing elections today.

Court must stay the poll because any illegality voids the election, and prevention is better
than later petitions always anyway.

The Court should decline because High Courts lack territorial jurisdiction over election
matters, which lie exclusively with Supreme Court alone always.
questions.solution: The option directly uses "bars judicial interference during the election process" and "except by election petitions after completion," matching the reference line. Since polling is imminent and the election process is underway, the bar principle points to post- election challenge routes rather than mid-process judicial interruption.

questions.questionText:
Principle: Dowry is often cloaked as "voluntary gifts" or "social expectations." The law aims to
prevent the undervaluation of women and their treatment as sources of financial extraction.
Whether a demand is made before or after marriage, it is legally treated as dowry if it is linked to
material extraction from the bride's family.
Facts: During the wedding of Ms. A and Mr. B, no dowry was discussed. However, six months
after the wedding, Mr. B’s family suggests that since Ms. A’s brother recently won a lottery, it
would be a "great social gesture" and "support for the couple’s future" if the brother gifted Mr. B a
commercial plot of land. When the brother refuses, Mr. B’s family starts treating Ms. A with
coldness and tells her she is "worthless" to their family. Based on the Supreme Court's
observations in the passage, how should this "gesture" be classified?
options:
It is a voluntary gift because it was requested after the marriage was already finalized and
was not a condition for the wedding.

It is not dowry because the demand was based on a "social gesture" and the brother’s sudden
wealth, not on a mandatory extraction.

It is dowry because it is a mechanism for material extraction that treats the woman as a
source of financial gain, regardless of when the demand was made.

It is a "social expectation" which, according to the passage, is a legally protected category of
gift-giving for a daughter's independence.
questions.solution: Why C is correct- The Supreme Court clarified that the lawdoes not distinguish between demands made before or after marriage. Since the demand for land was a form of "material extraction" that resulted in the woman being called"worthless," it fits the legal definition of dowry, regardless of the label used.

questions.questionText:
Ravi, a young entrepreneur, was accused of embezzlement of funds from his company. During the
trial, his lawyer requested a full-body medical examination, arguing that Ravi had been suffering from a
neurological disorder that could affect his memory and decision-making skills, potentially proving his
inability to commit the alleged crime intentionally. The prosecution objected, asserting that this was a
tactic to delay the proceedings. The magistrate was now faced with the decision of whether to allow the
medical examination under Section 54(1) of the CrPC. Should the magistrate allow Ravi's full-body
medical examination under Section 54(1) of the CrPC?
options: Yes, because Ravi has the right to a full-body medical examination to prove his innocence.
No, because the medical examination is irrelevant to the embezzlement charges.
Yes, but only if the examination does not delay the trial proceedings.

No, unless there is substantial evidence suggesting Ravi's neurological disorder directly influenced the
embezzlement.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The scope of the defence of Act of God has gradually narrowed in modern law.
Reason (R): Courts now expect individuals and authorities to anticipate and guard against
many natural events due to advancements in science, disaster forecasting, and infrastructure
planning.
In light of the above passage, choose the correct option:
options:
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true because technological advancements have
expanded the protection available under the defence.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false because courts continue to treat all
extraordinary natural events as unforeseeable.
questions.solution: The passage expressly states that the scope of the defence of Act of God has reduced over time because scientific and technological advancements now allow prediction of many natural events. Modern courts also impose higher standards of care due to improved forecasting systems, infrastructure planning, and safety expectations.

questions.questionText:
Samantha, a respected civil servant in the Ministry of Health, was unexpectedly dismissed from her
position shortly after she announced her pregnancy. Her dismissal was formally justified under the
doctrine of pleasure, which allows a civil servant's employment to be terminated at the government's
discretion. Believing her dismissal was directly related to her pregnancy, Samantha decides to legally
challenge her termination. She argues that her dismissal constitutes discrimination based on sex, violating
her constitutional rights under Article 15, which prohibits such discrimination.
options:
Samantha's challenge will likely fail because the doctrine of pleasure permits the government to dismiss any
civil servant without providing a justification, including for reasons related to health and capacity.

Samantha's dismissal is justified legally because the doctrine of pleasure allows for the dismissal of civil
servants who may require extended leaves of absence, which includes cases of pregnancy.

Samantha's challenge will likely succeed because dismissal due to pregnancy is seen as discrimination based
on medical condition, which is inherently linked to sex discrimination under constitutional law.

Samantha's challenge will likely succeed if she demonstrates that her dismissal was due to her pregnancy, as
this would constitute discrimination based on sex, explicitly prohibited under Article 15 of the Constitution.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): An agreement restraining the marriage of a major person is void even if it
satisfies all the essentials of a valid contract under Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
Reason (R): Every agreement made with free consent, lawful consideration, and between
competent parties automatically becomes legally enforceable without any exception.
In light of the above passage, choose the correct option:
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The passage explains that although agreements fulfilling the essentials under Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act generally become valid contracts, certain agreements are expressly declared void despite satisfying these requirements. One such exception is an agreement in restraint of marriage.

questions.questionText:
D stored large quantities of industrial solvent in tanks on his factory premises for
manufacturing purposes. Due to a crack in a tank, solvent escaped onto the plaintiff's
adjoining land, contaminating the soil. D argued he had taken all reasonable precautions and
was not negligent.
options:
D is not liable because he exercised reasonable care; the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher does
not apply to commercial manufacturing operations which constitute natural use of
industrial land.

D is liable only if the plaintiff proves D knew of the crack; strict liability under Rylands v.
Fletcher requires at minimum constructive knowledge of the defect causing escape.

D is not liable as the escape occurred due to a structural defect — an act of a third party —
which is a recognised defence under Rylands v. Fletcher.

D is strictly liable under Rylands v. Fletcher; industrial solvent stored in large quantities
is a thing likely to do mischief if it escapes, constituting a non-natural use of land.
questions.solution: Storing large quantities of a dangerous chemical substance that escapes and causes damage satisfies all elements of the rule — non-natural use, accumulation, escape, and resulting damage — without requiring proof of negligence.

questions.questionText:
Aarav was elected to the Lok Sabha on the ticket of Jan Pragati Party. After a dispute with
the party leadership, he did not submit a formal resignation from the party. However, he
wrote to the Speaker stating that he no longer accepted the Jan Pragati Party as his political
party, requested that he be seated separately from its members, and announced at a press
conference that he would act with the opposition bloc in all parliamentary matters. Before any
vote took place in the House, Jan Pragati Party sought his disqualification under the Tenth
Schedule. Is Aarav liable to be disqualified?
options:
Yes, because he may be treated as having voluntarily given up the membership of the
political party on whose ticket he was elected.

Yes, because he voted contrary to the direction issued by his political party without
obtaining prior permission before such voting.

No, because disqualification under Paragraph 2(1)(a) requires a contrary vote or
abstention in the House after a party direction.

No, because he did not submit a formal resignation and had not yet voted or abstained
contrary to any direction in the House.
questions.solution: The passage provides that a member may be disqualified if he voluntarily gives up the membership of the political party on whose ticket he was elected. Aarav’s letter to the Speaker and public declaration that he no longer accepted Jan Pragati Party as his political party directly attract Paragraph 2(1)(a), even though no contrary vote has yet occurred.

questions.questionText:
Following criticism of the Collegium System, Parliament enacts a constitutional amendment reviving
the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) with members including the Union Law
Minister and two eminent persons. The Government argues that judicial appointments require greater
democratic accountability and executive participation. Several senior advocates challenge the
amendment, contending that it compromises judicial independence. The petitioners rely upon earlier
constitutional precedents concerning the Basic Structure Doctrine. The Court is required to examine the
constitutional validity of the amendment. Which of the following correctly reflects the legal position?
options: The amendment is valid because Parliament possesses unlimited constituent power.
The amendment is valid because judicial appointments are exclusively a legislative policy matter.

The amendment is invalid because judicial independence forms part of the Basic Structure of the
Constitution.
The amendment is invalid because constitutional amendments relating to courts are completely prohibited.

questions.questionText:
Ramesh operates a pharmaceutical manufacturing unit in Uttarakhand. During an inspection on
March 10, 2023, the Drug Inspector found that Ramesh had failed to maintain proper records
under Schedule M and had also manipulated batch testing records for a narcotic drug in violation
of Chapter IV of the D&C Act. A complaint was filed against Ramesh on December 1, 2023,
alleging violations under Section 18(a)(vi) punishable under Section 27(d). Ramesh argues that
since the maximum punishment under Section 27(d) is two years, and the complaint was filed
after eight months, a Judicial Magistrate First Class has jurisdiction to try the case. Based on the
passage, which court has the proper jurisdiction to try Ramesh's case?
options:
Judicial Magistrate First Class, as the offence is punishable with imprisonment not exceeding
three years

Sessions Court, as offences under Chapter IV cannot be tried by a Court inferior to a Sessions
Court
Special Court under Section 36-AB, as narcotic drugs are involved.
Metropolitan Magistrate, as the complaint was filed within the limitation period.
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states that Section 32(2) mandates that "no Court inferior to that of a Court of Session shall try an offence punishable under this Chapter (Chapter IV)." Since Ramesh is charged under Section 18(a)(vi) punishable under Section 27(d), which falls under Chapter IV, only a Sessions Court has jurisdiction. Option (A) is incorrect because although Section 36-A permits JMFC trial for offences with imprisonment not exceeding three years, this is overridden by the specific mandat

questions.questionText:
A footwear brand applies to register “NIKSA” for shoes. An existing registered mark
“NIKSAH” already exists for shoes and is well-known in the same market. Consumers
frequently pronounce both similarly in local speech. The applicant argues that spelling
differences are enough and claims “no one owns a sound.” The Registrar objects on relative
grounds due to similarity and likelihood of confusion.
Which statement best reflects the relative refusal principle?
options:
Registration should be granted because minor spelling differences defeat confusion, and
relative grounds apply only to identical marks.

Registration should be refused only under absolute grounds, because similarity with
earlier mark is not part of relative examination ever.

Registration should be granted because well-known marks block only foreign applicants,
not domestic ones, so similarity is irrelevant.

Registration should be refused because relative refusal applies where the mark is identical
or deceptively similar to an earlier mark and causes confusion.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “deceptively similar,” » & “earlier mark,” and “causes confusion,” tracking the reference line’s exact grounds. “NIKSA” versus “NIKSAH” in the same goods category can mislead consumers, supporting refusal.

questions.questionText:
Arun, suffering from severe schizophrenia, believes that his neighbor is a demon
       trying to kill him. During a psychotic episode, Arun attacks the neighbor with a knife,
       causing serious injury. Medical evidence confirms Arun was incapable of
       understanding the nature of his act due to unsound mind. Is Arun criminally liable?
options:
He is not liable as insanity under Sec. 84 excuses him if he was incapable of knowing
       the nature of the act or that it was wrong.

He is liable because he caused serious injury to the neighbor and must be punished for
       his actions under the penal code.

He is not liable if it can be shown that the neighbor provoked him first or acted in a
       threatening manner towards him.

He is liable because he has a responsibility to seek treatment for his condition and
       control his behavior to prevent harm.

questions.questionText:
Vikram is a real estate agent engaged by Priya, a property owner, to sell her three apartments in Mumbai. The agreed
        commission is 2% of the sale value for each apartment sold. Vikram successfully sells the first apartment for ₹1.5
        crore after conducting proper due diligence and transparent negotiations. For the second apartment, Vikram
        secretly accepts a ₹2 lakh bribe from the buyer to undervalue the property, causing Priya to sell it at ₹80 lakh instead
        of its market value of ₹1.2 crore. For the third apartment, Vikram again conducts himself properly and sells it for
        ₹1.8 crore at fair market value. When Vikram claims his 2% commission on all three apartments, Priya refuses to
        pay any commission, arguing that his misconduct in the second transaction taints the entire agency relationship.
        Based on the passage, is Priya's refusal to pay any commission legally justified?
options:
Yes, because once an agent commits misconduct in any part of the agency business, the agent forfeits all
             remuneration for the entire agency relationship, not just the tainted transaction.

No, because under Section 220, an agent is not entitled to remuneration only for that part of the business in
             which the misconduct occurred, meaning Vikram can still claim commission for the first and third apartments.

Yes, because the passage states that agency is built on mutual trust, and Vikram's breach of trust in the second
             transaction destroys the entire foundation of the agency contract.

No, because Section 219 provides an absolute right to remuneration for any agent who performs work, and
             misconduct only affects the agent's liability for damages, not the right to be paid.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because under Section 220, an agent is not entitled to remuneration only for that part of the business in which the misconduct occurred, meaning Vikram can still claim commission for the first and third…. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): A divorced Muslim woman can claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC,
showing that secular maintenance remedies may operate alongside personal law.
Reason (R): In Shah Bano Begum v. Mohd. Ahmed Khan (1985), the Supreme Court held
that a divorced Muslim woman could claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, highlighting
the interaction between personal law and secular law.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion is true because the reference line expressly states that a divorced Muslim woman can claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, and it also frames this as an example of interaction between personal law and secular law. The reason is true and directly provides the judicial basis for the assertion by naming the case and its holding.

questions.questionText:
A logistics company accidentally delivers ten office chairs to a co-working space owned by Dev
instead of the neighbouring office that placed the order. Dev’s manager realises the mistake
but uses the chairs for two months during a busy season. When the supplier seeks payment or
return, Dev says there was no offer, acceptance, or mutual consent between them. The supplier
argues that the obligation arises not from agreement but from law.
Which conclusion best fits?
options:
Dev is not liable because offer and acceptance are always necessary before any legal
obligation arises.
Dev is not liable because mistaken delivery removes every duty to return or compensate.
Dev is liable only if the original buyer authorises the supplier to recover from him.
Dev may be liable because the obligation is imposed by law to ensure fairness and justice.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “imposed by law” and “fairness and justice,” matching the reference line. Dev’s use of the chairs despite knowing the mistake makes it appropriate to examine quasi-contractual liability independent of mutual consent.

questions.questionText:
The government has raised the purchasing prices of grains from farmers by 50% to provide maximum benefits to
        grain farmers. The threshold of grain is 10kg/acre a year. A was a child of a farmer family whose income solely
        depends upon the agricultural goods they produce on their agricultural land. To have the maximum benefit of a
        government decision, A’s family started growing grain over half of the agricultural land. They produce a total grain


1


        of 50 kg per year which only helps the family for survival. For his further study, A applied under EWS category
        reservation for admission to an average Government College. Will A get the benefits of EWS?
options:
A will get the benefits of the EWS category reservation as he belongs to the general category and his family
            income is less than Rs. Eight lakh.

A will not get the benefits of EWS category reservation as he doesn’t belong to the EWS category as his family
            income is above the given limit of Rs. Eight lakh.

A will get the benefits of the EWS category reservation as his family is able to produce only to fulfill their survival
            needs and A is taking admission in average Government College which depicts that the family is poor.

A will not get the benefits of the EWS category reservation because he is not eligible for reservation under EWS
            category as per the given Act due to non-fulfillment of all the essential elements.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: A will not get the benefits of the EWS category reservation because he is not eligible for reservation under EWS category as per the given Act due to non-fulfillment of all the essential elements. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
State P and State Q attempt negotiation, mediation and conciliation over an armed border
incident, but every effort fails. The situation worsens, troops remain mobilised, and both
States accuse each other of threatening regional peace. State P says that after failed peaceful
efforts, the matter should be referred to the Security Council. State Q says failed negotiations
merely end the dispute process and no further institutional step is required.
Which answer best follows from the stated principle?
options: State Q is correct because failed talks terminate all international settlement duties.
State Q is correct because the Security Council never receives unsettled disputes.
State P is correct because parties must continue only bilateral negotiation forever.
State P is correct because failed settlement may require Security Council reference.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line by recognising that failure of settlement may trigger reference to the Security Council. State P’s position is therefore consistent with the Charter mechanism described in the passage.

questions.questionText:
Based on the passage, what is the primary rationale behind the Supreme Court's refusal to allow a
Magistrate to try offences under Chapter IV of the D&C Act, despite Section 36-A providing for
summary trial by a Judicial Magistrate First Class for offences with imprisonment not exceeding
three years?
options:
Section 32(2) creates a specific mandatory jurisdictional bar that overrides the general
provision of Section 36-A.

All drug-related offences involve narcotic substances and therefore require the exclusive
jurisdiction of the Special Court.

The limitation period under Section 468 CrPC is automatically extended for all offences under
Chapter IV of the Act.

Section 36-AB grants exclusive jurisdiction to Special Courts for all manufacturing-related
offences under the D&C Act.
questions.solution: The passage explains that Section 32(2) "specifically mandates that offences punishable under Chapter IV are to be tried by a Court not inferior to a Sessions Court" and that this specific provision overrides the general provision of Section 36-A. The Court noted that "Section 36-A itself excludes offences triable by Sessions Courts," creating a mandatory jurisdictional framework.

questions.questionText:
A person applies for a loan from a bank based on the representation of his friend that he owns a house
worth 50 lakhs and that he is willing to mortgage it as a security for the loan. The bank sanctions the loan
and disburses the amount to the person. Later, the person defaults on the loan repayment and the bank
tries to recover the money by enforcing the mortgage. However, it turns out that the house belongs to
someone else and the friend had forged the ownership documents. The bank files a suit against the friend
for fraud and misrepresentation. Can the friend invoke the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the bank from
suing him?
options:
No, because he made a false representation of an existing fact to the bank, which acted upon it and suffered a
loss, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he did not make any representation to the bank, but only to his friend, who was not a party to the
suit, and he cannot be estopped by a third party.

Yes, because he made a representation in good faith and without any intention to deceive the bank, which
acted upon it at its own risk, and he cannot be held liable for any loss.

Yes, because he made a representation of a future fact, which was contingent on his ability to acquire the
house, and he cannot be estopped by a fact that did not materialize.

questions.questionText:
Amit, an employee at a tech company, approaches his colleague, Ritu, with a proposition. He offers to
pay Ritu Rs. 30,000 if she helps him hack into the company's database to access confidential client
information. Ritu agrees to assist Amit in carrying out the illegal activity. However, before they can
execute their plan, the company's cybersecurity team detects their suspicious behavior and alerts the
authorities. During the investigation, Ritu claims that she should still receive the promised payment
despite the failed attempt, as they had a valid agreement. Amit disagrees and decides to seek legal advice
in this situation. Which statement best strengthens Ritu's claim in court?
options:
The consideration in this contract is valid because Ritu agreed to assist Amit in hacking the company's
database.

The consideration in this contract is invalid because the promised payment was for engaging in illegal
activities, rendering the contract void.

The consideration in this contract is valid because Ritu upheld her end of the agreement by attempting to
assist Amit in hacking the database.

The consideration in this contract is invalid because Ritu did not receive any benefit from assisting Amit in
the illegal activity.

questions.questionText:
In May, the Supreme Court held that granting post-facto environmental clearances for
construction projects amounted to a gross illegality. However, in November, the Court recalled this
ruling, stating that the issue would be decided by a larger bench. A group of former civil servants
criticised this recall and urged the Court to restore its earlier position, citing worsening climate
events and severe air pollution. On what primary legal ground did the Supreme Court’s earlier
May ruling consider post-facto environmental clearances to be a gross illegality?
options:
Because post-facto clearances undermine the precautionary principle by allowing
environmental harm before assessment.

Because post-facto clearances reduce the revenue collected by the government through
environmental penalties.
Because post-facto clearances delay urban development and infrastructure growth.
Because post-facto clearances impose excessive financial burdens on project developers.
questions.solution: The illegality arises from the violation of the precautionary principle, as environmental impact must be assessed before potential harm occurs, not after damage has already been done. Incorrect Options:

questions.questionText:
A vacancy occurred in the Supreme Court of India. The President decided to appoint Justice Nitin
Khanna, a sitting Judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, to the Supreme Court. Before issuing
the warrant of appointment, the President consulted the Chief Justices of the Delhi High Court and the
Karnataka High Court, considering them suitable constitutional authorities. However, the Chief Justice
of India was not consulted because the President believed that consultation with experienced High Court
judges sufficiently complied with the constitutional requirement. The appointment was challenged for
violating the constitutional procedure. Decide the case as per the law before the introduction of the 99th
Constitutional Amendment.
options:
The appointment is valid because consultation with any judges considered necessary by the President is
sufficient in every case.

The appointment is invalid because consultation with the Chief Justice of India is mandatory when
appointing a Supreme Court judge other than the Chief Justice.

The appointment is valid because the President has complete discretion to appoint Supreme Court judges
without consulting any judicial authority.

The appointment is invalid because the President was required to consult every Chief Justice of all High
Courts before making the appointment.

questions.questionText:
Asha files an FIR alleging cruelty and dowry harassment against her husband Kunal. The
offence is cognizable and non-bailable, and the local SHO tells Asha that arrest is “mandatory
tonight” because otherwise the police will be blamed. Kunal’s lawyer produces documents
showing he has been cooperating and has a fixed job address. Without collecting any
supporting evidence beyond the complaint, the SHO arrests Kunal immediately. Kunal
challenges the arrest as routine and unjustified.
Which legal position best fits the Arnesh Kumar principle?
options:
Arrest is mandatory because cognizable and non-bailable offences require immediate
custody, and necessity inquiry is irrelevant today.

Arrest is optional only if complainant withdraws allegations, because police cannot act
without complainant’s continuing consent now.

Arrest is not automatic merely because offence is cognizable and non-bailable; power to
arrest differs from justification for arrest.

Arrest is lawful only if court issues warrant first, because police cannot arrest without
warrants in cognizable offences ever today.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “arrest is not automatic” and “power to arrest is different from justification,” matching the reference line’s words. On these facts, arrest based purely on label and without necessity analysis violates the stated principle.

questions.questionText:
Maya contracted to sell a one-of-a-kind vintage sports car to Ben. Ben planned to use it for
        weekend tours, a venture he had invested heavily in advertising. Maya then breached the
        contract by selling the car to a higher bidder. Ben sued, seeking a court order to force Maya to
        retrieve the car and complete the sale. He also claimed damages for his lost tour profits. What
        is the most likely primary remedy a court will grant Ben based on these facts?
options:
The court is likely to award monetary damages to cover Ben's reliance expenditures and his
        expectation of lost profits from the planned tours.

The court will order specific performance, compelling Maya to obtain the car and transfer it
        to Ben, as it is a unique good.

The court may decide to rescind the agreement entirely and order restitution of any benefits
        conveyed under the contract.

An injunction preventing any further sale of the vehicle paired with a substantial damages
        award is the probable remedy.

questions.questionText:
A competent adult suffering from progressive motor neurone disease executed a document titled
"Advance Medical Directive" stating she did not wish to be placed on ventilator support if she lost
capacity to breathe independently. She signed the document before two witnesses, both of whom
attested it. However, she did not present the document to a Judicial Magistrate for
countersignature as required under the Common Cause framework. Several months later she lost
capacity and doctors proposed ventilator support. Her family sought enforcement of the directive.
The hospital contended it was not validly executed.
The question before the court is whether a written directive signed by the patient and attested by
witnesses, but lacking the mandatory Judicial Magistrate countersignature, constitutes a valid
Advance Medical Directive under the Common Cause framework.
options:
The directive is valid; the Judicial Magistrate countersignature is a procedural formality
designed to assist authentication, and substantial compliance with the remaining requirements
suffices to give effect to the patient's clearly expressed autonomous will.

The directive is valid because the patient was mentally competent at the time of execution and
the document reflects her genuine and informed wishes; courts should give effect to the spirit of
the Common Cause framework rather than requiring strict adherence to each procedural step.

The directive is invalid; the procedural requirements laid down in Common Cause — including
countersignature by a Judicial Magistrate — are mandatory safeguards, and non-compliance
with any of them renders the directive unenforceable.

The directive may still be treated as valid evidence of the patient's wishes even if it does not
qualify as a formal Advance Medical Directive, since the right to self-determination under
Article 21 cannot be extinguished by procedural non-compliance.
questions.solution: The Common Cause framework requires an Advance Medical Directive to be in writing, signed by the competent adult, attested by two witnesses, and countersigned by a Judicial Magistrate who must be satisfied of the maker's competence and voluntariness. Failure to comply with the countersignature requirement renders the directive unenforceable as a living will, though it may inform the "best interests" assessment by the medical board and court.

questions.questionText:
The government launches a new scholarship scheme for rural students, with
       applications exclusively available through a mobile app. The app requires a video
       KYC where the applicant must sign their name on a piece of paper and hold it
       steady for a clear photograph. A student with cerebral palsy, which causes severe
       tremors in his hands, is unable to produce a stable signature and his application is
       rejected. He challenges the process. Which of the following principles from the
       passage is most central to his claim?
options:
The principle that digital access is a part of the right to life under Article 21, and
  the state has a duty to ensure its digital infrastructure is accessible.

The principle that thumb impressions must be accepted as valid signatures in all
  digital verification processes.

The principle that all electronic media must include audio descriptions and sign-
  language interpretation as per the RPwD Act.

The principle that any form of prompting or assistance is strictly barred during
  KYC verification to prevent fraud.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Sharma, a middle-class businessman, gives a gift a brand-new Toyota Fortuner to his
daughter’s husband at the time of her marriage. He claims that the gifts were given
voluntarily out of love and to maintain family prestige, and that no demand was ever made by
the groom’s family. Does this transaction amount to dowry under the Dowry Prohibition Act,
1961?
options:
No, because the gifts were given voluntarily without any demand from the groom’s side,
and Section 3(2) protects all voluntary presents made at the time of marriage.

Yes, because a luxury car like Toyota Fortuner is excessive in value relative to Mr.
Sharma’s financial status and is not of a customary nature in the community.

No, because the absence of any demand by the groom’s family is sufficient to take the
transaction outside the definition of dowry under Section 2.

Yes, because any valuable property or cash given by the bride’s family to the groom at the
time of marriage automatically constitutes dowry irrespective of voluntariness or custom.
S-20, Nandkishore Parikh Marg, Bapu Nagar, JAIPUR Ph. 7240060099 | www.lptedtech.com	22

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
questions.solution: The passage states that the present given at the time of the marriage without demand are excluded from the dowry if they are entered in the list ,;customary in nature and their value is not excessive, but in this case, he is a middle class businessman and the car is a luxury Toyota car which is excessive, hence exception does not apply here, and this transaction will fall under dowry. Option A is the closest distractor but wrongly assumes that voluntariness alone is sufficient.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Under modern occupation law, military control over territory cannot lawfully
extinguish the sovereign rights of the occupied state.
Reason (R): The modern law of occupation rests on the principle of the inalienability of
sovereignty, which treats sovereignty as not capable of being lawfully transferred by mere
military control.
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation
of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The assertion is true because the reference line explicitly states that “military control cannot lawfully extinguish the sovereign rights of the occupied state.” The reason is also true because it identifies the doctrinal basis “the principle of the inalienability of sovereignty” and explains why military occupation cannot legally transfer or erase sovereignty. Since the reason supplies the conceptual explanation for the assertion, it correctly explains it.

questions.questionText:
Avinash and Priyanka belong to a tribal sect of Hindus residing in a remote part of India. Their
community follows unique customs and traditions not commonly practiced by mainstream Hindu society.
They are third cousins once removed, with Avinash being three generations removed on the female side
and Priyanka five generations removed on the male side. Their community, however, traditionally
permits marriages within such degrees of relationship, viewing it as a way to strengthen familial bonds
and maintain tribal unity. Avinash and Priyanka, having grown up together and shared a deep bond,
decide to marry according to their tribal customs and rituals. Is the marriage between Avinash and
Priyanka valid under the Hindu Marriage Act, considering their degrees of relationship?
options:
Yes, because their tribal customs permit marriage within such degrees of relationship, which is recognized
under the Hindu Marriage Act when specific customs are followed.

No, because the Hindu Marriage Act explicitly prohibits marriage within three generations on the female side
and five generations on the male side, irrespective of any tribal customs.

Yes, because being third cousins once removed places them outside the prohibited degrees of relationship
under conventional Hindu law interpretations.

No, because the Hindu Marriage Act does not recognize any customs or traditions that contradict its primary
prohibitions against close familial marriages.

questions.questionText:
A Muslim man in a village dies intestate, leaving a widow and two daughters. The local
panchayat applies an old regional custom under which daughters do not inherit ancestral
house property, and the deceased’s brother is awarded the entire house. The widow
approaches a civil court, arguing that the personal law statute overrides “custom or usage to
the contrary” ” and makes Shariat the rule of decision for intestate succession. The brother
argues the custom is ancient and must prevail locally.
Which view best fits the Act’s rule?
options:
Custom prevails because village usage is the strongest source, and statutory personal law
cannot override it in family property matters.

Shariat prevails because Section 2 begins with “notwithstanding any custom or usage to
the contrary” for intestate succession.

Custom prevails because only marriage and talaq are covered; intestate succession is
excluded and left to local practices today.

Shariat prevails only if parties signed a declaration, because Section 2 applies only when a
Section 3 declaration is filed first.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary” and ties it to “intestate succession,” matching the reference line’s words. Therefore, the court should treat Shariat as the rule of decision and not apply the panchayat custom that excludes daughters.

questions.questionText:
Following a violent altercation during a village panchayat meeting, Naveen allegedly threw a corrosive
substance on Raghav, causing extensive burns on his chest and shoulder. An FIR was registered under Section 124
of the BNS, and the police arrested Naveen the same evening. While escorting him to the magistrate, the police
handcuffed him despite the fact that he had voluntarily surrendered, cooperated throughout the investigation, and
had no previous criminal record. Naveen challenged the use of handcuffs as illegal. Decide whether the action
taken by the police was legally justified.
options:
The action was unjustified because handcuffing can never be used against a person who cooperates during
investigation.

The action was justified because offences relating to acid attacks are treated as serious offences under Section 43 of the
BNSS, and it permits handcuffing of such offenders.
The police action was unjustified because handcuffing is permissible only after conviction by a criminal court.
The police action was justified only because the victim sustained visible burn injuries requiring hospitalization.

questions.questionText:
A coastal resort company continued operating tourist activities despite repeated cyclone
warnings issued by the Meteorological Department three days in advance. The company
neither evacuated the guests nor secured temporary structures erected near the beach. When
the cyclone eventually struck the area, several structures collapsed, causing injuries to tourists
and damage to surrounding property. The company argued that the cyclone was an Act of God
and therefore no liability could arise.
In light of the above passage, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
The company can successfully rely on the defence of Act of God because cyclones are
natural events caused entirely by forces of nature.

The company cannot rely on the defence because the cyclone was foreseeable and
reasonable precautions could have been taken to avoid the damage.

The company will not be liable because strict liability does not apply in cases involving
natural disasters of any kind.

The company can avoid liability because tourist injuries during natural calamities are
considered unavoidable consequences in law.
questions.solution: The passage states that for the defence of Act of God to apply, the event must be unforeseeable and unavoidable despite reasonable care. In the present case, cyclone warnings had already been issued several days in advance, making the event foreseeable.

questions.questionText:
State A and State B enter into an armed naval confrontation near a disputed maritime route.
During the conflict, State A invokes the 1956 draft Articles to challenge every military
movement of State B’s warships, arguing that the draft governs all law-of-sea situations,
whether peaceful or wartime. State B replies that the draft framework was limited to ordinary
peace-time legal regulation and cannot automatically govern wartime naval conduct.
Which conclusion best follows from the stated principle?
options:
State A succeeds because the draft governs all sea disputes during peace and armed
conflict.
State B succeeds because the draft applies to law of sea in time of peace only.
State A succeeds because wartime situations require stricter use of ordinary sea rules.

State B succeeds only if no nautical miles are involved in the dispute at all.
SCAN the OR for TaGs ]
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “law of the sea in time of peace only.” Since the dispute involves an armed naval confrontation, State B’s objection is consistent with the limited scope stated in the passage.

questions.questionText:
Kabir owns a logistics company and signs an indemnity clause with Rohan, his warehouse
supervisor, stating that Kabir will “fully indemnify” Rohan for any losses or claims arising
during warehouse operations. One night, Rohan deliberately breaks open a_ sealed
consignment and steals premium electronics, and is later caught. The buyer sues Kabir’s
company for loss, and Rohan demands that Kabir indemnify him for legal costs and any
liability.
Which option best applies the principle to these facts?
options:
Rohan can claim indemnity because the clause covers “any losses” during operations, and
wording overrides the nature of the act.

Rohan can claim indemnity because employer indemnity always applies to employees, even
when conduct involves deliberate wrongdoing.

Rohan cannot claim indemnity because indemnity will not cover unlawful or intentional
wrongful acts like deliberate theft in operations.

Rohan cannot claim indemnity because only third parties may enforce indemnity clauses,
and employees have no right to claim here.
questions.solution: The facts show deliberate breaking open of a consignment and theft, which is plainly an unlawful and intentional wrongful act. The reference line directly states indemnity will not cover such conduct, so Rohan cannot demand indemnification for his liability or legal costs arising from the theft.

questions.questionText:
Three accused (A, B, and C) are in police custody for a murder. On Ist June, A makes a
disclosure statement: I will show you the knife hidden under the loose brick in the abandoned
well. Pursuant to this, the police recover the murder weapon. On 3rd June, B and C separately
make identical statements: I will show you the same knife hidden in the same well. The police
do not discover any new fact from B or C. Under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
which of the following statements is most accurate?
options: The disclosure statements of all three accused are admissible.
Only A's disclosure statement is admissible.

None of the disclosure statements are admissible because joint or simultaneous disclosure
statements by different accused are inadmissible under Section 27.

B and C's statements are admissible as corroborative evidence under Section 157 of the
Evidence Act, even if not admissible under Section 27.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Only A's disclosure statement is admissible. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Chief Justice Devendra prepared a proposal recommending Justice Aakash Bansal for appointment
as a Judge of the Supreme Court. Before forwarding the recommendation to the Central Government,
the Chief Justice consulted the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court. Two judges supported the
proposal, while the remaining two submitted written opinions stating that Justice Aakash Bansal should
not be elevated because of concerns relating to his suitability. Nevertheless, the Chief Justice remained
convinced of the candidate's merit and forwarded the recommendation relying primarily upon his own
assessment. Decide the case as per the judgment given in Judges Transfer Case-III.
options:
The recommendation is valid because the opinion of the Chief Justice prevails over the views of the other
judges.

The recommendation is valid because consultation with the four senior-most judges was completed before
the recommendation was forwarded.

The recommendation is invalid because the Chief Justice cannot forward the recommendation when two
members of the collegium have expressed adverse opinions.

The recommendation is invalid because every recommendation must receive the unanimous approval of all
four senior-most judges before it can be forwarded.

questions.questionText:
A Muslim businessman wants his adopted daughter to inherit as per Islamic principles rather
than local customary practice. He files a formal declaration before the prescribed authority to
extend Shariat to adoption and wills, asserting he is Muslim, adult, and resident in the area
where the Act applies. His cousin challenges the declaration, saying the statute cannot be
voluntarily extended and applies only to matters already listed under Section 2. The
businessman argues the Act itself provides an option to make such a declaration for additional
matters.
Which position best fits?
options:
Declaration invalid because Shariat can never be extended by choice; only Parliament may
add matters and individuals cannot opt-in.

Declaration valid because Section 3 gives a Muslim person the option to make a
declaration extending Shariat to adoption, wills and legacies.

Declaration invalid because adoption and wills are already covered in Section 2, so no
declaration is necessary and authority lacks power.

Declaration valid only if cousin consents, because family rights are collective and personal
declarations cannot bind relatives at all.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “Section 3 gives... option” and “extending...

questions.questionText:
Greenfield Academy is a private unaided non-minority school in Delhi with 400 seats in Class I
and an existing pre-primary section consisting of 200 seats.
In 2024, the school reserves 50 seats in pre-primary for children from economically weaker
sections (EWS) under the RTE Act. However, it does not reserve any seats in Class I, arguing
that since pre-primary is the entry-level class, the 25% reservation requirement applies there.
Parents of EWS children challenge this, demanding that 100 seats (25% of 400) be reserved in
Class I.
Which position is legally sound?
options:
Greenfield must reserve 100 seats in Class I because Section 12(1)(c) mandates 25%
reservation at entry-level admissions only

Greenfield's reservation of 80 seats is legally compliant because schools can choose between
Class I and pre-primary levels

Greenfield must reserve 100 seats in pre-primary where it exists, as Section 12(1)(c)
applies to the lowest entry point

Greenfield must reserve 100 seats in Class I or pre-primary, whichever has higher
enrollment, to maximize EWS access
questions.solution: The passage states that Section 12(1)(c) requires private unaided schools to reserve "25% of entry-level seats (Class I or pre-primary where it exists)" for disadvantaged groups. The phrase "or pre-primary where it exists" indicates that if a school has pre-primary, that becomes the entry-level, and the 25% reservation applies there, not to Class I.

questions.questionText:
A vacancy arose in the Supreme Court, and the collegium recommended the name of Justice Arvind
Rao for appointment. After examining the recommendation, the President sought reconsideration, citing
certain intelligence inputs and returned the file to the collegium. The collegium reconsidered the material
placed before it, recorded detailed reasons in writing, and unanimously reiterated the recommendation of
Justice Arvind Rao. Despite the reiteration, certain officials in the Union Government contended that the
President was free to withhold the appointment until the collegium suggested another name. Decide the
case as per the judgment given in Judges Transfer Case-II.
options:
The President may indefinitely refuse to appoint Justice Arvind Rao because the recommendation of the
collegium is merely advisory.
The President may reject the recommendation and require the collegium to recommend a different candidate.

The President is bound to appoint Justice Arvind Rao once the collegium reiterates the same
recommendation after reconsideration.

The President must appoint Justice Arvind Rao only when the recommendation is approved by every judge
of the Supreme Court.

questions.questionText:
State A and State B have a boundary dispute over a river island. State A announces that
unless State B accepts its map within seven days, it will seize the island by armed patrols and
block State B’s vessels. State B proposes talks, fact-finding, and mediation through a neutral
regional organisation. State A argues that using pressure is lawful because the dispute
concerns territory and national pride.
Which position best reflects the principle governing such disputes?
options:
State A may use armed pressure because territorial disputes are outside peaceful
settlement duties.
State B is correct because States must resolve disputes by peaceful means.
State A may avoid settlement because national pride excludes international legal control.

State B is correct because mediation is unavailable in boundary-related disputes.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line because State B proposes peaceful methods instead of armed seizure. The principle requires States to resolve disagreements through peaceful means, especially where unilateral force may endanger international peace and security.

questions.questionText:
Dubo is a nation that follows the same constitution as that of India. The Government of Dubo introduced the EWS
        reservation policy after taking inspiration from India. The caste demography of Dubo is very diverse and to benefit
        all castes, the reservation was granted to most of the communities. The introduction of EWS further increased the
        overall total count of reservations in Dubo and breached the ceiling of fifty percent. The EWS reservation was
        challenged in the Apex Court of Dubo. Decide the constitutionality of EWS reservation in Dubo?
options:
Enactment of the Act introducing EWS reservation in Dubo is unconstitutional as it breaches the constitutional
             provision of Dubo’s Constitution exceeding the total reservation beyond 50%.

Enactment of the Act introducing EWS reservation in Dubo is not unconstitutional as it doesn’t breach any
             constitutional provision of Dubo’s Constitution.

Enactment of the Act introducing EWS reservation in Dubo is not unconstitutional as the same Act has already
             been introduced in India which is constitutionally valid.

Enactment of the Act introducing EWS reservation in Dubo is unconstitutional as the Act is inspired by the
             Indian EWS reservation policy, not serving the very purpose of the Act.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Enactment of the Act introducing EWS reservation in Dubo is not unconstitutional as it doesn’t breach any constitutional provision of Dubo’s Constitution. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A vacancy arises in the Supreme Court after the retirement of Justice B.R. Gavai. The Collegium
headed by the Chief Justice of India unanimously recommends the name of Justice Arun Palli after
consulting all four senior-most judges and recording detailed reasons in writing. The Union Government
expresses reservations regarding his elevation and returns the recommendation for reconsideration,
citing concerns relating to regional representation. After reconsidering the matter, the Collegium
unanimously reiterates the same recommendation without making any changes. The file is again sent to
the President, but certain government officials advise that the recommendation may continue to remain
pending until a different candidate is proposed. The constitutional validity of such advice is questioned
before the Supreme Court. Which of the following correctly reflects the legal position?
options: The Government is justified because the President possesses absolute discretion in judicial appointments.
The Government is justified because the executive has final authority after reconsideration.
The Government is not justified because regional representation overrides Collegium decisions.

The Government is not justified because a reiterated recommendation of the Collegium is constitutionally
binding upon the President.

questions.questionText:
A private chemical storage company in State M stores hazardous waste near the border.
Repeated leakage contaminates underground water flowing into State N. State M argues that
the facility is privately operated and not a government project, so international responsibility
cannot arise. State N replies that State M cannot allow its territory to be used for activities
contrary to the rights of neighbouring States.
Which response best reflects the relevant principle?
options:
State M succeeds because private activity within territory is outside environmental
responsibility.
State M succeeds because neighbouring States have no rights against private pollution.
State N succeeds unless State M directly ordered the company to pollute.
State N succeeds because States must not allow territory to harm other States’ rights.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “States must not allow territory” and “rights of other States,” matching the reference line. State M cannot avoid responsibility merely by pointing to private ownership if its territory is used for cross-border environmental harm.

questions.questionText:
A wife receives jewellery and valuable gifts from her family at the time of marriage. During
matrimonial disputes, she takes those items from the matrimonial home. Her husband files a
complaint under Section 406 IPC alleging criminal breach of trust. Applying the reasoning in
the passage, which of the following is most accurate?
options: The wife cannot be prosecuted because streedhan remains her exclusive property.

The wife is liable under Section 406 IPC because the property was located in the
matrimonial home.
The wife becomes liable if the husband had temporary custody of the jewellery.
The wife and husband become co-owners of all property exchanged during marriage.
questions.solution: Option A — Correct. This option directly reflects the Court’s reasoning.

questions.questionText:
Emma, a homeowner in a residential community, discovers that her neighbor, John, plans to build a
large fence that would extend onto her property and block her scenic view, which is against the local
homeowners' association rules. Emma requests a perpetual injunction to prevent John from constructing
the fence as planned. She argues that allowing the construction would result in a breach of duty owed to
her by the homeowners' association to maintain property values and aesthetic standards. Given the
principle that a perpetual injunction can be issued to prevent a breach of duty, is Emma likely to succeed
in her request?
options:
Yes, because the construction of the fence would directly breach a duty owed to Emma, making a perpetual
injunction necessary.

No, because John has the right to build on his property as he sees fit, regardless of the homeowners’
association rules.

Yes, because all constructions that might affect scenic views should be automatically stopped by perpetual
injunctions.

No, because the homeowners' association rules do not specifically prohibit building fences, only suggest
guidelines for them.

questions.questionText:
The Government of India, via an official gazette, declares a specific underground tunnel used
for transporting Metro cables as a “prohibited place” due to its proximity to a military bunker.
An employee records a video of the tunnel's security layout to show his friends how “cool” his
workplace is. He uploads the security layout publicly despite knowing it is restricted. He has
no intention of helping any foreign power. Is he liable under the OSA?
options:
No, because the passage states that Metro-related locations do not fall within the
definition of a “prohibited place” under Section 2(8).

No, because the employee lacked the “spy” intent, as he only wanted to show his friends
the workplace and not prejudice the safety of the State.

Yes, because the location is legally a “prohibited place” and the OSA penalizes acts relating
to such places if the conduct is prejudicial to State interests.

Yes, because recording any government-owned property without written permission is a
per se violation of Section 3 of the OSA.
questions.solution: Option C is correct because the passage distinguishes the MMCL office from “prohibited places.” If a location is specifically gazetted/defined as a “prohibited place”, Section 3 of the OSA is attracted. Recording a security layout of a sensitive site and uploading the security layout publicly are prejudicial to the interests of the State, regardless of a specific desire to spy for an enemy.

questions.questionText:
Riya slips on a wet floor in a shopping mall and fractures her wrist. She files a tort claim naming
