only the mall’s security guard, believing he “should have stopped people” from walking there. The
mall argues the guard is not the proper defendant because maintenance was handled by the mall
management and a separate housekeeping contractor. Riya refuses to add anyone else, saying
“someone must pay anyway.”
What best describes the impact of this mistake?
options:
Riya is safe because tort law allows suing anyone remotely connected, and courts will
automatically correct parties.

Riya’s case weakens because proper joinder is vital, and suing the wrong party or non-joinder
may weaken the claim.

Riya is safe because misjoinder never affects merits, so the court must grant relief once injury
is proved.

Riya’s case fails only if the guard proves he warned her personally; otherwise he remains liable
as sued.
questions.solution: The reference line directly addresses Riya’s situation she sued a potentially wrong defendant and refused to join other relevant parties. Since “suing the wrong party” and “non-joinder” can weaken the claim, her refusal creates a real risk of procedural and substantive weakness.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Muskesh Narangi, a politician from the Janta Party, is the Prime Minister of Sindhustan, a
country in South Asia having the same Constitution as that of India. Janta Party wanted to win the
upcoming election in Bengal, a state in Sindhustan. But the Janta Party lost the elections to another
party, CPP. A false memo accusing the CM of Bengal of corruption, nepotism and favouritism was
submitted by the opposition members of the Janta Party. In furtherance of the memo, the Union
Government appointed a one-man commission to inquire into the allegations levelled against the Chief
Minister. State Government of Bengal filed a petition under Art. 131 of the Constitution challenging the
authority and legality of the said commission. Is the suit maintainable?
options:
The present petition doesn't qualify under Art. 131 as there has been no actual cause of action and the present
scenario doesn't fit the criterion established in Art. 131.

The dispute involves a question of law or fact that transcends any statutory or constitutional rights and hence,
is maintainable under Article 131.

The allegations made by the plaintiff is merely a political propaganda and no question of law or legal rights
are involved and hence, the petition is not maintainable under Article 131.
As the dispute involves the Centre and the State, the suit falls under the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

questions.questionText:
A senior citizen, Mr. Das, files a maintenance claim against his daughter. The
       case is complex, involving multiple financial documents and legal arguments. Mr.
       Das, being frail and not well-versed in legal procedures, wants his lawyer to
       represent him before the Maintenance Tribunal. His daughter objects, citing
       Section 17 of the MWPSC Act, which bars legal representation. What is the most
       accurate current legal position on this issue, according to the passage?
options:
Mr. Das cannot have a lawyer because Section 17 of the MWPSC Act creates an
     absolute bar on legal representation to ensure proceedings are simple and informal.

Mr. Das can have a lawyer because High Courts have interpreted that the
     Advocates Act, 1961, which allows legal representation in all tribunals, overrides
     the bar in Section 17.

Mr. Das can only have a lawyer if the Tribunal grants special permission, as
  the bar in Section 17 is discretionary, not mandatory.

Mr. Das can have a lawyer, but the lawyer can only submit written arguments
  and cannot appear in person before the Tribunal.

questions.questionText:
"Goan Cashew Nuts" is a registered Geographical Indication in 2023, acknowledging the specific
attributes and quality of cashew nuts grown and processed in Goa. This GI status aims to safeguard the
reputation and economic interests of the local cashew industry. Within six years, there has been an
increasing problem of producers from other parts of India and abroad using the term "Goan Cashew
Nuts" on their products. The use of the "Goan Cashew Nuts" label on products not originating from Goa
misleads consumers into believing that they are buying authentic Goan cashews, leading to unfair
competition and financial losses for local cashew farmers and processors. What action can be taken by
the producers in light of the passage?
options: They can file for an action of infringement as the good is registered and within the protection period.
They cannot file for an action for infringement as the cashew nuts are not manufactured in Goa.
They can file for an action for penalty in form of fine and imprisonment under the 1999 Act.
They cannot file for an action for infringement as the requirements under section 21 and 22 are not met.

questions.questionText:
Sunita lodged a complaint alleging that her neighbour Meena shouted "shameless woman" at
her in the residential colony's common area at 8 PM when 20 residents were present. The
complaint states Meena knew Sunita's teenage son was standing nearby and the insult "was
calculated to make Sunita lose her temper and physically assault Meena in front of everyone."
Meena files a quashing petition arguing the words don't verbatim appear in the complaint and
no actual assault occurred. Based on the passage, what is the correct legal position?
options:
The complaint should be quashed because it fails to reproduce the exact words spoken
verbatim, which is mandatory for Section 504 proceedings

The complaint discloses Section 504 offence as it alleges intentional insult in circumstances
showing provocative potential and accused's knowledge of likely breach of peace

The complaint should be quashed because no physical assault actually occurred, and
Section 504 requires proof of accomplished breach of peace

The complaint is insufficient because it does not establish that the words "shameless
woman" are legally capable of provoking breach of public peace in all circumstances
questions.solution: The complaint satisfies all three Section 504 ingredients. First, intentional insult ("shameless woman" shouted publicly).

questions.questionText:
A courier company’s delivery rider, against express instructions, assaults a customer during an
argument about delayed delivery. The customer sues the courier company, arguing it must answer
for the rider’s act. The company argues it is not liable because assault was never authorised and
was purely personal anger. The customer argues a corporation can always be sued for what its
servants do.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
The company is liable because corporations can sue and be sued and are always responsible for
every act of every servant.

The company is liable only if the customer proves the company directors personally ordered the
assault.

The company may avoid liability if the servant acted outside the scope of authority, since
liability depends on authority.

The company is liable because any act committed during working hours is automatically
within the scope of authority.
questions.solution: The reference line directly supports this: corporate liability depends on whether the servant acted within the scope of authority. If the assault was a purely personal act outside job functions and instructions, the company can argue it should not be fixed with liability.

questions.questionText:
Yogi, a deeply religious man and owner of a house in the heart of the city, put it up for rent on
a weekly basis. For those who wished to use the same for religious purposes, he gave them a
discounted rate. As a result, the house remained occupied most of the time. The music played
through the loudspeakers during religious ceremonies caused constant noise and
inconvenience to the neighbours. Is Yogi liable for the tort of nuisance?
options: Yes, Yogi is liable because his neighbours face inconvenience due to his decision.

No, Yogi is not liable because he is not intentionally causing any inconvenience to his
neighbours.

No, Yogi is not liable because it is one’s right to practice their religion and use speakers for
the same.
Yes, Yogi is liable because the interference is beyond the reasonable limit.
questions.solution: The tort of nuisance is about the unreasonable interference with a person's use or enjoyment of their land. Yogi has the right to use his property, but that right is not absolute.

questions.questionText:
A group of residents blocks Vishakha from entering a public road leading to a protest site.
They argue that the matter is merely private inconvenience and has no connection with
constitutional liberty, because Vishakha was not arrested or detained in a room. Consider the
following Assertion and Reason:
Assertion (A): Wrongful obstruction of lawful movement may affect freedom of movement as
well as personal liberty.
Reason (R): Article 19(1)(d) protects citizens’ movement throughout India, while Article 21
protects personal liberty.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains the legal basis of A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain the legal basis of A.
Ais true, but R is false because Article 21 excludes movement-related liberty.
A is false, but R is true because only detention inside a room affects liberty.
questions.solution: the assertion links unlawful obstruction with freedom of movement and personal liberty. The passage provides that Article 19(1)(d) protects free movement, while Article 21 protects personal liberty, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.questionText:
A security guard, Ramesh, sees a man running with a bag from a shop at night. The
       shop had been burglarized earlier, and Ramesh genuinely believes the man is the thief.
       He tackles the man to stop him, but it turns out the man was a jogger carrying his
       sports bag. The jogger suffers minor injuries. Is Ramesh criminally liable for assault?
options:
He is not liable as he acted under a genuine and reasonable mistake of fact, which
       negatives criminal intention.

He is liable only if the jogger files a criminal complaint against him and pursues legal
       action in a court of law.

He is not liable because he was performing his professional duty to protect property
       as instructed by his employer in good faith.

He is liable because he caused injury to an innocent person without proper
       verification and due diligence under the circumstances.

questions.questionText:
Justice Rao, a distinguished judge at the High Court, found himself at the center of a controversy
when a political faction launched a campaign for his dismissal, displeased with his decisions that
frequently countered their policies. They argued that since all public officials serve at the government's
discretion, Justice Rao could similarly be removed from his position. Aware of the unique protections for
judges but unsure of the extent, Justice Rao prepares to defend his tenure. Given the judiciary's role and
constitutional guidelines, what is the most likely legal outcome regarding the attempt to dismiss him?
options:
The campaign to dismiss Justice Rao could succeed if it gains sufficient political support, as all public
officials, including judges, are subject to dismissal based on governmental needs.

Justice Rao could be dismissed if the administrative review finds his judicial decisions biased, aligning with
the political faction's claims.

The attempt to dismiss Justice Rao is likely to fail, given that judges typically enjoy a higher degree of
protection against dismissal to preserve judicial independence.

The political campaign against Justice Rao is valid, as it reflects a broader check on judicial authority by
elected representatives.

questions.questionText:
In proceedings under Section 504 IPC, the defence argues that the prosecution must prove
three elements: (i) the accused's words were objectively insulting according to dictionary
meaning; (ii) the complainant was subjectively provoked to anger or annoyance; and (iii) public
peace was actually disturbed within 24 hours of the insult. Which element(s), if any, correctly
state(s) the legal requirement under Section 504 IPC?
options:
All three elements correctly state Section 504 requirements as the offence demands
objective insult, subjective provocation, and actual disturbance

Only element (ii) is correct, as Section 504 is solely concerned with the complainant's
subjective experience of provocation regardless of other factors

None of the elements correctly state Section 504 requirements, which focus on intentional
insult, provocative capacity, and accused's mental state.

Elements (i) and (ii) are correct, but element (iii) is incorrect as actual disturbance within
specific timeframe is not required under Section 504
questions.solution: The passage establishes the three actual ingredients of Section 504: "(a) intentional insult; (b) the insult must be of such nature as to give provocation to the person insulted; and (c) the accused must intend or know that such provocation would cause another to break the public peace or commit any other offence." None of the defense proposed elements match these requirements. Element (i) incorrectly suggests "objective" dictionary meaning test—the passage requires contextual evaluation conside

questions.questionText:
Principle - A trademark is a sign, word, logo, or symbol that is capable of distinguishing the goods or
services of one trader from those of others. To be eligible for trademark registration under the Trade
Marks Act, 1999, a mark must be distinctive (not generic or descriptive of the goods/services), not be
identical or deceptively similar to an existing registered or well-known trademark and not be
misleading about the origin, nature, or quality of goods/services.
Acompany has applied for trademark registration for the following brand names and logos in India.
Based on the principle above, which option is most likely to be granted trademark registration?
options:
GlowMate — a wearable fitness tracker brand; the mark is distinctive, not similar to any existing
mark, and the company has begun commercial sales.

AppleBakery — a bakery brand selling apple-flavored cakes; the word “Apple” is already a famous
trademark in electronics.
Best Tea — a tea brand; the name is entirely descriptive of the product.

QuickFix — a repair services brand; the logo is identical to an existing registered repair company’s
logo.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: GlowMate — a wearable fitness tracker brand; the mark is distinctive, not similar to any existing mark, and the company has begun commercial sales. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
The city of Kanpur is situated on the bank of Holi River Ganga. The river holds special importance
for the people of the city as most of the people follow Hinduism and consider river Ganga sacred. To
worship the river, an annual fair is conducted, in which people offer prayers to river by throwing flowers,
sweets, idols and other objects used in Hindu worship. Mahima, an NGO worker requests the court to
ban this fair as it contaminates the water of river Ganga, which leads to mass sickness in city. Decide
whether the court can ban the Fair?
options: The court cannot ban the fair as it will be against Article 25 of the Constitution.
The court cannot ban the fair as it is a essential religious practice of Hindus to worship the river Ganga.
The court can ban the fair to protect the health of the people in the city.

The court can ban the fair as river worship cannot be considered as part of religion and therefore need not to
be protected.
questions.solution: Articles 25 and 26 are expressly subject to public health. The passage clearly states that religious freedom may be restricted where necessary to protect public health. Since the fair contaminates the river and causes widespread illness, the court may validly restrict or prohibit the practice in the interest of public health. Why other options are incorrect: A: Article 25 itself is subject to public health and therefore does not provide absolute protection. B: Even if the practice were considered essential, essential religious practices are still subject

questions.questionText:
A road accident victim, Salim, is taken to the nearest hospital with severe bleeding. The
hospital refuses immediate treatment because no family member is present to deposit money
and complete paperwork. By the time he is shifted elsewhere, his condition becomes critical.
The hospital says emergency treatment is a matter of private arrangement and payment, not
constitutional protection. Salim’s family argues that Article 21 includes health and emergency
medical care.
Which answer best reflects the principle?
options:
Hospital succeeds because emergency care depends only on payment and private hospital
policy.

Family succeeds because Article 21 includes the right to health and emergency medical
care.

Hospital succeeds because accident victims must first complete documentation before
treatment begins.
Family succeeds only if hospital had a prior contract with the injured person.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “right to health” and “emergency medical care,” matching the reference line. Salim’s case concerns urgent medical treatment after a serious accident, making Article 21’s emergency-care dimension directly applicable.

questions.questionText:
A complaint alleges both Section 504 IPC (intentional insult) and Section 506 IPC (criminal
intimidation). The accused argues these charges are mutually contradictory because if words
constitute insult they cannot simultaneously constitute threat, and the complaint should be
quashed for internal inconsistency. The prosecution argues both provisions can apply when the
same words both insult and threaten. Based on the passage, which position is legally sound?
options:
The accused's position is correct because Section 504 and Section 506 protect identical legal
interests and cannot be charged simultaneously

The prosecution's position is correct because Section 504 addresses provocative insults
aimed at breach of peace while Section 506 addresses threats aimed at causing alarm or
compelling action, protecting distinct interests

The accused's position is correct because charging both sections violates the rule against
multiple punishments for the same act under Section 71 IPC

The prosecution's position is correct only if the complaint alleges separate statements
constituting insult and threat respectively, not the same words serving dual purposes
questions.solution: The passage explicitly distinguishes the two offences: "Section 504 IPC turns on intentional insult plus provocation linked to breach of peace or another offence. Section 506 IPC centres on a threat intended to cause alarm or compel action/inaction by the victim...

questions.questionText:
Rajesh, a local vendor, regularly delivers tea to workers at the Omega Mining Corporation. One day,
while delivering tea within the designated safe zones of the mine, an unexpected explosion occurs in one
of the nearby tunnels. The explosion was due to negligence in following safety protocols by the mining
company. Rajesh suffers severe injuries from the blast. Despite Rajesh knowing the general risks
associated with entering a mining area, he had been assured that the areas he accessed were secure and
routinely monitored for safety. Omega Mining Corporation argues that Rajesh cannot claim damages


under the principle of 'Volenti Non Fit Injuria’ as he was aware of the risks of being in a mining area.
Rajesh decides to sue for his injuries. Will he succeed?
options: No, because Rajesh knew the risks associated with being in a mining area and still chose to enter the area.

Yes, because although Rajesh was aware of the general risks of a mining operation, he did not consent to the
negligence on part of the company that led to the explosion.

No, because delivering tea in a mining area inherently includes risks of accidents, which Rajesh should have
considered.

Yes, because the company failed to adhere to safety protocols, making any consent by Rajesh irrelevant to
the risks he faced.

questions.questionText:
States F and G sign a river treaty requiring that “all upstream States must reduce dam
releases to protect downstream ecosystems.” State H is an upstream State but never signed or
ratified the treaty and expressly refused to join. F sues H before an international forum,
claiming the treaty binds H because it affects shared river ecology. H argues it is a third State
and cannot be bound or benefited without its consent.
Which statement best matches the principle?
options:
H is bound because environmental treaties automatically bind all States, and consent is
unnecessary for third States in such matters always.

H is bound because a treaty can impose duties on any third State if two parties agree, and
third consent is irrelevant in law.

His not bound because third States are generally neither bound nor benefited by a treaty
without their consent, though custom may evolve later.

H is not bound only if it protests immediately; if it stayed silent for one month, treaty
binds it permanently as implied consent.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “third States... neither bound nor benefited...

questions.questionText:
Principle: The offence of money laundering is a "continuing offence." It is "born" when proceeds of
crime are generated and "dies" only when the accused person no longer possesses or controls those
proceeds. Culpability is based on the possession of such proceeds after the Money Laundering Act
or the specific predicate offence has been notified.
Facts: In 2002, Mr. Bajaj earned %20 Crores through an illegal mining scam (which became a
scheduled offence only in 2009). However, by the end of 2004, Mr. Bajaj had spent the entire 720
Crores on a series of luxury international vacations and consumable goods, leaving him with no
assets from that scam. In 2025, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) seeks to prosecute him under
the Money Laundering Act for the 2002 scam.
Is Mr. Bajaj liable under the Money Laundering Act according to the logic in the passage?
options: Yes, because the origin of the money was a criminal activity that is now a scheduled offence.

Yes, because the 2019 amendment clarified that any person who committed a predicate offence
is indefinitely liable.

No, because the offence "died" before the Money Laundering Act came into force or the offence
was scheduled, as he no longer controlled the proceeds.
No, because Article 20(1) completely prohibits looking at any act that occurred before 2005.
questions.solution: Why option C is correct? The passage provides a very specific definition of the "life cycle" of a Money Laundering Act offence.

questions.questionText:
Riya is preparing for the CLAT 2027 Exam. She practices mock test regularly in the evening and then
goes for a brisk walk to refresh herself. During one such walk, she notices her neighbor Tuntun Mausi
struggling to carry groceries into their house. Without being asked, Riya steps in and helps carry the
groceries inside. Later, Riya asks her neighbor for payment for the assistance provided. Determine
whether Riya's request for payment is legally enforceable based on the provisions enunciated under the
Indian Contract Act, 1872.
options:
The request for payment is enforceable because her neighbor took Riya’s assistance, even though it was done
voluntarily.
The request for payment is unenforceable because Riya's assistance was done at the desire of her neighbor.
The request for payment is enforceable because Riya performed a valuable service.

The request for payment is not enforceable because Riya's assistance was voluntary and not at the desire of
her neighbor.

questions.questionText:
A Metro Corporation official discovered a colleague is embezzling funds. To gather evidence, he
records the colleague’s phone calls and submits them directly to the Police as part of a formal
whistleblowing complaint. The Corporation argues this is a violation of the IT Act. How would
the Court likely view the “dishonesty” aspect of Section 66?
options:
The official is liable under Section 66 because all unauthorized recordings are
automatically deemed “dishonest” regardless of the motive.

The official might not be liable under Section 66 if the disclosure was made in “good faith
performance of duties” or to report a crime.

The official is liable under the OSA because recording any colleague's call is “prejudicial to
the interests of the State” as it disrupts office harmony.

The official is liable because the IT Act prohibits the sharing of any official information
with “unauthorised persons” like the Police.
questions.solution: Option B is correct because the passage mentions that Metro Rail Rules allow communication of info in “good faith performance of duties.” Since Section 66 requires a “dishonest or fraudulent” act, a whistleblower acting in good faith to report a crime might lack the “dishonest intention” found in the passage’s case. Option A is incorrect because he Court specifically noted that the unauthorised and dishonest sharing brought the case under Section 66; it implies the intent matters for the crimina

questions.questionText:
The Constitutional Law Society of a National Law University organised a panel discussion on
constitutional amendments affecting the judiciary. During the debate, one participant argued that after
the Constitution (Ninety-Ninth Amendment) Act, 2014, the President could appoint judges of the
Supreme Court after consulting any constitutional authority considered appropriate. Another participant
maintained that the amendment established a new constitutional body whose recommendation became an
essential part of the appointment process. A third participant asserted that the amendment merely
increased the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court without changing the existing method of judicial
appointments. The moderator asked the participants to determine which interpretation correctly
reflected the legal position created by the amendment. Decide the case.
options:
The President could appoint Supreme Court judges independently because the amendment removed all


procedural requirements relating to appointments.

The amendment required every Supreme Court judge to be appointed by the President on the
recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission.

The amendment merely altered the strength of the Supreme Court and did not change the process of
appointment.

The amendment required appointments to be made jointly by the President and the Chief Justice of India
without involving any other constitutional body.

questions.questionText:
Ina robbery case, the accused, while in police custody, makes the following disclosure: ‘I sold
the stolen gold chain to my friend, Rajesh, who runs a shop named 'Jewel Palace' on the main
road. I will take you to him.’ The police have no prior knowledge of Rajesh's involvement. They
follow the accused, locate Rajesh at the specified shop, and recover the stolen gold chain from
his possession. Is this disclosure admissible under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act,
1872?
options:
Yes, the entire disclosure is admissible under Section 27 because it led to the discovery of a
material fact the stolen gold chain.

No, the disclosure is not admissible under Section 27 because it merely identifies a person
(Rajesh).

Yes, the portion ‘I sold the stolen gold chain to my friend, Rajesh’ is admissible as it forms
a single transaction leading to the recovery, but the words identifying the shop are not
admissible.

No, the disclosure is not admissible because it amounts to a confession of the crime of
robbery, which is barred under Sections 25/26, and Section 27 cannot be used to
circumvent this bar.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, the disclosure is not admissible under Section 27 because it merely identifies a person (Rajesh). Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
In a seminar, a student argues that the 1976 amendment was merely a technical clean-up with
no political purpose. Another student counters that its design during the Emergency sought to
recalibrate power among institutions and reduce judicial checking. The professor asks the class
to identify the stated objectives that best explain why the amendment was so controversial.
They must pick the option that mirrors the amendment’s aims in one line.
Which objective-set most closely captures the intended direction of change?
options:
It aimed to decentralise power to the states, expand judicial review, reduce Parliament’s
authority, and strengthen federal autonomy against central dominance.

It sought to strengthen executive power, curtail judicial review, enhance Parliament’s
authority, centralise administration, and reshape the Constitution to match government’s
ideology.

It focused mainly on promoting free markets, privatising public enterprises, limiting
Cabinet advice, and restoring quorum rules in legislatures.

It primarily sought to increase judicial independence, expand High Court jurisdiction, and
make elections more frequent by shortening legislative terms nationwide.
questions.solution: The option directly mirrors the reference line’s phrases “strengthen executive power,” “curtail judicial review,’ “enhance Parliament’s authority,” and “centralise administration,” maintaining strong word-level correlation. It also reflects reshaping the Constitution to match the government’s ideological agenda as described.

questions.questionText:
Farah suffered severe burn injuries after her estranged brother-in-law deliberately threw a corrosive substance
at her during a dispute regarding inheritance of ancestral property. The Sessions Court convicted the accused and
directed him to pay compensation towards Farah's medical treatment and rehabilitation expenses. Separately,
Farah received financial assistance under the victim compensation scheme through the District Legal Services
Authority as well as additional financial support from the Prime Minister National Relief Fund. The accused
challenged the compensation order before the High Court, contending that the amount awarded by the trial court
should be reduced since Farah had already been compensated through government schemes. Decide the case.
options:
The High Court should reduce the compensation ordered against the accused because Farah has already received
sufficient financial assistance from government authorities.

The High Court should uphold only the compensation granted through government schemes because compensation
awarded by courts and government authorities cannot operate together.

The High Court should dismiss the argument given by the accused because compensation under Section 396 and
PMNRF is independent of and additional to compensation or fine directed by the court.

The High Court should direct Farah to refund the amount received from the Prime Minister National Relief Fund
before enforcing the compensation awarded by the trial court.

questions.questionText:
Priya accidentally discovers detailed maps and attack plans for a major armed
       insurrection against the central government in her brother's room. Fearing for her
       brother's life, she burns the documents and tells no one. It is later proven she knew the
       documents outlined a design to wage war. Is Priya criminally liable?
options:
No, she is not liable under Section 123 because she did not actively participate
              in creating the design and her concealment was a passive, private act.

Yes, she is primarily liable under Section 121A as an abettor to the conspiracy
              for actively protecting the plotters through her deliberate and secretive actions.

No, she is not liable because she is a close family member acting out of fear
              and love, which the law recognizes as a complete and valid defence to
              concealment.

Yes, she is liable under Section 123 for concealing a design to wage war with
              the intent to facilitate its execution by destroying critical evidence.

questions.questionText:
Kamla, a 62-year-old retired Ayurvedic practitioner, prepared a herbal mixture using leaves she
collected from her backyard garden to cure her neighbour Rekha's persistent cold and cough.
Kamla had successfully used similar remedies for 30 years. However, unknown to Kamla, the
particular leaves she used this time were from a toxic plant that had recently grown among her
usual medicinal herbs. Rekha consumed the mixture and suffered critical liver damage requiring
hospitalization. Kamla acted in good faith with no awareness of the toxicity. Decide Kamla's
criminal liability.
options:
Kamla is liable for causing grievous hurt as the injury was severe and resulted from her
voluntary act of preparing the mixture

Kamla is liable for rash or negligent conduct under Section 304A as she failed to properly
identify the leaves before administration

Kamla is not liable as she possessed neither intention nor knowledge of the harmful nature of
the mixture

Kamla is liable under strict liability principles applicable to administration of substances
affecting public health and safety
questions.solution: The passage emphasizes that "the subjective mental state of the accused remains the analytical fulcrum in determining guilt" and that liability requires either intention or knowledge. Kamla had neither—she genuinely believed the leaves were medicinal based on 30 years of experience and had no awareness of toxicity.

questions.questionText:
Match the following legal doctrines with their core meanings:
List I	List IT
A. Polluter Pays Principle | 1. The State holds natural resources as trustee for the public.
B. Precautionary Principle | 2. The person causing environmental harm must bear the cost of
restoration.
C. Public Trust Doctrine	8. Environmental action should not wait for scientific certainty.
D. Parens Patriae	4. The State may act as guardian for persons unable to protect
themselves.
options:
A-4, B-1, C-3, D-2
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: The Polluter Pays Principle places the cost of environmental restoration on the polluter, while the Precautionary Principle requires preventive action even without complete scientific certainty. The Public Trust Doctrine treats the State as trustee of natural resources, and Parens Patriae allows the State to act as guardian for vulnerable persons.

questions.questionText:
Senior Advocate V. Mohana is recommended for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court after
practising for over twenty-two years before various High Courts. During the appointment process, a
public interest organisation argues that she cannot be appointed because she has never served as a High
Court Judge. The Union Government seeks legal advice on whether prior judicial experience is a


mandatory constitutional requirement. The matter reaches the Attorney General, who is asked to
interpret Article 124. The dispute concerns the constitutional qualifications for appointment. Which of
the following correctly reflects the legal position?
options: The objection is justified because only High Court Judges are eligible for appointment to the Supreme Court.
The objection is justified because advocates cannot be directly appointed to the Supreme Court.

The objection is not justified because advocates with the prescribed constitutional experience are eligible for
appointment.

The objection is not justified because any practising advocate automatically becomes eligible irrespective of
years of practice.

questions.questionText:
The Republic of Zambara, a small African nation, had deposited ₹500 crore in an Indian bank as part of a bilateral
        aid agreement. The bank, citing alleged violations of international sanctions, froze the account and refused to release
        the funds. The Government of Zambara wishes to file a civil suit in an Indian court to recover its deposits. The bank's
        lawyers argue that foreign States cannot access Indian courts because they are not "persons" recognized under
        Indian law, and only Indian citizens or resident individuals can be plaintiffs. Based on the passage, is the Republic
        of Zambara entitled to file a suit in an Indian court?
options:
No, because the Code of Civil Procedure only recognizes natural persons and Indian corporations as valid
            plaintiffs, and foreign States must resolve disputes through diplomatic channels exclusively.


1

Yes, because Section 84 CPC permits a foreign State to sue in a competent court, especially where the suit is
            meant to enforce a private right vested in its ruler or an officer acting in a public capacity.

No, because Section 86 CPC requires the consent of the Central Government for any suit involving a foreign State,
            whether as plaintiff or defendant.

Yes, because foreign States have the same unrestricted access to Indian courts as Indian citizens under the
            principle of sovereign equality among nations.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because Section 84 CPC permits a foreign State to sue in a competent court, especially where the suit is meant to enforce a private right vested in its ruler or an officer acting in a public capacity. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
The Supreme Court accepted a new, uniform definition of the Aravalli hill range, restricting it to
hills rising at least 100 metres above local relief. This definition was prepared by a committee of
Union government officials. Environmental groups argue that the revised definition could allow
mining and commercial activities in large parts of the Aravallis, thereby weakening its role as a
dust barrier for Delhi, accelerating desertification, destroying habitats, fragmenting ecosystems,
and damaging groundwater recharge. A group of environmental organisations and residents files a
petition challenging the decision, claiming that it violates their right to life under Article 21.
Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action the petitioners can seek from the
Supreme Court, in line with established environmental jurisprudence?
options:
Direct the immediate implementation of the new definition while leaving environmental
protection entirely to future executive regulations.

Stay the new definition and appoint an independent committee to assess impact using the
precautionary principle.

Dismiss the petition on the ground that environmental policy falls exclusively within the
domain of the executive.

Allow mining activities to continue under the new definition, subject only to higher financial
penalties for violations.
questions.solution: Option B aligns with Article 21 and the precautionary principle, allowing judicial intervention to prevent potential irreversible environmental harm. The other options either avoid judicial scrutiny or permit environmental damage to occur before safeguards are assessed.

questions.questionText: During an armed conflict, State X receives credible intelligence that enemy forces have repeatedly used the rooftop of a functioning school over three consecutive days to relay troop coordinates. The school's lower floors continue to be used by approximately 200 students and remain in regular operation. The school is located near an active front line. Acting on this intelligence but without conducting a proportionality assessment or issuing any civilian warning, State X launches sustained missile strikes that destroy the entire building during school hours, causing extensive civilian casualties. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The attack is lawful because credible, repeated military use of a structure by enemy forces is sufficient under IHL to classify it as a military objective, and the principle of military necessity permits its destruction irrespective of continued civilian occupation.

The attack is impermissible primarily because enemy forces occupied only the rooftop while students occupied the lower floors, meaning destruction of the entire building exceeded the scope of any legitimate military objective.

The attack may be permissible because military necessity allows commanders to act decisively on confirmed intelligence of repeated military use, and the school's proximity to an active front line further diminishes its ordinary civilian character.

The attack appears unlawful because targeting a building with substantial civilian occupancy through sustained strikes, without proportionality assessment or civilian warning, likely violates both the principle of distinction and the principle of proportionality.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The attack appears unlawful because targeting a building with substantial civilian occupancy through sustained strikes, without proportionality assessment or civilian warning, likely violates both the…. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
The National Digital Assets Authority (NDAA) is a statutory body established under the National
Digital Assets Regulation Act, 2022. The Act empowers the NDAA to regulate digital assets, conduct
inspections, and issue binding directions to market participants. However, the statute is silent on
whether the NDAA has the power to institute legal proceedings or sue in its own name.
A dispute arises when the NDAA files a writ petition before a High Court claiming that certain actions
of a State Government are obstructing its regulatory functions. The State challenges the petition,
arguing that the NDAA is not a juristic person.
Applying the principle stated above, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options:
The NDAA is a juristic person because all regulatory authorities automatically have the right to
sue.
The NDAA is not a juristic person because its statute does not explicitly confer the power to sue.

The NDAA is a juristic person because interference with its functions gives it an inherent right to
approach courts.

The NDAA is not a juristic person only because writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is limited to
individuals.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The NDAA is not a juristic person because its statute does not explicitly confer the power to sue. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
A public university issues an order permanently barring Aman, a student activist, from entering
campus without giving him any hearing. Aman wants the Supreme Court to quash the order
immediately, saying any illegality can be corrected through the Court’s writ powers. The
university argues the Supreme Court can interfere only if a Fundamental Right is being enforced.
What is the most accurate statement?
options:
Aman can invoke Article 32 only if the challenge is framed as enforcement of a Fundamental
Right affected by the order.

Aman can invoke Article 32 for any illegal administrative order because the Supreme Court
can correct all forms of unfairness.

Aman can invoke Article 32 only after exhausting the internal university appeal and
approaching the District Court first.

Aman can invoke Article 32 only if the university is a private body, because writs are designed
mainly for private disputes.
questions.solution: The reference line’s exact wording “applies only to Fundamental Rights” means Aman must show that the university’s order violates a Fundamental Right and seek enforcement of that right. If he frames it purely as administrative unfairness without a Fundamental Right anchor, Article 32 relief will not ordinarily lie.

questions.questionText:
At an ATM outside a mall, a stranger held Vikram from behind, threatened him with a knife,
and forced him to enter a PIN and withdraw %20,000 from another person’s card already
inserted. The stranger snatched the cash and fled. CCTV shows Vikram typing the PIN and
taking the cash, and the bank files a complaint saying Vikram withdrew money “dishonestly.”
Vikram says every step was under immediate threat and he never chose to steal.
How should liability be evaluated?
options:
Vikram is not liable because blameworthy conduct usually requires both a wrongful act
and a blameworthy state of mind together for liability.

Vikram is liable because the cash withdrawal occurred by his hands, and criminal law
punishes the act regardless of mental state.

Vikram is liable because threat only reduces punishment, and the bank need not show any
guilty mind when money moves.

Vikram is not liable only if he files police report immediately otherwise silence proves
intent and completes the offence quickly each time.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “wrongful act” and “blameworthy state of mind,” capturing the core requirement that blameworthy conduct usually needs both elements together. Here, even if the physical act is visible on CCTV, Vikram’s immediate compulsion narrative challenges the presence of a blameworthy state of mind at the time of the act.

questions.questionText:
A partner in a law firm, using her apparent authority and firm letterhead, convinces a client to
        invest in her personal, unrelated business venture, which turns out to be a fraud. The client
        sues the law firm partnership for the losses. Will the partnership likely be held liable?
options:
The firm is liable under the principle of apparent authority created by using the firm's official
        stationery and status.

Liability would depend on whether the other partners had specific knowledge of this
        particular partner's fraudulent intentions.

No, because the fraudulent scheme was for personal gain and not in the ordinary course of the
        partnership's legal business.

Yes, because partners are jointly liable for all torts committed by a partner whenever they use
        firm resources.

questions.questionText:
The Parliament passes the Green Transition Incentive Act, 2025, offering tax rebates to
industries that voluntarily reduce carbon emissions by 30% within five years. However, the
law exempts defence and strategic sectors including public-sector steel and coal plants that
contribute nearly 40% of national emissions from compliance, citing "national security and
economic indispensability." A group of environmental activists challenge the exemption. The
Government defends its decision, citing differential treatment justified by Article 14's
intelligible differentia and Article 19(6)'s reasonable restriction clause in economic interest.
Which legal position is most sound?
options:
The exemption is unconstitutional because exempting sectors contributing 40% of
emissions directly undermines the State's duty under Article 14 to ensure equal climate
protection for all citizens.

The exemption is constitutionally valid as a pure policy decision, and courts will only
interfere if the Government demonstrates complete non-application of mind in framing the
classification.

The exemption may be constitutionally valid if the Government establishes a clear rational
nexus between the strategic sector classification and the legitimate object of the legislation.

The exemption falls exclusively within executive policy domain, and courts must exercise
strict judicial restraint, upholding it unless it is shown to be patently arbitrary without any
rational basis whatsoever.
questions.solution: The passage establishes that M.K. Ranjitsinh recognized climate protection as a fundamental right under Articles 21 and with Article 14's equality guarantee forming part of the constitutional basis.

questions.questionText:
A terminally ill patient with no prospect of recovery was being kept alive by ventilator support.
His family sought enforcement of his earlier oral statements that he never wished to be kept
on artificial life support. The hospital refused to withdraw treatment absent a court order,
citing uncertainty over the law. The family's counsel argued that under Common Cause (2018),
the patient's advance wishes constituted a binding living will.
The question is whether an oral statement of treatment refusal qualifies as a valid Advance
Medical Directive under the Common Cause framework.
options:
An oral statement of treatment refusal constitutes a valid Advance Medical Directive, as
the right to self-determination under Article 21 cannot be restricted by procedural
formalities requiring written documentation.

Any clearly expressed prior wish of a patient, whether oral or written, must be treated as
binding under Article 21 once the right to die with dignity is recognised as a fundamental
right.

An oral directive may be treated as valid if it is supported by consistent testimony of family
members and doctors, as procedural safeguards are intended to ensure authenticity rather
than mandate form.

An Advance Medical Directive must be in writing and executed with prescribed safeguards
by a competent adult, and an oral statement does not satisfy these requirements under the
Common Cause framework.
questions.solution: The Court mandated that advance directives must be written, signed, witnessed, and executed with safeguards. Oral statements, however genuine, do not fulfil these legal requirements.

questions.questionText:
Ananya discovered that she was pregnant despite regularly using contraceptive devices. She was not
willing to continue the pregnancy. She approached a Registered Medical Practitioner for termination at
19 weeks of gestation. The doctor refused to proceed immediately and informed her that approval from a
State-level medical board would first be necessary. Ananya challenged the decision before the court.
Decide the case as per the provisions of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971.
options:
The doctor acted correctly because every termination request close to 20 weeks requires approval from the
State-level medical board.

The doctor acted incorrectly because termination up to 20 weeks requires only the opinion of one Registered
Medical Practitioner under the Act.

The doctor acted correctly because pregnancies resulting from contraceptive failure can never be terminated
after 12 weeks of gestation.

The doctor acted incorrectly because termination of pregnancy under the Act never requires any medical
opinion before 20 weeks.

questions.questionText:
Laura and her neighbor Tom have been in a dispute over a shared driveway on their property
boundary. Tom recently began construction to extend his garage, which would block Laura's access to the
driveway. Laura seeks a perpetual injunction to stop the construction, claiming it unlawfully restricts her
access to her property. The case is scheduled for a hearing next month. Based on the principle that a
perpetual injunction can only be granted by a decree issued after an inquiry and hearing the merits of the
case, which of the following outcomes is most likely?
options:
Laura will immediately obtain a perpetual injunction because her access to the driveway is clearly being
blocked.

Laura cannot obtain a perpetual injunction until the court conducts a full inquiry and hears all merits of the
case during the scheduled hearing.

Laura will be granted a perpetual injunction without a hearing because the construction visibly infringes on
her property rights.
Tom will continue his construction as the court typically does not stop ongoing constructions.

questions.questionText:
Rajesh filed a private complaint alleging that Amit publicly called him a "fraud" and "cheat"
during a business meeting attended by 15 colleagues. The complaint states this humiliated
Rajesh and "provoked him greatly." However, the complaint contains no allegation that Rajesh
was provoked to break public peace or commit any offence, nor that Amit intended or knew
such provocation would lead to breach of peace. The complaint uses the exact words spoken.
Should the Magistrate take cognizance under Section 504 IPC?
options:
Yes, because the complaint reproduces verbatim the insulting words spoken, and Section
504 is satisfied whenever intentional insult occurs in public

Yes, because calling someone "fraud" and "cheat" in a business setting constitutes
intentional insult that inherently provokes breach of peace

No, because the complaint fails to disclose that the insult was capable of provoking breach
of public peace or another offence, or that the accused possessed requisite mental state

No, because Section 504 requires proof that public peace was actually broken immediately
after the insult, which is not alleged
questions.solution: The passage establishes three essential ingredients for Section 504: "(a) intentional insult; (b) the insult must be of such nature as to give provocation to the person insulted; and (c) the accused must intend or know that such provocation would cause another to break the public peace or commit any other offence." While the complaint alleges intentional insult (first ingredient), it fails to allege that the insult was such as to provoke breach of public peace or another offence, or that Amit in

questions.questionText:
Raghav, a 20-year-old male, was in a relationship with Kriti, a 19-year-old female, and both were
living in Mumbai, a city in the State of Maharashtra. However, lately, they had been facing issues in their
relationship, because of something Raghav did. Sometime later, Kriti forced Raghav to have sexual
intercourse with her. Extremely grieved by this, Raghav decided to file a charge of rape against Kriti.
Will Kriti be liable for rape?
options: Kriti is liable because she forced Raghav.
Kriti is not liable because she was in a relationship with Raghav.
Kriti is liable because she did something wrong because of this they faced issues.
Kriti is not liable because she is a female.
questions.solution: The passage defines rape under Section 375 as an offence committed by a man against a woman. Since Kriti is a woman, she cannot be prosecuted for rape under this provision, even if she forced Raghav into sexual intercourse. (Other offences may apply, but not rape under Section 375.) Why other options are incorrect: A: Although force was used, Section 375 is gender-specific and does not recognize a female as the perpetrator of rape. B: Their relationship is irrelevant to determining liability under Section 375.

questions.questionText:
The passage discusses the Supreme Court's recent observation that exempting minority
schools from the RTE Act may jeopardize children's Article 21A rights. What is the primary
constitutional tension identified by the Court that necessitates harmonious interpretation
rather than allowing one provision to trump the other?
options:
The tension between Article 30(1) protecting minority institutions' administrative rights
and Article 21A guaranteeing children's fundamental right to education

The tension between Article 45 directing early childhood education and Article 21A
mandating compulsory education for older children

The tension between Section 12(1)(c) reservation requirements and Article 30(1) protecting
minority institutions from state interference completely

The tension between Article 51A(k) imposing parental duties and Article 30(1) granting
minority institutions complete autonomy over admissions
questions.solution: The passage states the Court "emphasized that Article 30(1) minority rights and Article 21A child education rights must be harmoniously interpreted rather than one trumping the other" after noting that "exempting minority schools may jeopardize Article 21A rights of children studying therein." This identifies the core constitutional tension between minority institutions' administrative autonomy under Article 30(1) and children's fundamental education rights under Article 21A. questions.questionText:
State C ratifies a bilateral water-sharing treaty with State D. Five years later, after elections,
State C’s new government announces it will stop releasing water because the treaty is “unfair”
and domestic voters reject it. It claims political change gives it freedom to ignore the treaty.
State D argues that the treaty remains in force and must be performed, and that unilateral
refusal violates the good-faith performance requirement.
Which view best matches the treaty-law principle?
options:
State C may stop performance because elections override treaty duties, and domestic
politics is a complete excuse under international law always.

State C may stop performance because only signatory states are bound, and ratification is
not necessary for binding force under law.

State C must perform because every treaty in force must be performed in good faith, and
political dislike does not erase obligation.

State C may stop performance because treaties are only moral promises, and courts cannot
enforce inter-state agreements in law.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: The option directly uses “treaty in force” and “performed in good faith,” tracking the reference line’s pacta sunt servanda formulation. Therefore, State C’s unilateral refusal based on electoral preference breaches the good-faith performance requirement.

questions.questionText:
Harshita leaves a rare musical instrument with Priyanshu for repair and explicitly requests him to
return it by Monday evening because it is required for a recorded performance on Tuesday.
Priyanshu completes the necessary repair work on Monday morning but intentionally retains the
instrument for two additional days to exhibit it to a potential buyer of similar items. On Tuesday
night, an accidental fire originating from a neighboring shop spreads to Priyanshu’s premises and
completely destroys the instrument. Priyanshu argues that he is not liable because the fire was an
external event not caused by his negligence, and he had taken ordinary prudent care of the
instrument while it was stored.
Assertion (A): Priyanshu becomes strictly liable for the monetary destruction of the musical
instrument from Monday evening onwards.
Reason (R): A bailee's statutory exemption from accidental loss continues to protect them as long
as they maintain ordinary prudent care of the goods.
options:
Both Assertion and Reason are true statements, and Reason is the correct logical explanation
of Assertion.

Both Assertion and Reason are true statements, but Reason is not the correct logical
explanation of Assertion.

Assertion is a true statement, but Reason is an incorrect statement of law under the statutory
framework.

Assertion is a false statement, but Reason is an accurate statement of law regarding accidental
destruction.
questions.solution: the Assertion accurately reflects Section 161 of the passage; since Priyanshu failed to return the instrument by Monday evening, he became fully responsible for any subsequent loss from that exact time. Meanwhile, the Reason is an incorrect statement of law because the statutory protection does not continue to protect a bailee who is in active default.

questions.questionText:
Riya, a 21-year-old college student, became pregnant after being sexually assaulted by an
acquaintance. Due to fear of social stigma, she delayed seeking medical assistance. When she finally
approached the High Court, her pregnancy had reached 19 weeks. Riya argued that continuing the
pregnancy would severely affect her mental health. The State opposed her plea stating that mere
emotional distress cannot justify termination unless there is a medical emergency threatening her life.
Decide the case as per the judgment given by the Delhi High Court.
options:
The Court should reject the plea because termination is permissible only when continuation of pregnancy
threatens the physical survival of the woman.

The Court should permit termination because denying a woman the choice regarding motherhood violates
her right to live with dignity under Article 21.

The Court should reject the plea because pregnancies arising from sexual assault cannot be terminated after
the pregnancy crosses 12 weeks.

The Court should permit termination only if the State-level medical board confirms substantial foetal
abnormalities in the pregnancy.

questions.questionText:
Harish was asked by his company to deliver important documents to a client using the company
car. On the way, Harish felt unwell and requested his colleague Neeraj, who was accompanying
him, to drive the car so that the documents could be delivered on time. While driving, Neeraj
negligently caused an accident. Will the company be liable?
options: No, the company will not be liable because Neeraj was not an employee of the company at all.

Yes, the company will be liable because Neeraj was acting on the company's behalf to complete
the assigned task.

No, the company will not be liable because Harish personally requested Neeraj to drive the
company car instead.

Yes, the company will be liable only because it owned and provided the company car for the
work.
questions.solution: Neeraj drove in order to complete the company’s assigned task (delivery of documents). Even if he is not the regular driver, he was acting on behalf of the company to fulfil its objective.

questions.questionText:
Kunal angrily writes in his diary that he intends to burn his neighbour’s shed “next weekend.”
Two days later, while Kunal is out of town, a short circuit in the neighbour’s shed causes a fire
and the shed burns down. Police find Kunal’s diary during a separate inquiry and arrest him
for the burning, claiming his written intention proves guilt. Kunal argues he never performed
any act leading to the fire and was not even present.
How should liability be assessed on these facts?
options:
Kunal is liable because intention alone proves guilt, and the diary entry substitutes for the
act when harm eventually occurs later.

Kunal is liable because presence is irrelevant, and any earlier intention attaches to later
events, even if caused independently by accident.

Kunal is not liable because the guilty mind and the wrongful act must exist together, and
here the act occurred without his mind.

Kunal is not liable because diaries are privileged, so courts cannot ever use them, even if
they show intent to commit crime.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference words “guilty mind” and “wrongful act must exist together.” Kunal may have had a prior intention, but the shed burned due to a short circuit while he was away, meaning the wrongful act occurred without his corresponding guilty mind and conduct. Therefore, the ordinary basis for criminal liability is not satisfied.

questions.questionText: A constitutional provision requires judicial appointments to proceed through a three-stage process: a Judicial Appointments Commission composed primarily of sitting judges nominates candidates; the executive must then formally approve the nominee; and the legislature must ratify the appointment by a simple majority vote. A constitutional challenge argues that subjecting judicial appointments to the combined approval of both the executive and the legislature structurally compromises judicial independence and destroys the separation of powers. Supporters counter that the process reflects a carefully calibrated system of checks and balances. Which option best follows from the passage?
options: The arrangement is constitutionally problematic because requiring approval from both political branches executive and legislature creates a structural risk of the judiciary becoming politically subordinated, which is the precise mischief the separation of powers doctrine is designed to prevent.

The arrangement may be constitutionally acceptable because the doctrine of separation of powers does not require complete institutional isolation, and controlled interaction among constitutional organs through a checks and balances mechanism is recognised in modern constitutional systems.

The arrangement is unconstitutional because appointment powers over judicial officers belong exclusively within the judicial sphere, and involvement by the executive or legislature regardless of degree or form necessarily violates the principle of separation of powers.

The arrangement may be constitutionally acceptable as a checks and balances mechanism in principle, though the cumulative involvement of two separate political branches in a single appointment process may aggregate external influence over the judiciary beyond what the separation of powers doctrine can accommodate.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The arrangement may be constitutionally acceptable because the doctrine of separation of powers does not require complete institutional isolation, and controlled interaction among constitutional organs through…. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Suppose in the above question that when Ratan was stepping out of the bus, he asked Hasan to
park the bus nearby, even though he knew Hasan could not drive a bus properly. Hasan complied
with Ratan’s instructions and, while parking, met with an accident. Will Farhan be liable?
options:
No, only Ratan will be liable, as he negligently delegated his driving authority to Hasan
without proper authorization or consideration.

Yes, Farhan will be liable, as Hasan was acting as a conductor of the bus and was operating
within the scope of Farhan's authorized business operations.

Yes, Farhan will be liable, as Ratan was Farhan's employee who negligently delegated his
driving authority to Hasan within the scope of employment.

No, only Hasan will be liable, as driving the bus fell completely outside the scope of his
employment as a conductor and was not authorized.
questions.solution: Ratan negligently delegated driving to Hasan, but Hasan still acted within the employer’s operational sphere (parking the bus). Therefore, Farhan (employer) can still be vicariously liable through Ratan’s negligent delegation.

questions.questionText:
Deepika, a high-ranking officer in the Ministry of Transportation, faced allegations of procedural
lapses that potentially compromised a major infrastructure project. An inquiry was properly conducted,
where Deepika was fully informed of the charges against her and given ample opportunity to defend


herself. The inquiry was open, transparent, and included testimonies from multiple witnesses, both in her
favor and against. Despite presenting her case effectively, the inquiry panel found sufficient evidence of
her oversights that contributed to the project's delays and cost overruns. Based on these findings, the
decision was made to reduce her rank. Deepika believes the decision was harsh and is considering
challenging the reduction in rank in court. Given the thoroughness of the inquiry, what is the most likely
outcome if Deepika challenges her demotion?
options:
Deepika's challenge will likely succeed because any reduction in rank can be contested in court if the
affected party is dissatisfied with the outcome.

Deepika's challenge will likely fail as the inquiry was conducted with due process, providing her with all
rights to defend herself as mandated by Article 311.

Deepika can contest the outcome on the grounds of bias if she believes the inquiry panel was unfairly
predisposed against her, irrespective of the inquiry's conduct.

The court will likely overturn the reduction in rank because the evidentiary standards in such inquiries are
often not stringent enough to justify changes in rank.

questions.questionText:
Assume that the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), another statutory investigative agency, files a
writ petition under Article 226 before a High Court seeking to quash an FIR registered against it by a
State Police authority, claiming that the FIR interferes with its statutory functions. The State
Government challenges the maintainability of the petition, arguing that the CBI is not a juristic person
entitled to seek constitutional remedies.
Based on the principles discussed in the passage, which of the following is the most appropriate
legal position?
options:
The writ petition is maintainable because all statutory authorities automatically qualify as juristic
persons with enforceable constitutional rights.

The writ petition is not maintainable because investigative agencies cannot invoke Article 226
unless expressly authorised by statute.

The writ petition may be maintainable if the Court recognises the CBI as a juristic person capable
of enforcing legal rights under Article 226.

The writ petition is maintainable only if the fundamental rights of individual officers of the CBI are
directly violated.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reasoning in the passage. The maintainability of the writ petition depends on whether the Court recognises the agency as a juristic person with locus standi.

questions.questionText:
Twenty States conclude a multilateral “Ocean Plastics Convention” that sets uniform
standards for waste discharge, creates reporting duties, and establishes a review body.
Separately, two States sign a bilateral “Port Access Agreement” granting each other
discounted fees for three ports. In a seminar, a student claims both instruments are the same
type because both are treaties. The professor asks which classification best distinguishes their
legal character.
Which option best matches the treaty classification principle?
options:
Both are contractual treaties because all treaties are bargains, and no treaty can resemble
legislation or general norms ever.

Both are law-making treaties because all treaties create law, and bilateral agreements are
also general norms by default.

Ocean Plastics Convention is law-making, while Port Access Agreement is contractual,
because treaties classify into law-making and contractual forms.

Ocean Plastics Convention is contractual, while Port Access Agreement is law-making,
because multilateral treaties always serve private benefit only.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference line’s classification law-making versus contractual and applies it to the given examples. The multilateral standards-setting convention resembles law-making, while the bilateral port fee agreement is contractual and reciprocal.

questions.questionText:
Neeraj had been suffering from severe periodic mental disorder for several years and had
previously undergone psychiatric treatment involving multiple hospitalisations. According to
medical records, he frequently experienced episodes during which he lost touch with reality
and became incapable of recognising people or understanding his surroundings. One evening,
during such an episode, Neeraj suddenly attacked his neighbour with a sharp object under the
delusion that the neighbour was a dangerous supernatural being attempting to kill him.
Witnesses stated that immediately after the incident, Neeraj appeared confused, failed to
recognise his own family members, and repeatedly asked why strangers had entered his house.
Medical experts testified that at the time of the act, Neeraj was incapable of understanding
both the nature of his conduct and that it was wrong or contrary to law.
In light of the above passage and the interpretation laid down in Bapu Gujarat Singh v. State
of Rajasthan, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
Neeraj cannot claim the defence under Section 84 because violent acts involving
intentional assault are never protected under criminal law.

Neeraj may successfully invoke Section 84 because the facts indicate legal insanity existing
at the time of the act along with incapacity regarding both the nature and wrongfulness of
the act.

Neeraj cannot get the defence because periodic insanity and lucid intervals automatically
create a presumption of criminal responsibility.

Neeraj will not receive protection because medical evidence of insanity alone is irrelevant
under Section 84 of IPC.
questions.solution: The passage makes it clear that Section 84 of IPC applies only where the accused was suffering from legal insanity at the time of committing the act. Mere medical insanity is insufficient unless it results in incapacity to understand the nature of the act or that the act was wrong or contrary to law.

questions.questionText: G, a shipowner was carrying R’s zebra as a carrier by sea. During a turbulent stormy weather, the zebra turned hostile and behaved violently leading to injuries, despite the best efforts from the crew. Decide whether G could be held liable for negligence?
options: G can be held liable for negligence because he is the owner of the ship.
G can be held liable for negligence because R entrusted G with the duty to care.
G cannot be held liable for negligence because this was an act of god.
G cannot be held liable for negligence because he was not part of the crew.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: G cannot be held liable for negligence because this was an act of god. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
During a community cleanup event, a local business, GreenTech Solutions, accidentally dumped a
harmful chemical into a nearby river, causing significant environmental damage. The incident was a
result of mislabeled containers and not intentional. After the event, the community faced severe
repercussions on the local wildlife and water quality. GreenTech Solutions is now facing a lawsuit
requiring them to undertake specific actions to remedy the damage. Based on the principle that the
defendant must perform a positive act to rectify a wrongful act committed, what is the most likely court
order for GreenTech Solutions?
options: GreenTech Solutions will be ordered to pay a fine only, as their actions were accidental.

GreenTech Solutions will be exempt from any penalties or actions, as the containers were mislabeled and
they acted without knowledge of the wrongdoing.
GreenTech Solutions will receive a warning to prevent future occurrences, as the dumping was unintentional.

GreenTech Solutions will be ordered to actively engage in river cleanup and restoration efforts to directly
address the environmental damage caused.

questions.questionText:
The States of Sikandara and Milan commenced online lotteries, inter alia, in the State of Palampur.


The Government of Palampur declared the State to be a free zone from online and internet lotteries and
prohibited the sale of all computerized and online lottery tickets marketed and operated through vending
machines, terminals, electronic machines and tickets sold through internet in the state with effect from
the date of the notification. Pappu and Raghav are the lottery agents of the state of Sikandara and Milan.
Because of the recent notification passed by the state of Palampur, the states incurred heavy losses.
Owing to this, they both file a petition under article 131 in the Supreme Court.
options:
The petition will be maintainable as it involves interstate dispute and the Supreme Court has original and
exclusive Jurisdiction under Article 131.

Pappu and Raghav are agents of the state and are merely representing the state, and are private parties to the
dispute and therefore, they have no independent right to file the writ petition. Thus, the petition is not
maintainable under Article 131.

State of Karnataka will be held liable as its decision to prohibit the sale of all computerized and online
lottery tickets is arbitrary.
Both (A) and (C).

questions.questionText:
A foreign student, Elena, is detained by local authorities after a campus protest. No written
order is served, no statutory ground is shown, and she is kept in custody for two days without
access to counsel. The authorities argue that constitutional protection of life and personal
liberty is meant primarily for Indian citizens, and a foreign national must rely only on
diplomatic remedies. Elena files a petition claiming that Article 21 protects every person
against deprivation of liberty except by lawful procedure.
Which conclusion is most defensible?
options:
Elena fails because Article 21 protects citizens only and excludes foreign nationals from
liberty claims.

Elena fails because foreign students must use diplomatic channels before invoking
constitutional remedies.

Elena succeeds only if her home country formally supports her petition before Indian
courts.
Elena succeeds because no person may be deprived of liberty except by lawful procedure.
questions.solution: This option directly reflects the reference line by focusing on deprivation of liberty only according to procedure established by law. Since Elena was detained without written order, statutory basis, or procedural safeguards, her Article 21 claim is legally strong.

questions.questionText:
At a crowded airport security belt, Asha picks up a black laptop bag identical to hers and walks out,
believing it is her own. Thirty minutes later, she opens it in a taxi, realises it belongs to someone
else, and immediately returns it to airport security with the owner’s details. The owner still files a
complaint alleging theft because Asha physically carried the bag away. Asha argues she never had
a guilty mental state while taking it.
How should liability be approached?
options:
Liable because taking another’s property is theft per se and later return cannot erase the
offence once it is complete.

Liable because negligence is enough for dishonest taking, and confusion about bags still shows
a careless intent to deprive.

Not liable because punishment follows even without intention, and earlier periods allowed guilt
without proof of mind.

Not liable because mens rea means a guilty mental state accompanying a criminal act, and her
belief lacked guilt.
questions.solution: The option directly uses the reference words “guilty mental state” and “criminal act,” and applies them to Asha’s belief that the bag was hers. If her mental state lacked guilt at the moment of taking, the ordinary foundation for criminal liability is not satisfied.

questions.questionText:
Amit and Bala, disillusioned with the state, have a series of secret conversations. They
       meticulously draft a plan titled "Operation New Dawn," which details a future
       strategy to recruit members, procure weapons, and attack parliament to seize
       sovereignty. They hide this document but take no concrete steps to acquire weapons
       or recruit. Are they liable for any offence under the provided passage?
options:
No, they are not liable as their plan is merely a written document and they
               took no actionable steps like collecting arms, which is definitively required for
               an offence.

Yes, they are liable under Section 121 for waging war, as the detailed plan
               itself constitutes a concrete attempt to wage war against the Government of
               India and its institutions.

No, they are not liable as their concealment of the plan shows a lack of intent
               to actually carry it out, which negates the necessary criminal intent for any
               charge.

Yes, they are liable under Section 121A for conspiracy to wage war, as their
