               agreement with the shared intention to deprive India of its sovereignty is a
               complete crime.

questions.questionText:
Narang Samhati is a pro Hindu cultural organization, which works for preserving religious teachings.
The organization receives a complaint from nearby area that two nuns and a priest of St. Xavier Church
are trying to convert the Hindu people of locality by preaching sermons of Christianity. Narang Samhiti
wants church to stop propagating Christianity in locality and files a case in the Court. Decide whether
Organization's claim will succeed?
options:
The Organization's claim will succeed only if people have been already converted with the help of these
sermons.
The organization's claim will not succeed because the right to propagate religion is protected by Article 25.
The organization's claim will succeed because conversion is against Article 26 of the Constitution.

Organization's claim will succeed because they have right to protect their religion under Article 26 of the
Constitution.

questions.questionText:
Anil, a real estate tycoon, enters into a complex agreement with Bharti, his long-time friend,
concerning his vast estate. Anil is suffering from a terminal illness and wishes to ensure that Bharti's
family, who has been loyal to him for decades, is taken care of after his demise. The agreement includes
transferring ownership of one of his prime properties immediately to Bharti. However, the property in
question is tied to an ongoing legal dispute about the right of re-entry which Anil's competitor claims to
hold, pending a court decision. This right was established in a previous agreement signed by Anil's father,
which restricts the property's transfer until the dispute is settled. Bharti, following Anil's passing, wishes
to transfer the property to her daughter as a wedding gift. Is the property transfer legally valid?
options:
Yes, because Anil had a moral obligation to Bharti and acted on it, making the transfer enforceable under the
principle of promissory estoppel.
Yes, because the property was transferred to Bharti before the court's decision, making her the rightful owner.

No, because the property is subject to a right of re-entry, which is inherently non-transferable until resolved,
as per Section 6.

No, because the property is tied to spes successionis, making it non-transferable until the court confirms the
heir.

questions.questionText:
In April 2025, the Supreme Court observed that ten welfare bills had been stalled by a Governor
for over two years. Invoking Article 142, which allows the Court to pass any order necessary for
doing complete justice, the bench declared these bills as effectively assented to, bypassing the
requirement for a physical signature from the Governor. In the context of the November 2025
Advisory Opinion, which of the following best describes the constitutional validity of this specific
use of Article 142?
options:
It is constitutionally valid because Article 142 is an overriding power that allows the Court to
ignore the Separation of Powers to achieve complete justice.

It is invalid as the Judiciary cannot usurp the gubernatorial function of granting assent
without violating the Separation of Powers.

It is valid only if the President of India explicitly provides a post-facto confirmation of the
Court’s deemed consent order.

It is invalid because Article 142 can only be used for criminal cases and not for matters
involving state legislation or the Governor’s office.
questions.solution: The April Bench used Article 142 to grant deemed assent as an exceptional remedy for democratic stalemates, but the November Bench ruled this unconstitutional. It held that the Judiciary cannot "usurp" executive functions, as doing so violates the Separation of Powers a part of the Constitution's Basic Structure meaning the Court can command a decision but cannot make it for the Governor.

questions.questionText:
Mr. Sharma, an 80-year-old widower, gifted his self-acquired house to his only
        son, Rohan, in 2020 through a registered gift deed. The deed was a simple,
        unconditional transfer of title. For two years, Rohan provided for his father's
        needs. However, after a bitter argument in 2022, Rohan and his wife began
        neglecting Mr. Sharma, refusing to provide him with food and medical care. Mr.
        Sharma, unable to maintain himself, approached the Maintenance Tribunal
        seeking to revoke the gift deed and reclaim his house. Rohan argued that since
        the gift was unconditional, the Tribunal had no power to revoke it. What is the
        most likely outcome?
options:
The Tribunal will revoke the gift deed because Rohan's failure to provide
      maintenance is a direct violation of the Act's primary objective.

The Tribunal will not revoke the gift deed because, as per judicial precedent,
      an unconditional gift without a specific maintenance clause cannot be revoked
      under the Act.

The Tribunal will order Rohan to pay a monthly maintenance of ₹10,000 but
      will not revoke the gift deed, as that would be an excessive measure.

The Tribunal will revoke the gift deed because the Act's property protection
      provisions automatically create an implied condition of maintenance in every gift
      from a senior citizen to their child.

questions.questionText:
Meera was informed during a medical examination that her pregnancy had crossed 26 weeks. Doctors
found that the foetus suffered from severe abnormalities that would likely make survival after birth
extremely difficult. Meera approached the court for permission to terminate the pregnancy. The State
opposed the plea stating that the pregnancy had exceeded the statutory limit prescribed under the
Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971. Decide whether the court should permit termination under
the present law.
options:
The court should permit termination because emotional distress is sufficient to allow termination after 24


weeks.
The court should reject the plea because termination after 24 weeks is absolutely prohibited under the Act.

The court should permit termination because pregnancies above 24 weeks can be terminated in cases of
substantial foetal abnormalities.

The court should reject the plea because pregnancies beyond 20 weeks can never be terminated unless the
woman is a minor.

questions.questionText:
In light of the Supreme Court’s observations regarding the misuse of Article 32, consider the
following statements:
1. Article 32 forms part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
2. The Supreme Court is constitutionally bound to entertain every petition filed under Article 32
if a Fundamental Right violation is alleged.
3. High Courts under Article 226 have wider writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court under
Article 32.
4. The power to issue writs under Article 32 can be suspended during a National Emergency
through a Presidential Order under Article 359.
Which of the following options correctly identifies the statements that are legally accurate?
options: 1 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
questions.solution: Statement 1 is correct. In Kesavananda Bharati v.

questions.questionText:
Shyam and Ram are business partners with their business located in different parts of Uttar Pradesh
and Madhya Pradesh. A conflict arises between them regarding the shares of the company. In a rush of
anger, Shyam pushes Ram from the fifth floor of his apartment. As a result, Ram dies. Ram's family files
a petition in the Supreme Court under Article 131 for murder under Section 300 of the Indian Penal
Code.
options: Shyam is liable for murder under Section 300 of IPC as in a fit of rage and anger, he killed Ram.
Shyam will not be liable for murder as he had no intention to kill Ram and Ram was like a brother to him.
Ram's family cannot directly file for an action in the Supreme Court without first going to the lower court.

Supreme Court under Article 131 deals with disputes between two States or between the Centre and a State
and thus, Ram's family cannot file a criminal case against Shyam under Article 131.

questions.questionText:
Kumari Devi is one of the most famous temples in the state of Gujarat. Kumari Devi is worshipped by
a special sect of Hindus, who believe in only Female counterpart of Ardhanarishwara. The devotees do
not believe in any God, who is manifested in Male form. In 2018, An NGO files a PIL in Supreme Court
stating that these practices of sect have been adopted to make men feel inferior and thus is against
principle of equality embodied in constitution. The petitioner request that court should order sect to
worship gods in male form as well. Decide Whether NGO's claim will succeed?
options: NGO's claim will succeed because denying the male form of God is against the core idea of Hinduism.

NGO's claim will succeed because those religious practices can't be allowed which promote gender
discrimination.
Interference in Sect's way of worship is against Article 25 of the Constitution.
NGO's claim will not succeed because sect has right to manage its religious affairs under Article 26.

questions.questionText:
Magistrate receives a private complaint alleging Section 504 IPC. After examining the
complainant under Section 200 CrPC, the Magistrate is uncertain whether the allegations,
even if proved, would satisfy all ingredients of Section 504. The Magistrate decides to order a
limited inquiry by the local police station to verify facts before deciding whether to issue
process. The accused challenges this order. Which legal proposition is correct?
options:
The Magistrate's order is illegal because Section 200 CrPC, having already been complied
with, compels the Magistrate to either issue process or dismiss the complaint immediately
without further inquiry.

The Magistrate's order is authorized under Section 202 CrPC, which permits postponement
of process issuance and a preliminary inquiry to verify whether sufficient grounds to
proceed exist.

The Magistrate's order is illegal because once a complainant is examined under Section 200
CrPC, issuance of process becomes mandatory if any criminal offence is even prima facie
disclosed.

The Magistrate's order is valid only if the High Court first grants permission under Section
482 CrPC, since preliminary inquiries into private complaints require superior court
authorization.
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states that Section 202 CrPC "permits postponement of process issuance where the Magistrate considers it necessary to conduct a preliminary inquiry or investigation to verify whether sufficient grounds exist to proceed," describing it as "an optional safeguard against mechanical process issuance." The Magistrate's action falls precisely within this provision. Option (A) is the closest distractor as it correctly references Section 200 CrPC as the prior step, but the passage

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about a child born from a voidable Hindu marriage:
Statement I: If a voidable marriage is later annulled by a decree of nullity, the child born
from that marriage is protected under Section 16(2).
Statement II: The protection exists because the law separates the invalidity of the marriage
from the status of the child.
Statement III: Once a decree of nullity is passed, the child is treated as legitimate only if the
parents later remarry validly.
Which of the following is correct?
options:
Only Statement I is correct, because Section 16(2) applies only after a decree of nullity is
passed.

Only Statements I and II are correct, because the child is protected despite the voidable
marriage being annulled.

Only Statements II and III are correct, because legitimacy depends on later correction of
the marital defect.

All three statements are correct, because Section 16 protects the child but still requires a
valid marriage later.
questions.solution: Statement I reflects Section 16(2), which protects a child born from a voidable marriage where a decree of nullity has been passed. Statement II is also correct because the legal basis is separation between the invalidity of the marriage and the child’s status.

questions.questionText:
Amit is travelling in a taxi from Bhopal railway station to his office. Heavy rain causes traffic
to stop beneath a flyover. The taxi driver switches off the engine and parks at the extreme left
of the road to wait for the rain to reduce. While waiting, Amit steps out of the taxi to answer a
phone call, remaining beside the vehicle. At that moment, a large advertising signboard fixed
to the flyover above becomes detached due to poor maintenance and falls directly on Amit,
causing serious injuries. The taxi had no defect, did not strike any object, and nothing
connected with its movement, operation or condition contributed to the signboard falling. Amit
files a claim under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, arguing that he was still in the
course of the same journey and had stepped out only briefly. Is Section 166 the proper remedy
on these facts?
options:
Yes, because Amit's journey had not ended and the injury occurred while he remained
connected with the ongoing use of the taxi.

Yes, because Amit had stepped out only temporarily and the vehicle continued to be part of
the same transport activity.

No, because the injury resulted from an external event lacking a proximate connection
with the taxi's movement, operation, condition or use.

No, because compensation under Section 166 is confined to injuries suffered while a
claimant remains physically inside the motor vehicle.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
questions.solution: the signboard collapsed due to an independent external event. The passage explains that where the injury lacks a proximate connection with the vehicle's movement, operation, condition or use, Section 166 may not be the appropriate remedy.

questions.questionText:
Karan is prosecuted for strangling rival Mohit. Evidence: threatening messages one week prior;
Karan's vehicle near Mohit's residence on murder night; forensic ligature marks confirm
strangulation; DNA under victim's fingernails (indicating struggle) doesn't match Karan; no alibi.
Prosecution argues DNA absence means victim didn't scratch killer. Which principle resolves this
dispute?
options:
The last seen theory principle which requires independent corroboration to establish a
continuous and unbroken chain of incriminating events.

Circumstances must exclude every hypothesis except guilt, and exculpatory scientific evidence
cannot be ignored to convict on suspicion.

The TIP and dock identification principles which govern the reliability of witness testimony
when identifying a stranger in a criminal trial.

The FIR omission principle under Section 11 of the Evidence Act regarding the consistency of
the initial information provided to the police.
questions.solution: This directly tests scientific evidence principles. The passage states: "when scientific evidence is neutral or exculpatory—such as DNA mismatches...

questions.questionText:
A chemical manufacturing company stored large quantities of hazardous substances in tanks
located near a residential area. One night, an unexpected earthquake of extraordinary
intensity struck the region, causing the tanks to rupture and release toxic chemicals into the
nearby locality. The affected residents filed a suit against the company under the rule of strict
liability. The company argued that the escape occurred solely due to an extraordinary natural
event that could neither have been predicted nor prevented despite reasonable precautions.
In light of the above passage, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
The company will be liable because escape of hazardous substances automatically results
in liability, irrespective of the cause of escape.

The company cannot claim the defence of Act of God because strict liability does not
recognize any exceptions in cases involving dangerous substances.

The company may successfully rely on the defence of Act of God if the earthquake was
extraordinary, unforeseeable, and there was no human negligence contributing to the
damage.

The company will not be liable because all natural disasters completely exempt industries
from responsibility for damage caused to neighbouring property.
questions.solution: The passage explains that Act of God is a recognized exception to strict liability. If the harm is caused solely due to an extraordinary natural event that could not have been anticipated or prevented despite reasonable care, liability may not arise.

questions.questionText:
In 1977, during an Emergency proclaimed only in two border districts, the Union issues a
circular stating that Article 19 freedoms stand suspended in those districts, and a detained
journalist’s writ petition in the High Court is dismissed as “not maintainable” on the ground
that the High Court’s jurisdiction is restricted during the Emergency. The journalist argues
that Emergency provisions can operate only nationwide, not regionally, and that constitutional
cases must still be heard by normal benches.
Which option best reflects the set of Emergency-era changes relied upon?
options:
National emergency could apply to the whole or part of India, and Article 358 was
expanded to suspend Article 19 rights during emergencies.

Emergency could apply only to the whole of India, and Article 19 rights could never be
suspended even during emergencies anywhere.

High Courts retained full jurisdiction always, and constitutional benches required only
three judges with a simple majority in every case.

President’s Rule was reduced in duration, and tribunals were abolished, so all
constitutional disputes had to go to civil courts only.
questions.solution: This option directly uses the reference words “apply to the whole or part of India” and “expanded the operation of Article 358 for suspension of Article 19 rights during emergencies,” which matches the scenario of a geographically limited Emergency and suspension of Article 19 freedoms in those districts. It captures the Emergency-era logic used to justify regional application and Article 19 suspension.

questions.questionText:
Zenith Builders entered into a contract with Alpha Suppliers for the delivery of steel
machinery within 20 days. The contract included a force majeure clause stating that neither
party would be liable for non-performance caused by extraordinary natural events beyond
human control. Ten days later, an unprecedented landslide triggered by a severe earthquake
destroyed the only highway connecting Alpha Suppliers’ warehouse to the city, making
transportation impossible for several weeks. Zenith Builders sued Alpha Suppliers for breach
of contract due to failure to deliver the machinery on time.
In light of the above passage, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
Alpha Suppliers will be liable because contractual obligations must always be performed
regardless of natural events or practical difficulties.

Alpha Suppliers may be excused from liability if the earthquake and resulting landslide
qualify as an Act of God covered under the force majeure clause.

Alpha Suppliers cannot rely on the force majeure clause because Act of God applies only in
tort law and not in contract law.

Alpha Suppliers will automatically escape liability because every natural disaster
completely terminates contractual obligations between parties.
questions.solution: The passage states that although Act of God is primarily a concept in tort law, it is also relevant in contract law through force majeure clauses. Such clauses excuse parties from performing contractual obligations when extraordinary natural events occur beyond human control.

questions.questionText:
Kiran, an intern at the Municipal Water Board, records an official conference call which
includes a heated argument between two engineers regarding office leave policies, through the
official communication platform/system. She sends the audio to a friend purely for
entertainment, with no intention of harming the State or gaining money. The Water Board is
not a “prohibited place.” Which of the following best describes Kiran's legal position?
options:
Kiran is liable under Section 3 of the OSA because any unauthorized disclosure of
departmental information by an employee constitutes “spying.”

Kiran is not liable under the IT Act because her intentions were not “dishonest or
fraudulent” as she was merely seeking to entertain a friend.

Kiran is liable under the OSA because the Municipal Water Board is a government-funded
entity and thus qualifies as a strategic security-sensitive location.

Kiran is liable under Section 43 of the IT Act for unauthorized data extraction, even if her
actions do not qualify as spying under the OSA.
questions.solution: Option D is correct because the passage states that unauthorized recording falls under Section 43 (which relates to access/downloading without permission). Since the office is not a “prohibited place,” the OSA does not apply.

questions.questionText:
Sonal is waiting in a parked car beside a public road while her driver buys fuel coupons from a
nearby counter. A temporary festival arch erected by private organisers collapses during
strong winds and falls on the car, injuring Sonal. The car was insured, but it had no defect, did
not move, and did not hit the arch or its supporting ropes. Sonal files a claim before the Claims
Tribunal. The Tribunal records that the collapse of the arch had no connection with the
movement, operation, condition or use of the car, but still awards compensation against the
car’s insurer under Section 168, stating that it has the power to determine compensation and
specify the person who must pay. What is the likely legal position under the stated principles?
options:
The award may stand because Section 168 empowers the Tribunal to determine
compensation and name the payer.

The award may stand because the injury occurred in a public place while Sonal was seated
in an insured car.

The award is vulnerable because Section 168 requires proof that the owner personally
caused the injury.

The award is vulnerable because Section 168 applies after the case falls within the Motor
Vehicles Act.
questions.solution: the statutory requirement of a motor-vehicle accident is absent on the Tribunal’s own finding. Section 168 cannot create liability where the case does not first fall within the Motor Vehicles Act.

questions.questionText:
A famous actress, Ms. Sinha is arrested by the police at an airport at 1 PM on a Monday. She
is taken into custody, but the police, citing a flight delay, inform her that they will be taking a
later flight. They land at 4:40 PM later that day and travel to the police station from the
airport, where she is detained. The next day, at 4:00 PM, the police finally took her to the
Magistrate. Ms. Sinha’s lawyer contends that her fundamental rights have been violated.
Decide if there has been any violation of Article 22.
options:
The police have violated Article 22, as a flight delay is not a justifiable reason for not
producing her before a Magistrate on time.

The police have not violated Article 22, as the time spent traveling (via flight) is a
reasonable delay and should be excluded from the 24-hour calculation.

The police have violated Article 22, but the detention becomes lawful when he is produced
before the Magistrate on Tuesday.

The police have not violated Article 22, because the right to be produced before a
Magistrate within 24 hours is only applicable to arrests made within city limits.
questions.solution: option A is correct because only the time spent on the journey to the court is to be excluded. A delay caused by a flight delay or by waiting for a flight is not "journey time" and cannot be excluded.

questions.questionText:
During a National Emergency proclaimed under Article 352, an order was issued under Article
859 suspending the right to move courts for enforcement of certain fundamental rights. During
this period, Parliament enacted a special economic security law which made earlier foreign-
exchange reporting omissions punishable with imprisonment and heavy fines. Indovia
Minerals Pvt. Ltd., a corporation incorporated in Singapore and carrying on business in India,
was prosecuted for an omission committed before the new law was enacted. The Union argued
that Indovia Minerals could not invoke Article 20(1), since it was a foreign corporation and the
prosecution arose during the emergency period. Is the Union’s objection valid?
options:
No, because Article 20(1) protects accused corporations and survives Article 359
suspension.
No, because Article 20(1) protects Indian corporations only during Article 359 suspension.
Yes, because Article 20(1) protects natural persons alone, not prosecutable companies.

Yes, because Article 359 suspends all fundamental-right claims during any national
emergency.
questions.solution: Article 20(1) is not confined to citizens or natural persons. It can be invoked by non- citizens and corporations as well, if they are prosecuted under a criminal law.

questions.questionText:
Ratan was a bus driver authorised by the bus owner, Farhan, to drive the bus. Once, Ratan
stepped out of the bus to get a cup of tea. In the meantime, Hasan, the conductor of the bus who
had never been authorised or trained to drive the bus, started driving it to move it out of the way
of traffic., during which he met with an accident. Which of the following correctly identifies the
liability arising from the accident?
options:
Ratan will be liable, as he was supposed to take reasonable care while parking the bus so that
it was out of the way of traffic.

Farhan will be liable, as he was the owner of the bus and Ratan was acting under his
authorisation.

Both Ratan and Farhan will be liable, as Farhan authorised Ratan, who in turn authorised
Hasan.
Only Hasan will be liable, as driving the bus was outside the course of his employment.
questions.solution: Hasan is the conductor. The passage bases vicarious liability on employees acting within the scope of employment.

questions.questionText:
Sameer had been suffering from periodic mental disorder for several years and was medically
classified as a lunatic. His condition caused temporary episodes of unsoundness of mind,
followed by periods where he behaved normally and carried out daily activities rationally. One
afternoon, after planning a robbery for a few days, Sameer entered a jewellery shop,
threatened the owner with a knife, and escaped with cash and ornaments. During trial,
Sameer claimed the defence under Section 84 of IPC on the ground that he was suffering from
lunacy at the time of the offence.
In light of the above passage, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
Sameer will automatically receive the benefit of Section 84 because lunatics are
permanently treated as persons of unsound mind under criminal law.

Sameer can invoke Section 84 because any person medically categorised as a lunatic is
exempt from criminal liability irrespective of the timing of the act.

Sameer may not get the benefit of Section 84 if the offence was committed during a lucid
interval showing rational understanding and planning.

Sameer must be acquitted because periodic insanity itself is sufficient to negate criminal
intention under IPC.
questions.solution: is therefore correct because legal insanity depends upon the mental condition of the accused at the exact time of the offence.

questions.questionText:
The High Court receives a petition under Section 482 CrPC seeking to quash a complaint
alleging Section 504 IPC, on the ground that the complaint fails to disclose essential
ingredients of the offence and constitutes an abuse of process. The complainant contends that
since the Magistrate has already taken cognizance and issued summons, Section 397 CrPC
revision is the only available remedy and Section 482 CrPC is not maintainable. Which of the
following positions is legally correct?
options:
Section 482 CrPC jurisdiction is fully excluded once a Magistrate takes cognizance, making
Section 397 CrPC revision the sole legally available remedy for challenging such
proceedings thereafter.

Section 482 CrPC inherent jurisdiction remains available to prevent abuse of process, and
is distinguishable from appellate re-appreciation under Section 397 CrPC as the passage
confirms.

Section 482 CrPC and Section 397 CrPC operate identically at the post-cognizance stage,
and either provision may be freely invoked since both serve the same remedial purpose.

Section 482 CrPC becomes unavailable wherever Section 397 CrPC exists as a statutory
remedy, since specific statutory provisions always entirely displace the High Court's
inherent jurisdiction.
questions.solution: The passage directly states that where complaints "fail to disclose essential ingredients or constitute abuse of process, the High Court may exercise inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC to quash proceedings," and that "this power ensures prevention of unjust continuation of proceedings and secures justice." Crucially, the passage distinguishes Section 482 from “appellate re-appreciation under Section 397 CrPC" — confirming they serve different purposes rather than being interchangeable

questions.questionText:
A statute regulating export documents states: “Whoever brings prohibited goods into India in
breach of notification shall be punished,” without mentioning “knowingly” or “intentionally.” Riya, a
passenger, is caught with a sealed package placed in her bag by a travel agent, and she claims she
did not know it contained prohibited goods. The prosecution argues that because the statute is
silent on intention, guilt is automatic and knowledge is irrelevant. Riya argues guilty mind is
normally presumed unless the law clearly rules it out.
Which position best matches the passage principle?
options:
Defence barred: statutory silence always excludes mens rea; liability becomes automatic for
every offence, so knowledge is irrelevant.

Defence considered: guilty mind is generally presumed unless legislation clearly rules it out,
though words like knowingly are absent here.

Defence barred: strict liability covers all import offences; courts never examine intent or
knowledge, so her explanation cannot matter.

Defence must succeed: mens rea is always essential; no offence exists without explicit intention
wording, so the prosecution fails automatically.
questions.solution: This option directly mirrors the reference words “guilty mind is generally presumed” and “unless legislation clearly rules it out.” It correctly recognises that absence of words like “knowingly” does not by itself exclude mens rea.

questions.questionText:
Avinash, a senior civil servant in the Department of Education, was abruptly dismissed from his
position. Officially, the termination was justified under the constitutional principle that his employment
was at the pleasure of the President. This occurred shortly after Avinash exposed significant corruption
within the department. Believing his dismissal was in retaliation for his whistleblowing, and given that
there was no formal inquiry or specific reasoning provided, he decides to challenge this action legally.
Avinash contends that his dismissal was unjust and should be scrutinized for fairness. Given the
circumstances surrounding his removal, what is the most likely legal outcome?
options:
Avinash's legal challenge is unlikely to succeed, as the Constitution provides for termination at the pleasure
of the President, which is typically not bound by requirements for justification.

Avinash's legal challenge may succeed on grounds that his dismissal, without inquiry and following
whistleblowing activities, could be seen as arbitrary and unjust, possibly violating principles under Article 14 of
the Constitution.

Avinash cannot legally challenge the dismissal, as the doctrine of pleasure explicitly excludes the possibility
of judicial review for decisions made under this rule.

The court will likely uphold Avinash's dismissal on the grounds that the doctrine of pleasure allows for
unconditional termination, and whistleblower protection does not apply in cases involving constitutional
principles.

questions.questionText:
A Muslim woman claims a share in her father’s intestate agricultural land. Her uncle argues
that under the personal law statute, agricultural land is excluded, so local tenancy custom
applies and the land should pass only to male heirs. The woman argues that Section 2 still
makes Shariat the rule of decision for intestate succession and that excluding agricultural
land is unfair. The court must decide what the Act itself says on agricultural land.
Which statement best matches the passage principle?
options:
Agricultural land is excluded, so the Act’s Shariat rule does not automatically govern
inheritance rights in agricultural property.

Agricultural land is included, so Section 2 overrides customs in every kind of property
including agricultural land always today.

Agricultural land is included only for women, because the exclusion was inserted to protect
women and increase inheritance shares today.

Agricultural land is excluded only when the land is leased, but owned land remains within
Shariat rule for intestate succession.
questions.solution: This option directly uses “agricultural land is excluded,” matching the reference line. Even if the exclusion is criticised as unfair, the legal question here is what the Act provides, and the passage states the exclusion affects inheritance rights in agricultural property.

questions.questionText:
Arjun, deeply envious of his neighbour, instigates his friend Bharat to burn down the
neighbour’s empty house, promising him a reward. Bharat agrees and proceeds to the house.
After setting fire to the house, Bharat notices an expensive watch lying on a table inside and
decides to steal it before fleeing. The house is completely destroyed, and Bharat is later
apprehended with the stolen watch. Under these circumstances, what is Arjun's liability?
options:
Arjun is only liable for abetting the burning of the house, as his instigation was limited to
that specific act.

Arjun is liable only for abetting the theft, as it was a separate crime committed during the
act he instigated.

Arjun is not liable for any offence because the theft was committed, which makes Bharat
solely responsible for all acts.

Arjun is liable for both the burning of the house and the theft, as both crimes were
committed as a result of his initial instigation.
questions.solution: Why (a) is correct: The passage states that liability attaches if the act committed is the “probable and natural result of the instigation.” Arjun instigated only the burning of the house. Theft of the watch was a separate and independent decision taken by Bharat.

questions.questionText:
Karan is sitting inside an insured car parked near a public park during heavy rain. The driver
has stopped because visibility is poor. A large branch from an old roadside tree suddenly
breaks during a strong gust of wind and falls on the car, injuring Karan. The car had no
defect, did not hit the tree, and its position did not contribute to the branch falling.
Assertion (A): Karan’s claim against the motor insurer should not succeed merely because he
was injured while sitting inside an insured car.
Reason (R): A motor accident claim still requires a meaningful link between the injury and
the use of the vehicle, and an unforeseen natural event may weaken that link on the facts.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.solution: both the Assertion and the Reason follow from the passage. Karan’s presence inside an insured car is not enough by itself.

questions.questionText:
Rohan files a writ petition directly before the Supreme Court under Article 32 seeking dissolution of his
marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown. He argues that since the Supreme Court has the power under
Article 142 to grant divorce on this ground, it should entertain his petition and dissolve the marriage without
requiring him to pursue any other legal remedy. Based on the passage, which of the following is the most
appropriate legal position?
options:
The Supreme Court can directly entertain the petition under Article 32 because Article 142 permits divorce on the
ground of irretrievable breakdown.

The petition is not maintainable because a writ petition under Article 32 cannot be filed directly to seek divorce on the
ground of irretrievable breakdown.
The petition is maintainable only if both spouses jointly consent to the dissolution of marriage.
The Supreme Court must transfer the petition to the concerned High Court under Article 226 for disposal.

questions.questionText:
Priya, a resident of Mumbai, has filed a writ petition before the Bombay High Court under Article
226, challenging a government order that she claims violates her right to equality under Article
14. The matter is listed for hearing next month. In the meantime, she files a fresh petition under
Article 32 before the Supreme Court raising the identical challenge. Which option best aligns with
how the Supreme Court in the passage would view Priya's procedural choice?
options:
Priya's conduct is legally sound since Article 32 is an independent and constitutionally
guaranteed right that can be invoked at any point of time, and no provision of law expressly
bars simultaneous proceedings before the High Court and the Supreme Court on the same
issue

Priya's conduct amounts to a misuse of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction since she is invoking
Article 32 while an identical matter is already pending before an appropriate forum, which is
precisely the practice the Court has criticised in the passage

Priya's conduct is permissible because the matter involves a violation of a fundamental right
under Article 14, and the Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction over all cases involving
fundamental rights, irrespective of pending proceedings before any High Court

Priya's conduct, while procedurally irregular, is justified given that the Bombay High Court
has not yet passed any order in the matter, meaning that no High Court decision has been
bypassed or overridden by her approaching the Supreme Court directly
questions.solution: is correct because Priya's situation is factually identical to what the passage criticises — she has filed an Article 32 petition before the Supreme Court while an identical petition is already pending before the Bombay High Court. The passage expressly states that this constitutes a "gross misuse of the process of the court and of law," regardless of the nature of the right alleged to be violated.

questions.questionText:
At a traditional wedding in Udaipur, both families exchange gifts as per community customs.
The bride’s family gives the groom a gold chain, traditional attire, and some silver utensils
(total value approx. %4.5 lakh). The groom’s family gives the bride gold jewellery, clothes, and
household items (total value approx. 75 lakh) and no demand was made by either side. Later, a
complaint is filed alleging that dowry was given and taken. How should this situation be
assessed?
options:
It amounts to dowry because any exchange of valuable gifts at the time of marriage falls
within the prohibition under Section 2 of the Act.

It does not amount to dowry because the gifts satisfy all the conditions of the exception
under Section 3(2), they were given without demand, are customary in nature, not
excessive in value, and were entered in lists.

It amounts to dowry because the total value of gifts exchanged exceeds %5 lakh, which
creates a presumption of dowry under the Act.

It does not amount to dowry only because the gifts were exchanged mutually; mutuality
alone is sufficient to exclude the transaction from the definition of dowry.
questions.solution: The passage clearly states that presents given at the time of marriage without demand are protected under Section 3(2) if they are customary, not excessive having regard to the financial status of the giver, and entered in a list. In this case, all conditions are satisfied.

questions.questionText:
Four persons file applications under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act after suffering
injuries in different situations.
i. Rukmini is injured when a bus driver suddenly brakes to avoid a cyclist, causing her to be
thrown against the metal railing inside the bus.
ii. Farhan is injured when a parked delivery van’s loading ramp, left half-open during
unloading, slips and strikes his leg while he is helping remove cartons.
iii. Neel is injured while sleeping inside his parked car when a rotten branch from a roadside
tree falls during a storm and crushes the roof.
iv. Charu is injured when a truck’s worn-out tyre bursts while the truck is carrying goods,
causing the truck to overturn.
Which of the above claims are most likely to fall within the kind of accident for which Section
166 provides the procedural route?
options: Claims i, ii and iv only.
Claims i, iii and iv only.
Claims ii, iii and iv only.
Claims i, ii and iii only.
questions.solution: claims i, ii and iv have a real connection with the use, operation or condition of a motor vehicle. Rukmini’s injury is connected to braking during bus travel, Farhan’s injury is connected to the unloading use of the delivery van and its ramp, and Charu’s injury is connected to the truck’s worn-out tyre while carrying goods.

questions.questionText:
Aman voluntarily consumed an excessive quantity of alcohol and narcotic substances during a
celebration late at night. Several witnesses later stated that Aman had become completely
disoriented, was unable to recognise people around him, and appeared unaware of his own
actions. In that condition, Aman attacked a stranger with a metal object, causing serious
injuries. Medical evidence produced before the court showed that at the time of the incident,
Aman was incapable of understanding the nature of the act and was unable to distinguish
whether his conduct was wrong or contrary to law. Aman claimed the defence under Section 84
of IPC.
In light of the above passage, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
Aman cannot invoke Section 84 because voluntary intoxication can never amount to
unsoundness of mind under criminal law.

Aman will automatically get the defence because every intoxicated person is treated as
legally insane under Section 84 of IPC.

Aman may claim the defence if it is proved that the intoxication resulted in such complete
incapacity that he was unable to understand the nature and wrongfulness of his act.
Aman will get the defence as intention can not be formed if one is intoxicated.
questions.solution: The passage includes a person under intoxication within the category of medical insanity. However, merely being intoxicated is not sufficient to attract the protection of Section 84 of IPC.

questions.questionText:
Anika and Dev enter into a Hindu marriage. Later, Dev files a petition claiming that the
marriage is voidable because his consent was obtained by misrepresentation. During the
proceedings, Anika gives birth to a daughter, Myra. The court subsequently passes a decree of
nullity. Dev’s father argues that Myra cannot be treated as legitimate because the court’s
decree has undone the marriage, and Section 16 should apply only when the marriage was
valid under Sections 5 and 7 at the time of birth. What is the legal flaw in this reasoning?
options:
It assumes that a decree of nullity removes the child’s protection, although Section 16(2)
protects a child born from a voidable marriage.

It assumes that misrepresentation cannot make a Hindu marriage voidable, although the
defect may fall under Section 12.

It assumes that Sections 5 and 7 are irrelevant to marriage validity, although they provide
conditions of a valid Hindu marriage.

It assumes that the decree of nullity is unnecessary, although Section 16 protection arises
only before any court order.
questions.solution: Dev’s father treats the decree of nullity as destroying Myra’s legitimacy. The passage provides the opposite: Section 16(2) protects a child born from a voidable marriage where a decree of nullity has been passed.

questions.questionText:
Ishita approached a government-approved hospital for termination of her 19-week pregnancy. Dr.
Arjun, a Registered Medical Practitioner, conducted the procedure after obtaining the opinion required
under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971. Following the procedure, Ishita experienced
medical complications and her family filed a civil suit against Dr. Arjun, stating that the doctor should be
personally liable for the harm caused during the termination. During the proceedings, evidence showed
that Dr. Arjun had acted according to the requirements prescribed under the Act and without malicious
intent. Decide the case.
options:
Dr. Arjun will be liable because any medical complication arising from termination permits legal
proceedings against the doctor.

The suit against Dr. Arjun will not lie because the Act protects Registered Medical Practitioners for acts done
in good faith under the statute.
Dr. Arjun will be liable because protection under the Act applies only when the pregnancy exceeds 20 weeks.

The suit will succeed because doctors performing termination procedures in approved hospitals are not
protected from civil proceedings under the Act.

questions.questionText:
A was in love with B, his neighbor. B told A that she wanted to marry him and they eloped from their
home. Later, B's parents filed a complaint against A and A was convicted under a statute making it
unlawful to take any unmarried girl under the age of sixteen out of the possession and without the
consent of her parents. The girl taken by Defendant was 15 years old and she had told the Defendant that
mandatory minimum age under the law was 14 years and the defendant reasonably believed that the age
in statute was 14. Decide which of the following statements is true?
options: A will not be liable because B committed fraud with him.
A will not be liable because he made a mistake of fact.
A will be liable because he made a mistake of law.
Not A but B will be held liable for mistake of law.
questions.solution: A correctly knew B's actual age (15 years) but mistakenly believed that the legal minimum age under the statute was 14 instead of 16. His error relates to the contents of the law rather than any factual circumstance. Since mistake of law is not a valid defence, A remains liable. Why other options are incorrect: A: B did not deceive A about her age; the mistake concerns the legal age prescribed by the statute. B: The mistake is not one of fact because A knew B's actual age.

questions.questionText:
The National Vikas Party (NVP) secured a majority in the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly. A
majority of NVP legislators in the Assembly held a meeting and appointed a new party whip without
obtaining approval from the national leadership of NVP. The legislators argued that since they
constituted the majority within the legislature party, they were entitled to take decisions relating to the
functioning of the party inside the House. The original political party challenged the decision before the
Speaker. Decide whether the appointment of the new whip by the legislators would be legally valid.
options:
The appointment of the new whip would be valid because the legislature party has complete autonomy in
matters concerning the functioning of the House.

The appointment of the new whip would be valid because the legislature party and the original political party
possess equal authority under the Tenth Schedule.

The appointment of the new whip would not be valid because the legislature party derives its existence from
the original political party and cannot act independently of it.

The appointment of the new whip would not be valid because members of a legislature party are prohibited
from participating in internal party decisions under the Tenth Schedule.

questions.questionText:
After the panchayat elections, the Aam Party emerged victorious over the Angur Party. Later
at night, 6 members of the Angur Party decide to break into the property of the Aam Party’s
leader to damage the same. They reach the designated spot at night and cross the wall to
break into the property. However, out of 6, 2 of them do not enter the property to keep watch.
Just as the four members are about to cause damage, a security patrol arrives and apprehends
all six members. Based on this situation, which of the following is correct?
options:
The members are not liable for unlawful assembly, because they were apprehended before
they could actually cause any damage to the property.

Only 4 of them are liable for unlawful assembly as they entered the property, thereby
committing an offence; the other 2 are liable for abetment.
All 6 of them are liable for unlawful assembly as they had a common object.

None of the members are liable for unlawful assembly because not all six of them entered
the property. The minimum number for unlawful assembly is five, and only four committed
the act of trespassing.
questions.solution: An assembly becomes unlawful when the number of members is 5 or more and they have a common object that falls under any one of the categories as mentioned in the passage. Option A is incorrect because apprehension of the criminals is not a requisite criterion.

questions.questionText:
Five persons were charged under Section 103 read with Section 190 BNS for the murder of V.
During trial, two accused were acquitted as the prosecution failed to prove their participation in the
unlawful assembly. The remaining three accused were convicted under Section 103 read with
Section 190 BNS. On appeal, the defence argued that with fewer than five persons found to share
the common object, Section 190 could not be applied. The prosecution contended that even if Section
190 fails, the conviction can be sustained under Section 103 read with Section 3(5) BNS on the
same evidence. The question is whether the conviction under Section 190 can stand and whether
Section 3(5) may be applied in its place.
options:
The conviction under Section 190 fails once the common object is shared by fewer than five
persons; Section 3(5) may apply if common intention is established and no prejudice is caused to
the accused.

The conviction under Section 190 remains valid so long as at least two persons are convicted,
since an unlawful assembly may lawfully consist of fewer than five members after the court
returns its findings.

The accused must be acquitted entirely since Section 3(5) cannot be invoked at the appellate
stage where no specific charge was framed against them at the time of trial.
questions.solution: As held in Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, Section 190 requires a minimum of five persons.

questions.questionText:
Aarav Sharma was elected to the Karnataka Legislative Assembly as a member of the Jan Shakti
Party (JSP). He voted against the official direction issued by JSP during an important confidence motion.
He also participated in meetings of the People's Democratic Alliance (PDA) legislators and publicly
declared that he supported the policies of PDA. However, Aarav never submitted a formal resignation
from JSP. JSP thereafter filed a petition before the Speaker to disqualify Aarav under the Tenth
Schedule. Decide the case.
options:
Aarav cannot be disqualified because disqualification under the Tenth Schedule requires a written resignation
from the political party.

Aarav cannot be disqualified because attending meetings and supporting another party's policies are
protected political activities under the Tenth Schedule.

Aarav can be disqualified because his conduct may be sufficient to infer that he voluntarily abandoned
membership of JSP.
Aarav can only be disqualified if two-thirds members of JSP also join PDA along with him.

questions.questionText:
St. Xavier's Convent School, a Christian minority institution established in 1985, is unaided
and located in Mumbai. In 2024, the school refuses to admit Rajesh Kumar, a Hindu child from
an economically weaker section, under the 25% quota prescribed by Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE
Act, citing its status as a minority institution exempt under Pramati (2014). Rajesh's parents
file a writ petition seeking admission, arguing that their son's fundamental right under Article
21A is being violated. Based on the passage, which legal position is currently applicable?
options:
St. Xavier's must admit Rajesh under Section 12(1)(c) because the RTE Act applies to all
private schools regardless of status

St. Xavier's is exempt from Section 12(1)(c) obligations under Pramati (2014) as a minority
institution, both aided and unaided

St. Xavier's must admit Rajesh because minority institutions cannot deny admission based
on religion under Article 29(2) of the Constitution

St. Xavier's is exempt only if it receives state aid; unaided minority schools must comply
with Section 12(1)(c) requirements
questions.solution: The passage explicitly states that the Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) five-judge Constitution Bench "held that the RTE Act is entirely inapplicable to minority institutions—both aided and unaided" and "exempted minority institutions from all RTE obligations, not merely Section 12(1)(c)." As an unaided minority institution, St.

questions.questionText:
Raghav had been undergoing psychiatric treatment for severe mental illness for the last five
years and was medically diagnosed with schizophrenia. One evening, he killed his business
partner after a heated financial dispute. During investigation, it was found that immediately
after committing the act, Raghav hid the weapon, changed his clothes, and fled to another city
to avoid arrest. Before the court, Raghav pleaded the defence under Section 84 of IPC on the
ground that he was medically insane at the time of the act.
In light of the above passage, which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
options:
Raghav will automatically get the benefit of Section 84 because medical insanity itself is
sufficient to establish legal insanity under IPC.

Raghav cannot claim the benefit of Section 84 merely on the basis of medical insanity if his
conduct shows awareness of the nature and consequences of the act.

Raghav will get the defence because schizophrenia is recognised as a form of unsoundness
of mind under medical science.

Raghav can invoke Section 84 because any person suffering from prolonged mental illness
is presumed incapable of understanding law.
questions.solution: The passage clearly distinguishes between medical insanity and legal insanity. Merely proving that a person suffers from a mental illness is not sufficient to invoke Section 84 of IPC.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): An accused may fail to get the defence under Section 84 of IPC even after
proving that he was medically insane at the time of committing the offence.
Reason (R): Section 84 of IPC requires proof of legal insanity, and not every form of medical
insanity is recognised as sufficient in the eyes of law.
In light of the above passage, choose the correct option:
options:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of
Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true because proof of medical insanity
automatically establishes legal insanity.

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false because Section 84 does not distinguish
between medical and legal insanity.
questions.solution: The Assertion is true because the passage clearly states that medical insanity alone is not sufficient to claim protection under Section 84 of IPC. A person may be medically diagnosed with mental illness and still fail to satisfy the legal test required under criminal law.

questions.questionText:
A and B, friends, went together to confront C over a financial dispute. There was no prior plan to assault
C. When C made an insulting remark, A spontaneously struck C with his fists. C, physically stronger,
began to overpower A. B, who had not previously discussed violence, immediately picked up a heavy
stone lying nearby and struck C on the head, fatally injuring him. B argued before the Sessions Court
that since there was no pre-arranged plan to cause harm when they set out to meet C, no common
intention existed and Section 3(5) should not apply. The Sessions Court convicted both under Section 103
read with Section 3(5) BNS. On appeal, the question is whether common intention under Section 3(5) can
crystallise on the spot in the course of a confrontation that was not originally planned as a violent
encounter.
options:
Common intention under Section 8(5) may crystallise on the spot in response to developing
circumstances; if A and B shared a common intention to cause harm at the moment B intervened,
both are liable under Section 3(5) even in the absence of prior premeditation.

Common intention under Section 3(5) can only be established by evidence of a plan formed well
before the incident; an intention that develops spontaneously at the scene does not constitute
common intention within the meaning of Section 3(5), as the provision contemplates forethought.

Section 3(5) does not apply because A and B originally went only to confront C verbally; any violence
that ensued was beyond their initial purpose, making it an independent act of each individual
outside the scope of the joint plan originally formed.

B is independently liable for murder under Section 103, but A cannot be held liable under Section
3(5) for B's act because A was unarmed; Section 3(5) requires each participant to use the same type
or category of force as the person who commits the fatal act.
questions.solution: It is well-settled that common intention within the meaning of Section 3(5) may develop on the spot in the course of an unfolding confrontation. If, at the moment B struck C with the stone, A and B shared a common intention to cause harm to C, both are jointly liable for the consequences, notwithstanding the absence of any prior arrangement when they set out to meet C.

questions.questionText:
A couple was convicted under Section 306 IPC for abetting their daughter-in-law's suicide. On
appeal before the Constitution Bench, they argued that if the right to life includes the right to
die, abetting a constitutionally protected act cannot be an offence. They further argued that
Section 306 and Section 309 IPC stand and fall together — if one is unconstitutional, the other
must also be invalid.
The question is whether Section 306 IPC can survive independently of Section 309 IPC.
options:
Section 306 and Section 309 IPC are inseparably linked, such that if the offence of attempt
to suicide is held unconstitutional, the offence of abetment of suicide must also necessarily
become invalid.

Section 306 IPC creates a distinct offence that survives independently of Section 309 IPC,
as abetment of suicide punishes third-party conduct and is not dependent on the
criminality of the principal act.

Section 309 IPC may be valid while Section 306 remains constitutionally suspect, since
abetment involves a third party’s role and raises different considerations relating to
individual autonomy and criminal liability.

If suicide or its attempt is not punishable, abetment of suicide cannot be treated as an
offence, because criminal liability for abetment must necessarily depend upon the
punishability of the principal act itself.
questions.solution: Section 306 focuses on the culpability of a person who instigates or aids suicide. Its validity does not depend on whether the act of suicide or its attempt is punishable.

questions.questionText: D, a surgeon performed invasive surgery for appendix removal. The patient’s family wanted laser surgery instead, as it would heal earlier. D was of the opinion that the patient’s case is critical, therefore it would be in the best interest to perform invasive surgery. During the procedure which was conducted with due care and caution, the patient inadvertently developed an infection, which shifted to the intestines. The family blamed the doctor for negligence. Decide whether doctor could be held liable?
options: The doctor is not liable, because he was not negligent, he just chose an alternative medical procedure.
The doctor is not liable, because he was not aware of the potential consequence of invasive surgery.
The doctor is liable because he chose a procedure which amplified the complications.
The doctor is liable because he is responsible for the patient’s infection.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The doctor is not liable, because he was not negligent, he just chose an alternative medical procedure. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Two men, A and B, happened to be present at the same location when they simultaneously
attacked V — each acting on his own separate impulse after being independently provoked by
V at different moments. Both used weapons and V died. The prosecution charged both under
Section 103 read with Section 3(5) BNS, arguing that since both attacked the same victim at
the same time and place, they must have shared a common intention to kill. The trial court
convicted both. On appeal, the principal question before the High Court is whether
simultaneous action at the same place and time, without proof of a prior meeting of minds,
establishes common intention under Section 3(5).
options:
Simultaneous action by two persons against the same victim at the same time and place
raises a presumption of common intention under Section 3(5), which the accused must
affirmatively rebut by demonstrating independent motivation.

Since both accused used weapons and attacked the same victim, Section 3(5) is applicable
regardless of whether a prior meeting of minds is established, as the ingredient of "a
criminal act done by several persons" is satisfied on the undisputed facts.

Section 3(5) applies whenever two or more persons commit the same type of offence against
the same victim at the same time; the prosecution need not establish any pre-arrangement,
as the law treats synchronous violence as evidence of shared design.

Common intention under Section 3(5) requires a meeting of minds and is distinct from
similar intention; mere simultaneous or coincidental acts do not establish such shared
intention.
questions.solution: As held in Mahbub Shah v. Emperor, common intention is categorically distinct from similar intention.

questions.questionText:
A gang of four people planned to rob a jewellery shop. Three entered the shop, threatened the
owner at gunpoint, and looted the cash. The fourth, P, stood at the entrance as a lookout,
signalling to the gang when the street was clear. During the robbery, one of the three inside
shot and killed a shop assistant who raised an alarm. P was charged with murder under
Section 103 read with Section 3(5) BNS. P's defence was that he did not enter the shop, did not
fire the shot, and had no discussion about causing death. The Sessions Court convicted P for
murder. On appeal, the question is whether P's role as a lookout outside the premises
constitutes sufficient participation under Section 3(5) to make him liable for the killing inside.
options:
P is liable only for robbery and not for murder, because the killing was not part of the
original plan and constitutes an independent act of the co-accused that severs the chain of
common intention.

P may be held liable for murder only if the prosecution proves that he expressly authorised
the use of deadly force before the robbery commenced; murder, requiring specific intent,
cannot be imputed to a participant merely from his facilitative role.

P is liable for murder under Section 3(5) because he actively participated in furtherance of
the common plan by acting as a lookout, and the killing occurred during the execution of
that shared plan.
questions.solution: As established in Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor, standing guard and acting as a lookout constitutes active participation in furtherance of the common plan.

questions.questionText:
Amit orders his driver, Bhola, to pick up and drop off his aunt, Chameli, from the hospital every
day, through whichever route is suitable. One day, while Bhola was picking up Chameli from the
hospital, the usual route had a lot of traffic. Therefore, he decided to take a longer route that he
did not usually take and met with an accident. Is Amit liable?
options: Yes, Amit is liable, as he was the owner of the car.

No, Amit is not liable, as Bhola was driving outside the course of his employment when the
accident occurred.
Yes, Amit is liable under the principle of vicarious liability.
No, Amit is not liable, as Bhola was Chameli’s servant and not Amit’s.
questions.solution: Bhola was performing assigned duty (pick-up and drop). Route change due to traffic is still within employment.

questions.questionText:
In a coastal town, the local government plans to demolish a historic pier to construct a modern
marina, aiming to boost tourism and local economy. A group of residents, who believe the pier is an
essential part of the town's heritage and environment, seek a mandatory injunction to halt the demolition
permanently, arguing that it's crucial to preserve the town’s historical landmarks. They file a lawsuit just
as demolition preparations begin. Considering the principle that a mandatory injunction is used to grant
final relief and not interim reliefs except in exceptional cases like saving life, what is the most likely
outcome of their lawsuit?
options:
The residents will immediately receive a mandatory injunction because preserving historical landmarks is
crucial.

The residents will receive an interim injunction until the case can be fully reviewed, due to the irreversible
nature of demolishing the pier.

The residents will not receive a mandatory injunction because their case does not involve saving life or


similar exceptional circumstances.

The residents’ request will be denied as the local government has the authority to alter town structures to
benefit economic growth.

questions.questionText:
Karan, a senior officer in the Ministry of Commerce, was subjected to a formal inquiry regarding
alleged misconduct linked to procedural lapses in contract negotiations. Although an inquiry committee
was set up, Karan was neither informed of its schedule nor invited to participate in the proceedings. The
committee concluded its inquiry in his absence and recommended his dismissal based on the findings.
Shortly thereafter, Karan received a termination notice. Believing that his right to a fair hearing was
violated, Karan is considering challenging his dismissal based on the failure to involve him in the inquiry
process, as mandated by his constitutional rights. What is the most likely outcome if Karan decides to
challenge his dismissal in court?
options:
Karan's challenge will likely succeed because his dismissal, conducted without his participation in the
inquiry, violates Article 311, which mandates that a civil servant must be informed of the charges and given an
opportunity to defend themselves.

Karan's challenge is unlikely to succeed since the formal inquiry was completed, satisfying the legal
requirement for administrative proceedings against civil servants.

Karan cannot legally challenge the inquiry's outcome, as civil servants are subject to departmental discretion
in procedural matters.

The court will uphold Karan's dismissal as the existence of an inquiry, regardless of his participation, fulfills
the requirement under Article 311.

questions.questionText:
Sunita, a drug manufacturer in Gujarat, was inspected on January 15, 2022. The Drug Inspector
alleged only non-maintenance of documentation as required under Schedule U of the Drugs and
Cosmetics Rules, 1945, with no other irregularities. The prosecution filed a complaint on April 10,
2023 (approximately 15 months later), charging Sunita under Section 18-B punishable under
Section 28-A, which prescribes a maximum sentence of one year. Sunita moves an application to
quash the proceedings on the ground of limitation. Based on the passage, what would be the most
appropriate conclusion regarding the limitation issue?
options:
The complaint is barred by limitation, as the maximum sentence is one year and the complaint
was filed beyond one year

The complaint is not barred by limitation, as the limitation period under Section 468 CrPC
would be three years regardless of the actual charge

The complaint is not barred by limitation, as only non-maintenance of records under Section
18-B is alleged, which has a different limitation framework

The complaint is barred by limitation, as Section 28-A offences must be prosecuted within one
year from the date of inspection
questions.solution: The passage clarifies that when only Section 18-B violations (record maintenance) are alleged with punishment under Section 28-A (maximum one year), the limitation period would correspond to offences punishable with one year. Since the complaint was filed approximately 15 months after inspection, it would be barred by limitation under Section 468 CrPC (which provides that for offences punishable with imprisonment for one year, prosecution must be instituted within one year).

questions.questionText:
Five persons were tried for the murder of V, charged under Section 103 read with Section 190 BNS.
During trial, two accused were acquitted as the prosecution failed to prove their membership in the
unlawful assembly. The remaining three — X, Y, and Z — were convicted under Section 103 read with
Section 190 BNS. On appeal before the High Court, the defence argued that with only three persons
found to share the common object, Section 190 was inapplicable and the convictions must be set aside
entirely. The prosecution argued in the alternative that the same evidence established a clear common
intention among X, Y, and Z to commit murder, and requested the court to apply Section 3(5) instead.
The question before the High Court is whether X, Y, and Z may be convicted under Section 103 read with
Section 3(5) BNS when they were originally charged only under Section 103 read with Section 190 BNS,
and whether the court may apply Section 3(5) for the first time at the appellate stage.
options:
X, Y, and Z cannot be convicted under Section 3(5) at the appellate stage because they were charged
and tried under Section 190; substituting the mode of liability at the appellate stage without a fresh
charge violates the constitutional guarantee that every accused must be informed of the specific
charge against him.

The court must acquit X, Y, and Z entirely; since Section 190 is inapplicable due to the reduction
below five members, and Section 3(5) was never charged, the court has no jurisdiction to convict on
an uncharged mode of liability at the appellate stage.

Section 3(5) may be applied by the appellate court in place of Section 190 where the evidence on
record independently establishes common intention and active participation among the remaining
accused, provided the accused suffered no prejudice in their defence by the absence of a specific
Section 3(5) charge.

Since the substantive offence — murder under Section 103 — remains the same regardless of
whether Section 3(5) or Section 190 is the operative mode of joint liability, the appellate court must
uphold the conviction on the basis of each accused's individual presence at the scene, without
requiring the prosecution to establish either provision afresh.
questions.solution: The Supreme Court and the Privy Council have recognised that Sections 3(5) and 190 are interchangeable modes of establishing joint liability, both operating in conjunction with the same substantive offence. Where Section 190 fails due to the assembly falling below five, and the evidence independently establishes common intention and participation among the remaining accused, Section 3(5) may be applied without a fresh charge, so long as no prejudice is caused to the accused.

questions.questionText:
During a labour strike, Prakash entered a textile dyeing factory carrying a container of concentrated sulphuric
acid ordinarily used in industrial processing. While confronting the factory supervisor, he deliberately threw the
substance at him. The supervisor survived but suffered deep burns on his left arm and permanent stiffness in three
fingers, though his face remained completely unharmed. The police immediately arrested Prakash and produced
him before the Sessions Court. Prakash argued that Section 124 of the BNS would not apply because the victim
neither suffered permanent facial disfigurement nor entered a vegetative state. Decide the case.
options: Prakash cannot be punished under Section 124 because the victim did not suffer permanent facial disfigurement.

Prakash can be punished under Section 124 because causing partial damage or burn injuries through a corrosive
substance falls within the offence.

Prakash cannot be punished under Section 124 because the acid was an industrial chemical intended for lawful
commercial use.
Prakash can be punished only if the injuries permanently disable the victim or place him in a vegetative state.

questions.questionText:
Eight persons, including R, formed a group armed with lathis and iron rods and marched to
the house of a rival with the common object of demolishing his property. During the course of
the incident, when the rival resisted, one member of the group stabbed him with a knife,
causing his death. There was no prior discussion among the members about killing anyone. R
contended that he only intended to assist in demolition and had no knowledge that any
member would commit murder. The trial court convicted all members under Section 103 read
with Section 190 BNS. On appeal, the question is whether R can be held liable for murder
under Section 190 despite absence of prior discussion regarding killing.
options:
R is not liable for murder because he personally carried only a lathi and had no intention to
cause death; Section 190 requires proof of individual intention for the specific offence
charged.

R can only be convicted for rioting under Section 191(1) BNS because his personal object
was limited to demolition and not murder in this case; liability cannot extend beyond the
accused's own declared purpose.

R's liability under Section 190 depends on whether he individually participated in the
stabbing; since he was not directly involved, he cannot be held liable for murder.

R is liable under Section 190 as a member of the unlawful assembly when the offence was
committed; the murder was either in prosecution of the common object or was one the
members knew was likely.
questions.solution: As held in Lalji v. State of U.P., the essential requirement is membership of the unlawful assembly at the time of commission of the offence and that the offence was committed in prosecution of the common object or was a likely consequence known to the members.

questions.questionText: J a scientist was researching about the cure of foot and mouth disease in the cattle. He conducted experiments on several cows. However, the virus escaped and infected some cattle in the neighbourhood. The infected cattle had to be culled to prevent the infection from spreading further. The owners of the cattle were compensated. Meanwhile a few days later, a cattle auction was scheduled to take place. The cattle auctioneers demanded compensation as well. Decide whether J could be held liable for his negligence towards the cattle auctioneer?
options: J could be held liable for negligence as the loss to the auctioneers was foreseeable.
J could be held liable for negligence because auctioneers suffered economic loss.
J could not be held liable for negligence because it pertains to loss of profits.
J could not be held liable for negligence because the loss of the auctioneers was not foreseeable.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: J could not be held liable for negligence because the loss of the auctioneers was not foreseeable. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Vijay, a security guard at a private hospital, lights a bonfire 15 meters from the oxygen storage
unit on a cold December night to keep warm, despite having been instructed twice by the facility
manager not to light fires near hazardous areas. Vijay believes his experience of five years as a
guard makes him cautious enough to prevent any mishap. A sudden gust of wind spreads embers
to the storage unit, causing an explosion that kills three hospital staff members. Decide Vijay's
criminal liability under IPC.
options:
Vijay is not liable because he did not possess the specific intention to cause death or harm to
any individual

Vijay is liable for culpable homicide not amounting to murder as he had knowledge that his act
was likely to cause harm

Vijay is liable only for negligent conduct causing death under Section 304A as he lacked both
intention and knowledge of the specific consequence

Vijay is liable under the principle of strict liability applicable to hazardous activities involving
explosive materials regardless of mental state
questions.solution: The passage states that culpable homicide under Section 299 "may be predicated upon either the intention to cause death or knowledge that the act is imminently likely to cause death." Vijay had explicit knowledge of the risk—he was warned twice not to light fires near hazardous areas, and the oxygen storage unit's proximity (15 meters) made harmful consequences objectively foreseeable.
