questions.questionText:
Principle: Islamic law prescribes Mehr as a compulsory gift from the groom to the bride for her
financial security. However, the Supreme Court observed that in the Indian subcontinent, social
practices have led to the adoption of "dowry" alongside "nominal Mehr," which hollowing out the
protective purpose of the custom and undermines women's financial security.
Facts: In a wedding governed by Islamic law, the groom, Farhan, provides a Mehr of 2501
(described by the families as a "symbolic and traditional amount") to the bride, Salma.
Simultaneously, Salma’s father gives Farhan a premium SUV and 25 lakhs in cash as a "voluntary
gesture" to ensure his daughter lives comfortably. Two years later, Salma’s family files a case of
dowry harassment. Farhan’s lawyer argues that since Mehr was paid according to religious law,
the provisions of the Dowry Prohibition Act cannot be applied to their community. Based on the
Supreme Court’s observations in the passage, which of the following is correct?
options:
Farhan is not liable because the SUV and cash are considered "social expectations" that exist
outside the legal definition of dowry in non-Hindu marriages.

Farhan is liable because the SUV and cash constitute dowry, and the nominal Mehr of 2501
fails to fulfill the protective financial purpose intended by the law.

Farhan is not liable because the payment of any amount of Mehr, regardless of the size, legally
replaces and cancels out any allegations of dowry.

Farhan is liable because the Dowry Prohibition Act specifically prohibits any form
of Mehr that is less than the value of the gifts given by the bride’s family.
questions.solution: Why (b) is Correct: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that dowry is prevalent among all communities/religions, not just Hindus. It noted that when Mehr is "nominal" (a tiny, symbolic amount like 7501), it doesn't actually provide the financial security it was meant to.

questions.questionText:
The United Citizens Party (UCP) is a recognised national political party with members in both Houses
of Parliament. Fifteen out of its twenty-one Lok Sabha members publicly declared support for the
Democratic National Alliance (DNA) and began attending DNA parliamentary meetings. They also issued
a joint statement stating that their conduct demonstrated an effective merger with DNA under Paragraph
4 of the Tenth Schedule. However, the national executive committee of UCP neither passed any resolution
approving a merger nor announced any integration with DNA. A petition was filed before the Speaker for
disqualification of the fifteen members. Decide whether the merger is valid under the Tenth Schedule.
options:
The merger is valid because more than two-thirds members of the legislature party supported the merger
through their conduct.

The merger is valid because attending meetings and publicly supporting another political party amounts to
merger under Paragraph 4.

The merger is invalid because Paragraph 4 protects only complete mergers that involve all members of the
legislature party.

The merger is invalid because a merger cannot be inferred solely from the conduct of legislators without
action from the original political party.

questions.questionText:
During a state lockdown, the government restricts citizens from leaving their homes except for
essential purposes. A citizen challenges this restriction, claiming it violates their personal liberty
under Article 21. The government argues that Article 19(1)(d) allows reasonable restrictions on
the right to move freely and therefore personal liberty is not violated.
Based on CJ Kania’s view in the AK Gopalan case, which of the following statements is legally
correct?
options:
Restricting movement under Article 19(1)(d) automatically counts as deprivation of personal
liberty under Article 21.

Article 21 protects personal liberty broadly, so restrictions on movement under Article 19(1) do
not automatically violate it.
Only citizens are protected under Article 21, so the restriction is valid for non-citizens.
The lockdown restriction is unconstitutional because Article 19(1) rights are absolute.
questions.solution: Principle from the case: Kania CJ emphasized that “deprivation” under Article 21 is different from “restriction” under Article 19(1). Article 19(1)(d) protects freedom of movement for citizens, but restrictions on it (like lockdowns) do not automatically amount to deprivation of personal liberty under Article 21.

questions.questionText: V was the nephew of K. They were ensued in a legal battle for the title of a property. V believing that he is the real owner of the property, tried to remove K from the competition. V even threatened K to kill him, if he does not back down with his demands. One day, while K was sleeping, V tiptoed into his house and shot him. Next day, V got the papers of the land, from the court. Decide strictly on the principle mentioned in the passage, whether V could be held liable for extortion?
options: V is not liable for extortion because V got the papers of the land from the court.
V is not liable for extortion because there was no dishonest inducement.
V is liable for extortion because he threatened K to kill him.
V is liable for extortion because he killed K to get the ownership of the land.
questions.solution: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: V is not liable for extortion because there was no dishonest inducement. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

questions.questionText:
Argument: Article 21 of the Constitution protects “personal liberty,” which is broader than the
freedoms guaranteed under Article 19(1). While Article 19 deals with certain specific citizen
rights, Article 21 safeguards the general right to life and personal liberty for all persons.
Therefore, legislative restrictions under Article 19(1) cannot be applied to deprive a person of
personal liberty under Article 21.
Which of the following statements, if true, would most weaken this argument?
options:
Article 19(1) rights are essential components of personal liberty and deprivation of these rights
effectively amounts to deprivation under Article 21.

Article 22 of the Constitution provides for preventive detention and explicitly regulates
deprivation of personal liberty, showing that Article 21 is not absolute.

The protections under Article 19(1) are available only to citizens, whereas Article 21 applies to
all persons.

Courts have consistently interpreted Article 21 to include rights beyond those explicitly
mentioned in Article 19(1).
questions.solution: weakens this argument because it claims that Article 19(1) rights are essential components of personal liberty, so depriving these freedoms would count as deprivation under Article 21, directly challenging the distinction drawn by Kania CJ.

questions.questionText:
The Democratic Reform Party (DRP) officially announced its merger with the National People's
Front (NPF) through a resolution passed by its national executive committee. Following the
announcement, several members of the DRP in the State Legislative Assembly joined the NPF and began
functioning under its banner inside the House. A few rival legislators challenged their continuation in the
Assembly, arguing that the members had voluntarily abandoned their original party and should be
disqualified under the Tenth Schedule. Decide whether the members are liable for disqualification.
options:
The members are not liable for disqualification because they acted pursuant to a merger initiated by their
original political party.

The members are liable for disqualification because joining another political party always amounts to
defection under the Tenth Schedule.

The members are liable for disqualification because only the legislature party inside the House can authorize
a valid merger.

The members are not liable for disqualification because resignation from the original political party is
necessary before disqualification proceedings can begin.

questions.questionText:
Seven persons assembled with the common object of forcibly occupying a piece of disputed
agricultural land. Armed with lathis, they proceeded to the field. On reaching the land, one
member, without any prior discussion, drew out a country-made pistol — which no other member
knew he was carrying — and fired it, fatally injuring the landowner. The remaining six members
had no prior knowledge of the firearm. All seven were charged under Section 103 read with Section
190 BNS. The six surviving members argued that the common object was forcible occupation, not
murder, and that they had no knowledge that any member carried a firearm or intended to shoot
anyone. The Sessions Court acquitted all six under the first limb of Section 190 but convicted them
under the second limb on the ground that violence was a foreseeable consequence of an armed
assembly. The question before the High Court is whether the second limb of Section 190 is correctly
applied.
options:
All seven members are liable for murder under the first limb of Section 190 because killing the
landowner was directly in prosecution of the common object of occupying the land; his removal
was a necessary step, making the murder inseparable from the shared objective.

The six members may be liable under the second limb of Section 190 only if, given all the
circumstances, it was reasonably inferable that a member was likely to commit murder
specifically; a generalised foreseeing of violence or disorder is insufficient to satisfy the
knowledge requirement.

The six members are entirely exempt from liability for murder because the shooting was an
independent act unconnected with the common object; the second limb of Section 190 requires
knowledge of the likelihood of the specific offence, which cannot be inferred where no member
knew of the firearm.

Section 190 imposes absolute vicarious liability on every member of an unlawful assembly for
all acts committed during the assembly; since all seven were present when the fatal shot was
fired, they are collectively liable for murder without any further inquiry into individual
knowledge.
questions.solution: As clarified in Mizaji v. State of U.P., the second limb of Section 190 requires members to have known that the specific offence — in this case, murder — was likely to be committed.
